Coalition, opposition tie at 52 seats as Netanyahu's Likud gets closer to Eisenkot's Yashar - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:06:50 UTC
15:06:50 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party gained one seat this week, bringing the coalition bloc into a tie with the opposition bloc at 52 seats each, according to a Maariv poll released Friday, amid memorial events and protests marking the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre.
The opposition bloc lost one seat after Yair Golan's Democrats dropped by one mandate, while the other parties in the bloc remained unchanged. Within the coalition, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party lost one seat, while the Religious Zionist Party gained one. The Arab parties maintained their combined strength of 12 seats.
Respondents were asked, "If elections to the Knesset were held today, which party would you vote for?" Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party led the poll with 21 seats, followed closely by Likud with 20 and Naftali Bennett's B'yachad with 13. The Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu each received nine seats, while Otzma Yehudit secured eight.
The Joint Arab List, United Torah Judaism, and Shas each received seven seats, followed by the Religious Zionist Party with six and Ra'am with five. Amcha Yisrael and the Reservists and Economic Party rounded out the list with four seats each.
Opposition voters show greater motivation to vote
The poll found that 78% of respondents were certain they would vote in the upcoming elections, while another 18% said they expected to vote. The remaining 4% indicated they were unlikely to cast a ballot.
Opposition supporters expressed greater motivation to vote, with 86% of those planning to support an opposition party saying they were certain they would cast a ballot, compared with 81% of coalition supporters.
In head-to-head comparisons of candidates' suitability to serve as prime minister, Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot maintained his six-percentage-point lead over Netanyahu, receiving 46% support compared with the prime minister's 40%. The gap was unchanged from the previous poll.
Netanyahu, however, narrowed the gap with former prime minister Naftali Bennett to just two percentage points. Bennett received 44% support, compared with 42% for Netanyahu.
The prime minister also held a six-percentage-point lead over Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman, receiving 44% support compared with Liberman's 38%.
Majority oppose Arab party joining next coalition
The poll also found that 59% of Israelis oppose an Arab party joining the governing coalition after the elections, while 36% support such a move and 5% said they did not know.
By contrast, 53% of Israelis support including a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) party in the next governing coalition, while 41% oppose it and 6% said they did not know.
When asked whom they would prefer to serve as prime minister after the elections, 38% of Israelis chose Netanyahu, followed by Eisenkot with 24% and Bennett with 14%. All other candidates received single-digit levels of support.
The poll was conducted on October 7 and 8 among a representative sample of Israeli adults aged 18 and older, including Jewish and Arab respondents.
The poll was conducted by Lazar Research, headed by Dr. Menachem Lazar, in cooperation with Panel4ALL. A total of 4,667 people were invited to participate in the survey, with 700 completing it, matching the initial sample size of 700. The maximum margin of sampling error was 3.7 percentage points.

Finland is giving away its resources to tech giants on far too modest terms, according to Lassi Noponen, CEO of state-owned Business Finland.
"In Sweden, for example, Meta is involved in carbon capture in the Stockholm area, and that's a completely different scale of thing than 'lights for the running track'," Noponen said.
His "lights for the running track" jibe refers to how minor the conditions Finnish municipalities are setting for major companies building data centres — such as Google's promises to build saunas in Muhos and solar panels in Kajaani.
Noponen's opinion carries a good deal of weight. He leads Business Finland, a part of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment, which advises and assists foreign companies wanting to invest in Finland. The outfit is contacted by prospective data centre builders on a daily basis.
Noponen's phone rang while he was speaking with Yle. "That was about a data centre project," he grinned afterwards.
According to Noponen, data centres should be required to make investments of a completely different scale for Finland's benefit, compared to current demands.
Municipalities are currently negotiating with data centre companies, seeking tax revenue and local benefits — but Noponen said this would require coordination at the national level, since municipalities' bargaining power doesn't reach the level he's talking about.
Beyond calls for new electricity production — which Noponen also supports — he sees the electricity connection itself as a lever. Data centres typically receive their grid connection directly from state grid operator Fingrid. A pending law change would let Fingrid prioritise which applicants are first in line to receive scarce new connections.
"Research and development activity, or some other condition, could move a data centre builder higher up the priority list when we grant our limited electricity connection permits."
Tougher terms won't scare firms off
He further noted that companies could also improve their position by sourcing components and services from Finland — leveraging the country's strong power electronics industry, cooling specialists and wide subcontracting base.
Data centre projects do bring work and income to the construction sector and local hotels — but these effects don't last long. In contrast, Noponen's proposed conditions could deliver a broader, longer-lasting boost to Finland's economy.
He said that if Finland plays its cards right, a new 'data economy' could be born.
Throughout the time he spent speaking with Yle, Noponen repeatedly insists that Finland has a strong hand. Data centres are being built worldwide at a staggering financial pace. According to a September report by consultancy firm PwC (PricewaterhouseCoopers), companies are spending more than 700 billion euros on data centre projects this year alone.
"Finland is one of the best places to build because of our natural conditions," Noponen said, pointing to the country's cool climate, available land and electricity access — which PwC's report named as the biggest bottlenecks for data centres around the world.
Noponen doesn't think tougher conditions will scare off international data centre operators.
"I don't believe for a second that international data centre operators' interest in Finland will stop if we require things that build Finland's data economy over a slightly longer timeframe."
So lights for the running track really won't cut it?
"No, it won't."

India: CJP leaders allege mass detentions, decry 'emergency'
Published October 9, 2026last updated October 9, 2026
What you need to know
Here are our rolling updates from India on Friday, October 9:
- Cockroach Janta Party claims thousands detained ahead of Delhi protest march
- CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke to arrive in Delhi on Saturday
- Indian IT giants Tata, Wipro and HCL suspended from US green card filings
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
India's Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL suspended from US green card filings
In a setback for Indian IT workers, the United States has suspended Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL from its Permanent Labor Certification program.
The certification allows employers to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers.
The Indian companies are on a list of eight major tech firms, including Microsoft, which have been barred from applying for the program under which foreign employees can work permanently in the US.
The Trump administration said an alleged abuse of the program was behind its decision.
"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Thursday.
Sonderling said the suspensions were due to ongoing federal investigations into the companies.
Indian media reports have said that the move could potentially impact thousands of the country's IT professionals.
According to reported figures, Indian applicants secured nearly 70% of all US H-1B visa approvals in the 2025 fiscal year.
News agency ANI on Friday cited a report by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) as saying that the US green card freeze is a warning for the Indian IT sector to prepare for broader restrictions on foreign workers.
The New Delhi-based think tank advised that Indian IT companies should diversify export markets, strengthen delivery from India and expand local hiring in the US where needed, ANI reported.
It also called for more focus on artificial intelligence to reduce the sector's vulnerability to sudden changes in US policy, according to ANI.
India's Cockroach movement claims thousands detained ahead of Jantar Mantar march
As the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) ramps up its call for a protest march in New Delhi on October 10 over alleged voter roll manipulation, the youth-led movement has accused India's authorities of mass detentions of its members.
CJP spokesperson Deepak Baliyan and activists from across the country were among those arrested, CJP leaders said in a series of social media posts on Thursday night.
Baliyan was released later in the evening after being arrested by Rajasthan police at his house, CJP Co-Convener Ashutosh Ranka said on X on Friday.
Ranka claimed that at least 10,000 people were detained country-wide on Thursday.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke alleged on X that a group of the movement's volunteers from the state of Telangana were arrested by Madhya Pradesh police onboard a train in Bhopal.
The movement earlier said that a group of students from the western Indian city of Pune who were headed for the planned protest in Delhi were also detained. The CJP said they were being taken on a bus to an unknown location.
There have been no police statements on the alleged detentions so far.
Cockroach movement describes detentions as 'emergency'
Leaders of the CJP have railed against the alleged mass arrests, likening the situation to a "state of emergency."
"Why not just declare EMERGENCY?", Dipke said as he reacted to a video of the students from Pune purportedly being detained.
The last time an emergency decree was issued in India was under former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in the mid-70s. Emergency powers were applied by the Congress leader for 21 months, with civil liberties being suspended, most of the opposition being jailed and media censored.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) calls the period a "dark chapter" in India's history.
Another prominent CJP spokesperson Saurav Das accused the Modi government of being "at war with its own young citizens."
"Hello India. We are under a State of Emergency," Das wrote on X.
CJP's Abhijeet Dipke set to arrive in Delhi on October 10
Meanwhile, founder 'Cockroach' Dipke has said that he will land in Delhi on Saturday and march to Jantar Mantar.
"This intimidation is not going to work, Modi. The youth of this country are no longer scared of you," Dipke said.
Thousands are expected to converge at the capital's Jantar Mantar protest site on Saturday to participate in CJP's protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Jantar Mantar served as ground-zero for the viral online Cockroach movement's debut protest in July which culminated with the resignation of the then-education minister.
The CJP, opposition parties and their student units have been holding near-daily demonstrations against Kumar.
Around 130 million names have been removed from electoral rolls under an exercise called Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
Opposition leaders and critics say that those struck off the lists include a huge number of minority voters.
They accuse Modi's BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains, questioning the independence of the Election Commission of India (ECI), which is overseeing the exercise.
The ECI and the BJP deny the allegations.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily capsule of all the biggest headlines creating a stir in India.
Protests over the deletion of millions of voters from India's electoral rolls have gripped the world's largest democracy.
The bloc of parties opposing Prime Minister Narendra Modi — rallied by Modi's main political adversary Rahul Gandhi — has been taking to the streets of the Indian capital since Wednesday. In turn, Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were briefly detained on two consecutive days.
Now, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement has accused the Indian authorities of mass detentions ahead of their planned protest in New Delhi tomorrow.
Parts of central Delhi remain under heavy security, with reports saying that thousands of additional paramilitary personnel are being deployed to the capital over the protests.
In other news, Indian IT bigwigs Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL have found themselves among a list of companies suspended from the United States green card program.

Hong Kong needs tougher inspection regime, experts say after CK Asset building fiasco
Hong Kong lawmakers call for more inspectors and barring of errant contractors from government tenders after serious lapses at Kwun Tong project
Lawmakers and engineering sector leaders have called for a review of Hong Kong’s building inspection mechanism and a blacklist to bar errant contractors from government tenders, after Hong Kong’s first privately built “starter homes” project hit a snag over shoddy steel work.
The government should review the inspection regime and increase its supervisory manpower, lawmakers and engineers said on Friday, calling for inspectors to be stationed at construction sites of private-sector-built subsidised public housing estates rather than relying on spot checks.
The call came after the Buildings Department said on Thursday it had approved property developer CK Asset Holding’s plan to tear down and rebuild three of the six blocks at the Anderson Road development in Kwun Tong, with remedial work continuing on the rest.
Earlier investigations found the steel reinforcement in parts of the towers diverged significantly from approved plans, with fewer reinforcement bars used than required.

Eesti Laul 2027 gets 155 entries from over 20 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Eesti Laul 2027 gets 155 entries from over 20 countries
A total of 155 songs have been submitted to Eesti Laul 2027, Estonia's annual competition to pick its Eurovision Song Contest entry.
The deadline was Thursday lunchtime, and the 155 entries come from more than 20 countries, not only from neighboring ones such as Finland and Latvia, but from further afield too – including from the U.S. and Australia.
Sixty of the songs are in Estonian and 95 in other languages, including one in a made-up language. A "blind" jury of several dozen people will now assess all 155 offerings.
Spokespeople said this year's group of authors stands out for its international reach,.
"Estonian artists and authors are increasingly working across borders," said Eesti Laul producer Riin Vann, who noted a trend for a growing international entrant list, with this year's list of countries being a good example of that.
The broad-based jury of people working in the music business or related fields will now assess the submitted songs. These will be judged blindly, ie. just on the merits of the song, without knowing who the act or songwriter is.
A total of 12 songs will reach the main Eesti Laul final, with the winner to be decided on January 30 at the gala finals concert at the Unibet Arena.
ERR will reveal this year's shortlisted contestants at the end of this month, and the public will get the chance to all these songs at the end of November.
Estonia's Eesti Laul winner last year was Vanilla Ninja with the song "Too Epic To Be True," which did not make it through the Eurovision semi-finals. The semi-finals and grand final this year take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, in mid-May.

No outsider allowed to interfere in Persian Gulf: IRGC cmdr.

In a message released on Thursday marking the IRGC Navy Day, Commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps Major General Ahmad Vahidi stressed that security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz must be ensured by regional countries, describing the waterway as a strategic red line for Iran.
“Our strategy in this arena is clear, principled and unchangeable: security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz is indigenous and regional, and no extra-regional power has the right to threaten, establish a domineering presence in, or interfere in it,” he said.
General Vahidi described the Strait of Hormuz as a vital artery for global energy supplies, adding that safeguarding it is essential to protecting Iran’s national interests, public security and national dignity.
The commander also said the IRGC Navy is fully coordinated with the Iranian Navy and prepared to respond decisively to any enemy miscalculation involving unauthorized vessel movements through waters under its management in the region.
He cited the IRGC Navy’s capabilities, including precision-guided missiles, attack drones, fast vessels, electronic warfare systems and coastal defense networks, as elements of its readiness.
“Any threat from the US-Israeli camp will be met with this force’s vigilance, unified command and comprehensive readiness,” Vahidi said.
The general finally called on IRGC naval personnel to remain prepared to defend Iran and the strategically important Strait of Hormuz under the command of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, the Commander-in-Chief of the Iranian Armed Forces.

Tories overstate net zero cost by nearly £500bn in apparent spreadsheet error
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:00:41 UTC
15:00:41 KST

Kemi Badenoch’s flagship party conference policy document overestimated the cost of net zero by nearly £500bn, seemingly after someone accidentally double-counted figures on a spreadsheet.
The apparent error appears in a chapter on net zero in The Right Way, a 100-page policy document produced for the Conservative conference in Birmingham. Badenoch repeatedly used the phrase in her main speech.
Justifying the Conservatives’ decision to scrap the target of the UK reaching net zero emissions by 2050, introduced under Theresa May, the document says that estimates of how much this would cost the economy “have varied enormously”.
It goes on: “In 2020, the Climate Change Committee (CCC) estimated that its route to net zero would cost £957bn.” It cites the Sixth Carbon Budget produced by the CCC, the government’s climate change advisers, saying the report put gross economic costs at £1.4tn, falling to £957bn when savings were taken into account.
However, the figures in the report in fact total £478bn, half of what the Tory document said. The error appears to have arisen because a tally of all the costs in a CCC spreadsheet from the document also included the row showing totals for each individual column, thus doubling it.
A CCC spokesperson said: “We don’t recognise this number. The committee has previously offered to meet with Ms Badenoch and talk her through our advice. That offer is, of course, still open.”
The committee’s most recent analysis puts the expected cost of achieving net zero by 2050 at about £110bn, or about £4bn a year – 0.2% of GDP.
The error was spotted by the publication Carbon Brief, which informed the Guardian.
It is possible the Conservatives copied the figure without checking it. It appears to have been published in a report by the rightwing thinktank the Institute of Economic Affairs and also included in an article in the Spectator.
The Conservative document says it is intended to be a precise diagnosis of the UK’s problems. It is modelled in part on The Right Approach, produced by Margaret Thatcher’s Tory party in 1976, which set out some of the economic ideas later used in the 1979 election.
In a foreword, Badenoch notes that “as an engineer”, she is used to correctly diagnosing issues so they can be addressed. A later part of the report says: “To fix a problem we must first have an accurate understanding of what is causing it.”
The Conservatives and Badenoch’s office were contacted for comment.

‘A candelit spa, followed by an ice-cold plunge and a nightcap’: readers’ favourite European wellbeing breaks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:00:40 UTC
15:00:40 KST

An art nouveau spa in Stockholm
Tucked away off a pretty shopping street in a beautiful art nouveau building is one of Stockholm’s oldest spas, Centralbadet where a day ticket costs from £23. As winter darkness descends, candles are lit around the pool and a quiet calm envelops you. Swimming by candlelight is a treat. Next a sauna followed by an ice-cold plunge. Afterwards a nightcap is in order so it’s a brisk walk in the cold crisp air to Fotografiska restaurant. It’s a great spot to savour one of Stockholm’s best views; the old town Gamla Stan and the twinkling lights on Lake Mälaren. 
Sarah Rochfort
‘Completely timeless and immersive’: birdwatching in Norfolk
Birdwatching at the Cley and Salthouse marshes in Cley-next-the-sea, Norfolk. The two bird hides are meditative and relaxed spaces. The windows open directly on to the pools of saltwater where many different species of birds obliviously wander around. It’s a place that is completely timeless and immersive. Your only job is to gaze out at the birds. It’s a very popular spot for birdwatching but the atmosphere is friendly and quiet. Someone even let us have a go with their binoculars. We particularly enjoyed watching a nest of baby swallows huddled in the corner of the hide. The marshes cover a wide area and are so important for biodiversity, providing an essential resting place for resident and migratory birds. You might even spot a spoonbill, which have returned to the UK from 2010 after being absent for hundreds of years. Well worth a wellness visit, even if you don’t really know anything about birds (like me).
Petra
Hampshire’s Scandi sauna huts
A fresh ginger concoction, orange slices and a friendly sauna master greeted us at the Hello Outdoors shepherd’s hut sauna, which has a picture window overlooking the historic Lymington Sea Water Baths. The deep blue of the sky and water, Swedish sauna hats, the calming scent of our chosen essential oil, a soothing soundtrack and the option to ease the sauna heat with an exhilarating plunge in an ice-cold tub or more genial dip in the sun-warmed sea baths made for a very enjoyable and restorative couple of hours away from real life. We didn’t want to leave.
Claire Edwards
Forest bathing in Croatia
For five days in Radoboj, northern Croatia, we forest-bathed beneath the trees, walked slowly, practised breathing and meditation and ate simple local food. No luxury spa, no expensive treatments – just nature and time. I wore an Oura smart ring throughout. My resting heart rate fell markedly and, by day four, the ring recorded four and a half hours of restorative time. More importantly, I felt profoundly different. It completely overturned what I thought wellness travel was. Sometimes the most restorative place isn’t a spa. It’s a forest.
Bex Hamilton
Bath time near Sofia, Bulgaria
The natural mineral springs in Sofia mean bathhouses are a way of life. Bankya is on the outskirts of the city, so I travelled by bus to visit the Central Mineral Bath Bankya. This opulent bathhouse is owned by the Sofia municipality, meaning the atmosphere is a mix of the everyday council baths and extraordinary architecture from the early 20th century. You can visit from under €10 and, as well as the promised health benefits of the natural spring water, there is a thermal zone, a salt room, aromatherapy, saunas and steam rooms with an array of massages too.
Sarah Collings
The perfect spa and skiing combo in Poland
While skiing in Zakopane, Poland, we made a lot of use of Terma Bania, an incredible pool and spa centre right in the heart of the ski resort. There is something magical about watching the sun go down in blissfully warm water and surrounded by snow. There is an astonishing array of saunas, pools and steam rooms, surrounded by mountain views. We discovered there are also several thermal pool and spa complexes in the surrounding area, and ended up spending as much of our holiday in the spas as we did on the slopes!
Frances
Simmer by the loch in Argyll
The Lochside Sauna at West Coast Wellness (£17 for 2.5 hours) in Evanachan sits on the shore of Loch Fyne. Hidden away from the single track road, a 10-minute walk takes you to one of the most peaceful saunas in the UK. From the giant window, sit back and watch the water of the loch (keep an eye out for dolphins), slowly preparing yourself to make the short walk down and take a dip in between the heat. Alternatively there is a cold water plunge which if anything is colder than the loch! The centre also offers yoga and pilates sessions and there’s the delicious Inver restaurant just around the corner.
Lewis
Wild swimming and wildlife in North Yorkshire
Wild swimming at Pool Bridge Farm guarantees a wholesome retreat from the vibrant bustle of neighbouring York. Transformed from old fishing ponds, the sprawling site comprises four lakes and ample space for lounging and lunching. A revitalising dip is best paired with a stop in the sauna (£16.50), priming those brave enough for the raw, heady thrill of the next plunge. To top it off, head to nearby Wheldrake Ings nature reserve, one of North Yorkshire’s top wildlife destinations, especially for waterfowl. As the flood waters rise from autumn, so does the abundance of migratory birds. A serene natural scene to soothe the soul. 
Fin
Sensory walk in the Black Forest, Germany
My two teenagers and I stumbled on a wellness experience for the mind, body and soul while we were wandering around the Black Forest near our holiday base of Freiburg last summer. A friendly German walker with a tree branch for a stick and a large husky for a companion told us to try a barefoot sensory trail at Park mit Allen Sinnen (park of all the senses) as we walked along together through the forest. So we followed his advice. It involved walking barefoot over grass, sand, woodchips, stone, mud and more while trying to tune into our five senses. We began by putting our hands into hollowed-out trees with our eyes closed to guess what objects were placed there. There were bright, colourful flowers, natural scents to imagine and huts to relax and sit in full of sounds and smells to immerse ourselves in with eyes closed. We repeated these walks for three days, heightening our contact with our own senses – and treating ourselves to rye bread and cheese sandwiches with forest fruits berry juice from simple forest cafe cabins as a reward. 
Helen
Winning tip: County Donegal’s peerless sauna on the pier
If you find yourself on the wild coast of south County Donegal, head to the Sliabh Liag Sauna at Teelin pier. After a day of hiking (and maybe one or two pints of porter the evening before), the small wood-fired sauna right on the pier was the perfect unwind. We followed it up by taking a sea dip in the bay just steps away. If you have plenty of time, combine the sauna with a nearby boat trip to the unforgettable Sliabh Liag sea cliffs towering 601 metres (1,972ft) above the sea.
Peter Henry

Virgin unveils its future cross-Channel train as it gears up to take on Eurostar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
06:00:39 UTC
15:00:39 KST

Flash interiors, fancy food and maybe even a bar: Virgin has unveiled a mock-up of its future cross-Channel train, with a pledge to create “something genuinely new”.
The group is planning to launch rail services from London to the continent in 2030, with Eurostar facing competition for the first time since the opening of the Channel tunnel.
Virgin has ordered 12 trains from the manufacturer Alstom, and will hope to outshine Eurostar on design and customer experience as it fits them out.
While Virgin’s last stab at reimagining UK train travel may have peaked with the talking toilet seat on its intercity services in 2013, it has said the future trains will be inspired from its airline, cruise and hotel arms.
Although details are being kept firmly under wraps, it said it would draw on Virgin Atlantic’s airport lounges, or Clubhouses, for “pre-departure and onboard social spaces” with “more flexibility to work, relax or socialise in style”. Food will be influenced by its cruise line menu and the design by its Virgin Hotels brand.
Josh Bayliss, the chief executive of Virgin Group, said: “Virgin has a proud history in UK rail. With our latest venture we are drawing on more than four decades of experience across travel and hospitality to create something genuinely new.
“We’re confident that more journeys between the UK and Europe will be made by train. We’re adding capacity for millions more international rail journeys each year, growing the market as a whole. We’re looking forward to seeing our distinctive red and black trains travelling across Europe.”
Virgin will also look to connect its rail and airline networks, potentially bringing passengers from France for Virgin Atlantic flights.
The Office of Rail and Road on Thursday published an agreement with Eurostar for Virgin to maintain its trains at the Temple Mills international depot in east London, with track access in the UK confirmed until at least 2040.
Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia is also expected to launch cross-Channel high-speed services. It already runs international trains as far as Paris and recently announced its own €2bn order for 19 new trains from Hitachi, some of which are expected to be based in France and run through the tunnel to London.

Ukraine has returned to the club of ballistic missile-producing countries: what the first combat use of the FP-7 changed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
08:59:20 EEST
14:59:20 KST

Ukraine has returned to the club of ballistic missile-producing countries: what the first combat use of the FP-7 changed
Kyiv • UNN
Indigenous ballistic missiles give Ukraine new capabilities to strike targets at a considerable distance and reduce its dependence on partners’ long-range weapons.
The first combat use of Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile marked an important milestone in restoring the country’s own missile capabilities. After decades during which ballistic missile production in the country had effectively been lost, Ukraine once again acquired the capability to create such systems. FP-7 may now become the foundation for the further development of Ukraine’s missile program, UNN writes.
On October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported the first combat use of FP-7, developed by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point. The launch site and target were not disclosed, but it is known that the missile has a range of about 250 km and a warhead weighing approximately 200 kg.
Returning to the ballistic missile producers’ club
Ukraine already had its own missile industry. During the Soviet era, enterprises operating in our country produced, among other things, intercontinental ballistic missiles. After the collapse of the USSR, a significant portion of these production lines was shut down, and the missile industry declined.
We have a very powerful missile school. Even 10–20 years ago, Ukrainian rockets were launching commercial satellites into space
Therefore, the emergence of FP-7 is significant not only as the creation of a separate weapons system. Following the first combat use of FP-7, The New York Times called it "Ukraine’s return to the small group of countries that produce ballistic missiles."
What Ukraine’s own ballistic missile capability provides
The emergence of its own ballistic missile is also directly important for conducting the war. Serial production of FP-7 could expand Ukraine’s ability to strike targets at a considerable distance from the front line. As experts point out, potential targets could include command posts, ammunition depots, logistics hubs, repair bases, air defense systems, and other military facilities that Russia is attempting to move farther away from the front.
Ukraine is indeed gaining new capabilities on the battlefield. This is a new trump card. The emergence of our own ballistic missile capability changes the balance of capabilities and is of strategic importance. We will no longer merely react—we are gaining the ability to respond
According to him, if Ukraine can scale up FP-7 production, it will have greater freedom in choosing targets and will be less dependent on partners’ supplies of long-range weapons.
FP-7 could become the foundation for the further development of an entire line of Ukrainian ballistic missiles. It may be not just one specific product, but a technological base on which subsequent systems can be created—with different characteristics, ranges, warheads, and operational capabilities. The company (Fire Point—Ed.) has every chance of becoming one of the foundations of Ukraine’s ballistic missile program. It has good specialists and the relevant expertise, and, most importantly, it already has practical experience
The next stage for Ukraine could be the development of missiles with a longer range. Fire Point is simultaneously working on FP-9, which will have a greater range and be capable of striking Moscow.
Therefore, the development of FP-7 and subsequent Ukrainian missile systems could become one of the important elements of a long-term system for deterring Russia. But the key word here is serial production. Individual successful launches demonstrate technological capability, while stable mass production creates a real military capability
Thus, the first combat use of FP-7 was not simply a test of a new missile in the war for Ukraine. It marked the country’s return to the narrow circle of states capable of independently creating ballistic weapons.

QatarEnergy’s LNG expansion targets early 2027 production amid reports of $3bn loan

QatarEnergy is advancing its LNG expansion and has reportedly secured a $3 billion (€2.68bn) loan from Chinese banks as war damage and shipping risks constrain exports. Shipments through Hormuz are recovering, but remain far below pre-war levels.
QatarEnergy’s first production unit at its North Field East liquefied natural gas (LNG) project is expected to be ready to start up in November, Reuters reported on Wednesday.
LNG production is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027, two people familiar with the plans told the agency.
Last month, QatarEnergy chief executive and Minister of State for Energy Affairs Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi said the first unit was expected to come online in the first half of 2027. He warned that disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could delay equipment deliveries for later units.
North Field East includes four large production lines, known as trains, each designed to produce about 8 million tonnes of LNG a year. The project is intended to raise Qatar’s export capacity from 77 million to 110 million tonnes annually.
The expansion comes as Qatar works to recover from Iranian attacks on Ras Laffan in March. The attacks damaged two LNG production units, affecting around 17% of the country’s export capacity.
Al-Kaabi said last month that repairs to the damaged units could take three years, while undamaged facilities could return to normal operations within weeks of Hormuz reopening.
Bloomberg also reported on Wednesday that at least 12 empty LNG carriers owned or chartered by QatarEnergy were waiting near Qatar. LNG shipments through Hormuz rose in September but remained about 75% below February levels.
Chinese banks reportedly provide financing
Separately, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that QatarEnergy had secured a $3 billion (€2.68bn) loan from four Chinese banks, citing people familiar with the agreement.
The five-year loan was provided by Bank of China, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Agricultural Bank of China and China Construction Bank (Asia), according to the report.
The money is intended for general working capital. The loan was priced at 50 basis points, or half a percentage point, above the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, a US dollar lending benchmark.
The deal would add to Chinese banks’ lending in the Gulf, which rose more than fivefold to a record $11.5 billion (€10.29bn) in 2025, excluding bilateral loans, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
QatarEnergy had not yet responded to Euronews’ request for comment on the production timetable and reported loan.

From Aden to Sanaa, Yemenis struggle to deal with soaring living costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:53:04 UTC
14:53:04 KST

From Aden to Sanaa, Yemenis struggle to deal with soaring living costs
As fighting intensifies, Yemenis face a deepening economic crisis, with unpaid salaries and rising prices.
Sanaa, Aden and Marib, Yemen – As fighting intensifies across Yemen between the government and the Houthis, millions of people are confronting another battle far from the front lines: the deteriorating living and economic conditions in the country.
With salaries for large segments of the workforce either unpaid or irregularly disbursed – and the prices of goods and services rising – Yemen’s economic struggles have been compounded by a divided banking system that has made moving money between different parts of the country increasingly complicated.
From Aden’s struggling shoppers to displaced families in Marib and unpaid public-sector workers in Sanaa, Yemenis are being forced to make difficult choices about what they can afford, and what they must go without.
Aden: Food costs swallow salaries
In Aden, the internationally recognised Yemeni government’s interim capital in the south, the problem is not so much a shortage of goods in markets as people’s inability to afford them.
Salaries have failed to keep pace with the rising costs of food, rent, healthcare and transport, leaving workers with little money left over at the end of the month.
The consequences are evident in the smaller quantities and cheaper products that now make up shoppers’ baskets, and the decisions they are forced to make about what to cut back on.
Bushra Abdullah Abdulwarith is a government employee in Aden. She earns 78,000 Yemeni riyals ($50) a month at the black market exchange rate while typical household food costs in government-held areas run about 130,366 riyals ($83), according to estimates by the Yemen Economic Tracking Initiative. And that’s before she factors in the cost of rent, transport, healthcare and other household expenses.
The economic difficulties facing Yemenis like Bushra illustrate how more than a decade of war has devastated the economy. According to the World Bank, real GDP per capita has fallen by approximately 58 percent since 2015.
The fragmentation of Yemen’s monetary institutions between the government and the Houthis – who have operated their own institutions since seizing the capital, Sanaa, in 2014 – along with the disruption of oil exports, and declining international assistance have all contributed to the economic decline.
Bushra told Al Jazeera that rising prices have forced many households to give up almost all non-essential purchases and cut back on some expensive basics, particularly meat. Other families, she said, have resorted to buying food in smaller quantities, sometimes on credit or loans.
Reduced demand
The impact of rising prices is reflected not only in economic figures but also in the way people shop.
Ayman al-Maqtari, who works at a shopping centre in Aden’s Mansoura district, said that his customers now rarely buy non-essential items.
When it comes to the essentials such as rice, sugar, flour, and cooking oil, he has noticed that customers size up the price of each item before putting it in their baskets. They are also buying smaller quantities, for example, opting for a 5kg (11 pound) over a 40kg (90 pound) bag of rice.
“Many people have come to live day by day, or week by week,” Ayman told Al Jazeera, adding that more families are buying on credit when they run out of money before the end of the month.
The decline in purchasing power is also affecting commercial activity.
Across several streets and shopping centres in Aden, advertisements for discounts and special offers have become increasingly visible in shop windows and on retailers’ social media pages, as businesses attempt to attract customers and boost sales.
Weak demand, retailers say, is particularly evident for items that households can put off buying, such as clothing and household goods. A growing share of family income is spent on food, rent, healthcare and transport.
Limited pay increase
The Yemeni government approved a 20 percent cost-of-living allowance in May for public-sector employees in an attempt to ease the pressure of rising prices. But the amount is calculated based on each employee’s base salary, rather than their total pay, meaning the actual increase is relatively small for many workers.
Bushra, the government employee in Aden, said the increase has done little to improve her family’s financial circumstances. She described the allowance as “a temporary painkiller that does not reflect the scale of the actual pressure on people’s living standards”.
Her experience is far from isolated. In early October, the World Food Programme said its latest monitoring in accessible government-controlled areas showed that 74 percent of households were unable to meet their basic food needs.
One of the places where the crisis is evident is Marib, a government-controlled city east of Sanaa that is home to hundreds of thousands of displaced people. The sharp increase in the population over the war years, in what was previously a provincial backwater, has led to pressure on the city’s housing, employment and public services.
Government employees in Marib see their salaries disappear within the first few days after being paid, labourers struggle to find more than a few days of work and displaced families are forced to choose between buying water and milk.
Salah al-Zuhaifi works for a government institution in Marib. He said the war has separated him from his parents, who live in Houthi-controlled territory.
Alone in Marib, al-Zuhaifi said that inflation had eroded much of his salary’s purchasing power.
“No matter how much you earn, it will not be enough to meet your needs,” he said.
Abu Mohammed Nasser al-Asbahi, another government employee, described a similar struggle.
He told Al Jazeera that he earns 400,000 riyals ($250) a month, but more than half of that goes towards his rent, leaving little for his other expenses.
“We don’t even get to the first one-third of the month before the salary is gone,” he said, explaining that his family spends the rest of the month relying on loans and credit from local shops.
The healthcare sector in Marib has also been affected by widespread household spending cuts.
Pharmacist Khaled Mohsen told Al Jazeera that the rising price of medicines has prompted many patients to decline parts of their prescribed treatment and purchase only what they consider most essential.
People with chronic illnesses, meanwhile, have increasingly begun reducing their medication doses to make their supplies last longer before having to buy more, which creates serious health risks.
Houthi areas
Residents of Sanaa and other areas of Yemen’s populous northwest, controlled by the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – since 2014, are also facing a worsening economic and cost-of-living crisis similar to that affecting Yemenis elsewhere in the country.
Several factors are driving the crisis, particularly unpaid public-sector salaries, declining purchasing power, rising prices for goods and services, and the continuing consequences of the division of Yemen’s currency and banking systems in the early years of the war.
Many public-sector employees in Houthi-controlled areas have gone years without receiving regular salaries, with some sectors only receiving limited payments or half-salaries at irregular intervals.
Even when payments are made, they cannot cover families’ basic needs amid the rising cost of living.
Meanwhile, private-sector workers and business owners face growing pressures as a result of declining economic activity, multiple fees and levies, and a shortage of employment opportunities. The conditions have undermined incomes and job security.
The Yemeni riyal’s exchange rate in Houthi-controlled Sanaa is more stable than in areas controlled by the government. The Houthis have imposed strict monetary controls, banning the circulation of newer banknotes printed by the Yemeni government, and have also enforced a largely fixed exchange rate.
However, that does not necessarily translate into stronger purchasing power. Markets face difficulties caused by cash shortages and the division between monetary and banking systems operating in different parts of the country, including increased costs for moving funds.
That directly affects the many households relying on domestic and international remittances.
For residents in Houthi-controlled areas, the result is an economy in which the currency may be relatively stable, but livelihoods are precarious. Years of unpaid salaries and limited employment opportunities have left many families struggling to afford basic necessities, with few options beyond borrowing, cutting spending or relying on support from relatives.

Government rules out fuel excise cut despite business pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:53:00 UTC
14:53:00 KST

Government rules out fuel excise cut despite business pressure
The government says it has no plans to cut fuel excise despite a proposal from the Chamber of Commerce and Industry to do so, Climate Minister Erkki Keldo (Reform) said.
Lowering both fuel excises to the EU minimum would cut excise revenue by about €210 million a year, Keldo said. The government is observing whether a recent excise duty cut by Latvia will lead to a significant rise in consumers from Estonia heading south of the border to refill.
The Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kaubandus-tööstuskoda) has proposed lowering the diesel excise rate to the EU minimum for six months, from the current 42.8 cents to 33 cents per litre, at a time of soaring world diesel prices resulting mainly from the Middle East conflict.
"Reducing the excise rate is necessary to preserve businesses' competitiveness and curb inflation," said Mait Palts, director general of the chamber, in a letter to Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform).
The chamber also recommends creating a transparent, operational, data-based mechanism to assess how far diesel excise could reasonably be reduced in the event of sudden and exceptional circumstances — even temporary ones — and raised again once those circumstances have passed..
"Such an approach would ensure that the process of temporarily lowering the excise rate would be more operational, more transparent and based on data, and that the favorable excise rate would apply only during the period when it is economically justified," Palts said.
He added that several EU countries have cut excise, adding 18 out of the other 26 member states have lower rates than Estonia. Latvia's diesel excise duty is currently 33 cents per liter, Sweden's 11 cents, though Lithuania's (50 cents) and Finland's (51.1 cents) are higher.
"If Estonia has a higher excise rate than our nearby region and several other countries have decided to reduce it, even temporarily, this harms the competitiveness of Estonian businesses," Palts said.
Keldo said the fuel price rise is being driven not by taxes but by the world market, where supply has clearly fallen due to the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Higher fuel prices also do not translate to the same increase in tax revenues, since consumption falls, he added. Conversely, excise duty cuts do not fully get passed on to prices at pump, the minister said.
"We have to watch what our neighbors do, and we are watching very closely. Latvia has now made its first excise cuts. The Latvian Competition Authority's latest best knowledge says that 53 percent of the excise cut — essentially only half — reached pump prices," Keldo said.
As of Monday, diesel average €2.09 per liter at pump in Estonia compared with €2.12 in Latvia. The figures for gasoline were €1.94 per liter (Estonia) versus €1.96 (Latvia).
"What this shows is that the market as a whole is dynamic, and regional price differences and market competition affect it — there is no single solution here," Keldo said.
Latvia decided late last month to cut its excise duty rate on diesel fuel and unleaded petrol from October 1 until the end of this year.
Keldo said the chamber's proposal would cost the state budget a great deal. Taking both fuel excises to the EU minimum for all of 2027 would reduce excise revenue by approximately €210 million, he summarized.
The prime minister said the government is watching the fuel market primarily because Latvia is restructuring various taxes and introducing temporary measures; it would be advantageous to know how great the risk of cross-border trade is.
"We are assessing the situation and taking it seriously — what options there are for steps on cross-border trade if Latvia takes steps, or whether we need to take steps ourselves if price fluctuations from the world market affect our own price rises and inflation," Michal said.
Pump prices have risen by more than 60 cents per liter since the start of the Hormuz crisis in late February, and government decisions could affect the price by 10 to 12 cents per liter, he said, "perhaps more under some conditions."
"Possible costs in that case are about €10 million a month if we take excises to Latvia's level, and if we do more, the costs are greater. So about €120 million a year is the so-called minimum option," Michal added.
Keldo has been tasked by the government with monitoring world market fuel prices and the effect of price rises on consumer confidence and inflation.
Ahead of the mid-term elections, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened a diesel export ban on EU states if reserves were not released to counter soaring prices. The G7 countries earlier this week opted to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves.

How October 7 changed Lebanon and Hezbollah’s political reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:52:49 UTC
14:52:49 KST

How October 7 changed Lebanon and Hezbollah’s political reality
Analysts say Hezbollah’s decision on October 8 to join a ‘support war’ for Gaza changed Lebanon’s political reality.
Beirut, Lebanon – A day after the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel and the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Hezbollah made the decision to join the war, in what it said was support of the Palestinian people. It is a decision that analysts say has forever shaped Lebanese politics.
Experts said the group had underestimated the depth of Israel’s intelligence penetration in the run-up to the war, which later manifested in the bloody September 2024 pager attack and the assassination of much of Hezbollah’s leadership, including Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah.
“Hezbollah got sucked into a vortex which culminated in the decapitation of their leadership and the invasion of south Lebanon,” Nicholas Blanford, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and author of a book about Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera. “That dealt Hezbollah a major blow to their popular standing and galvanised the election of Joseph Aoun as president and the formation of a new government that took a much stronger line against [the group].”
Hezbollah’s decisions have left the group politically weakened. And while analysts say the group has not been defeated, despite claims to the contrary from some critics, it is no longer the political or military hegemon in Lebanon it once was.
‘A motion of events’
Before October 7, Hezbollah – a group representing Lebanon’s large Shia community – was the strongest political and military actor inside the country. The Iranian-backed group’s influence stretched across the region. Hezbollah was a key ally of the al-Assad regime in Syria and helped it retake territory from anti-Assad opposition groups. It also had connections with allies in places such as Iraq and Yemen.
Hezbollah had key electoral influence in Lebanon, where it often wielded its power to elect or collapse governments. It was also not against deploying its supporters against movements opposed to it, as in 2019 when they took to the streets of Beirut to beat back protesters calling for political reform of the country’s sectarian system, in which Hezbollah has become a key player in the years since the end of Lebanon’s 15-year civil war in 1990.
In the months leading up to October 2023, Hezbollah’s confidence was on clear display. Blanford pointed to examples such as a military parade in south Lebanon conducted by Hezbollah, and the group erecting tents in the Shebaa Farms – on territory that Lebanon considers occupied by Israel.
At the time, Israel was roiled by protests, and Nasrallah was delivering speeches predicting the imminent doom of Israel. The decision to join the fight against Israel in what became known in Lebanon as the War of Support came on October 8, 2023.
“October 7 set in motion a chain of events that Lebanon’s political system was not properly prepared to manage,” Jad Dilati, a political analyst from Nabatieh in southern Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “Hezbollah opened its support front for Gaza on October 8 completely unilaterally, without any cabinet decision or governmental consensus or even taking into account the positions of the southern [Lebanese] residents who were most affected and still are most affected by these actions.”
“Hezbollah opened the support front on October 8, genuinely believing that it was operating from a position of strength,” Dilati said. “Most of the South believed that Hezbollah was operating from a position of strength after it had spent years building precision missile capabilities, an elaborate tunnel network and these missiles that we were told can hit every building in Tel Aviv.”
Israel’s re-invasion
For the next 11 months, Israel and Hezbollah traded attacks, albeit with Israel hitting Lebanon more than five times for every Hezbollah attack. Tens of thousands from southern Lebanon and northern Israel fled their homes.
But in September 2024, Israel unilaterally intensified attacks. The Israeli-induced carnage came quickly and heavily, with nearly 500 people killed on September 23 alone. When Nasrallah was said to have accepted a ceasefire – according to Lebanese officials quoted in media reports – Israel ordered his assassination and the evacuation of areas of Beirut’s southern suburbs.
“When Nasrallah was amenable to a ceasefire, Israel was on the offensive and wasn’t going to return to the previous status quo,” Blanford said.
Israel invaded southern Lebanon in October 2024 and stayed in Lebanese territory for more than two months after a ceasefire was agreed in November. Despite the ceasefire, Israel continued to destroy homes and infrastructure in southern Lebanon and refused to pull its troops out of five locations on Lebanese territory. Next door in Syria, the fall of the al-Assad regime in December 2024 also dealt a blow to the group, as its land routes to receive weapons and funding from Iran were disrupted.
Over the next 14 months, Israel violated the ceasefire more than 10,000 times. Then in March 2026, Israel reintensified its war on Lebanon. The attacks came after Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel for the first time in more than a year as a response to the myriad ceasefire violations and the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, whom Hezbollah viewed as a religious and political leader.
Israel then invaded Lebanon again and launched widespread attacks on the country. It has killed more than 9,000 people in Lebanon since 2024 and displaced more than 1.2 million people, emptying entire regions of the country.
Hezbollah’s legitimacy crisis
Israel now occupies large swathes of Lebanese territory, stretching up to 10 kilometres (more than 6 miles) from the border at some points. Dozens of villages, once filled with agriculture and people, are now uninhabited piles of dust and rubble. Hundreds of thousands remain displaced.
This has had a massive impact on Lebanon. The World Bank says the country’s economy has contracted by more than 6 percent in 2026. After the 2024 conflict, the World Bank said Lebanon needed around $11bn for recovery and reconstruction. That figure is likely much higher now.
In the aftermath of past wars against Israel, such as in 2006, Hezbollah was able to support much of its community and supporters. Providing social welfare has been key to the group’s ability to maintain popularity and belief among its constituents.
But since 2024, the Lebanese state, along with much of the international community, has been working to expand its own services. The state is also openly claiming it is working to disarm Hezbollah, despite the group’s objections, as part of a framework agreement with Israel.
“Hezbollah is in a legitimacy crisis that it has not faced before,” Dilati said. “I wouldn’t say that there is a rupture in the community or a complete political realignment, but a big part of the communities that supported it for decades are saying that Iran left them behind, the war was fought on their land for someone else’s interests, and that they don’t want wars anymore.”
Still, while grumbles against the group are growing louder, analysts said Hezbollah remains the most popular representative among Lebanon’s Shia Muslims.
“Hezbollah is providing for their needs by and large, and there is no alternative politically for the Shia community at the moment,” Blanford said. “What is binding them to Hezbollah is the fact that several hundred thousand Shias were booted out of their homes and are living in non-Shia areas where they do not feel particularly welcome, and this can create a sense of vulnerability that naturally makes them gravitate to Hezbollah as communal protection, rightly or wrongly.”
The group also maintains fighting capacity, and despite critics calling it a spent force, analysts and foreign diplomats say its weakness has been overstated. Much of the group’s future depends on the outcome of regional events, particularly regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. But analysts said the status quo – in which the state is negotiating with Israel and trying to extend its influence across Lebanese territory, and Hezbollah adapts to waning domestic influence – could work against the group.
“The key thing is this looks like a long occupation, and you may get a situation where people who have not only lost their home but lost their village, orchards, banana plantations, tobacco fields and the rest of it may think life was good before and may start blaming Hezbollah,” Blanford said.

An outlaw motorbike gang police say puts "profits ahead of public safety" has been targeted by Australian and New Zealand authorities in a bid to undermine its criminal control.
The Lone Wolf Outlaw Motorcycle Gang has been assessed as posing a "very high threat" in organised crime in Australia.
Police say this is driven by its alleged involvement in illicit drug importation and trafficking, money laundering and violence.
A national day of action by a specialised task force on Thursday ended in 20 arrests and 69 charges laid.
Across Australia and New Zealand, Taskforce Morpheus conducted 18 search warrants, 10 firearms compliance checks and seized cocaine, MDMA, illicit tobacco and vapes.
The task force brings together all Australian state and territory police and Commonwealth law enforcement agencies.
Queensland Detective Superintendent Troy Pukallus said Lone Wolf used violence, intimidation and organised offending for financial gain.
"They have no regard for the impact their actions have on the safety and wellbeing of the community," he said.
Detective Superintendent Pukallus said police were sending a clear message that no matter how well-connected criminal gangs believe they are, authorities are committed to identifying, disrupting and dismantling organised crime networks.
Australian Border Force Commander Graeme Campbell said the illicit tobacco trade was a significant source of revenue for organised crime groups.
"With proven links between OMCG's (Outlaw Motorcycle Gang's) and illicit tobacco retail premises across Australia, profits are used to fund other serious criminal activity," he said.
Commander Campbell said authorities would continue to target groups that "exploit legitimate businesses", including tobacco shops, to "conceal and facilitate organised criminal activity".
NSW Police Force Raptor Squad Commander, Detective Acting Superintendent Brad Abdy said outlaw motorcycle gangs should expect to be targeted "wherever they operate".
"By combining intelligence and resources across jurisdictions, we're making it increasingly difficult for organised crime groups to profit from their criminal activity," he said.

Istanbul air pollution linked to more hospital visits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:50:44 UTC
14:50:44 KST

A haze hangs over Istanbul, as pollution affects older people. (AA Photo)
A study linked air pollution to more hospital visits in Istanbul, particularly among people over 65, after examining 3.94 million visits for asthma, acute bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Istanbul Technical University’s Eurasia Institute of Earth Sciences lecturer Dr. Özkan Çapraz analyzed hospital visits between 2013 and 2017. The research identified particulate matter smaller than 2.5 micrometers (PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter smaller than 10 micrometers (PM10) as pollutants significantly associated with the diseases.
The study assessed children, adults and people over 65 separately, with older people among the most sensitive groups. Levels of particulate matter and nitrogen oxides were highest in winter, followed by autumn and spring, while exceedance episodes declined in summer.
“Hospital visits increased when air pollution was high,” Çapraz told Anadolu Agency.
Human-induced emissions from vehicle exhaust and heating were more strongly linked to health problems than natural sources, Çapraz said. Nitrogen dioxide and fine particles from vehicle exhaust were associated with asthma, COPD and acute bronchitis.
The effects of pollution could appear several days later rather than on the same day, he said. Fine particles can reach deep into the lungs and trigger asthma and COPD, while areas with heavy traffic and household or industrial pollution face greater risks.
Ground-level ozone can irritate the respiratory tract, posing risks to children, older people, asthma patients and those active outdoors. Çapraz said sensitive groups should limit outdoor activity on polluted days.
He recommended hybrid or electric vehicles and natural gas instead of coal or wood for heating, and said industrial areas should be located outside cities.
Earlier research on Saharan dust found no major same-day effect on emergency asthma or COPD visits but a modest increase in acute bronchitis visits.

A collection of 525 rare works donated by Ottoman book and library history scholar İsmail Erünsal to Istanbul’s Süleymaniye Manuscript Library has been digitized and opened to public access worldwide.
The collection, assembled by Erünsal over decades through his personal efforts, includes unique copies, rare works and manuscripts written in the authors’ own handwriting. Among its highlights is a handwritten copy of the Divan by renowned Ottoman poet Şeyh Galib, believed to have been written when he was only 18 or 19 years old.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the donation demonstrated the importance of individual contributions to preserving cultural heritage and passing it on to future generations. He thanked Erünsal for donating the collection. “I sincerely thank our esteemed professor, Prof. Dr. İsmail Erünsal, for donating his collection so that these works, which he regarded as a trust belonging to our nation, could be better preserved, passed on to future generations and made available to more people,” he wrote on social media.
The ministry’s Directorate General of Manuscripts Institutions completed the collection’s maintenance, restoration, digitization and cataloging in about two months after it was donated to the Süleymaniye Manuscript Library on Aug. 6.
The digitization project now allows researchers and members of the public around the world to examine the manuscripts remotely, expanding access to works that are significant sources for the study of Ottoman literary and intellectual history.

Basalt columns in eastern Türkiye emerge as new route for climbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:50:24 UTC
14:50:24 KST

Climbers stand at the base of basalt columns in Kars.
Basalt columns formed 6 to 7 million years ago in the eastern province of Kars have become a new route for climbers and nature enthusiasts following their inclusion in academic literature.
The pentagonal and hexagonal prisms took shape during the Late Miocene epoch as cooling lava surfaced near Karagüney village in the Kağızman district. The distinct formations gained wider attention after being published in the Journal of Social, Humanities and Administrative Sciences, bringing them into the scientific literature.
Sitting at an altitude of 1,890 meters, the columns now draw outdoor sports enthusiasts and climbers from Kars and the neighboring province of Iğdır to the region. Their natural appearance and geological structure have made the site a new stop on climbing routes in the area.
Ali Öztürk, a member of the Iğdır Mountain Safari Club, said the geological structure offers a visually striking route for visitors.
“The columns have a very beautiful appearance. We came here with a 10-person team, made an exploration and created a new route,” he said.
Öztürk said climbers continue to chart new paths in the surrounding area and advised outdoor enthusiasts to see the basalt structures.
Amateur climber Hakan Duman said they had added the geological formation area to their routes and invited all climbers to see it.
Basalt columns form when volcanic lava cools and contracts, creating polygonal structures. The Kars formations emerged as lava cooled after surfacing near Karagüney village during the Late Miocene. The columns are found in a limited area at about 1,890 meters above sea level, where their pentagonal and hexagonal shapes are visible across the formation.

TOKYO, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Japan's real household spending fell 3.1 percent year-on-year in August, marking a ninth consecutive month of decline, government data showed Friday.
Average monthly consumption expenditure by households with two or more people stood at 310,975 yen (about 1,960 U.S. dollars), down 1.0 percent in nominal terms, according to data released by the Internal Affairs and Communications Ministry.
On a seasonally adjusted basis, real household spending edged up 0.1 percent from July, marking a second consecutive month-on-month increase.
Spending on food fell 1.4 percent, while outlays for energy and water bills dropped 5.2 percent as cooler temperatures reduced the need for air conditioning.
Spending on culture and recreation declined 4.3 percent, largely due to a pullback in domestic package tour spending following a surge during the previous year's World Exposition in Osaka, according to a ministry official.
Household spending is a key indicator of private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's gross domestic product. ■

"It threatens to increase noise and air pollution in Arlington by necessitating the diversion of certain flights into and out of Reagan National Airport," it continued.
According to the complaint, the National Park Service failed to take a "hard look" at the environmental impacts of the Arch project, as required by law.
The county filed the lawsuit to halt the agency's "feverish pace" toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the "hard look" mandated by the National Environmental Policy Act is completed before the agency commences "disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities."
Trump first unveiled the administration's plan to construct the Arch in October 2025, at the time hailing it as a monument to the 250th anniversary of American independence.

Xinhua Headlines: Drones tackle toughest rural delivery stretches in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:49:25 CST
14:49:25 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Express delivery now reaches more than 95 percent of China's administrative villages. In some rural areas, however, getting a parcel to the village requires more than just one mode of transport.
In Zizhong County in southwest China's Sichuan Province, for example, drones are being used on routes where winding roads make the last leg of the journey slow. This county currently has 131 drone routes serving 131 villages and plans to extend them to all 301 villages by the end of the year.
Some 300 km away in Quxian County, drones are also being tested on the return journey, carrying farm produce from villages to township delivery points.
SHORTER WAY IN
The route from Guide Town to Tongjiazui Village in Zizhong requires a delivery vehicle to travel 9.9 kilometers, which takes about 19 minutes, while a drone on this route covers 5.7 kilometers in roughly 6.5 minutes.
Around 85 percent of Zizhong is hilly, and many villages lie on slopes or in river valleys. Some remote villages previously received parcels only once every two or three days. In places without village service stations, residents sometimes had to travel to town to collect them.
Rao Yurong, who grows blood oranges in Yueliangxia Village, recently received a battery-powered sprayer she had bought online. It took the drone around seven minutes to fly from the township station to the village. Notably, Rao previously spent nearly an hour riding an electric bike to town and back to collect a parcel.
JD Logistics opened 78 routes in Zizhong in June and has since expanded the network to 131.
Drones handle only the last section of the journey. Trucks still carry parcels over long distances and from county-level facilities to township stations.
This service also relies on facilities and staff on the ground. Township landing sites and village collection points have been set up, with local workers handling parcel collection and sorting. Sichuan has also introduced financial support for eligible low-altitude logistics projects.
Similar services are being used where water, rather than hills, slows deliveries. In east China's Jiangsu Province, 32 rural drone routes are in regular operation. One route to Mudun Island on Hongze Lake has cut delivery time by approximately 50 minutes compared with the previous ferry-based service.
MAKING RETURN TRIPS COUNT
Most drones flying into villages still fly back empty. According to JD Logistics, about 99 percent of return flights on rural routes carry no cargo.
Quxian is trying to change this.
In August, local villager Yu Fengying sent several kilograms of peanuts and sweet potato starch noodles to relatives and friends outside the area. Instead of riding an electric scooter to town, she used a drone that had just delivered parcels to the village.
About eight minutes later, the package reached a central landing point in town and entered the conventional express network.
JD Logistics plans to expand this service across Quxian and use return flights to carry local products including daylilies, lemons and plums.
Farm produce requiring fast transit may be among the more suitable shipments.
During the 2025 sweet cherry harvest in Hanyuan County, Sichuan, drones carried fruit from mountainous areas to a mail processing center in around 15 minutes. Conventional vehicles needed one to two hours for the same trip.
In the course of a month, more than 550 flights transported 7,586 packages of cherries weighing a total of 22.76 tonnes.
For fresh fruit harvested within a short season, saving an hour or more in transport can help reduce the time between picking and onward shipment.
WHERE DRONES MAKE SENSE
The faster trip does not yet cost less.
On one Zizhong route, JD Logistics puts the comprehensive cost at roughly 5.6 yuan (about 83 U.S. cents) per parcel by drone, compared with 4.4 yuan by vehicle.
Drones carry approximately 30 percent of their available payload on average, while almost all return flights are empty.
Zhang Jianping, director of a low-altitude air traffic institute at Southwest Jiaotong University, said drones are most useful in places where mountains or water make ground transport difficult. Only a few such services have so far reached a scale that can support commercial operations, he noted, while most are still used alongside conventional transport.
Zhang said western mountainous areas have demand for transporting farm produce, daily necessities and engineering supplies, because difficult terrain, large elevation changes and limited road access can make ground transport slower or harder.
Fangxian County in central China's Hubei Province, meanwhile, is using several transport methods rather than relying on one. A national rural-delivery pilot project there uses conventional vehicles, autonomous delivery vehicles, drones and combined passenger-freight-express mail services, depending on local conditions.
Since the pilot began, average operating cost has fallen by 0.2 yuan per parcel, while daily inbound village mail volume has risen by 16.3 percent and outbound volume by 48.9 percent, according to the State Post Bureau.
In Sichuan, drones are also being used to carry matsutake mushrooms, cherries and highland strawberries, as well as bamboo, power-grid components and construction materials.
JD Logistics plans to expand rural drone services to more than 50 counties and districts across the provincial-level regions of Sichuan, Chongqing, Yunnan and Guizhou, all located in southwest China. ■

The proposed reduction would mark the first cut in Japan's consumption tax rate since the tax was introduced in 1989. The standard rate has been 10 percent since October 2019, while food and beverages are subject to a reduced rate of 8 percent, excluding alcoholic beverages and dining out. ■
