A central aim of the legislation is to make social media companies and other online platforms remove illegal deepfakes quickly.
Satire would remain legal, although Stampe acknowledged that distinguishing satire from unlawful manipulation could be difficult.
She said courts would have to decide whether particular content qualifies as satire or whether that label is being used to justify illegal material.
“It will certainly be difficult, but on the other hand, I also have respect for the fact that we have a very strong tradition of satire in Denmark,” she said.
Stampe hopes the legislation can take effect around the turn of the year.
Denmark expands exemptions from new nitrogen rules for fruit and vegetable growers
More Danish farmers will receive temporary exemptions from new fertilizer restrictions after concerns that the rules could make growing certain fruits and vegetables more difficult.
The Ministry of Nature and Animal Welfare announced that crops including melons, rhubarb, strawberries, table grapes and pumpkins will be exempt from the new nitrogen regulations throughout 2027.
Woody plants grown in nurseries will also be covered by the exemption.
The changes follow a review of the regulations approved by a majority in Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing, in September.
The rules, which take effect at the beginning of 2027, aim to reduce nitrogen pollution from agriculture by limiting fertilizer use.
Nitrogen runoff from farmland has contributed to the deterioration of Denmark’s marine environment.
However, agricultural experts and vegetable producers have warned that the restrictions could create significant difficulties for domestic food production.
The government initially planned to exempt mainly potato growers during the first year. The exemption has now been extended to additional fruit and vegetable producers.
“I am pleased that we have the opportunity to also exempt some berry and fruit growers who otherwise faced major challenges, so they get one more year to adapt,” Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said.
The exemptions apply only to 2027 and are intended to give affected growers additional time to adjust.
The ministry said the newly exempt crops account for a small share of Denmark’s total agricultural land.
As a result, it expects the changes to have only a very limited effect on the nitrogen reductions the regulations are intended to achieve.
Serum Institute expects high flu levels this winter
Influenza infections are expected to reach a high level in Denmark this winter, according to Statens Serum Institut (SSI).
“We expect a winter where influenza will once again be prominent, while COVID-19 appears to remain at a lower level,” Bolette Søborg, chief physician and head of section at SSI, said in an update published by the institute.
SSI expects both influenza A and B to circulate during the coming season.
“Both the number of influenza cases and influenza-related hospitalizations are assessed to potentially reach a high level,” the institute said.
Influenza A has dominated recent seasons, while influenza B has circulated at relatively low levels. SSI said this may mean that the population has less naturally acquired immunity to influenza B, which could make it account for a larger share of infections this season.
COVID-19-related hospitalizations, meanwhile, are expected to remain at a low to medium level.
People aged 65 and over are being offered free vaccinations against both influenza and COVID-19. SSI said the vaccines are expected to provide good protection against the two respiratory infections.
The institute also expects vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, to reduce serious illness among infants.
Since October last year, the Danish Health Authority has offered RSV vaccination to pregnant women. SSI said hospitalizations among infants fell by about 70% during the latest transmission season compared with previous years.
“We therefore also expect that the vaccination will significantly reduce the burden of disease among the youngest infants this winter,” Søborg said.
RSV is still expected to circulate among older children and adults, although for most people the infection causes symptoms similar to a common cold, including coughing.

Denmark proposes up to four years in prison for mediation councils that seek to prevent prosecution
The Danish government has introduced a bill that would make it a criminal offense to participate in a mediation council with the aim of preventing public prosecution of a crime.
The proposed penalty is a fine or up to four years in prison. The bill targets councils that attempt to settle criminal matters outside the Danish justice system.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a Social Democrat, introduced the proposal on Wednesday, arguing that such councils undermine the rule of law.
“It must come to an end that, for example, imams or prominent criminal families can exploit their position to act as judges of law and order and attempt to override the Danish rule of law,” he said.
The proposal revives a bill from the previous government that was not passed before a general election was called in February.
Police have encountered councils in Aarhus
Wammen said several police districts were aware of mediation councils, although he could not give a figure for how many exist.
In 2024, Jyllands-Posten reported that East Jutland Police had encountered such councils in western Aarhus for several years. The newspaper described them as widespread among groups with other ethnic backgrounds.
One anonymized police interview report described a case from 2020 in which a group of “important men” visited the parents of a man who had reported a violent assault.
The visitors wanted to avoid police involvement and suggested compensation for the assault, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Under current rules, a victim and perpetrator can agree to settle a conflict without police involvement, provided there is no criminal conduct such as coercion or witness intimidation. This has made it difficult for police to act against the councils.
The proposed law would also criminalize participation in a council when the purpose is to evade prosecution.
“What we are doing with this bill is that we are taking targeted action against those who sit at the head of the table,” Wammen said.
He cited wiretapping as a tool police could use to establish whether an illegal council was taking place.
“That is because this is something that takes place behind closed curtains and in environments that do not want to talk to the police. That is why we need better tools to combat it,” he said.
The government still needs a majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, to pass the bill. It is intended to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Danish cinemas pause screenings of “Naza” on anniversary of Hamas attack
Several Danish cinemas removed the documentary “Naza” from their Wednesday schedules on the third anniversary of Hamas’ attack in Israel, following a request from the film’s directors.
A review of listings on platforms including Kino and Nordisk Film Biografer showed that several cinemas had paused screenings for the day. Some are scheduled to resume showing the film on Thursday.
According to DR, the film’s Danish importer, Angel Films, passed on a request from directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor that the documentary not be shown on the anniversary.
The 80-minute film examines civilian casualties caused by Israel’s military operations in the Gaza Strip and the systems behind targeted killings of Palestinians.
It draws on anonymous testimony from Israeli military and intelligence personnel. The Israeli military has strongly criticized that method, and Israel has denied deliberately targeting civilians.
The documentary won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival in September.
It has also drawn anger from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. Both directors have been threatened with losing their Israeli citizenship for violating the honor of Israeli soldiers.
The directors’ request to pause screenings on the anniversary was circulated across Europe through film distributors, according to the Greek newspaper Greek City Times. The newspaper reported that several cinemas in Greece and the Netherlands had agreed to the request.
“Naza” premiered in Denmark on October 1.
Autumn holiday traffic could cause motorway delays across Denmark
Drivers should expect heavier traffic and possible delays on Denmark’s motorways at the start and end of the autumn holiday, the Danish Road Directorate has warned.
The busiest periods are expected to be Friday from 2 to 6 p.m. and Saturday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Traffic may also be heavier than usual during the final two days of the holiday.
The directorate, Denmark’s national road authority, recommends traveling outside the busiest hours.
Routes expected to see increased traffic include the E20 motorways across western Zealand and Funen, the E45 motorway in southern Jutland and motorways around Kolding.
Drivers crossing the Vejle Fjord Bridge on the E45 should allow extra time. Maintenance work has reduced the speed limit, and queues may form during busy periods.
Those heading to the ferry terminal in Aarhus should also allow more time to drive through the city. Roadwork on Marselis Boulevard means only one eastbound lane is open.
Drivers can check traffic conditions through the directorate’s Trafikinfo service or listen to P4 Trafik, the radio traffic service.

Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.

The incident happened June 30 during a screening of a match between Norway and Ivory Coast. The Swedish man was punched and suffered a ruptured artery. He died July 3.
The defendant is charged with assault under a section of the Danish penal code covering less serious violence. Prosecutors are also seeking an increased sentence because of his previous convictions.
Special prosecutor Maria Cingari said in July that he could face eight to 10 months in prison.

Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of Moderaterne, the Moderates, also commented after the Swedish man’s death, writing: “May the guilty party be judged harshly and fairly.”
The government has since announced plans to increase penalties in assault cases where the victim dies and the offender has previous convictions.
Prosecutors are also seeking a nightlife ban for the defendant. He has pleaded not guilty and is protected by a court-ordered name ban.
Two other people face separate assault charges in connection with the incident. One is accused of trampling on the Swedish man while he was lying down and assaulting another Swedish man. The other is accused of kicking the second man.
People collecting prescription medicine in Denmark may be asked to show identification as pharmacies respond to unauthorized access to information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register.
Danmarks Apotekerforening, the Danish Pharmacists’ Association, which represents the country’s pharmacies, said pharmacies are increasing checks when dispensing medicine and health information, particularly medicine with a risk of abuse.
“In practice, this means that it will normally not be sufficient to state one’s CPR number when picking up medicine,” the association said.
Customers may instead be asked to show a physical or digital health card or answer verification questions.
Additional checks may also apply when collecting medicine for another person. The association said bringing that person’s health card or other identification would be the easiest option. Otherwise, pharmacies may ask verification questions.
The changes follow recommendations from Samsik, the Danish Agency for Public Security.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” Samsik director Laila Reenberg said Tuesday.
PLO, the Danish Association of General Practitioners, which represents and advises general practitioners, has also asked its members to follow Samsik’s recommendations.
Samsik said authorities, organizations and companies should pay closer attention when CPR numbers, names or addresses are used to confirm someone’s identity and should generally use other information for identity checks.
Unauthorized people collected information on 8.8 million living, deceased and emigrated people over 10 days in September by abusing a private Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system.
The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, the Danish Data Protection Agency. The National Special Crime Unit is investigating the case.
Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.
Danish government proposes prison unit at Kærshovedgård departure center for convicted residents
Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday during her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.

Large search bill alerted Danish authorities to breach of 8.8 million CPR records
An unusually large invoice led Danish authorities to discover that unauthorized people had accessed personal records on 8.8 million people, an official said Tuesday.
A small Danish company had legal access to search the national CPR register. Each search carries a fee, and extensive activity produced a large bill.
“There is a very large amount being invoiced, which makes one aware that there has been a lot of activity,” said Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization.
Unauthorized users abused the company’s access for about 10 days in September.
Authorities have not identified the company.
The accessed information consisted mainly of names and addresses, Leihardt said. The CPR system is Denmark’s national register of personal information.
Authorities do not yet know who was responsible or how the company’s access was compromised.
“It is too early to say at this point who is behind it and what method has been used,” said Henriette Erbs of NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit.
She said cases of this type often involve cross-border crime.
Laila Reenberg, director of Denmark’s Agency for Public Security, said digital fraud was an obvious possible motive.
However, she said authorities did not yet know who collected the data or how they intended to use it.

The app’s functions will not change. Contacts, payment agreements, transaction history and other features will remain available.

The app will retain MobilePay’s blue color in Denmark and Finland. The logo will change to include the smiling symbol already used by Vipps in Norway and Sweden.
Hertzum said some users would adapt quickly, while others might need more time. The company said assistance would be available to people who need help with the change.

Egelund spoke after briefing two Folketing committees about the breach of Denmark’s national personal information register.
“I have requested a security review of the entire CPR system,” Egelund of the Moderates said.

Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information.

The CPR register can also contain details about marital status, births, family relationships, citizenship, Church of Denmark membership and guardianship.

NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating.
Authorities have not identified who was responsible. Egelund said investigators had not ruled out any possibilities, including international involvement.
Copenhagen apartment listings exceed 2,000 as housing market begins to slow
More than 2,000 owner-occupied apartments are for sale in Copenhagen for the first time since early 2024, according to housing website Boligsiden.
At the beginning of October, 2,057 apartments were listed in Copenhagen Municipality.
That was more than five percent higher than one month earlier and almost twice the number available one year ago.
The increase gives buyers more choice and could reduce competition for individual apartments, said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Sellers must now compete with more properties for buyers’ attention, she added.
Daetz said the changing balance had also led to larger price reductions on Copenhagen apartments.
Every district recorded an increase in listings over the past year.
Copenhagen S, which includes parts of Amager, had 530 apartments for sale at the beginning of October. That was an increase of more than 150 percent from one year earlier.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, said the figures showed that Copenhagen’s housing market was losing speed.
He pointed to slowing sales activity and smaller monthly price increases.
Across Denmark, the number of apartments for sale increased 6.3 percent over the past year.
However, listings of detached homes and terraced houses moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.9 percent nationwide.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.
The 2026 Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands to represent friendship
This year’s Danish Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands in a design focused on friendship and community.
Christmas Seal Foundation board chair Anne Glad Wagner and artist Martin Jørgensen unveiled the seal Monday at Copenhagen City Hall.
The design is titled “The best gifts cannot be wrapped.”
Jørgensen said the children represent the supportive community that young people experience during stays at Denmark’s Christmas seal homes.
“It is about helping children, and therefore I have made them the main characters,” he said. “The Christmas seal homes help children form bonds and believe in themselves.”
Jørgensen has a background in advertising. The foundation selected him because of a graphic style that combines warmth, humor and small visual surprises.
Christmas seals are special decorative stamps sold before Christmas to raise money for the five Christmas seal homes in Denmark.
The homes support as many as 1,000 children annually who experience problems including bullying, loneliness, low self-esteem and poor well-being.
Seal sales cover about five percent of the homes’ operating expenses. Private individuals, companies and foundations provide almost all other funding.
The Christmas Seal Foundation, a Danish charity that operates the homes, has had Queen Mary as its patron since 2004.
Denmark’s Christmas seals were first issued in 1904. This year’s design is the 123rd edition. Copenhagen postmaster Einar Holbøll originally proposed the idea.
Denmark faces mild start to week before cooler and wetter autumn weather arrives
Denmark will begin the week with mild temperatures before rain, showers and cooler conditions arrive from Wednesday, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, the national weather service.
“We will have a mild start to the week with many clouds and locally a little rain from time to time,” meteorologist Anne Borrits said.
A low-pressure system approaching from the southwest will bring more typical autumn weather during the second half of the week.
Monday will begin with some sunshine in eastern Denmark, while most other areas will remain cloudy.
Light rain is possible in Jutland, and temperatures will reach between 15 and 19 degrees Celsius. The highest temperatures are expected locally on Funen or Zealand.
Winds will be moderate to strong from the southwest. Coastal areas near the Skagerrak could experience gales Monday afternoon.
Skies will clear overnight into Tuesday, bringing dry conditions. Temperatures could fall to eight degrees in some areas, though most places will remain between 12 and 15 degrees.
Tuesday will be dry with periods of sunshine.
A low-pressure system will approach from the North Sea during Tuesday evening and Wednesday, bringing rain and later showers.
Conditions remain uncertain through Friday. Temperatures are expected to fall gradually, reaching between 10 and 15 degrees Thursday and Friday.
Strong winds are also possible along some coastal areas.
Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.
Elk dies after collision with car on motorway north of Copenhagen
An elk died after being struck by a car on the Helsingør Motorway near Nivå on Monday morning, North Zealand Police said.
A 36-year-old woman was driving north in the inside lane when the animal suddenly appeared a few meters ahead of her, according to her statement to police.
The collision occurred at 6:10 a.m. between the Kokkedal and Humlebæk exits.
The woman was apparently uninjured. The car’s windshield and rear window were shattered, while its roof and hood were damaged.
The elk was found dead about 100 meters from the vehicle.
Denmark has no naturally occurring wild elk population. However, Swedish elk were introduced to Lille Vildmose in Himmerland beginning in 2015. That population had grown to about 20 animals by 2020.
Authorities also plan to release elk into Gribskov National Nature Park in North Zealand this year.
Wild elk are occasionally seen elsewhere in Denmark. The animals can swim across the Øresund between Sweden and Zealand.
In mid-September, a farm owner near Hundested reported that a roaming elk had damaged a fence before disappearing toward Ullerup Forest.
Morten Elmeros, a senior adviser at Aarhus University’s Department of Ecoscience, previously said that animal had probably swum from Sweden.
Such crossings occur about once every 10 years, he said.
Electric bicycle injuries reach six-year high as imports approach 100,000 in Denmark
Electric bicycle injuries in Denmark reached their highest level in six years as imports of the vehicles continued to rise.
In 2025, 200 electric bicycle riders were injured in traffic, including 133 who were seriously injured. Eleven riders died, according to Danish Road Directorate figures analyzed by insurance company Alm. Brand.
Electric bicycles can reach higher speeds and usually weigh more than standard bicycles, potentially making injuries more serious, said Mathias Kjær Sigvaldason, Alm. Brand’s accident insurance director.
Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.
Imports of standard bicycles fell from slightly more than 500,000 in 2017 to about 350,000 in 2025. Electric models now represent more than one in four imported bicycles.
The figures cover imports, not consumer sales, for which no combined national data are available.
The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

A magnitude 6 geomagnetic storm will hit Earth – NOAA warns of heightened activity through October 11
Kyiv • UNN
NOAA forecasts a storm of up to magnitude 6 on October 9 following a coronal mass ejection from the Sun. Heightened activity will continue through October 11.
On Friday, October 9, Earth is expected to experience a geomagnetic storm reaching 6 on the Kp index. Elevated geomagnetic activity may be observed over the next 3 days, although its intensity will vary. This is indicated by a forecast from the Space Weather Prediction Center of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), UNN reports.
Details
According to experts, the geomagnetic storm will be caused by a coronal mass ejection that occurred on the Sun on October 6.
The strongest geomagnetic disturbances are forecast for the evening of October 9. The Kp index is expected to reach 6, corresponding to a moderate G2-level geomagnetic storm.
How long will the geomagnetic storm last
According to the NOAA forecast, geomagnetic activity in the coming days will be as follows:
- October 9 – up to 6, a G2-level geomagnetic storm.
- October 10 – up to 4, elevated geomagnetic activity.
- October 11 – up to 5, a weak G1-level geomagnetic storm is possible.
How a geomagnetic storm may affect people and technology
Geomagnetic storms can cause disruptions in high-frequency radio communications, affect satellite systems, and place additional strain on energy infrastructure.
At the same time, there is currently insufficient convincing scientific evidence that geomagnetic storms directly cause migraines, fluctuations in blood pressure, or worsened well-being in most people.
People who feel unwell should maintain their usual sleep schedule, ensure adequate water intake, and manage any existing conditions. In the event of pronounced symptoms, they should consult a doctor.

What is celebrated on October 9 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
07:08:37 EEST
13:08:37 KST

What is celebrated on October 9 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 9, Ukraine honors the Apostle James son of Alphaeus and celebrates Yakiv Studenyi. Around the world, people celebrate World Post Day, World Egg Day, Fire Safety Day, and other observances.
On Friday, October 9, Ukraine commemorates the Apostle James son of Alphaeus and recalls traditional autumn customs. Around the world, World Post Day and other themed observances are celebrated today. UNN рассказывает about the history and significance of these dates.
Commemoration Day of the Apostle James son of Alphaeus
According to the Revised Julian calendar, on October 9 the Orthodox Church of Ukraine commemorates the Apostle James son of Alphaeus—one of the 12 closest disciples of Jesus Christ. According to church tradition, after Christ's Resurrection he preached Christianity and suffered martyrdom for his faith. On this day, believers pray for spiritual resilience, patience, and the strengthening of their faith.
The Folk Holiday of James the Chilly
In the folk calendar, October 9 was called James the Chilly. Our ancestors associated this date with the approach of winter cold and the completion of the main autumn agricultural work. It was believed that on this day one should pay attention to family, share a meal, and prepare the home for the cold season. According to folk weather signs, people watched the weather, trying to predict what the coming winter would be like.
World Post Day
Every year on October 9, the world celebrates World Post Day, dedicated to postal workers and the development of international communications. The date was chosen to commemorate the establishment of the Universal Postal Union in 1874 in Bern, Switzerland. Today, the organization unites postal services from different countries, while the holiday reminds us of the importance of delivering letters, parcels, and documents even in the age of digital technology.
World Egg Day
In 2026, World Egg Day falls on October 9, as it is traditionally observed on the second Friday of October. The holiday was established in 1996 to draw attention to the nutritional value of eggs and their role in the human diet. This year, the date is particularly significant—World Egg Day marks its 30th anniversary. In various countries, culinary events, educational campaigns, and themed festivals are held.
Fire Prevention Day in the United States and Canada
On October 9, people in the United States and Canada traditionally reflect on the importance of fire prevention. The date is associated with the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, which destroyed a significant part of the city. This tragedy became one of the catalysts for the development of modern fire-safety regulations. During this period, educational events are held to explain evacuation procedures, the use of fire alarms, and ways to prevent household fires.
International Beer and Pizza Day
The holiday was established by Nick Saulino in 2016, when he decided to dedicate a special date to one of the most popular gastronomic pairings. Every year on October 9, pizza and beer lovers in various countries hold themed parties, tastings, and culinary gatherings.
Curious Events Day
October 9 is observed as Curious Events Day. This unusual holiday is dedicated to unsolved mysteries of history, strange coincidences, and phenomena that still have no definitive explanation. On this day, mystery enthusiasts recall stories about lost civilizations, mysterious places, and unusual events.
Sneaker Day
Another unofficial holiday on October 9 is dedicated to athletic footwear, which has long become part of everyday fashion. Sneaker Day promotes comfortable footwear and also highlights the development of sports culture and the influence of well-known brands on contemporary style.

German Spy Scandal – Could Ukraine and NATO Be at Risk?
Unknown

13:08:35 KST

The arrest of Germany’s former intelligence chief August Hanning in one of the country’s most serious espionage scandals in decades has exposed a suspected Azerbaijani connection – and raised broader questions about the vulnerability of Western intelligence networks as Russia intensifies its shadow war against Europe.
Hanning, 80, who headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was arrested on Tuesday, Oct. 6, on suspicion of espionage, attempted treason and illegally obtaining state secrets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
German prosecutors say he acquired nearly 2,000 intelligence documents through a former senior aide who continued working at the BND long after Hanning left office.
The documents reportedly included sensitive intelligence relating to Russia’s military activities, Iran’s nuclear program and information shared by Western intelligence partners.
German magazine Der Spiegel reported that investigators were examining whether Hanning used classified material to prepare an analysis for an Azerbaijani intelligence operative.
Azerbaijan has denied involvement, while German prosecutors have not publicly identified the foreign intelligence service concerned.
The case has emerged at a particularly sensitive moment for Germany, which is confronting growing Russian intelligence and hybrid threats while remaining a major supporter of Ukraine.
Budanov Heads to US With Ukrainian Negotiating Team for ‘Important Meetings,’ European Leaders Set to Join
How nearly 2,000 intelligence documents allegedly left the BND
At the center of the investigation is Hanning’s former office manager, identified by German prosecutors as Manfred D.
According to prosecutors, the two arranged in 2010 for Manfred D. to provide confidential information to Hanning in exchange for payment.
Manfred D. remained employed at the BND, working for successive intelligence chiefs until March 2026, giving him continued access to sensitive internal documents.
Prosecutors say he supplied Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents through June 2022, including material classified as secret.
Hanning allegedly used information from the documents to prepare analyses intended for foreign intelligence contacts.
The suspected breach is especially serious because some of the material was intended for Germany’s highest political leadership, including the chancellor’s office.
It also reportedly included intelligence originating from Germany’s allies, raising concerns about whether information shared by the CIA and other partner agencies was compromised.
Hanning denies wrongdoing. His lawyer has acknowledged that he possessed classified material but disputes allegations that he paid for or improperly disseminated it.
A German court ordered Hanning and Manfred D. to remain in custody on Wednesday, Oct. 7, pending further proceedings.
The Azerbaijan connection – what investigators know
The possible involvement of Azerbaijani intelligence has become one of the central questions surrounding the scandal.
According to Der Spiegel, investigators suspect Hanning was in contact with an Azerbaijani intelligence operative and prepared an analysis using information obtained from the BND.
Whether the analysis reached its intended recipient remains under investigation.
Azerbaijan rejected the allegations, describing the reports as unfounded and an attempt to damage German-Azerbaijani relations.
Hanning’s connections with Azerbaijan, however, extend beyond the current investigation.
He served on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum, an organization promoting ties between Berlin and Baku.
German newspaper Die Tageszeitung reported that Hanning was re-elected to the organization’s board as recently as August 2025.
Russia and Azerbaijan – a formal intelligence partnership
The suspected Azerbaijani connection has drawn attention to Baku’s established intelligence cooperation with Moscow.
On July 19, 2022, five months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) Director Sergey Naryshkin announced that the Russian and Azerbaijani foreign intelligence agencies had signed a cooperation agreement in Baku.
Naryshkin described the agreement as a framework for strengthening intelligence cooperation between the two countries.
The relationship continued despite Russia’s war against Ukraine.
During an April 2025 visit to Baku, Naryshkin met the heads of Azerbaijan’s Foreign Intelligence Service and State Security Service.
The Russian SVR subsequently described bilateral intelligence cooperation as constructive, mutually beneficial and based on trust.
The relationship raises a question in the Hanning case: If sensitive German intelligence reached an Azerbaijani intelligence operative, could it subsequently have been shared with Moscow?
There is no evidence that such a transfer occurred. However, classified BND assessments on Russia’s military activities or information supplied by Western partners could be particularly valuable to Moscow if obtained.
Secret German-Russian talks in Baku – Aliyev confirms meetings
The alleged Azerbaijani connection emerged months after another controversy involving confidential contacts between former senior German officials and figures close to Russian President Vladimir Putin in Baku.
A joint investigation by German weekly Die Zeit and public broadcaster ARD revealed that former German officials had been meeting Russian representatives in Azerbaijan since 2024.
The most recent gathering took place in July 2026.
Among the German participants were Ronald Pofalla, former head of Chancellor Angela Merkel’s office, and Matthias Platzeck, a former premier of Brandenburg.
Russian participants included Viktor Zubkov, a former Russian prime minister and senior Gazprom figure, and Valery Fadeyev, chairman of Russia’s Presidential Human Rights Council.
According to the German investigation, security agencies viewed the meetings as a potential Russian influence operation aimed at shaping Berlin’s approach to Moscow and its war against Ukraine.
The controversy reached the highest political level on July 21, when Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev was questioned about the meetings during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin.
Merz said he had no knowledge of the contacts.
Aliyev, however, acknowledged that Azerbaijan’s border authorities had confirmed the participants’ visits.
Aliyev maintained that his government had not been informed of the meetings.
“Our territory was simply used without our knowledge,” he said, adding that the overlapping travel records suggested a secret gathering had taken place.
“If this meeting serves to end the Ukrainian-Russian war, we, of course, welcome it,” Aliyev said.
Hanning traveled to Russia seven times after Crimea’s annexation
Further questions about Hanning’s international contacts emerged after independent investigative outlet The Insider identified at least seven trips he made to Russia between 2015 and 2019 – following Moscow’s illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014.
Some visits lasted less than 24 hours.
On July 6, 2016, Hanning flew from Munich to Moscow and returned to Berlin the following afternoon.
A similar short visit took place in May 2019.
The purpose of the trips and the identities of those he met remain unknown.
Significantly, the visits occurred during the period when prosecutors say Hanning was receiving classified documents from his former aide.
In September 2019, Hanning also attended an international Arctic-related gathering in Russia involving senior officials and representatives of foreign governments, according to reporting cited by Russian independent media.
He was reportedly invited as an honorary guest, separately from the official German delegation.
Russia’s shadow war – an alarming coincidence
The arrests occurred just one day after Germany’s current intelligence chief, Martin Jaeger, delivered a warning about Russia’s expanding covert campaign against Europe.
Speaking before lawmakers on Monday, Oct. 5, Jaeger said the threat posed by Moscow had entered a more dangerous phase.
He warned that Germany faced the possibility of direct confrontation as Russia intensified espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks and drone operations against European countries.
Jaeger described Russia’s activities as a shadow war threatening Germany’s security institutions and critical infrastructure.
German authorities have also examined suspected Russian involvement in drone-related incidents, including an attempted attack at Leipzig airport in August.
What could be at stake for Ukraine and NATO?
The suspected breach carries consequences far beyond Germany.
The BND is a major participant in Western intelligence cooperation, sharing assessments with NATO allies and partner agencies monitoring Russian military activities.
Germany has also become one of Ukraine’s most important European military supporters, providing weapons, air defense systems and other assistance as Kyiv continues resisting Moscow’s invasion.
Reuters reported that Hanning’s arrest had raised concerns among European intelligence services about potential damage to Germany’s intelligence-sharing relationships.

Aurora australis could light up parts of Australia tonight. Here's how to get the best view
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:04:06 UTC
13:04:06 KST

IN BRIEF:
- The aurora australis may be visible from Tasmania, southern Victoria and some parts of NSW on Friday.
- In Western Australia, the International Space Station will be visible for a few minutes as it crosses the sky.
Australians could be treated to a rare double helping of astronomical sights on Friday night, with forecasts pointing to a possible aurora australis and a chance to spot the International Space Station overhead.
While predictions for auroras can be difficult, astronomers say conditions are favourable for some parts of the country to catch a glimpse of the phenomenon, which occurs when charged particles from the sun interact with Earth's atmosphere.
Astrobiologist and astronomer at the University of Southern Queensland Professor Jonti Horner said the forecast was promising, though not for a particularly intense display.
"There is a chance tonight, and it's definitely worth letting people know," Horner told SBS News.
The International Space Station is also set to make a visible pass across Australian skies, giving stargazers a second reason to look up.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Will the aurora australis be visible tonight?
The likelihood of an aurora depends on something called a CME, or coronal mass ejection, where "big bursts of material and activity are flung outwards" from the sun into space.
By monitoring these events, observatories around the world can calculate whether the ejections will reach Earth.
CMEs are measured on the Kp index, a 0 to 9 scale that measures Earth's geomagnetic activity. A higher rank on the Kp scale predicts a better chance of aurora.
Horner said the CME could reach the "lower end" of Kp 6 on Friday night, meaning there was a "good chance" that Tasmania and some southern states will catch a glimpse of the aurora.
But his advice was tentative, because while astronomers could see the CME happening, there were multiple factors at play, like the potency of solar wind.
Where can you see the aurora australis in Australia?
Tasmania, Victoria and some parts of southern NSW may get a glimpse of the aurora.
"The further south you are, the better your chance, and Tasmania and New Zealand are always more likely than Queensland or WA, for example," said Horner.
Horner said a few astronomical factors are affecting the aurora's visibility tonight.
The first is our proximity to the equinox, when the sun is directly above the Earth, and day and night are approximately equal in length. This year's equinox occurred on 23 September.
The closer you are to the equinox, the higher the probability of a "decent aurora", Horner said, due to the tilt of the Earth in relation to the sun.
"When CMEs are coming in perfectly edge-on, they can get through our magnetic field a bit more easily than if one pole or the other is tilted towards the sun."
The moon is also at low brightness tonight, at around 3 to 4 per cent brightness in the lead-up to the new moon on October 11. This will improve aurora visibility, as the sky's darkness plays an important role.
"You're more likely to see the aurora if you're out of town, far from street lighting, because light pollution has an impact," Horner said.
"Basically, the more glow there is in the sky, the harder it will be to see the glow of the aurora. Now that applies to street lights, which are there all the time. It also applies to the moon. The full moon really limits our ability to see the night sky."
Aurora hopefuls are encouraged to find a spot facing south, with limited light pollution.
Can you see the aurora australis with the naked eye?
Horner warned it was "unlikely" people would be able to see much.
"You'll probably not see colour with the naked eye unless the aurora is incredibly intense, and this event probably won't be.
"Your eye will just see things in grayscale in black and white, but you might see that there's a bit of a glow to the south if it's quite a more intense aurora. You might even see structure in that glow; you might even see kind of patterns moving in it."
He advised aurora watchers to take a photograph with a smartphone on night mode or with a digital SLR camera; a long exposure time "could bring out some of the colour, the greens and reds".
If photos show an orange glow, "you're probably actually just seeing street lights; to be honest, you're seeing a bit of light pollution".
"But if you're getting red, then you're seeing some of the aurora. The red is usually higher in the atmosphere, so you can see it from further away. A lot of the time people are looking at this reddish glow to the south, and that's the very high altitude aurora."
"If you're getting greens, you're usually seeing a more intense aurora."
When will the International Space Station be visible?
The International Space Station (ISS), a large human-inhabited spacecraft that has orbited Earth for 24 years, will be visible crossing the night sky from parts of Western Australia on Friday evening.
The ISS orbits 400km above Earth — most of the time it is below the horizon and not visible. But on Friday evening it will be visible overhead Perth at 7.20pm.
"It will be about the brightest thing in the night sky, other than the planet Venus out to the west," Horner said.
Horner said the website Heavens Above allows people to set their location to pinpoint the time that the ISS will cross above them, as it moves in and out of visibility in a matter of minutes.

Barcelona team develops AI that detects ageing in blood stem cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:01:05 UTC
13:01:05 KST

ChromAgeNet has decoded chromatin architecture, the 3D organisation of DNA in the nucleus, distinguishing young from aged blood stem cells and opening new paths for cell rejuvenation.
Ageing gradually undermines the body's ability to regenerate, severely affecting the production of blood cells. In this race against the biological clock, analysing changes in blood stem cells is crucial to opening the door to interventions that can slow their decline and restore their original function.
A scientific team in Barcelona has developed ChromAgeNet, an artificial intelligence tool that detects ageing in blood stem cells by analysing the three-dimensional structure of their DNA.
Published in the journal "Aging Cell", the research, led by Maria Carolina Florian (IDIBELL) and Paula Petrone (BSC-CNS/ISGlobal), shows that the organisation of chromatin contains information that makes it possible to distinguish cells from young and aged mice.
A bridge between biomedicine and supercomputing
To train the model, the researchers applied convolutional neural networks to 3D images of the nuclei of mouse stem cells (source in Spanish). ChromAgeNet uses neural networks to decipher how DNA ages. AI makes it possible to detect subtle structural variations that are imperceptible to the human eye.
One of the main concerns when using neural networks in biomedicine is not knowing what they base their decisions on. ChromAgeNet overcomes that barrier by offering an explainable AI (XAI) system.
The tool managed, on average, to correctly classify around 68% of cells as coming from young or aged mice using images obtained with DAPI, a standard, low-cost stain.
In addition, ChromAgeNet stands out as an explainable AI, allowing researchers to investigate which image features contribute to its predictions. These analyses highlighted, among other regions, changes at the periphery of the nucleus associated with ageing.
The analyses showed that chromatin is compact and organised at the edges of the nuclei of young cells, while in aged cells it appears dispersed. As a proof of concept, the tool assesses how certain epigenetic drugs (source in Spanish) induce changes in chromatin organisation that are consistent with patterns more akin to those observed in young cells. This showcases the potential of the tool for screening treatments that could regenerate blood tissue and strengthen the immune system. The code and the image database are already available to the international scientific community.
Collaboration with AI research teams
As for the practical applications of this research, Dr Maria Carolina Florian, principal investigator at the Bellvitge Biomedical Research Institute (IDIBELL), explains to Euronews: "Currently, we have developed a tool that works as a proof of concept in murine haematopoietic stem cells. We are now working to optimise it and adapt it to human stem cells, with the hope of using it to evaluate new drugs that can act on nuclear architecture and be used to rejuvenate aged stem cells."
Maria Carolina Florian tells Euronews that this work "has found the ideal ground to become a real tool thanks to the expertise of Dr Paula Petrone (BSC and ISGlobal). We plan to continue developing it and expand it for use with human stem cells. In addition, we are applying for further EU funding and seeking to establish links with other scientists in Europe who are interested in the practical application of our work."
For her part, Paula Petrone believes that this research "shows that a deep-learning algorithm can tell apart young and aged stem cells by analysing images of cell nuclei stained with a low-cost substance called DAPI."
3D maps and open code to rejuvenate cellular architecture
The internal map of the cell nucleus reveals a distinctive signature: in youth, chromatin is tightly entrenched at the edges of the nucleus; with age, that architecture falls apart. Identifying these patterns could help to study the decline of blood stem cells and to assess potential strategies capable of regenerating haematopoietic tissue and triggering changes throughout the body.
To demonstrate the practical potential of the algorithm, the team designed a proof of concept: they applied the tool to aged cells exposed to various epigenetic drugs. The goal was to determine whether the molecules were able to produce changes in chromatin organisation consistent with a more youthful state.
To accelerate new discoveries, the team has released the tool's code and a public database of 3D images of stem cells, with the aim of finding drugs that reinforce the immune system and quality of life in old age.
Numerous international studies underpin the evidence for the fundamental role of the immune system in the ageing of the body, as Maria Carolina Florian points out: "In our laboratory, we have contributed by demonstrating the possibility of stimulating and rejuvenating aged haematopoietic stem cells to improve not only immune system function, but also life expectancy and the health of the organism as a whole."
Long-term promise, caution for now: the science behind ChromAgeNet calls for prudence
The new ChromAgeNet tool will help to understand the basic molecular mechanisms involved in the ageing of haematopoietic stem cells, which could become targets for therapies to rejuvenate them. "We hope to deepen our knowledge, consolidate our findings and identify new tools and drugs to improve the function of aged haematopoietic stem cells," Florian concludes.
"In future, this technique could be used to screen new drugs with rejuvenating potential. By treating aged cells with different candidate compounds, AI could use image analysis to identify those that induce changes consistent with a more youthful state," Paula Petrone tells Euronews.
For Dr Petrone, "Extending life expectancy is not as important as extending healthy life expectancy. The discovery of new drugs with rejuvenating potential could help, for example, to improve ageing of the immune system and thereby support healthier ageing."
The researcher nevertheless stresses to Euronews the need for caution: "We must be very careful not to overestimate our results. These new technologies take years to be developed, validated and eventually reach the clinic. Our research is just one small contribution to the study of how we age and to the search for strategies that can support healthy ageing."

EU faces gas supply shortage as winter looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:01:00 UTC
13:01:00 KST

BRUSSELS — The EU is facing a winter gas shortage that could leave it scrambling to replace lost energy supplies equivalent to the power used by 12 million homes, according to new reports shared with POLITICO.
The shortfall raises the prospect of a winter of soaring power bills and forced energy saving measures if the bloc fails to find adequate supplies elsewhere.
As the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy supplies, the EU faces an overall shortfall this winter of up to 14 billion cubic meters of natural gas — around 7% of the bloc's demand and enough to power between 10 and 12 million European households, according to a report by the Institution for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a U.S.-based energy think tank.
Advertisement
Those conclusions are echoed in a key report by a top European body of gas network operators that was presented to national energy officials on Thursday.
Natural gas is used widely to heat Europe's buildings, power its industry and generate its electricity. But the EU's gas reserves have fallen to their lowest level for the time of year since records began in 2011, at just above 70%, after high prices made it more attractive for traders to sell gas in the summer rather than store it for later use in the winter.
With gas prices at near-four-year highs and supply constrained due to the U.S.-Israeli war in the Middle East, Europe has limited supply options if the coming winter proves as cold as the last, IEEFA found.
While that doesn't necessarily mean the bloc will run out of gas, it does mean there could be 7 billion fewer cubic meters of stored gas to draw upon. That could force countries to buy gas at high prices on increasingly volatile global markets, or even require consumers to cut demand if fresh supplies are unavailable.
The EU's record-low reserves leave the bloc "with less of a buffer" against global supply disruptions, leaving it "vulnerable to price spikes," Ana Jaller-Makarewicz, IEEFA's lead European energy analyst, said in a statement. If countries are forced to exhaust stocks this year, that would also leave them with more to refill next year, continuing the feedback loop of low reserves and higher prices, she added.
The same risks were outlined in a 2026-2027 winter supply outlook published Thursday by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSO-G), an association of gas operators. The report warns that if imports of liquefied natural gas are limited or even “optimal” in the context of a cold winter, storage levels could fall as low as 11%, a baseline needed for strategic reserves that can't be easily tapped into.
Advertisement
If countries hope to restore their reserves to 30% by the end of winter — or else face increased exposure to future cold spells — volumes equivalent to 7% of the demand will either have to be curtailed or simply withheld from consumers, ENTSO-G warns.
Part of that pressure comes from a looming EU-wide ban on long-term supply contracts for Russian LNG, due to take effect in January, which will reduce European gas imports by an additional 7 billion cubic meters, according to the IEEFA report. Russian gas has been historically used to offset "swings in demand" over the winter, it said. "Now Europe depends on storage to get through winter."
To make matters worse, the IEEFA report argues, gas demand over winter has crept up in the past two years, while imports to the bloc have flatlined. That's left the EU leaning harder on its reserves over the winter period, with net drawdowns rising to 22.6 billion cubic meters in January this year, up from 18.8 billion cubic meters in January 2025 and 17.8 billion cubic meters in January 2024.
The alternative would be to import fresh LNG, a seaborne fuel that the EU increasingly sources from the U.S. But at current prices, importing the lost volumes would cost Europeans an additional €3 billion, a 12% rise over what the same volume would have cost last year, on top of already sky-high prices, according to the report. U.S. LNG production is also near full capacity, meaning those additional imports would further squeeze supply, Jaller-Makarewicz told POLITICO.
To some, a rise in prices is more likely. While ENTSO-G's tight market scenario assumes a "global deficit" that sees available LNG imports into Europe reduced by 20%, Laurent Ruseckas, a senior gas market analyst at S&P Global Energy, argues that reserves can only ever fall so low, "since a rapid drawdown early in winter will drive up prices," drawing cargoes to Europe from Asia.
"There is not much demand to destroy in Europe," he added, pointing out that the war in Ukraine already destroyed 20% of the bloc's industrial demand. "And it didn't come back."

Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.
One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.
“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.
In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.
Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.
Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Journalists’ Syndicate, whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.
Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.
The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.
For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.
“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

====================================================================================================

How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:00:37 UTC
13:00:37 KST

A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.
But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.
Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet.
Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia.
Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica.
However, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River.
He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself.
Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest.
They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies.
“It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,” Magdalena said. “Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping.
“Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,” he said. “It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.”
The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journal Phytotaxa confirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies.
Harris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was “incredible”.
“I was just so excited, absolutely elated,” he said.
Magdalena said: “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.”
The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction.
Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as “large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.”
The team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List designation.
Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown at Kew Gardens.

Winner of Nobel Peace Prize to be announced in Oslo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
04:00:01 UTC
13:00:01 KST

STOCKHOLM, October 9. /TASS/. The Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday in Oslo.
Unlike other Nobel prizes, the award ceremony for the Nobel Peace Prize takes place in Oslo and not Stockholm, in accordance with the last will of renowned Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel. The document specifies that the prize should be awarded to a person, "who has done the most or best to advance fellowship among nations, the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and the establishment and promotion of peace congresses." In his will, the scientist also specified that the prize should be awarded by a committee of five members appointed by the Norwegian parliament. Traditionally, the committee includes retired Norwegian politicians and former party leaders.
Nowadays, the century-old wording is interpreted quite broadly, frequently drawing criticism toward the committee’s decisions. In recent years, the list of laureates included politicians, rights activists, political activists, and humanitarian organizations recognized for achievements across a wide range of fields.
The Nobel Peace Prize 2025 was awarded to Maria Corina Machado "for her tireless work promoting democratic rights for the people of Venezuela and for her struggle to achieve a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy".
Possible candidates
Traditionally, nominations for the prize can be made until January 31. After that, the right to nominate is reserved for committee members, who can exercise it at their first meeting, usually in February.
The full list of nominees is kept strictly confidential and may not be made public until after the 50th anniversary of the award. Each year, however, information about the nomination of certain candidates is leaked to the media by organizations or individuals with the right to nominate. These include former and current members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee and its advisors, previous Peace Prize laureates, members of national parliaments, university professors specializing in history, philosophy, law or theology.
The record number of contenders - 376 - was reported in 2016. A total of 287 candidates have been nominated for the 2025 edition of the prize: 208 individuals and 79 legal entities. According to media reports, US President Donald Trump was one of them. A number of public figures and political leaders spoke publicly about his nomination, including from Israel, Cambodia and Pakistan. A member of the House of Representatives of the US Congress, Anna Paulina Luna, also mentioned this.
Haakon Gjerlow, the head of the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), which regularly publishes lists of potential contenders, named the Save the Children charitable foundation, Sudanese volunteer network Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), the International Space Station (ISS), the International Court of Justice of the United Nations, and the International Criminal Court (ICC) as possible laureates.
About the award
The Nobel Peace Prize was first awarded in 1901. There were years when no winner was announced, the last time being in 1972. The reasons for no award being given include World Wars I and II, disagreements among committee members, and a "lack of worthy candidates."
The award ceremony is in Oslo on December 10, on the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death. This year’s monetary prize amounts to 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million).
Nobel Week kicked off in the Swedish capital of Stockholm on October 6. Winners of the prizes in medicine, physics, chemistry and literature have already been announced.
