US-based Kashmir filmmaker Arfat Sheikh walks free from ICE detention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:00:50 UTC
12:00:50 KST

Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh has been released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention on bond after being detained on September 24, according to a statement by a campaign of his friends and relatives to free him.
Sheikh, whose work has explored conflict in his native India-administered Kashmir, was detained by ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security, while coming off a plane from California at the Washington Dulles International Airport, the campaign said.
It said Sheikh's bond was granted on Tuesday and he was released on Thursday, adding that the deportation case against him continues.
The campaign said Sheikh, who lived in Alexandria, Virginia, entered the US in 2019 on a student visa to pursue graduate studies in film at Georgia State University and filed for asylum in 2020.
The campaign said he had a pending immigration application and was authorised to work and live in the US.
DHS said on Wednesday Sheikh was arrested on September 24.
It said Sheikh "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance." A pending application does not confer legal status in the US, DHS said, adding he will receive due process.
President Donald Trump's administration said in August it was working "to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently."
Trump has pursued an immigration crackdown and deportation drive that he says aims to improve domestic security.
Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
Saffron Kingdom
Sheikh's first feature film, 2024's "Saffron Kingdom," won Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival and the Wake Forest Film Festival.
Sheikh, who hails from India-administered Kashmir, won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival.
The film explored conflict in Kashmir through the journey of a family from Srinagar in India-administered Kashmir in the 1990s to Atlanta in 2019.
Muslim-majority Kashmir is claimed in full by both Hindu-majority India and Islamic Pakistan, but each control only part of it and have fought wars over the territory. India revoked Kashmir's constitutional autonomy and annexed it in August 2019.
A significant proportion of Muslim Kashmiris favour the right to self-determination as promised by several UN Security Council resolutions, seeking either full independence or accession to Pakistan.
In May 2025, India and Pakistan fought a brief war using missiles, fighter jets, drones and other weapons, which ultimately led to US involvement.
US President Trump helped broker a ceasefire during the military confrontation, an intervention later publicly praised by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, while India maintained that the truce was reached through direct bilateral military communications and that Trump had played no role in it.
Sheikh, who grew up in India-administered Kashmir during the 1990s, told TRT World in a 2024 interview that his film "Saffron Kingdom "was born from his desire to reclaim his people's narrative, who have often been negatively depicted by Indian cinema."
"This film is my way of breaking Bollywood's hegemony over our narrative. It's about debunking the lies they have been peddling for years," he said.
In the interview he recalled traumatic memories of being locked in a room with his family while the Indian military tortured his uncle.
His father, a renowned Kashmiri musician, was murdered while travelling to northern Indian state of Punjab. "His death was reported in newspapers, but each paper had its own version of events. We were not even given his body," he said.

Can China use its widening US yield gap to boost the yuan’s global role?
Beijing could leverage the yuan’s low interest rate to increase the currency’s worldwide use, an expert says
The 10-year US Treasury yield was 5.22 per cent on Thursday, compared with 1.69 per cent for Chinese government bonds on their first trading day after the National Day holiday – a gap of about 3.5 percentage points, compared with a record 3.7-percentage-point gap on September 9.
Jiang Zhenlong, an associate research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Finance and Banking, argued that higher US yields weakened the appeal of yuan assets and added pressure on the exchange rate and capital flows, but also raised dollar funding costs.
“The China-US yield inversion presents an asymmetric effect: pressure on the asset allocation side and benefit on the financing side,” he wrote in the latest issue of China Money Market, a central bank-affiliated magazine.

Berechenbare Risiken – unberechenbare Politik? Warum Deutschland jetzt aus Worten Gesetze machen muss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Berechenbare Risiken – unberechenbare Politik? Warum Deutschland jetzt aus Worten Gesetze machen muss
Mit berechenbaren Risiken kann die forschende Pharmaindustrie umgehen – mit politischer Unberechenbarkeit nicht. Warum eine Standortklausel nun ein erster Schritt in Richtung Verlässlichkeit am Standort Deutschland sein kann.
In der Ökonomie gibt es eine fundamentale Unterscheidung, die für das Verständnis unternehmerischer Entscheidungen zentral ist: Das Risiko und die Ungewissheit. Risiko lässt sich berechnen, einpreisen, managen. Man kennt die Spielregeln – auch wenn man nicht weiß, wie das Spiel ausgeht. Ungewissheit hingegen entzieht sich jeder Formel, weil sich die Spielregeln selbst immer wieder verändern.
Wer neue Technologien entwickelt, Produktionskapazitäten aufbaut und langfristige Zukunftsprojekte anstößt, ist bereit, Risiken einzugehen. In kaum einer Branche zeigt sich das deutlicher als in der forschenden Pharma- und Biotech-Industrie. Denn bis ein neues Medikament bei Patientinnen und Patienten in der Versorgung ankommt, vergehen 10 bis 15 Jahre milliardenschwerer Forschung und Entwicklung. Und die Wahrscheinlichkeit, auf dem Weg zu scheitern, liegt bei über 90%. Mit diesem Risiko können wir umgehen. Es ist fester Bestandteil unseres Geschäftsmodells, das auf Innovation ausgerichtet ist. Es ist auch Voraussetzung für die bahnbrechenden Fortschritte, die in der Medizin in den letzten Jahren erzielt wurden.
Was Zukunftsentscheidungen jedoch lähmt: Ungewissheit durch politische Sprunghaftigkeit.
Wer Zukunftsversprechen formuliert, im Alltag der Gesetzgebung aber vor allem den Rotstift an Innovation und Fortschritt ansetzt, konterkariert jegliche Industriepolitik und erstickt Vertrauen im Keim – da hilft das stärkste Signal nicht mehr.
Genau diese erleben wir in der politischen Diskussion zuletzt zu oft. Genau diese Sprunghaftigkeit haben wir als forschende Gesundheitsindustrie in Deutschland in den letzten Monaten in aller Deutlichkeit zu spüren bekommen. Auf der einen Seite ein ambitioniertes Bekenntnis zum Pharmastandort Deutschland im Koalitionsvertrag – eine Pharmastrategie unter der Regie des Bundeskanzleramtes. Ein starkes Signal!
Auf der anderen Seite dann aber gravierende Eingriffe in bestehende Spielregeln. Eine Gesetzgebung, die einzig und allein darauf abzielt, wieder einmal Finanzlöcher auf Seiten der Kassen zu stopfen – maßgeblich auf Kosten der Industrie durch künstliche Preisdeckel und Zwangsrabatte. Wer Zukunftsversprechen formuliert, im Alltag der Gesetzgebung aber vor allem den Rotstift an Innovation und Fortschritt ansetzt, konterkariert jegliche Industriepolitik und erstickt Vertrauen im Keim – da hilft das stärkste Signal nicht mehr.
Ein gefährlicher Dominoeffekt
Wenn Vertrauen schwindet, explodiert ein Industriestandort nicht mit einem lauten Knall. Vielmehr setzt eine leise Kettenreaktion ein, bei der ein Dominostein den nächsten umwirft. Und klar ist: Die ersten Steine des Gesundheits- und Forschungsstandorts Deutschland sind längst gekippt – mit direkten Folgen für Wirtschaft, Versorgung und Sicherheit:
Abfluss von Risikokapital: Milliardenschweres Risikokapital ist global mobil und fließt in jene Märkte, in denen Innovation ein erfolgreiches Geschäftsmodell sein kann. Schon heute vereinen die USA über 50 Prozent des weltweiten Pharmamarktes auf sich, auf Deutschland entfallen lediglich 4-5 Prozent. Mit Regulierung, die Innovation entwertet, verliert Deutschland weiter an Attraktivität und private Investitionen fließen in Zukunft noch häufiger in jene Märkte, die mit strategischer Konsequenz innovationsfreundliche Rahmenbedingungen schaffen.
Verlust an Forschung und Innovationskraft: Wo Kapital abwandert, schrumpft auch die wissenschaftliche Substanz. Der europäische Anteil an der globalen Pharma-Forschung ist in den letzten Jahrzehnten drastisch von über 40 auf knapp 30 Prozent gefallen; der Anteil an klinischen Studien hat sich binnen einer Dekade auf 9 Prozent halbiert. Auch Deutschland ist längst zurückgefallen: Im Global Innovation Index der WIPO zählen wir erstmals nicht mehr zu den zehn innovationsstärksten Volkswirtschaften der Welt.
Gefährdung der medizinischen Versorgung: Ein Markt, der Innovation nicht fair honoriert, ist unattraktiv für medizinische Durchbrüche. Schon heute sehen wir, dass Deutschland seine Rolle als globaler Versorgungspionier verliert: Jedes dritte in den USA neu zugelassene Medikament erreicht Patientinnen und Patienten in Deutschland nicht mehr. Besonders alarmierend: Bei zwei Dritteln dieser Therapien handelt es sich um Präparate mit anerkannt hohem Innovationsstatus.
Verlust von Souveränität: In Zeiten geopolitischer Umbrüche und fragiler Lieferketten sind medizinische Schlüsseltechnologien längst zu einer Währung für nationale Resilienz geworden. Wer Forschung und Produktion im eigenen Land vernachlässigt, gibt Handlungsspielräume auf und gerät bei der Versorgung der eigenen Bevölkerung in gefährliche Abhängigkeiten.
Chance auf einen Perspektivwechsel
Zukunftsfähigkeit, Innovationskraft und Souveränität lassen sich nicht durch kurzsichtiges Flickwerk verteidigen. Um den Dominoeffekt, der unseren Gesundheitsstandort erfasst hat, zu stoppen, braucht es jetzt ein Umdenken; weg von Verteilungsdebatten hin zu einem verlässlichen Bekenntnis zu Innovationen.
Erstmals wird medizinischer Fortschritt nicht mehr einseitig von der Kostenseite gedacht, sondern daran gemessen, was die forschende Gesundheitsindustrie durch Forschung, Entwicklung, Produktion und hochwertige Arbeitsplätze für unser Land leistet.
Dazu gehört auch, dass wir uns ehrlich machen: Die finanzielle Schieflage der Kassen entsteht durch strukturelle Ineffizienzen im System, nicht durch medizinischen Fortschritt. Ganz im Gegenteil: Innovative Medizin ist kein Kostenfaktor, sondern eine Investition in die Zukunft. Der konsequente Einsatz modernster Diagnostik, digitaler Prozesse und innovativer Therapien könnte schon heute jährlich über 40 Milliarden Euro freisetzen – direkt im Gesundheitssystem und indirekt als positiver Effekt auf Wirtschaft, Wachstum und Wohlstand.
Die Politik hat jetzt die Chance, einen Perspektivwechsel einzuleiten. Eine Expertenkommission hat jüngst konkret vorgeschlagen, wie Unternehmen, die in Deutschland investieren, von einem Teil – wohlgemerkt: nur einem Teil – jener zusätzlichen Belastungen ausgenommen werden können, die mit dem GKV-Beitragssatzstabilisierungsgesetz eingeführt wurden. Diese Vorschläge zur Verknüpfung des Herstellerabschlags mit einer sogenannten Standortklausel liegen nun auf dem Tisch. Und sie sind schon bemerkenswert: Erstmals wird medizinischer Fortschritt nicht mehr einseitig von der Kostenseite gedacht, sondern daran gemessen, was die forschende Gesundheitsindustrie durch Forschung, Entwicklung, Produktion und hochwertige Arbeitsplätze für unser Land leistet. Ein Ansatz, der Industriepolitik, Sozialpolitik und Geopolitik endlich zusammendenkt.
Denn erst dann sendet die Bundesregierung die notwendige politische Verbindlichkeit.
Dabei wird uns keineswegs etwas geschenkt: Die Kassen werden mit einem erhöhten Herstellerabschlag von 15,5% weiterhin auf Rekordniveau durch die Industrie gestützt – Unternehmen, die nachweislich vor Ort Werte schaffen, Arbeitsplätze sichern und Forschung verankern, erhalten lediglich die Chance, die zusätzlichen Belastungen zu reduzieren. Das ist kein Geschenk – sondern die Korrektur einer massiven Fehlsteuerung. Eine vorausschauende, ressortübergreifende Standortstrategie hätte von vornherein auf positive Anreize gesetzt, statt bestehende Strukturen zu schwächen. Umso wichtiger ist es, dass daraus nun schnell ein wirksames, unbürokratisches Gesetz wird – und dass weitere Schritte folgen. Denn erst dann sendet die Bundesregierung die notwendige politische Verbindlichkeit. Denn milliardenschwere Investitionsentscheidungen in die Zukunft Deutschlands folgen keinen Kommissionspapieren – sondern verlässlichen Taten, die die Grundlage für eine Pharma-Strategie werden können, die Deutschlands Wettbewerbsfähigkeit wiederherstellt und den internationalen Herausforderungen gerecht wird.

Storm Simon seen exploding into major hurricane before hitting Mexico

Storm Simon seen exploding into major hurricane before hitting Mexico
MEXICO CITY, Oct 8 - Tropical Storm Simon is forecast to rapidly strengthen into a major hurricane before striking Mexico's Pacific coast this weekend, threatening destructive winds, life-threatening flooding and dangerous storm surge, the US National Hurricane Center said on Thursday.
Simon was about 245 miles (395 km) south of Manzanillo at midday, with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kph), the Miami-based center said. It was moving west at 5 mph and is expected to turn northward on Friday, approaching southwestern and west-central Mexico late on Saturday.
The hurricane center said Simon was likely to become a hurricane later on Thursday and intensify into a "very dangerous" Category 4 hurricane before reaching the coast.
A hurricane watch was in effect from the port city of Manzanillo to vacation hotspot Punta Mita.
Forecasters warned Simon could dump 8 to 15 inches (20 to 38 cm) of rain across parts of southwestern Mexico through Sunday, with isolated totals of up to 25 inches (64 cm) possible in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. The rainfall could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in mountainous areas.
A dangerous storm surge was also possible near and east of where the storm's center makes landfall, the center said, with large and destructive waves expected along the coast. Swells generated by Simon were forecast to create hazardous surf and rip current conditions over the coming days.
Private forecaster AccuWeather said Simon could make landfall in western Mexico on Sunday with wind gusts of 120 to 130 mph (193 to 209 kph) near the point of impact and storm surge of up to 15 feet (4.6 meters) in the worst-hit areas. It said some of the same regions affected by Hurricane Polo late last month were now facing another tropical threat.
AccuWeather also said tropical moisture from Simon could spread into the US Southwest next week, bringing 1 to 2 inches (2.5 to 5 cm) of rain to parts of New Mexico, eastern Arizona, southern Colorado and western Texas, with higher totals possible in southern New Mexico. REUTERS

What's next?
St Kilda will undertake an independent review of its AFLW football program, with Brad Lloyd appointed to lead the review.
St Kilda's disastrous AFLW season has led to coach Nick Dal Santo stepping down after six seasons in charge, ahead of an independent review of the football program.
With four rounds to go until the end of the regular season, the Saints sit at the bottom of the AFLW ladder with eight losses from as many games.
St Kilda's percentage is a league-worst 37.2. The team is averaging 23 points per game in attack, while conceding an average of 62 points a game.
The situation reached a critical point after last weekend's game, where the Saints lost by 30 points to the Western Bulldogs in Ballarat.
Ashleigh Richards kicked a point at the 17-minute mark of the final term, for what proved the team's only score of the game.
This meant the Saints avoided becoming the first team in AFLW history not to score in a full game.
In a club announcement on Friday, St Kilda confirmed Dal Santo's decision.
Saturday's (home) match against Collingwood will be Dal Santo's final game as senior coach.
"Nick has made a significant contribution to our AFLW program across six seasons and will always be an important part of our football club," St Kilda CEO Carl Dilena said.
"His care, commitment and leadership have been unwavering, and we thank him for everything he has given to the program, including leading the team to its maiden finals appearance last season."
Dal Santo was quoted in the statement saying he was proud of "where we've been able to take this program", but that he had been giving thought to whether continuing was the right decision for him and the club.
"It's been a privilege to coach this group and help shape its formative years in the competition.
"I have a strong love for this club. I wanted to contribute to women's football, and with a daughter of my own, it's great to see a pathway for young females with football ambitions.
"I'm looking forward to finishing my time as coach alongside the group this weekend and wish them every success for what comes next."
St Kilda confirmed that football administrator and executive Brad Lloyd from Apogee Sports would lead an independent review into the program.
Lloyd has previously led reviews at AFLW clubs Richmond and Carlton.

Sacred splashes: ancient Chinese ritual of ‘elephant washing’ for good fortune
Unknown

Sacred splashes: ancient Chinese ritual of ‘elephant washing’ for good fortune
The tradition came to an end in the late Qing dynasty, after a parade elephant went rogue, crushed a general’s carriage, and killed a eunuch
In ancient China, royal families washed elephants to pray for good fortune – until one elephant went rogue and brought the tradition to an end.
Elephants had been spotted and documented in China as early as 4000 BC. They are believed to have once been familiar animals in the Central Plains before gradually migrating south to more remote regions.
From the Han dynasty (202 BC–220), elephants were presented as tribute to the royal court. They carried deeply auspicious meanings: the Chinese word for “elephant”, xiang, is a homophone for auspiciousness, xiang – the core half of ji xiang, which means “good fortune.”

NHAI in SC against HC’s blanket ban on tree felling, says impedes infra projects
NEW DELHI: In what appeared to be a clash between environment protection and strategic infrastructure in a border state, the Supreme Court on Thursday asked Punjab govt its plan on allocation of land for compensatory afforestation in lieu of tree felling necessitated for construction of highway and public projects in the state.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta told a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the Punjab and Haryana HC has imposed a blanket bank on tree felling without the HC’s prior permission which had brought to a standstill that strategic road projects in the border state even though necessary permission for these had been obtained from statutory authorities.The bench said the HC’s concern was legitimate as the forest cover in Punjab has been reduced to 3.67% of the geographical area, which is lesser than the 4.87% forest cover in the arid Rajasthan. The HC, while imposing a blanket ban on tree felling, had flagged the poor forest cover in the state and said, “It appears that the functionaries of the state of Punjab are neither serious nor they seem conscious of the impending ecological catastrophe.
In view of the inactivity of the respondents, it requires drastic remedial measures by this court. Accordingly, this court prohibits the cutting of any tree of any age/species in Punjab, without permission of this Court, till the next date of hearing.”In another case, the HC had said trees would be permitted to be cut if the state makes available and allots public land for the purpose of compensatory afforestation (planting of five times the number of trees cut) within a radius of five km of the place where the trees are felled. It had said that if the state failed to provide such land, then the cutting of trees would not take place.Mehta said that in linear highway projects, there may not be suitable land within five km of the project for afforestation and requested the court to relax this norm to enable afforestation at the nearest possible location.

- The move deepens Meta’s rivalry with TikTok, while both firms face pressure over teen safety and tighter rules on children’s use of social media.
AI generated
BENGALURU/MEXICO CITY - Facebook and Instagram-owner Meta has banned advertisements by ByteDance, the Chinese parent of TikTok, on its platforms in the United States and a handful of other countries, a company spokesperson said on Oct 8.
The move marks an escalation in the long-running rivalry between Meta and ByteDance, whose video-sharing app TikTok has emerged as one of Meta’s most formidable competitors for user engagement, creators and advertising dollars.
Meta’s ban takes effect immediately in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, and extends to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries, Meta said.
“We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps,” Meta said.
“Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience.”
TikTok and ByteDance did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment on Meta’s move.
TikTok’s website shows that it does not support links that open or log users into other social media apps. However, users can still add links to their profiles that direct people to those platforms’ websites.
Meta has been urging TikTok and YouTube to follow steps it agreed to take on teen safety in August following a settlement of up to US$18 billion (S$23 billion) with US states over social media harms to children.
Meta in August agreed to impose daily usage limits and restrict nighttime usage by children who use Facebook and Instagram, and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content.
TikTok has not publicly commented on Meta’s campaign, but it reached a settlement with Alabama in September that requires the social media platform to impose new usage limits and enhance age-verification measures for users in the state, resolving claims that it endangered children and misled consumers about its safety.
TikTok operates in the US as a majority American-owned joint venture after a deal aimed at safeguarding US user data and averting a US ban on an app used by more than 200 million users in the country.
Bloomberg News first reported Meta’s ban earlier on Oct 8. REUTERS

UK PM Burnham's Labour fends off left-wing Greens in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

UK PM Burnham's Labour fends off left-wing Greens in London
LONDON, Oct 9 - Andy Burnham's Labour Party won an election for a parliamentary seat vacated by former leader Keir Starmer on Friday, fending off a strong challenge from the left-wing Green Party in a boost for the British prime minister.
Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of the local council, won the seat in the central London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras with 12,292 votes, compared with 8,928 for Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader.
The victory, which had been expected, will buoy Burnham, installed as prime minister by lawmakers fearful Starmer's unpopularity was opening the way for a challenge by the populist Reform UK party at the next national election.
After losing left-wing support to the Greens earlier this year, Labour looks to have won many voters back, a result which triggered more questions about the leadership of Polanski, who had promised to make his party "an eco-populist" movement.
POLANSKI VOWS TO STAY ON AS GREEN PARTY LEADER
The 43-year-old former actor and hypnotherapist, who had some success in drawing voters away from Labour before Burnham came to power, has come under fire after party members passed a Zionism is Racism motion. The move, which called for "the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine" was criticised by Jewish groups, other parties and most Green Party lawmakers.
After the fiercely contested vote, Polanski who did not vote, answered his critics, saying he would stay on as leader, and described the result as part of "Andy Burnham's honeymoon".
Yet he did not get a full endorsement from the party's former leader, Caroline Lucas, who struggled to contain her anger over what she said was his lack of leadership over the motion on Zionism at last week's annual conference.
Asked whether he should stay on as leader, she told the BBC: "I think just let's see what happens in the coming days and weeks."
"I want him to speak now about what has happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday."
Labour's Abdi-Wali, who arrived in Britain as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a defeat for "those who seek to divide us".
"We have a responsibility to defend what we've built and pass it on," she said. "Throughout our campaign, we chose hope, and the people of Holborn and St Pancras chose it with us. And now it's time to deliver."
POLANSKI FACES DOWN CRITICS
It was an early test for Burnham, whose predecessor, Starmer, stood down as a lawmaker in September after being ousted as prime minister in July.
Under Starmer, Labour had also ceded ground to the Green Party, which made record gains in London in May's local elections with its widening appeal among younger, left-leaning voters in the capital and other urban areas.
The Greens have fallen back in opinion polls since, after Burnham made policy pitches that boosted Labour's standing among voters to the left, including a tougher line on Israel and a more ambitious approach to relations with the European Union.
Polanski, who is Jewish, was questioned repeatedly after the by-election over the conference vote on Zionism and the Green leader seemed again to distance himself from it, saying only that he believed displacement of Palestinian people and "ongoing genocide" were racist.
For now, he said, the Green Party should take their fight to Burnham's Labour and focus on whether the governing party's budget on October 28 delivers.
"So many people told me on the doorstep that they want to give Andy Burnham a chance," Polanski told broadcasters. "Well, he's got a chance now. Let's see what he does with it." REUTERS

Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro wins third-place candidate’s support against Lula
Brazil's right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro secured third-place finisher Augusto Cury's endorsement on Thursday, strengthening his position against incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva ahead of the runoff. Cury won nearly three percent in Sunday's first round. A Datafolha poll put Bolsonaro ahead with 52 percent against Lula's 48 percent.
Right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Thursday gained the support of Augusto Cury, the third-place candidate in Brazil's presidential election, bolstering his chances against incumbent leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
"My support is not a blank check," Cury said in a statement, after winning nearly three percent of the vote in Sunday's first round of voting, compared to Bolsonaro's 47 percent and Lula's 45 percent.
Bolsonaro, 45, is the eldest son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest for plotting a coup after losing Brazil's last election in 2022.
Prior to the announcement, the younger Bolsonaro was leading in polls on Thursday, which gave the senator 52 percent compared to Lula's 48 percent, according to the Datafolha institute.
Read moreThousands protest Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, fearing far-right return
Lula, 81, downplayed the polls as he sought to secure a fourth term.
"I don't assess polls, I don't work like that. I work knowing that I need to have more votes than Flavio to win the election. I have 17 days to do that," he said at a press conference Thursday.
While Bolsonaro is hoping to bank on his allegiances in the final stretch of the campaign, Lula has been strengthening his presence on social media, where the right has an upper hand.
Thousands of people demonstrated on Thursday in Sao Paulo and other cities against the return of the far right to power in Brazil, a day after a similar march in Rio de Janeiro.
Renan Santos, the fourth most popular candidate with 2.6 million votes, has refused to support either leading candidate.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Singapore film festival rejects South Korean party’s calls to drop The Assassin(s)
Organisers said the political thriller will open the festival amid growing backlash in South Korea over claims of historical distortion
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
The Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) is standing by its decision to screen South Korean political thriller The Assassin(s) as its opening film, despite calls from South Korea’s conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP) to withdraw it over allegations of historical distortion.
The film, directed by Hur Jin-ho and starring Yoo Hae-jin, Park Hae-il and Lee Min-ho, has drawn criticism in South Korea over its fictionalised portrayal of a real-life 1974 assassination attempt on then president Park Chung-hee, which resulted in the death of his wife, first lady Yuk Young-soo.
SGIFF said it was aware of the discussions surrounding the film but would retain it as the opening title of its 37th edition, which runs from October 21 to November 1.
“SGIFF respects the creative vision of the filmmakers behind The Assassin(s), which remains the festival opening film of our 37th edition,” the festival said.

Houthis claim attack on Riyadh airport as airlines suspend flights to Saudi capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:28:58 UTC
11:28:58 KST

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis say they have struck Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport with a ballistic missile, badly damaging a plane and leading some airlines to suspend flights to the capital.
The group provided no evidence, and Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on the claim.
However, three people briefed on the matter told Reuters that shrapnel from an interception or another projectile left a Saudia Airlines commercial plane heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at a terminal on Thursday.
They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the time but they could not rule out any injuries.
Witnesses heard explosions in Riyadh, including a large blast at the King Khalid international airport. One witness told the Associated Press that fire and ambulance crews were deployed. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from the airport in a video verified by Reuters.
The witness, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that outgoing flights were halted, and that passengers were instructed to evacuate the airport.
Lufthansa and Air India confirmed they were suspending flights to Riyadh. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from the airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT on Thursday, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports.
It comes after Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport, in the country’s southwest.
The Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, attempting to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and warning workers to stay away from energy plants, which would be targeted.
Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh.
The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to take back territory from the Houthis.
The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month, appearing to gain ground in the country’s south-west on Wednesday as the group approached the city of Taiz.
Independent observers said earlier this week there was danger the group was on course to capture Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure the major port city of Aden.
Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.

Aysu Bicer
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Britain’s Green Party has conceded defeat in a by-election for the central London constituency of Holborn and St. Pancras, acknowledging that its candidate and party leader Zack Polanski will not become a member of parliament.
A Green Party spokesperson said the party would finish in second place, describing its performance in the traditionally safe Labour constituency as a sign of its growing political influence.
“It is clear now we will come a close second in this by-election. Taking the fight to Labour in one of its safest seats shows just how far the Greens have come,” the spokesperson told the BBC.
The party said it would continue pressing the Labour government on affordable housing, public ownership of water and climate change.
“Greens will be there every single day, holding Labour to account and demanding the change people voted for,” the spokesperson added.
Turnout in Thursday’s by-election was confirmed at 38.76%, lower than that recorded in the 2024 general election.
The constituency became vacant after former Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced last month that he would step down as a member of parliament.
Holborn and St Pancras has long been considered a safe Labour seat. However, the Green Party has gained momentum since Polanski became its leader, with the by-election providing a significant challenge to Labour in the constituency.

FIFA chief urges greater support for young African players at CAF conference
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:21:34 CST
11:21:34 KST

PRAIA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- FIFA President Gianni Infantino called for greater opportunities for young African footballers on Thursday as the Confederation of African Football opened its Strategy Conference on Cabo Verde's Sal Island.
The conference, held from October 7 to 9 in Santa Maria, brings together African football leaders to discuss the development of the game across the continent and review African teams' performances at the 2026 World Cup ahead of the 2030 tournament.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Infantino said young African players should not have their prospects limited by where they were born, local news agency Inforpress reported.
"African talent has shaped and is increasingly shaping the world. We must provide opportunities for that talent to shine on the global stage," Infantino said.
He said FIFA had invested about one billion U.S. dollars in African football through its Forward development program over the past decade.
He praised Cabo Verde's national team, known as the Blue Sharks, for its passion and resilience at the World Cup.
CAF President Patrice Motsepe stressed the importance of cooperation among national football associations, governments and sports ministries.
He said the conference would give CAF's 54 member associations an opportunity to discuss their concerns in greater depth than at ordinary general assemblies.
"At general assemblies, there is not enough time to discuss each association's concerns in depth, highlight good results and, above all, identify areas where there is room for improvement and where we need to do better. That is why today and tomorrow are also about listening," Motsepe said.
Cabo Verde Football Federation President Mario Semedo said hosting the conference reflected international recognition of the country's football development efforts and provided an opportunity to promote Cabo Verde as a tourism destination and host of international events.
The gathering includes presidents of CAF's 54 member associations, regional football officials, national team coaches and international experts. ■

Australia expects sufficient east coast gas supply in Q1 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:20:49 CST
11:20:49 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Australia's east coast gas market is expected to have sufficient supply to meet domestic demand in the first quarter of 2027, with a projected surplus of between 5 and 15 petajoules (PJ), the government said.
In a statement released on Friday, the Department of Industry, Science and Resources said the latest forecasts from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) and the Australian Energy Market Operator indicated that gas supply would comfortably meet household and industrial needs from January to March 2027.
According to the ACCC's September 2026 Gas Inquiry report, the projected surplus is 9 PJ lower than previously forecast, mainly due to declining gas production in southern states and increased export demand.
Despite the downward revision, the department said the east coast gas market can meet domestic demand, maintain gas exports without affecting local supply, and replenish gas storage facilities.
Given the positive supply outlook, the Australian government will not initiate a formal review of potential gas supply shortfalls for the quarter.
The department said it would continue conducting quarterly assessments of domestic gas supply until the government's Domestic Gas Reservation Scheme comes into effect. ■

Ethiopian drones deliver strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray — TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:20:01 UTC
11:20:01 KST

NAIROBI, October 9. /TASS/. Ethiopian drones delivered a series of strikes on Eritrean army units that entered the country’s region of Tigray, the Africanews television reported citing independent conflict monitor ACLED and eyewitnesses.
According to ACLED, the attacks occurred in the early hours of October 8 and targeted the city of Adigrat, where Eritrean troops that earlier crossed into Ethiopia were stationed. The drones targeted the Eritrean army’s personnel and military vehicles.
Eyewitnesses said multiple explosions were heard in the Adigrat area. A local resident said several Eritrean military trucks were destroyed. Another eyewitness said he saw military vehicles hit by drones. The third local said Eritrean troops have started to pull back to the north.
Ethiopian and Eritrean governments have not yet commented on the strikes.
Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea deteriorated in recent months as Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) jointly with Sudan and Egypt - a claim that the three countries strongly rejected. In early October, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara, with Eritrea subsequently announcing that diplomatic ties with its neighbor have been severed.
The Ethiopian government’s remarks about the need to secure reliable access to the Red Sea coast remain an additional source of tension. Earlier, Eritrea’s authorities accused Ethiopia of plotting to put these plans into practice by seizing the port of Assab. Addis Ababa maintains that it plans to resolve the issue peacefully.
Ethiopia lost access to the sea in 1993 after Eritrea declared independence following a referendum. Eritrea was formerly an Italian colony and later a British protectorate. In 1952, it was incorporated into Ethiopia as an autonomous region, but in 1962 Emperor Haile Selassie dissolved the federation and annexed the territory.

Putin, Pezeshkian Talk ‘Peace’ in Turkmenistan While Fueling War in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:12:03 UTC
11:12:03 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged support for Tehran and offered to help resolve its conflict with the US during talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan on Thursday, Oct. 8 – reaffirming a strategic partnership that has helped sustain Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
The two leaders met in Avaza, on the Caspian Sea coast, ahead of Friday’s Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit. Both governments have been strengthening political, military and economic cooperation amid extensive Western sanctions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Pezeshkian used the meeting to criticize Washington’s foreign policy, thank Moscow for its diplomatic support and reveal that Tehran was preparing revised proposals for ending its conflict with the US.
Putin plays peacemaker for Tehran
Putin opened the meeting by praising bilateral relations under the comprehensive strategic partnership agreement signed in January 2025.
He portrayed Iran as seeking peace rather than bearing responsibility for the regional conflict.
“We know that Iran is making genuine efforts to end the conflict that erupted in the region through no fault of its own – not Iran’s fault,” Putin said.
He added that Tehran had put forward new proposals for a peaceful settlement and offered Moscow’s assistance.
“For our part, we are ready to do everything within our power to help you resolve this situation,” Putin told Pezeshkian.
German Spy Scandal – Could Ukraine and NATO Be at Risk?
Pezeshkian challenges Washington, details US backchannels
Pezeshkian responded by praising Moscow and criticizing what he described as Washington’s attempts to dictate global policy.
“The United States is now trying to dictate its views to countries around the world,” Pezeshkian said, arguing that Russia and Iran shared a commitment to resisting unilateralism.
The Iranian president thanked Putin for Moscow’s diplomatic backing, particularly at the United Nations.
“Thanks to your assistance, they have been unable to impose their unilateral approach on us,” he said.
Pezeshkian also revealed that indirect diplomatic exchanges between Tehran and Washington were continuing through intermediaries.
“We have once again revised the American proposal, and once that process is finalized, we will communicate the results,” he said.
He maintained that Tehran had never abandoned negotiations, even when military attacks occurred during diplomatic discussions.
Iranian drones and missiles – the cost for Ukraine
For Ukraine, the Avaza meeting underscored the security consequences of Russia’s military partnership with Iran.
Since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones have become a principal weapon in Russia’s repeated strikes against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
Moscow initially relied on Iranian drone supplies before establishing domestic production of Iranian-designed systems, enabling Russian forces to expand the scale and frequency of their attacks.
Western governments have also reported Iranian transfers of short-range ballistic missiles to Russia, raising concerns about further military cooperation.
The relationship extends beyond weapons deliveries. Russia’s extensive battlefield experience in Ukraine, particularly in drone technology and electronic warfare, has raised concerns that military expertise could flow back to Tehran.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned about the wider consequences of military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran.

The mixed fortunes of Australia's last South African touring party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:11:49 UTC
11:11:49 KST

The members of Australia's touring party from the 2018 South Africa series have endured various fortunes in the eight years since.
Some have seen their careers go to new heights, while others struggled to recapture their form from before the ball-tampering saga.
Others never featured for Australia again.
As Australia plays its first Test in South Africa since 2018, here is a look at where everyone from the previous tour ended up in the years that followed.
Steve Smith
It is somewhat of an indictment on where Australian cricket has gone since the last South Africa tour that Smith is still by far the team's best batter.
Although, a glass-half-full view might suggest that it is a sign of Smith's incredible longevity.
While he is not at the peak of his powers like he was on the last tour, Smith is still the trump card in the line-up and will be the wicket South Africa's bowlers most covet.
Smith has retired from all white ball formats and is primarily a Test cricketer at the international level.
David Warner
Arguably Australia's main antagonist in 2018, Warner last represented Australia at the T20 World Cup in mid-2024.
Following his ball-tampering suspension, Warner never quite recaptured his form, particularly in the Test format.
Warner averaged 48.63 in Tests prior to the 2018 South Africa tour and finished his career averaging 37.28 in 38 Tests afterwards.
He is now a T20 gun for hire in various competitions around the world.
Cameron Bancroft
Bancroft's international career suffered the most out of the three players banned from the 2018 tour, having been the man caught by the Supersport cameras trying to hide a piece of sandpaper from the umpires.
The right-hander has played just two Tests since. The last of those came in 2019, and his Test career looks just about done.
Still just 33, Bancroft remains a prolific domestic run scorer, and ranked third in terms of runs in the Sheffield Shield last year. He has 33 first class centuries to his name.
Joe Burns
Burns was one of the players drafted into the Australian XI for the final Test in 2018 after the suspensions of Smith, Warner and Bancroft.
He enjoyed a productive 2019 at the Test level before playing the last of his Tests for Australia on Boxing Day in 2020.
Burns later became a T20 specialist for Italy, averaging 45.16 in eight matches across 2024 and 2025 to help the Italians qualify for their maiden T20 World Cup this year, but was left out of Italy's World Cup squad.
Pat Cummins
Cummins's Test career was in its infancy in 2018, having just returned to the side following years of injury issues.
Since then he has become one of the finest all-format bowlers as well as Australia captain.
Under Cummins's tenure, Australia has won an ODI World Cup and the ICC Test Championship, both in 2023.
He has been named in the Test Team of the Year on four occasions, and was named Test Cricketer of the Year in 2019.
Peter Handscomb
Another player who came in for the final Test in 2018, Handscomb has forever been on the periphery of Australia's Test side.
Handscomb was famously the man who told the Australian team that they'd been caught ball tampering, after chatting to then-coach Darren Lehmann on a walkie-talkie while flipping an Aussie rules football in between his hands.
Considered a specialist in spinning conditions, Handscomb has added just seven Tests to his career since the 2018 series, but is an outside chance to feature again in India next year after recently being added to the Australia A side.
He was the leading scorer in the last Shield season, scoring 724 runs at an average of 34.47 in very bowler-friendly conditions.
Josh Hazlewood
Hazlewood enjoyed some of his best years as a Test bowler following the 2018 tour.
The right-arm paceman averaged 25.77 with the ball prior to that series and has seen that average dip to an elite 21.17 in the years that have followed.
Hazlewood is still prolific when he is able to get on the park, but his body has given him problems over the last few seasons.
The 35-year-old was restricted to just four Tests last year, but still took 16 wickets at an average of 17.93.
Jon Holland
Holland was one of the players who didn't play a single Test during the last South Africa tour, and has mostly remained on the outer since.
His two Test appearances following the 2018 tour yielded just four wickets at an average of 75, and he was unsurprisingly surpassed in the spin pecking order.
Nevertheless, Holland continued to enjoy his time in domestic cricket, helping Victoria claim a Sheffield Shield title in 2018–19.
Holland's first class career ended in 2023 when he was let go by Victoria after 95 Shield appearances.
Usman Khawaja
Khawaja played all four Tests as Australia's number three in 2018, but his struggles in that series were no indicator of what was to come.
After being left out of the Test side in 2020 and 2021, Khawaja returned for the New Year's Test in 2022 and had an incredible stint as one of Australia's openers.
Khawaja scored eight of his 16 Test centuries after his return in 2022 and averaged 48.05 as an opener, one of the best marks by an Australian.
He retired from Test cricket following Australia's Ashes triumph against England last summer and is now a T20 specialist for domestic leagues after also retiring from Shield cricket.
Nathan Lyon
Lyon remains a mainstay in Australia's first-choice Test XI, just as he was in 2018.
Despite being the oldest player in Australia's team, no spinner has been able to claim Lyon's spot as the non-pace bowling option alongside Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins.
Lyon's body has slowly begun to show signs of aging in the past few years, and he played just two of the five Tests against England in last summer's Ashes.
His performances in the Bangladesh Tests suggest he won't be an automatic selection in South Africa.
Mitch Marsh
Marsh played all four Tests against South Africa in 2018, but struggled to kick on from that series in the years that followed. He was the man with the ball in hand when the ball-tampering storm erupted.
He had a strong 2023, scoring a century and four 50s to end the calendar year with an average of 67.50, but managed an average of just 18.86 the following year and saw his Test career come to an end after Boxing Day.
Marsh has since retired from Test cricket but remains in Australia's ODI and T20 sides, captaining the country in the shortest format.
His name gets mentioned with regards to a Test return every once in a while, but that ship appears to have sailed with Australia well-stocked with all-rounder options.
Shaun Marsh
The other Marsh brother also played all four Tests in the 2018 series, but struggled thereafter.
Marsh was relied upon heavily during the suspensions to Smith, Warner and Bancroft, but did not play another Test once the trio were cleared to return.
He played his last first class match in 2023 and his last T20 in the BBL at the end of 2024.
Marsh is one of 10 former international cricketers involved in the CLT10, India's first luxury-format indoor cricket league.
Glenn Maxwell
Maxwell has not played a single Test since 2017 but remains a white ball superstar.
He played a key role in Australia's T20 World Cup and ODI World Cup wins, in 2021 and 2023 respectively.
He retired from ODIs in 2025 but still plays for Australia in the T20 format and is considered one of the most dangerous short-form players in the world.
With less international cricket on his plate, Maxwell is a gun for hire for domestic T20 leagues around the world.
Tim Paine
Paine was thrust into centre stage following the sandpaper debacle on the 2018 tour, captaining Australia in the final Test of the series in Smith and Warner's absence.
The Tasmanian keeper retained the captaincy even when Smith returned, and eventually led his country in 23 Tests.
Paine's reign as captain came to an end when he resigned in November 2021 after explicit messages he'd sent to a co-worker in 2017 resurfaced.
He ended his playing career at all levels in 2023 and took up coaching. Currently he is the head coach of Pakistan Super League side Multan Sultans.
Matt Renshaw
Renshaw was among those drafted into the Australian side for the final Test of the 2018 series in Johannesburg.
He played three more Tests in 2023, including one against South Africa, but managed just nine runs in four innings.
Renshaw received a Test recall earlier this year against Bangladesh, but managed just eight in his sole innings at the crease.
The left-hander has been most effective for Australia at the T20 level, where he averages 38.83 at a healthy strike rate of 125.94.
Jhye Richardson
Richardson has been the nearly man of his generation of Australian cricketers.
He did not feature in the 2018 Tests, but made his debut the following year, shining with six wickets in two Tests.
However, repeated injury issues halted his once-bright career, allowing him to play just two Tests in the last seven years.
He currently features in Australia A's Tests against India A. If his body holds up, he should be back in Test calculations in the not too distant future.
Chadd Sayers
Sayers was another one of Australia's inclusions for the Johannesburg Test in 2018, and it wound up being the only Test he would ever play.
A prolific Shield performer in the lead-up to the South Africa series, a knee injury ruined his 2018–19 season.
Sayers continued to play for South Australia and eventually retired from first class cricket at the end of the 2020–21 season.
Following his retirement, Sayers spent some time as a runner for SANFL side Woodville-West Torrens.
Mitchell Starc
Starc's career has gone from strength to strength since 2018, and he remains one of the most feared new ball bowlers in world cricket.
Nearly 37, Starc is as fast as ever and remains an integral part of Australia's Test line-up.
At the end of the 2018 series, Starc had taken 182 wickets at an average of 28.17 in 43 Tests.
Since then, he has taken a further 263 wickets at an average of 24.70 in 64 Tests, and his career mark of 445 Test wickets is the most by any left-arm bowler.

three ceramic sculptures diffuse distinct fragrances evoking puglia’s landscapes

three ceramic sculptures diffuse distinct fragrances evoking puglia’s landscapes
three olfactory sculptures by coco brun diffuse scents of puglia's sea, earth and vegetation, composed with perfumer laurène sourdillon of givaudan.
Coco Brun translates Puglia’s eroded landscapes into ceramics
Landscape Memories is an olfactory installation by French artist and designer Coco Brun that translates the landscapes of Puglia, southern Italy, into three ceramic sculptures that diffuse distinct fragrances. Developed during the D.Puglia residency, curated by Gordana Zgonjanin, the project draws on research into the region’s coastline, where erosion and the shifting relationship between land and sea shape the terrain.
The three sculptures take their forms from caves and underground geological formations. Surface patterns derived from 3D scans of Puglian caves are reproduced through ceramic extrusion, developed and produced in Milan with SuperForma. A programmed printing process builds the surfaces layer by layer, while the clay’s behavior during printing, drying, and firing produces visible drips, twists, and irregularities. The sculptures share a modular system that can be assembled in different configurations, with integrated openings allowing air and fragrance to circulate.
Ceramic sculptures diffuse scents of Sea, earth, and vegetation
Artist and designer Coco Brun collaborates with perfumer Laurène Sourdillon of Givaudan Paris for the creation of the three scents, Marino, Terra, and Bosco, which represent the sea, earth, and Mediterranean vegetation. Each fragrance can be experienced separately within its corresponding sculpture. As the scents circulate simultaneously through the exhibition space, they overlap to create a fourth olfactory impression that was never composed independently. Its perception changes with air currents, visitors’ positions, and the timing of the experience.
The fragrances are diffused through ORB, a dry-air olfactory diffusion device developed by Genius Loci and integrated into the sculptures. Each rechargeable sphere features an artisan-crafted, perforated casing inspired by organic forms found in the landscape.
Landscape Memories sensory Installation beyond the gallery
Presented at Villa Saporiti during the Lake Como Design Festival 2026, as part of Border / Confine, curated by Giovanna Massoni and Francesca Prandelli, the installation brings ceramic forms into dialogue with an invisible, shifting material. The project is being developed further, with redesigned sculptures and new textile and graphic works planned to extend the installation across two and three dimensions in future presentations in 2027.
project info:
name: Landscape Memories
artist: Coco Brun | @c_o_c_o_brun
perfumes: Laurène Sourdillon, Givaudan Paris
ceramics: SuperForma srl, Milan – Mattia Ciurnelli, Lorenzo Falegnami, Silvio Caniglia
olfactory diffusion device: ORB by Genius Loci
photographer: Federica Livia | @federicalivia__, Rebecca Pissina | @repsss

Green Leader Polanski’s Westminster gamble fails in Holborn and St Pancras

Green Leader Zack Polanski listens to successful Labour Party candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali's acceptance speech after her victory in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election in London on Oct. 9, 2026. | Carl Court/Getty Images
LONDON — Zack Polanski’s bid for a Westminster seat ended in defeat Friday as Labour comfortably held Holborn and St Pancras in a by-election.
Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali won the central London House of Commons seat with 12,292 votes, a majority of 3,364 over Green Leader Polanski, who came second with 8,928.
The poll was triggered when Keir Starmer stood down as an MP last month after being ousted as U.K. prime minister.
Advertisement
It is a symbolic early boost for Starmer’s replacement Andy Burnham, who has shifted the ruling Labour Party to the left since taking charge and toughened the U.K.’s stance on Israel amid criticism that Starmer’s response to the war in Gaza was flat-footed.
The north London seat has been held by Labour since its creation in 1983 — but the left-wing Green Party poured significant resources into trying to get its high-profile leader elected.
Abdi-Wali got 45% of the vote – down four points on Labour’s 2024 general election result. Polanski won 33% of the votes cast — a 22-point leap on the party’s 2024 result, but still some way short of taking the traditionally-safe Labour seat.
Labour Party candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali is hugged by a supporter after winning the Holborn and St Pancras by-election in London on Oct. 9, 2026. | Carl Court/Getty Images
A defeated Polanski – who had gambled on getting a toehold in parliament to boost the Greens’ profile – insisted he would stay on as party leader, telling broadcasters: “I’ve taken a loss tonight, but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion.”
His rival for the Green candidacy Hamza Chowdhury — a Green councillor in Camden — said: “This is a fucking win mate. Labour might be celebrating now but wait till 2029 when we wipe the floor with them.”
Polanski told Sky News Friday he is “disappointed” by the result, but put his defeat down to voters wanting to “give Andy Burnham a chance.”
Advertisement
He argued the Green Party’s fortunes have changed because Labour has moved closer to Green positions. “We’ve now got a different prime minister who is in a honeymoon, who is talking a lot of the language I’ve been talking about for the past year,” he said. “So I see that as a result.”
Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the U.K. as a child refugee from Somalia, meanwhile said her victory was “deeply personal” and vowed to work with Burnham to tackle homelessness. She said she wants to see Thames Water — the giant private water company that serves her constituents — brought into public ownership.
U.K. polling expert John Curtice said the Holborn result is “still by far and away [the Greens’] second best ever result in a parliamentary by-election” — but warned the Greens are “now operating in a more politically competitive environment.”
“The trouble is that when you manage to bring down an unpopular leader of your opponents, you’ve then got to deal with the consequences, which in this case is that Labour have put in place somebody who is more popular,” Curtice said of the party’s boast that it helped persuade Labour MPs to oust Starmer in favor of the more left-wing Burnham.
A Labour official said voters who were not giving the party a hearing earlier in the year were now listening again.
Curtice pointed out that while Labour is enjoying a substantial Burnham bounce they are “still short of where they were in 2024.”
Advertisement
Green dissent
Polanski’s defeat also comes as Green Party divisions spill into the open after members passed a controversial motion declaring Zionism to be a form of racism at their party conference last weekend.
One London councillor said the move had been “electoral suicide,” and shortly after polls closed Thursday the veteran former MP Caroline Lucas told the BBC that Polanski, who did not attend the vote in Brighton, “should have been there” and should now “show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.”
Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas — a former party leader who was the first Green MP to be elected to the House of Commons — said: “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks.”
Pushed on Lucas’ criticisms, Polanski told Sky News Friday that she is a “significant figure,” but that members are “entitled to have different opinions.”
A senior Green local politician allied to Polanski, granted anonymity to discuss internal matters, said: “You can’t really force a coup” in the Green Party — highlighting that a leadership election is not due for another year.
Polanski did not say if he agrees with party members who voted for the Zionism motion, which has been sharply criticized by Israel, rival British parties, and the chief of the Jewish Greens, when questioned at the by-election count.
Advertisement
He told broadcasters: “As I say, the displacement of the Palestinian people, the genocide, is clearly racist.”

Christa Pike case underscores prevalence of botched executions in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:05:00 UTC
11:05:00 KST

Christa Pike case underscores prevalence of botched executions in US
Experts say methods such as lethal injection promise more humane form of execution but are frequently marred by mishaps.
The botched execution of Christa Pike has sparked debate about the death penalty in the United States, where lethal injections, experts say, are frequently marred by mishaps and incompetence.
The attempted execution of Pike, a woman sentenced to death for her participation in the murder of a classmate when she was 18 years old, was called off after two doses of pentobarbital failed to kill her on September 30.
Witnesses reported that she continued to breathe, snore and lift parts of her body off the gurney to which she was strapped even after the lethal injections were administered. Pike’s lawyers said that she had regained consciousness at the hospital on October 6 but faces a long path to recovery.
Governor Bill Lee announced a pause on executions in the state and promised a “comprehensive, third-party review” of the incident, the second case this year in which Tennessee authorities have called off an execution after a failed lethal injection attempt.
The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment when asked by Al Jazeera why the execution attempt failed and whether it planned to try to execute Pike again.
While the case has attracted nationwide attention, experts say that botched execution attempts, largely carried out through lethal injection, are a disturbingly common feature of capital punishment in the US.
“This is an opportunity for everyone to stop and really carefully examine all of the ways in which this execution went wrong and to make good decisions about how to move forward, if we’re going to move forward with this method of execution,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit research group based in Washington, DC.
Medical issues
Of the various methods of execution in the US, lethal injection is by far the most common. It is also among the least reliable.
States such as Tennessee, Idaho, Alabama, Arizona, Texas and Oklahoma have all recorded at least one botched execution via lethal injection since 2022, and a survey of executions in the US between 1890 and 2010 found that lethal injections were botched at more than twice the rate of all other methods.
Researchers attribute the poor record of lethal injection to a number of factors, including the difficulty of carrying out what amounts to a medical procedure in a prison setting without access to qualified staff.
Major medical organisations bar members from assisting in executions on the basis that it violates their mandate to do no harm, meaning that prisons rely on staff members or officials with dubious credentials to carry out the procedure.
“Lethal injection has all of the delicacies of a medical procedure: all of the error-prone qualities, all of the need for precision. But it has been warped to fit the needs of execution settings,” said Corinna Barrett Lain, a professor at the University of Richmond School of Law and author of a book on lethal injection.
She explained that she has witnessed botched executions that drag on for hours and include prisoners being punctured with needles more than a dozen times. “It’s this really bad combination of a delicate procedure that is not performed in a delicate way.”
Pharmaceutical companies also restrict the use of their products in executions, meaning that some states acquire drugs used in lethal injection through facilities called compounding pharmacies.
Such pharmacies often prepare medications not manufactured commercially, and the drugs they produce are not as extensively scrutinised as mass-produced medications. Some states have also sought to stretch existing stockpiles of drugs used in lethal injections, though they can become expired or faulty.
The risks are compounded by the people the lethal injections are administered to.
Those on death row often spend years or even decades waiting for their execution. Since many are of an advanced age, they are more likely to have health issues that can further complicate the procedure.
Botched executions often feature failed attempts to locate a vein or set an IV line.
While state officials have yet to offer an explanation of why Pike’s execution failed, her lawyers had previously argued that she had small veins and a blood condition that were likely to complicate a lethal injection effort.
After the lethal injections, Pike’s lawyers described her arms as swollen and burned.
Maher, the head of the Death Penalty Information Center, said those symptoms suggest the injection may not have properly reached her bloodstream.
“Everyone has speculated that the drugs were administered to her but did not enter her bloodstream in sufficient amounts to kill her,” she said. “It’s likely that her veins were blown, or that the needle went through the vein.”
Popular method
When the lethal injection drugs fail to be properly administered, executions can be drawn out and, in some cases, unnecessarily painful for prisoners.
After the first dose of pentobarbital was administered to her, Pike reportedly stated that she felt her arm was “about to burst open”.
In May, Tennessee also called off the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff struggled for more than 90 minutes to establish a backup IV line.
In February 2024, the state of Idaho likewise suspended the execution of Thomas Creech, a man in his 70s, after an execution team failed to properly insert an IV after eight attempts in his arms, legs and feet.
Despite such incidents, lethal injection has become the primary method of execution in 28 of the 29 states that still allow capital punishment, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The first execution via lethal injection occurred in Texas in 1982.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, 39 people were killed by lethal injection in 2025, compared with five by lethal gas and three by firing squad. The last electrocution of a prisoner took place in 2020, and older methods such as hanging have not been employed since the 1990s.
Michael Radelet, a professor of sociology at the University of Colorado who has tracked botched executions, says that lethal injection has taken the place of older forms of execution that came to be seen as outdated and draconian.
Such methods also resulted in grim spectacles that distressed observers. Prisoners being electrocuted sometimes caught on fire or disturbed witnesses with the smell of burning flesh.
“Lethal injection is relatively new, but it’s part of a long-term trend going back hundreds of years in search of a more ‘humane’ method of execution,” Radelet told Al Jazeera.
But he added that the method’s promise of a more peaceful and clinical procedure has been belied by its poor record.
He also pointed to autopsies that show that, despite the relative sterility of the procedure, prisoners still experience pain.
Critics say such information calls into question the widespread use of lethal injection and whether it should be discarded altogether.
“Lethal injection, from the very start, was about a humane-looking execution, not a humane execution,” said Lain, the law professor. “There’s a big difference.”

Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:03:41 UTC
11:03:41 KST

Labour has seen off the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a result that will relieve Andy Burnham and dent Zack Polanski’s position as a decisive power player on the left of British politics.
The byelection, called after former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from the seat in September, was considered a two-horse race between the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, and the Green party leader, Polanski. Abdi-Wali received 12,292 votes, 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 8,928, 33% of the vote.
Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4% down from the 2024 general election.
In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us” in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.
“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me. I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden and this is Britain.”
Labour’s victory provides assurance for Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister, and reinforces polling that shows he has recovered some public support lost by Starmer, his predecessor in Downing Street.
However, the low turnout suggests Burnham still faces an uphill battle in urban areas, particularly in the capital where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.
Polanski’s loss caps a bruising week for his eco-populist party, which fell into turmoil after it voted on Sunday to adopt a policy declaring Zionism a form of racism, raising questions about his leadership.
Shortly after polls closed, Caroline Lucas refused to say whether Polanski should stand down. Speaking to BBC Newsnight, the former Green party leader said: “I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday,” when the motion was voted on. Polanski abstained and campaigned in the constituency instead.
Speaking to the BBC after the result came in, Polanski insisted he would remain in his post. “Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green party,” he said. “We’re a party of 220,000 members. I’ve taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion and we’re going to grow.”
The motion at the centre of the fallout said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism” and called for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. The head of the Jewish Greens condemned the motion and said she might leave the party, although it was supported by some Jewish Greens.
The motion passed in a vote by Green members at the party conference despite opposition from four of its five MPs. Even members who supported large parts of the motion were unhappy about its narrow conception of Zionism, which some fear could brand those in favour of the idea of a Jewish homeland, but not specifically the modern-day state of Israel, as racist.
Asked after the result whether he believed Zionism was racism, Polanski said he “grew up in a Zionist household” with the “idea that region was a land without a people and a people without a land”. But he said after educating himself he doesn’t “believe that’s true, and what we’re seeing is an ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people. I believe that’s clearly racist.”
Speaking to the Guardian after her win, Abdi-Wali said local people at the school gates found the Greens motion “divisive”, adding: “It just speaks to the larger divisive discourse that set off and I don’t want to engage in that kind of thing.”
On Labour’s stance on Palestine, she said: “The work Ed Miliband has been doing on Gaza, Palestine and Israel has resonated really well with local people. He’s been taking action and not just speaking.”
The Greens’ standing in the polls, and Polanski’s personal approval ratings, had fallen in recent months after a peak in popularity last summer, exemplified by the party’s seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February.
The Greens ran a strong ground game, dispatching thousands of members to knock on doors in the constituency, even before Polanski was selected as the party’s candidate. But the 8,928 votes cast for Polanski compares to the nearly 11,350 his party and Andrew Feinstein – a pro-Gaza figure on the left – received combined in the seat in 2024 suggests the Greens have not significantly expanded their base of voters in the constituency.
On the contest’s low turnout, Liam Conlon, Labour MP for Beckenham and Penge and the campaign leader for Abdi-Wali told the Guardian: “We performed better tonight than we did in May at the local elections here. That shows you the direction of travel.”
Midway into the race, George Galloway, running in “self-exile” outside the UK, put his name on the ballot in a move that many Green supporters said could pull votes away from Polanski. In the end, he received 314 votes.

When politicians write bad erotic fiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

This column has, once again, been overlooked for the Nobel Prize in Literature — although there’s still hope for the Peace Prize.
Asked by Declassified if it could justify this blatant discrimination, the Nobel committee hung up the phone.
Advertisement
Politicians can, of course, make great writers, and several have won Nobel’s literature prize, including Britain’s Winston Churchill in 1953, and Peru’s Mario Vargas Llosa in 2010. The latter — who ran for president in 1990 — won the prize “for his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual’s resistance, revolt, and defeat.” But has he ever referred to British Conservative grandee Jacob Rees-Mogg as a “Haunted Pencil”? No, he has not.
There are, however, a lot of very bad books written by politicians.
Former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson — very much the “Winston Churchill if you ordered him off Temu” — published a book in 2004 called “Seventy-Two Virgins — A Comedy of Errors” (the last four words also being the summary of his Covid policy) about a terrorist group targeting the U.S. president on a visit to London. It was described in the Guardian some 15 years later — after Johnson became prime minister — as ” sexist, racist, fundamentally undiplomatic.”
But the undisputed king when it comes to politicians letting out their inner writer is France.
In 2023, Bruno Le Maire, then the country’s economy and finance minister, published the novel “Fugue Américaine,” which drew instant criticism and mockery, mainly because of an explicit sex scene (unhappy French people were quick to point out that they had been screwed by the government for years).
Then there’s Marlène Schiappa, former government minister and writer of raunchy books under the pen name Marie Minelli, with titles such as “Osez les sexfriends,” “Sexe, mensonge et banlieues chaudes” and “Comment transformer votre mec en Brad Pitt en 30 jours.” When she was junior social affairs minister, Schiappa appeared on the cover of Playboy, although she was not naked in the magazine (great news for those who buy Playboy only for the articles).
Advertisement
Former President Valéry Giscard d’Estaing published several erotic novels, including “La Princesse et le Président,” which features sex scenes set in the presidential palace.
But perhaps the most intriguing of all is current President Emmanuel Macron, whose erotic novel about the early days of his romance with Brigitte has, alas, never seen the light of day. Perhaps he’s keeping it back for political gain and will promise to publish the steamy tome if the people of France promise to vote for a centrist candidate in April’s election.

Key takeaways from US Senate debate in Michigan between El-Sayed, Rogers
