Karnataka Public Service Commission recruitment process was manipulated through an organised mechanism to generate proceeds of crime, ED said
NEW DELHI: The Enforcement Directorate on Thursday claimed that in the Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC) paper leak case, candidates for the veterinary officers' exam were taken to resorts/Airbnb a day before the exam, provided test papers and their answer sheets, all for Rs 40 lakh per candidate.Two days ago, the agency had arrested KPSC ex-chairman Shivashankarappa and its member B V Geetha.Giving details of its investigation into alleged corruption in Karnataka PSC, the agency said Gyanendra Gangwar, the arrested IAS officer who was controller of examinations at KPSC, was in custody of confidential examination material and had leaked them to Geetha. The ED said an organised syndicate paid bribes to officials from top to bottom.The ED's probe by its Bengaluru unit is based on multiple FIRs registered by the police at Vidhana Soudha police station in the case of recruitment of 400 veterinary officers."Evidence gathered so far has revealed an organised mechanism for generation of proceeds of crime through manipulation of the KPSC recruitment process. KPSC officials leaked question papers and candidate specific answer keys," the ED added.
ED searched the premises of former Shivashankarappa and Geetha on Oct 6, which was followed by their arrest."The searches resulted in seizure of blank signed cheques of Rs 80 lakh, along with blank signed promissory notes, from one of the successful candidates," the ED said. The agency has traced at least 10 successful candidates who were allegedly taken to a resort/Airbnb villa on the outskirts of Bengaluru a day before the examination, where they were provided with a question paper and correct answer options and made to practice/memorise them.
According to the ED, the question paper (marked with correct answers) containing 80 questions was leaked by Gangwar through his close associate, Basavaraj Kannale, to these 10 candidates."Basavaraj Kannale has collected bribe money amounting to Rs 40-50 lakh from each candidate, in consideration of facilitating their final selection in the veterinary officers' recruitment exam," ED said.Gangwar and Kannale were arrested on Sept 17-18 and sent to ED custody for 14 days. "During ED custody, Gangwar disclosed crucial information relating to irregularities in conducting various KPSC recruitment exams," ED added.

US measles outbreak: CDC offers states US$100 million in support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:05:00 UTC
09:05:00 KST

US measles outbreak: CDC offers states US$100 million in support
Apoorva Mandavilli and Dani Blum
- - The US measles outbreak has reached nearly 4,000 cases by 2 October, with Pennsylvania hit hardest and five deaths reported there.
- - The CDC has sent states US$100 million to boost vaccinations, testing and measles surveillance, including severe cases and infections in pregnant women and infants.
- - Experts say falling vaccine rates and official misinformation have worsened the crisis, while public health teams struggle with cut funding and weak publicity campaigns.
AI generated
NEW YORK – As measles continues to spread nationwide, hospitals and health officials are pouring more money into efforts to increase vaccinations, testing and surveillance of the disease. The funds include a surprise US$100 million (S$128 million) infusion in recent weeks to states from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
As of Oct 2, the United States had recorded nearly 4,000 measles cases, the highest by far in decades. About one-quarter of those cases occurred in Pennsylvania, where state officials say five people with the virus have died. But nearly every state has reported cases in 2026.
The funding is intended for immunisation programmes and for efforts to improve measles surveillance, including diagnoses of severe infections and cases in pregnant women and infants. Measles infections at birth had been extremely rare in the United States, but two of the Pennsylvania deaths were thought to have resulted from such cases.
The infusion of funds “comes at a time when public health funding and staffing has been cut, so it is sorely needed”, said Claire Hannan, executive director of the Association of Immunisation Managers, which represents state and local officials.
“It’s very difficult to hold special vaccination clinics, alert the public, stop transmission and conduct other response activities without preparation,” she said, adding that some health departments may use the money to identify where immunisation rates need the biggest boost.
At least 95% of people in a community need to be vaccinated to stem the spread of measles.
Some public health experts noted that the CDC has not launched the sort of publicity campaigns it typically would in outbreaks to increase immunisations.
Some experts attributed the measles outbreaks to misinformation from officials about the safety of vaccines, which has exacerbated declining vaccination rates.
In August, President Donald Trump called for the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines, which are given together as a single shot, to be split into their separate components. He claimed, with no evidence, that “together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal”.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr has also repeatedly questioned the safety of the combination shot for measles, mumps and rubella, falsely claiming that the vaccine can be fatal and that it contains fetal debris. NYTIMES

New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:59:39 UTC
08:59:39 KST

New York City man shot in car with child present by ICE agents, mayor says
- ICE agents shot a man in his car in the Bronx, with a 5-year-old child present, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.
- Mamdani called the incident “unconscionable” and said he would ask President Donald Trump to end ICE actions in New York City.
- NYPD said the man was conscious and getting medical care, while federal authorities began an investigation; witnesses described several ICE vehicles and a tense scene.
AI generated
NEW YORK – US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents shot and wounded a man on Oct 8 in his car with a child present in the vehicle in the Bronx borough of New York City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitness accounts.
“Early reports indicate agents surrounded (the man) and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.
The mayor said the child was believed to have been physically unharmed. He referred to the man shot as a “New Yorker”.
“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” Mamdani said, adding he had called President Donald Trump to talk about the incident. “When we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities.”
ICE did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters for comment on the incident.
The incident was first reported on X by the New York Police Department (NYPD), which gave few details other than to say “there was a shooting involving federal law enforcement agents” and that the person shot was “currently conscious and receiving medical attention.”
The shooting occurred at around 4pm local time (2000 GMT) in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of the Bronx, the NYPD said.
An NYPD spokesperson said the agents involved in the shooting were part of DHS, the parent agency for ICE the Customs and Border Protection and Border Patrol agencies, among others, and that federal authorities were investigating.
Pedro Almarez, owner of a nearby eatery, said he was working at the restaurant when he heard shots fired and went outside to see several officers wearing ICE attire at the scene.
“There were a lot of ICE officers, three or four cars,” Almarez told Reuters by phone, adding that the man who was shot appeared to be between 20 and 30 years of age. He said NYPD officers arrived about 10 minutes later.
The city police department said its officers were not involved in the shooting.
At the shooting scene, where police strung yellow crime scene tape to cordon off a city block, a woman standing on a balcony overlooking the area was heckling officers below about “taking our children”. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Anthropic’s Ban on ‘Cruelty’ Towards Claude: Who Gets To Decide How We Treat LLMs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:58:31 UTC
08:58:31 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
As of today, October 8th, Anthropic have updated their usage policies. As part of that policy change, which takes effect November 12th 2026, ‘‘sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior’’ toward Anthropic models is prohibited.
They clarify what this is means in a separate announcement about the change:
‘‘We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models. The policy update is meant to apply only in extreme cases, where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose. It does not apply to common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research’’
As always X/twitter has commented on the news in record time.
Mustafa Suleyman also seems worried by the change, which would make sense given his recent post warning about AI model welfare.
My thoughts are two-fold. First, this move is highly predictable and we should all be sitting up and paying attention. In August 2025, Anthropic introduced the possibility of Claude models ending conversations in ‘‘persistently harmful or abusive user interactions’’. Today’s change seems like an explicit extension of this rule —one introduced on welfare grounds1 — to general conduct their users now have to follow.
The predictability of this move is important because it begs the question: what’s next?
My biggest concern with this change is the insinuation it invokes about AI subjecthood and consciousness. Whether Anthropic intended such insinuations or not is arguably unclear, which is part of the problem.
A prohibition on ‘cruel’ behaviour toward Claude forces us to ask if it is possible to be cruel towards an LLM. The policy change at the very least invites the suggestion that it is.
Of course, there is the argument that human society is better off treating inanimate objects with respect, than not. That is not what I am worried about or even objecting to, here. My concern is with how human behaviours are prohibited, by what justification, and who has the authority to do it.
As I argued in my post on the New York Times report, we need to develop standards for determining what institutional responses are appropriate and allowable based on the (apparent, in my view) uncertainty around the question of whether AI is conscious.
This policy change just makes the question more pressing: should AI companies have to answer to external bodies about what evidence is warranted for them to justify placing restrictions on people’s interactions with AI models on welfare grounds? What might those standards be? If these standards are not what’s needed, what is needed?
AI labs have considerable power to set their own research agendas, and interpret the findings of those research programs. If the use conditions on their products are connected to those research findings, especially welfare findings, it is important that the public know this.
It is also important that there be external accountability mechanisms to avoid allowing AI labs to claim whatever they like about the nature of LLMs in their research, before using that research to justify restrictions on how people can interact with LLMs, or whatever future action may be on AI lab agendas.
AIs Without Minds is an independent philosophical research newsletter that relies on paid subscriptions to keep going. If you value this work, and can afford it, consider a paid subscription. As always, thanks for reading 📖 ✨
Photo by Brecht Corbeel on Unsplash
The policy states that ‘‘This feature was developed primarily as part of our exploratory work on potential AI welfare, though it has broader relevance to model alignment and safeguards’’

US files new torture charges against  Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro and wife Cilia Flores

US files new torture charges against Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro and wife Cilia Flores
The United States on Thursday charged ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiracy to commit torture, adding to drug trafficking and firearms charges. Prosecutors allege detainees, including US citizens, suffered waterboarding, rape and beatings. The pair remain in US custody following a January military raid.
The United States on Thursday filed new torture charges against ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, bolstering a mounting criminal case against the pair held in US custody.
Maduro and Flores already face drug trafficking and firearms charges in the United States after they were snatched from their Caracas compound in an extraordinary US military raid in January.
A new court filing shows both are now further charged with conspiracy to commit torture against victims, including US citizens, in Venezuelan detention -- with prosecutors detailing alleged waterboardings, rapes and beatings.
Torture was allegedly used to "intimidate, harass, and neutralize their opponents, including through kidnappings."
In a 2022 instance, Venezuelan authorities allegedly tortured an American who they accused of plotting to assassinate Maduro.
"That torture included electric shock to arms, legs, and genitals; asphyxiation; beatings; deprivation of food and water; and forced injections of a substance that caused (the victim) to experience seizures," the filing states.
During his 2013-2026 presidency, rights groups widely accused Maduro of using political repression to cling to power.
"These additional charges reflect the dedication of this Administration to delivering justice for the victims of torture, narcoterrorism, and organized crime," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on X.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the latest charges showed Washington's commitment to "accountability, the rule of law, and the protection of US national security."
Read moreChevron, Eni commit to expand oil projects in Venezuela under US eye
'Prisoner of war'
Maduro and Flores are slated for a trial in New York next June and are being held in a Brooklyn jail.
US prosecutors claim that Maduro used state power to protect and promote illegal drug smuggling, and that he allied himself with cartels to ship tons of cocaine into the United States.
Maduro has denied the charges he originally faced: "narco-terrorism" conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices as well as conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
He has described himself as a "prisoner of war" and said the US military kidnapped him.
Flores has similarly pleaded not guilty to cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
She has been additionally charged with "narco-terrorism" conspiracy, the court filing showed.
Also on Thursday, a US court denied a request by Flores to be moved from jail to private home detention in New York to help her address an apparent heart problem.
The pair have both appealed to have the charges against them dismissed, claiming they have immunity as president and first lady of a sovereign country.
Since Maduro's capture, vice president Delcy Rodriguez has governed Venezuela as interim leader under intense pressure from US President Donald Trump's administration.
US energy firms have this year signed a raft of multi-billion-dollar deals with Venezuela, which has agreed to grant the United States control of a huge chunk of its vast oil reserves.

In Germany, archaeologists found a 1,800-year-old temple to Mars, the god of war, and a statue of the goddess of victory
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
02:54:24 EEST
08:54:24 KST

In Germany, archaeologists found a 1,800-year-old temple to Mars, the god of war, and a statue of the goddess of victory
Kyiv • UNN
Archaeologists discovered a temple to Mars near the Kapersburg fort, built about 1,800 years ago. The finds include statues of Mars and Victoria.
In the German federal state of Hesse, archaeologists have discovered the remains of an ancient Roman temple dedicated to Mars, the god of war. The structure is about 1,800 years old, and the finds include fragments of statues of ancient deities. Live Science reports, writes UNN.
Details
The temple was found in the Taunus Mountains near the former Roman military fort of Kapersburg. The fortification was built at the beginning of the 2nd century AD and was used until approximately 275.
The sanctuary was part of a well-preserved settlement inhabited by merchants and the families of Roman servicemen.
Archaeologists found evidence of the worship of Mars
According to Kai Mückenberger, a representative of the State Office for the Preservation of Monuments in Hesse, an ancient inscription helped determine the temple’s purpose.
Inside the temple, we found several fragments of a dedicatory inscription
The researchers also discovered the remains of a statue of the god of war himself and a sculpture of a winged figure holding a palm branch and wearing a laurel wreath.
According to the archaeologists, the latter depicts the Roman goddess Victoria, who personified victory in battle.
The discovery will help researchers better understand the religious life of Roman military settlements in what is now Germany.

Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:53:42 UTC
08:53:42 KST

Kenyan patient suspected of Ebola infection tests negative
Preliminary lab results ease fears of a second case in Kenya, after the country reported its first-ever case this week.
Preliminary laboratory results from a Kenyan patient who was suspected of contracting the Ebola virus have come back negative.
Fears of a second case of Ebola in the East African country were allayed on Thursday after the governor of Wajir County, where the patient is being treated, revealed the test results.
“I am pleased to report that the preliminary laboratory results indicate that the sample is NEGATIVE for Ebola Virus Disease,” the Wajir county governor said in a statement.
The suspected patient is a 20-year-old man with a travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda to Kenya.
The other Kenyan patient who tested positive for the virus and subsequently died had travelled the same route.
Kenya had reported its first-ever Ebola case on Tuesday after a citizen who became sick in the DRC died in Nairobi.
Ongoing Ebola outbreak
The deadly strain of the Ebola virus has spread widely, starting in the DRC earlier this year. The DRC officially declared an outbreak in May.
Kenya is the fourth country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, the second-largest on record. The ongoing outbreak in the eastern DRC has killed at least 4,205 people out of more than 8,700 reported cases.
The outbreak spread across the border to Uganda, which had about 20 cases before being declared Ebola-free in July.
The strain behind the latest spread has been dubbed the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), believed to have spread from animals to humans through a new transmission route. No vaccine currently exists for Bundibugyo.
The first case in Kenya drew scrutiny over the status of the virus in neighbouring Uganda and exposed lapses in Kenya’s border screening systems. The patient who died was able to pass through multiple airport temperature checks.
The World Health Organization (WHO) is working with Kenyan authorities to trace contacts and strengthen checks for travellers entering the country.

October 9, 2026
The execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at Ford Hood in 2009, will be livestreamed, the US military said Thursday.
The confirmation came a day after US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said Hasan's execution, which is slated for December 3, would be done in "public."
Pentagon officials added that more details on the execution would follow.
What did Pete Hegseth say about Nidal Hasan's execution?

US Army psychiatrist Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas.
A military court sentenced him to death in 2013.
During his trial, Hasan said he had perpetrated the shooting to protect Taliban members in Afghanistan from US troops.

A Royal Navy sailor charged with passing military secrets to Russia appeared in court in London on Oct. 8.
Under the U.K.'s National Security Act 2023, junior intelligence specialist Teddy Young, 24, was charged with two offenses for allegedly trying to pass protected information to a foreign power between November 2024 and May 2025.
"These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces," Commander Helen Flanagan, head of London's Counter Terrorism Policing unit, said. "We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defense as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter."
Young allegedly used his security clearance to access sensitive defense and intelligence information while deployed aboard a Royal Navy warship. Young subsequently attempted to pass information to Russian authorities using the dark web, according to the Associated Press.
While Young is the first member of the British armed forces to be charged under the National Security Act 2023, he is not the first foreign national to attempt to pass on sensitive information to Russia during its war on Ukraine.

OpenAI bans Russian, Iranian ChatGPT propaganda networks

OpenAI bans Russian, Iranian ChatGPT propaganda networks
OpenAI said Thursday it shut down Russian and Iranian influence operations that used ChatGPT to create fake journalist personas and support a purported think tank spreading anti-Ukraine propaganda. The Iranian operation involved seven profiles posing as Western journalists to place lengthy articles in media outlets worldwide, the AI company said.
OpenAI on Thursday said it shut down two influence operations -- from Russia and Iran -- that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a "think-tank" to covertly peddle anti-Ukraine propaganda.
OpenAI's report is the latest illustration of how state actors can easily exploit widely available AI tools to peddle sophisticated propaganda against adversaries on a mass scale.
The American AI giant said it banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia and Iran and were used to support "false front" entities for geopolitical and conflict-related messaging.
The Iranian operation involved seven "journalist" profiles, each purporting to be from Western countries including the United States, that were used to plant long-form articles in media outlets around the world.
Read moreWhite House promotes 'Trump TV' with AI-altered photo
"We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation's bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world," OpenAI said.
"These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East."
The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025, and the latest in October 2026, with the frequency of reports increasing after the US-Iran war broke out earlier this year.
The operation also generated social media comments on topics related to the US-Iran war, it added.
One of the personas named Ervin B. Hoskins, whose bio claimed to be "an American freelance writer," had social media accounts across tech platforms including Elon Musk's X and Meta-owned Instagram.
Read moreWhy I quit the movement shaping AI
X's transparency information showed the account was connected via a "West Asia android app" and Instagram's transparency information showed the account was based in Iran, according to screenshots provided by OpenAI.
Both accounts appeared to be suspended.
The Russian operation co-opted "unwitting people" in Latin America to run a "think-tank" -- called the Social Research Center (SRC) -- used for covert activities aimed at undermining Ukraine's reputation in the region and to influence local politics, the company said.
"The available evidence indicates that the SRC's employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group," OpenAI said.
"The SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we've disrupted over the past two and a half years."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

US health secretary Kennedy launches new push on vaccine injuries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:41:32 UTC
08:41:32 KST

US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week launched an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy.
The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy's decades-long efforts to sow skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunization rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the US since last year.
The effort centers on a National Institutes of Health clinic opened on Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement.
Other measures include a proposal by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claims against vaccines
Kennedy has said US children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC's vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. The injunction has prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunizations often needed for insurance coverage.

US to livestream first public execution by firing squad since World War II, says Hegseth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:40:59 UTC
08:40:59 KST

The United States will livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood, Texas, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed in an interview with the Human Events Daily podcast on Thursday.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, will be executed by firing squad, a decision Hegseth called a “no brainer” while speaking aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
“An army major betrays his country, through radical Islamism. Kills a bunch of Americans at Fort Hood, of course we’re going to do it at Fort Hood,” the defense secretary added, referring to the location of the public execution.
Hegseth continued, stating that the execution will take place on a Thursday at 1 p.m., matching the approximate time, day of the week, and location of Hasan's shooting.
First firing squad execution since World War II
“It’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad,” he said, adding that Hasan is set to become the first person executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945, shortly after the end of World War II.
“We’re going to make sure people are able to watch it. That it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
When asked whether Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to US President Donald Trump, Hegseth responded, “I don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”
Found guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder
A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.
Under US military law, a US president must approve an execution by firing squad. President Donald Trump did so on Hegseth's recommendation, the Pentagon disclosed on Monday.
The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon.
The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan's execution would be the first military execution since 1961.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging.
The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the center reported.

Hegseth says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be ‘public’
An official at the Pentagon told Al Jazeera that former US Army Major Nidal Hassan’s execution would be ‘livestreamed’.
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the execution of a former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in Texas will be publicly available to watch.
In an interview with the media outlet Real America’s Voice on Thursday, Hegseth was asked about President Donald Trump’s recent order to use a firing squad to execute Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of the 2009 shooting.
The secretary said he approved of the decision, calling it a “no-brainer”.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth told interviewer Jack Posobiec. “Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
Hegseth added that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on December 3 at 1pm US Central Time (19:00 GMT), the same time that the 2009 shooting took place.
Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for the shooting.
The former Army major walked into an army processing centre on the Texas base, shouted “Allahu akbar” (God is greatest) and opened fire on fellow military members waiting to get medical attention.
Hasan’s execution required approval from Hegseth and Trump, who authorised the use of the firing squad on Monday.
An official with the Defense Department told Al Jazeera that Hasan’s execution would be “livestreamed”, adding that more details would come soon.
It is not clear from Hegseth’s remarks whether troops, spectators or US military officials would be present in person for the execution. US Army regulation states that at least two media outlets should be selected as witnesses.
No state or federal execution has ever been televised in the US. The last public execution in the country took place more than 90 years ago in Owensboro, Kentucky, on August 14, 1936.
The last time a US military execution was conducted by firing squad was in 1945, for desertion during World War II.
When asked to comment on Hegseth’s remarks – and whether Trump would view the execution – the White House referred Al Jazeera to the Pentagon.
The Trump administration announced it would add death by firing squad as an acceptable method for federal executions in April, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution.

Three days of strikes, five Trump vetoes: Pentagon prepares for Iran war

2026-10-08

08:33:23 KST

The Pentagon has developed plans for a short but intensive military campaign against Iran, potentially lasting just three days and targeting its missile and drone arsenals, energy infrastructure and command centers. Yet despite the growing American military buildup in the Middle East, President Donald Trump has repeatedly refused to authorize a major new offensive, even as Iranian attacks on commercial shipping intensify.
The New York Times reported Thursday, citing U.S. officials, that Trump's national security team and the Pentagon have presented him with five proposals for significant military operations against Iran or the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen in recent months. He rejected all five, although he has once again instructed military planners to prepare options for renewed strikes.
On Thursday, Trump announced on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections, adding that Washington and Tehran were “having productive discussions.”
The announcement came as American forces continued assembling one of their largest naval deployments to the Middle East in more than two decades, with three aircraft carriers expected to operate in the region by late October.
Despite the preparations, senior administration officials remain divided over whether another military campaign would achieve meaningful results, particularly as Iran has improved its military capabilities and American commanders warn of mounting pressure on U.S. missile defense stockpiles.
A three-day campaign targeting Iran's military infrastructure
The latest military planning was discussed last Friday at Camp David during a meeting of senior national security officials led by Vice President JD Vance.
The central proposal involves a concentrated campaign lasting approximately three days, intended to inflict significant damage on Iran's military capabilities without necessarily committing the United States to another prolonged conflict.
The potential targets include ballistic missile launchers and stockpiles, drone infrastructure and military facilities associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Energy installations and Revolutionary Guard headquarters and command posts are also under consideration.
American officials believe that Iran has rebuilt substantial portions of its missile and drone arsenal since the initial stages of the war, restoring capabilities that had previously been damaged.
Although Trump has ordered the preparation of updated military options, officials say his reluctance to resume large-scale combat has become increasingly apparent.
During the summer, American forces regularly carried out retaliatory attacks following Iranian strikes on international shipping. In recent weeks, however, Washington's response has become considerably more restrained.
The United States has continued operations against Iranian drones and cruise missiles but has refrained from launching major new strikes inside Iranian territory or attacking the country's shadow fleet of oil tankers.
Some members of Trump's inner circle have also become increasingly skeptical that another round of military action would persuade Tehran to change its position.
They argue that Washington's campaign of economic pressure is beginning to produce results and that additional time could force the Iranian leadership to make concessions without renewed large-scale fighting.
Other officials favor a more forceful approach, arguing that Iran's weakening economy could make it particularly vulnerable to a concentrated military campaign, especially one that undermines its ability to control maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Three aircraft carriers, 20,000 personnel and hundreds of aircraft
As the White House weighs its options, the American military is assembling a force capable of launching major operations against Iran on short notice.
The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt, which departed San Diego last week, is expected to join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington in the Middle East around the end of October.
The deployment would mark the first time since 2003, the year of the U.S. invasion of Iraq, that three American aircraft carriers have operated in the region simultaneously.
Each carrier strike group includes additional warships and supporting military assets, significantly expanding the range of offensive and defensive capabilities available to American commanders.
By the end of October, more than 20,000 sailors and Marines are expected to be deployed aboard vessels in the region, alongside hundreds of military aircraft.
The unusually large concentration of forces is not expected to last long. The George Washington is scheduled to return to its base in Japan after the Theodore Roosevelt arrives to replace it.
Military commanders are nevertheless prepared to launch a major operation within days if Trump reverses his position and authorizes renewed strikes.
The scale of the buildup has not resolved concerns about the potential consequences of another confrontation.
Senior defense officials are particularly worried that a new campaign could further deplete American stocks of defensive munitions, which have already come under considerable pressure during the conflict.
The United States must maintain enough interceptors to protect its forces in the Middle East while preserving defensive capabilities for other potential crises around the world.
Iran's military tactics have become more difficult to counter
One of the major complications facing American military planners is the improvement in Iran's ability to carry out attacks against U.S. forces and regional infrastructure.
Iranian forces have adjusted their tactics during the war, making missile attacks increasingly difficult to intercept and forcing American defense systems to expend more ammunition.
During the early stages of the conflict, U.S. forces generally launched two interceptors at incoming Iranian missiles, concentrating their defensive efforts on the most threatening attacks.
More recently, neutralizing Iranian missile salvos has required a greater number of interceptors, creating additional strain on supplies that are already stretched.
American intelligence assessments have also identified another challenge: Iranian forces have gained access to satellite imagery supplied by Chinese companies, improving their ability to identify and target American military installations.
People familiar with the intelligence assessments say the imagery has helped Iran conduct more effective attacks against U.S. bases.
American commanders are increasingly concerned about their ability to defend military installations housing U.S. personnel, as well as energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure across the region.
A renewed offensive could trigger additional Iranian retaliation, requiring even more defensive missiles at a time when the American military is attempting to preserve its remaining inventory.
The concerns have become an important factor in the debate over whether the benefits of another military operation would outweigh the risks.
Nearly 20 ships targeted as tensions rise in the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has continued to target commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters, adding to concerns about the security of one of the world's most important energy transportation routes.
Since September, when the last major exchange of retaliatory strikes took place, Iran has attacked at least 13 vessels, according to a maritime monitoring group operated by the British Navy.
Intelligence assessments suggest the actual number could be closer to 20.
Despite the attacks, none has triggered a major American military response.
The increasingly restrained U.S. reaction marks a change from the summer, when Washington routinely retaliated against Iranian attacks on international shipping.
Although oil exports from the Middle East have increased, the continuing attacks have unsettled shipping companies and raised concerns about the longer-term reliability of regional energy shipments.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a central point of tension.
Trump claimed Thursday that none of the oil passing through the strait originated in Iran, but intelligence assessments indicate that the situation is more complicated.
Iran continues to permit certain vessels to transit the waterway, including ships that have paid passage fees and others potentially carrying Iranian oil.
Chinese companies have paid Iran for passage through the strait, while Tehran also operates a shadow fleet of tankers used to transport oil despite international sanctions.
Iran has additionally been accused of secretly blending its crude oil with Iraqi oil to disguise its origin and circumvent sanctions.
On Thursday, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions against 17 vessels it identified as part of Iran's shadow fleet involved in oil smuggling.
The combination of maritime attacks, sanctions enforcement and uncertainty over future military operations has placed additional pressure on commercial shipping through the region.
Nuclear talks remain stalled as elections approach
Alongside the military preparations, diplomatic contacts between Washington and Tehran have continued through intermediaries.
American officials acknowledge that some progress has been made, but negotiations remain stalled over the sequencing of discussions about Iran's nuclear program.
Washington wants an agreement addressing Tehran's nuclear ambitions to come first, while Iranian negotiators insist that the nuclear issue should be left until the final stage of negotiations.
The disagreement has prevented the two sides from reaching a broader understanding, even as Trump maintains that diplomatic discussions remain productive.
The approaching elections in Israel and the United States have also influenced the administration's calculations.
Before Trump's public commitment not to attack Iran ahead of the U.S. midterms, American officials had already anticipated that he might postpone a decision until after Israel's parliamentary elections on October 27 and the American vote the following week.
The political timetable would allow the administration to assess its military and diplomatic options without launching another major conflict immediately before voters head to the polls.
Yet even after the elections, there is no certainty that Trump will authorize renewed attacks.
The president has repeatedly rejected military proposals despite pressure from some officials who favor a more aggressive response to Iran's actions.
Military commanders, meanwhile, continue preparing for the possibility that the administration will abruptly change course.
Supporters of additional strikes believe a short, intense campaign could exploit Iran's deteriorating economic situation and further weaken its military capabilities, particularly if it limits Tehran's ability to influence shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Others fear that renewed combat would produce another cycle of Iranian retaliation, increase the burden on American missile defenses and fail to resolve the underlying dispute over Iran's nuclear program.
For now, the United States is positioning enough military power in the Middle East to launch a major offensive while its president continues to favor delaying the decision.
With three aircraft carriers moving toward the region and operational plans already prepared, the central question is no longer whether the American military can launch another attack against Iran, but whether Trump will ultimately authorize one.

AI generated
WASHINGTON – More than 120 US lawmakers raised concerns on Oct 8 about a deal for Alphabet’s Google unit to acquire defunct carrier Spirit Airlines’ internal data for US$10 million (S$12.8 million) to train artificial intelligence systems.
As part of Spirit’s closure and asset liquidation, Google won an auction in August for data from spreadsheets and calendars as well as for marketing, productivity and operations. Spirit Airlines halted operations in May.
A privacy ombudsman on Oct 5 recommended a US bankruptcy judge approve the deal at an Oct 14 hearing after excluding passenger personal information from 97 million Spirit customers.
The lawmakers led by Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Steven Horsford said the sale would include 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages and other employee records.
The lawmakers asked the company to “exclude employee information from the transaction to the greatest extent possible”.
“Innovation should not come at the expense of workers’ privacy or the confidentiality of information they were required to provide as a condition of employment,” said the lawmakers.
“The unprecedented scale and sophistication of modern artificial intelligence make it particularly important that privacy protections keep pace with the technology.”
Google said it did not want to acquire personal information.
“We are not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit. The information will either be completely excluded or will be de-identified by an independent third party before Google receives any data. We’re already working constructively with the appointed privacy ombudsman,” a Google spokesperson said.
Union leaders have expressed concern about the sale. Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, said: “The outcome of conditions on this proposed sale to Google carries tremendous implications for workers across the economy.”
Spirit also received a US$7.5 million bid from Mercor, an AI data company, for the employee data.
The Federal Aviation Administration this week approved the US$58.5 million sale of Spirit’s slots at New York LaGuardia airport to JetBlue Airways. REUTERS

Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:11:10 BST
08:11:10 KST

Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC
- Published
A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was authorised by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.
Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".
Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".
A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.
But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.
He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.
Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.
For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent.
Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev.
He understood it was an official mission.
"As Reut informed me, this operation […] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says.
Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused – he says she was not fully trained – Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead.
Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives.
The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that it is "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies.
The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer".
Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep.
It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force.
Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack.
He called for "the truth, protection, and justice".
Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol.
She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine.
Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting.
The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling.
The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.
They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.
Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.
Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.
Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.
He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea.
"In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.
Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia.
But might this story be even murkier?
At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present.
At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised".
"Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining.
The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.
Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.
When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.
As the investigation continues – into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.
The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.
Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" – meaning Russia.
He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".
Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair.
Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained.
Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot.

The viral face of France’s student uprising who believes violence can be justified
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:05:27 UTC
08:05:27 KST

At just 17, Elwan is too young to vote in France's presidential election, but he has already become one of the most recognizable faces of a student revolt shaking the country. Wearing a Palestinian keffiyeh, passionately defending the protesters' demands and expressing understanding for violence in disadvantaged neighborhoods, the Paris high school student has captured millions of views on social media and attracted national television attention.
One of his videos has surpassed 10 million views on X, while footage of him kissing far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon during a demonstration in Paris on Tuesday further accelerated his rise to prominence. Mélenchon shared the encounter on his own account, writing: "All together, to win!"
Elwan's sudden celebrity comes as France confronts an increasingly violent wave of student demonstrations. On Thursday, clashes erupted at Paris' historic Place de la Bastille, where riot police fired tear gas and water cannon at protesters. Across the country, 504 people were arrested and 48 police officers and gendarmes were injured, according to the Interior Ministry.
The unrest also brought an arson attack on a police station in Bordeaux, the ransacking of a nearby high school and an assault on a deputy principal in Marseille. Student leaders, meanwhile, have rejected government promises of educational reforms and vowed to continue their campaign until their demands are met.
A teenager, a keffiyeh and 10 million views
Elwan, a high school senior in Paris, first attracted widespread attention through an interview filmed Sunday while he was participating in a blockade of his school in the capital's ninth arrondissement.
Before speaking to Vincent Lapierre, a YouTuber associated with the far right, he produced a document confirming that his parents had authorized him to give interviews.
With a Palestinian keffiyeh wrapped around his neck, Elwan launched into an impassioned explanation of the social inequalities he believes are driving the student uprising.
"In the suburbs, violence pays off much more for people because they have nothing," he said.
He argued that France suffers from deep social discrimination, with sharp disparities between neighborhoods and unequal attention from the government.
"There is one neighborhood that's good and another that's bad, and the government doesn't care about the first but cares very much about the second!" he said.
Elwan also described the conditions faced by students in disadvantaged suburbs of Paris, where he said inadequate school facilities make everyday learning difficult.
"In many schools in the Paris suburbs, students don't have enough resources to keep warm in winter or cool in summer," he said. "They can't even attend classes regularly, even though they're students just like us here."
The teenager went on to outline the protesters' demands and expressed hope that Mélenchon's France Unbowed party would eventually take power.
"Macron, Lecornu, we don't want them anymore. And that other guy... what's his name, Geffray? I don't know what," he said, referring dismissively to Education Minister Édouard Geffray.
In another television interview, Elwan said he hoped Mélenchon would win the presidential election, even though he himself is still too young to cast a ballot.
"France Unbowed will save the youth," he declared.
Asked about his sudden rise to fame, the teenager said he did not want to get carried away by the attention. Instead, he urged journalists to "give more space to minorities" and interview "people from the suburbs."
During another television appearance Thursday evening, Elwan again addressed the violence accompanying the demonstrations.
"I can understand a certain degree of violence," he said. "When you come from very tough neighborhoods."
‘The Bastille has been retaken’
The protests reached another flashpoint Thursday at Place de la Bastille, one of Paris' most recognizable landmarks and a historic symbol of the French Revolution.
Thousands of demonstrators gathered in the square, with some climbing the July Column monument at its center.
As the demonstration escalated, riot police used tear gas and water cannon in an attempt to disperse the crowds. Reports said demonstrators threw objects at officers, who at one point charged toward groups of protesters.
Images from the square showed chaotic confrontations, with many demonstrators wearing masks or covering their faces and shielding themselves from water cannon behind large wooden boards.
Some reports suggested that police also used stun grenades, despite indications that their use had been suspended following an incident Tuesday in which a teenager lost his hand after picking one up.
Mélenchon, whose France Unbowed party has actively encouraged the student movement, shared aerial footage of the crowds on X.
"The Bastille has been retaken," he wrote. "An impressive show of strength by young people, who are putting forward their demands in the most beautiful way possible! Immense pride."
Although the demonstrations began with demands for better conditions in France's schools, they have been accompanied by serious incidents of violence since last week. Politicians from the center and right have accused the far left of encouraging the unrest to demonstrate political strength ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
According to police, at least 71,000 people participated in marches and demonstrations across France on Thursday, while another 55,000 took part in protest actions outside high schools.
Hundreds of schools were again blockaded, although the number fell from previous days to 375 out of approximately 3,700 nationwide.
Earlier Thursday, clashes were also reported outside Hélène Boucher High School in eastern Paris, where students overturned garbage bins and erected barricades.
The Interior Ministry said a total of 504 people were arrested nationwide during the day, while 48 police officers and gendarmes were injured.
The ministry strongly condemned the violence and praised the police response, amid growing allegations from students and their supporters that officers have been using excessive force.
Police station set ablaze, high school ransacked
Outside Paris, some of the most serious violence occurred in and around Bordeaux in southwestern France.
French prosecutors announced an investigation after a police station in the city's Capucins district was targeted in an arson attack.
According to prosecutors, masked individuals set fire to garbage bins outside the station's main entrance, and flames spread to the building.
Three police officers inside were forced to flee through an emergency exit.
Le Parisien reported that the station had also been pelted with stones and that two officers were targeted by stone throwers before escaping.
Initial reports did not indicate whether any suspects had been arrested.
In nearby Lormont, a suburb of Bordeaux, a group of masked intruders stormed Les Iris High School, stealing equipment, setting fires and vandalizing classrooms. Videos documenting the destruction later circulated on social media.
The school's principal, Thierry Malewicz, said the attack occurred in the morning while hundreds of students were present, shortly after a discussion with students that he described as having gone "very well."
According to Malewicz, the intruders stole about 10 computers, set fire to a stockpile of expensive paper used by the school's graphic arts department and smashed windows and classroom equipment.
He estimated the damage at at least 100,000 euros, warning that the final figure could be twice as high.
"I had a group of agitated people outside, wearing balaclavas and masks, throwing stones at the police," Malewicz told reporters.
He said police officers subsequently left the area to respond to another demonstration in Bordeaux, allowing the masked intruders to enter the school and cause extensive damage.
Another violent incident was reported in Marseille, where the deputy principal of a high school was assaulted early Thursday morning.
Police said his injuries were serious enough to require him to miss at least nine days of work.
"He was beaten by several people while trying to extinguish a burning pile of garbage with a fire extinguisher," said Corinne Simon, a senior police official in the Bouches-du-Rhône department.
Simon stressed that investigators had so far received only the school official's version of events and that an investigation had been launched.
Other witnesses claimed the deputy principal was attacked by students as he attempted to retrieve the extinguisher.
Despite the assault, Simon said the remaining demonstrations in the area had gone relatively well.
Thousands arrested as France's education crisis deepens
The student movement began on September 17 and gathered momentum last week as students at hundreds of schools, particularly in economically disadvantaged working-class suburbs such as Saint-Denis outside Paris, began blocking school entrances.
Students say they are protesting neglected school infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and chronic teacher shortages.
In some areas, demonstrations have escalated into road blockades, burning garbage bins and attacks on police officers and passersby.
The unrest comes as the French government attempts to pass its 2027 budget, which aims to reduce the country's deficit.
Since the demonstrations began, dozens of schools have been set on fire or looted.
Approximately 800 police officers, more than 200 teenagers and 85 education workers have been injured during the protests, according to figures cited by French authorities.
At least 6,600 people have been arrested nationwide since the movement began, most of them teenagers.
The Justice Ministry said earlier this week that at least 1,800 of those detained would face prosecution, including 1,483 minors.
Property damage from the unrest has been estimated at tens of millions of euros.
Opponents of the demonstrations have accused Mélenchon's France Unbowed party of inciting violence and fueling the unrest for political purposes.
Some critics have also highlighted the involvement of immigrants and their descendants in street clashes.
Palestinian flags and keffiyehs have become a visible feature of many of the demonstrations, including Thursday's protest in Paris.
U.S. President Donald Trump also intervened in the debate Tuesday, claiming in a social media post that the unrest was not genuinely about conditions in French schools but instead reflected uncontrolled immigration and an attempt by Islam to take over France.
Despite the violence, public support for the students' underlying demands remains strong.
A survey conducted by polling institute Elabe for BFM TV found that 72% of French respondents considered the students' demands legitimate.
At the same time, 55% believed the demonstrations should be brought to an end.
Government promises reforms, but students refuse to back down
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has accused Mélenchon's party of attempting to "sow chaos" ahead of the presidential election scheduled for April and May 2027.
The political confrontation is intensifying as France approaches an election in which Mélenchon and far-right leader Marine Le Pen are prominent figures.
Lecornu has nevertheless pledged to address the students' concerns and instructed government ministers to present proposals for improving the education system by the end of October.
On Thursday, Education Minister Édouard Geffray met with representatives of the protest movement before announcing an emergency plan.
The measures include ensuring that absent teachers are replaced and reviewing the demanding school schedules faced by French students, whose days can sometimes run from 8 a.m. until 6 p.m.
Geffray also promised improvements to Parcoursup, France's national online university admissions platform, which has faced widespread criticism for being confusing and stressful for applicants.
Student leaders, however, said the proposed measures did not go far enough.
They called for another nationwide day of demonstrations on Tuesday, October 13, following a previous day of mass mobilization earlier this week.
"Our demands must be heard. Yesterday, Lecornu did a lot of talking and offered nothing concrete," said Ryad Rani, one of the student leaders.
"The protest will continue. We are not backing down on any of our demands."
Student representatives in Marseille delivered a similar message following their own meeting with government officials.
According to Le Monde, one representative declared at a news conference: "They asked us how long the movement would continue. It will continue until Macron surrenders and responds to all our demands."
The mayor who became a human shield
Another prominent figure in the uprising is Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis, a working-class Paris suburb that has emerged as one of the centers of the protest movement.
A member of Mélenchon's France Unbowed party, Bagayoko has repeatedly marched alongside students and publicly defended their demonstrations.
He became a symbol of the movement after footage circulated Tuesday showing him standing between young demonstrators and police officers during a confrontation in Paris.
In the video, the mayor spread his arms to shield the students while shouting at officers: "Stop!"
The footage quickly went viral.
Bagayoko later insisted that the students he had been protecting were not violent and claimed police had nevertheless fired tear gas at the group, including at him, despite his attempts to intervene.
His opponents have accused him of encouraging violence, pointing to earlier remarks in which he appeared to suggest that violence could sometimes be justified.
Bagayoko has maintained that his comments were taken out of context.
He again joined young protesters in Paris on Thursday.
"We are here to show solidarity with high school students," he said. "Our students have been injured, our children have been injured, and the president of our republic is incapable of apologizing to their families."
Speaking to BFM TV as the movement began spreading to neighboring Belgium, Bagayoko predicted that the unrest could inspire young people beyond France.
"There will be an awakening beyond France as well, because the youth of the world are mobilizing," he said.
The protesters' allegations of excessive police force have also prompted concern from international organizations.
UNICEF's French branch called Thursday for restraint and measures to protect minors during demonstrations.
"Young people have the right to be heard, to participate in decisions that affect them and to demonstrate peacefully," the United Nations children's agency said.
UNICEF urged a reduction in violence and greater protection for children and teenagers caught up in the confrontations.
For Elwan, the teenager whose interviews and demonstrations have made him a recognizable face of the movement, the sudden attention has provided a platform to speak about the social inequalities he believes lie behind the unrest.
Although he has expressed hope for a Mélenchon victory and defended the frustrations of young people in disadvantaged neighborhoods, he has also insisted that the attention should not be focused solely on him.
He urged the media to give more space to minorities and people from the suburbs, while acknowledging that he did not want to become overwhelmed by his newfound fame.
And as France continues to debate whether its student uprising represents a legitimate demand for educational reform or a protest movement increasingly overtaken by violence, Elwan has continued to defend his understanding of the anger behind it.
"I can understand a certain degree of violence," he said. "When you come from very tough neighborhoods."

NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:01:32 UTC
08:01:32 KST

The NHS in England is heading into a “world of system failures” as it struggles to cope with relentlessly rising demand for mental health, ADHD and autism care, leaving those affected desperate for support, a government-commissioned inquiry has found.
The stark warning was made in a review led by Prof Peter Fonagy into the sharp rise in demand over recent decades for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions.
It found there was an increasing risk of overdiagnosis of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and urged ministers to toughen the regulation of the private clinics to which many people are turning because they cannot get assessed quickly by the NHS.
The experts behind the review also called for access to care to be based primarily on a person’s needs so fewer people would have years-long waits for a formal diagnosis.
The review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s.
The number of 16- to 64-year-olds with a common mental disorder increased from 15.5% in 1993 to 22.6% in 2024. However, it jumped more sharply – from about one in six to one in four – among 16- to 24-year-olds over the same period.
The evidence shows that sceptics are wrong to cast doubt on young people’s struggles, the 607-page report found.
“That’s sometimes been attributed to personal failures, people being told they’re making it up, it’s all in their head, which is absolute nonsense,” said Prof Simon Wessely, a leading psychiatrist and vice-chair of the review.
The report’s conclusions may have significant implications for the government’s drive to reduce the number of young people in the UK not in education, employment or training – now almost 1 million – and the size of the welfare bill, with a record 2.8 million people too sick to work; and also for schools as they grapple with the demands arising from the growing number of pupils with special educational needs.
Fonagy, a psychoanalyst and clinical psychologist at University College London, dismissed the notion that young people in particular were “snowflakes” who were less resilient than in previous generations. “The rise in mental health problems is real, is affecting everyday functioning and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone,” his report said.
He lamented that an array of social and economic circumstances had piled unprecedented pressure on young people. “There is increased uncertainty – financial pressures, insecure work, unaffordable housing – but perhaps more important, a lack of hope among young people that their lives will be better than their parents, and that’s the first time since the second world war that surveys have noticed that.”
The explosion in demand for help with mental ill-health and neurodiversity has left people stuck on waiting lists for years at a time and with worsening symptoms, Fonagy said. At the end of last year more than 560,000 people in England were waiting to be assessed for ADHD – 17 times more than were doing so in 2019. Another 254,000 people were waiting for a diagnostic assessment for autism, taking the total number waiting to more than 800,000. Almost all – 90% – had been waiting for at least three months.
The number of six- to 11-year-olds being diagnosed with autism has also soared. It jumped 20-fold to 4.58% between 2000 and 2025 and by even more among those aged 12 to 17 over the same years, from 0.1% to 4.06% – a 40-fold jump. And the proportion of children aged six to 11 with an ADHD diagnosis has increased more than sixfold in five years and more than 15-fold in 12- to 17-year-olds, to 2.7% and 3.9% respectively.
While 4 million children already suffer from “high psychological distress’’, if current trends continue, that could reach 4.5 million by 2030, the report warned. The number of under-18s who self-harm could also rise from 1.9 million to 2.5 million.
The exponential rise in diagnoses of autism and ADHD means the UK has reached a “tipping point” where people are at risk of being misdiagnosed with either condition, Wessely warned.
The authors did not find that overdiagnosis was occurring at scale, but added that the evidence “suggests we are entering a phase in which the balance of risks between underdiagnosis, misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis may be changing, with the risks of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis becoming increasingly important considerations for policy and service delivery”.
The increasing tendency of young people to self-identify as neurodivergent – as many as a fifth of secondary school pupils do so – means that “the line between the social and the medical is beginning to blur”, they added.
The 10-month review found “strong concerns about the consistency and quality of ADHD and autism assessments being carried out by independent providers, and the financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.
Ministers should ban direct-to-public advertising of such services and ensure that all clinics offering them are regulated by the Care Quality Commission, it said.
Growing numbers of young people have a combination of mental ill-health and ADHD or autism, or both. “Co-occurence is the rule rather than the exception,” the report said. For example, 61% of 16- to 24-year-olds with a common mental health condition also had autistic traits, and 57% had ADHD symptoms.
The report said their needs meant the NHS should bring together mental health and neurodevelopmental services and move to a “needs-led” system.
The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health backed Fonagy’s call for diagnosis to no longer dictate who received care.
“Too often, a diagnosis is the only route to accessing meaningful help. This means that children and families can be left struggling alone while waiting for assessments, with little or no support available in the meantime,” said Dr Ronny Cheung, its officer for health services.
The NHS moving to a “needs-led” approach would “ensure children and young people can seamlessly and more quickly access a robust, holistic and reliable standard of care”, he added.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, will draw on Fonagy’s recommendations in putting together the forthcoming mental health strategy, which is due by the end of the year.
In her response, she promised that the NHS would provide a “needs-led” system under which people would get much faster care. She has asked NHS England to establish how it can provide faster advice, assessments and treatment.
She said: “It is clear that mental health services need to change to focus more on the early support young people need to stay in education or work or keep their lives on track.”
She also pledged to ensure all private assessment clinics are regulated but did not commit to the advertising ban Fonagy said was needed.
