New Ofsted inspection regime damaging teachers, survey says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:01:31 UTC
08:01:31 KST

School inspections in England continue to damage the mental wellbeing of teachers and senior leaders, according to a survey commissioned by Ofsted that casts doubt on efforts to reduce the stress caused by inspectors’ visits.
The independent survey of school leaders who had undergone the revised inspections since last year found that 88% said it had “negatively affected” the mental wellbeing of school staff, including 29% who said it affected them “a lot”.
School leaders called the results a “damning indictment” of Ofsted’s attempts to reform after a coroner’s finding in 2023 that an Ofsted inspection contributed to the mental health deterioration and death of headteacher Ruth Perry.
The Guardian reported last week that education secretary Lucy Powell wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” after hearing complaints that the new format was stressful and damaging to teachers’ mental health.
Martyn Oliver, Ofsted’s chief inspector, said: “The data published today shows that we are on the right track. We are inspecting first and foremost in the interests of children and maintaining high standards, while at the same time improving the experience for the hard-working professionals in our nurseries, schools and colleges.
“I know that workload and wellbeing in education continue to be challenging, and I don’t take that lightly. We will keep listening to feedback from professionals and parents alike as we continue to improve what we do.”
But Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “It is extremely serious that the health of so many educators is being undermined and we do not understand how [Ofsted’s] chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver can then say the system is on the right track. This is clearly not the case.
“The feedback that we receive from our members shows a devastating toll on wellbeing and several have told us they will leave the profession before undergoing another Ofsted inspection. These are highly experienced and resilient professionals who will be lost to the education system.”
Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the wellbeing and workload findings “should stop everyone in their tracks”. He urged Ofsted to release the full survey data rather than a summary.
“Ofsted is once again trying to put a positive spin on a truly terrible situation, showing the profession why it cannot be trusted,” he said.
“The evidence is clear that the framework is still creating unacceptable levels of pressure, workload and stress. It is a damning indictment – certainly not a vindication.”
Fewer than one in four schools agreed to be surveyed after their inspections, leading the authors, IFF Research, to note that its findings had limitations.
Ofsted highlighted the results from all categories, including childminders and further education providers, showing that six out of 10 respondents said their inspection would help them improve.
More than three-quarters of those inspected under the new approach said it had been conducted respectfully, collaboratively and empathetically, while a similar proportion said the inspections “successfully identified” their best elements.
But Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the National Education Union, described the overall results as “rose-tinted,” and added: “Lucy Powell has indicated a readiness to review.
“We want to see a new system that is more supportive, but also fair and effective. It is what the profession is crying out for.”

Michael Robotham's latest novel sat in his bottom drawer for 35 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Michael Robotham's latest novel, Tell Me Something True, is his most autobiographical yet
Michael Robotham was a 22-year-old journalist working for a Sydney newspaper when he began writing his first novel in the early 1980s.
"[It] was going to be my great Australian novel … [and] win me every prize in the world," Robotham tells ABC Arts.
He finished it six years later, when he was living in London. It came very close to being published.
Set in a small country town based on his hometown of Gundagai in the Riverina region of NSW, the novel had the working title Blessed Are the Meek.
"I missed out by a single vote in an acquisitions meeting for a major publisher," Robotham says.
"I was told that it was really the setting … They just felt it was a little bit too hard for them to market, because this was obviously well before Jane Harper and Liane Moriarty and few Australian-set books had ever done well internationally."
He consigned the manuscript to his bottom drawer and spent the next decade working as a journalist and then as a ghostwriter.
Robotham returned to Australia in the 90s, but when he eventually began writing a new novel he recalled the advice he'd been given and set it in the UK.
That book, The Suspect — the first instalment of what would become the popular Joe O'Loughlin series — triggered a bidding war at the London Book Fair before it was published in 2004. It has since sold more than 1 million copies worldwide and was adapted for television in 2022.
Now, two decades later, Robotham has finally set a book in Australia.
Tell Me Something True, Robotham's 20th novel, is a "seriously rewritten and re-imagined" version of that first manuscript.
"All the story and the characters remain the same, but it's been in the bottom drawer since the 1980s," he says.
A tale of brotherhood
Robotham wrote the first version of Tell Me Something True on a Remington typewriter, so the first step of the rewriting process was transferring it to a computer.
When he cast an appraising eye over the original story, he recognised both strengths and weaknesses in his work.
"I read some sections and thought, 'Wow, that guy could really write! Whatever happened to him?!' And then I read other sections that I thought, 'Oh, that's so naive. That was a 20-year-old … who was very self-indulgent and full of himself.'"
He also found that the world had moved on in many ways.
"There was no such thing as a sensitivity reader all those years ago," he says.
"It's amazing how you'd put things in books 20 years ago that you wouldn't put in a book today."
But the most significant change was structural. The original story unfolded chronologically.
"Back then, it was the story of Arlo Hackett and his brother Luke … and into their life I dropped this very feisty, opinionated teenage girl, Saxon, who arrives in a stolen car," he says.
"I wasn't writing it as a crime novel. I saw it as a coming-of-age novel and a story about brotherhood and family."
In the published version, Robotham created a second storyline set in the present as Arlo returns to his hometown of Yulara after his release from prison.
To contemporary readers, Tell Me Something More belongs to a well-established tradition in Australian publishing of mysteries set in the bush, also known as outback noir, kicked off by Jane Harper's 2006 novel, The Dry.
But, as Robotham good-humouredly points out, his novel predates the trend by decades.
"I did this first," he says. "Well before the others did it, I'd done it."
Small-town secrets
Robotham describes Tell Me Something True as his most autobiographical work.
"It's my most personal book in a sense," he says. "There are scenes in it that are lifted straight out of my childhood."
Robotham's father was a teacher, and the family moved often when he was a child.
His primary school years were spent in Gundagai, a town of 2,000 people on the Murrumbidgee River known, among other claims to fame, as the resting place of 19th-century bushranger Captain Moonlite.
While Robotham says the town is easily recognisable to anyone familiar with its geography and history, he chose not to use its name in print, renaming it Yulara instead.
"In small towns there is only one high school and one high school principal and only one senior police officer," he says.
"I didn't want people playing a guessing game as to whether I based any of this on real-life characters."
As the popularity of outback noir attests, a small town is a fertile setting for a fiction writer.
"Small country towns are very slow to forgive," Robotham says.
"They're full of secrets and yet they're places where it's almost impossible to keep a secret."
In Tell Me Something True, the newly freed Arlo attempts to resume life in Yulara, but encounters hostility from the town's residents, many of whom he's known his whole life.
His mother is in a nursing home and the house he grew up in is in disrepair.
With nowhere else to go, he sets about fixing up the house.
As he reflects on his past, told in flashbacks, he begins to question the events that led to his imprisonment.
"Initially you're asking readers to accept a narrator who spent 12 years in prison for being an accessory to a terrible rape and murder," Robotham says.
"And you're thinking, 'How am I going to go along with this? Do I want to spend time with this man?'
"But as his story unfolds, you realise how badly wronged he's been."
Literary influences
Robotham says he can see his early literary influences in Tell Me Something True, from John Irving's The World According to Garp (1978) and Hotel New Hampshire (1981) to John Steinbeck's 1937 novella, Of Mice and Men.
Also an enthusiastic reader of Australian fiction, Robotham's number one choice in the Top 100 Australian Books was Illywhacker by Peter Carey.
Shortlisted for the 1985 Booker Prize, the novel tells the story of the memorable and idiosyncratic Herbert Badgery.
"He's a 139-year-old con man who relates the story of his life, and you can't believe a word of what he says … and I loved that," Robotham says.
"I read that in my 20s and thought Peter Carey was a genius."
Robotham is also an admirer of Year of Wonders by Geraldine Brooks, his former colleague-turned-fellow novelist.
"It's an astonishing piece of research," he says.
"I'm in awe of people who write historic fiction. The idea of capturing that period of history of the plague years in that tiny, isolated village in Britain — I thought she did a remarkable job."
Robotham acknowledges we're at a crucial moment in global publishing thanks to the encroachment of AI.
"There was something like a million extra books published in the last year because they've been generated by AI. There's going to be a tsunami of AI slop," he says.
"But I'm a realist … It might make mistakes now, but AI will get better."
Robotham is currently part of a lawsuit in the US accusing tech companies of stealing authors' work to train their language models.
"I hate the idea that we're going to probably cave into the AI companies and give them some sort of right to Australian copyrighted material," he says.
"To me, it's like someone robbing your house and then saying to you, 'Don't worry about it, I'll give you your toaster back'."
Michael Robotham will be at Sydney Writers' Festival's Homegrown at the State Library of NSW on October 10.
ABC Radio National will count down the Top 100 Australian Books on air on October 17 and 18.

US Health Secretary Kennedy launches new push on vaccine injuries
- US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr has launched an HHS-wide push to study and record health problems reported after vaccination.
- The plan includes a new NIH clinic, better VAERS reporting, and electronic health records for vaccine adverse events.
- The move has raised alarm among public health experts as Kennedy faces legal challenges over vaccine policy changes and falling US immunisation rates.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr this week launched an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) said on Oct 8.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunisation policy.
The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly US$5 billion (S$6.4 billion) across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy’s decades-long efforts to sow scepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunisation rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the US since 2025.
The effort centres on a National Institutes of Health clinic opened on Oct 5 to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement.
Other measures include a proposal by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Kennedy has said US children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by US President Donald Trump.
Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and selected new panellists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices.
The injunction has prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunisations often needed for insurance coverage. REUTERS

Why Trump is targeting green card path used by Microsoft, other tech firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Why Trump is targeting green card path used by Microsoft, other tech firms
- Trump has suspended PERM green card sponsorship for Microsoft and other tech firms, saying the system is abused and should protect US workers more.
- PERM lets employers seek permanent residency for foreign staff after wage checks and 60 days of job adverts, but delays and backlogs are common.
- The administration is also tightening H-1B rules and plans a PERM overhaul, while companies face pressure to train and hire more American workers.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - From the start of his second term, US President Donald Trump has made it a top priority to restrict opportunities for non-Americans to gain entry or remain in the United States. In the latest action on that front, his administration said on Oct 8 that it would indefinitely suspend the ability of a number of technology companies, including Microsoft Corp, to sponsor foreign employees for permanent residency in the US.
Such companies have been relatively heavy users of the government’s Permanent Labor Certification process, a step in the path towards a green card, which confers permanent residency. The administration alleges there have been widespread abuses of the programme. Earlier in 2026, the administration took steps to overhaul the H-1B visa programme, arguing it also has been exploited by employers.
What’s the Permanent Labor Certification process?
The process, known as PERM, is a government system for vetting applications by employers who want to secure green cards for foreign workers. Typically, employers file applications on behalf of foreign employees who are already working for them in the US on a temporary basis.
First, an employer is required to have the Department of Labor determine a minimum wage for the relevant position based on the job duties and geographic market. After that, the employer must advertise the job for 60 days to test whether there are qualified American workers interested in applying. When the recruitment period concludes, the employer can submit an application for permanent labour certification, which can take well over a year to clear because of large processing backlogs.
The Labor Department is required to consider whether there are Americans “willing, qualified and available” to do the same work and whether the employment of the foreigner will negatively affect the wages and working conditions of comparable US workers.
In fiscal 2025, it approved some 138,000 applications. Another 3,400 were denied and 6,700 withdrawn.
The approvals cover a wide range of occupations. The top eight are software developers; computer systems analysts; meat, poultry and fish cutters and trimmers; data scientists; fast food and counter workers; project management specialists; software analysts; and landscapers and groundskeepers.
How is PERM different from the H-1B programme?
H-1Bs, which are temporary work visas, are the primary pathway to hire foreign workers with at least a college degree for specialised occupations. The maximum time a worker can stay in the US on an H-1B visa is generally six years. If an employer wants to retain the worker long term in the US, it can apply for a permanent labour certification. In that case, the H-1B can be extended continuously if at least a year has passed since the employer filed for the certification. The biggest PERM filers have historically been the largest employers of H-1B workers.
Arguing that employers have used the H-1B programme to displace American workers, the Trump administration earlier in 2026 revamped an annual lottery for 85,000 visa slots to favour the most highly paid workers. It has also announced a US$100,000 (S$128,000) fee for new H-1B workers hired from outside the US, but courts have blocked the imposition of it.
How important is PERM to the tech industry?
A large proportion of PERM applications are for positions in the tech industry. In 2025, almost a third of all approved applications were for software and computer systems analysis roles. Microsoft was the top PERM filer in fiscal 2025. Green card sponsorship, which begins with a PERM filing, is an important recruitment and retention tool of employers competing for high-skilled foreign talent.
Why is the programme under scrutiny from the Trump administration?
The Trump administration has been sharply critical of Silicon Valley’s reliance on foreign workers and has pressured tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers. In announcing the suspension, Vice-President J.D. Vance did not specify alleged abuses but accused Microsoft and other companies of “importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do”.
In addition to Microsoft, the administration has suspended use of the PERM process for staffing firms Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp, Infosys Ltd, Tata, Wipro Ltd, HCL Technologies Ltd and Capgemini SE.
This is not the first time the administration has brought enforcement actions against US companies on the basis of alleged abuse of PERM. A unit of OpenAI reached a US$3.2 million settlement in August with the Justice Department to resolve allegations of discrimination against US workers. And the Labor Department took the rare step earlier in 2026 of suspending PERM applications by software firm Cloudera Inc over recruitment violations.
Justice Department investigations launched during Trump’s first term into alleged PERM recruitment violations by Apple Inc. and Meta led to large settlements.
What changes are planned for PERM?
The Trump administration plans to overhaul the regulations governing the PERM process, which were last updated more than two decades ago. A Labor Department rule currently under review at the White House would modernize how the agency reviews applications and bring a new emphasis to protecting American workers, the administration has said. The Russians have recalled World War I technologies to protect oil refineries from Ukrainian drones – how effective is this
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

The Russians have recalled World War I technologies to protect oil refineries from Ukrainian drones – how effective is this
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is developing barrage-balloon nets against Ukrainian drones. Experts doubt the system’s effectiveness because of the wind, the speed, and the maneuvering of the targets.
Russia is developing barrage balloons to protect oil refineries from Ukrainian long-range drones. An attempt is being made to adapt technology used as far back as World War I to modern threats. This is reported by Defense Express, writes UNN.
Details
The new system consists of 2 small balloons, between which a net made of thin cables is stretched. According to the developers’ concept, drones should become entangled in it or be destroyed upon collision
To prevent drones from simply flying over the barrage, the Russians have provided for automatic adjustment of its altitude using radar data. However, the effectiveness of such a mechanism against maneuvering targets remains questionable.
Experts doubt that the system will stop Ukrainian drones
As Defense Express notes, during the tests the Russians used a small drone whose characteristics were significantly inferior to those of Ukrainian long-range strike drones.
It is unknown whether the net will withstand a collision with a heavy drone moving at a speed of hundreds of kilometers per hour. In addition, the system may prove ineffective against simultaneous attacks from different altitudes.
Another problem is strong wind, which could damage or tear down the barrage balloons. At present, several similar Russian projects remain at the development stage.
Similar systems were actively used during World War II, in particular to protect London from German V-1 rockets. However, according to data cited by Defense Express, barrage balloons intercepted only about 5% of those rockets at the time.

Ex-German Chancellor Schröder attends Putin's birthday bash
October 9, 2026
Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder attended Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday party, the Kremlin said Thursday.
Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.
"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands.
Schröder was visiting Hyperglobus branch after joining board
Schröder, who is 82 years old, was in Moscow visiting one of the branches of the new Hyperglobus supermarket chain. The ex-German chancellor was named to the chain's supervisory board last week.
Hyperglobus was originally part of German retail company Globus Holding, which operates the Globus supermarkets in Germany and the Czech Republic.
Globus Holding also had supermarkets in Russia, but divested its stake last year, with those stores thus being spun off into seperate company Hyperglobus.
What backlash has Schröder faced in Germany over his Russia ties?
Schröder, a member of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), served as Germany's chancellor from 1998 to 2005.
Since leaving the chancellery, Schröder has worked for Russian state-owned energy firms and has also maintained personal contact with Putin.
Schröder's fondness for Russia has drawn controversy, particularly since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, and he has also faced calls by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.
Schröder, however, has survived the attempt to be kicked out of his party.

AI use ups homework scores, but slashes exam marks: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:52:26 UTC
07:52:26 KST

‘LLM users show lower cognitive effort’ (representative image)
NEW DELHI: Evidence cited by World Bank suggests that unrestricted use of generative AI can improve what students submit as part of classwork while weakening what they actually learn - a warning with implications for countries such as India.World Development Report 2026 devotes a section to 'Generative AI and the Erosion of Knowledge, Learning, and Human Skills', cautioning that tools such as ChatGPT can reduce the mental effort through which reasoning, writing and knowledge are built.Its strongest evidence comes from China. A study covering students in classes VII-XII found self-reported AI use rising from almost zero to around 80% between 2022 and 2025. Six months after its first use, homework scores improved 18% even as students spe-nt less time on assignments, while monthly in-class examination scores fell 20%. Students who had ever used AI also scored, on average, 5-7% lower in senior high-school and college entrance exams.The report cautioned that the study had not yet been peer-reviewed and reflected the early phase of AI adoption.Gaurav Nayyar, who led the World Bank team that prepared the report, said the evidence points to both opportunity and risk in education.
"If students outsource the learning process to AI, then... that will be a problem," he told TOI.He said the evidence so far appeared more encouraging when AI was used by teachers rather than directly by students, pointing to its use in personalising and customising instructions to suit different learners.
Other research reviewed by World Bank points in the same direction. Participants using large language models for research displayed lower cognitive effort and weaker reasoning, while studies found mental effort declining even when output quality improved. Students given unrestricted AI access also performed worse later when the technology was withdrawn.The report warns that if students use AI to complete homework, the "productive struggle" central to learning can disappear, potentially weakening foundational skills in reasoning and writing.But it does not argue against AI in education. A synthesis of experiments across China, Ghana, Nigeria, Turkiye and US found that 30 sessions of AI-powered tutoring produced learning gains equivalent to at least 0.5 years of schooling, particularly when AI complemented teachers and included safeguards against shortcuts. "AI can augment human capabilities," the report said, "but it must not replace the processes through which more advanced skills are acquired."

Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

Kremlin: Russia agrees with Rubio that Ukraine conflict is in a stalemate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:50:27 UTC
07:50:27 KST

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying on Thursday that Russia agreed with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the Ukraine conflict was in a stalemate.
"Yes, we agree with him," Russian news agencies quoted Peskov as saying on the sidelines of a meeting of leaders of ex-Soviet states in Turkmenistan.
State news agency RIA quoted Peskov as saying it was up to diplomats to find ways of moving towards peace.
"The art of diplomacy precisely involves finding some way out that would allow moving onto a peaceful track," Peskov was quoted as saying.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet Ukrainian representatives on Friday in Miami to discuss new ideas and try to produce a unified proposal for resolving the war, an American source familiar with the plan said on Thursday.
No immediate prospect for three-way summit
Peskov was quoted as saying he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Putin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and US President Donald Trump.
He restated the Kremlin's position that Russia wanted an overall solution to the conflict and was not interested in temporary measures, like a limited ceasefire.
"We are not for a fragmented solution, we are for a comprehensive solution that will allow for sustainable settlement for many, many years, for decades," the agencies quoted him as saying.

Mayor Ruslan Martsinkiv said the victim was a civilian security guard who had been protecting an outbuilding when fragments from a Russian drone damaged the structure.

Opposition calls on A-G to take legal action against PM, Likud attacks Gil over Oct 7 interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:49:56 UTC
07:49:56 KST

Likud said on Thursday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's former military secretary, Avi Gil, was trying to divert attention from his own failures after telling N12 News and Israel Hayom that Netanyahu's chief of staff allegedly tried to change the official record of the prime minister's schedule.
In a public statement, the party said that on the morning of the October 7 massacre "Avi Gil knew about the approaching attack and chose not to wake the prime minister in time."
According to Likud, Gil received a text message from the military secretariat's intelligence officer on warning signs at 3:55 a.m., including SIM cards being activated in the central Gaza camps and Khan Yunis, Hamas activating its emergency communications, and unusual activity by Mohammed Deif.
According to Gil's interview, an intelligence assistant received an alert about a message detailing suspicious actions near the Gaza border but decided not to wake the military secretary or the prime minister, believing the situation was not urgent enough.
Gil only woken up at 6:12 to receive information, according to interview
Gil said he was woken at 6:12 a.m. by a call from the office of former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Ronen Bar, and was briefed on information about the SIM cards and reports of Hamas operatives moving underground only upon calling Bar on a secure line at 6:17 a.m.
Gil said he then called Netanyahu twice, once at 6:29 a.m., waking him up and telling him "Hamas has launched extensive fire, a large-scale surprise attack. I am gathering information and will call you as soon as possible," and a second time at 6:40 a.m., telling him "We are at war."
Netanyahu responded to the interview in a post on his X/Twitter account in which he wrote "The left's campaign of lies will never defeat the truth," on Thursday evening.
Eisenkot, Liberman, Golan call on A-G to pursue legal action
The Yashar! party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, called on Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara to pursue legal action over suspicions that Netanyahu gave the state comptroller and the public false and distorted information about the failures surrounding October 7.
The party cited reporting and statements that it said supported the allegations, “as revealed by journalist Ronen Bergman’s investigation in Yedioth Ahronoth and statements by Maj.-Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, who served as Netanyahu’s military secretary, in Israel Hayom and on Channel 12 News.”
The statement also accused Netanyahu of presenting a partial and distorted account of security documents from before the massacre. It alleged that he omitted significant warnings and intelligence assessments about Hamas’s growing strength, its closer ties to the Iranian axis, and the danger of escalation with Israel.
In his interview, Gil stated that there are discrepancies between what the public has been told and what actually happened, calling for the formation of a state commission of inquiry.
“The document submitted to the state comptroller does not reflect what really happened. It is part of the truth, but not the whole truth,” Gil had said.
Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman criticized Netanyahu over the allegations: “I call on the attorney-general to order an immediate investigation into the prime minister and his aides on charges of treason and conspiracy. I call on the IDF chief of staff to prevent any attempt to use the IDF for political purposes, solely to change the public agenda just before the elections.”
The Democrats chairman Yair Golan also sharply criticized the prime minister: “This is an earthquake. The testimony of Maj.-Gen. (res.) Avi Gil is among the most serious ever heard in Israel. Netanyahu’s culpability and responsibility for the massacre of 1,200 people and the abduction of 251 people have never been clearer. Netanyahu committed a grave crime against the residents of the Gaza border communities, survivors of captivity, and the entire people of Israel.
“I call on the attorney-general to order a comprehensive criminal investigation into these suspicions, including an examination of the involvement and responsibility of everyone in the Prime Minister’s Office, up to the most senior level. The preservation of all original recordings, minutes, and documents must be ensured immediately. Netanyahu must account for the decisions made before the massacre and any possible attempt to obstruct the examination of responsibility afterward," Golan said.
Oct 7 council says interview just 'tip of the iceberg'
The leader of the October 7 council also responded to Gil's interview, saying “Tonight, it is no longer possible to claim they did not know. Maj.-Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, who sat alongside Netanyahu in the most confidential meetings and served as his military secretary, is speaking out openly and confirming in his own voice what we have revealed in recent days. And tonight, we say clearly and unequivocally, this is only the tip of the iceberg.”
Corinne Baum and Miriam Sela-Eitam contributed to this report.

US President Donald Trump on Thursday said comments he made that Iran could "take out" California cities had been misinterpreted and that he was instead referring to the need for people to tolerate higher gas prices.
Trump made the remarks at a political rally in Nebraska on Monday as he spoke about Americans' wartime economic sacrifices.
"Remember, with the war, it's just artificial, it's a little bit high, it's a small price to pay," he said then.
"It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it's going to be over with very soon."
California's Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans quickly rebuked the remarks.
Trump explains comment in Truth Social post
"What I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon," Trump said in a Truth Social post on Thursday.
"If you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" he continued, saying he loved both cities.
Trump has shrugged off cost-of-living concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before.

US military to livestream execution by firing squad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:46:02 UTC
07:46:02 KST

US military to livestream execution by firing squad
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has announced plans to livestream the execution of a former US Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people at a military base in Texas, arguing that Americans should witness the consequences of such crimes.
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major sentenced to death for a 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, is scheduled to face a military firing squad on December 3. The execution would be the first carried out by the US military in more than six decades and the first by an Army firing squad since World War II.
Speaking to conservative commentator Jack Posobiec on Thursday, Hegseth defended the decision to execute Hasan at the same installation where he carried out the massacre.
“He’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.
MAJOR NEWS!!! @SECWAR REVEALS FORT HOOD SHOOTER’S FIRING SQUAD EXECUTION WILL BE PUBLIC Sec. Pete Hegseth says Nidal Hasan will be executed by soldiers at Fort Hood on December 3 at 1 PM—the same time as the 2009 attack. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” @JackPosobiec
— Real America's Voice (RAV) (@RealAmVoice) October 8, 2026
The Department of War subsequently confirmed that the execution would be livestreamed for public viewing, with further details to follow, according to the Washington Post and AP.
Hasan, a US-born Muslim and former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at a military processing center at Fort Hood on November 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. He reportedly shouted “Allahu akbar” – Arabic for “God is great” – during the attack.
The gunman had previously exchanged emails with radical Islamic cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen. During his court-martial, Hasan admitted responsibility for the massacre, claiming he had acted to protect fellow Muslims from American military operations in Afghanistan.
He was convicted of premeditated murder and attempted murder in 2013 and sentenced to death. The US Supreme Court declined to review his conviction in March 2025, clearing the way for US President Donald Trump to approve the execution earlier this month following a recommendation from Hegseth.
The execution is scheduled for 1 PM on December 3, at approximately the same time of day as the original attack. Hasan could still seek to delay his execution through a separate legal challenge in civilian federal court.
The last US military execution took place in 1961, when an Army private was hanged after being convicted of the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-orld girl.
Capital punishment by firing squad remains legal in five US states – Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah – although the method is rarely used.
Public executions are even more unusual in modern American history. The last widely recognized public execution in the US took place in Kentucky in 1936, when a convicted murderer was hanged in front of thousands of spectators.

Mexico’s Sheinbaum announces creation of group to tackle online content inciting violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:40:57 UTC
07:40:57 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Thursday that she is creating an interagency working group to address the spread of harmful content online.
“I am forming a working group to demand that digital platforms remove content as soon as they identify statements or actions that incite violence, abuse or harassment,” Sheinbaum said at her daily news conference, referring to websites and social media platforms.
She said the group will include representatives from the Secretariat of Security and Citizen Protection, the Digital Transformation Agency and academic institutions as well as experts.
Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said the group will work on a decree establishing obligations for digital platforms.
The initiative is expected to be developed next week and will seek to strengthen the detection, reporting and timely removal of content that directly incites violence.
It would also establish mechanisms for early-stage risk identification, socio-emotional counseling and mental health support directly tailored for adolescents and young people while involving parents, educators and other adults.
Sheinbaum said the government has identified three or four similar incidents in recent years, highlighting the need for preventive measures against violence linked to online content.
The announcement came after an attack on Oct. 1 at a secondary school in Torreon in the northern state of Coahuila. Two 18-year-old brothers who were former students at the school entered the facility armed with machetes, killing a teacher and injuring four other people, according to authorities.
The government said the proposed measures aim to strengthen prevention and establish greater responsibility for digital platforms in addressing content that directly incites violence.
The initiative comes amid growing government scrutiny of the role of social media in the spread of violent content and its potential impact on young people.

ICE Emails Discuss Using Palantir-Supported Tool to Investigate Voter Fraud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:40:11 UTC
07:40:11 KST

As the Trump administration has carried out a nonstop effort to undermine the midterm elections this year, the Department of Homeland Security appears to have looked into whether it could use a Palantir-supported tool to track people it believes have voted illegally.
The revelation is found in a tranche of documents obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request and published this week by Democracy Forward, a legal advocacy group. As well as revealing that DHS officials have investigated over 150 nonprofit groups in search of evidence they’re helping noncitizens register to vote, the documents show how Immigration and Customs Enforcement is now central to federal voter fraud investigations.
More specifically, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)—one of ICE’s two major components—is spearheading the effort to uncover voter fraud, with its Innovation Lab (known internally as iLab) developing tools for agents.
ICE, it seems, wants to build “a system that is going to get good at determining how to find people to investigate and potentially bring action against,” Chinmayi Sharma, an associate professor at Fordham Law School who has closely tracked the Palantir-supported tool called ELITE, tells WIRED.
“You would want to build off of what already exists, what might already have the infrastructure and data sources that you would want,” says Sharma.
“iLab’s processing focuses on DOJ voting rolls and [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] data; criminal histories are currently excluded, with efforts underway to address this,” a worker in HSI’s Countering Transnational Organized Crime unit wrote on May 26 in an email with “Voter Fraud” in the subject line. (Like other workers, their name was redacted in the records released to Democracy Forward.)
“Coordination with iLab continues,” they wrote, “particularly on ingesting processed voter roll data into the ELITE enforcement system to enhance lead management, analytical review, and investigative tracking.”
The existence of ELITE, which stands for Enhanced Leads Identification & Targeting for Enforcement, was first reported in January by 404 Media, which revealed that ICE agents using the tool can create maps featuring potential deportation targets, pull up files on each target, and see a “confidence score” on the person’s current address.
“Voter roll data has never been integrated into ELITE,” a Palantir spokesman tells WIRED.
ELITE was again mentioned in a July 7 email with an attachment named “Fraud WAR”—WAR typically refers to a weekly activity report—from a DHS worker who shared an update on the agency’s “election integrity investigations,” including the news that Connecticut, Georgia, Kentucky, Missouri, Michigan, and New Mexico had “been enriched by the iLab and are pending Palantir entry into ELITE.”
What specifically was enriched and pending Palantir entry is unclear from the records, but in another email in the same chain, a DHS official said that someone from the agency would send the update to the White House.
“ICE does not disclose the existence of investigative methods and techniques,” an agency spokesperson tells WIRED.
“While ICE Homeland Security Investigations is not able to comment on any active investigations, HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.
The White House did not comment on ICE’s possible use of ELITE to track noncitizen voters in a statement provided to WIRED.
The claim that noncitizens are voting in numbers sufficient to sway the outcomes of US elections has been a central narrative pushed by the Trump administration in the run-up to next month’s midterms. All available evidence shows that noncitizen voting is vanishingly rare.
DHS, under secretary Markwayne Mullin, has led the charge on identifying noncitizen voters but has so far only found a handful of possible cases. Earlier this week, the Justice Department announced it had brought charges in 16 cases involving foreign nationals allegedly committing voting-related crimes. (All were lawful permanent residents.) Last month, a whistleblower alleged that federal employees directed by DHS leadership may have broken the law when they searched state websites for illegally registered voters.
While Mullin and the Trump administration have been vocal with their claims about noncitizen voting and short-term victories ahead of the midterms, in the background, ICE appears to have been working on tools that will work in the long term.
The May 26 email sent under a “Voter Fraud” subject line characterizes a weekly report as emphasizing “a network-based investigative approach, prioritizing organization and facilitation analysis over individual leads, now stated as a strategic direction.”
The language used in the documents related to the agency’s new approach to identifying voter fraud suggests this system was not live or even in pre-deployment at the time, but rather being built for the future, Sharma believes.
“I could be wrong,” says Sharma, “but there's a reason you choose to build voter fraud [investigations] within DHS when it does not intuitively fall within what you would think of as DHS's purview, and I think it's because of the authorities, the infrastructure, the vendor relationships, the contract vehicles, and privileges. There's just a lot of synergies you can take advantage of.”

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 9, 2026
US freezes Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys green-card applications
The Trump administration froze on Oct 8 some green-card filings by Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine top universities, widening a visa crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.
The twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programmes – potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers – while putting some of the country’s top research universities on notice.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” Vice-President J.D. Vance said.
He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
‘Public’ execution by firing squad for military base shooter
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing squad execution of convicted military base shooter Nidal Hasan will be “public,” according to a video shared on Oct 8 by the Pentagon.
“He’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec in a clip posted on X by various official Pentagon accounts.
“People need to understand that... there’s serious consequence for these types of things,” Hegseth said, speaking aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier.
France pledges 3,000 substitute teachers after protests
France’s education minister on Oct 8 promised 3,000 substitute teachers for the country’s worst-off high schools, after tens of thousands took to the streets nationwide to demand better education and less police brutality.
Students have blocked entrances to hundreds of high schools for more than a week, with squads of riot police deployed - occasionally resulting in violent clashes.
High school students across the country - most aged 15 to 18 - have complained of absent teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
Russian strike on buses kills 30 in frontline Ukrainian city
Ukraine on Oct 8 accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians after 30 people were killed when two buses were blown up in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, in one of the deadliest single attacks for weeks.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky vowed that the attack “will not go unanswered” after photos posted by local authorities showed the burnt-out metal shell of the vehicles, with bodies and debris strewn across the road.
“Russia is trying to destroy all life in (the) Donbas (region) and the world must respond to this,” he wrote on Telegram, warning that the death toll could rise.
City must ‘stick together’ during crisis, says Haaland
Erling Haaland said Manchester City must “stick together” in uncertain times after being found guilty of over 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules.
City face a severe points penalty or even expulsion from the Premier League after an independent commission found they used “sham” commercial contracts to inflate revenue and cut costs by over £900 million (S$1.5 billion) between 2009 and 2018.

60 Million Children Have Been Automatically Enrolled in Trump Accounts. Here’s What Parents Should Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:38:49 UTC
07:38:49 KST

Sixty million American children were automatically enrolled into “Trump Accounts” on Oct. 1, President Donald Trump announced.
Roughly 10 million of the investment accounts for kids have also been created by parents or guardians following the program’s launch on July 4, meaning that the automatic enrollments bring the total number of enrollees to 70 million. That figure represents every American child under 18 with a Social Security number, according to the White House.
“Today we celebrate our next historic … step to ensure every American child has a fair shot at the American dream,” Trump said Wednesday in the Oval Office. “The U.S. government is automatically creating a tax-free investment account for every child to grow over the course of their lives and to be used to their benefit and for their benefit after they turn 18.”
More than $4.5 billion has been deposited into Trump Accounts since they went live this summer, including $1.3 billion in federal seed money, $2.6 billion in philanthropic donations, and over $600 million from family and friends of account owners, according to the White House, which added in a press release that there is “more on the way.”
Here’s what to know about Trump Accounts following the latest announcement.
What are Trump Accounts?
Trump Accounts are special tax-deferred investment accounts for American children under the age of 18.
Accounts for newborns and many young children will receive seed deposits from the federal government or philanthropists Michael and Susan Dell, with amounts depending on their birth year and zip code. Parents, friends, family, or others also have the option of contributing up to $5,000 per child into the accounts each year.
Money in the Trump Accounts will be invested in a fund that tracks the performance of the S&P 500 Index, which includes roughly 500 of the largest publicly traded U.S. companies.
The funds can only be accessed after a child turns 18, at which point their account will become a traditional Individual Retirement Arrangement (IRA) account. While the accounts will be under children’s names, they will be managed by parents or guardians until the owners turn 18.
The accounts, established under Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” are intended to help build long-term wealth for American children.
“Our studies found that when a child has an account like this, they are way more likely to graduate from high school, to go into college and graduate to buy a home, to not be incarcerated, to be a contributing member of society, and it improves the mental health of both the child and the parent, even with a relatively small sum,” Michael Dell said during an event in Washington, D.C., earlier this year.
Madeline Brown, a senior associate at the public policy think-tank the Urban Institute, tells TIME that the “infrastructure” created by the Trump Accounts “provides lots of opportunity.”
She argues, however, that the program does not adequately address wealth gaps in the U.S. and should give more money to lower-income families, rather than distributing the same amounts to various groups.
“There's no essentially guaranteed other money for lower income kids,” she says. “In a structure that was aiming to reduce inequality, you would see additional annual contributions for lowest income kids, ideally from the federal government.”
Who’s eligible to get a Trump Account, and to receive seed deposits?
All American children who are under the age of 18 and have a valid Social Security number are eligible for a Trump Account. With the automatic enrollments announced by Trump on Wednesday, the White House says every eligible child in the U.S. should now have an account.
Certain kids are also eligible to receive funds in their Trump Accounts from the federal government or Michael and Susan Dell.
Once accounts are opened for children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, they will automatically be seeded with a one-time, tax-free government payment of $1,000.
Due to an additional $6.25 billion investment from the philanthropists Michael and Susan Dell, children born from 2016 through 2024 who live in zip codes where the median family income is at or below $118,000 will also receive a $250 deposit into their Trump Accounts once they’re activated. Children living on military bases also qualify for the deposits.
An analysis of Census Bureau data by Investopedia showed that roughly 71% of children under 10 will qualify for the $250 deposit. That is expected to amount to about 25 million children, on top of those who receive the seed money from the government.
"We've seen what happens when a child gets even a small financial head start, their world expands," Michael Dell, who was with Trump in the Oval Office on Wednesday, said in a video statement.
How can you claim your child’s account?
To claim a child’s account, their parents or guardians must go to TrumpAccounts.gov to download the official Trump Accounts app. There, they must verify their identity and relationship to their child before claiming the account.
This process is still required to claim accounts for children who have been automatically enrolled in the program.
“Eligible children must also have their Trump Account claimed to receive the one-time $1,000 seed contribution from Treasury,” the Treasury Department wrote in a release on Oct. 1.
How will enrollment in Trump Accounts work moving forward?
In a notice published in the Federal Register, the Treasury Department estimated that an additional two million accounts would be created for children every year moving forward as a result of the auto-enrollment system.
“An eligible individual should not lose the opportunity to receive contributions or investment growth merely because no adult completed an election,” the Treasury wrote in the notice.
Brown says that “reducing friction” in the enrollment process is important. She called the automatic enrollments a “step in the right direction.”
But she stressed that many people are not aware that they have access to the accounts. One study produced by Brown and her colleagues at the Urban Institute showed that lower income families were less aware of Trump Accounts, aligns with research demonstrating how financially secure individuals and households are often more knowledgeable about financial products and opportunities.
Read More: The Problem with Trump Accounts
“We just need to continue emphasis on education and outreach, including in different languages with trusted messengers,” Brown says.

Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections
President Donald Trump on Thursday ruled out attacking Iran before the US midterm elections on 3 November, saying Washington was holding "productive discussions" with Tehran.
Trump's post on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices on Thursday driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to those elections.
"I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," he wrote.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," he added, without providing additional details.
The Atlantic magazine reported on Wednesday that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop options to strike Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms. The New York Times published a similar report on Thursday, saying the plans were being developed despite Trump's "ambivalence".
The rise in crude oil prices has also been fueled by persistent tensions in the Strait of Hormuz - a strategic chokepoint for the global oil trade - as well as hostilities between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
In a recent sign of those tensions, an oil tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar reported being struck "by multiple projectiles," causing an unspecified number of casualties, the UKMTO maritime agency said Wednesday.
Polls suggest that US voters are strongly dissatisfied over rising fuel prices, linked to the conflict launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February.
The US leader has repeatedly insisted in recent weeks that the United States has effectively won the Iran war, despite ongoing unrest and a recent security threat that forced the withdrawal of American bombers from a base in England.
But Trump's claims that prices will fall as soon as the Iran war is over have so far fallen on deaf ears with voters.
The midterm elections will shape the final two years of Trump's presidential term as his Republican Party risks losing its current grip on Congress.
Although Trump is not on the ballot, he is heavily involved in the campaign, holding numerous rallies in an attempt to limit the damage or even turn the political tide.
Trump has warned he faces a possible third impeachment if Democrats retake the House of Representatives, and the White House is preparing for a slew of investigations into corruption and abuse of power.
The US president also on Thursday sought to calm a furor over his comments at a rally earlier this week that Iran could "take out" the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Trump, 80, blamed the "fake and artificial news" for misinterpreting the remarks, which Democrats pounced on.
"In actuality, what I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" Trump said on Truth Social.

The Ukrainian "Bebradron," with a range of up to 45 km, has received approval from the Ministry of Defense — what is known about the new strike UAV
Kyiv • UNN
The strike "Bebradron," with a payload of up to 7.5 kg and a range of 45 km, has passed codification by the Ministry of Defense. The drone can already be procured by the military.
The Ukrainian strike drone "Bebradron," capable of carrying up to 7.5 kg of payload and operating at a range of up to 45 km, has undergone codification by the Ministry of Defence. Military personnel can now officially purchase it with state funds. This was reported by the developer company BlueBird Tech, writes UNN.
Details
"Bebradron" is a fixed-wing, aircraft-type tactical drone created in Ukraine to perform combat missions at medium ranges.
According to the manufacturer, the drone reaches speeds of up to 150 km/h, remains airborne for 30 minutes, and transmits video and telemetry to the operator in real time.
What is special about the Ukrainian development
The drone is launched using a compact pneumatic catapult manufactured by BlueBird Tech. This makes it possible to use the drone without large launch equipment.
Military units can now purchase it directly and officially use it on the battlefield. Thus, pilots have more opportunities to engage enemy targets
In addition to the strike version, the developers created the modular "Bebradron KIT" platform and the "Bebradron-M" training modification for operator training.
Codification means that the drone has undergone the necessary official procedures and can be supplied to the Security and Defence Forces of Ukraine. At the same time, the volume of future state procurements has not yet been reported.

The two countries, which are under heavy Western sanctions, have reinforced diplomatic and military ties.

Ukraine and Western countries have accused Iran of supplying Russia with Shahed drones and short-range missiles for use in the Ukraine war. Russia has also been accused of supplying data to Iran for its attacks on US targets in the Middle East.

Serviceman recruited by Russia while AWOL detained for directing strikes on Ukrainian forces
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
The operation to expose the suspect was carried out with the assistance of the Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
The Russian agent was a mobilized serviceman from the Poltava region who directed fire at the positions of his assault regiment and adjacent units of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
The investigation established that the Russians were primarily interested in the coordinates of the largest concentrations of Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel and equipment, as well as training grounds where the suspect underwent combat training.
According to SBU cyber specialists, the man was recruited by Russian intelligence services after he was AWOL from his military unit and began looking for easy ways to make money through Telegram channels.
After being recruited, he was instructed to return from his unauthorized absence to his unit and gather intelligence to help direct Russian strikes.
The SBU documented the man transmitting the geolocation of his battalion's temporary deployment site to the Russians before leaving his military unit under the pretext of going to a hospital.
Instead of visiting a medical facility, he went into hiding at his home in Kremenchuk.
SBU officers took advance measures to secure the positions of Ukraine's Defense Forces in the area of enemy intelligence activity and detained the spotter.
During searches, officers found a smartphone that was used to coordinate his actions with his Russian handler. To maintain secrecy, the agent used an anonymous chat and regularly deleted his correspondence.
SBU investigators notified the detainee that he was suspected under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

NEW DELHI: A group of 42 retired judges on Thursday slammed the opposition's attack on Election Commission, claiming that it appeared to be a calculated campaign driven by "vested political interests" with little regard for the potentially devastating consequences of destabilising the world's largest democracy."India's constitutional bodies are under sustained attack. EC stands at the centre of this assault. Even the higher judiciary, which we hold in high esteem, and statutory agencies have not been spared. These attacks are not reasoned critique," they said in an open letter.Former Supreme Court judges Hemant Gupta and Pankaj Mittal and several former chief justices of high courts, besides retired judges of various HCs were signatories to the statement, which defended the EC's Special Intensive Review (SIR) of electoral rolls, arguing that a clean roll protected every genuine vote.They said they held no brief for any political party but in moments like these, silence was no longer a neutral choice. A party that governed this nation for over five decades now claims that the very system which elected it is rigged."They said activist outfits with a long record of selective litigation lent these claims a veneer of legality. "They file petitions one after the other. They seldom file proof. The courtroom becomes a stage, and when the judgement is delivered, it is criticised whenever it does not serve their interests."
The uproar over SIR appeared both sudden and remarkably convenient, the judges said. "Tell citizens often enough that their vote does not count, and they stop believing in the ballot. When the ballot loses meaning, the street gains it. Unrest begins with a narrative. Anarchic and fringe elements then occupy the vacuum," the group said.While some of these groups were homegrown, some took their cues from beyond borders, they alleged. They appealed to political parties to not delegitimise elections and take their grievances to EC and the courts with evidence.

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro leads President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by six percentage points in the first poll done since the Oct. 4 first round of the presidential election.
Ahead of the Oct. 25 runoff, the PoderData/Aya poll released Thursday said Bolsonaro has 53% support, compared with 47% for Lula.
The survey was done on Oct. 5-7 through calls to both cellphones and landlines, with 3,000 interviews in 705 municipalities across Brazil’s 27 states. It has a margin of error of 1.8 percentage points.
The poll marks a change from PoderData/Aya’s poll before the first round, which showed the two candidates tied at 50%. In the new poll, Bolsonaro gained three percentage points while Lula lost three.
The first round was closely contested, with Bolsonaro winning 47.03% of valid votes to Lula’s 45.16%. The Oct. 25 runoff will decide the presidency.
Lula, seeking another term, will face Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, in the runoff. Both campaigns are seeking support from voters whose candidates were eliminated in the first round.
Other major pollsters are also expected to release runoff surveys, giving more indications of how the race is developing ahead of Oct. 25.
Brazil’s electoral system requires a candidate to receive more than 50% of valid votes to win the presidency in the first round.
With neither candidate reaching that threshold, Lula and Bolsonaro advanced to the runoff.

Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' book does not worry Cummins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:25:27 UTC
07:25:27 KST

Australian captain Pat Cummins says the team has "moved on" from the infamous Sandpapergate incident.
Usman Khawaja, who played in the 2018 Cape Town Test that saw three players suspended over ball tampering, is preparing to release an autobiography.
What's next?
Khawaja's book will be released next month, a week after Australia's Test tour of South Africa.
Pat Cummins says he is not fazed by the prospect of the so-called Sandpapergate incident being raised in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, which will be the first from any Australian player who played in that 2018 Cape Town Test.
Cummins confirmed today Khawaja had called to inform him he was writing the book, which will be released days after the end of Australia's first Test tour of South Africa since the infamous match.
How much will be written about the ball-tampering scandal that rocked Australian cricket remains to be seen.
Khawaja is a childhood friend of former opening partner David Warner, who copped a 12-month ban for the ball-tampering scandal.
At the time, Warner was painted as the architect of the ploy, with captain Steve Smith also suspended for a year and Cameron Bancroft nine months.
There was a report at the time that Khawaja had suggested the team should take joint responsibility for the incident, rather than just the three players.
However, a Cricket Australia investigation found no other player had knowledge of the plan to apply sandpaper to the ball, a point that has long been maintained.
Australia's bowlers have also previously issued a statement saying they did not know a "foreign substance" would be taken onto the field.
There is no suggestion Khawaja's autobiography, which has been penned without a ghost writer, will suggest anything other than what the investigations found.
Cummins was asked ahead of Friday's first Test in Durban if Khawaja had specified how much detail he would go into and if he would agree with his former teammates' version of events.
"You would have to ask him," Cummins responded.
"It's obviously a long time ago. All the investigations, everything was done back then. Answered every question a million times.
"It was dealt with then. All I can say is as a group we've moved on. [I'm] very happy with the last eight or nine years, how we've been as a group and evolved.
"He didn't go into too much detail … As always, it was, 'No worries. You can tell your story. That's fine.'"
It has been hard to escape talk of the 2018 series in the lead-up to the first Test.
Cummins noted on Thursday there was a larger-than-normal media turn-out in Durban, with this also the battle between the world's top-two sides.
Beyond the ball-tampering scandal, the 2018 series was littered with clashes between the two teams from the middle of the pitch to dressing-room stairwells.
But tensions have thawed significantly since, with neither side expecting similar dramas.
"It was quite a big series that 2018. It was pretty full on," Cummins said.
"After that, I think pretty much every Test team in the world felt like they'd made some adjustments.
"This group is quite a different group in how we approach playing and I'm really proud of how the guys have been since that 2018 series."

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November's US midterm congressional elections, asserting that the two countries are having "productive" talks about ending the six-month-old war.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd."
The war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump's domestic approval ratings downward and is weighing heavily on his fellow Republicans as they seek to preserve their narrow legislative majorities in November's election.
Some 60% of Americans - including one in four Republicans - disapprove of how Trump is handling the situation in Iran, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The conflict has pushed gasoline prices sharply higher at a time when voters say their top concern is the cost of living.
Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but he has not offered a detailed plan for exiting the war.
Proposals exchanged aimed at ending war, opening Strait of Hormuz
Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer.
Iran's state media reported on Thursday that Tehran would not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium stockpile, citing the head of the country's Atomic Energy Organization, days after US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make "meaningful" reductions in its enrichment capacity.
The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied.
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on July 14 following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu, and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.

UK: Two Latvian men arrested for breaking into RAF base
October 9, 2026
Two Latvian men have been arrested for breaching the perimeter fence at an RAF base used by the US military, UK police said Thursday.
The two UK residents, aged 36 and 32, were arrested by counterterrorism police at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in southeastern England, 70 miles north of London.
Police said they were being held on suspicion of trespassing, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the UK."
A former World War II airbase, RAF Molesworth, is now a non-flying facility that is managed by the US Air Force.
It houses intelligence personnel from US Africa Command and the NATO Intelligence Fusion Center, which provides information to the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe.
The incident comes after several men were arrested amid an alleged terror plot at another UK air base last month.
What do we know about the incident at RAF Molesworth?
According to a statement from Counter Terrorism Policing London, officers from the Ministry of Defense Police and Cambridgeshire Constabulary began investigating an incident at approximately 10 p.m. local time on Wednesday after an abandoned vehicle was found near the edge of the base.
Police later discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence and arrested the two suspects at around 2 a.m. on Thursday.
The men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage. They were later arrested on charges of entering a prohibited place with the intent to harm the UK.
Both men remain in police custody. Due to the nature of the offense, the matter is being investigated by counterterrorism police.
Is this related to the RAF Fairford incident?
On September 27, authorities discovered three suspicious vans near RAF Fairford, a British air base from which US bombers launched strikes against Iran. This triggered a widespread investigation that led to seven arrests.
Last weekend, the US Air Force brought home all the bombers deployed to the base.
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of the counterterrorism unit, said that while UK authorities are "very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites", there is "nothing to suggest" the incident at RAF Molesworth is related to what happened at RAF Fairford last week, although she added that the investigation was still in its "very early stages."
The US European Command acknowledged the incident but declined to comment on specific force protection measures.

The STF’s First Panel unanimously convicted him of using his position as a federal lawmaker to seek foreign sanctions against Brazilian authorities, including Supreme Court justices and the Prosecutor General.
Bolsonaro operated from the US and sought measures by the Trump administration against Brazilian officials, according to the court.
Moraes said Bolsonaro’s actions were intended to pressure authorities and interfere with the judicial proceedings. The court rejected his appeals.
Bolsonaro has been living in the US since 2025. Brazilian authorities would need to secure his return for the prison sentence to be physically carried out in Brazil.
The justice also ordered the Superior Electoral Court to be notified that Bolsonaro’s political rights remain suspended while the effects of the final criminal conviction remain in force.
