Iran to respond to U.S. views on 7-day plan to end war in coming days: FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:14:21 CST
06:14:21 KST

TEHRAN, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday that his country will in the coming days submit its response to the U.S. views on its proposed plan to end the war, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Speaking on the sidelines of a funeral ceremony in Tehran, Araghchi said that the negotiations are continuing and that Tehran and Washington are exchanging messages through mediators.
He said Iran has received the U.S. views on its seven-day plan and is "currently reviewing" them.
Iran conveyed its plan to the United States to cease hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz on Sept. 22 through mediators on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Under the plan, Tehran proposed ending the war and reopening the waterway within seven days, provided that the United States accepted its conditions. Iranian authorities have repeatedly said that ending the war on all fronts, including Lebanon, and reopening the Strait of Hormuz are the sole focus of the ongoing diplomatic process.
However, U.S. Vice President JD Vance said in a Monday interview with Reuters that "Iran must make a meaningful reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy U.S. demands and end the war."
On Thursday, Mohammad Eslami, president of Iran's Atomic Energy Organization, responded that uranium enrichment is an "inseparable" part of the nuclear industry, and Tehran will not back down despite U.S. threats and military operations, according to Tasnim.
Eslami said that Iran's nuclear program is in compliance with its safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency and the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war on all fronts.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement. However, the two sides failed to make sufficient progress as tensions continued to escalate. ■

Venezuela's Maduro, wife face new U.S. charge over alleged torture
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:14:18 CST
06:14:18 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were charged by U.S. authorities on Thursday with conspiracy to commit torture, according to an indictment filed in federal court in Manhattan.
"He (Maduro) authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," the indictment said.
Maduro had previously been charged with narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine importation conspiracy and weapons-related offenses, to which he pleaded not guilty.
A U.S. judge ruled in July that Maduro and Flores will go on trial on June 1, 2027.
Maduro's lawyers have sought to have the case dismissed, arguing that he was the incumbent president of Venezuela at the time of his capture and was therefore entitled to immunity from foreign criminal jurisdiction.
On Jan. 3, U.S. forces launched a military operation in Venezuela and forcibly seized Maduro and his wife before transporting them to New York. The couple has been held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn since their capture in Caracas. ■

Türkiye, France sign roadmap to deepen defense, security ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:14:17 CST
06:14:17 KST

ANKARA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye and France have signed a roadmap to further develop bilateral relations in defense and security, the Turkish Defense Ministry said Thursday.
Speaking at a weekly press briefing, Turkish Defense Ministry Spokesman Zeki Akturk said the roadmap aims to strengthen bilateral defense ties based on common interests and to create a more institutionalized framework for cooperation.
The roadmap envisages regular defense and security consultations, cooperation against hybrid threats, intelligence sharing, closer air defense coordination and improved system interoperability, Akturk said.
It also calls for coordinated training and capacity-building activities in third countries, he added.
Under the framework, meetings will be held alternately in Paris and Ankara, with the first session scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026.
Meanwhile, the country's Ministry of Family and Social Services and the European Union (EU) Delegation to Türkiye signed a protocol in Ankara on Thursday to enhance cooperation on social integration and education programs for foreign nationals in Türkiye.
According to Turkish media Daily Sabah, under the Social Cohesion and Education Assistance Program for Foreigners signed by the two sides, the EU will provide 402 million euros (449 million U.S. dollars) to support vulnerable foreign families in the country.
"We will continue to support families' basic needs, such as food, shelter and education, through regular cash assistance," said Turkish Minister of Family and Social Services Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas. ■

Anti-migrant protests spark violence, arson in South African cities

2026-10-09
05:13:59 CST
06:13:59 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Anti-migrant protests turned violent in South Africa on Thursday, with mobs torching vehicles, looting foreign-owned businesses, and exchanging gunfire in both the coastal hub of Durban and Johannesburg's iconic Soweto township, according to local authorities and police.
The fresh wave of unrest marks a sharp escalation in months-long anti-immigrant demonstrations that have drawn widespread international scrutiny over xenophobic violence in Africa's most industrialized economy.
In downtown Durban, KwaZulu-Natal province, a chaotic rally demanding the immediate closure of a local refugee processing center descended into rioting. Fire crews reported at least seven vehicles set ablaze along Dr Pixley KaSeme Street and Park Lane, while crowds vandalized and looted nearby shops belonging to foreign nationals.
Police intervened with riot units to disperse the crowd and safely evacuate asylum seekers trapped inside the facility.
KwaZulu-Natal police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said tensions erupted after a South African protester was allegedly assaulted by a foreign national, leaving the victim with a severe leg fracture.
"Unplanned marches create volatile situations like this," Netshiunda told reporters, confirming that three foreign nationals were arrested over the assault. He added that a lodge and a warehouse were partially destroyed by arson before emergency crews contained the blazes, and heavy police patrols remain deployed.
Meanwhile, in Soweto, South Africa's largest township, nine vehicles were torched outside the Department of Home Affairs office following intense violent clashes between local residents and foreign traders.
Xolani Fihla, spokesperson for the Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department, confirmed officers are investigating reports that live ammunition was fired at local demonstrators. While no casualties were reported in Soweto, police cautioned that the atmosphere remains highly explosive.
Tensions have been stoked in part by vigilante grassroots groups, such as Operation Dudula, which have mobilized local youth to forcibly close foreign-owned corner shops, known locally as spaza shops, and demand the deportation of undocumented migrants.
Socioeconomic analysts attribute the recurring waves of xenophobic turmoil to South Africa's staggering unemployment rate, which sits above 32 percent, and widespread poverty. Foreign nationals, largely hailing from other African countries such as Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi and Nigeria, are frequently scapegoated by local communities for straining township housing, public healthcare, and informal retail sectors.
The latest flare-up follows a landmark Constitutional Court ruling that mandated the Department of Home Affairs to process asylum applications from all foreign arrivals, regardless of whether they entered the country legally. A subsequent Sept. 28 official circular directing local refugee centers to implement the court mandate sparked intense public anger among anti-migrant groups.
Addressing the civil turbulence, Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi, who chairs the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration, emphasized that the judiciary's decision "must not be interpreted as legalising unlawful migration," as the government seeks to balance constitutional human rights obligations with border control concerns.
Xenophobic outbreaks have historically strained Pretoria's diplomatic ties with regional allies across the African Union, while threatening regional trade integration under the African Continental Free Trade Area. ■

Roundup: Ebola slows in parts of DR Congo, but new hotspots, cross-border spread surface
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
05:13:47 CST
06:13:47 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is showing signs of slowing in some areas, but grim challenges persist, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) have warned.
"While transmission is going down overall, new hotspots continue to appear, including in areas close to the border with South Sudan," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told a media briefing Wednesday.
According to the latest figures released Wednesday by the DRC health authorities, the outbreak had recorded 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 deaths as of Oct. 6.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, has affected 64 health zones across seven provinces since it was declared in mid-May.
UNEVEN EPIDEMIC TRENDS
On Thursday, Africa CDC reported that confirmed cases had declined by 24 percent in Ituri, the outbreak's epicenter, and 19 percent in North Kivu province over the past three weeks, compared with the previous three-week period.
Wessam Mankoula, an Africa CDC official, cautioned that the declines should be interpreted carefully, as insecurity and community resistance continued to hamper surveillance and reporting in several affected areas.
Of the 64 affected health zones, 47 continued to report active transmission, while 11 had recorded no new cases for more than 42 days, he said.
Community deaths remain a major concern. According to Africa CDC, between 60 and 70 percent of reported Ebola deaths continue to occur outside health facilities, while shortcomings in contact tracing suggest that many infections remain undetected.
"Of course, there is some of the underreporting," Mankoula said, stressing that the official figures did not capture every infection.
Tedros also warned that contact tracing remained below the level required to contain transmission, despite significant improvements in surveillance and community engagement.
CROSS-BORDER SPREAD RAISES CONCERN
The regional threat posed by the outbreak has become increasingly evident following Kenya's confirmation of its first imported Ebola case.
The patient, a 40-year-old Kenyan businessman who had lived in the DRC, developed symptoms in September and sought treatment at several health facilities before traveling to Nairobi on Oct. 3 via Uganda, according to Africa CDC.
Tests later confirmed infection with the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, and he died on Monday.
Kenyan authorities were monitoring 55 contacts, including passengers and crew members aboard the flight from Uganda's capital Kampala to Nairobi, Tedros said Wednesday.
Africa CDC said health authorities from the DRC, Uganda and Kenya had held a joint meeting to reconstruct the patient's travel history and coordinate contact tracing across the three countries.
Both WHO and Africa CDC advised against blanket travel restrictions, emphasizing the importance of screening, early detection, contact tracing and information sharing.
"Transparency should be rewarded, not punished," Tedros said, commending Kenya for promptly reporting the case.
VACCINE, TREATMENT TRIALS ADVANCE
Though no vaccine or treatment specifically approved for Bundibugyo virus disease is currently available, efforts to develop them are making progress.
Africa CDC announced Thursday that Phase Ib clinical trials of a vaccine candidate developed by the University of Oxford had begun in Uganda on Oct. 6, while another candidate developed by Moderna had received ethical approval for Phase Ib trials in the country.
The Africa CDC said the DRC had received 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, which is approved for use against the Zaire Ebola virus but has not been proven effective against the Bundibugyo virus.
Under a protocol-governed compassionate-use program, 7,775 healthcare and other frontline workers had been vaccinated as of Oct. 7. Another 848 frontline workers had received the vaccine under a separate research protocol known as BRAVO, although vaccination under that program has been suspended due to supply shortages.
Clinical trials of experimental treatments are also progressing, with 654 participants enrolled in therapeutic trials, according to Africa CDC.
Tedros said the advances reflected months of work by communities, health authorities and international partners, but warned that the epidemic continued to unfold against the backdrop of a prolonged humanitarian crisis.
According to Africa CDC, the ongoing outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, the second-largest worldwide and the largest ever recorded in the DRC. ■

Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives

Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives
The National Medal of Science is given annually to scientists and engineers for major contributions in their fields.
United States President Donald Trump has awarded the country’s most prestigious honours in science and engineering to executives from top technology firms including SpaceX, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia.
On Thursday, Trump presented the National Medal of Science to billionaire SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Lisa Su of the semiconductor firm AMD.
Two more recipients received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation: Michael Dell of Dell Technologies and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.
At the award ceremony, Trump credited the honourees with “helping pioneer an incredible future for America”.
“Because of these people here, we will always be on top. No one else can compete with us,” Trump said.
Five of the six people receiving medals on Thursday were born outside the US. Four are among the 10 wealthiest people in the world, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
The award ceremony took place hours after the Trump administration announced it was suspending Microsoft and other top tech companies from using the H-1B visa system, which allows companies to hire skilled foreign workers and put them on a path towards permanent residency in the US.
The suspension, officials said, was due to the companies allegedly using the system in a fraudulent manner.
White House builds ties with Silicon Valley
The medal ceremony was the latest example of what critics see as an increasingly close relationship between Silicon Valley tech executives and the second Trump administration.
Powerful companies like Amazon, Meta and Nvidia contributed money to Trump’s second inauguration, and several high-profile industry leaders attended his swearing-in, including Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.
Trump, for his part, has pledged to slash regulations and position the US “as the world leader in artificial intelligence”.
He has also touted self-regulation in the AI industry amid concerns about the safety of the technology.
Several of the tech entrepreneurs honoured on Thursday have forged close ties to the White House, through political and business dealings.
The South Africa-born Musk, for example, was the largest contributor to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and has been a supporter of right-wing causes around the world, which he amplifies on his social media platform, X.
He briefly served as a special adviser to the president during the first months of Trump’s second term, helping to lead the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and its efforts to downsize the federal government.
Around the time he left DOGE, however, Musk and Trump had a public falling-out over the president’s tax-and-spending plans.
The two have since reconciled. On Thursday, Trump hailed Musk as “our modern-day Thomas Edison” and an “industrial titan”, citing his work with the aerospace company SpaceX and the carmaker Tesla.
“Few Americans in history have done more to advance America’s national interest than Elon in one field after another,” Trump said.
Another honouree, Dell, has been a financial backer of the president’s efforts to launch Trump Accounts, a scheme to enrol American children born during Trump’s second term into government-backed investment accounts.
Dell and his wife Susan Dell committed $6.25bn to the programme last year.
Separately, the White House entered into a deal in August for the US government to take a 15 percent cut of any AI chip sales that Nvidia and AMD make with China.
Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder, later invested in the struggling US tech firm Intel. He is reported to be among the donors financing Trump’s plans for a new White House ballroom.
The National Medal of Science was first awarded in 1963 to Theodore von Karman, a pioneer in aerospace engineering who fled anti-Semitism in Europe during World War II.
He went on to help found the Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology.
Nominations for the award are solicited by the National Science Foundation, and the recipients are ultimately selected by a committee appointed by the president.

The Space Force has finished transferring the last of the Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard members covered by the Personnel Management Act that created a hybrid full-time/part-time force.
The last cohort of transfers—Air Force Reservists transitioning to part-time jobs in the Space Force—swore in to their new service on Oct. 1. The main transfer ceremony took place at Los Angeles Air Force Base, Calif., with some service members joining via video teleconference, according to a service release.
Over the past two and a half years, hundreds of Reservists and Guardsmen have transferred into the Space Force as part of the groundbreaking effort to consolidate space-focused units and personnel and create a force with no components that will allow Guardians to transition between full-time and part-time positions with fewer bureaucratic hurdles.
The Space Force Personnel Management Act, passed in late 2023 as part of the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act, laid out the process for those transfers to take place, starting with the Air Force Reserve. A year later, lawmakers voted that space missions in the Air National Guard would also be absorbed by the Space Force instead of creating a separate Space National Guard.
Officials said implementing the Personnel Management Act, or PMA, would be a yearslong process.
In May 2024—before the transfer of Air National Guard space mission into the Space Force was finalized—USSF announced a six-month window for members of the Air Force Reserve to apply to transfer into the new service on a full-time basis. Officials then conducted a series of boards, eventually selecting 380 Reservists for transfer by April 2025.
Then, in August 2025, USSF started accepting applications from Air National Guardsmen to transfer on a full-time basis. Another board selected 99 Guard members in early 2026 for transfer.
Separately, in September 2025, the Space Force announced it was accepting applications for Air Force Reservists to transfer in for part-time positions. In April, the service said it selected 247 individuals to do so, and the first part-time Guardians came aboard in July.
The Oct. 1 transfer ceremony was for the last of the part-time cohort. Guard and Reserve members can still join the Space Force through the prior service program, but the main movement is complete.
“The recently completed transfer cohort represented the final PMA-directed movement of [Air Reserve Component] members in the designated space-mission population,” a Space Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
As part of the transition, the Space Force started assuming the Air National Guard’s space missions on Oct. 1, 2025.
The Space Force never opened a window for Air National Guardsmen to transfer into part-time work roles. The spokesperson noted that USSF “will continue to evaluate manpower requirements and the potential need for subsequent transfer windows as part of the overall growth model.”
The new members serving in a part-time capacity are called Guardians “Not on Sustained Duty.” They will be required to serve the equivalent of at least 36 days—48 four-hour Inactive Duty Training periods and 12 Annual Training days—per year to have a “good year” toward retirement.
The former Reservists and Guardsmen joining the Space Force bring deep experience to the service at a time when it is looking to grow dramatically—that’s important, officials say, to match the coming surge of brand-new Guardians.
Too many new Guardians with little experience entering at the lowest ranks could wreak havoc on the service’s grade structure, Deputy Chief of Space Operations for personnel Katharine Kelley said last month at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
“We’re trying to balance not having all of our accessions be brand new in terms of experience,” she said. “We’re looking for ways to make sure that we can kind of balance this as a sourcing model and a sustainment model for people.”

Counter-Drone Task Force Taps Directed Energy Systems for December Shoot-Off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:04:05 UTC
06:04:05 KST

The Pentagon’s counter-drone task force recently selected four directed energy weapons it will test in a December shoot-off to identify lasers and microwave systems that could defend U.S. military installations from future aerial attacks.
The three laser weapons and one microwave system are the first to be selected for the Joint Interagency Task Force 401’s counter-unmanned aircraft systems directed energy pilot program, according to a Pentagon announcement. The pilot is a congressional requirement in the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act.
“High-energy lasers and high-powered microwave systems are tools that can be effectively used in a layered drone defense,” Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF 401, said in the announcement. “This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland.”
The four weapon systems selected to participate in the shoot-off at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah are:
- AeroVironment’s Palletized High-Energy Laser system
- Epirus’ Leonidas High-Powered Microwave system
- Kord Technologies’ Firefly High-Energy Laser system
- Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon system
In May, JIATF 401 selected Grand Forks Air Force Base, N.D. and Whiteman Air Force Base, Mo.—along with Fort Huachuca, Ariz.; Fort Bliss, Texas; and Naval Base Kitsap, Wash.—to “support rigorous testing and operational assessments across diverse environments” for the pilot effort. U.S. Northern Command and the Federal Aviation Administration are also involved in the pilot, the announcement states.
The announcement of the four systems selected for the shoot-off comes seven months after an incident involving the firing of a military counter-drone laser on the southwest border that prompted the FAA to shut down all flight traffic over El Paso. The Pentagon and the FAA then quickly completed a “data-informed Safety Risk Assessment” of a high-energy laser counter-drone system which found that the counter-drone technology does “not pose undue risk to passenger aircraft.”
Epirus’ Leonidas system is the only high-powered microwave selected for the shoot-off so far. The Army awarded a $43.5 million contract to Epirus in July 2025, which included the delivery of two Integrated Fires Protection Capability High-Power Microwave, or IFPC-HPM Generation II systems, which rely on “weaponized electromagnetic interference” to down drones.
AeroVironment’s Palletized High-Energy Laser system features the firm’s LOCUST X3, a 30-kilowatt system the Army selected in September with a production contract valued at roughly $465 million.
Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon is available in 2-kilowatt and 5-kilowatt versions. The 5-kilowatt system plugged into the Army’s Forward Area Air Defense Command and Control network to defeat Group 3 drones weighing up to 1,320 pounds during the September 2024 Red Sands Integrated Experimentation Center in Saudi Arabia, according to Boeing.
Kord’s Firefly High-Energy Laser is a palletized, mobile system that features scalable power from 5-kilowatts up to 30-kilowatts. It relies on advanced AI detection and tracking algorithms to “detect, track, intercept and defeat incoming drones at standoff ranges,” according to Kord, a subsidiary of KBR.
JIATF 401 plans to evaluate additional directed energy technologies that could be selected to participate in the shoot-off event, according to the announcement.
“Directed energy gives commanders another option within a layered defense, complementing existing counter-UAS capabilities with a scalable, safe, and effective way to respond to drone threats,” Ross said. “This pilot program will give us vital information in a real-world environment so we can employ these systems to protect the homeland.”
The Air Force is looking to up its counter-drone capabilities to defend bases, a mission it refers to as “point defense.” The service’s primary weapon system for doing so is the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon, but officials have declined to identify what that system is. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
It’s unclear how much the service has spent or plans to spend on new counter-drone tech. The Air Force requested more than $1.5 billion for SUADS in the fiscal 2027 budget, most of it for missile defense components, according to budget documents. Additional counter-drone systems are being acquired with the assistance of JIATF 401, but those are not listed in the budget request and both Air Force and JIATF 401 officials have declined to provide funding details.
The Air Force Research Laboratory has experimented with high-powered microwave systems to down drones—in 2023, AFRL used the Tactical High-power Operational Responder, or THOR, to disable a drone swarm.

President Donald Trump's envoys will meet Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss "new ideas" and seek a unified proposal to end the war with Russia, two US sources told AFP news agency.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the talks scheduled to take place on Friday after a day in which a reported Russian strike on buses killed 30 people in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, one of the deadliest attacks in weeks.
"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelenskyy said on Thursday.
"The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."
Zelenskyy said his chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, as well as Ukraine's top officials: Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia will take part in the talks in Florida.
The US-led peace efforts to end the Ukraine war have been largely stalled, with Washington focused on its war with Iran despite Kiev saying Russia has ramped up aerial attacks.
But US officials said they were making a fresh effort in an enlarged format, following visits to Moscow and Kiev by last month by Witkoff, Trump's business friend-turned-roving envoy, and the president's son-in-law Kushner.
"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region," one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.
"The American negotiators also invited national security advisors from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union."
Energy costs
US officials said the envoys would discuss "security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war prosperity plan, and other aspects of the conflict."
They added that the Europeans had expressed "frustrations" to Washington about energy costs — which Trump has blamed on Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel refineries, rather than his Iran war.
"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.
"So, the United States is trying to mediate with the sides with the goal of creating a unified proposal."
Zelenskyy said last week that the United States wanted to revive peace efforts by trying to broker a new round of talks with Ukraine and Russia and hold it by the end of October.
The Kremlin said last month that three-way talks on ending the war could take place in October.
Previous rounds of talks have failed to yield tangible progress towards peace, with Moscow unwilling to drop its maximalist conditions to end the fighting.
Trump said earlier this week that he had a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although it was expected to focus on the reported death of a researcher at a Russian plague lab.
In a sign that Ukraine was under discussion, Witkoff was seen by AFP reporters traveling with Trump on Air Force One on Wednesday on a campaign trip to Texas for the US midterm elections.

Polls close in Holborn and St Pancras byelection as Labour hopes to retain seat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:00:29 UTC
06:00:29 KST

Polls have closed in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a test of whether Andy Burnham can unite Labour’s voters or whether Zack Polanski can peel off support from the party’s progressive flank.
Labour is seeking to retain Keir Starmer’s former north London seat, where he won a majority of more than 11,000 votes in the 2024 general election.
The byelection is seen as a measure of the political landscape under Burnham, almost three months into his premiership.
It is a significant first electoral test for Burnham, who succeeded Starmer in July, as part of a wider battle for younger leftwing voters who became disillusioned with the party under Starmer’s leadership over issues such as housing, the climate crisis and the war in Gaza.
Polanski has sought to run an energetic campaign involving thousands of activists, leaving the Green party conference early after his speech in an attempt to prove he and the Greens are a serious rival to Labour, despite the latest polling.
The Greens are hoping to reproduce their byelection victory in Gorton and Denton in February where they overturned a Labour majority.
However, the political landscape has shifted since then. Shortly after their byelection win in Greater Manchester, YouGov polling put the Greens on 21%, a few points ahead of Labour.
But the latest YouGov survey put the Greens 16 points behind Burnham’s Labour, which was on 27%. The poll came as Burnham proposed a more ambitious pitch to progressives at his first Labour conference as prime minister.
Holborn and St Pancras has a large number of students, younger voters and renters, with almost half of residents aged between 18 and 34, while about 45% were born overseas.
Polanski has argued that electing him would increase pressure on Labour to deliver more radical policies, including stronger rent controls, greater action on the climate crisis and public ownership of Thames Water.
But the leader of the Greens has faced questions about his own authority and was accused of being unable to articulate his thoughts on motions that became policies at his party’s conference.
In an interview with the Guardian last Friday, Polanski described the contest as “probably 50/50” and that it was “really on a knife-edge” while also insisting his leadership did not depend on victory.
Asked whether losing the byelection would undermine his position, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.”
Senior Green figures privately fear a defeat could severely damage his reputation amid concerns the party’s increase in members has not translated into an advantage in campaigning.
Labour has fielded Sagal Abdi-Wali, the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in Britain as a child refugee after her family fled civil war in Somalia.
She has emphasised her longstanding connections to the area, presenting herself as locally rooted, and with experience of community work, homelessness and housing policy.
The closing days of the byelection campaign were overshadowed by a row within the Green party after members voted at their conference to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813 despite opposition from four of the party’s five MPs.
Polanski, who is Jewish, left the conference early to campaign in north London and did not participate in the vote.
As polls closed on Thursday, Burnham said the Green party’s Zionism motion was “completely wrong”.
Speaking to journalists on a trip to Berlin, the prime minister said it showed “terrible judgment on behalf of the Green party” and “shouldn’t be supported in any way, shape or form”.
The Labour leader called on Polanski “to say that it will be reversed and it won’t be Green party policy”, adding: “In my view, all political parties in the UK should do everything they can to support the two-state solution between Israel and Palestine.”
The byelection result may provide some insight into whether Burnham’s recovery in national support is translating into Labour’s inner-city strongholds, and into whether the Greens can continue to attract younger and progressive voters.
It will also offer a test of Polanski’s argument that the Greens can put pressure on the government from the left, even as Labour seeks to reclaim voters it lost under Starmer.
Polls closed at 10pm on Thursday and the result is likely to be announced between 2:30am and 4am on Friday.

EU cyber and science researchers are testing Chinese AI models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:54:20 UTC
05:54:20 KST

BRUSSELS — The European Union's cybersecurity agency and in-house research center have each begun experimenting with open artificial intelligence models from China, three EU officials have told POLITICO.
The Joint Research Centre (JRC) — the EU’s in-house scientific research center — is evaluating “publicly available open-weight models” originating from China, European Commission spokesperson Maciej Berestecki confirmed. The head of ENISA, the bloc's agency responsible for cybersecurity, also said in an interview that his team was now testing Chinese AI.
The experiments with Chinese models at the JRC are part of a broader research project to evaluate artificial intelligence that also includes leading models from the United States and Europe, Berestecki said. “Models from different origins are included in a comparative scientific evaluation of their capabilities, performance, limitations and risks,” he said, adding that the JRC is also looking into their potential scientific applications.
Advertisement
AI safety and security — topics currently under intense scrutiny following a series of incidents in which advanced AI models hacked real-world networks during testing activities — are not the core focus of the JRC’s testing activities, according to a different Commission official, who was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive material.
Open-weight models are those whose core components are publicly released, allowing anyone to run the model and study how it works. China’s approach to AI has leanedmore towards open models than the United States. Some major U.S. tech and AI companies, including chips giant NVIDIA, are investing in open-weight models.
Forced to choose
The U.S. and China are locked in a race to dominate in the technology, with Europe largely sitting on the sidelines. Without a viable European frontier model, European private and public organizations may be left to choose between American and Chinese providers for advanced AI applications.
In a recent speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested Europe should not try to win the frontier AI race. A top German tech company told POLITICO this week it was dropping Europe's leading AI lab Mistral in favor of open-source Chinese models.
The JRC has not entered into any “bespoke access” or licensing negotiations with the relevant Chinese developers, Berestecki said. The models are run on the center’s “secure, on-premises scientific infrastructure” and the Commission is not intending to use Chinese models for its own purposes, he added.
EU cyber agency ENISA — which has gained access to advanced models from top U.S. AI firms Anthropic, OpenAI and Google — is also experimenting with “a couple” of open-weight Chinese models, its executive director Juhan Lepassaar confirmed in an interview on Wednesday.
JRC and ENISA have been tasked with working together to set up an AI testing platform under a recent EU action plan on AI and cyber, the European Commission's attempt to respond to the growing concerns after a series of incidents involving AI systems breaking out of testing environments and breaking into other organizations' digital systems.

AI generated
PARIS – France’s education minister on Oct 8 promised 3,000 substitute teachers for the country’s worst-off high schools, after tens of thousands took to the streets nationwide to demand better education and less police brutality.
Students have blocked entrances to hundreds of high schools for more than a week, with squads of riot police deployed – occasionally resulting in violent clashes.
High school students across the country – most aged 15 to 18 – have complained of absent teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
In a bid to placate the anger, Education Minister Edouard Geffray on the evening news said the teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected of around 3,700 high schools.
The Interior Ministry said 71,500 took part in protests across the country, most outside their schools, with police detaining more than 500 people.
In Paris, where some 24,500 took to the streets, a few fireworks streamed up into the sky as students from schools and universities rallied in Bastille Square.
Crowds of students climbed the famous monument at its centre, some waving the French flag and singing the national anthem.
A student sat with his legs dangling on the top of a bus stop, clutching a sign reading: “Reason for absence: Too busy fighting for our future.”
Jeanne, a 15-year-old student from a top Paris high school, said she wanted to show solidarity with pupils in less privileged areas outside the capital.
“There shouldn’t be people who are more educated than others when we’re all in the public education system,” she said.
Marianne, a 20-year-old university student who also did not want to give her second name, said she objected against excessive police force in recent days of protest.
“For me, that’s just unacceptable,” she said.
‘We want action’
Some demonstrators have started fires and vandalised bus shelters. In response, police have used tear gas, batons and blast balls, prompting rights groups and the children to accuse them of using disproportionate force.
A 15-year-old lost a hand on Oct 5 after police fired a stun grenade, and the government has suspended the use of the weapon.
Police on the evening of Oct 8 said they used tear gas in Bastille to disperse some “high-risk profiles”.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu in a televised address on the evening of Oct 7 promised a plan to respond to the crisis by the end of October.
Although he denied security forces had been given “orders to confront” the protesters, many were unconvinced.
“We don’t want words, we want action,” 17-year-old Camille told AFP at a student march in the western city of Nantes.
Outside one high school in Rennes, 18-year-old Hanaa told AFP she was “disappointed and unconvinced” by Lecornu’s remarks.
‘Fundamental issues’
Assane Seck, father of a 15-year-old student in a Paris suburb, told AFP that at his son’s school, “a teacher in one subject or another is missing” almost every day.
“There are genuine, fundamental issues that deserve reflection,” he said.
Economy Minister Roland Lescure said this week there was room to address demands for more school resources within the highly constrained 2027 budget.
In the current draft, education has the second-largest increase in funding – after defence – with a boost of 1.4% to €90.9 billion (S$130 billion).
A report from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development found that France spends 24% more per student on upper secondary education than the OECD average – but markedly less at earlier stages, particularly primary schools.
The country’s recent PISA score – an annual survey which assesses the performance of education systems by measuring the skills of 15-year-old students – was France’s worst since the rankings began in 2000.
Hundreds of students, police and teaching staff have been injured since the protests began, and thousands of people – mostly children – have been arrested.
The police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct.
The unrest has erupted just months ahead of the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron. AFP

South Africa protests turn violent amid rage over asylum ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:43:34 UTC
05:43:34 KST

South Africa protests turn violent amid rage over asylum ruling
Several cars torched and foreign-run businesses forced to shut in Johannesburg’s Soweto and coastal city of Durban.
Anti-migrant protests in two cities in South Africa have turned violent, with the government blaming disinformation about a court ruling on asylum seekers.
Violence erupted on Thursday in Johannesburg’s Soweto township and the east coast port city of Durban, with two dozens cars set ablaze and foreign-run businesses forced to close, police said.
The unrest followed demonstrations demanding that refugee centres stop processing asylum applications.
Acting National Police Commissioner Lieutenant General Puleng Dimpane on Thursday said 10 vehicles were torched in Johannesburg and 14 in Durban, where three people were arrested.
In Soweto, a Reuters reporter saw residents carrying groceries out of a shop they said was owned by a person from Somalia, whom they chased away. Those residents fled after police arrived.
In Durban, a Reuters reporter saw cars torched in the urban centre, where foreign-owned shops were also looted. AFP reporters in the city said police opened fire with rubber bullets to disperse protesters who reportedly set alight a business run by foreigners.
The protesters are opposed to a July Constitutional Court decision that removes procedural barriers to seeking asylum, including for people who entered South Africa irregularly, lacked asylum transit visas, or missed reporting deadlines.
On Thursday, the government’s Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration held an urgent briefing to address overcrowding at asylum offices after implementing the ruling. A day prior, the committee said all its offices were overwhelmed by the number of incoming applications.
Government spokesperson William Baloyi said the violence was triggered by people spreading deliberately false information about the constitutional court ruling.
Baloyi said the court decision had been widely misrepresented, and that it did not automatically grant refugee status, permanent residence or other legal rights to undocumented migrants.
“We are deeply concerned by what is going on now,” he added.
Months of protests by populist, anti-immigrant groups against undocumented foreign nationals, demanding they leave South Africa, have led tens of thousands to flee, some repatriated by their governments.
Three decades since apartheid ended, South Africa remains deeply unequal and about a third of people are out of work. Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fuelling crime and straining public services, although such claims are not supported by evidence.

American Express fined $US350m for insufficient anti-money laundering program
US bank regulators fined American Express $350 million ($501 million) after they determined the lender's programs to identify potential money laundering were insufficient and the company potentially missed billions of dollars in suspicious activity.
The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Reserve announced the enforcement action on Thursday, saying the company, primarily via its national bank, failed to maintain a sufficient anti-money laundering compliance program, including inadequate resources, inexperienced staff, weak training and internal control gaps.
American Express did not admit or deny the regulators' findings.
The OCC said "systemic breakdowns" in its monitoring and reporting meant the lender failed to identify, evaluate and sufficiently report about $US13 billion in suspicious activity over the past decade.
"The OCC expects banks of American Express’s size and complexity to devote sufficient resources to ensure compliance with laws and regulations designed to detect and prevent money laundering, which are critical to both economic and national security,” said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould in a statement.
The OCC said American Express focused on risks in its relatively narrow deposit products, while not devoting sufficient attention to its much larger credit card business. The regulator also identified shortcomings in customer due diligence and identification programs.
In a statement, American Express CEO Stephen Squeri said the bank was "fully committed" to addressing the concerns and continuing to improve its compliance.
"While we have made meaningful progress, we know there is more work to do," he said.
Mr Squeri also said the penalty and the costs of meeting the regulators' requirements were not expected to affect guidance for 2026 and 2027.

Key Event
Gas prices remain stable due to sufficient supply forecast, new ACCC report finds
Gas buyers on Australia's east coast contracted 51 petajoules (PJ) of gas in the first half of this year for supply in 2027 — more than double the volume contracted compared to the same time in the previous year.
The ACCC's latest Gas Inquiry report has shown commercial and industrial gas users, and other large gas buyers, contracted more gas at this point in the supply cycle than in the previous four years.
Gas buyers contracted 43 PJ of gas for supply in 2028, exceeding volumes contracted at the same stage in either of the past two years, the ACCC said.
Average prices under long-term contracts for 2027 and 2028 supply remained steady at around $12 to $13 per gigajoule (GJ) during the first half of 2026, it added.
"It is encouraging to see gas users securing more gas at broadly stable long-term prices, which is important for business certainty," ACCC Commissioner Anna Brakey said.
The report also shows wholesale gas prices on Australia's east coast appear largely unaffected by elevated international prices.
"Most new gas supply agreements entered into between April and June 2026 were struck at fixed prices rather than linked to international commodity markets," Ms Brakey said.
The ACCC’s next gas inquiry report is scheduled for December 2026.

Two Melbourne-based finance companies and their manager have been ordered to pay more than $470,000 in penalties over "the systematic exploitation of migrant workers and adverse action".

Florida Air Force Bases Evacuate Planes, Personnel as Hurricane Isaias Bears Down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:40:01 UTC
05:40:01 KST

The Air Force has begun evacuating stealth fighters, gunships, and special operations planes ahead of Hurricane Isaias’ expected landfall over the Gulf Coast this weekend.
Severe storms can be devastating for Air Force bases, endangering lives, damaging aircraft and buildings, and battering runways.
As of Oct. 8, three bases in Florida have begun flying out F-35 Lightning IIs, AC-130J Ghostriders, and MC-130J Commando IIs.
Tyndall Air Force Base, Fla.—which was ravaged by Hurricane Michael in 2018—began moving out aircraft Oct. 8 including F-35s from the 325th Fighter Wing, a base spokesman told Air & Space Forces Magazine. Some aircraft were in the air in the morning, the spokesperson said, but the situation remained “fluid,” and it was unclear how many would ultimately fly out. The wing declined to say where the planes were going, citing operational security concerns.
Isaias is currently gathering strength in the Gulf of Mexico, with maximum sustained winds increasing to nearly 85 miles per hour, the National Hurricane Center said Oct. 8. That qualifies as a Category 1 hurricane, but the center’s forecast predicted Isaias’ winds could reach 110 miles per hour, or near Category 3 strength, over the next 24 hours.
Isaias is expected to hit the United States’ northern Gulf Coast sometime between late Oct. 9 and early Oct. 10, the center said. Parts of Alabama, Georgia, and the Florida panhandle could also face tornadoes.
“Isaias is expected to remain a dangerous hurricane through landfall, and gusty winds are expected well inland after landfall,” the center said. “A life-threatening storm surge is expected from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Suwannee, Florida.”
Bases in the region are on guard. Tyndall moved to Hurricane Condition 2 status on Oct. 8, meaning destructive winds of 58 miles per hour or greater were possible over the next 24 hours. Tyndall also limited installation access to mission-essential personnel, residents, and other authorized personnel, and facilities such as child care centers, the fitness center, and the commissary began closing throughout Oct. 8.
Another Florida installation, Eglin Air Force Base, flew its airworthy aircraft—including planes assigned to the 96th Test Wing, 53rd Wing, and 33rd Fighter Wing—to safer locations on Oct. 8. Aircraft that could not fly were placed in hangars for protection.
Civilian authorities in the Eglin region have also ordered some residents to evacuate. Eglin commander Col. Chris Keithley issued his own limited evacuation order for service members, Pentagon employees, and dependents living in certain parts of Okaloosa County, Fla., authorizing them to be reimbursed for their evacuation travel and saying they are not to return until directed to do so.
Eglin’s 96th Medical Group Hospital and pharmacies closed, but emergency operations, labor and delivery, and inpatient services remain open, the base said.
“The safety of our Airmen, their families, and our community is our highest priority,” Keithley said in a statement. “As we prepare for the potential impacts of Hurricane Isaias, we are taking proactive steps to protect our people and aircraft entrusted to our care. Relocating our aircraft is a deliberate decision that reflects our responsibility to be good stewards of taxpayer resources while preserving our ability to execute the mission.”
The home of Air Force Special Operations Command, Hurlburt Field, Fla., moved to Hurricane Condition 3 on Oct. 7 and limited base access to mission-essential personnel.
A spokesperson for Hurlburt also told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the base’s 1st Special Operations Wing had started flying out its AC-130s and MC-130s.
The wing commander also ordered roughly 1,000 Hurlburt residents in privatized military housing to evacuate by 5 p.m. on Oct. 8. Hurlburt said it doesn’t expect the storm surge to reach or damage housing structures, but that rising water levels could inundate a critical station that would interrupt vital wastewater, sewage, and potable water services.
Almost eight years ago, Tyndall was wrecked by Hurricane Michael when the Category 5 storm struck on Oct. 10, 2018. Aircraft that were not able to be flown out beforehand—including F-22 Raptor fighters—were damaged, some beyond repair, when their hangars were hit, and numerous buildings sustained damage that the Air Force called “catastrophic” at the time. Tyndall took years to recover, and its F-22 operations moved first to Eglin before ultimately settling at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Va..
In March 2019, Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska experienced severe flooding, caused by the combination of a bomb cyclone’s violent weather and the melting of record snowfall. Those floods left dozens of buildings and much of Offutt’s flightline partially submerged, and prompted the base to evacuate several aircraft.
News Editor Greg Hadley contributed to this report.

Cuba says US lacks authority to restrict trade with island nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:38:08 UTC
05:38:08 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said Thursday that the US lacks the authority to decide which countries or companies can sell fuel, trade or invest in Cuba, arguing that Washington's measures also target the wider international community.
“The US government has no authority whatsoever to decide who can and cannot trade fuel or any other product with Cuba, invest in our country or help our people,” Rodriguez said on the US social media platform X.
Rodriguez said Washington lacks both the “practical and moral authority” to determine what is legal under international law and the rules of free trade.
He accused countries and companies that comply with US restrictions of becoming “accomplices” in what he described as the “collective punishment” of the Cuban people.
Rodriguez said Washington's measures are directed not only against Cuba but also against other members of the international community that maintain commercial or economic ties with the island.
The Cuban foreign minister also accused Washington of seeking to impose a naval blockade and an “energy siege” against the island.
He said the US has no right to stop or inspect vessels in international waters or take military action against ships based on what Washington considers suspicious activity.
Rodriguez further accused the US of seeking to “usurp” sovereign resources and territories belonging to other countries, without providing details.
Cuba has repeatedly criticized US sanctions and trade restrictions, which Havana refers to as a blockade, arguing that they have a broader impact on the Cuban economy and population.
Washington has maintained extensive economic restrictions on Cuba for decades and has imposed additional measures in recent years targeting Cuban state entities and other sectors of the economy.
The latest dispute comes as Cuba faces shortages of fuel and other essential goods, while Havana has increasingly focused its criticism on measures it says restrict the island's ability to obtain energy supplies from abroad.
Rodriguez concluded by saying Cuba is protected by international law and rejected the legitimacy of the US measures.

Afghan women facing arrest for dress code violations: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:37:00 UTC
05:37:00 KST

Afghan women facing arrest for dress code violations: UN
October 8, 2026
At least 52 women and one girl were arrested or detained in the Afghan cities of Herat and Kabul between July and September of 2026, according to a statement released by the United Nations on Thursday.
"Women were detained for not wearing a chador [an all-enveloping, cloak-like garment], having visible hair, wearing colourful scarves or makeup, or being in public without a mahram [male chaperone]," the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said.
According to the mission, the detained women were released after being held for several hours. It also warned that the number of cases could be higher due to underreporting.
UNAMA said it was "gravely concerned" by the arrests, detentions, and threats of arrest.
The mission stated that the detentions violate women's and girls' rights to freedom of movement, expression, and autonomy. The detentions also expose them to severe social stigma in traditional Afghan society, UNAMA said.
In June, Afghan authorities opened fire on a rare protest in Herat over the arrests and detentions of women for alleged dress code violations. According to witnesses and the UN mission, at least one person was killed and several others were injured.
What restrictions do women in Afghanistan face?
Since seizing power in 2021 as US-led forces withdrew from Afghanistan, the Taliban government has imposed severe restrictions on women and girls, including banning them from attending school beyond the primary level and limiting what they can wear and where they can go.
In public, women must wear a full hijab, which includes a headscarf, a long robe that covers the body, and a face covering. The Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice enforces these rules.
Earlier this week, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued four arrest warrants for senior Taliban officials, accusing them of committing crimes against humanity by systematically depriving women and girls in Afghanistan of their rights.
Hovewer, the Taliban rejected the decision, calling it a politically motivated violation of Afghanistan's sovereignty.

SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir High Court ordered Thursday revival of Kashmir student’s passport so that she can complete her MBBS in Iran.The authorities had impounded Ibra Khan’s passport based on a CID adverse report about an FIR against her father in 1997, although she was born in 2005. The report cited “aspersions” against Khan’s father in relation to the case and “apprehensions that she may join anti-India forces”.“This court has the highest concern towards the security of the country. In a very limited intervention and keeping in view that the appellant (student) has completed half her MBBS, we dispose of the appeal by directing that the passport be revived for the remaining period of her course,” a division bench of Chief Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal said.Khan is pursuing MBBS at Tehran University of Medical Sciences. She was issued a passport in Oct 2024 but received showcause notices March 27, 2026 and April 9, 2026 from passport authorities over her father’s case before her passport was impounded on May 4, 2026.Khan moved the HC but a single-judge bench dismissed her petition saying it found no reason to interfere in the decision by authorities and citing an alternative remedy of appeal under Passports Act, 1967.
Khan then approached the division bench. Her counsel Salih Pirzada argued that she began pursuing MBBS in 2024 but owing to the prevailing turmoil in the region, she returned to India. It was during this period that she received the notices, followed by the passport’s impounding without clear reasons.
J&K’s additional advocate-general (AAG) cited the adverse CID report and claimed Khan had not replied to the show-cause notices, leaving authorities with no alternative but to impound the passport.Following this, the division bench of Justices Bhati and Nargal called for the CID report, which cited the case against Khan’s father and “apprehensions” about the security and sovereignty of the country.Khan’s counsel Pirzada contended that the state had not been able to pinpoint the reasons for such apprehensions given that the case against her father dated to 1997 whereas she herself was born eight years later.The division bench eventually allowed Khan’s appeal by ordering the passport’s revival, saying the authorities were free to impose conditions and directing her to comply with any such riders.

One Palestinian killed, dozens injured during Israeli settler attacks on West Bank olive harvest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:23:22 UTC
05:23:22 KST

The third anniversary of October 7 was a bloody one for Palestinians in the West Bank, with a Palestinian killed and 16 injured amidst a spree of attacks by Israeli settler mobs, as well as raids and road closures by the Israeli army.
Settler attacks targeted Palestinians harvesting their olives in the villages surrounding Nablus, including Beita, Beit Imrin, Sebastia, and Al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya, where settlers planted Israeli flags along the entrance to the village. In the Ramallah area, settlers torched a car used by Israeli-Russian journalist and activist Andrei Kharzhanovsky and American journalist Jasper Nathaniel. In Aqraba, east of Nablus, Israeli settlers beat the AFP photojournalist Jaafar Ishtayeh, seriously injuring him and requiring him to receive hospital treatment.
The wave of settler attacks turned fatal in the town of Burqa, northwest of Nablus, when settlers opened fire on Palestinians harvesting their olives in the village groves and in the neighboring Ramin plain on their privately-owned lands, killing 44-year-old Ali Hassan Bazzari and injuring and wounding nine others. Bazzari was the father of four children, the oldest aged 17, and the youngest only 18 months old. He served as an officer in the Palestinian security forces and volunteered in the local emergency committee in Burqa.
Abu Bilal Bazzari, a Palestinian man in his fifties, was one of the wounded in the attack and an eyewitness to the killing of his cousin, Ali Hassan Bazzari. He told Mondoweiss that “the family had gone to the Ramin plain early in the morning, as we do every year.” That was when they encountered the group of settlers on their land.
“Without any context or warning, they began to threaten and harass us,” Abu Bilal said, adding that his family did not leave the groves despite the settlers’ harassment, but the settlers did not back down.
“They made some calls, and soon another group of around eight settlers arrived, and they started to assault us violently. One of them hit me with a club on the head, and my brother, his wife, and another cousin were injured, too, but more settlers kept arriving.”
According to Abu Bilal, Israeli forces arrived at the scene after more Palestinians showed up to fend off the settlers. Ali, Abu Bilal said, was among those who responded to the calls for help, only to be shot by an Israeli soldier upon his arrival. “He was wounded, but the Israeli forces blocked access to anybody from the village trying to reach the location, including the ambulance, and eventually Ali bled to death,” he said.
Israeli media said that one Israeli settler was injured during the clashes, quoting the Israeli army saying that a soldier “neutralized” Ali Hassan Bazzari after he ran at him carrying a “suspicious object.”
Palestinian anti-settlement activist and resident of Burqa, Ghassan Daghlas, told Mondoweiss that people in the villages surrounding Nablus, including Burqa, have historically relied on income from working inside Israel, but after October 2023, Israel revoked all work permits for Palestinians in these areas. “For them, the olive harvest is their only opportunity to secure some extra income to sustain themselves,” Daghlas said. “They will continue to try to go to their groves despite the threats by settlers, because they have no other choice.”
Ahead of the third anniversary of October 7, the Israeli army announced a complete closure of the West Bank between the fifth and seventh days of the month, while Palestinians reported settlers rallying online group chats to storm Palestinian roads and villages. Checkpoints connecting Ramallah to the surrounding villages and to the northern West Bank were closed in both directions. Many Palestinians reported waiting for hours at the checkpoints of Atara, north of Ramallah, Nabi Saleh, west of the city, and Deir Jarir, in the villages east of Ramallah.
This is the fourth year in a row that the Palestinian olive harvest season is disrupted in the West Bank, exacerbated by the over 150 new settler outposts that have been established on Palestinian lands, dozens of which continue to be legalized by the Israeli government. According to the Palestinian Settlements and Wall Resistance Commission, Israel has confiscated over 64,000 dunams (6,400 hectares) of Palestinian land in the West Bank since October 2023.

‘Nothing will stop us’: French student protests show few signs of ending
Students on Thursday barricaded a Parisian high school with garbage bins before police shot tear gas at them as France’s nationwide protests showed little sign of ending. At least a dozen demonstrations supporting the high school students’ movement were planned across the country while 375 schools were fully or partially closed.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Students barricaded a high school in northeastern Paris with garbage bins on Thursday before police moved in with tear gas, as France’s nationwide protests showed few signs of ending.
The Hélène Boucher high school has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital and was one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protests Thursday. Riot police gathered in side streets as students converged on the school. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid being recognized.
Read moreLive: French government vows to boost teacher numbers in bid to ease school crisis
At least a dozen demonstrations supporting the high school students’ movement were planned across France later in the day, including a rally at Place de la Bastille in Paris, where tear gas and a water cannon were fired at protesters.
Police have made more than 6,600 arrests since late September, when students, most of them under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, according to the interior ministry. The education ministry said 375 schools were fully or partially closed Thursday.
Pressure mounts on government
While the number of school closures was down compared to Tuesday, pressure is mounting on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
The protests against the underfunding of schools – many of them struggling with dilapidated facilities and insufficient staff – have drawn troublemakers not concerned about the aims of the protest movement as well as unions and political groups.
In a TV address, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lamented the “violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalized, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults”.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
He took aim at “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles”. France goes to the polls for a presidential election in April. “We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth”, Lecornu said.
At the lycée, 18-year-old university student Emma Khelil came to offer support to those at the barricades at her former high school. She told The Associated Press that she’s really concerned about police violence.
“We’re here to defend our rights, not to lose an eye or a hand,” Khelil said. She also said that she had noticed insulation problems and water leaks in the school building and had even seen rats on occasion. Other students confirmed that they’d seen rats too.
Read more'We're fed up': Paris students rise up in a movement that shows no sign of slowing
She was not convinced by Lecornu’s efforts to calm the situation.
“I don’t think the movement is going to lose momentum. As long as things don’t change, we’re going to see the movement grow stronger, and potentially a convergence of struggles, especially with the next presidential election coming up,” she said.
Not long after she spoke, police surrounded a nearby square. The crowd surged, and tear gas was fired.
‘Nothing will stop us’
Smoke from burning garbage nearby hung in the air at Place de la République as hundreds of high school and university students prepared to march toward Place de la Bastille, the demonstration’s focal point.
Some carried signs bearing their schools’ names; others held placards reading “More money for repression than for our education”, and “Who protects us from the police?”
“We’re here, we’re demonstrating, and we won’t stop. Until October, November, December if necessary. Nothing will stop us,” said Sofia Ferdials, 18, a student at Paris 8 University.
Dounia Gergeon, a 39-year-old school librarian, said she joined the demonstration at Place de la Bastille because she shared students’ concerns and worried about a broader crisis facing young people anxious about their futures. At the middle and high school where she works, time was set aside for students to discuss their demands.
“They do not feel supported,” she said. “They feel cornered and forced to work under these conditions.”
Authorities deployed tear gas and a water cannon at the protesters, some of whom hurled projectiles at riot police.
Read moreWhat France's student protesters want – and what the government is offering
Protests in Belgium and Italy
France is not the only country to be dealing with student-related protests.
In Belgium, Willy Demeyer, the mayor of Liege, issued a ban on public gatherings until midnight on Oct. 16, citing a “real, serious and imminent risk” of further clashes and vandalism.
City police said they used water cannon and tear gas on Wednesday to hold back several hundred protesters. Authorities sent emergency text messages advising shopkeepers to close due to rioting.
Nearly 90 people were arrested and several police were injured. Police reinforcements were sent from the capital, Brussels, and from Antwerp, and more are coming. Smaller protests have been held in Mons and Charleroi.
Belgium’s Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said on social media that the “perpetrators will have to answer for their actions before the courts”.
The Belgian protests, organised through online chat groups, include demands for more teachers and smaller classes as well as complaints about education reform in Belgium, but are also likely inspired by events in France.
Student protests have spread to several Italian cities, though on a much smaller scale and over a broader set of domestic grievances. Activists have explicitly invoked the French movement with the slogan “let’s do as they do in France”, while organising school occupations, assemblies and marches.
In Turin, students occupied several high schools over building conditions, education funding and increased military spending. In Rome, students occupied one high school and walked out of another, while students in Naples added opposition to a planned migrant detention centre to their demands.

Saudi nursery hit by debris as Houthis target Riyadh airport
Unknown

2026-10-08

Breadcrumb
Saudi nursery hit by debris as Houthis target Riyadh airport
The Saudi civil defence agency said a kindergarten and a medical complex in Riyadh were damaged by debris from a missile interception on Thursday, as Yemen's Houthis announced attacks targeting the capital's airport.
Two witnesses said that a plane at the airport belonging to national flag carrier Saudia had cracks and holes in its fuselage. A source briefed on the matter said three planes suffered damage.
Saudi Arabia leads a pro-government coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen's civil war. The Iran-backed group has repeatedly targeted Riyadh since the conflict roared back to life in July, vowing to hit critical infrastructure and disrupt Saudi airspace.
The scale and frequency of the attacks on the Saudi capital have been unprecedented in the eight months of wider war in the Middle East.
The Houthis announced three attacks on Thursday against Riyadh airport. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group also launched missiles at an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
Recent attacks have also targeted oil infrastructure in the world's largest crude exporter.
The Houthis on Thursday warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted two missiles fired towards Riyadh.
The kingdom's civil defence agency said "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in the city. It did not say if there were casualties or provide details of the damage.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Shelter in place
After resuming their fight against Yemen's internationally recognised government following a four-year lull, the Houthis last month seized all of the country's Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive.
The group, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014. Riyadh's military coalition intervened in 2015 to support the government.
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to roll back the Houthis' advance, despite an ambitious counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory, including the area around a crucial sea route for global energy flows.
In Riyadh, diplomats were instructed to shelter at their respective embassies, some of them told AFP, after explosions echoed around the city on Thursday morning.
There were no text alerts warning residents, as there had been in the past.
An interior ministry campaign has repeatedly warned residents against sharing unauthorised information, images or footage of missiles, drones and their impacts, warning that violators of legal consequences.
Several residents told AFP that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
"My daughter called me," one parent told AFP on condition of anonymity, saying she was "completely distraught".
Two people working in Riyadh's business hub, the King Abdullah Financial District, told AFP that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
'Heightened vigilance'
Numerous flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, according to information posted for passengers.
The airport did not immediately acknowledge disruption, pointing only in a short statement to the "necessity" of contacting airlines before travelling.
The United States urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to "exercise heightened vigilance" following the attacks at the airport, which US government employees now need "special authorisation" to use.
Previous attacks killed a Sudanese national at Riyadh airport, as well as an Egyptian and an Algerian national at Abha airport, civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
A humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
After declaring its counter-offensive, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides have not reported any major changes on the ground.
The rival claims have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
The Houthis recently seized areas south of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, cutting it off from the government's temporary capital in Aden and sparking shortages and soaring prices for food and energy.

Ukrainian strikes blast Russian frigates at Novorossiysk
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:19:50 BST
05:19:50 KST

A single Ukrainian drone attack on Novorossiysk has significantly degraded the land-attack cruise missile capability of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, accounting for forty per cent of its Kalibr-capable surface ships, according to a Defence Intelligence update published by the UK Ministry of Defence.
In its update on Thursday, Defence Intelligence said: “Ukraine has launched two large scale uncrewed aerial system (UAS) attacks against the Russian Novorossiysk Naval Facility and Commercial Port within the last two months. The 08-09 September 2026 attack led to successful strikes against a GRIGOROVICH class frigate and a SVIYAZHSK light-frigate.”
It went on: “Both vessels have likely sustained sufficient damage to prevent them taking part in KALIBR Land-attack Cruise Missile (LACM) firings into Ukraine, likely for the short-medium term. This single attack has significantly degraded the LACM strike capabilities of the Black Sea Fleet, representing 40% of the KALIBR-capable surface fleet.”
Two ships out of action amounting to two fifths of the capability says as much about the size of the remaining fleet as it does about the damage. Russia has been firing Kalibr missiles at Ukrainian cities and infrastructure from Black Sea platforms since the opening days of the full-scale invasion, and the surface ships able to carry them have never been numerous.
The Admiral Grigorovich class are Project 11356R frigates, the newest conventional surface combatants the Black Sea Fleet has, each able to carry Kalibr in a vertical launch system. Defence Intelligence describes the second vessel as a Sviyazhsk light-frigate, a smaller Kalibr-armed surface combatant.
Ukrainian strikes drove Russian warships out of Sevastopol over the course of 2023 and 2024, and the Krasnodar Krai port became the main operating base for what remained. Pushing the fleet east was supposed to put it beyond easy reach.
Defence Intelligence uses a probability yardstick in which “likely” sits between 55 and 75 per cent, so the assessment that both ships cannot take part in Kalibr firings is a confident judgement without being a certainty. The phrase short to medium term carries no fixed definition, though repairs to a vertical launch system and the surrounding structure on a frigate are not quick work, particularly in a yard under periodic attack.
UK Defence Intelligence publishes its guidance on the use of probabilistic language at this link.
