Major League Baseball proposes shortening its regular season as it pushes for a salary cap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:16:21 UTC
05:16:21 KST

Major League Baseball proposed shortening its regular season to 154 games from 162 as it attempts to convince players to approve a salary cap in the league's next collective bargaining agreement. The new shortened schedule would begin in 2029.
MLB's CBA expires Dec. 1, after the conclusion of this season's World Series. The most contentious issue is the introduction of a salary cap on players. MLB is the only major American sports league without a cap. The league has failed to convince the players' union to adopt one in several previous CBA negotiations.
A 154-game season was used between 1904 and 1960, except for 1918 and 1919 when the schedule was abbreviated because of World War I. For the past 66 years, 162 regular season games has been the standard, though some seasons have been shortened. Lopping off eight games "is good for player health, while also creating a new national broadcast window to showcase our most exciting teams and players," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "A shorter regular season unlocks making October even better for our fans — with fewer weekday afternoon games, a longer Division Series, and more opportunities to see the game's best pitchers on the biggest stage."
As part of the proposal, MLB wants to cement Monday as an exclusive broadcast window for one or two games to "increase national exposure for the sport." The league could conceivably sell a package of Monday-only games to a streaming service looking to increase subscriber and advertising revenue. Every team not playing in the national game or games would have an off day. Teams that play Monday would be off on Thursday, MLB said.
In addition to lowering the number of regular season games, MLB would extend the divisional round of the playoffs to seven games from five and would allow the higher-seeded teams in both the wild card round and in the divisional round to choose their lower-seeded opponent.
The Major League Baseball Players Association responded to the MLB's proposed changes by claiming the league "once again made clear that all of its proposals are contingent on players' agreement to a salary cap, a system that guts player rights and compensation, as well as its other anti-player proposals."
An MLB spokesperson confirmed that Thursday's proposed changes are contingent on adopting a cap – and a salary floor, which would force teams to spend a certain amount on players. Still, the MLBPA said it would review the proposed changes. "Players will weigh in on these proposals and we will respond at the bargaining table," MLBPA said in a statement.

As Jane Norman first reported, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has just confirmed the delay of the implementation of the ATO's controversial credit card ban.
The tax office announced last week it would stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills from December, in response to the Reserve Bank's ban on credit card surcharges.
It justified the move saying it would cost $200 million a year to absorb the fees.
But after pressure from small businesses, Chalmers says the government has "stepped in" to ensure the transition period is extended.

Why a Starbucks takeover of Chipotle would — and wouldn't — make sense for both companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:12:33 UTC
05:12:33 KST

Starbucks has reportedly explored buying Chipotle Mexican Grill, but investors are split on whether the megadeal would make sense for both companies.
The coffee giant has been working with advisers on a takeover proposal of the fast-casual chain in recent months, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.
If Starbucks bought Chipotle, it would combine two of the largest U.S. restaurant chains. With about $31 billion in annual domestic sales, Starbucks is the second-biggest U.S. chain by sales. Chipotle sits in the number seven spot, with more than $11 billion in annual system-wide sales in its home market.
The report sent Chipotle stock up about 6% on Thursday, while shares of Starbucks fell slightly after dropping more sharply earlier in the day. It is not unusual for deal rumors to lower the potential acquirer's value and increase the target's share price, but investor reactions show that a prospective takeover comes with pros and cons for each side of the deal.
To be sure, it is unclear if Starbucks will even pursue the takeover. D.A. Davidson analyst Matt Curtis wrote in a note to clients on Thursday that he views the odds of a deal being completed as "relatively low" — about 20%.
A Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC that the company does not comment on rumors and speculation. Chipotle did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
Why it makes sense:
1. The Niccol connection
Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol knows more than a thing or two about Chipotle.
Before joining the coffee company in 2024, he was chief executive of Chipotle for more than six years. He led a turnaround of the burrito chain, helping it bounce back from a series of foodborne illness outbreaks that had turned into a full-blown crisis for the company.
In the wake of Niccol's departure, traffic to Chipotle restaurants fell in 2025, as budget-conscious consumers visited its restaurants less often. These days, the chain looks like it is starting to get back on track, with signs of "encouraging progress," Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said on the company's earnings conference call in late July.
Still, its shaky 2025 means that the stock is trading at a 20% discount from a year ago, even with Thursday's big move. And since Niccol left, shares have lost about 40% of their value.
2. Building the next Yum
Chipotle would be a splashy acquisition for Niccol. More than that, it could create a new restaurant conglomerate, following in the footsteps of Yum Brands, Restaurant Brands International and Roark Capital-backed Inspire Brands.
Multi-brand restaurant companies are more diversified, which can be more attractive to investors. While Starbucks is still a much larger chain than Chipotle, the difference in their categories means that one's poor performance could be offset by growth at the other.
Moreover, Starbucks could help Chipotle grow more quickly in international markets; the burrito chain only has about 100 locations outside of the U.S., while Starbucks has about 23,000.
Other restaurant companies have set a blueprint for that strategy: Yum has leaned on its international experience from KFC and Pizza Hut to launch Taco Bell outside of the U.S. And Restaurant Brands has leaned on Burger King's international expertise to grow Popeyes' international footprint.
3. Potential synergies
With any strategic acquisition, investors hope for synergies that justify the price tag and explain why the deal makes sense. A coffee shop and a burrito restaurant do not have much overlap in ingredients, but there are other potential benefits for both companies and their investors.
Combining Starbucks and Chipotle would open up potential cost cuts, like layoffs for some now-redundant corporate roles.
The two chains also have significant overlap in their U.S. real estate footprints. Roughly 90% of Chipotle restaurants are within one mile of a Starbucks cafe, according to a research note from Stephens analyst Jim Salera published on Thursday. Both companies could benefit from shared real estate development and even operating efficiencies as a result.
But real estate is not the only area where they overlap. Many Starbucks customers also frequent Chipotle restaurants. As one entity, they could leverage that overlap through a combined rewards program, Salera suggested.
4. Alignment in business model
Unlike many big restaurant players, both Chipotle and Starbucks operate most of their U.S. locations, although Starbucks also has thousands of licensed cafes in its home market.
That marks a difference from Chipotle's last strategic owner — McDonald's.
The burger giant, which franchises the vast majority of its U.S. restaurants, made a majority investment in the upstart Mexican-inspired chain in 1998. But by 2006, McDonald's divested its ownership. Its restaurant investments, which also included Boston Market, were labeled a distraction by Wall Street as the Golden Arches struggled.
Before it sold its stake, McDonald's tried to franchise some of Chipotle's restaurants to its own franchisees. But Chipotle's leadership, including founder Steve Ells, pushed back. It was one sign of the cultural misalignment between the two brands.
Chipotle also resisted efforts to make it more similar to McDonald's, declining suggestions like adding drive-thru windows and a breakfast menu.
Why it doesn't make sense:
1. Starbucks' ongoing turnaround
Niccol joined Starbucks more than two years ago to lead a turnaround of the embattled coffee chain. Early signs show that his efforts have improved its U.S. business — but the company is not done yet. Starbucks is aiming to be "the world's greatest customer service company," Niccol wrote in a memo to employees in September, part of a broader push to improve customer loyalty.
Starbucks also has other deals that it is reportedly considering. In September, Reuters reported that the company was considering selling a majority stake in its Japan business. The country has been the chain's largest overseas company-operated market since it formed a joint venture to operate its cafes in China less than a year ago.
Integrating a new chain into the company would be a big distraction for Starbucks at a time when many investors think it should still be focusing on itself.
"Starbucks is still executing its turnaround strategy, and acquiring Chipotle could consume significant senior management time on financing, integration, organizational design, systems, and personnel," BTIG analyst Pete Saleh wrote in a note. "Why introduce another major strategic initiative before demonstrating that Starbucks can deliver sustainable margin recovery?"
2. The price tag
Starbucks' turnaround has also been expensive, which hasn't pleased investors.
The company has been investing heavily in labor, cafe makeovers and store equipment to improve its service and the overall customer experience. Even layoffs and store closures, which will cut costs in the long term, have weighed on its quarterly earnings.
But Chipotle would be an even bigger expense. Even with shares' recent struggles, the company still has a market cap of roughly $42 billion. If Starbucks pursues the acquisition, it would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover.
Starbucks had about $9.4 billion in debt at the end of June. William Blair analyst Sharon Zackfia estimated that its leverage would balloon to about six times if the company paid a 20% premium and sought to finance the potential deal primarily through debt. An all-stock deal would not weigh on earnings as much, although Zackfia estimates it would still dilute earnings per share by about 10%.
3. Niccol's experience
At Chipotle and Starbucks, Niccol was tasked with turning around struggling restaurants. But his corporate experience so far has not prepared him for a deal of this size.
Merging two colossal restaurant companies would be a massive undertaking, potentially at the expense of the individual success of both brands.
Two-brand restaurant companies often struggle to keep both operating with same-store sales growth, Citi Research analyst Jon Tower wrote in a note to clients. Additionally, he said internal employees usually gravitate toward the brand that is perceived to perform better or offer more career opportunities.
While the size of the deal makes the takeover unique, the restaurant industry already has plenty of examples of mergers and takeovers that did not work for either party.
The latest example comes from Jack in the Box, which bought Del Taco in a $585 million deal in 2022. At the time that the deal was announced, executives said it was "strategically and financially compelling."
During the period that Jack in the Box officially owned Del Taco, shares of the company cratered 73%. The burger chain shuttered dozens of locations as its sales struggled. And Del Taco reported even worse results, including more than a year straight of quarterly same-store sales declines.
More than three years later, Jack in the Box sold Del Taco to a franchisee for about $119 million.

Merz turned into ‘Ukrainian chancellor’ – Moscow
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has effectively become a “Ukrainian chancellor,” showering Kiev with more taxpayer-funded aid despite mounting discontent at home, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has said.
Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Zakharova criticized Merz’s visit to Kiev on Sunday, during which he pledged billions in additional assistance, including funding for long-range weapons production. The announcement came amid plunging support for his governing coalition and a series of electoral setbacks for his Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Zakharova suggested that Merz was so eager to escape his domestic troubles that he “practically fled from the festivities in Bremen” marking the 36th anniversary of German reunification.
“The new face in Ukrainian politics, [or] a ‘Ukrainian chancellor’ as Merz has been dubbed in German political circles, didn’t come empty-handed – he announced yet another generous gift to his ‘friend’, Zelensky,” she said sarcastically.
German taxpayers will foot the bill, Zakharova argued, suggesting that Merz was deliberately adding to their burden despite growing public dissatisfaction with his policies.
She also questioned whether the chancellor could genuinely be unaware of Ukraine’s rampant corruption, pointing to a series of high-profile scandals involving Vladimir Zelensky’s inner circle and senior officials.
Zakharova cited a September survey by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology (KIIS), in which 50% of respondents identified corruption as the country’s most pressing problem. Some 72% said graft had worsened since the escalation of the conflict with Russia in 2022, while the same proportion blamed Zelensky and his associates.
Given what she described as Kiev’s efforts to suppress dissent, Zakharova argued that the findings were particularly revealing.
“Ukraine is so mired in corruption that it has become impossible to cover up its real scale by any means,” she said.
Merz has faced similar criticism from German opposition politicians. In July, Alternative for Germany (AfD) lawmaker Markus Frohnmaier told RT’s Rick Sanchez that Merz “is the chancellor of Ukraine and not the chancellor of Germany.”
Veteran left-wing politician Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), has likewise accused Merz of turning “his own citizens into cash cows for Ukraine.”
Meanwhile, an INSA poll published earlier this month put support for Merz’s CDU/CSU alliance at a record low of 18%, compared with 30% for the AfD, which remains Germany’s most popular party.
The chancellor’s Christian Democrats also suffered successive electoral defeats last month in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The CDU finished a distant second in Saxony-Anhalt with 17.5% of the vote and failed to clear the electoral threshold in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, securing just 4.9%.
Despite the setbacks, Merz, who has previously criticized Germans for not working enough hours, has refused to change course.

The conference will present the framework for examining acts of bravery and sacrifice carried out by IDF personnel during the fighting on the day of the massacre.
“The purpose of the process is to provide appropriate recognition for extraordinary acts of heroism carried out during the battles, thereby preserving and passing on the legacy of battlefield courage to future generations,” the IDF said.
The military added that the process would be conducted “meticulously, with close examination of the details and accuracy of the facts, and with sensitivity and transparency.”
The IDF also will address acts of heroism by civilians during the October 7 battles. Cases involving exceptional civilian bravery that are deemed appropriate will be referred to the advisory committee to the president, under the existing mechanism for awarding the President’s Civilian Bravery Award.
“Additional appropriate cases referred to the President’s Residence will also be examined by the committee, as were the cases brought before it until now,” the IDF said.
The launch follows months of public criticism over the prolonged delay in formally recognizing soldiers who fought in the battles to halt the Hamas assault.
In July last year, ynet reported that the military planned to establish a committee to examine thousands of recommendations that had accumulated from units in the field, but the process was delayed.
The IDF repeatedly said it could not move forward until its in-depth operational investigations into the October 7 battles had been completed. The process also was delayed by the ground campaign in Lebanon and the fighting against Iran. With those investigations now gradually reaching completion, the military says the awards committee can finally begin its work.
Throughout the war, some officials also voiced concern over possible political interference in decisions determining who would receive military commendations and decorations.
The precise timetable for presenting the final candidates and awarding the honors remains unclear. The IDF says the committee’s work will be thorough and is not expected to be completed quickly.

Syria reopened the historic Great Umayyad Mosque in the northern city of Aleppo on Thursday, 13 years after it was taken out of service following extensive damage during the country's civil war.
Aleppo Governor Azzam al-Gharib attended the reopening ceremony, according to state-run Alikhbariah TV.
“Today, we are honored to reopen one of the houses of God, restoring Aleppo's great mosque after difficult years in which it was subjected to destruction,” al-Gharib said.
He said the mosque, dating to the Umayyad era, had for centuries served as a center of learning and religious life in the historic city.
The governor also recalled the mosque's role during the Syrian uprising that began in March 2011, saying demonstrations against the former regime had emerged from the site.
The mosque and its surroundings witnessed intense fighting between former regime forces and opposition factions from 2012 to 2016, repeatedly changing hands.
It was taken out of service in 2013 after suffering extensive damage, including to its dome, arcades and historic minaret, during fighting and bombardment.
Following the fall of the Bashar Assad regime on Dec. 8, 2024, Aleppo's Endowments Directorate began restoration work aimed at preserving the mosque's architectural and historical character.
The Great Umayyad Mosque, also known as the Great Mosque of Aleppo, is one of Syria's oldest and most significant mosques.
Its construction dates to the Umayyad period in the early eighth century, with most historical accounts attributing its establishment to Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik.

Breadcrumb
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on 14 July following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
President Donald Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.

US suspends Microsoft, Adobe from filing for green cards
October 8, 2026
The Trump administration on Thursday said it was suspending major tech firms, including Microsoft, from applying for a program that allowed their foreign workers to work permanently in the US.
US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling accused those tech firms of abusing the program — the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) — that had so far been a legal pathway for workers to apply for green cards.
"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said.
Sonderling said the suspensions were due to ongoing federal investigations into those firms.
There are good reasons that Indian media firms covered the issue so urgently because many of those firms are either Indian or rely on thousands of Indian professionals who've moved to the country.
Trump administration accuses Microsoft of abusing program for green cards
Vice President JD Vance said the PERM system required companies to advertise work in the US before they applied for green cards for foreign workers due to a lack of qualified American job applicants.
"They'll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They'll go out there and say that 'We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.' And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants," Vance claimed.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
The announcement came hours before US President Donald Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.
Microsoft says majority of its workers are Americans
Microsoft said in a statement that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information, saying the majority of its workers are Americans and that a large part of the H-1B filings have to do with the status of people already based in the US.
"We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings," the company said.
The H-1B visa program is another part of the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration, as concerns have long persisted that the visa for skilled workers has displaced Americans in favor of lower-cost foreign labor.
Microsoft employs 125,000 US workers and 103,000 international workers, according to the company's 2025 annual report.

One potential option would be for that to come at the expense of Beau Webster, who batted at number seven in the recent Test series against Bangladesh.
The South Africans has already confirmed they will play two spinners in Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, in a clear sign of how they believe the wicket will play.
"Everyone brings something a little bit different to it, and it's just trying to work out what we think the best combo is," Australia captain Pat Cummins said.
Green is a chance to return for Australia in the second Test, while Inglis is recovering well and is expected to fly back to South Africa before the series ends.
Australia is also confident Marnus Labuschagne has shown signs he can return to form at number three, after a century in a warm-up game last weekend.
The 32-year-old has not reached three figures in any of his past 39 completed Test innings, and was briefly dropped for last year's tour of West Indies before fighting back.
"He doesn't need to go searching for something that he doesn't already have," Cummins said.
"I think it's him finding his way back to when he was at his best, and we've seen that in the last six months.
"I know a lot of it hasn't translated into Test runs, but we love what he's bringing, we love his approach.
"He's hitting the ball beautifully in the nets, I know it doesn't guarantee success out in the field, but we think he's really well placed."
Australia has spoken about the need to potentially play this Test at a different tempo to many recent ones, which have been dubbed as "fast-forward cricket".
"We've got to get a little bit better, and we can get a bit better at, getting to the grind," Cummins said.
"It might not be the glamorous stuff, but it's that grinding out a session, going for two runs an over, not these major falls or not these whirlwind innings at the time.
"We haven't played too many of those Test matches in the last few years, particularly in Australia, they've been quite fast-paced.
"A lot of our success has come off these big moments, with a Travis Head hundred or Starcy [Mitchell Starc] running through the top order."

Autism and ADHD traits appear to follow different social paths to mental health problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:00:09 UTC
05:00:09 KST

Children who show traits of autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder often face elevated risks of emotional and behavioral problems as they grow up, but the social pathways connecting these traits to mental health are complex. A long-term study published in Psychological Medicine suggests that difficulties with classmates, schoolwork, and family members do not simply follow neurodevelopmental traits in a straight line. Instead, day-to-day social struggles and mental health challenges appear to be linked in both directions over time, which may create self-reinforcing cycles as students develop.
Autism spectrum disorder, commonly known as ASD, involves differences in social communication, social interaction, and patterns of behavior or interests. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is characterized by ongoing patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Both conditions exist on a continuum, meaning that many children display noticeable traits without having an official clinical diagnosis. Even when these traits fall below diagnostic thresholds, children are at elevated risk of emotional distress, including internalizing problems like anxiety and depression, or externalizing problems like anger and disruptive behavior.
Earlier research suggested that everyday hardships may help explain these links. For instance, a 2018 longitudinal study tracking youth from childhood to age 18 found that elevated autistic traits increased the risk of developing depressive symptoms, an association partly explained by social hardships such as bullying. In a similar vein, a 2020 study of adolescents indicated that childhood ADHD symptoms predicted teenage depression in part through academic setbacks and peer problems.
Strained relationships with parents and peers also helped account for the link between attention difficulties and later depression in a 2013 study of two samples of young people, although academic struggles did not independently explain that link in that research.
Because autistic and ADHD traits frequently co-occur in the same individuals, researchers faced a challenge in untangling which specific social hurdles stem uniquely from each set of characteristics. Many previous studies examined either autism or ADHD in isolation, making it difficult to understand how distinct traits relate to social adjustment across different settings.
“In school settings, many children show mild ASD or ADHD traits that do not meet diagnostic criteria, yet they may still experience difficulties with peers, learning, or relationships with adults,” lead author Eriko Hashimoto, a doctoral student in the Graduate School of Humanities and Sciences at Ochanomizu University in Tokyo, told PsyPost. “These children may fall outside formal support systems.”
“However, we still know relatively little about how such traits relate to social adjustment and mental health over time,” Hashimoto explained. “Together with my supervisor and co-author, Professor Hiroyuki Ito, I wanted to address this gap by examining these developmental associations over several years in a large, community-based sample of school-aged children.”
To investigate these questions, Hashimoto, Professor Hiroyuki Ito of the Faculty of Core Research at Ochanomizu University, and their colleagues analyzed data from a large population-based cohort involving all public elementary and junior high schools in a medium-sized municipality in Chubu, Japan. The final analysis included 9,619 students from an initial group of 11,549 enrolled children. Students were surveyed once per school year from fourth through ninth grade, with data from 11 grade cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. By gathering information from students, their parents, and their homeroom teachers, the authors were able to capture behavioral and emotional patterns across both home and classroom environments.
Parents reported on their children’s autistic tendencies using a shortened version of the Autism Spectrum Screening Questionnaire and assessed ADHD traits using the ADHD Rating Scale-IV. Students completed questionnaires detailing their subjective difficulties in three areas: keeping up with classwork, conflicts with teachers, and arguments with family members. Problems with classmates were evaluated using the peer relationships subscale of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, combining ratings from students, teachers, and parents into a single composite score.
Mental health outcomes were grouped into two broad categories. Internalizing problems, reflecting inward emotional distress such as anxiety and depression, combined child self-reports on a depression scale with parent and teacher ratings of emotional symptoms. Externalizing problems, capturing outward behavioral difficulties such as hostility and aggression, brought together student self-reports with adult ratings of conduct problems. The researchers used cross-lagged structural equation modeling, an advanced statistical technique that tests whether one variable predicts changes in another variable over time while controlling for student sex and grade level.
The analysis produced standardized coefficients, which express how strongly one measure predicted later changes in another. By the guidelines the authors used for this kind of analysis, values around 0.03 count as small, 0.07 as medium, and 0.12 as large.
The findings indicated distinct developmental patterns for autistic and ADHD traits. Autistic traits showed consistent links over time with subsequent peer difficulties, showing standardized coefficients between 0.146 and 0.190 across grade transitions, which fall in the large range. Autistic traits were also linked with later internalizing problems, with small-to-medium coefficients ranging from 0.068 to 0.097. In contrast, autistic traits were not consistently associated with later academic struggles or conflict with teachers.
ADHD traits showed a different pattern of associations. Elevated ADHD traits were linked to subsequent externalizing problems, with coefficients between 0.064 and 0.118, with the strongest associations appearing during late elementary school. ADHD traits were also associated with higher levels of academic difficulties over time, particularly in fourth and fifth grade, but showed weak and mostly inconsistent links to later internalizing problems directly. Instead, academic difficulties themselves predicted later internalizing symptoms during elementary school, suggesting that learning struggles may act as an intermediate pathway linking attention difficulties to emotional distress.
Rather than revealing one-way effects, the analyses indicated notable bidirectional processes. For instance, while peer problems predicted increases in subsequent internalizing symptoms, higher levels of internalizing symptoms were also associated with worsening peer problems over time. Similarly, externalizing behaviors predicted more frequent conflicts with teachers and parents in later years, and those strained adult relationships were linked with subsequent increases in behavioral difficulties. Academic problems consistently predicted greater family conflict in the following year, with coefficients ranging from 0.105 to 0.163.
The social environment also appeared to feed back into parent ratings of neurodevelopmental traits. Experiencing peer problems was linked to higher reported autistic traits in later grades, with coefficients up to 0.164. In an analogous manner, elevated externalizing behaviors predicted higher reported ADHD traits in subsequent waves. These patterns suggest that neurodevelopmental traits may not be fixed and could shift with a child’s social experiences, though they could also reflect changes in how parents perceive and rate their children’s traits once problems emerge.
“One important message is that ASD and ADHD traits showed different patterns of association with later difficulties,” Hashimoto said. “These findings highlight the importance of considering not only children’s individual characteristics but also the social environments in which they develop.”
These findings align with prior research into how childhood difficulties unfold over time. The results are consistent with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that childhood ADHD traits were linked to greater psychological distress in midlife, partly through experiences of social exclusion in adulthood, though that research followed individuals into adulthood while the current study tracked youth through junior high school.
The observed connections also touch upon research covered by PsyPost in 2025 linking ADHD symptoms to emotional problems across development, though that earlier project pointed to shared genetic factors, based on twin data, as an underlying driver rather than school-based social pathways.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. “This study does not demonstrate causality,” Hashimoto noted. “The findings show temporal associations, not proof that one factor directly causes another.”
“It is also important to emphasize that children with elevated ASD or ADHD traits are highly diverse; our results describe group-level patterns and should not be interpreted as predictions for any individual child,” she pointed out. “In addition, we examined ASD and ADHD traits dimensionally in a general school population rather than focusing specifically on children with clinical diagnoses.”
There are a few other things to keep in mind. Many of the associations, including most links between the traits and later mental health problems, were small to medium in size. Also, the questionnaire used to evaluate autism primarily captured a relatively narrow set of characteristics, focusing mainly on Asperger-type social and behavioral traits rather than the full spectrum.
Future research could build on these findings by incorporating direct observational measures alongside questionnaires and testing whether supportive social settings can buffer these links. The authors suggest that early support for academic organization, peer relationship skills, and positive communication between families and schools might help interrupt these cycles, though the study did not test any interventions.
The study, “Longitudinal associations among autism and ADHD traits, social maladjustment, and mental health in school-aged children,” was authored by Eriko Hashimoto, Hiroyuki Ito, Megumi Hamada, Takahiro Nakajima, Nobuya Takayanagi, Mitsunori Myogan, Yasuo Murayama, and Masatsugu Tsujii.

Commentary: To Trump, the Cornell Seven are victims. It's a familiar refrain for him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:58:04 UTC
04:58:04 KST

To Trump, the Cornell Seven are victims. It’s a familiar refrain for him
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A former Cornell student says she was drugged and gang-raped by fraternity brothers in 2024; she sued the men and the university after prosecutors declined to file criminal charges.
- President Trump says the accused won’t get a fair shake, as New York’s attorney general opens a criminal investigation and Cornell hires a second independent investigator.
- Students have staged protests, and more than 60,000 alumni and supporters have pledged to withhold donations, demanding transparency and reform in how the university handles sexual assault cases.
Believe women.
The message should have been codified during the #MeToo 2010s after decades, if not centuries, of women reporting sexual assaults and authorities doing little to nothing to help them. Tangible proof of change was everywhere: Bill Cosby fell from grace. Harvey Weinstein wound up in jail. And though it took awhile, the Tate brothers are finally behind bars.
Institutions would finally take claims of rape seriously, and young men would have a better understanding of consent and the consequences. Or not.
Last month, a former Cornell University student identified only as Jane Doe sued seven fraternity brothers and the university, claiming the school failed to protect her and punish the perpetrators. Doe says she was plied with drugs and alcohol and gang-raped by the men during a party at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024. Cornell conducted an internal investigation and suspended or expelled some of the men, but prosecutors did not bring criminal charges against any of the accused.
There’s no point asking how we got back here, when President Trump himself is proof that some folks never budged in the first place.
Trump said Friday that the accused men “won’t get a fair shake,” in response to a reporter’s questions about the case and the appointment of a special prosecutor, Letitia James. In painting the accused as victims, it appeared the president was speaking from personal experience.
A New York prosecutor has reopened an investigation into gang rape allegations at a Cornell University fraternity in response to a lawsuit
Trump was found liable in 2023 for sexual abuse and battery in a lawsuit filed by the writer E. Jean Carroll. She said that in a dressing room in a high-end department store in 1995 or 1996, Trump pushed her against a wall, pulled down her tights and sexually assaulted and penetrated her before she was able to flee. In the civil trial, Carroll said that the assault made her “unable to have a romantic life again.” She was awarded $5 million in damages. Trump still denies all wrongdoing, calling the allegations a “hoax” and the rulings politically motivated.
In 2005, when he was a reality TV host, Trump bragged on a hot mic about sexually assaulting women in his now infamous “Grab ‘em by the pussy” boast. He promptly apologized when the recording was leaked before the 2016 election, only to walk it back after he won, suggesting the recording was a deepfake (it was not).
And he expressed more than one well wish for Ghislaine Maxwell, convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime companion, after her arrest on a multitude of sex-related charges in 2020.
James, the New York state attorney general, will lead a criminal investigation into the Cornell Seven case after public backlash over the local district attorney declining to pursue charges. She won a $454-million judgment against Trump in 2024, with a judge finding that his businesses defrauded lenders by inflating assets. The financial penalty was later ruled “excessive” and wiped out, but the finding of business fraud still stands.
Is it any wonder that Trump is siding with the men in the Cornell case?
And now, a second independent investigator has been brought on by a Cornell committee to look into the university’s conduct. She is former federal prosecutor Sally Yates, who famously served as acting U.S. attorney general for 10 days in 2017, until Trump fired her for refusing to defend his administration’s travel ban (aka the “Muslim ban”).
The Cornell Seven became a national story when in September, Doe filed a 101-page lawsuit alleging that during the frat party, multiple men gave her alcohol and ketamine, then repeatedly sexually assaulted her. One of the men allegedly sent a message to a 50-person Snapchat group alerting his frat brothers that a woman was available for sex.
All of the Cornell Seven have denied wrongdoing.
Trump says he was wrongly accused of a pattern of sexually abusing women based in part on his own words.
Doe’s complaint alleges that the university only temporarily suspended some of the men and that others “were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays.” Cornell denies that this was the only punishment it handed down. The New York Times reported Tuesday that two of the fraternity brothers were expelled, two more were suspended, and one who had already graduated was barred from campus. The remaining men were handed lighter punishments.
Considering Trump’s track record of demonizing powerful women, there’s little doubt that the appointment of James by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, and the addition of Yates, will aid in his politicization of the Cornell Seven case. But the public outcry against the university and the accused men speaks volumes about how out of step the president is with many Americans who are willing to stand by a woman’s claim of rape until proved otherwise.
Holding signs that read “Justice for Jane Doe,” Cornell students staged a sit-in Wednesday and vowed to not spend any money on campus, in a statement against sexual violence and how the university has handled her case. It was one of many acts of protest by Cornell students. Over 60,000 alumni and supporters of the university also signed a petition pledging to withhold donations until Cornell meets their demands for transparency and reform in cases of sexual assaults.
They represent a familiar refrain: Believe women.

Israeli settlers take Palestinian olives, and their harvest traditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:57:29 UTC
04:57:29 KST

Israeli settlers take Palestinian olives, and their harvest traditions
As Israeli settlers harvest olives on Palestinian land, farmers face growing violence and the loss of a tradition passed down through generations.
Ramallah, occupied West Bank – The video shared in Israeli settler groups shows two men bashing an olive tree with long wooden sticks. Smiling and congratulating one another, they try to knock the olives to the ground. They call the result “Pure Olive Oil”.
But as Palestinian activist Bashar Qaryouti explained, the two men don’t own the land, the trees, or the olives.
They’re Israeli settlers who set up an illegal settlement outpost on private property in the village of Qaryut, in the northern occupied West Bank, and made their way into this olive grove, some 200 metres (656 feet) away from Palestinian homes.
“No one has come near here for about three years, thank God,” one of the two men in the video says in Hebrew.
Local Palestinians know the man by name, and he does little to hide. The man is Avichai Suissa, an Israeli settler sanctioned by the European Union, United Kingdom – and previously by the United States – who runs a farm on the outpost. It was established more than a year and a half ago, and videos like this help Suissa raise donations for it.
On his campaign page, he says the goal is to rebuild and expand the farm, which was once dismantled by the Israeli army, to prevent it from falling “into enemy hands”.
“We’re gradually starting to work our way into the area,” Suissa said in the video.
But the land belongs to Palestinians – residents of Qaryut – who have not been able to reach it since the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. “A few months ago, farmers tried to plough their land, but the army stopped them,” Qaryouti said.
Worst year yet
“After we complained, the army declared the area a closed military zone a few days ago, so settlers are going to other lands, to other olives to steal,” Qaryouti explained.
Suissa and others are part of a growing movement of settlers who have intensified their campaign against the olive harvest. The campaign, part of a settler pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank, has turned the olive harvest season in October into a source of fear and danger.
Many Palestinians in the occupied West Bank describe this year as the worst yet in terms of settler attacks, and the season has barely started.
On Wednesday, armed Israeli settlers on tractors raided lands between the villages of Ramin and Burqa, in the northern occupied West Bank. They opened fire on farmers heading to their trees.
Ali Bazzari, a 44-year-old farmer, was killed. His only “crime”, the family says, was trying to pick his olives.
Witnesses say the Israeli army prevented ambulances from reaching the wounded. Palestinians had to carry the injured through the mountains to hospitals.
The Israeli Rights Group Yesh Din says it documented 109 incidents of violence directly related to the harvest in 75 Palestinian communities between September 27 and October 6, an average of 11 per day.
Longtime tradition
Israeli settlers are increasingly attempting to adopt the rituals of the olive harvest season, while pushing out the Palestinians who have kept those traditions for generations.
Several new farms have been set up in the occupied West Bank. One shares videos of olives being pressed. Others invite Israelis to “join in” the experience.
Palestinians say the videos circulating show a disregard for the actual owners of the land taken by the settlers, and a clear attempt to appropriate the season, imitating its rituals and claiming them as their own.
Those rituals – things like collective picking, singing, and shared meals on the farms – are rooted in a deep connection to the land.
The olive harvest season may be an exhausting time of the year for Palestinians, with its hard work and long hours in the sun, but it’s a rewarding one. Olive farmers traditionally gather for family get-togethers, with neighbours and friends volunteering to help one another harvest the olives, in a cultural tradition known as “ouneh”.
The season has a light-hearted element, with debates about whose land produces the best oil, who should charge the most, and who knows how to pick the most olives and not drop any to the ground.
Older generations pass down lessons from history, such as the best time to harvest and how to nurture the trees – an inherited knowledge of climate, agriculture and the land itself.
“They planted so that we can eat. We plant so they [will] eat,” a well-known Arabic saying goes. It highlights the continuity of this inheritance, and the responsibility towards future generations.
Last harvest?
These trees, which are meant to be protected, nurtured and passed on, are being taken away – not only by settlers, but by soldiers, too.
Hazem Sanaf, 61, stood on a nearby hill in the village of Beit Rima and watched as Israeli bulldozers ploughed through his lands in late September, after he had received an Israeli military order. The bulldozers destroyed and uprooted more than 400 trees belonging to Hazem and his neighbour, some of them decades old, and his only source of income.
“They just want to take our olive trees from us,” he said, his eyes reflecting his pain.
Hazem is not alone. Several Israeli military orders to uproot olive trees have been handed out across the occupied West Bank. Some have been carried out, while others await their turn.
In the past, the Israeli military has cited the need to clear land of trees to prevent security threats or ambushes on troops. But Palestinians say it reflects a pattern of dispossession and impoverishment.
According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission (CRRC), Israeli settlers and soldiers have destroyed approximately 50,000 trees this year alone.
Fuad Daraghmeh, from the village of al-Lubban Asharqiya, near Ramallah, carried the thick, broken stem of a tree.
“I took care of it for 30 years,” he said, and headed home. He did not say what he planned to do with the stem, but others said that their trees had been uprooted before, and that they had managed to nourish them back to life.
Others are resigned to saying goodbye to the trees. They sit by the bulldozed trees with small hand tools, picking the last fruit of what they believe is their last crop.
Palestinians have been watching videos of settlers harvesting their olive trees, including the one shared by Suissa.
Beyond the pain, one remark keeps coming up: the method used by Suissa in vigorously beating the tree is no way to treat it, and no way to harvest olives.
“The people who have tended to their lands for decades know that,” one Palestinian activist, who did not wish to be identified for security reasons, said.

Ukrainian-Made FP-1 Drones Hit Russia's Largest Oil Refinery 2,500 Km From Border

Ukrainian-Made FP-1 Drones Hit Russia's Largest Oil Refinery 2,500 Km From Border
Ukrainian forces have struck Russia’s largest oil refinery in Omsk, more than 2,500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, using upgraded FP-1 long-range drones, Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the company, the attack targeted the Omsk Oil Refinery, operated by Gazprom Neft, which has an annual processing capacity of 22.23 million tons of crude oil.
Fire Point reported a successful hit on the facility, followed by a fire.
Russian independent outlet Astra also reported a fire at the refinery, citing its own OSINT analysis.
According to Astra, residents of Omsk reported explosions after authorities issued a drone threat warning across the region. An OSINT analyst subsequently examined an eyewitness photograph and identified black smoke rising from the refinery.
Omsk region Governor Vitaly Khotsenko acknowledged the incident, stating that one drone had reached the city's northern industrial hub. He did not specify whether the refinery had been damaged.
The Omsk Oil Refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil processing facilities and a major asset of Gazprom Neft. According to some estimates cited by Astra, the plant accounts for approximately 10% of Russia’s total oil refining.
On October 8, Astra reported a suspected fire near the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in Russia’s Republic of Bashkortostan, approximately 1,400 kilometers from the Ukrainian border. The incident was later confirmed by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

UP investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach detained in Vienna while on assignment
Mykhailo Tkach, head of the investigative journalism department at Ukrainska Pravda, has been detained in Vienna while carrying out an assignment from the editorial team in connection with the search for the fugitive prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko. We consider his detention unlawful and are demanding his immediate release and an official explanation from the Austrian law enforcement authorities.
Mykhailo was in Austria with his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko. At present, we do not know where Yaroslav is or what has happened to him. We demand that his whereabouts be established immediately and that his safety be confirmed.
The editorial team currently has no direct contact with Mykhailo. According to the information available to UP, he has been taken into custody and is in contact with a lawyer.
We have already informed the Embassy of Ukraine in Austria and the Austrian Embassy in Ukraine. We call on Ukrainian diplomats to take all necessary measures as a matter of urgency to protect our journalists, establish their whereabouts and facilitate Mykhailo's release.
We call on the Austrian authorities to immediately explain the grounds for Mykhailo's detention, ensure that he has access to legal and consular assistance, and allow him to contact the editorial team and his family.
We are also appealing to international journalism organisations and human rights organisations to support our colleagues and help protect their rights.
Mykhailo and Yaroslav travelled to Vienna to do their jobs as journalists. As editor-in-chief, I insist that journalists' safety and their right to carry out their professional duties must be guaranteed. We expect the Austrian authorities to act without delay, provide transparent explanations and fully respect our colleagues' rights.
Sevğil Musaieva
Editor-in-Chief, Ukrainska Pravda
