Russia has spent a decade trying to stop people from bypassing internet censorship. Now it plans to spend nearly 60 billion rubles over three years on traffic filtering.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:42:18 UTC
04:42:18 KST

Russia has spent a decade trying to stop people from bypassing internet censorship. Now it plans to spend nearly 60 billion rubles over three years on traffic filtering.
Russia is preparing a new wave of restrictions on tools used to bypass internet blocks. The budget for the next three years includes a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering. The Digital Development Ministry wants to make mobile internet much more expensive for VPN users, and there are plans to put companies’ corporate networks under strict oversight by the Federal Security Service (FSB). Dozens of other restrictions have accumulated in recent years. We looked back at the main ones to show how the state has methodically cut Russians off from the free internet — and where we are on that timeline right now.
VPN services were banned from bypassing Russian internet blocks (2017)
On November 1, 2017, a new Article 15⁸ was added to the law “On Information, Information Technologies, and Information Protection” to address VPNs and other ways to bypass internet blocks:
Measures to prevent the use within the Russian Federation of information and telecommunications networks and online resources that provide access to online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation.
The authorities did not ban VPNs outright. Instead, they required providers to filter their Russian users’ traffic and block access to resources on the banned list. If providers failed to comply, Russian telecommunications operators were required to block their VPN services on instructions from Roskomnadzor, Russia’s internet regulator. The only exemptions were for the authorities themselves and companies that needed unrestricted access “for technical purposes necessary to support their operations.”
Internet providers were banned from explaining how to bypass blocks (2018)
In February 2016, the Association for the Protection of Copyright on the Internet proposed administrative fines for promoting VPN use to access banned websites. Roskomnadzor supported the idea but proposed fining only internet providers. An agency spokesperson said in April that inspections had uncovered “several instances in which telecommunications operators posted information about ways to bypass blocks on their block notification pages.”
In the end, no separate fine was introduced. But starting November 1, 2017, telecommunications operators were required to comply with rules governing “posted information about restrictions on access to online resources.” Roskomnadzor published the corresponding order in March 2018. It prohibited the following on block notification pages:
- News content
- Information about ways to access online resources containing information to which access is restricted under Federal Law No. 149-FZ
A center was created to manage Russia’s internet, along with equipment to filter traffic and block access (2019)
After their failed attempt to block Telegram in 2018, the authorities learned from their mistakes and passed a law on the “sovereign internet.” It took effect on November 1, 2019.
Among other things, the law allowed centralized control over the Russian segment of the internet. To that end, the authorities established a Center for Monitoring and Management of the Public Communications Network within the Main Radio Frequency Center, which reports to Roskomnadzor. The new center was supposed to be able to take control “in the event of threats to the stability, security, and integrity” of internet operations in Russia.
To counter such threats, every telecommunications operator was required to install TSPU, or “technical means of countering threats.” These hardware and software systems allowed Roskomnadzor to filter traffic at its discretion and block sites and services it deemed objectionable. The agency later made extensive use of TSPU to target VPNs and other tools for bypassing blocks. If you want to understand exactly how TSPU works, watch this five-hour video.
In October 2023, Roskomnadzor head Andrey Lipov said that all communications nodes in Russia were “100% covered by TSPU.”
Mass blocking of VPN services began (2021)
In May 2021, Lipov threatened to block VPN services that continued to ignore Russian legal requirements. The agency began targeting individual providers the following month. Roskomnadzor made its plans public in advance so the blocks would not affect companies using those VPN services “to keep technical processes running at businesses and organizations.”
By the end of the year, the agency had said it was restricting VyprVPN, Opera VPN, Hola! VPN, ExpressVPN, KeepSolid VPN Unlimited, Nord VPN, Speedify VPN, IPVanish VPN, Betternet, Lantern, X-VPN, Cloudflare WARP, Tachyon VPN, and PrivateTunnel.
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
All instructions for bypassing Russian internet blocks were banned (2023)
On July 31, 2023, a new provision allowed authorities to add online resources to the unified register of banned websites for another reason:
Article 15¹. Unified register of domain names, website page addresses, and network addresses identifying websites containing information whose distribution is prohibited in the Russian Federation
5. The grounds for adding the information specified in Part 2 of this article to the register are:
m) information about ways and methods of providing access to online resources and/or information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation;
Fines were introduced for VPN service operators (2025)
On September 1, 2025, a new Article 13.52 was added to the Code of Administrative Offenses:
Violation of the rules governing the use within the Russian Federation of hardware and software tools for accessing online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted
It provides for fines for refusing to cooperate with Roskomnadzor or to block Russian residents’ access to banned resources. The fines can reach 80,000 rubles for individuals and 500,000 rubles for companies. Repeat violations carry steeper penalties: up to 200,000 rubles and 1 million rubles, respectively.
Using a VPN became an aggravating factor in criminal offenses (2025)
On September 1, 2025, a new item was added to the Criminal Code’s list of aggravating factors:
committing a crime using hardware and software tools for accessing online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted
Now, if a court finds that an offender used a VPN to commit any crime, it can impose a harsher punishment. It can even deny offenders certain forms of leniency under the Criminal Code, such as sentencing limits for those who voluntarily report their crimes to the authorities or enter into a pretrial cooperation agreement.
VPN advertising was banned, and fines were introduced for it (2025)
On September 1, 2026, a new provision was added to Article 5 of the law “On Advertising,” which sets out general requirements:
10⁸. It is prohibited to distribute advertisements for hardware and software tools that provide access to online resources and information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted under the laws of the Russian Federation
At the same time, fines for such advertising were added to the Code of Administrative Offenses (Part 18 of Article 14.3). The maximum fine is 80,000 rubles for individuals and 500,000 rubles for companies.
Major Russian companies began detecting users with active VPNs (2026)
In April 2026, the Digital Development Ministry forced major Russian companies with the most heavily visited websites and services to detect active VPNs on users’ devices. The companies were required to block those users’ access and, according to RBC, share data about their VPN connections with Roskomnadzor. In theory, this was meant to help the agency gather information about VPNs that successfully bypass blocks or go entirely undetected, so it could block them more effectively.
Authorities tried to cut VPN services off from Russian hosting providers (2026)
On June 26, 2026, the law “On Information, Information Technologies, and Information Protection” was amended to prohibit Russian hosting providers from serving VPN services that bypass Russian internet blocks:
Article 10²⁻¹. Specific rules governing hosting providers’ activities
5¹. A hosting provider may not supply computing capacity for storing information in an information system permanently connected to the internet to owners of information and telecommunications networks or online resources (a website and/or website page, information system, or computer program) that provide access to online resources or information and telecommunications networks to which access is restricted within the Russian Federation under this Federal Law, if those owners have applied to the hosting provider and have not complied with the requirements set out in Paragraph 1 of Part 7 of Article 15⁸ of this Federal Law.
Okay, folks, this brings us to the present day…
Roskomnadzor would monitor corporate VPNs that bypass blocks
Since 2017, the authorities have officially allowed companies to use VPNs that can bypass Russian censorship “for technical purposes necessary to support their operations.” Companies must also determine in advance which employees will use such a VPN.
A new bill to combat phone and cyber fraud would require companies to notify Roskomnadzor that they use corporate VPNs, though it is unclear how. The government and the FSB would also jointly approve rules for using these services and set requirements for employees who have access to them.
Using Russian hosting providers would become even harder for VPN services
The same bill would create a new Roskomnadzor register of individuals and companies that use servers in Russia to host VPN services. If caught bypassing blocks, they would be barred from entering into contracts with any provider in Russia for a full year. The government would develop procedures for Roskomnadzor and hosting providers to exchange this information.
Charges for international mobile internet traffic would be introduced to combat VPNs
According to Forbes, the Digital Development Ministry’s plans to charge mobile subscribers for international internet traffic first became known in March 2026. At the time, the ministry proposed an additional charge for subscribers who used more than 15 gigabytes of international traffic. This would put VPN users in a bind: When they connect to foreign servers, all their traffic becomes international. Using a good VPN on a mobile phone without additional workarounds would become very expensive.
At the time, telecommunications operators asked for the measure to be postponed. But officials have now returned to the idea. According to Kommersant, the government is proposing to raise the free international internet traffic allowance to 50 gigabytes and, for now, introduce the additional charge only on 5G networks.
The authorities plan to allocate even more money to combat VPNs
The draft federal budget for 2027–2029 provides for a sharp increase in spending on traffic filtering and internet blocks using TSPU. The annual subsidy to the Main Radio Frequency Center had been set at 9,870,441,200 rubles for 2027 and 9,844,821,700 rubles for 2028. The new draft budget simply puts a 1 in front of each figure. The planned subsidy for 2029 is roughly the same: 19,870,474,200 rubles. That amounts to nearly 60 billion rubles over three years. By comparison, in 2024, the authorities planned to spend almost the same amount, 59 billion rubles, on upgrading TSPU — but over six years (through 2030).

Sweden counts its difficult waters as an advantage
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
20:41:19 BST
04:41:19 KST

The Baltic archipelago that makes sonar so unreliable also gives a navy that knows it cover, concealment and freedom of manoeuvre, the commander of the Royal Swedish Navy’s 4th Naval Warfare Flotilla told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Captain Anna Jonsson, whose flotilla operates in the waters around Stockholm, opened a panel on countering undersea threats by describing the conditions her crews work in.
She said: “Sweden and my unit operates in a complex underwater environment. Our archipelago consists of tens of thousands of islands, narrow passages, shallow waters, and highly variable seabed conditions. Below the surface, rocks, wrecks and seabed formations create a challenging environment for our sensors.”
The behaviour of the water itself compounds everything the seabed is already doing. “Add variations of depth, temperature and salinity to that, and the performance of the sonar and underwater systems can change significantly from one area to another,” she said.
Her argument was that none of this amounts to a handicap for the navy that has learned to live in it. “Complexity is not necessarily a disadvantage always. For the force that understands the environment, it can provide cover, concealment and freedom of manoeuvre,” she said. “This has shaped the Swedish naval platforms, sensors, weapons and tactics for generations.”
That inheritance shows in what the Swedish navy buys, since small shallow-water submarines, mine countermeasures vessels, and corvettes built for the archipelago are a different proposition from blue-water designs, and the tactics that go with them have been refined over decades of operating in exactly these conditions.
“Sweden is in some way a small state. I have limited resources within my flotilla, but we still need to achieve combat effectiveness,” she said. “It’s important for us to understand the underwater terrain better than our adversary.”
The chair observed that the Baltic condenses problems that navies meet in diluted form elsewhere, with the Black Sea the closest comparison, and that anti-submarine warfare there is a different business from where NATO navies usually operate.
Commodore David Burton, who leads the alliance work on an allied underwater battlespace network, said understanding the environment is built into how NATO is organising its experimentation, with Allied Command Transformation targeting demonstrations region by region. The Baltic has had its turn, the Mediterranean has had another, and the High North comes next.
Sweden brought all of this into NATO when it joined.

EU’s fight to break China’s raw material dominance isn’t going well
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:40:20 UTC
04:40:20 KST

BRUSSELS — It was meant to be Europe's escape from the web of Chinese critical mineral supremacy.
But two years after it took effect, the EU's Critical Raw Materials Act is not on schedule. Just one in four critical mineral projects granted special status under the law is on track to be ready on time, according to new analysis shared with POLITICO.
On Friday, EU industry chief Stéphane Séjourné will unveil a new list of critical mineral projects that will receive privileged access to funding, accelerated permitting and help from Brussels to find buyers.
Advertisement
The idea is to make Europe a major producer of materials essential to clean energy, tech, and defense manufacturing. It's currently a heavy importer.
But progress on the first round of 47 projects, announced early last year, offers little hope for the bloc’s ambitions.
“At least one in three mining and processing strategic projects is either late, stalled, at risk, or no longer exists, and only about a quarter are clearly on track,” said Diego Marin, policy officer for raw materials at the European Environmental Bureau, citing publicly available sources. The findings will be published in a report later this month.
Financial, regulatory, and political hurdles are blocking European mining projects, the industry says, despite the Critical Raw Materials Act’s aim to speed up the time it takes to get the shovels in the ground.
The EEB's findings were echoed in an industry call in August, where 23 projects named in the first round claimed some were facing “immediate jeopardy,” in a letter sent to the Commission and obtained by POLITICO.
Those same companies also believe that announcing more strategic projects will create more problems. However, a Commission official dismissed that claim, saying that some of those projects had received direct funding from the Commission, and claiming the companies believe new projects would "dilute their status."
Advertisement
The EU unveiled 47 projects in March 2025, covering 14 of the bloc’s 17 designated strategic raw materials—from lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite for electric vehicle batteries and rare earths for magnets used in wind turbines, to tungsten for military equipment and gallium for semiconductors. It also includes 13 projects from outside the bloc.
These were designed to deliver the EU’s raw materials targets: by 2030, the bloc aims to mine at least 10 percent, process 40 percent and recycle 25 percent of its own needs, while sourcing no more than 65 percent of any one material at any processing stage from a single non-EU country.
Breaking Europe’s dependence on China for key metals is at the heart of the policy, a goal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen highlighted in her State of the Union speech last month. “We are more than 80% dependent on China for many critical raw materials [and] 90% for some rare earths,” she lamented.
Outgoing Euromines president and former CEO of Swedish miner LKAB Jan Moström, who says Europe is a long way from meeting its targtets, in an interview at the 2025 European Industry Summit in Antwerp. | John Thys/AFP via Getty Images
A Commission official said that if all goes to plan, the EU will meet its 2030 goals for lithium, cobalt and rare earths, but results for other materials are mixed, with shortfalls in nickel processing and recycling and across the manganese supply chain. They did not give hard figures, though.
Industry skeptical
“Unless something happens that is absolutely not foreseen today, we will be far, far away from reaching the targets, even if they are quite low,” said Jan Moström, former CEO of Swedish mining giant LKAB and outgoing president of Euromines. He said better access to financing and faster permitting was key.
The EU is under additional time pressure as a pause on China’s export controls on rare earth minerals is due to expire in January.
Advertisement
Global think tank ODI found in June that “out of 60 projects, 14 are unlikely to contribute by 2030 because their estimated start of production falls between 2029 and 2031,” and that “three out of four are either behind their expected schedule or impossible to verify using up-to-date public evidence” — backing up the EEB’s numbers.
A European Court of Auditors report this year also revealed that “many projects will struggle to secure supply for the EU by 2030” and that there was “no proper tracking of results.”
The European Commission questioned the current validity of the ECA's findings, saying it “audited a period of policy that does not cover everything we've done since this mandate. So the Court of Auditors had very relevant points that we took into account in our policy, but should absolutely not be seen as a fair assessment of the work we've done with the von der Leyen Commission number two,” said a Commission official.
Desperate times
Since adopting the Critical Raw Materials Act in 2024, Brussels has rolled out a flurry of initiatives to get projects moving. They include a proposed critical raw materials center, for which Parliament is seeking €2 billion; the "RESourceEU" plan that’s mobilized more than €2 billion; a mechanism to identify suppliers; and plans to revise water rules and speed up environmental impact assessments.
But industry leaders say the EU is moving too slowly.
“I'm still to be convinced that it makes any difference,” Michael Staffas, CEO of Swedish miner Boliden, told POLITICO when asked about the benefits of being designated as a strategic project. Boliden's subsidiary Somincor was granted strategic status for a copper and zinc mine in Portugal.
Advertisement
The “strategic project” label promised faster permitting and help securing public and private finance, with permitting deadlines of 27 months for mines and 15 months for processing and recycling projects.
"In Sweden you have different authorities that can basically object to a permit process and that in itself creates way longer time than 27 months, just the legislation,” said LKAB CEO Johan Menckel, whose company currently has three strategic projects.
One is the Per Geijer deposit, home to Europe’s largest rare-earth deposits, which the local indigenous Sámi community opposes, arguing it would harm their reindeer-herding tradition.
A 2023 view from the highest point of the Covas de Barroso complex in Portugal, the site of Europe's largest lithium deposit. | Henrique Campos/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Karin K Niia, a Sámi reindeer herder, said in comments that the EU will be complicit in cultural genocide if the project goes ahead.
Europe's lithium hope
Europe’s biggest bet to escape China’s foothold in battery metal supply chains is the Barroso lithium mine in Portugal, run by UK-based mining company Savannah Resources. The company says the mine could supply enough lithium for around half a million electric-vehicle batteries a year.
Advertisement
“I don't think the strategic project stamp and the [Critical Raw Materials Act] have been absolutely essential, but it wasn't also supposed to be. It was supposed to, in my understanding, be important to set a framework under which Europe can do the right thing faster, better, and for the better benefit of the next generation of Europe,” Savannah’s CEO Emanuel Proença said, calling it just another piece of a very big puzzle.
Europe’s lithium-refining ambitions are also faltering: France’s Viridian Lithium went bankrupt after failing to secure funding, while Portugal’s José de Mello Group was unable to finance its planned €492 million refinery — despite both projects winning strategic status in the EU’s first round.
Viridian Lithium spokesperson Luc Pez said the strategic project label was a ‘curse.’
Rio Tinto’s Jadar project in Serbia, one of the non-EU projects to gain strategic-project status, was meant to provide double Barroso’s lithium capacity and cater to up to 25 percent of Europe’s demand. That, however, was suspended because of permitting issues and became a widely protested project amid allegations of corruption and environmental concerns.
That reflected the simple fact that people don't like mines in their backyard — an obstacle for mining projects worldwide, but especially in Europe, which is densely populated and has strong civil society.
"These projects had strategic status, EU money and fast-track permits, and it still wasn't enough," said EEB's Marin. "If the supply push can't deliver even under those conditions, the EU has to take demand reduction and sufficiency seriously. We can't permit our way out of a market problem."

Why Morocco is deepening ties with Israel despite public anger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:33:11 UTC
04:33:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Morocco is deepening ties with Israel despite public anger
Morocco’s recent elections took place amid widespread disillusionment with electoral politics. Even the historic appointment of Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the country’s first female Prime Minister was largely seen as just a minor reshuffling of ministers. Real political power remains in the hands of the ‘Commander Of The Faithful’, King Mohammed VI.
And, while general election ballots were still being counted, the Moroccan Front for Supporting Palestine and Against Normalisation was leading three days of action across 45 cities to demonstrate opposition to normalisation with Israel. The people clearly felt that the streets were a much better space to have their views heard, and possibly change their political reality.
Abraham Accords
To understand Moroccan politics, the most important thing to know is that the King is still very much in charge. Although reforms following the 2011 Arab Spring gave the elected parliament some extra powers, the King still maintains executive authority over religious affairs, defence, foreign policy and national security matters. Therefore, different election results don’t necessarily signal change in Moroccan government policy on anything beyond traffic safety reforms.
The clearest example is Morocco’s increasingly friendly relationship with Israel. Despite the latest Arab Opinion Index finding that 89% of Moroccans opposed recognition of Israel (with only 6% supporting it), the government has announced that Morocco and Israel will upgrade their diplomatic relations to full embassies with ambassadors.
To really rub salt into the wound, it was also announced that Israel’s office will be relocated to Mehdi Ben Barka Avenue. Ben Barka was a Moroccan revolutionary socialist leader whose kidnapping and murder in 1965 was recently revealed to have been a Mossad operation.
Naturally, normalisation with Israel has provoked massive opposition among the Moroccan public, especially after the Gaza genocide. Even before the recent protests against normalisation, Moroccans have spent the past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza showing their solidarity with the Palestinians despite the risks of government repression.
Already in October 2023, it was being reported that ‘hardly a day goes by’ without a rally for Palestine led by a coalition of left-wing parties, trade unions, civil associations and Islamist organisations. Emmanuel Macron couldn’t even visit Israel without a demonstration being held outside the French consulate in Casablanca denouncing “the criminal position of the French government, which supports genocide in Gaza.”
The Moroccan security forces would forcibly break up a similar demonstration a year later, denouncing Macron for calling Hamas ‘barbaric’, with some activists requiring hospital treatment.
Mobilisations for Palestine continued elsewhere across 2024. In September, a national day of action resulted in simultaneous rallies in 50 cities demanding that humanitarian aid be allowed into Gaza. Meanwhile, students and university alumni organised the UM6P campaign to oppose normalisation with Israel in Moroccan universities, with specific opposition to ties with the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, known for its co-operation with the Israeli military.
The mobilisations escalated further in 2025, when Israel’s violation of the first Trump ceasefire agreement brought tens of thousands onto the streets in some of the biggest protests Morocco had seen so far. The government was said to have ‘tolerated’ most protests; however, anyone who had “implicated the monarchy in their complaints” was liable to be arrested.
The contradiction remains, however: the same public that shows such strong opposition to Moroccan foreign policy never utters even the mildest criticism of the monarch behind it.
Morocco’s official line is to position itself as a ‘mediator’ between Israel and the Palestinians, making the defence that this alignment allows it to influence Israel in a positive direction rather than just being treated as an enemy state. However, since the recent Gaza genocide, almost nobody actually believes this.
Quid pro quo
The more logical place to look for an explanation for Morocco’s warming towards Israel is Western Sahara, most of which has been illegally occupied by Morocco since 1975, despite the Polisario Front being recognised by the UN as its legitimate representatives. The United States and Israel are two of only a handful of states that recognise Morocco’s de facto sovereignty over Western Sahara as ‘legitimate’. This took place in 2020 as part of Donald Trump’s Abraham Accords.
The quid pro quo seems obvious here: Israel/the US recognise Morocco’s illegal annexation, and in return Morocco recognises Israel.
It should be noted that, although illegal, Morocco’s occupation of Western Sahara is far less violent than Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians. The most crucial difference is that Western Saharans, including the indigenous Sahrawi people, are legally treated as Moroccan citizens by the government and are permitted to move across the territory and into Morocco proper should they wish. They are not reduced to stateless non-citizens with no rights like Palestinians are.
Israel is also becoming an important supplier for the Moroccan military. According to the Jerusalem Post, Israel was the 3rd largest source of Moroccan military imports in 2019-23. These ties became public enough that in 2022 the Israeli military’s Chief of Staff even made an official visit to Morocco, though since the Gaza genocide they haven’t dared to be so brazen.
In August 2025, Morocco also conducted training exercises using EXTRA guided rockets provided by Elbit Systems (Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer), giving them access to precision medium-range munitions. Morocco also agreed to a $500m deal with Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) to provide its Barak MX air defence system. Although this has not been publicly acknowledged, Reuters reported that Morocco will also purchase a $1 billion Ofek spy satellite from IAI to replace its existing satellites.
Not only has Morocco become a close military ally of Israel, but it is also making itself increasingly dependent on Israeli systems and technological infrastructure in the long term, making it difficult for even an anti-normalisation government to reverse the trend.
So what next for Morocco? So long as opposition is restricted to just expressing opinions against the treatment of the Palestinians, it’s likely that the government will continue to cosy up to Israel with impunity. This may even become more apparent if the United States continues to cut down on its forces in the region, leaving Israel as the more direct Western military outpost offering to protect local authorities from their own populations.
A potential flashpoint for popular opposition will be the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco is co-hosting and is currently busy preparing infrastructure for. If it goes smoothly, it will likely boost Moroccan soft power. However, the recent storming of Ceuta, where 70,000 Moroccans were so desperate to get into Spain that 141 drowned themselves trying, is not a sign of a happy country.
Daniel Lindley is a writer and trade union activist in the UK.

A teen tried to navigate Canadian mountains with Claude. His trek ended in an emergency rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:31:23 UTC
04:31:23 KST

The route up the Widowmaker Arete, a 1,700-foot wall in British Columbia, is deceptively described as “mostly easy slab climbing”, interspersed with “short steep sections that can include finger cracks, blocky face climbing”. It requires careful planning, and the right equipment.
When 16-year-old Bryce Vincent Gowryluk found himself facing its sheer headwall last week, he had neither. He did, however, ask the AI chatbot Claude for directions.
Last week, Gowryluk had to be rescued after those directions proved wildly incorrect, in the latest incident to raise questions about the growing reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation.
On Saturday morning, Gowryluk took a gondola up to the top of Grouse Mountain and, while ascending, asked Claude to plan a route to nearby Crown Mountain and back. After navigating scree and more than 2,000ft of elevation gain, the summit promises 360-degree panoramic views of Greater Vancouver, the Fraser valley and the Capilano watershed.
Typically, the trek takes eight hours and hiking guides warn it is not for beginners.
As Gowryluk, a keen indoor climber, navigated down the Crown Pass and up through Crater Slabs and into a boulder-strewn valley, the directions from Claude took him away from the planned course.
He found himself at the final headwall of the Widowmaker Arete – a climb that requires ropes, cams and a clear plan for ascent. As he climbed, Gowryluk soon realized the terrain was far too steep and that he was stuck at the base of a cliff. He phoned his mother, then called emergency services for help.
Police notified North Shore Rescue, which sent a helicopter, but Gowryluk was too close to the rock face for the rotors, so two members of the rescue team were hoisted down to lift him up. He was flown to the rescue base near the Cleveland Dam.
In their debrief the rescue crew said Gowryluk was “far off” his intended route. While the incident is believed to be the first time a hiker has been lost because of AI, it is the latest in a string of mishaps in the mountainous region of south-western British Columbia, where hikers increasingly rely on imprecise mapping directions.
In July, three people were rescued after they planned a route on the Howe Sound Crest Trail using Google Maps, which gave them wildly inaccurate time estimates, suggesting a route that often takes as long as 14 hours could be done in just over five.
Search manager Paul Markey warned that mountaineers should not rely on the directions of artificial intelligence, and that proper prepartion was key.
“In this particular case, the boy had a headlamp. He had good clothing. He had he had a good pair of boots, spare battery and spare food. He was was pretty well equipped for hiking and scrambling. But he was certainly not prepared or equipped for rock climbing,” Markey said.
“Claude in this particular situation, has never been in the area that this 16-year-old boy found himself in. Claude can only go so far with regard to describing what the area may be like.
“There’s definitely a trend towards using electronic applications as opposed to map and compass skills. But is really no substitute for the good map and compass training and education.”
He noted that in some cases apps give too much information. “We have found that some of the apps have identified trails in areas where, really, our preference as a rescue team would be that those trails or routes are not actually identified,” he said, adding that people see routes they think are good trails only to get into difficulty.
“The main thing is: do not blindly rely on a on AI as as a route planning tool. It can never substitute for good education, good training, a good experience, good decision making in the field.”

She Designed Meta’s New AI Logo. Then Came the Hate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:30:00 UTC
04:30:00 KST

Bay Area lettering artist Jesscia Hische knew that when she took a freelance gig to design the M logo for Meta’s new AI assistant Muse, it was bound to make some people angry. “AI is such a third rail, and Meta is such a third rail,” she tells me.
Still, as a small business owner who relies on client work to keep her two brick-and-mortar art and stationary shops in Oakland afloat, she says she needed the money. “New Work! (Don’t be mad at me),” Hische wrote in her newsletter last month. “I worked with Meta on an icon and logotype for their latest release: Muse, which just launched! It’s Meta’s foray into the AI agent / personal assistant world. I know folks have big feelings about both AI and Meta, but this has been a really fun project for so many reasons.”
The news quickly went viral on Threads, where dozens of fellow designers criticized Hische for selling out. She responded to the haters by trying to explain the decision:
“For the past year, I pretty much have 2-4 payrolls in my account at any given time, which if you own a small business, you know is pretty precarious,” she wrote. She added that she had also invested $100,000 in Studioworks, an admin platform she runs for creatives, and $30,000 in Drawling, her art shop for kids in Oakland, where she hosts classes and workshops. “I have 4 people on payroll including myself, my mom, and two shop employees,” she added. Nothing she said seemed to help.
“Disgusted,” wrote one user. “It’s not about money, it’s about ethics.”
Another person responded saying, “Doing this job is like doing a hit for the mob, and being surprised later when the mob takes you out too.” Other users posted photos of Hische’s house and speculated about her wealth and finances.
Hische had expected some pushback from the artist community, but the level of vitriol caught her off guard. Even if people didn’t like Meta, she felt the company should be commended for hiring an independent artist rather than using generative AI. But the backlash made it clear just how unpopular generative AI has become in some circles, to the point that working for one in any capacity is seen as a betrayal.
We spoke on the phone last week about the backlash, her design process, and whether she was instructed to not make the Muse logo look like a butthole.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Zoë Schiffer: In your newsletter, you acknowledge that people have complicated feelings about Meta and about AI. Did that make it hard for you to take this job?
Jesscia Hische: The last year or two, my client work has been really slow, and my client work is what supports the other things I do, because the brick-and-mortar businesses are not hugely profitable. My margins are razor thin. I think between the two shops, I had like $10,000 in profit last year. I can't sustain myself on $10,000 a year.
So when the Meta project came around, it was like, alright! Let's get some money in the account so I can pay my staff and I don't have to feel so stressed out every time I have to run a pay cycle.
What were you hired to do, specifically?
I specialize in logo refreshes. I did the redesign of Squier from Fender, I redesigned Jeni’s Ice Cream a few years ago and did Southern Living magazine. When I work on logos, I want them to look like they went to the spa for a weekend—not that they went and got a ton of plastic surgery, you know? Just fresh and new, where you're like, “Oh, something's different. I can't tell what, but I like it.”
The [Meta] team had done an exploration of the M internally. They knew it wasn't quite right. It’s just a bunch of product designers and engineers designing type. Some of them are very skilled at typography, but it's just such a super unique thing to be able to draw letterforms. They wanted to refine what they had already done in terms of the M.
It was a huge sprint for that M. I did the work in two days. There were 32 different versions. The logotype took another two weeks.
What did the team tell you they wanted to change?
They had drawn the M as a single stroke, a vector stroke. It was the same width all the way around. When something is just a mono-weight stroke with no adjustments, there's not a lot of subtlety around the shape. This is where the fun happens with type design. As strokes touch each other and join, it creates this heavier pocket, visually. You get these little inky moments. And what type designers often do is sort of play with subtracting and adding bits of weight.
Their big ask was, “We want this thing to feel inspiring and creative and to get people thinking that Muse is a fun thing you can play with, not that it's like this very rigid, engineered, cold thing.”
How much do you get paid for a project like this?
I charged what I thought was an amazing fee for a two-day sprint for a big company, which was like $12,500. That’s an amazing amount of money to make in two days, but it’s not life-changing.
Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang has been talking about the logo recently, noting he’s happy it doesn’t look like a butthole, unlike some of Meta’s competitors.
I do think the “don't make it a butthole logo” thing was probably something they had top of mind internally. But for me, the discussions were more about looking at the Meta infinity loop logo and wanting the Muse logo to look like it was part of the same universe.
How did you decide to start talking about the work publicly?
I wanted to share it because I like sharing about my work. Within my newsletter group, everybody knows that my husband worked for Meta for ages, so they know that I have an association with the company.
I also wanted to acknowledge that AI is a very sensitive topic for people, but acknowledge it to an audience that understands my relationship to both Meta and AI.
I noticed that you responded to a bunch of the people criticizing you. Why?
Generally, if something happens online where there's a misunderstanding, I've been able to just come at [whoever is posting about me] and say “Hey, I hear you,” in an open and conversational way. I’m not trying to persuade them, I’m trying to say, “I agree with this part, but have you considered this?” That's always kind of worked for me in the past to help de-escalate stuff.
But with this, I made a comment about how hopefully, because of this job, I won't have to carry $50,000 in credit card debt through the holidays for my shop, because I have to do a bunch of inventory purchasing. Then that got taken out of context by someone being like, “This rich girl spends $50,000 on Christmas.” And I was just like, OK, wait, someone will see that and not the original post, and then all of a sudden it spins into this story about me being like a kajillionaire sitting on like a pile of emeralds, yelling at poor suffering artists, which is the opposite of my whole vibe.
How did it feel to you, when all this was happening?
The first day when I was like replying to people, I was not torn up about it at all, because I was like, “Oh, these people just don't understand that I'm a small-business owner, that I want to pay my employees. This helps me offer a health plan to like one of my employees. This is good!” And also, this company isn’t hiring me to use AI, I didn’t use AI at all in the process. Isn't this ultimately the future that we want? Large companies hiring independent artists to do things?
But then, as it started to escalate, it just blew up way bigger than I could have ever anticipated. It wasn't just a handful of people talking about it online. It felt like the entirety of Threads, you know? One of the things I have the hardest time with is feeling really misunderstood. I love teaching, but I'm not a guru that's making a predatory $1,500 course or whatever. I tend to charge $35 for a five-hour workshop.
I’m very intentional about things, and I don't just flippantly say yes to things that I obviously feel conflicted about, but I'm also like, this didn't feel like one of those conflicts just because they were paying me as an artist, and I wasn't using AI at all, you know?
So I felt deeply sad. I felt like I had been hit by a truck. For the two days following it, I sat in my bed and sobbed. It just made me feel so awful, like everything I have done up to this point, all the good decisions I tried to make, the free resources I've put out, have been for nothing.
Did it make you regret taking the job?
Not exactly. There was one camp of people who were like, “Of course, do the work if you need to, but just don't talk about it.” But I felt like I was doing a good thing for artists by commending a company that is hiring artists instead of making generative work.
Where do you think the reaction comes from, for designers in particular? Is it fear?
I mean, the fear is real. There’s real fears about AI's impact on commercial art. My husband and I really got into it at one point, because he was working on AI and really excited about it, and I was vehemently anti-AI. Eventually I started seeing the infrastructure, low-level data-processing side of it and how useful it is for things outside of creativity. Then I was like, OK, well, there are silver linings to using this thing. I think that softened the edges for me. My husband also came around to AI’s impact on commercial art, which helped.
Most of the folks in AI are like, “AI helps creativity because it makes human-made things more valuable!” Maybe in fine art, but that's not how commercial art works. Of course, there’s anti-AI purists, and their whole thing is that AI is built on theft, which is true. I think I’m going to benefit from the Anthropic settlement, because they've definitely scraped my books.
I don't use AI for generative art or anything like that. I just use it for admin and for help with coding and web building. But anytime that AI takes the place of a person or does the heavy lifting on stuff that requires human creativity, that's when it becomes problematic.
This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

AI generated

The Atlantic Has Its First Hurricane of the Season. Here's What To Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:28:57 UTC
04:28:57 KST

A storm is heading towards the gulf coast, ending what was a quiet start to the Atlantic hurricane season. Tropical storm Isaias intensified into a hurricane early Thursday morning—making it the first hurricane four months into the Atlantic season. Currently a strong Category 2 hurricane, Isaias could reach Category 3 before making landfall sometime in the next two days.
Here’s what to know.
What areas are in Hurricane Isaias’s path?
The storm is expected to make landfall along the central Gulf Coast on Friday night or early Saturday, bringing the threat of heavy rain and flash flooding to the regions in its path. A hurricane warning is currently in place from Ocean Springs, Miss., to the Bay-Gulf County line in Florida.
Some coastal residents of Florida’s Okaloosa County have been put under evacuation order. Officials have also asked out-of-town visitors to leave the impacted area, and all three county airports are scheduled to close Thursday evening. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has declared a state of emergency for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions.
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey also issued a state of emergency for 40 counties. And the state’s 53rd Annual National Shrimp Festival, set to take place in Gulf Shores, Ala., was cancelled due to the storm.
Oil companies operating in the Gulf of Mexico have begun cutting production and evacuating non-essential personnel from facilities in preparation for the storm. It’s a risky time to be slowing down production. America’s emergency oil stockpile is at the lowest level since 1982 as the war in Iran has squeezed the supply chain and pushed up prices.
Why has it been a “quiet” Atlantic hurricane season?
It’s been a relatively quiet hurricane season along the Atlantic. Hurricane Isaias now holds the record as the latest forming first hurricane in the Atlantic Basin—breaking the previous record set in 1905 by Hurricane Four by a mere three and a half hours, according to Accuweather. Isaias is the ninth named storm of the Atlantic season—and the first to reach hurricane strength.
The lull is attributable to El Niño. The phenomenon increases vertical wind shear across the Atlantic, making it harder for thunderstorms to turn into hurricanes. It also temporarily warms up the Pacific Ocean—which often leads to more hurricane activity on a coast that doesn’t typically see a lot of hurricanes.
There have been a number of hurricanes in the Pacific this year. By Sept. 28, the number of named storms in the region was at 20, with nine reaching hurricane strength.
Will El Niño intensify the storm?
El Niño is not likely to intensify the storm. In fact, it often has the opposite effect, weakening hurricane activity along the Atlantic.
Even still—the storm’s impact will be felt. The National Hurricane Center said on Thursday morning that the storm is expected to "remain a dangerous hurricane through landfall.”

====================================================================================================

Eye Cells May Have Been Rejuvenated for the First Time in People
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:20:04 UTC
04:20:04 KST

Three people have received an innovative treatment designed to rejuvenate vision cells. In a presentation at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Ophthalmology, researchers from Life Biosciences reported that the treatment appears safe, and two of the recipients show early signs of improved vision.
The study is among the first approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration using a novel strategy of reprogramming cells to restore their normal function—essentially rejuvenating them. The scientists used a modified version of a reprogramming strategy that earned a Nobel Prize in 2012 for turning mature, adult cells back to an embryonic-like state from which they could become any of the cells in the body—including healthy new versions of diseased or older cells. In that work, Japanese scientist Shinya Yamanaka used four genes to trigger the cellular time warp.
In the current Phase 1 trial, which is ongoing, scientists used three of the four factors to perform a modified reprogramming of diseased retinal ganglion cells in the eye in people with a form of glaucoma—not returning the cells all the way back to their embryonic-like state, but to a point before they stopped functioning properly. Retinal ganglion cells have long arms that connect them from the retina in the eye to the optic nerve, which transmits visual signals to the brain. In some people, over time, fluid in the eye fails to drain properly, putting pressure on the retinal ganglion cells, which lose their delicate connections to the optic nerve, causing loss of vision. While the cells don’t necessarily die, they become dramatically less able to do their job of transmitting critical visual signals.
To try to restore their function, in the trial, scientists injected specially designed proteins, or transcription factors, coding for three of the genes into the vitreous: the gel-like fluid cavity at the back of the eye near the retina. It’s an advantageous location to test such a therapy, since it’s protected from the body’s immune defenses which could attack the newly made proteins. The proteins then did their work to reprogram the damaged and aging cells so they became functional again.
The experimental therapy is based on work from the lab of David Sinclair, professor of genetics at Harvard Medical School and co-founder of Life Biosciences. It's a test of his theory that aging cells lose their ability to work properly because they accumulate too many confusing instructions for which genes they need to turn on or off—so-called epigenetic noise that disrupts the original marching orders cells follow. Sinclair believes that restoring the proper epigenetic information, and removing the epigenetic “noise” by reprogramming the cells to a younger, more functional state could address diseases associated with aging, such as glaucoma.
“We are scientifically reversing epigenetic age to restore youthful function,” Sinclair says.
“We think of it as restoration,” says Sharon Rosenzweig-Lipson, chief scientific officer at Life Biosciences, who presented the new data at the conference. “We’re restoring the code back to what it was when [the cells] were healthy and functional.”
Full reprogramming with the four Yamanaka factors comes with a risk of cells growing out of control and forming teratomas, a type of tumor that can sprout partially or fully developed tissues like teeth, muscle, and bone. Sinclair’s goal was to exploit this reprogramming process to help cells regain their proper instruction manual, and together with his graduate student Yuancheng Lu, launched studies involving just three of the genes, dropping one that is most associated with cancers. There was no guarantee that using three of the factors would trigger reprogramming, since all of the previous studies employed all four. And for three years, Lu learned why—while working with mice with age-related vision loss like glaucoma, he struggled to reprogram retinal ganglion cells with only three of the factors. Experiment after experiment failed. Frustrated, Lu sought out Sinclair, hoping to move onto another project. “He said reversing aging is probably the hardest biological question in the world, and if it were easy, it would have been done already,” Lu says. But there was at least one element working in Lu’s favor. “Removing the fourth factor allowed the three other factors to be small enough to fit into the viral tool we used to deliver them into [animals],” he says. “If the three genes were a little bigger, then we couldn’t fit them into the viral vector.”
In 2018, Lu finally succeeded and texted Sinclair images of the first mouse with glaucoma that had regenerated the delicate connections between the retinal ganglion cells and the optic nerve that had been lost. When Lu asked Sinclair what he saw, Sinclair replied: “the future.”
Lu and Sinclair published their findings in 2020, and that therapy is very close to the one that Life Biosciences ended up using in its trial in people. Two days before the trial was launched in June, Rosenzweig-Lipson gave Lu the good news that the experiment he had worked on for three years was ready to test in the first people with glaucoma. “I was in the lab, and I couldn’t believe it,” Lu says. “I know these patients are suffering. My own family has the macular degeneration risk allele, and I carry the risk allele. So it means a lot to me. My great aunt died when she crossed the street because she couldn’t see well, so I feel like it’s destiny helping these people.”
While the study’s main goal is to show that the therapy is safe, two of the three participants showed early signs of improved vision as well, Rosenzweig-Lipson says. All three took a test before receiving the therapy to establish their visual field by noting when they could see strategically placed lights that flashed above, below, or to the left or right when they looked straight ahead. Eight weeks after receiving the reprogramming factors, two of the participants had improvements in their visual fields. “In places where they weren’t seeing as well, or weren’t identifying lights, we are now seeing better evidence that they can,” says Rosenzweig-Lipson.
She says the results are encouraging enough to begin testing a higher dose—three times that of the initial one—to determine if the treatment remains safe, and, ultimately, what dose would bring the biggest improvement in vision to patients.
The results could also lay the foundation for including people with another eye disease, NAION, which occurs mostly in people over 50 and is similar to a stroke in the eye. NAION causes sudden vision loss when retinal ganglion cells stop functioning for still unknown reasons. If the reprogramming factors can restore the function of some of these cells, the researchers are hopeful that people could regain some of their vision and avoid the blindness that results if left untreated.
So far, the researchers have not seen any adverse effects from the therapy: only side effects related to the injection, they say, and not the reprogramming itself. To be safe, however, the three factors can only be activated in the presence of the antibiotic doxycycline, which acts as an on-off switch for the treatment. After receiving the injection of the three factors, the participants took doxycycline for eight weeks, which ensured that the factors were active and produced the proteins needed to reprogram the retinal ganglion cells. Once they stopped taking the antibiotic, the proteins were no longer made. If further studies show that additional reprogramming is needed to improve vision, they could begin taking the antibiotic again to reprogram more aging or damaged cells.
These initial results will fuel additional studies on using the same method to rejuvenate other cells. Sinclair’s lab has reported promising findings with brain, knee, back, and liver cells in animals.
If the approach continues to be safe and show benefit, eye diseases could be just the beginning of rejuvenating different cells. “We have a wide array of [animal data] support now to suggest that it’s not just a one-organ phenomenon, but that it’s something that transcends organs and potentially has opportunities across a wide range of age-related diseases,” says Rosenzweig-Lipson.

Sinn Fein, which leads Northern Ireland's power-sharing government alongside its main pro-British rival, said a number of its representatives and party members received correspondence from police, without naming them.
"Sinn Féin will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents who should be allowed to live in peace and free from sectarian intimidation," the party said in a statement.
Gerry Carroll, a lawmaker from the smaller People Before Profit party, said separately that he had received an invitation from police to attend a voluntary interview under caution in connection with the protest.
The dispute has destabilised the British-run region's fragile devolved government - a key plank of the 1998 peace deal - with Sinn Fein's partners the Democratic Unionist Party calling for O'Neill and other lawmakers to be prosecuted.
"A political title is not a shield, and no one is above the law," the party said in a statement on Thursday. REUTERS

'We always respond in kind' — Zelensky addresses Ukrainian attacks on Russian data center
Responding to journalists' questions in a press pool chat on Oct. 8, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine will continue to retaliate against Russia for strikes on Ukrainian data centers.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky said about striking Russian data centers. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
The President's comments follow Ukrainian strikes on a Yandex data center in Russia's Ryazan Oblast on Oct. 8. The attack caused internet disruptions for several banking services, as well as for Google, RuTube, and the website of Russian Railways.
Yandex Cloud later acknowledged an "incident" and power supply problems, warning that the outage could affect other parts of its cloud network and advising customers to move some services elsewhere while engineers worked to restore operations.
"We responded to them," Zelensky told reporters when asked about the Yandex attack. "I cannot share all the details."
The attack came after Russian forces struck Ukrainian data centers and internet providers in late September. Officials said the strikes disrupted service for around 100,000 households as Moscow expands its attacks on Ukraine's internet infrastructure.
"As Russia is not achieving its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said about the attacks.
Zelensky clarified to reporters that Kyiv's retaliation against Russia will not match Moscow's targeting of children after Russian strikes killed dozens across Ukraine, including multiple minors, on Oct. 8.
"Let me tell you frankly: Ukraine certainly, most certainly, does not retaliate against children," Zelensky said. "It does not. And it never will. But certain adults will soon receive a response."

Meet the German spymaster turned treason suspect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:14:34 UTC
04:14:34 KST

The former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service built a lucrative second career trading on his security expertise. Now prosecutors accuse him of profiting from secrets belonging to the state.
August Hanning spent seven years at the top of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, with access to some of the country’s most closely guarded secrets. Then came a second act: private consulting, corporate intelligence and business stretching across Europe, into Russia and Asia.
Now, the 80-year-old former spymaster is himself at the center of an espionage investigation, after German federal prosecutors arrested him Tuesday on suspicion of treasonous espionage, attempted treason and other espionage offenses. They allege he obtained a stream of secret intelligence from his former chief of staff and used the material to benefit his private consulting business.
“It’s catastrophic for Germany and for Western intelligence services. Everyone is in shock. The scale of it is enormous, especially at a moment like this,” said one EU intelligence official, who — like others in this report — was granted anonymity to discuss a clandestine arena. “And given that investigators stumbled across this while working on an entirely separate case, we’re likely to learn much more.”
Advertisement
For the BND, the case comes at an uncomfortable moment. Just last week, German parliamentarians began debating a new law proposed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government to grant the agency sweeping new authority, as part of an effort to return Berlin’s foreign intelligence service to the top ranks of global espionage. The timing is equally awkward for European intelligence more broadly. With Russian hybrid attacks continuously targeting Europe, governments across the bloc are rewriting decades-old security laws to give their spy agencies greater powers and be taken more seriously.
Prosecutors say Hanning’s former chief of staff, identified under German privacy rules as Manfred D., supplied him with roughly 2,000 BND documents between 2010 and June 2022. Many contained classified information intended exclusively for internal intelligence work, including material used to brief senior German officials.
In comments to German newspaper WELT, a lawyer representing Hanning said some of the allegations against the ex-spymaster were true but that he did not harm Germany.
“He was in possession of confidential documents. Incorrect, however, is the accusation that he had passed on information contained therein to the detriment of the Federal Republic of Germany — let alone [for] payment. Further investigations will show that,” he said.
In one case, prosecutors suspect Hanning used classified material to prepare an analysis for an employee of foreign intelligence service. They also allege he maintained a relationship with a representative of another foreign intelligence service for several years, passing along political information that was partly based on material obtained from Manfred D.
Prosecutors have not publicly identified either foreign service but German media has named Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan. Azerbaijan has denied any connection.
Advertisement
“In intelligence services, everything is logged — who accesses which documents and when. If an analyst working on right-wing extremism suddenly started looking at intelligence on China, that would raise red flags. But the position of chief of staff has access to virtually everything, so it wouldn’t look suspicious because of the seniority of the position,” said a second EU intelligence official.
Chiefs of staff often stay on when directors change, unless they don’t get along with the incoming boss, the official added.
“Every intelligence service will now be looking at what information it shared with the BND and assessing what damage may have been done,” he said.
Revolving door
Hanning led the BND from 1998 to 2005, before serving as state secretary at Germany’s interior ministry until 2009. Once out of government, he wasted little time entering the private sector.
In July 2010, Hanning and his wife established Hanning Consult. It was in the spring of that same year that Manfred D. agreed to provide him with intelligence from inside the BND in exchange for payment, according to the prosecutor’s statement. Hanning then used that information in his private consulting activities, they added.
Roderich Kiesewetter, a Christian Democrat lawmaker on the Foreign Affairs Committee in the German parliament, said that within Germany there is a “very widespread network” of people who use the contacts and knowledge acquired while they were in service to influence Berlin’s policy on behalf of foreign governments like Russia and China.
Advertisement
“It’s not only sad, it’s damaging the reputation of Germany,” Kiesewetter told POLITICO. “You could also say if you want to talk to Russia, take former members of the government or former members of the secret services.”
Hanning also became involved with Samuel Danilowitsch, a German businessman, who led the Swiss corporate intelligence consultancy, Pluteos. There, Hanning eventually became chairman and the two were listed as attending a 2019 Moscow gathering focused on Europe-Russia relations, attended by Russian political and business figures, where the annexation of Crimea was brought up as a “necessity” rather than a choice. Pluteos did not respond to a request for comment.
From around 2014, Hanning joined British consultancy G3 as a senior adviser, according to archived web pages seen by POLITICO. He later oversaw its work involving Russia and the former Soviet republics, according to German media outlet Correctiv. G3 did not respond to a request for comment.
In 2019, Hanning was invited as a “guest of honor” to a gathering organized by Russia’s Security Council of officials and experts from Arctic Council countries. It was chaired by former secretary of the Security Council of Russia, Nikolai Patrushev, one of the most powerful figures in President Vladimir Putin’s security orbit. As part of the cultural program, the group visited the remote Valaam Island monastery where Hanning was pictured next to Patrushev.
Delegates from Arctic Council countries visited the Valaam Island monastery on Oct. 2, 2019. August Hanning stands on the far right of the front row, next to senior Russian security official Nikolai Patrushev. | Valaam monastery
Hanning has also publicly ventured into some of the more politically explosive questions surrounding Russia’s war on Ukraine.
In 2024, he told WELT TV that he considered it “very likely” that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy knew about the 2022 operation that destroyed the Nord Stream pipelines. Days later, Hanning went further, suggesting an agreement between senior Ukrainian and Polish figures was behind the attack. Germany has since charged a Ukrainian national it identified only as Serhii K., with his trial due to begin in Hamburg in October.
Advertisement
None of those business relationships, contacts or statements establishes a connection to the espionage case now facing Hanning, though they paint a picture of the influence he continued to amass after leaving the German government. Prosecutors have not accused him of spying for Russia.
The steakhouse heiress
Investigators got onto Hanning’s trail starting with an extraordinary custody dispute involving Christina Block, an heiress to a German steakhouse empire.
Block is accused by the Hamburg Public Prosecutor’s Office of orchestrating the abduction of her two youngest children from their father in Denmark. Prosecutors in that case say Block and two men commissioned an Israeli security team to seize her children, then aged 10 and 13, from their father, Stephan Hensel.
According to the indictment, masked men beat Hensel and took the children across the Danish-German border, to southern Germany. The children were reunited with their father in Denmark four days later, under a court order. Block denies knowing about the abduction.
In September 2025, Hamburg investigators searched Hanning’s home and business premises in connection with the Block case, according to local media. Prosecutors suspected Hanning and a retired police officer had accepted a contract worth more than €100,000 to intercept the children on their way to school in November 2022. The plan ultimately failed as their father noticed suspicious figures and alerted Danish police.
German broadcaster Taggeschau reported that the investigators, in the search of Hanning’s premises, discovered around 2,000 digital BND documents that ultimately triggered scrutiny of his handling of sensitive government information. Federal prosecutors took over the resulting investigation in May 2026.
Advertisement
Manfred D. had been Hanning’s chief of staff at the intelligence service and subsequently served several of Hanning’s successors, remaining in a senior position until March this year.
Both men are now in custody.
“He’s reflecting the Germany between 1998 and 2011, so he has not the feeling of having done something evil,” said Kiesewetter. “He was just mirroring [the] state policy of the center-right Christian Democratic and conservative political alliance.”

IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has told senior U.S. government and military officials that a renewed military escalation with Iran could force Israel to postpone its general election, currently scheduled for October 27, according to a source familiar with the discussions.

The IDF and U.S. military have remained in close coordination since the end of the latest round of fighting with Iran. Israeli military intelligence is meanwhile building an extensive new target bank inside Iran, covering ballistic missiles, launch and production infrastructure and sites connected to Tehran’s nuclear program. The IDF declined to comment on Zamir’s reported remarks.
The warning fits a broader pattern of heightened preparations ahead of the election. International Criminal Court building in The Hague. Photo: Tony Webster, CC BY 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons
Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office has sent requests to the Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security, and to several other countries it did not name, asking them to detain and extradite nine current and former officials of the International Criminal Court in The Hague. The office announced the requests in a press release on its website.
The list includes former ICC prosecutor Karim Khan, the court’s president Tomoko Akane, first vice-president Rosario Salvatore Aitala, second vice-president Reine Alapini-Gansou, and judges Luz del Carmen Ibáñez Carranza, Sergio Gerardo Ugalde Godínez and Haykel Ben Mahfoudh.
It also names two people who no longer sit on the court: former president Piotr Hofmański and former judge Bertram Schmitt.
The Russian press release gives outdated titles. It calls Hofmański the court’s president and Ibáñez Carranza its first vice-president, which were their posts from 2021 to 2024. Hofmański’s term on the court ended in March 2024. The current president, Akane, appears in the release only as a judge.
Khan also no longer works at the court. In July 2026, the ICC’s Assembly of States Parties removed him from office after sexual misconduct allegations. Russia’s request still refers to him as the ICC prosecutor.
In December 2025, the Moscow City Court found all nine guilty in absentia of bringing a knowingly innocent person to criminal liability, unlawful detention, and an attack on persons enjoying international protection. The charges were quite unique, as one of the criminal articles relates to “the preparation... of an attack on a representative of a foreign state... for the purpose of provoking war or complicating international relations.”
Khan received 15 years in a penal colony. The others received sentences ranging from three and a half to 15 years.
The Prosecutor General’s Office repeated its earlier claims. It said Khan “unlawfully brought citizens of the Russian Federation to criminal liability” and that the ICC presidium, “in the absence of legal grounds,” instructed judges to issue “knowingly unlawful” arrest warrants. According to the office, these decisions violated international law and were made “in the absence of any evidence.” It also cited the 2016 presidential order withdrawing Russia’s intention to become a party to the Rome Statute, adding that Russia “does not recognise its jurisdiction.”
As in December, the press release does not name the Russian citizens. The Investigative Committee had previously confirmed that the case was opened in response to the March 2023 warrants for Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova. The ICC holds them responsible for the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.
Since the warrant was issued, Vladimir Putin has limited his travel to countries friendly to the Kremlin. He then defied the court in September 2024 by visiting Mongolia, a state party to the Rome Statute. Mongolia’s refusal to arrest Putin led to a formal “Non-Cooperation Finding” by the ICC, which referred the matter to the Assembly of States Parties.

‘War lives in me’: Gaza playwright Ali Abu Yasin wins English PEN award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:12:33 UTC
04:12:33 KST

‘War lives in me’: Gaza playwright Ali Abu Yasin wins English PEN award
Ali Abu Yasin, honoured for his artistic resilience, has endured Israeli bombardment, displacement and personal loss over the past three years.
London, United Kingdom – Ali Abu Yassin, a playwright from Gaza who continued writing even as Israel’s genocidal campaign devastated the world around him, has won a prestigious award in London.
“This prize is great not only for me, but for Gaza, Palestine, and all the Palestinian people,” Ali Abu Yasin, who was named on Thursday as “Writer of Courage 2026” by the literary group English PEN, told Al Jazeera.
The 62-year-old began writing plays and mastering the oud as a teenager in al-Shati refugee camp in Gaza, one of the largest in the Strip and a target of recent attacks.
“It’s how I was born, I’ve wanted to express myself using art since my childhood,” he told Al Jazeera.
After the war began in October, 2023, Abu Yasin stopped writing plays and instead wrote about life under Israeli bombardment.
Abu Yasin said for the first two years, he wrote about the situation in Gaza as Palestinians fled and feared for their lives.
“There was no theatre; it was impossible to have a theatre because Gaza was being destroyed,” the writer said, shaking his head.
Since 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza and the majority of survivors have been displaced several times over.
Abu Yasin works with actors who now rehearse their lines in makeshift tents, against the sound of gunfire.
“I was near death four, five times. I saw people around me die. We lived by chance, and those who died, died by chance,” Abu Yasin told Al Jazeera.
“My son was trapped under rubble; my house was bombed. So, during those two years, I was trying just to provide some safety to my family. To protect them from famine. And to document what was happening, so the world can hear my voice before I die.”
After a break, he wrote several screenplays that he hid and carried with him throughout displacement.
In 2004, Abu Yasin began working with the Said Al-Mishal Theatre, a hub for Palestinian culture in Gaza City that was levelled in a 2018 Israeli bombing.
Leading playwrights and theatre directors described the attack as “obliteration of this symbol of Palestinian culture and identity” in a letter to The Guardian newspaper.
In 2008, Abu Yasin began writing the Gaza Monologues, a series illustrating life in Gaza, both moments of joy and of pain.
A few weeks ago, Abu Yasin left Gaza with the support of an artist residency programme in France.
“I didn’t actually leave the war. The war lives in me, Gaza lives in me,” he said.
He has found himself conserving small amounts of water and minimising waste, habits he developed by living through the humanitarian crisis.
The award ceremony aligns with his trip to France, allowing him to attend in person largely by fortunate coincidence. For English PEN, the privilege of an in-person ceremony at the British Library is not taken for granted.
“For many years, writers living in Gaza have been among those with the most limited freedom of movement in the world. We recognise this and the direct impact it has on their freedom of expression,” an English PEN spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
Abu Yasin’s recent play, 50 Minutes, was shown in Gaza and tells the story of genocide and mourning. Actors rehearsed in a makeshift tent in a car park, many of them without any previous theatre experience.
Abu Yasin was nominated by the British academic and cultural critic Jacqueline Rose, who won the 2026 PEN Pinter Prize.
The Writer of Courage “is awarded to an author who is active in defence of freedom of expression, often at great risk to their own safety and liberty, and shares the PEN Pinter Prize with the winner,” says English PEN.
The organisation is the United Kingdom branch of PEN International, a global association of writers dedicated to “championing freedom of expression and literary advocacy worldwide”.
PEN America, its United States counterpart, came under fire in recent years as some alleged it did not support Palestinian writers. PEN America faced a boycott, leading to the resignation of its president in 2025.
English PEN, which operates independently from the US group, joined PEN International in calling for an arms embargo on Israel and condemning the killing of Palestinian writers.
Rose described his work as “a call for justice, a cry of outrage and a spiritual quest” in a press release.
“He has been the consistent chronicler of the harshness and cruelty of Palestinian existence, and the mentor of young people struggling to pluck meaning from the debris of their lives.”
Rose came to prominence with her 2005 book, The Question of Zion, a psychoanalysis of Zionism.
Abu Yasin has three children and 16 grandchildren. All are in Gaza except for his son, Amjad Abu Yasin, who is an actor in France.
“In Gaza, we have simple dreams. We want to live in peace and to live in freedom. We want the sky and the seas to be open,” he said. “We just want some freedom.”
