UAE blocks Israeli flights after flydubai cockpit attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:10:47 UTC
01:10:47 KST

Breadcrumb
UAE blocks Israeli flights amid reports of dispute over flydubai cockpit attack
The UAE has withdrawn landing permission for Israeli airlines attempting to repatriate passengers stranded in Dubai, forcing the cancellation of flights amid tensions over the handling of an suspected hijacking attack aboard a flydubai aircraft last week.
Israeli carriers Arkia, El Al and Israir cancelled flights scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday after Emirati authorities revoked the necessary authorisations, leaving passengers scrambling for alternative routes home.
Arkia said it had been working with the relevant authorities to restore permission but had been unsuccessful.
"Arkia has engaged with all relevant parties to regain authorization and operate the flights," the airline said in a statement cited by the Times of Israel.
"Unfortunately, these efforts have so far been unsuccessful, and we are therefore forced to cancel the flights."
The airline said affected passengers would receive full refunds, while those able to reach another destination served by Arkia would be offered a discount on flights to Israel.
The cancellations follow the suspension of flydubai's services to Tel Aviv after a violent incident aboard flight FZ1073 on 30 September, when an Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the aircraft's Indian captain with an emergency axe.
The Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, plunged more than 16,000 feet in approximately 30 seconds as the confrontation unfolded in the cockpit.
The wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to intervene and overpower the co-pilot. Two off-duty pilots subsequently took control and landed the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Emirati prosecutors have described the incident as an attempted terrorist attack, although investigators have yet to establish the suspect's motive.
Flydubai subsequently suspended its Tel Aviv services until at least 14 October, disrupting a major air link between the UAE and Israel.
The suspension initially left an estimated 10,000 Israelis stranded in Dubai and other destinations, prompting Israeli authorities to arrange special repatriation flights.
According to Israel's Transportation Ministry, at least 7,415 passengers had returned by Tuesday aboard special flights operated by Israeli carriers or commercial services through Abu Dhabi.
However, the latest withdrawal of landing permissions has disrupted the final stage of the operation, which Israeli authorities had expected to conclude on Thursday.
The precise reason for the Emirati decision remains unclear, although the dispute has exposed disagreements over how the aviation crisis has been handled.
A source close to the UAE, speaking to The Jerusalem Post, criticised Israeli officials for describing the flights as a rescue operation, arguing that the terminology wrongly suggested that Israelis were in danger in the Emirates.
"'Rescue flights' is a term used for a country where it is dangerous to be. That is simply not the case," the source said.
The source also claimed that flydubai had been prepared to resume flights to Israel under revised security arrangements, similar to those used by Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways, but that Israeli authorities had rejected the proposal.
The claims have not been independently confirmed.
Etihad has continued operating between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv, increasing services to help accommodate stranded passengers.
The dispute comes as authorities in several countries investigate the flydubai incident and the apparent security failures that allowed the suspect to operate flights to Israel.
Saudi Arabia has launched an aviation safety investigation into the incident, while the UAE is conducting a separate criminal investigation.
According to Reuters, Saudi authorities have notified international aviation agencies that they will examine the incident under established international safety procedures.
The UAE, where the aircraft is registered, is participating in the Saudi-led investigation, while Israel has expressed willingness to assist but has not been formally included.
The episode presents an unusual challenge for relations between Israel and the UAE, which established diplomatic ties under the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.
Direct commercial flights became one of the most visible symbols of normalisation, facilitating tourism, business and investment between the countries.
However, there has been no indication that the aviation dispute represents a wider suspension of diplomatic relations, with commercial flights through Abu Dhabi continuing despite the disruption in Dubai.

Nicolas Maduro, wife face torture charge in new U.S. indictment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:07:00 UTC
01:07:00 KST

Nicolas Maduro, wife face torture charge in new U.S. indictment
Deposed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now facing an additional charge of conspiracy to commit torture as federal prosecutors filed a superseding indictment in the Southern District of New York on Thursday.
"As alleged in the indictment, the Maduro regime subjected over a dozen American citizens to torture while held in custody of the Venezuelan government — including drugs, electrocution, sexual assault, and more," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on social media. "They will now answer for their crimes."
The couple were already facing a slew of charges, including narco-terrorism conspiracy; cocaine importation conspiracy; possession of machine guns and destructive devices; and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
The 30-page superseding indictment accuses the couple of overseeing a system of political repression that relied on Venezuela's military, intelligence agencies and security forces to torture their opponents, silence dissidents and maintain power.
"To undermine Venezuelan democracy and entrench themselves in power, these same leaders presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens," prosecutors wrote. "That torture included electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims' families, including children."
Maduro and Flores were indicted by a federal grand jury in January on charges stemming from what prosecutors said was his role in a scheme to import "thousands of tons" of cocaine into the United States and enrich themselves, their family and senior members of the Venezuelan government.
The U.S. military took the couple into custody in an overnight operation and brought them to the U.S. to face the charges. They have pleaded not guilty to the initial charges.
Prosecutors allege Maduro ordered political opponents detained and tortured, received regular updates on interrogations and instructed officials to intensify abuse. During one briefing about a defiant prisoner, Maduro allegedly told officials to "squeeze them harder."
During political unrest in 2014, Maduro allegedly proposed abducting five to seven military officers suspected of disloyalty and extracting information through torture. According to the indictment, Flores agreed with the proposal.
The indictment also includes cases involving U.S. citizens subjected to electric shocks, drowning, severe beatings and other abuse while detained in Venezuela. One American arrested in 2022 was allegedly given injections that caused seizures.
A U.S. citizen detained in 2023 was severely beaten and tortured by Venezuelan intelligence officers, prosecutors said. One officer allegedly told the prisoner he had been kept alive because his U.S. citizenship made him useful in a potential prisoner exchange.
At a bail hearing for Flores on Thursday, her lawyer asked for the arraignment on the new charge to be delayed since they just received the indictment that morning, which was allowed by the judge.
Flores' lawyer argued she should be allowed release on bail with strict conditions due to health concerns related to her heart. The judge denied bail for Flores, noting she had access to "considerable funds" and calling the charges "serious allegations."
The case against the couple was brought in the Southern District of New York, where Maduro and 14 others were first indicted in March 2020, during the first Trump administration.

LISBON -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Russia's war against Ukraine is at a stalemate but could escalate into a broader regional conflict if the deadlock pushes either side toward increasingly dangerous actions.
Speaking in Lisbon on the final stop of a three-country swing through NATO allies Iceland, Greece, and Portugal, Rubio said Washington believes the war ultimately requires a negotiated settlement and remains ready to facilitate diplomacy.
His remarks came as a Russian strike on two buses in the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people on October 8, according to local authorities.
Asked by RFE/RL about Russia's attacks on Ukraine and the security of NATO's eastern flank, Rubio called the conflict “a very dangerous war” that has reached reached a stalemate, which generally ends either through negotiations or escalation.
The first option requires both sides to make difficult compromises. The second could involve Russia or Ukraine intensifying the conflict in an attempt to change the military balance.
“That’s very dangerous,” Rubio said.
He warned that escalation could include Russian sabotage in neighboring NATO countries, a strike, or other actions that could rapidly widen the conflict.
That could “quickly turn what is a war between two countries to a much broader, far more dangerous regional conflict,” he said.
“In the end, we do not believe that there will be military solutions...We think this war needs to end, and the negotiated settlement is sooner and better.”
Portugal's foreign minister backed diplomatic efforts to end the war, saying Russia's invasion violates international law and that any settlement should respect Ukraine's sovereignty.
Rubio also recast the debate over NATO defense spending, describing increased military outlays as an investment in defense rather than simply “spending more.” He said stronger individual NATO members would strengthen the alliance and its deterrence.
Rubio said NATO is fundamentally a defensive alliance and that its credibility depends on the capabilities of its members.
“NATO is important. For NATO to matter, NATO has to be strong,” he said. “For NATO to be strong, NATO's member states need to be strong.”
He said NATO members have different circumstances and cannot all contribute in the same way, but each should develop the strongest capabilities it can. “
He also called for greater cooperation on advanced military technology and the next generation of weapons, saying allies need to work together to meet future threats.
Asked whether European allies could continue to rely on the US amid possible changes to the American military presence in Europe, Rubio stressed the importance of maintaining strong NATO capabilities and deterrence.
He did not provide details on future US troop deployments but said the alliance's members share responsibility for maintaining its strength.
Rubio also sharply criticized Iran when asked about concerns surrounding the use of Portugal's Lajes air base and allegations raised by Amnesty International over potential violations of international law.
He declined to comment on a Portuguese investigation, saying it was a matter for Portuguese authorities.
Rubio instead accused Amnesty International of failing to focus on alleged abuses by Iran's government against protesters, including the "murders in cold blood of tens of thousands of people in the streets.”
“Those are war crimes. Those are crimes against humanity. Those are crimes committed against their own people,” Rubio said.

Bear kills man, seriously injures woman in their home in Mongolia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:05:55 UTC
01:05:55 KST

Bear kills man, seriously injures woman in their home in Mongolia as encounters rise across Asia
A bear killed a man and seriously maimed a woman in their home in the outskirts of Mongolia's capital, authorities said Thursday, warning that sightings of the animals have skyrocketed across the country this year.
The man in his 40s and the woman in her 50s were attacked on Wednesday night in the Bayanzurkh district on the outskirts of Ulaanbaatar, the city's environment department chief Munkhbayar M told a news briefing.
The woman fled after sustaining injuries and sought help from neighbors, and she is being treated in a hospital, he said.
A team of 35 rangers is trying to locate and kill the bear.
Bear sightings have risen in Mongolia, with 24 confirmed sightings in Ulaanbaatar so far this year, compared with just two in 2018 and one in 2019, Munkhbayar said. Across Mongolia, 754 bear sightings have been reported in 11 provinces and the capital in 2026. Of those, 80% involved cubs or female bears accompanied by cubs.
Investigations are underway to determine what has caused the rise in sightings. Authorities have issued bear-hunting permits across eight provinces and are seeking to procure tranquilizer dart guns to support rangers in rural areas.
A bear that was hunted and examined in the eastern province of Khentii was found to have no food in its stomach, Baljinnyam N, an official at the Environment and Climate Change Ministry, told reporters.
As a result, authorities banned in September the harvesting of nuts and berries from mountainous areas for this year, he said.
Bear attacks increasing in parts of Asia
A spike in human-bear encounters has been reported in other parts of Asia recently.
In September, prosecutors said at least six people had been killed in bear attacks in Russia's vast Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk over a one-month period, and an official in a neighboring region reported bears had put one town "under siege."
Prosecutors said they opened a probe into criminal negligence, accusing local officials of failing to control bear numbers.
Russia's brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990, from around 130,000 to almost 308,000 in 2026, according to Russia's natural resources ministry.
Meanwhile, Japan has also recorded a sharp rise in bear sightings and attacks on humans in recent years, including in the outskirts of towns and cities. A record 13 people were killed by bears in Japan last year, and there has been a jump in encounters as the animals emerge hungry from hibernation.
The animals have been seen on airport runways, walking on golf courses, roaming near schools and causing panic in supermarkets and hot spring resorts almost on a daily basis.
The problem was so bad that last year, the U.S. State Department warned Americans in Japan to be alert for bears.
 The causes are complex and include variations in food available — something potentially linked to climate change — as well as rural depopulation, experts say.

U.K., Israel both claim a moral win with apparent truce in diplomatic feud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:02:43 UTC
01:02:43 KST

U.K. and Israel appear to reach tense truce, but diplomatic feud highlights Israel's strained ties with Europe
London and Tel Aviv — The U.K. and Israel appeared Thursday to have narrowly avoided a major diplomatic confrontation, reaching a compromise to allow Britain's nearly 200-year-old consulate in east Jerusalem to remain open, but under a new name and with a significantly reduced staff.
Israel had threatened to shut the facility down completely in a dispute over British sanctions barring the import of goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The agreement — which has been framed very differently by London and Tel Aviv — may prevent the tension between the two longstanding allies from escalating, but it has highlighted how strained ties have become between Israel and several European governments over Israel's ongoing actions in the Palestinian territories.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said talks with the U.K. had taken place "with the aim of preventing further deterioration in relations," following weeks of escalating tension.
The dispute began in September when London announced sanctions — along with 11 other Western nations — targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The measures include a ban on goods produced in the settlements and sanctions against companies and individuals involved in facilitating settlement expansion.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described the measures as the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Israel retaliated by giving Britain 30 days to close its east Jerusalem consulate. The facility has been operating since 1839, when Jerusalem was still part of the Ottoman Empire, predating the founding of Israel by more than a century. The consulate has historically operated independently of the U.K. Embassy in Tel Aviv, as Britain's principal diplomatic link with Palestinian officials in east Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
On Thursday, both governments sought to claim the diplomatic high ground.
Saar, in his statement, presented the agreement as a demonstration of Israel's willingness to respond to measures taken against it.
"It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response," he wrote. "We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour Government brought us here."
Saar insisted Israel had followed through on its September vow to retaliate for the sanctions, including by lifting the U.K. consulate's previous diplomatic status.
Under the new arrangement, Britain's consul general and 19 diplomats will leave Israel, while no more than seven diplomats will remain at the renamed mission, according to Saar.
Israeli officials have not said explicitly whether the remaining diplomats at the mission would retain their accreditation and diplomatic immunity, but Britain's top diplomat Miliband said in his statement that, "without an understanding, we would not have the necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises," indicating that those protections were likely part of the negotiations.
Miliband also said in his statement that the U.K. did "not accept that the Government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem," reaffirming Britain's longstanding position that "East Jerusalem is occupied territory."
Miliband said the newly renamed U.K. Mission would remain independent and operational, continuing to work with Palestinians. He also pledged to rebuild Britain's diplomatic presence in the coming months and ruled out any retaliatory measures — as long as "credible" discussions with Israel continue.
Both sides appeared to have moderated their responses because their bilateral security and business ties are too important to risk, Israeli political scientist Jonathan Rynhold told CBS News on Thursday.
The U.K. is an important economic market, and it punches above its weight diplomatically on the global stage, said Rynhold, a senior researcher with the Begin-Sadat Center at Israel's Bar Ilan University.
"They found something to do without blowing the whole relationship up," Rynhold said of the compromise.
Israel regards Jerusalem as its capital, while Britain and much of the international community do not recognize Israeli sovereignty over east Jerusalem, which Israel captured from Jordan in the 1967 Six-Day War and subsequently annexed.
The dispute comes amid a broader deterioration in Israel's relations with several European governments.
Spain has withdrawn its ambassador from Israel and imposed an embargo on arms sales to the Jewish state, while France formally recognized Palestinian statehood last year, drawing rebukes from the U.S. and Israel. Israel has also clashed with Ireland and Norway over their recognition of a state of Palestine.
The other nations that joined the U.K. in September in announcing sanctions or plans to impose sanctions targeting West Bank settlements were Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden.

French, US and Russian astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space

French, US and Russian astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
SpaceX brought France's Sophie Adenot and fellow astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and Andrey Fedyaev back to Earth on Thursday after an eight-month mission on board the International Space Station that saw Adenot become the first French woman to walk in space.
Four astronauts returned to Earth from the International Space Station on Thursday after hurrying there eight months ago to replace an ailing colleague and his crew.
SpaceX brought the US, French and Russian flyers back with a splashdown in the Pacific off the coast of Los Angeles.
NASA’s Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France’s Sophie Adenot and Russia’s Andrey Fedyaev departed the orbiting lab on Wednesday, eager to reunite with their families after a lengthy separation. Their replacements arrived three weeks late because of capsule repairs, stalling this crew’s homecoming.
They couldn’t wait to feel the breeze on their faces, hit the shower and, for Adenot at least, plunge back into water sports.
“We are so excited to be back on Planet Earth after an incredible mission on the International Space Station,” Meir radioed moments after splashing down. While still in orbit, she said the crew had “a lot of mixed, swirling emotions” and would miss the “extraordinary views of our home planet”.
Read moreExclusive: French astronaut Sophie Adenot recounts her ‘miracle’ mission from orbiting ISS
Meir and her crew left the planet in February to replace four station occupants who were sent home early after one of them – NASA's Mike Fincke, now retired – fell ill. It was NASA's first medical evacuation in 65 years of human spaceflight.
The new foursome watched with pride two months later as the Artemis II astronauts flew around the moon. They also celebrated the United States’ 250th birthday up there, with Meir joining the Boston Pops with her piccolo for a Fourth of July concert.
Meir took part in four spacewalks, while Adenot ventured outside three times for maintenance and upgrades to the 28-year-old outpost.
In the middle of all the work, the astronauts found time for fun, throwing a dance party last month and holding regular cooking demonstrations complete with aprons and a chef's toque.
Meir presented a how-to video for curly-haired spacewomen like herself, while Hathaway kept his bushy moustache – a space rarity – groomed to perfection. He grew the naval aviator-style moustache before rocketing into orbit as a way to honour his Navy ties, and found it no harder to maintain in weightlessness than on Earth. Some ground controllers grew moustaches in solidarity.
Will his moustache disappear now that his mission is over?
“It’s kind of become a little bit of my brand up here,” Hathaway said in August, “so I don’t know if it’ll go away right away or I’ll end up keeping it for a while.”
Seven astronauts remain aboard the space station, representing the US, Russia and Canada. The outpost has welcomed 298 visitors from 26 countries since the doors swung open in 2000, by NASA's count.

====================================================================================================

Does deliberating on politics make you look weak or wise? New research weighs in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:00:50 UTC
01:00:50 KST

New research suggests that taking time to weigh options before taking a stance on a political issue can improve how others view your moral character, but only if they disagree with your position. When people share the same political views, pausing to deliberate tends to have little effect on how their character is judged by their allies. The findings were published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin.
Political disagreement is an inescapable feature of democratic societies, but it often leads to negative social outcomes and interpersonal hostility. In a 2016 Pew Research Center survey, 47 percent of Republicans and 35 percent of Democrats viewed members of the opposing party as more immoral than the average American, numbers that rose to 72 percent and 63 percent by 2022. People tend to view their own political beliefs as correct and unbiased, often interpreting disagreement on moralized issues, which are issues that many people view in terms of right and wrong, as evidence that the other person lacks good moral character.
Prior research suggests that the speed of a decision sends a strong signal about a person’s inner moral compass. For example, a 2013 study found that people judge someone who quickly makes the right moral choice more favorably than someone who pauses to deliberate first, since taking time can look like hesitation or doubt about what is right.
“We knew from some past work that when people think deeply about a moral choice, others would judge them less extremely,” lead author Zachary N. Grey, a PhD candidate in the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto who researches with the Center for Mind and Morality Lab and the Morality, Affect, and Politics Lab, told PsyPost.
“If someone deliberated about whether they should return a wallet, then they would be seen as less of a good person if they returned it (the morally good thing), but they would also be seen as less of a bad person if they decided to keep it (the morally questionable thing),” Grey explained. “This was because deliberation signaled uncertainty. If someone does something wrong, then it’s better if they at least felt conflicted about doing it. If someone does something good, then it’s often best if they didn’t think twice about it.”
However, other findings indicate that learning about an opponent’s reasoning can soften hostility. A 2020 study found that people tend to assume their ideological opponents lack good reasons for their positions, and that reading arguments for the opposing side led them to form more favorable impressions of those opponents.
At the same time, appearing torn on an issue carries social costs. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 showed that expressing political ambivalence resulted in lower perceived likeability, particularly among participants who agreed with the target person’s overall position.
Grey and his colleagues at the University of Toronto designed the new study to connect these ideas. They reasoned that deliberating about a political issue might send two signals at once: that a person is thoughtful, and that they are uncertain. Thoughtfulness should count in a person’s favor no matter which side they take, but uncertainty might be welcome in an opponent and unwelcome in an ally.
“The catch is, this would imply that there would be some level of social risk to thinking things through when that process is observed by people who share your political views,” Grey said. “In their eyes, deliberating before landing on ‘the right position’ might make you seem less committed. Part of polarization might come from this pressure that people feel to display strong conviction in their political beliefs.”
“To us, however, the realm of politics seemed to be the sort of place where people ought to be more deliberative,” Grey added. “Doesn’t it seem praiseworthy for someone to ‘do their homework’ when it comes to politics? Wouldn’t it be great if people engaged in some perspective taking, or considered how other people might be affected by their political commitments? So, we wondered whether we could expect the original pattern of results for political deliberation, or whether something different might happen.”
In the first experiment, the scientists recruited 194 American adults to read 12 short descriptions of political issues, including carbon taxes, gun control, affirmative action, immigration, and universal healthcare. For each scenario, participants indicated whether they personally supported or opposed the policy or position.
Participants then read about a hypothetical person who either agreed or disagreed with their chosen position. This person was described as responding either “after long and careful deliberation” or “quickly and immediately.” Afterward, participants rated the person’s moral character on a 1-to-7 scale, assessing whether they viewed them as a good person who wants to do what is right.
The researchers found that participants consistently rated people who agreed with them more positively than those who disagreed. When the target person agreed with the participant, deliberating made no statistically significant difference: these targets averaged about 5.3 on the 7-point character scale either way. When the target disagreed, deliberation raised ratings from about 3.7 to about 4.1, a modest boost that still left opponents well below allies.
The second experiment involved 400 participants and used a similar design, but it added measures to examine what observers inferred from deliberation. Participants rated how thoughtful the target person seemed, assessing if the person had considered the issue deeply. They also rated how certain or conflicted the person appeared to be about their final decision.
This second experiment replicated the initial findings and shed light on why the pattern emerged. For targets who agreed with the participant, deliberation sent two opposing signals. It made the person seem more thoughtful, which was associated with improved character ratings.
At the same time, deliberation made agreeing targets seem less certain, which was linked to lower character ratings. These two influences pulled in opposite directions and canceled each other out, resulting in no statistically significant total effect on moral character judgments for allies.
For targets who disagreed with the participant, deliberation again made the person seem more thoughtful, which was associated with higher character ratings. It also made them seem less certain, but in this experiment that uncertainty was not reliably linked to character judgments in either direction. Overall, disagreeing targets who deliberated averaged about 4.5 on the 7-point character scale, compared to about 3.9 for those who decided quickly.
In the third experiment, the researchers recruited 302 participants and adjusted the wording to ensure participants were not being nudged toward an interpretation of thoughtfulness. Deliberating targets were simply described as responding “after deliberating,” and non-deliberating targets as responding “without deliberating.” The researchers also added a control condition where no information about deliberation was provided.
The results largely mirrored the previous experiments, though the formal test of whether deliberation affected allies and opponents differently was not statistically significant this time. Disagreeing targets who deliberated were judged more favorably than those who decided without deliberating (about 4.0 versus 3.75 on the 7-point scale), and more favorably than targets in the control condition. Character ratings in the control and no-deliberation conditions did not statistically differ from each other.
For targets who agreed with the participant, deliberation again showed no statistically significant effect on character ratings compared to the control or no-deliberation conditions. This pattern suggests that the positive influence of deliberation on opposing targets does not depend on loaded wording. This time, the uncertainty signaled by deliberation was also linked to more favorable ratings of opponents.
“The main takeaway from this work is that, at least when it comes to politics, the benefits of appearing thoughtful can help to offset the costs of appearing uncertain,” Grey told PsyPost. “If you’re working through something like a political issue, there’s no need to rush through it: a little bit of cognitive effort might go a long way. You’ll likely come off as being a better person in the eyes of those who disagree with you, and those who agree probably won’t think any less of your character.”
Drawing on earlier research, Grey also distinguished the active process of deliberation from simply holding mixed feelings. “We emphasize within the paper that people do not seem to necessarily infer thoughtfulness from mere political ambivalence,” he explained. “Thoughtfulness has the benefit of being seen as a form of cognitive effort, which is pretty praiseworthy. On the other hand, merely being ambivalent (endorsing reasons that both support and oppose a given position) doesn’t seem to give the same benefit on its own.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study used brief, written scenarios to describe political disagreements. In the real world, political conversations involve body language, tone of voice, and other social cues that might change how a pause in conversation is interpreted.
Participants also rated both deliberating and non-deliberating people in quick succession, which may have made deliberation more noticeable than it would be in everyday life. A supplementary experiment in which each participant saw only one version largely reproduced the results.
Observers may have assumed that an opponent who deliberated held a more moderate version of the opposing view, and because the study did not measure how extreme people thought the targets’ views were, it could not separate that impression from perceived uncertainty. Future research could investigate how perceived extremity interacts with decision speed.
The research focused exclusively on American participants and American political topics, leaving open how these patterns play out across other political cultures. In addition, the scientists only measured judgments of moral character, meaning that traits like warmth, competence, or assertiveness might respond to deliberation differently.
The study, “Diverging Effects of Deliberation: How Perceived Thoughtfulness About Political Issues Affects Character Judgments,” was authored by Zachary N. Grey, Paul Bloom, Jason E. Plaks, and Yoel Inbar.

====================================================================================================

Strong social networks predict higher fertility rates in new study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:00:47 UTC
01:00:47 KST

Communities where people report high levels of social support and frequent social interactions tend to have higher birth rates, regardless of their economic status. This pattern suggests that strong social networks within a region may help sustain population levels even as birth rates decline globally. The findings were published in the journal Biodemography and Social Biology.
Birth rates are dropping across much of the developed world. Several nations are approaching what demographers call lowest-low fertility, defined as fewer than 1.3 children per woman. This shift is drastically altering population pyramids and economic forecasts worldwide. Finland currently faces this steep decline, dropping from a fertility rate of 1.87 in 2010 to 1.30 in 2025.
This rapid downward trend has challenged the assumption that robust social welfare programs naturally protect against falling birth rates. Finland offers paid parental leave, heavily subsidized childcare, and home care allowances. Yet, its fertility rate has fallen faster than in many neighboring countries.
Researchers often look to economic conditions, such as recessions or housing costs, to explain why people choose to have smaller families. Economic indicators alone do not fully explain recent demographic shifts, particularly in Nordic countries where financial safety nets are strong. As a result, demographers are searching for alternative explanations. Family formation is an inherently social process, leading scientists to investigate how social environments influence childbearing.
Social capital broadly refers to the networks, resources, and shared norms that exist within a community. Previous research on family planning usually focused on the individual level, testing whether a specific person’s network of friends and relatives encouraged them to have children. Less is known about how the overall social atmosphere of a geographic region impacts its aggregate birth rate.
Eetu Soini, a psychology researcher at the University of Helsinki, led a team to investigate this gap in the literature. The researchers wanted to see if community-level measures of social cohesion corresponded to regional variations in fertility. Finland exhibits substantial regional differences in birth rates, with lower numbers in the southeast and higher numbers in the northwest coastal areas. The team hypothesized that municipalities with stronger social ties would report higher birth rates.
Soini and his colleagues analyzed data from a large national health survey conducted between 2012 and 2017. The survey included 100,750 adults across 299 Finnish municipalities. The researchers used this data to calculate regional estimates for seven different components of social capital. These components included perceived social support, frequency of social interactions, community participation, cultural engagement, general trust, trust in people, and loneliness.
To measure social support, the survey asked participants who they believed truly cared about them and who would provide practical help if needed. For social interactions, participants reported how often they communicated with people outside their household in person, by phone, or online. The researchers used a statistical technique to mathematically adjust the survey responses so they would accurately reflect the true age and sex demographics of each specific municipality.
The team then compared these localized social metrics to municipality-level fertility data spanning from 2018 to 2020. They incorporated a three-year lag between the survey data and the birth records to see if existing social conditions preceded current fertility trends. The researchers used spatial statistical models to account for the fact that neighboring regions often share similar demographic traits. By using these spatial models, the researchers could filter out hidden variables that cluster geographically.
The team adjusted their models for population size, population density, religious affiliation, and a composite score of regional socioeconomic status. The socioeconomic score combined local data on tax income, education levels, and unemployment rates.
The researchers found that municipalities with higher levels of expected social support had higher total fertility rates. Regions where residents reported more frequent social interactions also saw higher birth rates. These associations remained even after adjusting for all demographic and socioeconomic variables.
The specific source of the social support did not change the main outcome. Support expected from romantic partners, relatives, friends, and other associates were all linked to higher regional birth rates. The local socioeconomic status, by contrast, showed no association with fertility rates in any of the models.
The study also analyzed specific age groups to see who was most sensitive to these regional social factors. The link between social support and higher fertility was strongest for individuals between the ages of 20 and 39. The association peaked specifically among people in their twenties.
The researchers suggest that young adults often face more uncertainty in their careers and finances. This precariousness might make a supportive social environment especially relevant for their transition to parenthood. Older age groups may already have established careers and stable incomes, making them less reliant on broader community support.
Not all forms of social capital were linked to birth rates. The researchers found no association between a region’s fertility rate and its levels of general trust or trust in people. Community participation, such as involvement in sports clubs, health organizations, or political groups, was also unrelated to fertility. Engagement in cultural events and regional rates of loneliness similarly showed no association with birth rates. These null findings suggest that the recent rise in public loneliness may not be a driving force behind demographic changes.
The researchers performed additional calculations to ensure that people simply delaying childbirth did not skew the results. Demographers call this a tempo effect, where the average age of mothers giving birth rises and temporarily depresses the annual birth rate. Even after adjusting for changes in the average age at birth, the regions with higher social support from relatives and more frequent social interactions still demonstrated higher fertility rates.
The study relies on cross-sectional data, meaning it captures a snapshot of a population at a specific time. This design prevents researchers from determining whether high social capital directly causes people to have more children. It is entirely possible that the reverse is true, where a higher birth rate fosters greater social cohesion. Having children often connects parents to new community networks, such as schools, daycares, and youth sports leagues, which could increase overall regional interactions.
Comparing broad regional metrics does not always perfectly mirror individual behavior. A regional correlation between social support and fertility might reflect community-wide norms that encourage family growth, or it could simply be the mathematical sum of individual choices. Future research will need to separate individual influences from neighborhood effects to better understand how local environments shape family planning. Investigating how social capital affects the decision to have a first child versus subsequent children could also provide more specific insights into these population trends.
The study, “Regional social capital and fertility rate: Municipality-level analysis in Finland,” was authored by Eetu Soini, Kateryna Golovina, Hans Hämäläinen, Anna Rotkirch, Venla Berg, Suvi Parikka, and Markus Jokela.

Global health officials — as well as the world's media — have been particularly alert to pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the Covid-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China.
However, the cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined.

Xinhua Headlines: Where the Long March began, China's new journey unfolds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:00:41 CST
01:00:41 KST

NANCHANG, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The former ferry crossing is about half an hour's walk from the home of Sun Guanfa, 77, in Yudu, a hilly county in east China's Jiangxi Province.
For his father, the journey from this riverbank more than nine decades ago was part of an epic.
In October 1934, some 86,000 soldiers of the Red Army crossed the Yudu River to embark on what later came to be known as the Long March.
In a country beset by foreign invasion, social turmoil and destitution, the fledgling Red Army, led by the Communist Party of China (CPC), was fighting for national independence and the liberation of the Chinese people. But at the time, it was encircled by the overwhelming and much better-armed Kuomintang forces.
What followed was an epic military maneuver: from Yudu, Red Army troops trekked roughly 12,500 kilometers across China, crossing snow-covered mountains and treacherous marshlands, all the while battling enemy forces. They eventually reached the country's northwest, where, in 1936, they were joined by several other Red Army branches, marking the victorious conclusion of the Long March.
This military maneuver preserved the Red Army. It also gave the CPC a new foothold in northwest China, from which it built up its strength, fought back against invading Japanese troops and eventually toppled the corrupt Kuomintang regime, leading to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
In Yudu, the Long March is not simply a chapter in a history book. It is a family story.
More than 17,000 residents joined the departing army. Only 277 were recorded as eventually returning home, said Zhong Min, a guide at a museum built beside the river to commemorate the departure.
Her voice still catches when she says that number.
Her maternal great-grandfather died fighting the encirclement campaigns. Her husband's grandfather marched away with the troops and was never heard from again. Sun's father fell in a battle that saw the forces of the Red Army reduced to just over 30,000.
"We are not telling other people's stories," Zhong said. "We are telling our own families'."
Here, the Long March is measured not only in kilometers and battles, but in the people who left home knowing they might never return.
For Sun, the legacy of that generation is deeply personal. Under a local tradition, Sun was adopted as the son of the soldier who left the riverbank and never returned, so that the soldier's family line could continue.
"People of my father's generation were willing to give their lives so ordinary people could be liberated," Sun said.
On the same riverbank in 2019, Chinese President Xi Jinping spoke of what had enabled the Party and the Red Army to come back from the brink of destruction time and again: firm ideals and convictions, and strong willpower.
"We must not forget our Party's original aspiration and founding mission," said Xi, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission. The Party's long-stated mission, dating to its founding in 1921, is to seek happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation.
During the visit, Xi placed a flower basket at a monument commemorating the Red Army's departure and bowed in tribute. He then walked behind the monument to a railing overlooking the river and stood there for a long while.
The river remains. For Xi, it was also a place from which to look ahead to China's future.
"We came to this place to revisit what it was like when the Red Army set out," he told local people gathered nearby. "Today we are on a new journey -- to build a modern socialist country. We must carry on the work of those who came before us, gear up anew, and set out once more."
That new journey was unfolding against a vastly changed backdrop. When Xi visited Yudu, the nationwide campaign he had launched to combat poverty was entering its final stage.
It would culminate in the elimination of absolute poverty in a nation of 1.4 billion. Nearly 100 million rural residents were lifted out of poverty under Xi's "targeted poverty alleviation" campaign, which mobilized the entire Party and the nation.
Xi announced the victory, as a key part of building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, in 2021 when the CPC marked its centenary.
During his 2019 visit, Xi saw for himself whether the former revolutionary base areas were on track to meet their poverty-reduction targets.
At Sun's home, he walked through the main hall to the backyard and checked the kitchen and the bedrooms. There was rice and cooking oil in the kitchen, and the bathroom was clean.
Xi asked about the family's income and how Sun's son and daughter-in-law made a living, where their children went to school, and what the school meals were like.
"By the time they grow up, we will have achieved the rejuvenation of our nation," Xi said, pointing to Sun's two grandchildren.
China aims to basically realize socialist modernization by 2035 and build a great modern socialist country in all respects by the middle of this century, according to the vision set by the Party.
Earlier, at the museum where Zhong served as a guide, Xi had stopped before a map of China made from straw sandals.
The display recalled how local people worked through the night to make straw sandals for the soldiers, many of whom fought barefoot. They also dismantled doors, bed boards, roof beams and even timber intended for coffins to build pontoon bridges, helping the soldiers cross the Yudu River.
"The country has developed and people's lives have improved, but we must remember where it all came from," Xi said. "We must not forget our revolutionary forefathers and those who died for the revolution, or the people of the old revolutionary base areas."
Nowadays, golden waves of selenium-rich rice ripple around the 700-year-old village, and rows of modern vegetable greenhouses stand nearby. In the residential area, white-walled houses with gray-tiled roofs sit amid trees, while pavilions nestle between them.
"Now we have wages from working, rent from our guesthouses and dividends from our shares," Sun said. "Our annual income has tripled to more than 200,000 yuan (around 29,000 U.S. dollars)."
The transformation extends well beyond Yudu.
Much of southern Jiangxi, once cut off from the outside world by rugged mountains, is far more connected. High-speed rail links it with the city of Shenzhen, the country's economic powerhouse close to Hong Kong. Expressways also reach every county, and paved roads now extend into villages.
For local business owners, it no longer means spending two days and two nights on the road to source a critical part. Now they can hop on a high-speed train, pick up what they need in the morning and return that afternoon, drastically speeding up the development of a prototype.
The change is not only about getting around. Industries such as non-ferrous metals and advanced materials, electronics and information technology, and textiles and apparel have taken root here. For ordinary people, the changes are closer to home. Housing has improved, drinking water is safer, and schools and medical care are more accessible.
More people can now earn a living without leaving their hometowns. In March, the Hong Kong Polytechnic University launched a facility dedicated to research into smart wearables and smart clothing in Xingguo, a county next to Yudu.
This summer, Yudu welcomed students from more than 170 universities across China who came to retrace the Long March at the places where it began. Many realized that the Red Army soldiers who set out were their age.
"Standing where those young soldiers began their journey gave me a deeper understanding of what they accomplished," said Liu Fanshuo, an undergraduate studying automation.
Today, five modern bridges span the Yudu River near the crossings where local people once built pontoon bridges to help the Red Army cross.
On the banks, Sun pours hot tea for tourists whose lives might have been very different had those soldiers never crossed. ■

WTO raises 2026 global merchandise trade growth forecast to 3.9 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
00:00:40 CST
01:00:40 KST

GENEVA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The World Trade Organization (WTO) said on Thursday that global merchandise trade is expected to grow by 3.9 percent in 2026, up from its March forecast of 1.9 percent, driven by supply chain adaptation and strong investment in artificial intelligence (AI).
While raising the forecast for merchandise trade growth, the WTO's latest Global Trade Outlook and Statistics report lowered the outlook for commercial services trade in 2026 over the impact of the Middle East conflict.
The forecast for services trade volume growth in 2026 has been revised down to 3.3 percent from 4.8 percent in March.
In 2027, growth rates in volume terms for merchandise and services trade are expected to rise to 4.1 percent and 6.4 percent, respectively, depending on a timely resolution of the Middle East conflict, the report said.
In the report, the WTO projected global GDP growth at 2.6 percent and 2.9 percent in 2026 and 2027, respectively.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said the figures "reflect trade resilience in action."
Meanwhile, WTO Deputy Director-General Johanna Hill told a press conference held on the same day that while the system has proven resilient, that does not necessarily mean it is robust.
"Vulnerabilities remain, and WTO members are working to address them. Strengthening the multilateral trading system will help ensure that the global economy is better equipped to deal with future shocks."
According to the report, merchandise trade volume grew by 3.5 percent in the first half of 2026, exceeding expectations despite the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict.
The performance reflected the ability of supply chains to adapt to shocks affecting energy, fertilizer and transport markets, the report noted.
The report showed that crude oil exports from the Middle East fell by roughly 24 percent and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports by 47 percent in the first half of 2026. But increased shipments from other suppliers helped limit the decline in global exports to around 6 percent for crude oil and just 1 percent for LNG. Fertilizer markets also adjusted despite severe disruption, the report said.
Another factor contributing to the higher merchandise trade growth forecast is "a stronger-than-expected" surge in AI-related capital investment, said the report.
In the first half of 2026, AI-enabling goods such as semiconductors and servers accounted for 47 percent of global merchandise trade growth, with trade in these products up 67 percent year-on-year, accelerating from already rapid growth in 2024 and 2025.
As the Middle East conflict disrupted transport and travel services, services trade growth slowed from 14 percent year-on-year in value terms in the first quarter of 2026 to 10 percent in the second quarter, the report showed.
It noted that other services, especially digitally delivered services such as computer and financial services exports, remained resilient and continued to support overall services trade growth. ■

Florida judge allows lawsuit against Shah of Iran’s alleged ‘chief torturer’ to move forward
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:00:23 UTC
01:00:23 KST

The alleged “chief torturer” for the deposed Shah of Iran is a step closer to trial for human rights abuses after a Florida federal judge rejected his demand to halt a lawsuit brought by three former political prisoners.
Parviz Sabeti, who was reported last year to have lived in a quiet upscale central Florida community, is accused of being the former head of Savak, the shah’s secret police and intelligence agency. The plaintiffs say they discovered his whereabouts only after a photo of Sabeti at a 2023 protest against the Iranian government was posted on social media by his daughter.
He could now be made to answer as early as next year to civil claims under the Torture Victim Protection Act (TVPA) that he directed and took part in the detention and torture of thousands of the shah’s political opponents in jails in Tehran and elsewhere until the Islamic revolution swept the regime from power in 1979.
Sabeti has denied allegations that that he was personally involved or that Savak tortured detainees, and claimed that he “always opposed torture”.
Tuesday’s sealed order by the district court judge Gregory A Presnell rejected Sabeti’s argument that a statute of limitations on the allegations should be strictly enforced and a summary judgment issued in his favor.
In August 2025, Presnell rejected a motion by Sabeti’s lawyers to dismiss the case outright, ordering the parties to conduct discovery on whether the TVPA claim was time-barred, and said he would listen to arguments about why the deadline should not be extended.
Sabeti’s lawyers dispute that he was difficult to find and sue before 2023, filing dozens of documents which they said proved he had lived openly in Florida under his real name, including property records, media articles, and a photograph of Sabeti with George HW Bush and his son Jeb Bush, a former governor of Florida.
In May, attorneys for the three Iranian plaintiffs filed a response presenting dozens of documents and articles of their own to try to bolster their argument that there were extraordinary circumstances in the case that warranted an extension of time to bring the claim.
They included the Guardian’s September 2025 story that chronicled Sabeti’s departure from Iran and his low-profile new life in Florida, where the lawsuit asserts he “has spent the last four decades out of the public eye, concealing his whereabouts and identity”.
As the Guardian reported last year, Sabeti was identified as a fiercely loyal ally of the shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, in a secret analysis by the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) written in 1978, which was not released until 2018.
According to the complaint, he was “widely recognized as one of the most powerful and feared men in the shah’s regime … with the authority to apprehend, interrogate and prosecute opponents throughout the country”.
The plaintiffs, Iranian men living in California aged 68 to 85, claim they were among thousands of people rounded up as perceived opponents of the shah by Savak, Iran’s notoriously brutal internal security and intelligence agency, and subjected to abuses at Sabeti’s personal direction.
Among their claims made under the TVPA are that their captors used rape, electric shocks, near-drownings and forced nail extraction against political prisoners. They say they were abducted by Savak in Tehran, beaten into giving false confessions and served prison time.
The lawsuit details the alleged use of a torture device nicknamed Apollo, an electric chair named after the early US space program, which featured a metal helmet that amplified victims’ screams into their own ears.
Sabeti has previously insisted he was not involved in the detention, torture or execution of prisoners. A 2023 report on the website of the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran, a dissident group, cited an interview Sabeti gave to the Persian channel Manoto in which he characterized his government employment as clerical work.
Court papers list seven attorneys for Sabeti. None replied to the Guardian’s request for comment by the time of publication.
Claret Vargas, senior staff attorney for the Center for Justice and Accountability, an advocacy group representing the three Iranian plaintiffs, welcomed Presnell’s ruling, which she said allows the case to move forward towards discovery on the TVPA allegations against Sabeti. The court previously dismissed the state law claims.
“I’m very glad that our clients will be able to pursue justice after all these years, and everybody deserves justice for torture regardless of who was in charge, or the regime that tortured them,” she said.
“Perpetrators of torture should not escape accountability simply because the survivors were forced to live with fear for decades.
“We don’t yet know the specific legal basis for the court’s decision, but it’s a really important milestone for our clients to be able to bring forth this case and really address [their allegations].”
Donald Trump’s war in Iran has brought new scrutiny of the resilience of the country’s hardline Islamic regime, and the strength of the opposition to it among a sizable Iranian expat community in the US.
Washington DC-based Reza Pahlavi, the former shah’s son, has positioned himself as a possible new leader if the current regime falls, although questions remain over his level of popular support.
In June, Pahlavi, 65, was forced to distance himself from far-right supporters who flew banners and wore shirts with the Savak emblem at rallies.
Divisions between various opposition groups of Iranians in the US were highlighted by the killing in Canada earlier this year of the Iranian activist Masood Masjoody, a critic of the US-led war and the campaign to install Pahlavi as the country’s next leader.
According to the Associated Press, Masjoody’s sudden disappearance in February was followed by a threatening post on X in Farsi directed at other activists by a since-deleted account named for Savak.

“The time of containment in the face of hostile [acts] against the State of Israel is over,” Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said Thursday, warning that Britain’s Labour government risks losing its influence in the region as Jerusalem responds to a series of sanctions and diplomatic measures.
Speaking in an interview with The Jerusalem Post at the newspaper’s Diplomatic Conference in Jerusalem, Sa’ar defended his decision to shut down the British Consulate in Jerusalem on Thursday – the deadline for closure – saying, “Every state that works and acts against the State of Israel must understand that we will take our revenge.”
The decision to close the consulate is the latest in a series of retaliatory measures following the British government’s imposition of sanctions on Israel on September 8.
In addition to closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem, Israel has removed British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat, terminated British training activities for Palestinian Authority (PA) security forces in the West Bank, and barred 12 British elected officials from entering the country, along with other British citizens accused by Israel of antisemitic or anti-Israel activity.
The closure also means the departure of approximately 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, from the Jerusalem mission.
British consulate in east Jerusalem downgraded to limited diplomatic mission
Sa’ar authorized the British government to operate a task force of only seven diplomats in the mission building with a limited scope of activity.
He told the Post that Israel had deliberately targeted areas in which the United Kingdom previously maintained a diplomatic or security presence, including Jerusalem, the West Bank, and Gaza.
“Any country that pursues a one-sided and unbalanced policy against Israel will lose its influence and relevance in our region, including in Gaza and Jerusalem.”
“We didn't choose this path. It was the Labour government that chose that. But we had to react,” he said.
Sa'ar accuses UK Labour government of increasingly hostile policies toward Israel
Sa’ar accused the Labour government, which came to power in July 2024, of pursuing an increasingly “hostile” policy toward Israel, pointing to measures targeting Israeli officials, organizations, trade negotiations, and military cooperation.
Despite the deterioration in relations, Sa’ar insisted that diplomatic dialogue between Jerusalem and London would continue.
“I’m always for dialogue,” he said, although he expressed little optimism about a significant change in British policy under the current government.
Asked whether he believed relations could recover while Labour remained in power, Sa’ar pointed to the party’s recent conference, claiming that government ministers had avoided an event organized by Labour Friends of Israel while attending one hosted by Labour Friends of Palestine.
“I believe this tells you the direction, and therefore I want to be realistic,” he said. “It doesn’t mean we don’t give [them] a chance. We always give a chance for a different path.”
Sa'ar says Britain risks undermining valuable intelligence and security cooperation with Israel
The foreign minister also stressed that Israel continued to provide the UK with valuable assistance in intelligence and security cooperation, suggesting that London was undermining a relationship from which it benefited.
“We help the Brits: security, intelligence, a lot of issues. They know it,” he said. “I think they are making a mistake in their approach.”
Sa’ar drew a distinction between legitimate criticism of Israeli government policy and what he described as punitive action against the Jewish state.
“It’s one thing to criticize, and it’s a different thing to act against you,” he said.
Colombia to open embassy in Jerusalem next week
Turning to Israel’s wider diplomatic relations, Sa’ar announced that Colombia would inaugurate an embassy in Jerusalem on October 14, thus becoming the 10th country to establish an embassy in the Israeli capital.
“Next Wednesday, we are going to inaugurate the 10th foreign embassy in Jerusalem, which will be the Colombian embassy,” he told the conference.
“When I entered my ministry, it was less than two years ago, there were five [embassies in Jerusalem]. Next week, we’re going to have 10.”
Sa’ar also revealed that Israel had already reached an agreement with the Democratic Republic of the Congo to open an embassy in the capital, which would become the 11th foreign diplomatic mission in the city.
“We already agreed about the 11th embassy with DRC. And that will be very soon,” he said.
Sa'ar hopes more countries, including Brazil, will open embassies in Jerusalem
The foreign minister expressed hope that additional countries, including Brazil, could eventually follow, linking the expansion of Jerusalem’s diplomatic presence to Israel’s efforts to strengthen its international standing.
“This is a diplomatic battle over the truth,” Sa’ar said, arguing that Jerusalem’s historical connection to the Jewish people remained central to Israel’s diplomatic efforts.
“Jerusalem was always the capital of one nation, and that’s the Jewish people, from the times of King David more than 3,000 years ago, until this very day,” he said.
Returning to the UK in his closing remarks, he suggested that London’s refusal to recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital did nothing to diminish that historical connection.
“Everyone knows Jerusalem,” Sa’ar said, “even if it is not recognized by the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom.”

Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman warned that the United States is expected to recognize a Palestinian state within approximately two years, claiming that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is aware of the move and is working to advance it.

Senior US and Russian authorities, including special US envoy Jared Kushner, have discussed the prospect of an American investor joining the Nord Stream pipelines that once supplied Russian gas to Germany.
The talks involved Kushner – US President Donald Trump’s son-in law, and Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, five people familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday, Oct. 8.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Any deals will have to be negotiated by Russia with DFC [US International Development Finance Corporation] and Treasury and must benefit United States taxpayers and companies,” a White House official told the news agency when asked about the discussions, adding that there had been “no Nord Stream discussions recently.”
Business as a possible path to peace
Kushner, who has been working alongside his counterpart US senior envoy Steve Witkoff to broker an end to Russia’s war, reportedly sees business deals as key to securing peace.
An agreement on Nord Stream would essentially allow American investors to profit from gas flowing to Europe – once an unconditional ceasefire is achieved.
Late September, Dmitriev headed to New York for talks with the Trump administration, with the agenda previously agreed upon with Russian President Vladimir Putin. His visit followed an earlier meeting between Putin and US representatives on Sept. 5, when Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Moscow, before heading to Kyiv for the first time only a day later.
Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
According to Reuters, it is not clear how much of these meetings focused on the pipelines. However, two of the sources said the issue was still on the table.
Dmitriev, who has long lobbied for Russian gas sales to Germany to resume, also met representatives of the US Energy and Treasury departments last month to explore possible energy projects between the two countries.
His representative declined Reuters’ request for a comment.
Nord Stream pipelines remain under EU and US sanctions
How serious Washington is about reviving Russian gas supplies to Germany – Europe’s largest energy consumer – remains uncertain.
One US official told Reuters that a deal was unlikely in the medium term given the obstacles involved.
Currently, both pipelines are under US and EU sanctions. This would make any possible deal practically illegal. While Trump has the power to waive or ease US sanctions, doing so could become more difficult should the Democrats take control of Congress in the upcoming November midterm elections.
Germany and other EU countries are also expected to push back, as they rearm in response to the growing threat from Russia and work to tighten sanctions on Russian gas and on more than 3,000 Russian individuals and entities.
The Nord Stream pipelines, which provided Europe with Russian gas, remain closed due to EU sanctions. The decision has been in effect since the beginning of the war in 2022. Germany previously relied on the two pipelines for more than half of its gas imports.
In September 2022, several Nord Stream pipelines were severely damaged by a series of underwater explosions, with the latest suspect arrested on Aug. 19, 2026 in Croatia.
According to Reuters, a spokeswoman for Germany’s Economy and Energy Ministry said that Berlin has since found other suppliers. Reopening the pipelines would require approval from the German government, which has no wish to do so, she added.
Zelensky questions economic talks
Speaking in Pryluky earlier on Thursday, President Volodymyr Zelensky questioned how economic cooperation with Moscow could be discussed while peace efforts remained at a standstill.
“One cannot… negotiate with Russians about future economic projects,” he said, describing the situation as a “diplomatic stalemate.”
Zelensky has also announced that Ukrainian negotiators would travel to the US for talks on Friday, Oct. 9-10, urging Trump to step up pressure on Russia.
The two presidents previously met on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, at which high-level talks were held the last week of September. During the meeting, Zelensky outlined Ukraine’s positions on a potential energy ceasefire, trilateral talks with Putin, domestic Patriot missile production, and growing Russian threats to Europe.
During the same summit, 51 countries signed a joint statement backing Ukraine and urging Russia to accept an immediate, unconditional ceasefire. So far, the Kremlin has rebuffed every such proposal.
Dmitriev, who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund, has become one of Moscow’s main channels to Washington. He has previously held talks with US officials on sanctions waiver for Russian oil and prisoner exchanges.

A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.
The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding.

The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024.
Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers.
Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine.
“These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year.

Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia.
In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers.

Nearly 50 Arrested as Police Target Western Balkan Drug Network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:56:00 UTC
00:56:00 KST

Nearly 50 suspects have been detained following an international crackdown on a Western Balkan drug syndicate allegedly linked to murders, kidnappings, and grenade attacks across Europe, Europol announced on Thursday.
The multi-year investigation culminated on October 6, when police searched 42 properties across Slovenia and Spain. Law enforcement arrested 36 suspects on the action day—34 in Slovenia, one in Spain, and one in Croatia—adding to 11 members previously detained during the probe.
The syndicate comprised nationals from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Türkiye, and the Netherlands. To move cocaine, cannabis, amphetamine, MDMA, and methamphetamine from Belgium, the Netherlands, and Spain to destinations across Europe, the group allegedly hired drivers—chiefly from Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Bulgaria—to conceal illicit cargo within regular commercial shipments using trucks, vans, and cars.
To coordinate logistics, syndicate members relied on encrypted platforms, including SKY ECC and CryptCom. When shipments were lost or financial disputes erupted, the network allegedly turned to severe violence to maintain control and enforce discipline. Investigators tied the group to alleged shootings, homicides, an attempted murder in Spain, the abduction of a group member, and hand grenade strikes directed primarily at syndicate members and their relatives.
On the October 6 action day, officers seized 66 kilograms of narcotics—including 51 kilograms of cannabis and 15 kilograms of amphetamine—along with cash, jewelry, and firearms.
Europol clarified that these raids built upon years of prior evidence gathering: between February 2022 and September 2026, officers directly investigating this specific network had already physically intercepted 253 kilograms of cocaine, 404 kilograms of cannabis, 18.8 kilograms of methamphetamine, 825 grams of MDMA, and 550 liters of acetic anhydride, a chemical precursor used in drug manufacturing. Police had also confiscated ammunition, several handguns, and an automatic firearm fitted with a suppressor.
However, physical seizures accounted for only part of the syndicate's alleged traffic. By decrypting intercepted SKY ECC communications, investigators uncovered extensive additional operations. Prosecutors now expect to charge the suspects in connection with an unseized additional 2.5 metric tons of cannabis, 474 kilograms of cocaine, 104 kilograms of heroin, 30 kilograms of amphetamine, 11.6 kilograms of MDMA, 18,000 ecstasy tablets, and 1,000 units of psychoactive mushrooms.

The men, 32 and 36, were picked up at 2am inside the base, in an investigation that began four hours earlier when military police discovered an abandoned vehicle outside the facility.
Military police, helped by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence before finding and arresting the men, initially on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage.
The suspects, Latvian nationals currently resident in the UK, were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023 – namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
Counter-terror police are now leading the investigation due to the nature of the incident, which comes a few days after the US withdrew B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire amid concerns about a possible Iran-directed attack.
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counter-terrorism policing London, said there was nothing at this stage to suggest a connection to September’s incident near RAF Fairford, but said investigators were yet to determine what the men had been doing.
“Our investigation into this incident is at its very early stages. A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage and inquiries are very much ongoing,” she added.
Investigators said it was unclear at this stage if there was a hostile state link to the men’s presence on the base, if they were criminals or whether they had ended up on the site in a misjudged state of late-night exuberance.
The abandoned vehicle was taken to a nearby police location. Initial searches led concerned officers to call in explosives specialists to carry out further checks, though nothing concerning was understood to have been found.
A police cordon was also briefly imposed on part of the A1 south of Peterborough and around the village of Glatton, as a precaution, but has been lifted. Officers were carrying out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation, counter-terror police added in a statement.
Both men remained in police custody on Thursday.
RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre, which provides military intelligence to Nato, and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe, which provides similar service for the US military’s European command, though not Centcom, which is responsible for Iran.
The head of the armed forces, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, said he had “confidence around the safety and security of our bases” as he visited troops on a military exercise in Wales earlier on Thursday.
The chief of defence staff cited the “enormously close relationships from an intelligence perspective and operationally with the US” as reasons for his confidence, but said the US had removed its bombers from Fairford as a precaution.
“The decision to remove the bombers, which don’t ordinarily live there … to take them back was an operational decision to reduce the risk,” he added. The bombers were suddenly redeployed on Sunday, amid reports that the US feared Iran could orchestrate a drone attack on B-1 planes on the ground.
British sources remain sceptical that Iran would have the capability to launch an attack of such sophistication, though the investigation into why five men driving three white vans descended on a village next to Fairford continues.
Mark Rowley, the Met police chief, said the public would “see more progress on this investigation”, and urged them to trust the police as they worked with spy agencies MI5, GCHQ and intelligence partners internationally.
The five men arrested near RAF Fairford, all British nationals in their 20s from London, have been released on police bail without charge, as has a sixth, a dual UK-Iranian national, who was arrested subsequently.
A seventh man, aged 22, who was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, was also let out on bail on Thursday.
Rowley acknowledged the threat landscape appeared to have changed. “We’re dealing with an increased tempo of terrorists and also of threats that are directed by foreign states such as Iran and Russia,” he said in a radio interview.
