St. Francis of Assisi Meets Antoni Gaudí, an event at the embassy in Madrid
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:27:34 CEST
00:27:34 KST

The Italian Embassy in Madrid celebrated the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi and the 100th anniversary of the death of Antoni Gaudí with the event “Francisco y Gaudí: lenguajes, vida y actividades de lo sagrado.” The event featured a dialogue between Father Giuseppe Buffon, OFM, rector of the Pontifical Antonianum University and professor of Church History, and Italian architect Chiara Curti, a professor at the Antoni Gaudí Faculty in Barcelona and author of publications on the Catalan architect, including the recent *Gaudí vivo* (Edizioni Ares). 
    To celebrate in Spain the figure of St. Francis of Assisi, patron saint of Italy, and his message of peace, brotherhood, and care for creation, the Embassy chose to place him in dialogue with Antoni Gaudí, a central figure in Barcelona’s architectural and religious heritage.
                                    
The coincidence of the two centennial anniversaries in 2026—as stated in a press release—provided an opportunity to bring together two figures who are distant in time and background but united by a profound connection between faith, life, and expression. Building on this relationship, Father Giuseppe Buffon and Chiara Curti developed the dialogue around three central themes: the Nativity scene, creation, and self-emptying.
                                    
The program allowed the audience to recognize points of contact and iconographic parallels between Francis and Gaudí, highlighting how faith can become experience, work, and culture. The event thus contributed to a shared understanding of Italian and Spanish cultural and religious heritage.
                                    
Father Giuseppe Buffon explored the legacy of the Franciscan message, focusing in particular on the significance of the Greccio Nativity scene, on fraternity, and on care for creation. Chiara Curti explained how faith and the observation of creation guided Gaudí’s work on the Sagrada Família, leading to his decision to devote himself entirely to the church and to identify himself as a “collaborator with the Creator.”
    The event was included in the program of the National Committee for the celebrations marking the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi and among the events of the Year of Gaudí. “Two anniversaries that differ in era and context, but which the calendar brings together this year, offering us the opportunity to create a dialogue between two very different figures, united by a profound connection between faith, life, and language. “I am particularly pleased that this event is part of the program organized by the Italian National Committee for the celebrations marking the eighth centenary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi, as well as among the official events of the Year of Gaudí,” stated the Italian Ambassador to Spain, Giuseppe Buccino Grimaldi, in his welcome remarks.
                                    
“Beyond the historical distances that separate them, both figures were able to translate the spiritual dimension into a lived experience and a universal language, helping to make the heritage of the two countries a shared legacy,” he emphasized.

NEW DELHI: Should Arvind Kejriwal’s AAP and MK Stalin’s DMK join INDIA bloc’s fight against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR? Well, the answer would surely be “yes”, as far as the allies of the bloc are concerned.Now to the more difficult question: Will Arvind Kejriwal’s AAP and MK Stalin’s DMK join INDIA bloc’s fight against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over SIR? Well, there is no straight answer to this one.The AAP and the DMK have a common enemy in the Congress. Uddhav Thackeray’s Shiv Sena (UBT) has now urged the two parties to set aside their differences with the grand-old-party to fight against "dictatorship". In an editorial in the party mouthpiece 'Saamana', Shiv Sena (UBT) said, “The entire country has been witnessing protests against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), but the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) have stayed away from it."
-
The absence of both parties, who have officially withdrawn from the INDIA bloc, has highlighted the existing differences within the opposition camp on the strategy and format of the protest against irregularities in the SIR process.
'A very critical request'
Former Congress leader and senior political commentator Sanjay Jha feels Shiv Sena (UBT)'s suggestion to both the DMK and the Aam Aadmi Party to join the INDIA bloc is a very practical, very reasonable, and at the moment, a very critical request.
"This is not about, at the moment, anything other than the fact that Indian democracy is in peril. It is unlikely that the CEC is going to resign of his own volition. It is pretty apparent that the government of Mr. Modi is going to be stubborn, and they will stonewall any effort by the opposition to demand and get accountability. Public protests don't seem to make any difference to the government. So the more the merrier," Sanjay Jha says.While the AAP has openly announced it will not be a part of the INDIA bloc’s protest and said “we are fighting this battle in our own way, the DMK has spoken in different tones.DMK spokesperson Saravanan Annadurai accused Rahul of adopting inconsistent positions on the electoral roll revision exercise and questioned why developments in Tamil Nadu had not received the same attention as the broader campaign against the Election Commission.In a post on X, Annadurai called on Rahul Gandhi to clarify his stand on allegations concerning names allegedly removed from Tamil Nadu’s electoral rolls during the SIR process.The DMK spokesperson also referred to a statement attributed to Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge that governments elected after the SIR exercise should be dissolved and sought clarification on why Rahul Gandhi had not publicly endorsed that position and whether such a stand would also apply to Tamil Nadu.Interestingly, a day later, DMK senior leader TKS Elangovan backed Rahul Gandhi on protests against the Election Commission (EC), saying that citizens have a right to protest against the government.“It is the right of citizens to fight against the government’s wrongdoings. That is what Rahul Gandhi did yesterday. Still, this government does not want him to protest because Gyanesh Kumar is being very useful to the BJP. Because of him, the BJP captured power in many states. In all these states, re-elections should be held,” Elangovan said.
Will DMK, AAP join SIR protests?
The DMK and the Congress had a very unpleasant parting of their two-decade-old ties after the 2026 assembly elections in Tamil Nadu, which the alliance lost to actor-politician C Joseph Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam TVK. While the TVK emerged as the single largest party, it fell short of a majority. The Congress rushed in to help Vijay not just form the government but also eventually join it. Making Congress a part of the government was something the DMK had resisted all along. The Congress move offended the DMK to no end. Since then, MK Stalin’s party has been unrelenting in its attacks on the Congress at all forums from Chennai to Delhi. The Congress, on its part, maintains that it kept the DMK in the loop while shifting loyalties to the TVK.The DMK is missing no opportunity to drive a wedge between the new allies. On Thursday, it lashed out at Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay-led TVK for not explicitly naming the BJP government over the arrest of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi after a protest in the national capital demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.Questioning the TVK's statement, Elangovan pointed out that it failed to identify the authorities responsible for the action against the leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha. "Who arrested Rahul Gandhi? They should condemn and explicitly mention the name of the BJP government," Elangovan told PTI videos.With the TVK establishing itself as the third pole of Tamil Nadu politics, at least for now, the Congress will have to choose one against the other, and to that extent its ties with the DMK will remain frosty for now. More so, after the TVK has officially joined the INDIA bloc. But the DMK’s measured criticism of the Congress-led INDIA bloc protests may offer a ray of hope to the opposition bloc allies of a future softening of stand by M K Stalin.Now, let’s turn to AAP. Here’s where untangling the strains in the ties may be very difficult, if not impossible. Relations between the Congress and the AAP have always been uneasy and tumultuous. AAP was initially a part of the INDIA bloc.However, ties between Kejriwal’s party and the Congress were never smooth given their competing political interests in several states. AAP attended the first three meetings of the INDIA bloc. The high point in their ties came in the run up to the 2024 Lok Sabha elections when the two parties agreed to a joint contest in Delhi, Haryana, Goa, Punjab and Gujarat.The alliance did not work and the ties ended for all practical purposes after the results were out. In July 2025, Kejriwal formally announced the end of ties.Uddhav Thackeray’s party has reminded Kejriwal of his bitter experiences with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union home minister Amit Shah and the Election Commission.“While Kejriwal was the chief minister of Delhi, he was put behind bars in a "false" case. Kejriwal's defeat was engineered by deleting names of voters from his constituency, it alleged. So, it is not in the AAP's interest to stay away from the INDIA bloc,” the Shiv Sena (UBT) wrote in its editorial.
'All parties should look at larger picture'
Sanjay Jha is confident that these parties will eventually join the opposition protest. He argues it is extremely crucial that the opposition includes everyone.“Whether there are any small, petty differences, whether there is any degree of discomfort with one or the other partner, everyone has to look at the larger picture. And the larger picture is that today people are out on the streets because they're concerned about the future of their vote and the future of democracy,” Sanjay Jha says.
“And I believe it is very likely that the DMK and Arvind Kejriwal will join, because this is the time to put aside any petty squabbles and think of the larger goal of the country,” he adds.But this may be easier said than done. The Congress and the AAP are the main rivals in Punjab, where assembly elections are due early next year. The two parties are already engaged in a bitter war of words in Punjab, where AAP is defending its only government and the Congress is going all out to defeat Kejriwal’s party and reclaim its lost glory and government in the state.So, let’s see if this political compulsion decides the future course of ties between the two parties or the “larger goal of the country”?

Moldova is ready to take in more Ukrainian refugees this winter if Russia inflicts another humanitarian crisis upon the country through its targeted mass attacks, President Maia Sandu said on Oct. 8.
"Since 2022, more than one million Ukrainians fleeing the war have arrived in Moldova, and around 100,000 have found a home here. If this winter in Ukraine is as difficult as the whole world expects, we are ready to receive as many people as need safety," Sandu said at the Moldova Security Forum in Chisinau, as reported by Moldovan media outlet Newsmaker.
Russia's targeting of Ukraine's energy infrastructure last winter led to prolonged blackouts and heating outages across the country during sub-zero temperatures.
Speaking about preparations for the coming winter, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Ukraine is better prepared than last year, but warned that Russia has strengthened its own capabilities by stockpiling jet-powered drones and missiles.
At the Moldova Security Forum, former Moldovan Prime Minister and current Presidential Special Envoy Dorin Recean also said that Moldova is preparing for the coming winter logistics-wise, as Ukraine and Moldova's energy grids are interconnected.
Moldova has dealt with repeated violations of its airspace during Russia's attacks against Ukraine.
After five Russian Banderol missiles and drones, exploded on the country's territory during the overnight attack against Ukraine on Oct. 3, Sandu warned that "(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova."
In response to the growing threat, Moldova announced on Oct. 7 that it plans to build protective shelters at border crossings with Ukraine where border guards and people in nearby areas can take cover during drone incursions.

UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham in Berlin
United Kingdom

UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham in Berlin
- Published
The UK and Germany will face threats together, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said as he reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships.
On his first official European trip, apart from visits to Ukraine, Burnham met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and was greeted with military honours in Berlin.
Speaking to reporters at the German capital's Federal Chancellery, the prime minister said both countries were facing hybrid attacks "on a regular basis" and "it makes sense" to take them on together.
The pair formally ratified the 2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity.
Burnham said the treaty would "improve our security here in Europe" but also help grow the economy and living standards.
"The Kensington Treaty [is] the first treaty between Germany and the UK since the Second World War - it really is a significant moment," he said.
He added that the UK government would now "seek to progress" Germany joining Gcap, the Global Combat Air Programme led by Italy, Japan and the UK to develop a next-generation fighter aircraft.
He outlined partnerships "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".
He mentioned collaboration on quantum technology and space, adding he was aiming to host the first joint meeting of the UK and German cabinets next year.
The Berlin talks come after intelligence services warned of rising threats, including last month when Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Meanwhile, French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the European Union, in an interview with the BBC's economics editor Faisal Islam.
Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was "very committed to securing deeper cooperation" and to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe".
He told reporters a closer relationship with Europe was in the interests of growth and tackling irregular migration.
In recent weeks he has mentioned the prospect of eventually rejoining the bloc.
The German leader replied: "From our German side, I can assure you that we will do anything what we can do to bring the UK closer and closer back to Europe, to the European continent, to the European Union."

The meeting comes as European leaders have been warning that the threat of hybrid attacks against Europe by Russia has intensified.
Hybrid attacks can include potentially destabilising activity such as cyber attacks, sabotage or misinformation.
Sir Mark Lyall Grant, former UK national security adviser, explained that hybrid warfare "falls somewhere between peace and war - it's in that sort of grey zone, an area where Russia has been extremely active for some time".
He told Radio 4's Today that while Russia had posed a threat to the UK since Vladimir Putin became president in 2001, there had been an "intensification" in response to European support for Ukraine following Russia's invasion.
"We know Russia has been mapping undersea cables in the North Sea; that's something I'm sure Andy Burnham will be talking to Chancellor Merz about because it affects both the UK and Germany," he added.
Last month, a senior Russian diplomat was summoned by the British government over an "egregious and reckless attack" on Leipzig airport, while the EU's foreign affairs chief also summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels.
It is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.
Meanwhile, questions have been raised this week about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a former spy chief on suspicion of espionage.
The talks also come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny.
Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory.
Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and following setbacks in regional elections.
Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future.

Five things to know about the situation in the south of Yemen today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:24:48 UTC
00:24:48 KST

In the south of Yemen, a recent escalation of fighting is displacing many families. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) teams are responding by supporting health facilities and reaching people through mobile clinics. Here are five things to know about the current situation in the south of Yemen.
1. What is currently happening in Yemen and on its western coast?
In September 2026, the Ansar Allah forces launched a rapid military operation down the western coast of Yemen, seizing strategic areas like the city of Mocha and Bab Al-Mandab Strait. The incursion reached the vicinity of the third largest city in Yemen, Taiz, with roads and access to the south being blocked. In return, the internationally recognised government in Aden, backed by Saudi Arabia, announced a counter-offensive on 5 October, and fronts are reported to be progressing towards Bab Al-Mandab and Dhubab. Today [8 October], territorial control remains unclear.
This escalation has led to a significant influx of displaced people fleeing the captured areas across the west coast. It further increases the needs of people who are already grappling with years of conflict and humanitarian crisis, as well as extremely high levels of acute malnutrition, cholera and acute watery diarrhoea, measles, and other communicable diseases.
2. What is the humanitarian situation?
Across Yemen, more than 22 million people are in urgent need of humanitarian support and around 5.2 million people are displaced, according to UNHCR.1
This latest escalation is taking place against the backdrop of an already severe and chronically underfunded humanitarian crisis in the country. More than 200,000 people have been displaced due to the insecurity in the past month, according to the UN.2  As MSF teams have observed in recent mobile clinics, displaced people have had to undertake very long journeys to reach safer areas, often on foot, across desertic lands, with high temperatures and limited access to food and shelter.
Many have settled around Lahj governorate, and in the outskirts of Aden. They are in critical need of medical and humanitarian support, including water and sanitation services in the informal places where they settle, such as schools and mosques. The risk of waterborne diseases, like cholera, is increasing rapidly in the current conditions.
The ongoing escalation is adding new pressure to an already overstretched medical system. The availability of health facilities, which was already affected by the humanitarian crisis, is now affected by the resumption of hostilities, as facilities have less capacity to respond to people’s ever-increasing needs.
3. What are the most pressing medical needs that MSF teams are seeing?
Food insecurity and loss of livelihoods is leading to an increase of malnutrition cases, cholera is on the rise, and access to health services and referrals are compromised.
In the many camps across Lahj and Aden governorates, 70 per cent of the patients treated by MSF mobile clinics are women and children. People present with skin infections, fever, diarrhoea, and communicable diseases. The long walks have caused foot injuries and ear and eye infections. Displaced people who cannot find shelter in host communities, and formal or informal camps have been seen by our teams on the road or sleeping under the shade of trees.
4. How is MSF responding?
MSF is focusing on continuity of care, while supporting the health authorities to respond to increased medical and humanitarian needs. Medical needs were already very high in Mocha, a port city, before the escalation, with many of the women arriving for labour at Mocha General hospital being malnourished.
We continue to support the paediatrics and maternity services at Mocha General hospital, where we received 567 patients between the 10 September and 6 October at the emergency department, and assisted in 45 deliveries.
In the general healthcare centre supported by MSF in Khokha, north of Mocha, the medical teams are providing an average of 130 to 160 consultations per day, with 2,122 patients seen at the triage during the same period. The cholera treatment unit has also been reactivated in the healthcare centre of Khokha.
In early September, we pre-positioned emergency medical kits in the two general healthcare centres in Khokha and Mafraq Al-Mocha, as well as in Dhubab's general healthcare centre. Up until now, our teams have not treated trauma injuries directly.
In response to the needs of displaced people, we sent mobile clinics across Aden and Lahj governorates, with 775 total consultations since 15 September. Twenty children were diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition. Assessments across south Yemen are being carried out to identify camps and improvised settlements where people have limited access to healthcare.
To support the health authorities in their response to the emergency, we are carrying out capacity building activities in Ibn Khaldoun hospital in Lahj, and four trauma kits were sent to Taiz hospitals. MSF is also providing support to trauma services and donations at the emergency department of Al-Jumhouria hospital in Aden.
We continue to further assess ways of adapting our operations to respond to people’s emerging needs.
5. What more can be done?
An urgent and rapid scale-up of the humanitarian response is needed to address acute and growing needs. Displaced people who are living in dire conditions urgently need food, water and sanitation services, shelter, and essential items.
Humanitarian organisations and the authorities must ensure and expand access to healthcare for the people affected by the crisis. Displacement, insecurity, and overstretched services are leaving many unable to reach urgently needed care.
In this context of heightened insecurity, civilians and healthcare must be protected at all times.

UK announces new round of Russia sanctions targeting financial services, 'shadow fleet'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

00:24:26 KST

UK announces new round of Russia sanctions targeting financial services, 'shadow fleet'
LONDON, Oct 8 - Britain's Foreign Office announced on Thursday new sanctions targeting individuals and entities it said were involved in the production or transport of Russian oil, facilitating military manufacturing and circumventing financial services sanctions.
The 38 new designations are part of Britain's effort to squeeze Russia's ability to fund and equip its war in Ukraine, targeting the oil revenue, financial channels and military supply chains that sustain Moscow's war economy.
The package included:
• A further 12 oil tankers which Britain says are operating as part of Russia's shadow fleet and helping Moscow evade sanctions on oil exports
• Three crypto exchanges and two payment platforms suspected by Britain of being used by Russia to circumvent financial sanctions. Britain said two of those entities had processed and facilitated transactions with the A7 illicit finance network
• Seventeen entities and individuals involved in the supply of goods deemed by the UK, US and EU to be critical for the Russian war effort, including Russia-based importers of machine tools, electronics and materials used to produce missiles and drones
A statement from Russia's embassy in London, reported by state news agency RIA Novosti, said: "Each new sanctions package is intended to demonstrate the resolve of the British authorities, but in reality it highlights the ineffectiveness and futility of the course they have chosen." REUTERS

BBC pays compensation to PinkNews couple over false sexual misconduct allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:23:31 UTC
00:23:31 KST

The BBC has apologised and paid “substantial” compensation to the couple behind the PinkNews website, after conceding that stories accusing them of sexual misconduct were false and defamatory.
In a sweeping admission, the BBC accepted at the high court that a 2024 iPlayer documentary about the PinkNews founder Benjamin Cohen and his husband, Anthony James, called PinkNews: Behind Closed Doors, had made “a series of very serious, false, and defamatory allegations”.
The corporation also accepted that an accompanying news article had made “false and extremely harmful” allegations that the pair had placed inappropriate pressure on young female staff members to act as surrogates for them.
The claims were widely reported. Downing Street described the claims of sexual misconduct made against the couple behind PinkNews, the world’s largest LGBTQ+ website, as “very concerning”.
The accusations also meant that the pair were subjected to investigations by the Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service, which safeguards the interests of children involved in family court proceedings. The investigations took place before a hearing concerning the couple’s son, who was born via a surrogate.
Cohen felt compelled to resign as a trustee of a global disability charity, his legal team told the court. James resigned as an associate non-executive director on the board of Bedfordshire hospitals NHS foundation trust.
“These allegations were false and extremely harmful to the claimants’ reputations,” said the couple’s legal team. “They were – unsurprisingly – picked up and republished by other national media outlets and across social media.”
The BBC’s barrister said: “On behalf of the defendant, I accept everything that my learned friend has said. The BBC retracts and apologises unreservedly for the defamatory allegations made in the programme and the article.”
In a joint statement after the hearing, Cohen and James said the BBC still had questions to answer about how the allegations ever reached publication.
“The BBC ignored warnings about the veracity of these allegations and chose to broadcast false claims to millions of people,” they said.
“When this began, we were new dads and our son was just six months old. What should have been one of the happiest periods of our lives was instead thrown into chaos, impacting our business, our colleagues and our family. This included being subjected to additional investigations by social workers.
“Throughout all of this, our greatest fear has been for our son’s future. We have worried about the day he goes to school and other children find these false allegations online. We have worried about what he might read about his dads, what his friends might say and what that could do to him.
“Today’s apology cannot erase what happened, but it means that when that day eventually comes, the truth will be there.”
Cohen and James launched legal action last year. The case will no longer go to trial after the BBC apologised and agreed to pay compensation, described as “substantial”. The couple are donating it to the Multiple Sclerosis Society and Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Charity.
The documentary and accompanying BBC article have been removed. The corporation said: “The BBC has reached a settlement with Ben Cohen and Anthony James. We will not be issuing any further comment.”

Marco Rubio calls Portugal 'ideal gateway' to Europe for US during Lisbon visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:22:31 UTC
00:22:31 KST

As one of the smallest members of NATO and the European Union, Portugal is keen to cultivate its relations with bigger countries
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Portugal on Thursday for the final stop of his tour of three NATO allies.
The visit comes a day after he urged European countries to preserve Western civilisation by upholding the values and traditions of ancient Greece during a speech in Athens.
“Portugal is a great ally, very cooperative ally of the United States and a country with which we already have a solid and growing relationship. And we visit these countries in order to reinforce those ties,” Rubio said before departing Athens. “That’s the purpose of the trip.”
Rubio is expected to thank Portugal for allowing the US to use its Lajes Field air base in the Azores for operations linked to the Iran war.
On Saturday, Portugal's attorney general's office said it was examining whether the use of Lajes Field air base was lawful, following a formal complaint by the small left-wing party Left Bloc.
Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel said the country's approval for US military operations did not cover actions violating international law.
Rubio also met Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro in Lisbon, but neither spoke to reporters.
Rubio praises Portugal’s defence spending
Rubio praised Portugal’s investment in defence, stressing that defence spending "is not a hostile act" and that NATO members must "be strong" and "have capabilities".
"NATO exists, more than anything else, as a defensive alliance that acts as a deterrent against hostility, and it has served us well for decades. If we want it to continue to serve us, we must ensure that it remains strong," he said.
Rubio also highlighted economic ties, describing Portugal as "the ideal gateway, from a geographical and economic point of view" for US technology companies seeking access to Europe.
He noted that US investors put more than $20 billion (€17.2 billion) into Portugal last year, while Portuguese companies invested over $2 billion (€1.72 billion) in the United States.
Rubio also praised Portugal’s efforts to combat drug trafficking, noting that Portuguese authorities, working with US agencies, have seized 200 tonnes of cocaine in recent years.
A long history of cooperation
Unlike neighbouring Spain, where Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez refused to allow the US military to use Spanish bases for attacks on Iran, Portugal has taken a more moderate approach, allowing Washington to use Lajes Air Base following the outbreak of the conflict.
The base was first used by the US during World War II, before Lisbon and Washington signed a formal agreement governing its use. Its long runway accommodates heavy military aircraft.
Scaled back after the Cold War, the base is now mainly used to refuel transatlantic military flights.

Russia denies second illness case amid Siberia 'plague' concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:20:46 UTC
00:20:46 KST

Russia on Thursday denied reports of a second case of illness in its Siberian region of Irkutsk amid quarantine measures following reports of a possible “plague” outbreak.
Citing the press service of Russia’s consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor, state news agency Tass reported on Thursday that the agency described information circulating on social media about the issue as “incorrect.”
The statement said no incidents involving pathogenic microorganisms were identified and that compliance with “proper control measures during work with pathogenic microorganisms” has been confirmed.
“Comprehensive preventive and anti-epidemic measures have been implemented. There are no epidemic risks to the population of the city of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region,” it said.
The watchdog also said that as of Wednesday, monitoring had been completed for over 90% of contacts in the Irkutsk region and no health issues linked to infectious diseases were found.
On Friday, Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said he convened an extraordinary meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission following reports of a suspected “highly dangerous infectious disease” in a resident.
Rospotrebnadzor said at the time that an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown aetiology.”
On Friday, local outlet People of Baikal reported that the institute employee, identified in the report as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, allegedly broke a test tube containing “pneumonic plague.”
The outlet reported that she became ill after allegedly breaking the test tube late last month and was hospitalised in the town of Shelekhov, where she died Friday evening.
The Kremlin said the “overwhelming majority” of reports regarding the situation were “false information” and urged citizens to heed Rospotrebnadzor’s official statements.
The watchdog said on Monday that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was “calm.”
US President Donald Trump said the same day that Washington was closely monitoring the reported case of “pneumonic plague” in Russia and pledged assistance.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia a day later to provide full transparency on the situation.
Meanwhile, the World Health Organization said on Wednesday that it was seeking additional information from Russia on the death of the institute employee and reports of the death of a second employee.

Ben-Gvir celebrates October 7 arrest of Ra'am party activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:20:46 UTC
00:20:46 KST

Breadcrumb
Ben-Gvir celebrates arrest of Ra'am party activists on October 7
Israel's extremist National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has celebrated the detention of supporters of a Palestinian political party within Israel's 1948 boundaries, comparing their motorcycle convoy to the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
This comes amid mounting efforts by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government to exclude Palestinian parties from the country's forthcoming elections.
The incident occurred on Wednesday, the third anniversary of the attacks, when motorcyclists carrying green flags associated with the Islamist-leaning Ra'am party, led by Mansour Abbas, travelled along roads in the Negev region of southern Israel.
Videos circulating on social media showed the convoy waving the party's banners, prompting accusations from right-wing Israeli politicians that the scenes resembled those of the 2023 attacks.
Ben-Gvir posted a photograph on X showing a motorcyclist lying bound on the ground, claiming police had intervened against riders who were breaking the law and frightening local residents.
He said the convoy had briefly evoked images of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas-led fighters entered southern Israel from Gaza.
"They forgot one little detail: The national security minister is Itamar Ben Gvir, and the policy has changed," he wrote, adding that officers had made arrests and issued fines.
However, subsequent Israeli police accounts focused on alleged traffic offences rather than the political affiliation of the riders.
According to Israeli broadcaster i24NEWS, police intercepted the convoy near Ohalim Junction after receiving reports of dangerous driving.
Officers said several motorcyclists attempted to evade a police roadblock, with one rider losing control of his scooter and crashing while attempting to escape.
The rider was detained after police discovered he was allegedly driving without a valid licence or insurance. His scooter was removed from the road.
Police have not publicly established that displaying Ra'am flags constituted an offence, and the total number of arrests remains unclear.
The incident comes amid attempts by Netanyahu's governing coalition to exclude Palestinian political parties from Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
On 23 September, Israel's Central Elections Committee, dominated by Netanyahu's coalition, voted 18-5 to disqualify both Ra'am and the Joint List, an alliance comprising Hadash, Ta'al and Balad.
Netanyahu's Likud and Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) were among the parties that formally petitioned to exclude Ra'am, alleging links to organisations associated with Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood.
Ra'am rejected the allegations, maintaining that there was no evidence it supported armed struggle against Israel.
Israel's Supreme Court unanimously overturned the bans on 2 October, ruling that the evidence presented did not meet the legal threshold for disqualifying the parties.
However, the court indicated that it was prepared to uphold the exclusion of Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh over comments he made about the 7 October 2023 attacks, prompting him to withdraw his candidacy.
The effort to exclude Abu Shehadeh also received support from opposition parties, demonstrating that attempts to restrict Palestinian political representation have extended beyond Netanyahu's governing coalition.
Opposition parties have also supported attempts to disqualify Jewish Hadash politician Ofer Cassif, a vocal critic of Israel's war on Gaza.
The controversy is particularly striking given Ra'am's history of cooperation with Israeli governments.
Ra'am became the first independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition in 2021, helping bring Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid to power and ending Netanyahu's 12 consecutive years as prime minister.
However, the decision provoked fierce criticism from other Palestinian political parties, particularly Hadash and Balad, which accused Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas of abandoning Palestinian national demands in favour of limited economic concessions.
Critics argued that participation in a government led by Bennett, a hard-right former settler leader who opposed Palestinian statehood, risked legitimising Israel's oppression of Palestinians.
Abbas defended his approach as a pragmatic means of securing investment, improving public services and addressing crime and discrimination affecting Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Despite its willingness to participate in Israeli coalition politics, Ra'am now finds itself among the parties targeted for exclusion from the forthcoming election.
The controversy comes as the participation of Palestinian political parties could prove significant in the formation of Israel's next government, with mainstream opposition leaders also divided over whether they would accept Arab parties as coalition partners.

Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro and his wife charged over torture allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:20:39 UTC
00:20:39 KST

Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro and his wife charged over torture allegations
The new US charge adds to the existing drug trafficking case against Venezuela’s former president and first lady.
Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were charged in the US state of New York with conspiring to commit torture in connection with allegations that they tortured political opponents to maintain their power.
The indictment, filed on Thursday in a Manhattan federal court, adds one count of conspiracy to commit torture to the drug trafficking charges the couple already faced.
It alleges that Maduro and Flores were part of a conspiracy that used torture and other abuses to repress and punish political opponents. Prosecutors say the conspiracy ran from at least 1999 through 2025 and involved Venezuelan military, intelligence and law enforcement officials.
The indictment details several cases of alleged torture. One detainee was allegedly subjected to electric shocks and asphyxiation after being arrested following a 2018 drone attack that the Venezuelan government said was an attempt to assassinate Maduro.
The alleged abuses also extended to United States citizens detained in Venezuela, three of whom were cited in the indictment. In one case, in January 2025, Venezuelan intelligence officers arrested an American citizen who was not their intended target and beat him repeatedly over two days, which caused permanent injury to his eye. He was reportedly released about a year later and was warned by Venezuelan officials not to disclose that the government had abused him.
Prosecutors allege that Maduro personally directed or was regularly briefed on the abuse of detainees. In one instance, the indictment says Maduro was told that a detained military officer remained defiant and responded by ordering officials to “squeeze them harder”. Prosecutors say he went so far as to suggest specific torture methods for unrelenting victims.
In other cases, prosecutors allege Maduro was told about beatings, electric shocks and simulated drowning and directed officials to apply additional “pressure”. According to the indictment, Flores was present at some of the meetings where detainees and their treatment were discussed.
“The indictment … alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable. The members of Maduro’s broad conspiracy were not just sitting behind a desk,” said federal prosecutor Jamie McDonald at a news conference. “These members of the conspiracy were holding the shovel. American citizens were tortured, and so were thousands of Venezuelans, we allege.”
Maduro and Flores pleaded not guilty to the drug charges and have been held at Brooklyn’s Metropolitan Detention Center since their capture. Their trial is scheduled for June 1, 2027.
The charges pile on an ongoing criminal case against Maduro and Flores. A superseding indictment accuses Maduro of working with cartel groups to move cocaine through Venezuela towards the US.
Maduro was abducted and imprisoned on January 3, after US President Donald Trump authorised a military raid in Caracas.

London voters go to polls for Holborn and St Pancras by-election
The vote in London’s Holborn and St Pancras parliamentary seat tests whether Burnham can restore faith in Labour.
Londoners are voting in a special by-election in the electoral district of Holborn and St Pancras, where the Green Party is posing a threat to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour Party.
Zack Polanski, leader of Britain’s left-wing Greens, was among candidates bidding on Thursday to win the parliamentary seat vacated by the resignation of former Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Labour has held the seat continuously since its creation in 1983. Thursday’s vote is widely considered a two-horse race with the Greens, with thousands of activists from both parties out canvassing in recent weeks.
The vote is seen as a first test of whether Burnham can restore voters’ faith in Labour, which saw its popularity among left-wing voters plunge over the war in Gaza.
The by-election also offers him a chance to rob the Greens of the momentum they have built up under Polanski, the 43-year-old self-styled “eco-populist” who became party leader in September last year.
Green gains in areas of London contributed to Labour’s dismal local election results in May, which helped set in train a process that culminated on July 20 with Starmer’s resignation and his replacement by Burnham.
He has since adopted a tougher position on Israel and seeks to blunt the Greens’ rise by laying out a more left-wing vision for the UK.
Polanski, as the Greens’ candidate, faces Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali, a local council leader who arrived in Britain as a child refugee from Somalia in the 1990s and is expected to be declared the winner.
Polls are scheduled to close at 10pm local time (21:00 GMT) and the result is expected to be announced in the early hours of Friday.
The other candidates are: Barmy Brunch of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party; Ewan Cameron, Conservative Party; independent candidate Tom Darwood; Clare Fischer of the Climate Party; George Galloway, Workers Party; Tyler Johnson, Restore Britain; Briony Anne Lonbay Kapoor of Rejoin EU; Peter Newman of Reform UK; Ketankumar Pipaliya, UK VOICE; Jonathan Silberman of the Communist League; Helen Spiby-Vann, Christian Peoples Alliance; Patrick Thomas Stillman, Liberal Democrats; Ben Walker, UKIP.

Lebanese parliament speaker warns against UNIFIL departure without replacement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:16:54 UTC
00:16:54 KST

Wasim Seifeddine and Ikram Kouachi
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri on Thursday warned against the exit of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNFIL) without a replacement.
This came during a meeting between Berri and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, according to a statement from the speaker’s office.
The two discussed developments in Lebanon and the region, including political and security developments amid Israel's continued violations of the ceasefire agreement and daily attacks on southern villages and towns, the statement said.
The meeting also addressed Lebanon's relations with the EU and the bloc's potential role in supporting the country, particularly reconstruction efforts, as well as Beirut's position in favor of maintaining UNIFIL's presence in southern Lebanon.
Berri warned against reaching a point where UNIFIL's mandate expires without a replacement under the UN umbrella.
He said such a development would constitute “an attack on international legitimacy and its UN resolutions” and negatively affect the EU and its role.
Berri stressed that “the problem remains the same: Israel’s failure to comply with its obligations under all agreements.”
UNIFIL's mandate is set to expire at the end of 2026, while Lebanon insists on maintaining its presence as an element of stability in the south.
UNIFIL has been deployed since 1978 under UN Security Council resolutions to monitor the cessation of hostilities and help maintain security and stability in the area.
Lebanese president meets Kallas
During his meeting with Kallas, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun reaffirmed his country’s commitment to negotiations with Israel.
Regarding the situation in southern Lebanon, Aoun said the Lebanese army is “fully carrying out its duties” in areas where it has deployed south of the Litani River under the “framework agreement,” while Israel “continues to refrain from implementing its provisions.”
Israel has continued attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing 4,386 people and injuring 12,413, according to the latest Lebanese Health Ministry figures dated Sept. 25, 2025.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-sponsored framework agreement in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army in areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued attacks on southern Lebanon and remains in control of areas of Lebanese territory, some occupied for decades and others seized during more recent wars and military operations.
Aoun also said Lebanon looks forward to signing a strategic partnership with the EU based on “deep historical and cultural ties.”
He thanked Kallas for the European Council's intention to approve the deployment of a civilian-military mission to Lebanon under the EU's Common Security and Defense Policy to provide advice, training and equipment.
Aoun also praised EU efforts to “avert a vacuum in the post-UNIFIL phase,” saying Lebanon is counting on European support to find an alternative arrangement.
He said Beirut wants any replacement force to operate “under the UN flag.”

Helsinki requires visible faces in schools but rejects headscarf ban
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
18:16:24 EEST
00:16:24 KST

Helsinki will require pupils, teachers and other staff to keep their faces visible in schools and nurseries under new safety guidelines, while rejecting proposals for a blanket ban on headscarves and other face-covering clothing.
The decision follows a Helsinki City Council meeting on Wednesday, 7 October, where councillors considered two proposals seeking restrictions on face coverings in educational institutions.
The new guidelines will require people to remain identifiable during school activities, including lessons, examinations and other situations involving interaction or safety.
The requirement will also extend to nurseries and adults collecting children, although officials say staff will assess individual situations rather than apply an automatic prohibition.
Helsinki's education director, Satu Järvenkallas, told Helsingin Sanomat that the city was not introducing a headscarf ban but clarifying existing safety requirements.
"We do not want to interfere with people's clothing, but have clarified the identification guidelines from a safety perspective," Järvenkallas told the newspaper.
Under the guidelines, pupils will continue to wear religious head coverings such as hijabs, which leave the face visible. Garments that conceal the face, including niqabs, burqas and balaclavas, will generally conflict with the identification requirement during school activities.
Exceptions will be assessed according to circumstances, including health-related reasons for wearing face masks.
The guidelines will apply across Helsinki's schools, educational institutions and early childhood education facilities. The city intends to introduce them following the council's consideration of the proposals.
The debate began after the Finns Party's council group proposed banning headscarves covering the head or face in schools. National Coalition Party councillor Seida Sohrabi submitted a separate proposal targeting garments such as niqabs, burqas and balaclavas.
The council rejected an outright clothing ban, and the Finns Party failed in its attempt to return the matter for reconsideration.
City officials argued that a general prohibition would raise concerns about equality and religious freedom under existing legislation.
The city's equality and non-discrimination advisory body also opposed the proposed ban, calling for restrictions to be assessed to prevent discrimination.
During the council debate, Sohrabi said she had received reports suggesting that face-covering clothing had become more common in educational institutions.
Left Alliance councillor Sandra Hagman criticised the identification requirement to HS, warning that it might prevent employees and adult students who wear niqabs from participating in education.
Social Democratic councillor Mahad Ahmed also questioned whether face-covering garments presented a problem in Helsinki schools. “The Muslim community and Islam have been discussed a great deal in politics recently. We must ensure that Islamophobia does not become a normal part of political discourse, especially in the city council,” Ahmed told HS.
The guidelines will also require employees' faces to remain visible during teaching activities.
Elsewhere in the Helsinki metropolitan area, Vantaa has already introduced restrictions on face coverings during the school day. Espoo has also considered similar measures.
Helsinki's education department plans to issue the revised safety instructions to schools and nurseries as soon as possible.

E.ON Next deal to buy Ovo Energy leaves UK with just ‘big three’ energy suppliers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:16:14 UTC
00:16:14 KST

Almost three-quarters of households in Great Britain are now served by just three energy suppliers, after E.ON Next completed a deal to buy Ovo Energy despite fresh concerns about competition in the energy market.
The takeover concluded on Thursday after Britain’s competition watchdog cleared it, despite concerns that the shrinking number of household energy suppliers could mean bill payers will have less choice and suppliers will have less incentive to lower bills.
While there will be no immediate change for the 4 million households supplied by Ovo, the sale means that E.ON Next, which already supplies 5.6 million households, will hold 25% of the household energy market – or 13.45m gas and electricity accounts – and become Great Britain’s second-largest energy supplier.
The supplier’s hold on the market is narrowly behind Octopus Energy, which holds a 26% share or 14.3m accounts, and ahead of legacy energy incumbent British Gas, which was once the top supplier but today serves about 23% of the market or 12.5m accounts.
It also deals a blow to the decade-long efforts to dismantle the dominance of what were the “Big Six” energy suppliers to increase competition and lower energy prices.
Tom Goswell, the energy supply lead at Cornwall Insight, a leading consultancy, said: “The big six have become the big three, and there have been questions raised over how this will impact household choice and the health of the market.”
Those concerns were rebuffed by Chris Norbury, chief executive of E.ON UK, who described the market as “fiercely competitive” and said the company’s “flexibility and scale” would allow it to “deliver for customers now and to transform for the energy system to come”.
The legacy big six suppliers – British Gas, EDF Energy, E.ON UK, SSE, Scottish Power and npower – dominated about 85% of the energy market in 2016 when a landmark investigation by the CMA warned that customers were overpaying by roughly £1.4bn to £1.7bn every year due to weak market competition.
As a result of the E.ON deal, about 90% of Great Britain’s household energy supply market will be held by only five suppliers when including EDF Energy and Scottish Power alongside the big three.
Although there was a surge in new energy start-ups after 2016 – led by Octopus, Ovo and Bulb Energy – the market began to shrink after SSE sold its household supply business to Ovo in 2019, and dozens of suppliers went bust during the 2021/22 energy crisis.
Octopus became the biggest supplier in the market after taking on 1.5 million customers from Bulb, which became the biggest casualty when it went into administration in 2022.
“Larger suppliers do bring with them a degree of stability, and after about 30 firms dropped out of the market, leaving customers wondering who would be sending their next bill, stability is not something to dismiss lightly,” Goswell said.
“The concern with fewer suppliers is that the pressure to compete eases off, taking with it some of the incentive to keep prices low and offer something different. The big suppliers have the resources to give people real choice, and the test over the next few years will be whether households who shop around find a genuine range of deals waiting for them rather than three versions of the same thing,” he added.

Syria arrests 5 former Assad regime militia, intelligence members for crimes against civilians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:15:59 UTC
00:15:59 KST

Sahin Demir
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Syrian security forces arrested five former militia and intelligence members affiliated with the ousted Bashar al-Assad regime for their involvement in massacres and serious crimes against civilians, the Interior Ministry said Thursday.
The ministry said internal security forces carried out intelligence-based operations that led to the arrests.
Among those arrested was Shahin Hamdan al-Shahin, one of the founders of the Shawaheen Regiment militia during the former regime.
Al-Shahin began working with the former regime’s Air Force Intelligence Directorate in 2015 under the command of Suheil al-Hassan before helping establish armed groups, according to the ministry.
It said he was directly involved in massacres against civilians, particularly in eastern Hama province and along the Ithriya-Raqqa road in 2017.
The ministry said he later commanded groups involved in killings, arrests, torture and destruction in Palmyra and areas extending to Deir ez-Zor province until 2019.
In a separate operation, authorities arrested four former regime members for their involvement in massacres and serious violations against civilians.
The ministry identified two of them as Nabil Adnan Ismail and Ghazi Mohammed Ismail -- group commanders within militias affiliated with the former regime’s Air Force Intelligence Directorate.
They were involved in kidnappings, looting and massacres, including direct participation in incidents in the village of Aqrab, as well as kidnapping civilians and extorting money from them, according to the ministry.
The other two suspects, brothers Taher Youssef al-Mohammed and Talal Youssef al-Mohammed, served with the Air Force Intelligence Directorate and the Scientific Studies and Research Center.
The ministry said the brothers were involved in repression and arrests and exploited their positions to access detainees’ files and extort their families.
Investigations into the five suspects are continuing before their referral to judicial authorities, it added.
The arrests come amid continuing security operations targeting former regime officials and military personnel involved in crimes committed during Syria’s nearly 14-year conflict.
On Sept. 18, Syrian authorities arrested five senior air force officers and commanders who served under Assad for their involvement in planning, directing and carrying out airstrikes on populated areas.
Since Assad’s overthrow on Dec. 8, 2024, Syria’s new administration has launched security operations targeting former regime figures and personnel implicated in abuses during the conflict.
Assad, who ruled Syria for nearly 25 years, fled to Russia after anti-regime forces captured Damascus, bringing decades of Baath Party rule to an end.

Russia said Thursday it views the potential deployment of additional NATO troops in the Baltic states as an escalation.
“We unequivocally view the potential deployment of additional NATO contingents – including US troops – and the establishment of corresponding military infrastructure in the Baltic states as an escalation,” Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told journalists.
Zakharova said such plans, which she claimed are “harbored by the Washington administration,” run counter to its stated aim of “fostering diplomatic and political avenues to de-escalate tensions in Europe.”
“All these confrontational moves align with the North Atlantic Alliance’s plans for the accelerated militarization of Russia’s western border regions under the false pretext – as we have already discussed today – of a so-called threat from the East,” Zakharova said.
She reiterated that Russia has no plans for an armed conflict with Western Europe, noting that Russian President Vladimir Putin and Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov have repeatedly made such statements.
“One might ask those who voice such things – or those who can at least explain what they mean – how they justify these fantasies. What do they cite as the goals, objectives, or reasons for the actions they fabricate?” Zakharova said.
She also accused the EU of embarking on a “path of confrontation” with Russia, arguing that this path would “only exacerbate Europe's problems.”
Zakharova described Germany as a party to the Russia-Ukraine war on Kyiv's side and accused the current German government of seeking war, citing German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s recent visit to Ukraine.
Merz visited the Ukrainian capital over the weekend and announced a further €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in military aid to Kyiv.

Meloni says proud to be called 'woman from Ciociaria' in fluffed jibe
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:14:03 CEST
00:14:03 KST

Premier Giorgia Meloni said Thursday
she was proud to have been called "a woman from Ciociaria" in a
fluffed jibe by a political opponent who said he had actually
meant to call her a "loudmouth".
                                    
The man, a local councillor at Pontedera near Pisa, said he had
meant to call the premier a "caciarona" a Roman dialect word for
a loud, rowdy, or boisterous woman.
                                    
Instead, he said he mistakenly used the word "ciociara", meaning
a woman from Ciociaria, a formerly mostly agricultural
southeastern part of the Lazio region, towards Campania.
                                    
Irked, Meloni posted on social media:
"Personal attacks—regarding my physique, my family, and my
origins. But today, the tone changes. And the level of discourse
shifts. Because a gentleman from the Democratic Party, a certain
Floriano Della Bella, stated during a Pontedera City Council
meeting that Meloni is a 'Ciociara'—using the term in the most
derogatory sense.
                                    
"He was reprimanded for this by the Council President—himself a
member of the PD—who added: 'Please, use language befitting your
role.'
"So, for these gentlemen, being 'Ciociaro' is something to be
ashamed of, and calling someone that is tantamount to an insult.
                                    
"What's more, they consider it a term that shouldn't even be
uttered in an institutional setting. I'm afraid I disagree. And
I am proud to be called a Ciociara.
                                    
"Because Ciociaria is one of the most beautiful, ancient, and
extraordinary regions of our Italy.
                                    
"A land of Popes and military leaders, of saints and artists, of
writers and poets.
                                    
"Cicero, Gaius Marius, Boniface VIII, Saint Thomas Aquinas,
Marcello Mastroianni, Vittorio De Sica, Nino Manfredi, and so
many other men and women who have shaped our history over time.
                                    
"They constantly speak of 'the people,' respect, and cohesion.
                                    
"Yet, in a single stroke, they insult nearly half a million
Italians, branding them as inferior, ignorant, and second-class
citizens.
                                    
"But it is they who are the ignorant ones. Long live Ciociaria!"
she concluded.

EU, China at trade crossroads amid strict market access plans threatening new trade war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:13:49 UTC
00:13:49 KST

The EU and China have reached a crossroads in economic relations as the bloc grapples with state-subsidized overcapacity, economic dependence, and deindustrialization, while member states push for market restrictions to help shrink the trade deficit and Beijing warns of a trade war.
Top European and Chinese trade officials are meeting in Beijing for the second round of talks to address widening structural imbalances.
The talks follow an initial session held in Brussels in June, which focused on trade rebalancing, export control, intellectual property, and reforms for the World Trade Organization (WTO).
The EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), aimed at strengthening the bloc’s industrial production amid the threat of unilateral external dependence and deindustrialization, involves steps particularly targeting China.
The draft includes measures to protect and boost industrial capacity in key sectors by imposing strict origin rules in public procurement and providing incentives for local producers.
China argues that the draft and the further protectionist measures it brings to the table will introduce investment barriers for Chinese firms and systematically discriminate against them.
The leaders of France and Germany called on the European Commission earlier this week to implement new trade protection tools including restrictions on market access.
The letter calls for a mechanism to enable systematic and resolute responses, including the immediate suspension of market access.
As Europe’s trade deficit with China more than doubled over the past decade to reach $359.8 billion in 2025, friction between the two parties intensified.
The EU’s imports from China rose 6.4% while its exports to China dropped 6.5% last year.
Manufactured products made up 97.3% of all Chinese imports to Europe, with electrical equipment and industrial machinery accounting for the largest categories of goods at $164.9 billion and $106.5 billion, respectively.
European policymakers are concerned that subsidized Chinese manufacturers are gaining a larger market share in Europe across foundational sectors such as automobiles, chemicals, and electronics.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned the European Parliament last month that a second China shock is coming, mirroring the 1990s steel crisis that hurt Western industrial bases.
With the EU’s IAA in March, Germany joined France in a major shift from its historically cautious stance toward protectionist measures, demanding even tougher interventions against China.
Decision-makers in Brussels are planning to develop a series of new trade defense tools in addition to the measures in the IAA, such as a rapid-response mechanism to counter economic coercion and a requirement for European firms operating in key sectors to source materials from at least three distinct countries.
Among the proposals are a solidarity fund to shield European producers against potential Chinese retaliation and a power to be granted to the Commission to impose tariffs similar to those under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 in the US.
China responded with a warning that the EU’s IAA proposal and the measures implied in the Franco-German letter would lead to unfair competition, violate World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, and trigger a trade war.
The Chinese Commerce Ministry said on April 27 that the IAA draft would create an investment barrier, as the legislation covers emerging strategic sectors like batteries, electric vehicles (EVs), solar panels, and critical raw materials, potentially restricting foreign investment, including from China.
Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi said China and the EU must jointly defend multilateralism and free trade against the emerging anti-globalization trends in a phone call with his German counterpart, Johann Wadephul, on Sept. 22.
Chinese trade officials reiterated that politicizing trade and weaponizing national security will further disrupt global supply chains without helping improve Europe’s underlying industrial competitiveness issues.
The EU negotiation delegation will brief European leaders on the outcome of the Beijing talks during the European Council summit next week.
The bloc’s newly proposed trade defense instruments and market restrictions could be enforced as early as December, depending on the consensus reached during the council meeting.

Musk goes on rant after India rejects ‘oligarch’ claim: What makes Starlink controversial

NEW DELHI: SpaceX CEO and the world's richest man Elon Musk on Thursday went on a rant explaining how the Starlink's satellite internet services will help the "least served" in India. Musk had just a day earlier alleged that his telecom firm was facing regulatory hurdles in India due to "oligarchs", a claim which was strongly rejected by the Indian government.Also read: Rahul Gandhi reacts to Musk's remarks; Starlink boss says 'thank you'The SpaceX chief then launched a tweet blitz posting about thrice in just a span of 10 minutes."Starlink will help the least-served in India," he said in a post at 6:18pm.He followed it up with another post at 6:25pm, writing, "Starlink provides Internet connectivity to the least-served, enabling self-education and prosperity by giving people access to sell their products worldwide!"Three minutes later, Elon posted again: "People who oppose @Starlink hurt only the least-served. The wealthy or those living in large cities already have good Internet, so they don’t understand."
Musk's comments come as a Starlink delegation is attending the India Mobile Congress organised in the national captial.Musk's claim about Starlink serving the "least-served" in India is somewhat ironic, as India already ranks among the countries with the lowest internet charges in the world."The last decade was about scalability, penetration, affordability.
We have discussed many times of how voice prices have crashed, data prices have lowered by almost 97%, which has led to greater penetration," information & technology minister Jyotiraditya Scindia said on Thursday.On the other hand, Starlink will reportedly cost Rs 8,600 per month, with an additional Rs 34,000 one-time hardware charge.
What Musk claimed & what the govt replied
"Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are … This is a crime against the people of India!" Musk said in a post on Wednesday.The telecom ministry rejected Musk's claim stating, "Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all three licensees""The Department of Telecom has issued licences to all satcom companies as well as provisional spectrum. Now the issue is pending with MHA for security clearance. As soon as it is cleared, they will get it. It has nothing to do with one company," minister of state for communications Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani told reporters on the sidelines of the India Mobile Congress.READ ALSO: 'Remain alert, stay indoors': India issues advisory for citizens in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
Why Starlink has sparked controversy
The logic behind Starlink is simple: Get internet to places where conventional networks are difficult or too expensive to reach. But Elon Musk’s satellite internet service has increasingly become much more than a tool for connectivity. Its growing use in war zones, conflict areas and during internet shutdowns has turned Starlink into a strategic technology and raised questions over who controls access to it.Critics have raised concerns about the company’s links with US intelligence and military agencies, arguing that a privately controlled satellite network could have implications for national security and sovereignty.
Starlink uses thousands of small satellites in low-Earth orbit, around 550km above the planet. Unlike traditional communications satellites positioned around 36,000km away, these satellites can transmit data with lower latency. Users connect through a small receiver with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically links with satellites passing overhead. The satellites can also transfer data between themselves using laser links.
What are the major concerns
A 2024 report by the Kutniti Foundation, had described Starlink as “a wolf in sheep’s clothing”. The foundation argued that Starlink’s global satellite network gives it capabilities that go beyond conventional telecom services and could create strategic concerns for countries such as India.
US intelligence links: Kutniti has highlighted Starlink’s links with US intelligence and military agencies, including publicly known contracts involving Musk’s companies.
Dual-use technology:The foundation argues that Starlink can provide high-speed internet while also supporting capabilities such as high-definition imagery and live video transmission.
Control beyond borders: Unlike traditional telecom networks that rely on infrastructure within a country, Starlink’s satellites operate from outside national territory, raising questions over regulatory control.
Security requirements: Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said Starlink has not yet fulfilled all required security conditions. India’s licence will be issued only after those requirements are met.
Furthermore, the satellites also raise security questions. Satellites travel at roughly 11,000 km/h to 28,000 km/h orbiting the earth and can also be used to monitor activity inside the territory of a country.

Ex-police chief who had affairs with two officers guilty of gross misconduct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:11:42 UTC
00:11:42 KST

A former chief constable showed a sense of entitlement, dishonesty and lack of integrity by having sexual relationships with two subordinate officers, including engaging in sexual activity while on call to lead major incidents, a misconduct hearing has ruled.
The panel found that the behaviour of Scott Chilton, 53, who retired as chief constable of Hampshire and the Isle of Wight before the hearing, amounted to gross misconduct.
Chilton was found to have had “consensual sexual relations” when he was a chief inspector or superintendent with a woman identified as Officer A, including while he was on duty. When he applied to be chief constable – and during his tenure – he “repetitively and dishonestly” denied this relationship.
The hearing in Eastleigh, Hampshire, was told that a consensual relationship with another woman, Officer B, began within weeks of Chilton becoming chief constable.
He was found to have “abused his position for a sexual purpose” and should have declared the relationship. When it came to light, he “behaved inappropriately” to Officer B, putting pressure on her to conceal what had happened.
Chairing the panel, Michelle Skeer of His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services said Chilton’s behaviour showed “persistent dishonesty and lack of integrity”. She said his actions suggested he did not think the rules applied to him.
“He was in the highest position of trust as the most senior officer in the constabulary and ought to have known the foreseeable risk of harm by having a covert relationship,” Skeer said.
“He repeatedly lied by act and omission about both his relationships with Officer A and Officer B and he knew that this was wrong. His conduct was a serious, deliberate and sustained attempt to mislead … to subvert any negative impact on himself.”
Skeer said Chilton had been privy to confidential and sensitive information on colleagues, security and national policing matters. “There was evidence that he was discussing issues which he shouldn’t have been discussing with Officer B during WhatsApp message exchanges.”
She added that Chilton had attempted to bully Officer B into “keeping quiet” by asking her to “delete and double delete” their messages and not to go to events that his wife would attend, which showed the power imbalance between them.
She said Chilton had engaged in sexual activity with Officer A while on duty and in silver command, which meant he would have been the officer in charge if a major incident had occurred.
Skeer added that “his actions were driven by his own entitlement” and the “abuse of his position was for personal gain and ultimately his own sexual gratification”.
She said Chilton had acted in a domineering fashion towards his colleagues in an attempt to “control the narrative” in relation to responding to press inquiries about the allegations.
Attention also focused during the hearing on disciplinary proceedings against another prominent Hampshire police officer, the former DCI Roger Wood.
In February 2025 a disciplinary hearing concluded Wood had inappropriate relations with two junior colleagues and would have been dismissed had he not already resigned.
Before his case, Wood claimed to have “damaging information” about Chilton and during the proceedings stated that the chief had “had affairs”.
John Beggs KC, who presented the case against the former chief constable, said Chilton had discussed using the force solicitor to prevent Wood from speaking to the press, adding: “He was trying to use his position as a chief constable to advance his own best interests.”
Since Chilton became chief constable in February 2023, there have been about 20 misconduct cases in Hampshire in which officers were accused of various forms of sexual behaviour. About five of these have included behaviour against junior officers.
Chilton retired in April 2025 after a career spanning 33 years that included acting as a lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council on national investigation standards and coordination.
At the start of the hearing, James Berry KC, representing Chilton, said his client would not be attending the hearing because of “medical issues”.
Chilton said in a statement that he admitted the second relationship but not the first. He said he accepted that by not disclosing that relationship he fell short of the standards police officers were judged by.
He added: “These were personal matters, rather than issues affecting policing or public safety, and at no point did this relationship influence policing decisions, operational matters or the discharge of professional responsibilities.”
He said his “deepest regret” was for his family “for the hurt caused by my poor judgment and actions”.
Chilton would have been dismissed if he had not resigned, the panel said. He has been placed on the College of Policing barred officers list, so he can never again become a police officer.
