Were Oct. 7 records altered? New allegations target Netanyahu's inner circle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:56:05 UTC
23:56:05 KST

The October Council, an organization representing former hostages, bereaved families and survivors of the October 7 massacre, has appealed to Shin Bet chief David Zini, Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Cabinet Secretary Yossi Fuchs and State Archivist Ruti Abramovitz, raising concerns that individuals close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have concealed information related to the events of the massacre, ynet learned Thursday morning.
"According to people in the prime minister's inner circle, transcriptionists were threatened and pressured to alter official transcripts," the letter states.
The appeal by the October Council families follows a July 2024 report by Nadav Eyal in ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth revealing that Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, Netanyahu's military secretary at the time of the massacre, had contacted the attorney general to express concerns that attempts had been made to alter official transcripts in the Prime Minister's Office during the war.
Even before that report, officials in the Prime Minister's Office had alleged that attempts were made during the war to change some of the transcripts of security Cabinet discussions and even transcripts of security-related telephone conversations.
The former military secretary said in media interviews that he had noticed early in the war that Netanyahu associates were engaged in what he described as a "disproportionate collection of materials."
He added that a stenographer in the Prime Minister's Office had told him that Tzachi Braverman, Netanyahu's former chief of staff, who was later implicated in the "late-night meeting" affair and whose appointment as ambassador to Britain was delayed, had demanded that the stenographer change the recorded time of a conversation Gil held with Netanyahu on the morning of October 7.
Asked whether he could assess why Braverman had done so, Gil replied: "First of all, this is a pattern of criminal conduct by people who think they can do whatever they want, and the chief of staff behaved like someone who could do whatever he wanted."
According to Gil, "It's possible they were already working on the narrative we're seeing now, portraying the prime minister as the only one functioning when the chaos began, supposedly because he had issued all the necessary instructions from the very beginning. That's a serious but plausible scenario."
"There's another possibility, one that is far more serious. Eleven minutes passed between the first and second calls. During that time, I received intelligence and information I didn't have during the first call, intelligence and information that I passed on to the prime minister during the second call. And if they can prove that this intelligence and information already existed at 6:29 a.m., that would mean someone already knew at that point what was going to happen. In other words, there had been a betrayal."
Allegations against Netanyahu and Braverman
In the October Council's letter, which alleges that transcriptionists in the Prime Minister's Office were threatened and ordered to alter official transcripts, the families raised a question:
"The transcriptionists are heroes who came forward and told the military secretary what had happened. Otherwise, the alteration of the transcript would never have been discovered. Who knows how many other transcripts were changed?"
The families' letter further stated: "An associate of Avi Gil, who was serving as Netanyahu's military secretary at the time, told us what Gil had revealed to him about the alleged alteration of the transcript.
"'Braverman definitely changed the time in the transcript. The transcriptionist told Avi that she had said to him, "But Tzachi, I'm not allowed to. The time is 6:40 a.m. It's recorded in the computer.'
"'He told her, 'Don't argue with me. Change it to 6:29 a.m. I was on that call."
"'That was her testimony to Avi. She then says that Tzachi looks at the transcript [after it was altered] and enthusiastically tells her, "Look how sharp the prime minister is. As soon as he's woken up, he immediately gives instructions."
"And that, of course, was a lie. The transcriptionists felt they were being asked to do something they weren't allowed to do, so they turned to Avi. They told him that Braverman would walk around carrying stacks of transcripts. He had collected a large amount of material."
The families added in their letter: "Another senior official, who had extensive information, documents and records related to October 7 in his possession, told us: 'I have three hidden folders containing all the documents related to October 7. One will go to the State Archives and the other two will go to the state commission of inquiry. For now, everything is being kept in safes at different locations because I'm afraid the documents could fall into the wrong hands.'
In their appeal to the senior officials, the families added: "One of the most senior officials serving on October 7 told us: 'It bothers me that the prime minister of Israel is breaking the law and the system doesn't know how to deal with it. He takes transcripts from sensitive discussions, presents half-truths from them in a manipulative way and tries to turn them into the truth, even though he knows that isn't the case.
"'If he has already taken it upon himself to exercise authority he doesn't actually have to release excerpts, then why release fragments of sentences taken out of context?
"'Netanyahu publishes 55 pages, and I was there. I saw a large portion of the original documents. Who gave you the authority to publish partial quotations rather than the full discussion?
"Yet Netanyahu repeatedly chooses to present only part of the picture rather than the whole story in an attempt to manipulate the public."
The families' letter to the Shin Bet chief, the attorney general, the Cabinet secretary and the state archivist also stated: "Another senior official, who headed a security agency at the time, testified: 'As time passes and more reports emerge on the matter, it is becoming clear that we did not necessarily know everything and that some people chose to conceal things from us.'"

Germany to buy 4 more frigates to track enemy submarines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:54:07 UTC
23:54:07 KST

Ayhan Simsek
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Germany’s parliamentary budget committee approved the purchase of four more frigates on Thursday from Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems, raising the navy’s order to eight identical warships for anti-submarine warfare.
The Defense Ministry said the Bundestag’s budget committee cleared the additional ships from Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems, or TKMS. Lawmakers already approved the first four of the same type on July 8. Industry has pledged that the first of the eight ships will join the fleet in 2029.
The vessels are MEKO A-200 DEU frigates, a design TKMS sells in adapted versions to allies and partners. The ministry said those export ships have been in service for years and have proved themselves.
“Germany is taking responsibility for conventional defense in the alliance,” said the ministry. “For that, we have pledged NATO a range of capability contributions under capability and defense planning.”
“Alongside other capabilities, the navy will make an important contribution to defense and deterrence in the North Sea and Baltic Sea region, as well as in the Atlantic and the High North, through sea-based anti-submarine warfare,” it said.
Exit from Damen contract
The ships replace a plan that assigned sea-based submarine hunting to the F-126 frigate.
That program had been led by Damen, a shipyard group based in the Netherlands, as general contractor. After major performance failures, Germany ended the contract following a full assessment, according to the ministry.
The navy then reviewed alternatives available on the market and concluded that the MEKO A-200 DEU frigates are suitable for anti-submarine warfare and for Germany’s NATO commitments, it said.
“The procurement of eight frigates of a single ship type also offers the German navy considerable advantages in operation, maintenance and repair, as well as training,” said the ministry.
Damen, the Dutch shipbuilder, disputes the German government’s account and argues that the cancellation was politically motivated. The company is seeking nearly €4.7 billion ($5.25 billion) from the German government for the scrapped F-126 frigate program.

In Sickness and in Health: An Israeli Writer Throws Her Lot in With the Country
"Israel is neither a country, nor a nation," the writer Amos Oz once told an audience in Portland, Oregon. "Actually, it is a fiery collection of arguments." For Israeli journalist Ruth Margalit, Israel is a collection of fiery people, too – all kinds of people, from contentious political extremists like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir to Sayed Kashua, the eminent Palestinian writer driven all the way to the United States by Israel's demoralizing treatment of its Palestinian citizens.
Margalit's nonfiction debut, "In the Belly of the Whale," which was released on September 22, draws from years of studying some of Israel's biggest personalities in granular form. The result is a searing, deeply compassionate – sometimes even comically absurd – view of Israel, "a place vigorously debated but little understood," as her introduction says.
Margalit strings together, in one efficient volume, published in the United States by Steerforth Press in collaboration with Altneuland Press internationally, a variety of characters she has covered over the last decade, a checkered pantheon of Israeli personalities and provocateurs told through close narratives, her vivid observations cutting close to her subject's bones.
Characters like Miri Regev and Ben-Gvir, easy targets for liberal contempt due to their outsized influence and media antics – to say nothing of their actual politics – come across as people who could be the eccentric aunt or uncle pressing buttons around the family dinner table. At an event hosted by Haaretz, Margalit describes Regev's spectacular persona: "Standing in front of the audience, her expression set between a smirk and a scowl, she clutched the lectern with one hand. 'I was always told to start a speech with a quote; it makes for a cultured impression,' she began. 'So here goes. As the famed Chinese philosopher Sun Tzu once put it' – she switched to accented English – 'Cut the bullshit! Cut the bullshit!'"

South Korea tested a hypersonic weapon for the first time amid deteriorating relations with North Korea
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:53:08 EEST
23:53:08 KST

South Korea tested a hypersonic weapon for the first time amid deteriorating relations with North Korea
Kyiv • UNN
Seoul conducted the first test of an HGV capable of maneuvering at low altitudes and striking targets precisely. The launch took place after a mine exploded at the border.
South Korea conducted the first test of a hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV), which is capable of carrying out high-precision strikes against targets. The launch took place amid growing tensions in relations with North Korea. Yonhap reported this, writes UNN.
Details
South Korea conducted the first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) on Thursday, the presidential office of Cheong Wa Dae said. It was apparently a show of force directed at North Korea amid heightened inter-Korean tensions following a recent mine explosion at the border.
The test was conducted to verify key hypersonic technologies, including flight trajectory and speed, as a strategic asset capable of delivering sudden, high-precision strikes against enemy targets, presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jun said in a written statement to the press.
President Lee Jae-myung personally observed the launch, accompanied by Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul and other officials.
An HGV is a missile system that uses a booster to build up speed and climb into the upper layers of the atmosphere, after which it separates from the booster and glides at lower altitudes at hypersonic speeds.
Lee’s office did not disclose the location of the test, but reports said the launch took place from a barge at the Agency for Defense Development’s test center in Taean, approximately 130 kilometers south of Seoul.
According to Kang, the launch tested heat-shield materials designed to withstand extremely high temperatures, guidance and control systems, as well as the vehicle’s ability to perform irregular maneuvers at low altitudes.
Unlike traditional ballistic missiles, after separation the HGV lowered its flight altitude, made horizontal and vertical course corrections, and precisely hit the target, she said.
Update
The unannounced launch on Thursday is widely viewed as a response to the September 21 mine explosion on the South Korean side of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), which seriously injured two South Korean servicemen. Seoul determined that the explosion was caused by mines planted by North Korean military personnel in violation of the armistice agreement.
Tensions rose after the explosion: Pyongyang categorically denied responsibility and threatened retaliation if the South took any measures in response.
The government of Lee Jae-myung, which seeks rapprochement with Pyongyang, came under criticism for its passive response to the mine explosion.
Critics accused Lee and his officials of taking an excessively soft stance in order not to provoke the North.

The NBA and the International Basketball Federation (FIBA) reaffirmed their commitment Thursday to launching a new professional men's basketball league in Europe despite EuroLeague clubs rejecting a proposal to join forces.

The project has been targeting a launch in 2027, although the final structure and timetable remain under discussion.
EuroLeague, meanwhile, currently featuring 20 teams, is pursuing its expansion plans, including a possible increase to 24 clubs.

Byzantium recognises Damian as Bulgaria’s first patriarch in October 927
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:52:07 UTC
23:52:07 KST

Author
Ivo Ivanov
Byzantium recognises Damian as Bulgaria’s first patriarch in October 927
Thursday 8 October 2026 16:18
Thursday, 8 October 2026, 16:18
The ruins of the Patriarchal Basilica in Drastar (present-day Silistra), on the banks of the Danube.
PHOTO bulgarianhistory.org
Font size
In 927, Bulgaria and Byzantium (the Eastern Roman Empire) signed a peace treaty under which Constantinople officially recognised the autocephalous Bulgarian Church as a patriarchate for the first time, acknowledging its status as equal to that of the Eastern patriarchates and the Church of Rome. A later historical list, dating from the 12th century, names Damian as the first Bulgarian patriarch and associates him with the Danube city of Drastar.
The following historical events led to Byzantium’s recognition of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church’s independence.
On 27 May 927, the medieval Bulgarian ruler Tsar Simeon the Great died. After fighting numerous wars against Byzantium, Bulgaria’s principal rival during the Middle Ages, Simeon had sought recognition as ruler not only of the Bulgarians but also of the Romans, or Byzantines. He did not achieve this during his lifetime.
Coin bearing the image of Tsar Peter I.
PHOTO wikipedia.org
Simeon was succeeded by his son Peter I. The young tsar launched a military campaign in Thrace, forcing Byzantine Emperor Romanos Lekapenos to negotiate. In early October 927, the two sides concluded what became known as the Deep Peace.
Constantinople recognised Peter as Basileus of the Bulgarians. To seal the agreement, the Bulgarian ruler married Maria, a granddaughter of Emperor Romanos Lekapenos. At their wedding, Maria took the name Irene, meaning “peace”.
Under the same agreement, Patriarch Stephen II of Constantinople reaffirmed the Bulgarian Church’s independence and recognised its patriarchal status.
Until then, the Bulgarian Church had been an autocephalous, or self-governing, archbishopric. It had acquired this status in 870, during the reign of Prince Boris I, who established Christianity in Bulgaria after 866.
The Round Church in Veliki Preslav, built during the reign of Tsar Simeon I (893–927), is a masterpiece of early medieval European architecture.
PHOTO wikipedia.org
In 924, following the death of Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos of Constantinople, Simeon proclaimed himself Basileus of the Bulgarians and Romans. Joseph I was then consecrated as patriarch. These unilateral Bulgarian actions, however, were not recognised by Byzantium.
Little is known about Damian, the first Bulgarian patriarch recognised by Constantinople.
Apart from his name, almost nothing is known with certainty about Damian. Numerous, often contradictory theories concern his identity, the dates and location of his ministry, and the extent of his ecclesiastical authority. His name first appeared in a published historical work in 1680, in Charles du Cange’s Historia Byzantina.
Miniature from the Madrid manuscript of John Skylitzes’ Chronicle: Emperor John Tzimiskes takes the royal icon of the Virgin Mary, the captive Tsar Boris II and his family from Preslav to Constantinople.
PHOTO Archive
During his research, du Cange discovered a collection of ecclesiastical lists from the chancery of the Patriarchate of Constantinople in the Royal Library in Paris. The documents are now held by the National Library of France. Among them was a 12th-century list of the primates of the Bulgarian Church and its successor, the Archbishopric of Ohrid. The document, also known as the Du Cange List, was published in the catalogue accompanying Historia Byzantina, a collection of translations of Byzantine texts.
The source states: “Damian held ecclesiastical office in Dorostol, now called Dristra. In his time, Bulgaria too was granted autocephalous status. By order of Emperor Romanos Lekapenos, he was proclaimed patriarch by the imperial council, and was later deposed by John Tzimiskes.”
PHOTO wikipedia.org
Why does the document place Damian in Silistra rather than in the royal capital of Preslav?
One possible explanation lies with the author of the list, Archbishop John Komnenos of Ohrid. The Byzantine cleric may have wished to diminish the Bulgarian patriarch’s standing by presenting him as the Metropolitan of Drastar and emphasising his expulsion by Byzantine Emperor John Tzimiskes. Following the death of Tsar Peter, Tzimiskes invaded Bulgaria, capturing first the capital, Preslav, and then Drastar, also known as Dorostol.
Yet the Du Cange List names another church leader after Damian: “German, also called Gabriel, who served as bishop in Voden and Prespa.”
Emperor John I Tzimiskes’ campaign against Drastar – a 14th-century miniature from the Manasses Chronicle.
PHOTO Archive
These brief accounts have led Professor Plamen Pavlov and several other Bulgarian historians to argue that Damian refused to submit to Byzantine authority after the capture of Preslav and the imprisonment of Tsar Boris II. According to this interpretation, the patriarch fled Drastar and moved the seat of the Bulgarian Patriarchate westwards, to Sredets and the Bulgarian territories that remained independent under the future Tsar Samuel.
The circumstances of Patriarch Damian’s death, however, remain unknown.

Amazon overhauls aging devices lineup with higher-priced Alexa tablet, dumping the budget Fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:51:27 UTC
23:51:27 KST

Amazon on Thursday debuted a set of new, pricier Alexa tablets and said it's ditching its budget-friendly Fire lineup, marking a significant shift in the e-commerce juggernaut's devices strategy.
The company unveiled 8-inch, 11-inch and 12-inch models, which start at $230 and run up to $550. All devices are available for preorder on Thursday and will begin shipping Oct. 14.
Amazon has historically sold its devices at or near the cost of manufacturing them, partly to undercut competitors with extremely cheap prices, but also with the goal of promoting its other products and services. It's hoped that for every $80 Echo smart speaker it sells, users will purchase movies, audiobook subscriptions or items from its sprawling webstore, which tend to have higher margins.
The company has recently taken steps to make more money from its devices business under CEO Andy Jassy, who succeeded founder Jeff Bezos in 2021. Last year, it introduced pricier versions of its Echo smart speakers and began charging non-Prime members a subscription for Alexa+, the souped-up version of its digital assistant.
The $550 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs more than double the price of the $155 Fire HD 10, Amazon's base model, and puts it more in line with Apple's iPad, which runs from $449 to $1,199.
The launch comes as Amazon and other device makers are grappling with a historic surge in memory prices. Amazon in August boosted prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs and other hardware, citing the memory crunch. And earlier this year, Apple raised its prices on MacBooks and iPads, while Nintendo hiked the price of its Switch 2 console.
Amazon denied that rising memory costs played a role in its decision to charge more for the Alexa tablet. But Panos Panay, the company's devices boss, acknowledged that the shortage made it "quite tricky" to build a premium tablet at a reasonable price without making any "trade-offs."
"I think the team did a good job designing without making that trade," Panay told CNBC in an interview. "They gave you the full craftsmanship of a product, but are able to keep it at that price point."
The company said the Alexa tablet's improved speed and performance, artificial intelligence features, and upgraded design warrant a higher price tag and put the devices on par with "the best tablets on the market."
Amazon added a sleeker, sturdier aluminum backing, higher resolution display and faster processors. On the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, the highest-end model, it incorporated "Nanomatte" display technology that was developed in partnership with Corning to "dramatically reduce screen glare."
One of the most notable upgrades is that all of the devices run Google's Android operating system, a major departure from earlier models, which relied on a custom Android version dubbed Fire OS and used Amazon's own app store, limiting the number of apps that were available.
It's also the first time Amazon has attached a set of devices to the Alexa brand, the company's automated assistant first launched in 2014 via the Echo smart speaker. Alexa is front and center in the new tablets, via a "dynamic tab" on the home screen that offers recommendations and lets users quickly pick up where they left off reading or watching a TV show. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to ask questions.
The company also introduced a new feature called "On-Screen Intelligence," where users can ask Alexa to look at what's on their screen and make suggestions or take actions.
In a demo, Panay showed how users could watch a TikTok clip of someone cooking on a grill and ask Alexa to shop for a burger press used in the video. Users can also pull up a game schedule and add every date to their calendar, Amazon said.
"She'll do the homework, and if things work out, she's going to bring up a shopping list where I can just hit buy now," Panay said.
Amazon said it will continue to support the Fire lineup for four years after the final shipment and consumers can continue using their devices as they do today, but it is no longer manufacturing new units. The Fire lineup includes a 10-inch and 8-inch model as well as two versions targeted for kids.

At least 30 people were killed Thursday and another 18 wounded when Russia dropped a bomb on two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk, in what is shaping up to be one of the deadliest weeks in Ukraine in recent months. 
The mass casualties came a day after 22 people, including five children, were killed and another 54 wounded when a Russian missile struck a residential building in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s birthday.
Thursday morning’s attack, in which a glide bomb struck the two buses in Kramatorsk, is already one of the deadliest single attacks Ukraine has suffered since the start of the war. For several weeks, Ukrainian forces have been conducting a counteroffensive in this sector and say they have already recaptured several square kilometers of territory.
Officials in Kramatorsk accused Russia of committing a “war crime.” Images from the scene showed the wreckage of the buses and charred bodies.
The capital, Kyiv, was also attacked again Thursday, with three people killed and 13 wounded in strikes there. Police in the city said bomb disposal experts also neutralized two unexploded ballistic missile warheads, each weighing about half a ton, after they landed near residential buildings.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly warned in recent days that Russia is preparing an unusually large-scale attack on Ukraine. Moscow has not denied that, stressing that future strikes would be in retaliation for recent Ukrainian drone attacks inside Russia, which have badly damaged Russian oil facilities and warehouses belonging to e-commerce companies and have also caused fatalities.
According to assessments in Kyiv, Russia is seeking to severely damage infrastructure ahead of winter in order to create electricity shortages in Ukraine. In recent days, local companies have already been forced to announce planned power outages and conservation measures.
A public awareness campaign relaunched this month is now urging Ukrainian families to prepare for emergencies, stockpile drinking water and obtain alternative power sources in case of prolonged winter blackouts.
Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to strike deep inside Russia. Russian technology giant Yandex said Thursday that one of its data centers in the western Russian region of Ryazan was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, forcing the site offline and potentially disrupting online services. It was the first time Kyiv had struck a target of this kind.
Ukraine, for its part, said its forces attacked a large oil refinery complex in the Russian city of Salavat, about 1,200 kilometers east of Moscow. Ukraine’s General Staff described the complex as one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities.

Polish SIM cards found inside Russian drones in Poland, raising new questions over 2025 incursion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:50:34 UTC
23:50:34 KST

Polish SIM cards were found inside some of the Russian drones that entered Polish airspace during a mass incursion in September 2025, Polish outlet RMF24 reported, citing findings from a Polish prosecution investigation.
SIM cards can allow drones to connect to local cellular networks for functions such as communications, data transmission, telemetry, or navigation-related services. However, investigators have not said what the Polish SIM cards found in the Russian drones were used for. The details remain classified.
The SIM cards were discovered in some of the Russian Gerbera drones recovered after the incursion, RMF24 reported.
Investigators have not disclosed whether the SIM cards were stolen or obtained illegally.
The investigation into the September 9–10, 2025 incursion was ultimately closed after prosecutors failed to identify those responsible for violating Polish airspace.
More than 30 drones entered Poland
The incursion took place overnight on September 9–10, 2025, during a large Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine. More than 30 Russian Gerbera drones entered Polish airspace from the east and came down at 27 locations across the country, according to RMF24.
Polish forces intercepted and shot down multiple drones, with the Territorial Defense Forces deployed to search for wreckage and other objects that came down on Polish territory. Poland also maintained contact with NATO command throughout the operation.
The incident prompted Poland to close four airports – Warsaw Chopin, Warsaw-Modlin, Rzeszów-Jasionka and Lublin – because of the military activity.
Polish officials described the airspace violations as unprecedented and a serious threat to national security. The incident marked the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine that Polish forces had used weapons against Russian aerial objects that entered the country's airspace.
The mass incursion subsequently became the subject of a criminal investigation into the violation of Polish airspace and the threat to public safety.
Investigation closed without identifying perpetrators
After months of investigation, Polish prosecutors closed the case because they were unable to identify the perpetrators, according to Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office spokesman Marcin Kozak, as cited by RMF24.
Most of the case files, including the justification for the decision, are classified.
Last September, Poland downed four of 19 Russian drones. This September, drone reached NATO’s missile shield in Redzikowo, and troops guarding it called 112
Prosecutors cleared Poland's military response
Investigators also examined whether the Polish military had responded properly to the drone incursion.
According to RMF24, prosecutors concluded that the military acted in accordance with procedures. Polish troops had the right to use force and shoot down hostile objects, and prosecutors found no irregularities in their response.
The investigation was therefore closed both over the failure to identify the perpetrators and over the assessment of the Polish military's actions.

Hurricane Isaias just set a new record for late-arriving Atlantic storms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:50:23 UTC
23:50:23 KST

Isaias is officially the first hurricane of this year’s Atlantic season—marking the latest arrival of a first hurricane in the region since reliable tracking began.
As of this writing, the Category 1 hurricane is about 385 miles (620 kilometers) off the U.S. Gulf Coast and is expected to make landfall late on Friday or early on Saturday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Isaias’s winds are currently about 80 miles per hour (130 kilometers per hour), with “additional strengthening” expected before landfall, NOAA said in its recent forecast.
As Scientific American previously reported, the Atlantic hurricane season has been historically quiet this year. That’s in no small part because of a strong, brewing El Niño, which typically dampens Atlantic hurricanes with unfavorable wind conditions. The region had seen no hurricanes form between June and September—an unparalleled dry spell.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Officials officially upgraded Isaias’s status from a tropical storm to a hurricane—a storm with wind speeds at or above 74 mph (119 kph)—at 3:30 A.M. UTC on October 8. According to meteorologists, that’s the latest first hurricane since satellite tracking began. (Prior to that, a hurricane that didn’t make landfall could go unnoticed, making it hard to say if this is the latest-forming storm for the region ever.)
Still, Isaias beat the previous record by a stunning 27 days, hurricane researcher Brian McNoldy wrote on social media.
“There was beginning to be some uncertainty about whether the Atlantic would get any hurricanes at all this season, but having the first one occur so late in the season is undoubtedly a result of the very strong El Niño building in the central Pacific Ocean,” McNoldy tells Scientific American. “Activity in the deep tropical Atlantic has been shut down this year due to the El Niño–induced wind shear, so the Gulf is one of the few places where this could happen.”
Like any hurricane, Isaias poses a real danger: Officials have put a hurricane warning—meaning, extreme wind and rain conditions are expected—in effect for parts of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida. Dangerous storm surge is possible from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. There is also the possibility of “isolated tornadoes” in parts of Alabama, Florida and southwestern Georgia, according to NOAA.
“Preparations to protect life and property should be rushed to completion,” the agency said.

More killed in Kramatorsk as Russia targets Ukraine’s transportation system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:50:20 UTC
23:50:20 KST

More killed in Kramatorsk as Russia targets Ukraine’s transportation system
Russia’s attacks on trains, buses and ports are paralysing Ukraine’s transport network and endangering civilians.
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian glide bomb struck two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian town of Kramatorsk on Thursday morning, killing at least 30 people and wounding 18, regional authorities said.
Ukrainian officials said the attack was deliberate. When dropped from planes on the Russian side of the front line, such bombs can glide to fixed coordinates on the ground, in this case, a street in the town that lies about 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) from the front line.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” regional administration head Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill the maximum number of people.”
“Russia consciously disregards all conceivable rules of warfare and norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians,” he wrote.
Filashkin ordered the suspension of the movement of all public transportation in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk as Russia intensifies attacks, paralysing Ukraine’s transport infrastructure, from trains and minibuses to gas stations, bridges, seaports and freight ships.
“This is a new Russian tactic,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “They used to focus on depriving Ukraine of power, on switching off electricity and heating; now their task is also to immobilise the infrastructure, create a transportation collapse.”
“Unfortunately, Russia’s tactic has a certain effect with their strikes on railroads, gas stations,” he said. “They coerce to peace on their conditions.
“They also strike the public psychologically, disrupt the usual lifestyle in general.”
Throughout the war, Russia has denied it targets Ukrainian civilians, a statement that means little to Ukrainians. During the first eight months of 2026, 15,280 civilians were killed or injured, according to the United Nations – a toll that is 55 percent higher than during the same period in 2025.
With no civilian planes in the sky since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, trains, buses and trucks have become a lifeline for Ukrainian civilians and businesses, as well as for transporting military and humanitarian supplies.
Trains handle almost two-thirds of Ukraine’s freight volumes, including the export of steel slabs, grains and vegetable oils that keep the economy afloat.
At least 521 locomotives have been hit by drones and shelling since 2022, three-fifths this year alone, Ukrzaliznytsia, the state-run railway monopoly, said in late September.
Some locomotives were struck while in motion, and drones have occasionally hit passenger carriages, causing fires, deaths and injuries.
The largest such attack killed five passengers in January in the northeastern Kharkiv region, an act of “terrorism” that was “not militarily justified”, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
‘The Russians improved their comms’
Hitting moving trains and buses has become possible because a new generation of Russian drones are no longer the slow, unmanned aircraft that can be jammed electronically or shot down with a machinegun or even an assault rifle.
Jet-powered, with bigger payloads, they are piloted by human operators who use a wireless mesh network, in which each drone serves as a relay node.
“They’re operated manually. The Russians improved their comms,” Andriy Pronin, one of the pioneers of drone warfare in Ukraine, told Al Jazeera.
Occasionally, the signal reaches the drones through a modem on the ground, on a rooftop or even inside somebody’s apartment – switched on by Ukrainians recruited by Russian intelligence, he said.
Locating the modems before attacks is “complicated, but doable”, Pronin said.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, prosecutors and officials, hundreds of recruits, including teenagers, have been offered money via Telegram. They often did not realise the consequences of their actions and have been arrested and convicted.
The video feed and geolocation are often backed by smuggled Ukrainian SIM cards or signals from mobile phone providers in neighbouring, pro-Moscow Belarus, officials believe. These drones can now get almost anywhere in Ukraine, including once-safe western regions.
A train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson crossed into Poland on September 14, just 30 minutes before a Russian drone struck another passenger train’s locomotive at Yahodyn train station in western Ukraine. Former CIA chief David Petraeus was on a nearby train and reportedly described the attack as “terrifying” and “the act of a truly barbaric leader”.
Ukrainian civilians are equally terrified.
When a daytime Russian drone attack began on September 23, Alyna realised that her workplace was in the most vulnerable place in Kyiv’s central railway station.
She works in a cafeteria located almost in the middle of a massive overpass that stretches above 14 main tracks between the station’s main buildings.
The howling air raid siren and the booms of exploding jet-powered kamikaze drones sent the 24-year-old Kyiv resident scurrying down the stairs and farther on to the subway station.
The drones hit a nearby market, sending black plumes of smoke into the sky and burning to the ground the rotund, modernist building known as the Puck.
“Everything was whistling and rattling above me,” Alyna told Al Jazeera just after another air raid alert ended and passengers began re-entering the station. She withheld her last name for security purposes.
Minutes after the conversation, one more air raid siren forced the passengers out of the railway station, and a drone hit by an interceptor turned into a black cloud in the sky a couple of kilometres east of the building.
The attacks are not limited to trains – Russian drones target petrol stations, buses and minibuses, and seaports, paralysing Ukraine’s exports of grain, vegetable oils and steel.
“You go to a minibus and can hear how [drones] buzz right next to it,” Tetiana Melikhova, a university professor in Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern city with a pre-war population of 720,000, told Al Jazeera.
Her 18-year-old student, Tetiana Bubynets, and two other civilians aged 31 and 48 were killed by an AI-driven drone that was programmed to strike a petrol station on July 6.

Russia has begun experiencing major internet problems following an attack on a Yandex data center — which services are not working

In Russia, the disruptions have affected operators, social networks, Gosuslugi, banks, and government websites. The outages occurred after a fire at a Yandex data center.
Large-scale disruptions to internet services have occurred in Russia — in addition to media outlets, social networks, and "Gosuslugi," problems have been recorded among mobile operators, T-Bank, the presidential grants website, and Channel One, UNN reports, citing Astra.
Details
The service "Sboy.rf" reported problems accessing the Russian websites of Tele2, Rostelecom, Megafon, MTS, Channel One, the website "президентские-гранты.рф," T-Bank, and other resources.
Among Russia's regions by the number of complaints about communication problems, Moscow, St. Petersburg, Novosibirsk Oblast, Krasnodar Krai, Moscow, Sverdlovsk, Nizhny Novgorod, and Rostov oblasts are leading.
In addition, according to Downdetector, disruptions have occurred at "Gosuslugi," Russian Railways, "Avito," "VKontakte," and other public companies.

How ‘Digital Oblivion’ Is Helping Russia Rewrite the Past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:49:23 UTC
23:49:23 KST

The disappearance of independent journalism, firsthand accounts and historical archives from the internet is helping Russia and other authoritarian states rewrite history and shape collective memory, researchers warn.
From altered reporting on the Beslan school siege to vanishing articles documenting anti-government protests, the loss of online records — a process that researchers call “digital oblivion” — is contributing to public “amnesia” about key events that autocrats find unhelpful.
As artificial intelligence becomes a gateway to news and information, the researchers warn that gaps in the historical record combined with a flood of propaganda can shape the answers people receive about the past.
“Digital tools are used to consolidate what would have otherwise been a more painstaking process,” Steven Feldstein, a researcher with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said at a recent panel at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at the City University of New York.
Autocratic leaders who have long relied on violence, intimidation and legal harassment to consolidate power have added powerful digital tactics to their toolkit. These can make independent accounts of key events harder to find, unsafe to publish or impossible to verify.
Digital oblivion can involve a government’s or a company’s deliberate removal of a website or archive, or can be the quiet disappearance or blocking of online photos, blogs or social media posts. Records can also become inaccessible through broken links and obsolete media formats, even when the cause is unclear.
The erasure can be ad hoc or systematic. It is more expansive than old-school censorship.
“Contemporary autocratic politics is all about a ‘glorious past.’ The thing that needs to happen is the ‘past’ needs to be cleaned up,” said panelist M. Gessen, co-founder of Kronika, an initiative to preserve independent journalism.
Documentation of large-scale anti-Putin protests in Moscow in 2015 has become difficult to find online, as has material tracing the development of Russia’s LGBTQ+ movement, Gessen said.
In some cases, reporting remains available while passages challenging the official account disappear.
A Russian translation of “The School,” journalist C.J. Chivers’ account of the 2004 Beslan hostage crisis for Esquire, was heavily edited around the tragedy’s 20th anniversary, according to a 2025 analysis by Mediazona using the Wayback Machine.
The translation had been preserved on the website of Pravila Zhizni, the magazine that replaced Russian Esquire after it lost its license in 2022.
Mediazona’s analysis found that parts of the online article changed, including a passage describing how most of the deaths occurred after Russian troops stormed the school. The article’s conclusion that the siege had shaken faith in the Russian government and its ability to protect the Russian people also disappeared.
An investigation by Citizen Lab, a Canada-based research group, documented extensive blocking of content on Ukraine, Belarus and LGBTQ+ issues, as well as accounts belonging to independent media and users opposing Putin or supporting Ukraine, on Russian social network VKontakte.
At times, ordinary people have voluntarily become tools of digital oblivion, the panelists said.
Gessen cited the example of a Belarusian woman who deleted photos documenting her participation in anti-government protests following President Alexander Lukashenko’s disputed 2020 re-election in order to protect herself.
China’s restrictions on information about the June 4, 1989, Tiananmen massacre mark an early success story for digital oblivion. Online censorship makes accounts of the military’s crackdown on the student-led protests difficult to find on the Chinese internet, while documentation of subsequent protests in Hong Kong has also been heavily restricted.
The panelists said similar pressures on the public record can emerge in democracies.
Gessen recalled the case of a U.S. scientist who removed language about climate change from existing research and inserted language acceptable to the Trump administration to safeguard funding from the National Institutes of Health.
Panelists also pointed to the Trump administration’s removal of information from government websites and changes that have made studies and reports harder to find online.
AI is accelerating the impact of these disappearances, the researchers warned. Digital oblivion regularly leads to large language models being trained on faulty and incomplete sources, or censored information. Decisions by AI companies about which material to use and how to present it can then influence what people know and understand about a historical event.
“AI companies have become increasingly opaque in how they are training their models,” Sarah Myers West, co-director of the AI Now Institute and an expert on technology policymaking, said at the panel, titled “Digital Oblivion: How Autocrats Engineer Forgetting.”
A flood of low-quality, AI-generated content often called “AI slop” can create further noise, making reliable accounts harder to find.
Pro-Kremlin information operations have demonstrated how large volumes of misleading content can influence AI responses.
NewsGuard, a company that analyzes misinformation, said in a March 2025 report that the pro-Kremlin disinformation network Pravda was flooding search results and material retrieved by AI chatbots with false claims and propaganda.
A separate NewsGuard analysis showed a video produced by Russian influence operation Storm-1516 was provided by an AI chatbot as evidence that Ukrainian soldiers had burned an effigy of U.S. President Donald Trump and promoted other false claims about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
A November 2025 analysis by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue identified roughly 900 political websites that have linked to Pravda network articles, with the majority citing them as credible sources.
The institute said the network had published more than 6 million articles since its launch in 2014 and was publishing new content every few seconds.
Efforts to preserve that record are growing, such as in librarians’ work to save data and archives, citizens protesting data-center construction and communities rejecting Flock cameras.
In Russia, activists are working to safeguard the history of the LGBTQ+ movement as state restrictions threaten both its participants and its archives.
Readers can also reduce their exposure to manipulated narratives by consulting original reporting and verifying information through multiple reliable sources, rather than through the framework, and lack of context, of an AI platform, panelists said.
But preserving access to reliable information also requires action from governments as AI infrastructure becomes increasingly embedded in institutions, schools and systems, they argued.
“They need to have real incentives to train their models on facts,” said Gessen.

British colonization worsened Australia's bushfire risk by creating landscapes more prone to burning : Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:49:18 UTC
23:49:18 KST

Saadet Gokce
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Forest expansion and thickening following British colonization created landscapes more prone to burning, amplifying the influence of climate change and worsening Australia's bushfire crisis, according to a study published in Nature on Wednesday.
The study was conducted by researchers from the University of Melbourne in collaboration with the Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation.
The study involved the reconstruction of 1,000 years of vegetation history in Croajingolong National Park, one of southeastern Australia's most fire-prone forest regions.
The study found that colonization triggered cascading changes, including increased fire temperatures, a fourfold increase in eucalypt cover, the transformation of open woodland into forest, and increased soil erosion.
The paper's lead author Michael-Shawn Fletcher said that the research provides scientific evidence for the value of cultural burning and the need to integrate Indigenous knowledge into contemporary fire management strategies, according to a statement from the University of Melbourne.
"When Country is cared for, climate does not dictate wildfire," he said, adding that the Gunaikurnai people have been caring for the environment for thousands of years, keeping much of the landscape as open woodland.
"Climate records show that seasons of comparably dangerous fire weather, such as those seen during Ash Wednesday and Black Saturday, reoccurred in the region repeatedly before colonization, yet the open landscape maintained by cultural burning protected the land from catastrophic fire," Fletcher said, arguing that colonization ended that practice, leading forests across the region to expand and thicken and eventually increasing the amount of fuel in the landscape.
Australia breaks ground in $1.2 billion rare earths mine project
Separately, in Australia's Northern Territory, a 1.8 billion Australian dollars ($1.2 billion) rare earths mine reached a major milestone Thursday as construction finally began after two decades in development, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.
The project is backed by the US and Australian governments and Australia's richest woman, Gina Rinehart.

CIS, SCO security services practice repelling terrorist UAV attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:48:58 UTC
23:48:58 KST

MINSK, October 8. /TASS/. Security services of Russia, Belarus, Iran, Kazakhstan, China, and Uzbekistan held a joint exercise in Minsk to practice thwarting terrorist attacks with the use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on a site with a large gathering of people and on a critical infrastructure facility, as well as a joint counterterrorism operation to eliminate an illegal armed group that had infiltrated a populated area.
The special forces’ operations took place as part of the final phase of the Eurasia-Antiterror 2026 exercise, organized by the Belarusian KGB with the support of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Anti-Terrorism Center (ATC) and the Executive Committee of the Regional Anti-Terrorism Structure (RATS) of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) during the CIS-SCO Counterterrorism Forum currently taking place in Minsk.
"The exercise involving the competent authorities of the CIS and SCO member states was organized as part of cooperation between the two international organizations, which provides for the simultaneous execution of specific training tasks united by a common concept and scenario, as well as the location and timing of their conduct," the CIS ATC press office reported. In total, the competent authorities of 10 states - Russia, Belarus, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, China, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan - took part in this year’s exercise.
During the first phase, the exercise was conducted within the national territories of the participating states to practice joint operations by security agencies and financial intelligence units of the CIS member states aimed at countering the financing of terrorism, as well as operations by security agencies of the CIS and SCO member states aimed at identifying and suppressing the activities of international terrorist organizations. Under the coordination of the operation headquarters established under the CIS Anti-Terrorism Center and the Executive Committee of the SCO Regional Anti-Terrorism Structure, the participants practiced the exchange of current significant information using the CIS and SCO shared information systems. At the conclusion of the exercises in the Belarusian capital, the participants toured an exhibition of weapons and special equipment.
The CIS Anti-Terrorist Center emphasized that anti-terrorist exercises are an important element in the development of a system of practical cooperation among the special services of the CIS and SCO member states. The exercise participants gain experience in planning, preparing, and conducting joint counterterrorism operations, and refine the forms and methods of coordinated actions to detect and prevent terrorist acts, taking into account changes in the operational situation, current challenges, and threats.
This was the second time that joint CIS-SCO counterterrorism exercises were held--the first took place in Kyrgyzstan in 2023. A distinctive feature of the Eurasia-Antiterror 2026 exercise was the participation of special operations units from six countries in carrying out training tasks on the territory of a single state.

Six of the seven were killed in various parts of Gaza City.
Two people were killed in a drone strike on a car, while one was killed in a drone attack on a tent in an encampment for displaced people, the rescue service and al-Shifa hospital said.
"Two people, a woman and a child, were killed and others were wounded when Israeli aircraft bombed a residential building" in Gaza City, the civil defence said.

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen claimed responsibility for the latest attack on Riyadh’s airport, saying a ballistic missile caused damage, but provided no evidence. The Saudis had no immediate comment about the claim.
The Houthis’ military spokesman later said the group had fired additional ballistic and cruise missiles at airports in Riyadh and the southwestern city of Najran, claiming the attacks disrupted flights.
Riyadh’s airport “closed again,” global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said Thursday afternoon on X. It said the last landing was more than 80 minutes earlier and the last takeoff more than 90 minutes earlier.
Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks with Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday and promised to "do everything" to help end the Middle East conflict, Russian news agencies reported.
"We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation," said Putin ahead of a regional summit in the Central Asian nation of Turkmenistan, adding that Iran had made "real efforts to end the war" since US-Israeli attacks started on February 28.
Putin noted the "positive evolution" in relations between Iran and Russia.
The two have reinforced diplomatic and military links since Russia launched its offensive in Ukraine in February 2022, becoming increasingly reliant on each other.
France and Saudi Arabia are studying several options involving French military assets to help protect the Yanbu oil terminal, France's Armed Forces Chief of Staff, General Fabien Mandon, said on Thursday.
"It's at the study phase at the moment with Saudi Arabia. We are examining different options to protect the Yanbu terminal, which has been attacked and is essential for hydrocarbon trade," Mandon told a parliamentary hearing.
He added that France had already deployed around 2,000 troops to the region to help protect Gulf allies, including Qatar and Kuwait.
The Israeli army said Thursday that one soldier was killed and three others were slightly wounded in south Lebanon, where the military has occupied a band of territory since invading in March in response to Hezbollah attacks.
"Captain Eliav Haim Tzapalamus, aged 21, from Haifa, a combat officer in the 603rd Battalion, 7th Brigade, fell in combat in southern Lebanon," the army said.
A commercial plane belonging to state-owned Saudi Arabian Airlines (Saudia) was heavily damaged by fire while parked at a terminal in Riyadh airport on Thursday, three people briefed on the matter said, attributing the damage to either shrapnel or a direct hit by a projectile.
The sources said that the plane was believed to be empty of passengers at the time, but could not rule out any injuries as a result of the incident.
Saudi Arabia's government media office, its civil aviation authority and Saudia Airlines did not respond to emailed requests for comment.
The United States imposed sanctions Thursday targeting "the remnants of Iran's shadow fleet" of tankers used to transport oil products to foreign markets - the latest move to ramp up pressure in its war against Tehran.
"Today's action effectively neutralises the vast majority of Iran's remaining shadow fleet network," the US Treasury Department said in a statement.
The aim is to deprive Tehran of funds needed to "wage war in the region," added Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Thursday's move takes aim at 17 vessels said to have moved millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, alongside petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets across South and East Asia.
The Treasury Department designated companies that own these vessels, accusing them of operating in the petroleum or petrochemical sectors of the Iranian economy.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told AFP on Thursday that the bloc was expanding its naval mission in the Red Sea, where more ships are requiring escorts as the war in Yemen escalates.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis last month seized control of the country's entire Red Sea coastline, including the Bab al-Mandeb strait, as the previously dormant conflict reignited.
The EU, which launched Operation Aspides in 2024 when the Houthis were previously targeting Red Sea and Gulf of Aden shipping, said last month that the mission had raised its alert level as the fighters again threatened the key waterway.
"The list of ships that need escorting is increasing," Kallas told AFP in an interview during a visit to Lebanon.
She said the EU had been urging members of the bloc to supply more vessels for the mission and "the good news is that the member states are already providing more ships."
"We have Belgium coming in with new ships, and two more member states who are providing or actually contemplating providing new ships, so to make it stronger (so) that we can actually cater for all those that need escorting," she added.
"The minimum amount that we actually need is 10 ships. We don't have that right now, but we are working on getting this there," she said.
"Clearly maritime security is one of our priorities."
The United States urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to "exercise heightened vigilance" Thursday following Houthi attacks targeting Riyadh's airport, which US government employees now need special authorisation to use.
"The US Mission is aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh as of 8 October and reminds all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance," the State Department's consular affairs arm said on X, adding that "US government employees working in Saudi Arabia now require special authorisation" to use the transit hub.
Donald Trump said Thursday that the US is having productive discussions with Iran and will not launch an attack on the country before US midterm congressional elections in November.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. He said the US blockade of Iranian ports remains in effect and that oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.
"We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd," Trump wrote.

The aim is to deprive Tehran of funds needed to "wage war in the region," added Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Thursday's move takes aim at 17 vessels said to have moved millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, alongside petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets across South and East Asia.
The Treasury Department designated companies that own these vessels, accusing them of operating in the petroleum or petrochemical sectors of the Iranian economy.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told AFP on Thursday that the bloc was expanding its naval mission in the Red Sea, where more ships are requiring escorts as the war in Yemen escalates.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis last month seized control of the country's entire Red Sea coastline, including the Bab al-Mandeb strait, as the previously dormant conflict reignited.
The EU, which launched Operation Aspides in 2024 when the Houthis were previously targeting Red Sea and Gulf of Aden shipping, said last month that the mission had raised its alert level as the fighters again threatened the key waterway.
"The list of ships that need escorting is increasing," Kallas told AFP in an interview during a visit to Lebanon.
She said the EU had been urging members of the bloc to supply more vessels for the mission and "the good news is that the member states are already providing more ships."
"We have Belgium coming in with new ships, and two more member states who are providing or actually contemplating providing new ships, so to make it stronger (so) that we can actually cater for all those that need escorting," she added.
"The minimum amount that we actually need is 10 ships. We don't have that right now, but we are working on getting this there," she said.
"Clearly maritime security is one of our priorities."
The United States urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to "exercise heightened vigilance" Thursday following Houthi attacks targeting Riyadh's airport, which US government employees now need special authorisation to use.
"The US Mission is aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh as of 8 October and reminds all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance," the State Department's consular affairs arm said on X, adding that "US government employees working in Saudi Arabia now require special authorisation" to use the transit hub.
Donald Trump said Thursday that the US is having productive discussions with Iran and will not launch an attack on the country before US midterm congressional elections in November.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. He said the US blockade of Iranian ports remains in effect and that oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.
"We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd," Trump wrote.

The ministry said the attacks "represent a grave violation of the Kingdom’s sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region and the safety of civilians, civil objects, and air navigation" in a post on X.

EU diplomatic arm under fire for bowing to US pressure over disinformation conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:48:19 UTC
23:48:19 KST

The EU diplomatic service pulled its backing from a disinformation conference after US pressure, angering MEPs and NGOs who say it undermines the bloc's own defence of civil society.
The EU's diplomatic service is facing criticism from lawmakers and civil society after withdrawing its backing for a disinformation conference at the last minute, following pressure from Washington.
The European External Action Service (EEAS) pulled out of the conference, one of the few European-level gatherings devoted to the issue, saying its programme did not align with EU positions. Critics say the move contradicts the bloc's own approach to protecting civil society.
"We have decided to have the EEAS logo removed from the material associated with the conference in view of the content of the program," said Christian Wigand, the EU's lead spokesperson for foreign affairs, on Thursday.
"The organisers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the positions held by the EU," he continued.
Critics say that withdrawing support from an NGO-led initiative because of a clash with the EU's official position undermines the European Democracy Shield, a framework intended to protect civil society and journalists from governmental pressure and foreign interference.
"Pressuring European governments to drop a disinformation conference to hide its own role in spreading disinformation is not diplomacy. It is foreign interference, and Europe should call it that," said MEP Alexandra Geese (Germany/Greens/EFA).
The EEAS declined to say which parts of the conference did not align with EU views. It quietly asked organisers to remove its logo from the conference material just days before the event began.
Canada and Lithuania also asked for their logos to be removed following pressure from the US State Department, Euronews can confirm.
"Pulling support from the conference at the last minute is a hugely irresponsible move, especially from the EEAS. It shows a lack of commitment to actually fighting disinformation. That looks like the EU is treating disinformation as a commodity," Domen Savic, co-founder of the NGO Državljan D, told Euronews.
The conference, organised by the NGO EU DisinfoLab, is taking place on Wednesday and Thursday in Vilnius, Lithuania.
For MEP Brando Benifei (Italy/S&D), the EEAS's withdrawal of support is a serious matter that deserves a full explanation.
"Frankly, it is difficult to see how the Vilnius discussions are so at odds with the EU’s stated position. Nor does it seem that we are filling this void with stronger European democracy by hiding our logos," Benifei told Euronews.
In EU jargon, FIMI stands for foreign information manipulation and interference. The latest EEAS report on the subject, published in March, names China and Russia as hostile actors conducting such operations in Europe but does not mention the US.
The programme includes a panel titled "USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back", featuring two researchers and Alex Finley, a former CIA official.
"There are no good and bad interferences in our democracies, the ones we decide to ignore versus the ones we agree to counter. My approach to the fight against FIMI is country-agnostic, and so it should be for the EEAS," MEP Nathalie Loiseau (France/Renew), chair of the special committee on the Democracy Shield, told Euronews.
"The Trump government publicly states that they want to help the far right rise to power in Europe. If the Commission does not even dare to recognise US interference, because they fear Trump, we are lost," said MEP Kim van Sparrentak (the Netherlands/Greens/EFA).
"With this mentality I'm starting to question whether the European Commission can credibly lead and coordinate our European responses to hybrid threats," she added.
The decision was taken at a very high level within the EU institutions and caught even officials working directly on the issue off guard, Euronews understands.
A few days before the conference, Michael Shellenberger, a right-wing US commentator, emailed several speakers. He asked whether they had received government funding and what they hoped to achieve with their sessions.
"Do you regard the US government as a source of foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) in Europe? Have you had any contact with the State Department or another US agency about your work or this conference?" reads the email, seen by Euronews.
At the same time, others argue that Brussels should not bicker with Washington, least of all over an NGO-led conference, because transatlantic unity is needed to confront what they see as the West's real enemies.
"I regret that the US feels it is being perceived as a FIMI actor by the EU. When it comes to FIMI, the EU should remain firmly focused on the threat posed by Russia and other hostile actors. Full stop," MEP Tomas Tobé (Sweden/EPP) told Euronews.
By contrast, some argue that withdrawing support at the last minute from a conference that is one of the few serious European-level venues where experts, civil society and private actors discuss disinformation sends a clear message to the community to steer clear of US interference.
"The US actions are hardly surprising, the disinformation community has already been under increasing pressure since Donald Trump returned to the White House, but it has never been so blatant," Mattia Caniglia, an affiliate lecturer at the University of Glasgow, told Euronews.
"EU institutions and the majority of member states react to these incidents like the world was still the one we had in 2010, but things have changed. Sacrificing the support to an NGO not to put important dossiers in peril will not work; standing for what we believe in will," he said.
Vincenzo Genovese contributed to the reporting.

Draft law aims to protect investors in fund liquidation process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:46:41 UTC
23:46:41 KST

The draft law on the troubled funds aims to protect the rights of nearly 460,000 investors.
Lawmakers from Türkiye’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) have drafted new legislation aimed at safeguarding investor rights and ensuring transparency during the liquidation of investment funds hit by the ongoing financial crisis, state-run Anadolu Agency has reported.
The proposal, which is expected to be submitted to parliament in the coming days, would provide for the liquidation of assets worth up to 1 million Turkish lira for 455,578 investors.
The draft seeks to identify each fund’s assets and their rightful owners, liquidate fund assets without causing unnecessary economic losses and distribute the resulting cash proceeds fairly among investors.
To account for past cash flows and help balance investor losses, investment values would be updated using the arithmetic average of changes in the consumer price index (CPI) and domestic producer price index (D-PPI). Withdrawals would be calculated under a “first-in, first-out” method.
The proposal also envisions interim payments of up to 1 million lira per investor, provided that the amount does not exceed the investor’s net investment or finalized claim.
If available cash is insufficient to cover all payments, funds would be distributed proportionally among eligible investors. The Capital Markets Board (SPK) would be authorized to determine payment priorities, including making payments beginning with investors who have the smallest net investment amounts.
The draft would establish a voluntary reimbursement mechanism for investors who exited funds before liquidation and earned returns deemed above normal market conditions due to inaccurate asset valuations. Reimbursement calculations would be based on objective market benchmarks, including comparable fund returns and relevant market indices.
Under the proposal, responsibility for investor losses could extend to fund founders, portfolio management companies and individuals or entities found responsible for shortfalls in liquidation proceeds. Assets seized during criminal investigations could also be used to compensate investors.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) would be authorized to sell or liquidate assets that cannot be directly transferred to funds and channel the proceeds to affected investors.

German president says Berlin will remain committed to Europe during France visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:45:42 UTC
23:45:42 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Germany would remain committed to Europe despite political and economic changes in the country, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said Thursday.
“The Germans will remain good Europeans, despite all the changes taking place here -- economically, politically, and especially in security policy,” Steinmeier said after meeting French President Emmanuel Macron during a state visit to France, according to German newspaper Die Zeit.
“Germany can only be successful as a European Germany, closely embedded in the EU. That is true and will remain so for us,” he added.
“If Germany and France do not move forward together, Europe will not move forward at all,” Macron said.
He said cooperation between the two countries was important to “strengthen our democracies and their vitality” at a time when “conspiracy theories and skepticism sometimes gain the upper hand.”
The two presidents also discussed challenges facing their countries, with Steinmeier saying political polarization and the growing strength of radical political forces were making it more difficult to form governments and govern.
“We will not escape our growth crisis if everything remains as it is,” Steinmeier said, adding that “reforms have become even more difficult.”
The meeting was also a farewell visit, as both Steinmeier and Macron are due to leave office next year.
Steinmeier's visit is the first state visit to France by a German federal president in 13 years, according to the German government.
Macron, for his part, said the two countries “understand the price of war, the need for reconciliation and the value of peace.”
“Our friendship, which is etched in history, is our greatest strength and represents promise for all of Europe,” Macron said.

Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:43:19 UTC
23:43:19 KST

Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles
Saudi Arabia says two of the missiles intercepted were headed towards the capital, Riyadh.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has intercepted ballistic missiles allegedly fired by Yemen’s Houthis towards cities in Saudi Arabia.
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said his forces intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles heading in the direction of the Saudi capital Riyadh, and one missile in the direction of the city of Khamis Mushait, close to the Yemeni border, on Thursday.
Separately, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency said in a statement on X that falling debris from an intercepted missile had caused material damage to a kindergarten and medical clinic complex in Riyadh. It did not indicate if there were any casualties.
Yahya Saree, Yemen’s Houthi military spokesman, said the Iran-aligned group launched a ballistic missile towards King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Thursday afternoon, claiming that the missile had successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic.
Witnesses told The Associated Press news agency that they heard several explosions in Riyadh on Thursday, including one at the city’s airport that halted flights. Al Jazeera could not independently confirm the reports.
In recent days, the Houthis have warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating in the kingdom’s airspace, except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, is a target for the Houthis.
Following the latest reports, Air India said on Thursday that it had cancelled flights to and from Riyadh until at least the weekend, and the Germany-based Lufthansa Group airlines said they were suspending flights to Riyadh through October 16, according to the Reuters news agency.
The US embassy in Saudi Arabia meanwhile urged its citizens in the country to remain vigilant, saying they should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions.
Saudi Arabia’s Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks, claimed by the Houthis on Tuesday and Wednesday. At least three civilians were killed and 36 injured, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the attacks on the two airports, saying in a post on X that they “represent a grave violation of the Kingdom’s sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region and the safety of civilians, civil objects, and air navigation”. Oman and Egypt also condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi airports.
These were not the first Houthi strikes on Saudi airports. On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Fighting intensifies in Yemen
Meanwhile, inside Yemen, explosions have been reported near the airport in the Houthi-controlled Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, according to local sources.
The cause and impact of these explosions are not immediately clear.
In a post on X, a spokesman for Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces said at least 1,370 Houthi fighters were “neutralised” in 1,729 operations, and at least 300 vehicles were destroyed or disabled.
Al Jazeera’s Hadeel al-Yamani, reporting from Taiz in Yemen, said intense fighting is raging between armed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis in al-Shamayatayn, al-Maafer and the southern and western countryside of Taiz governorate.
“The Houthis are pushing into rural areas that have not seen conflict for years, aiming to open a supply route because their lines towards al-Kadaha and al-Waziiya, which link Aden, Lahij and Taiz, are nearly cut off by advancing government forces”, she said.
Al-Yamani added that pro-government forces are within striking distance of al-Waziiya and the Kahboub Mountains overlooking Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Pro-government forces have reported more than 2,000 operations against the Houthis, and are preparing for a “dangerous escalation”, she said.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to data released by the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The IOM described the crisis in a statement on Wednesday as alarming, with the number of people displaced surging from the 76,000 recorded in mid-September.
