Investigation Finds That Former High-Ranking Uzbek Security Official Acquired UAE Citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

In April 2023, when he was serving as deputy head of the Presidential Security Service, Otabek Umarov – Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s son-in-law – reportedly acquired citizenship in the United Arab Emirates. He’s also alleged to be the owner of around $7 million worth of Dubai real estate.
Those are the central allegations of a new investigation published by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service, Ozodlik.
Under Uzbek military law, which governs the position Umarov held at the time, holding a second citizenship is prohibited. Since acquiring citizenship typically includes swearing an oath of allegiance, many countries bar security (and other) officials from doing so – a second passport represents possible divided loyalties and a counterintelligence risk.
As OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and [the process] requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.”
Umarov was shifted out of his security service role in November 2024, in the extended wake of the assassination attempt on Komil Allamjanov.
Allamjanov, at the time of the October 2024 attempt, had recently stepped down from his role as deputy head of the presidential administration. He has since returned to government service, as an adviser to the powerful head of the presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva (the president’s eldest daughter). As of January 2026 he was also appointed to a seemingly bespoke role: advisor-ambassador and representative of the presidential administration in the United States.
Umarov, meanwhile, was named first deputy chairman of Uzbekistan’s National Olympic Committee – his father-in-law, the president, is the chairman.
According to OCCRP and Ozodlik, at some point in 2025, Umarov became the owner of 13 properties in Dubai, worth around $7 million. The properties previously belonged to his younger brother, Oybek Umarov, who purchased them in 2021 and 2022, according to leaked Dubai real estate data obtained by OCCRP.
It is not clear precisely how or when they came to be listed with Umarov’s name on the deeds, whether the properties were gifted or purchased.
While Umarov has notably expensive tastes – for example, he’s been pictured wearing a limited edition Richard Mille watch valued at up to $1.9 million – his government position doesn’t quite explain his apparent wealth. Uzbek officials do not have to disclose their income declarations publicly.
OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Public commercial registries show no record of [Otabek Umarov] owning private companies during his time as deputy presidential security chief.” His brother, however, does have extensive business holdings, including in banking, cement, and metalwork.
A high-ranking government source told The Diplomat in late 2024 that Umarov’s assets and businesses were held in the names of others, including Ulugbek Shadmanov who was implicated in an apparent attempt to manipulate the U.S. sanctions system to target Allamjonov and another Uzbek official in the months before the assassination attempt. Shadmanov was earlier named in the Pandora Papers as connected to an offshore company, though there are few details available. In December 2024 he was detained in Dubai and extradited rapidly – apparently without the proper legal process – to Uzbekistan, regardless of the fact that he held what’s known as a “Golden Visa” in the UAE. Despite high-powered legal representation and a campaign on his behalf, very little has been reported since about his case.
Ultimately, the OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation raises far more questions than it answers; that’s the nature of investigations into the opaque underbelly of Uzbek politics (and those of the UAE, to boot). As I told Ozodlik, we don’t know exactly how Umarov acquired UAE citizenship, who was involved, and who knew about it. As noted above, the process to acquired UAE citizenship necessitates a nomination by a royal court or senior official. It’s nearly impossible to believe that Umarov’s role and connections were unknown at the time to the UAE’s authorities.
Then there are questions of what comes next. Uzbekistan does not officially recognize dual citizenship. Holding a second citizenship isn’t illegal per se – though it does violate laws related to Umarov’s specific position at the time. Nevertheless, “voluntarily acquiring a passport of a foreign state” is listed as possible grounds for revocation of Uzbek citizenship.

The strategic-sites list already covers state institutions, energy facilities, defense-industry companies, mobile-network operators and other infrastructure regarded as essential to national security.
"Karash Invest" belongs to Hristo Gebrev, the son of arms manufacturer Emiliyan Gebrev. The company produces explosives and runs warehouses for weapons and ammunition. Its manufacturing facility is near Smyadovo, where the new plant is also planned.
The second company added to the list, "Aheloy OPM," is owned by Boris Redanski. Its stated business activities include the production and trade of weapons and ammunition, including thermobaric munitions.

The development followed explosions at "EMCO" ammunition warehouses in the village of Belitsa near Tryavna that month. The Prosecutor’s Office launched an arson investigation and said it was examining all possible leads, including potential external interference.
"EMCO" is owned by Emiliyan Gebrev. Several of his facilities have been affected by explosions in recent years, while Russian nationals linked to Moscow’s military intelligence were implicated in earlier incidents. Eye contact may act as a learning “switch” for babies’ brains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

Direct eye contact from an adult speaker appears to guide how infants choose which words to learn by aligning the baby’s brain activity with the adult’s. A new study suggests that this one-way neural coordination may help link an adult’s communicative gaze to an infant’s selective word learning. The findings were published in Nature Communications.
Infants grow up in busy environments where many sights and sounds compete for their attention, requiring them to figure out which information is worth learning. To navigate this challenge, babies rely on social signals known as ostensive cues, which are communicative acts like direct gaze or infant-directed speech that indicate an adult intends to share information. The central focus of the new study is interpersonal neural coupling, a measure of how much activity in one person’s brain predicts later activity in another person’s brain.
Past developmental research has shown that social cues play an active role in how young minds acquire language. For example, a 2003 study indicated that nine-month-old infants learned unfamiliar foreign speech sounds when interacting with a live person, but did not learn when watching identical recorded video lessons. Expanding on how social cues operate in the brain, a 2017 study found that when an adult made direct eye contact with a baby, their brainwaves synchronized more strongly than when the adult looked away.
Even so, scientists still faced an unresolved question about what this shared brain activity accomplishes. As the authors of a 2020 review noted, it remained uncertain whether brain-to-brain synchrony helps infants learn or represents an incidental byproduct of two individuals watching the same event. In a related vein, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 showed that communicative infant-directed speech heightened attention-related brain activity in toddlers and was linked to better word learning.
The research team, which included first author Wei Zhang of Nanyang Technological University and Victoria Leong, a professor in the School of Social Sciences at Nanyang Technological University and the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Cambridge, set out to address this question. “We had previously published a seminal demonstration that eye contact modulates adult-infant neural synchrony,” Leong told PsyPost. “The current study replicates (across two countries) and extends these findings to show that neural synchrony underpins infants’ selective learning in social contexts.”
The researchers tested 47 infants who were roughly nine months old, with an average age of 286 days. The sample consisted of 29 infants from the United Kingdom and 18 infants from Singapore. All infants were developing typically, with the British infants coming from English-speaking households and the Singaporean infants coming from bilingual English-Chinese families.
During the experiment, infants sat facing a monitor that displayed pre-recorded video clips of a female speaker reciting three different artificial languages. Each artificial language was constructed from four three-syllable words, like “pe-tu-do” or “di-lo-ga,” spoken continuously at a steady pace without pauses or emotional inflections. In these sequences, syllables within a word always occurred together, while syllables crossing between words occurred together only a third of the time, mimicking how real speech contains statistical patterns that help infants identify word boundaries.
To isolate the impact of eye contact, the speaker wore glasses with polarizing lenses, paired with an adjustable polarizing filter on the camera, while looking straight ahead. In the full gaze condition, the glasses appeared transparent, leaving her eyes entirely visible. In the partial gaze condition, the lenses were darkened like sunglasses, and in the no gaze condition, the lenses were made completely opaque. Adjusting only the filter on the camera allowed the researchers to manipulate how visible her eyes were while her own view remained unobstructed, so her delivery would not differ between conditions.
Each experimental block included a familiarization phase and a testing phase for each gaze condition. During familiarization, babies watched the speaker recite an artificial language for 60 seconds while their visual attention and brain activity were recorded using electroencephalography, a non-invasive technique that detects electrical signals through sensors on the scalp. During the testing phase, the infants heard either valid words from the language or artificial nonwords made by joining syllables that crossed word boundaries. The researchers measured how long babies looked at the screen, relying on the tendency of infants to look longer at less familiar sounds when they have recognized the underlying patterns.
The behavioral results showed that infants learned selectively depending on the speaker’s gaze. Infants showed evidence of learning only for the language paired with the full gaze condition, looking an average of 1.22 seconds longer at nonwords than at words, a small to moderate effect. In contrast, learning was not statistically significant for the languages accompanied by partial gaze, where the difference was 0.76 seconds, or no gaze, where the difference was 0.34 seconds.
“We let the infants listen to all three languages and it turned out they were selective in what they learned,” Leong said in a news release from the University of Cambridge. “They’re not just passive sponges. They heard all three languages, but only learned the one, which was when they could see the speaker’s eyes.”
This learning preference did not stem from differences in general visual attention. Infants spent roughly equal amounts of time watching the speaker across all conditions, averaging about 23 seconds in the full gaze condition, 21 seconds in the partial gaze condition, and 23 seconds in the no gaze condition. In addition, statistical analysis showed that the link between total looking time and learning was not statistically significant.
Kaili Clackson, a study co-author from the University of Cambridge, described the gap between looking and learning this way. “Even when the infants seemed to be staring at a screen attentively, unless there was eye contact, nothing was going in – the information washed over them,” Clackson said in the release. “The brain synchrony shows that it’s a selection process.” She added, “These cues are really powerful because when you preface new information with them, they tell the baby: this is important, you need to listen.”
When comparing the two geographic groups, Singaporean infants watched the speaker on screen longer than British infants did, which the authors suggested might reflect an interest in a speaker with unfamiliar Western facial features. However, learning performance itself did not differ significantly between the Singaporean and British infants. Both groups responded similarly to the presence or absence of the speaker’s gaze.
Leong noted that this pattern sheds light on early cognitive development across backgrounds. “This suggests that although there are already cultural differences in what we pay attention to or find novel from 9 months of age, the brain’s learning mechanisms set infants up to learn in a fundamentally similar way across cultures,” she told PsyPost.
To examine brain connections, the authors focused on alpha rhythms, a type of brainwave that in infants cycles about 6 to 9 times per second, using data from the 42 infants whose recordings were usable. Because the speaker’s brain activity had been recorded while she filmed the videos, the researchers could test whether patterns in her brain activity predicted later patterns in the infants’ brains as they watched.
This adult-to-infant coupling predicted learning better than chance, explaining about 25 percent of the variation in learning compared with about 20 percent for models built on shuffled data. The infants’ own internal brain connectivity did not predict learning, but it was linked to their scores on a parent-reported checklist of early communicative gestures, explaining about 34 percent of the variation compared with about 22 percent for shuffled data.
The team also evaluated neural entrainment, which is the tendency of a listener’s brainwaves to track the rising and falling loudness of speech. Full gaze strengthened this tracking at a few recording sites, but entrainment did not predict learning. A statistical mediation analysis suggested that adult-to-infant coupling may link the speaker’s eye contact to infant learning: coupling was stronger with full gaze than with no gaze, though not reliably different from partial gaze, and stronger coupling went along with greater learning. The authors call this result preliminary, partly because the coupling measure was selected for how well it predicted learning.
“Eye contact helps the baby decide what is important to learn in a social context, acting as a ‘switch’ to synchronize their brainwaves with those of the speaker and facilitating learning,” Leong told PsyPost.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that eye contact promotes aligned brain activity between interacting individuals. However, that earlier study examined spontaneous synchrony between familiar adult pairs rather than adult-to-infant coupling during learning.
Beyond theoretical insights into early development, the authors noted practical takeaways for parents and caregivers. “As parents, we need to be conscious of the need to use social cues like eye contact and calling your child’s name, as these cues don’t just focus your child’s attention, they activate the learning process,” Leong said in the release.
“If you’re on your phone and distracted when you’re trying to give them instructions or teach them something, there’s less of a likelihood that they’ll take it seriously or learn compared to if you put your phone down and look them in the eye,” Leong added in the release. “This is an important way of signaling your intentionality, your seriousness, that you want them to pay attention and learn something.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study involved a modest sample size of 47 infants for behavioral testing and 42 for brain recordings, meaning subtle effects in the partial gaze condition might be detected more reliably in larger groups. Additionally, the infants watched pre-recorded videos rather than interacting with a live adult, and the study did not test everyday interactions or phone use directly. Notably, infants in this study succeeded in learning statistical word patterns from video, in contrast to the 2003 findings where infants required live interaction to distinguish non-native speech sounds.
There are a few other things to keep in mind regarding the findings and measurements. The authors noted that eye contact may play a different role in communities where adult-infant interaction relies more heavily on touch and physical closeness, as observed in some Arab cultures. Methodologically, the researchers analyzed brainwaves within a single shared frequency band of 6 to 9 Hertz to meet computational requirements, even though adult alpha waves typically peak higher. Finally, while the statistical models highlight an association, experimental manipulations would be needed to establish whether neural coupling directly causes learning gains.
The study, “Adult-to-infant unidirectional neural coupling mediates selective social learning in infants from the United Kingdom and Singapore,” was authored by Wei Zhang, Kaili Clackson, Stanimira Georgieva, Lorena Santamaria, Vanessa Reindl, Valdas Noreika, Nicholas Darby, Vaka Valsdóttir, Priyadharshini Santhanakrishnan, and Victoria Leong.

Italy approves Meloni's electoral reform in confidence vote ahead of 2027 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:00:36 UTC
23:00:36 KST

The Chamber of Deputies has passed electoral law reform by 227 votes to 164, despite possible Constitutional Court objections. Italy now formally enters the election campaign, with an early vote increasingly likely.
Italy's Chamber of Deputies approved a new electoral law on Thursday, clearing the way for its use in the next general election, due in 2027.
The legislation, backed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government and formally known as the Stabilicum, - dubbed the Melonellum by opposition parties, - passed by 227 votes to 164 in a secret ballot.
The vote effectively marks the unofficial start of the election campaign. While the current legislature runs until September 2027, speculation about an early election is already circulating in the corridors of parliament, though as we explain below, a vote before 14 April remains unlikely.
The immediate political battle now shifts to alliances. Meloni has so far ruled out joining forces with National Future, the party of MEP Roberto Vannacci, while the opposition has yet to agree on a common leader. Significant divisions remain within the centre-left, particularly over the war in Ukraine, where Democratic Party secretary Elly Schlein and Five Star Movement leader Giuseppe Conte remain at odds.
Meloni moved quickly to claim the vote as a show of unity.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right split, today we answer with facts: we are united, solid and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens," she wrote on social media.
During the sitting, opposition MPs protested, brandishing placards reading: "Rigged law", "No to the fix" and "With Meloni diesel at 3 euros".
"Seats first. That is your slogan. We will vote firmly against this electoral law, which has been designed not for voters but to protect those already elected. With our progressive alliance we will be able to win under any electoral law and change Italians’ lives," said Elly Schlein in her explanation of vote.
Five Star Movement leader Conte also used exceptionally harsh words, arguing that the law has been written to ensure victory for the current ruling coalition.
He concluded: "There is only one further detail missing to guarantee your future control of Parliament: specifying that the majority bonus goes to a prime minister with light-coloured eyes".
How the new Italian electoral law was approved
The governing majority held firm in the secret ballot. This was the third parliamentary reading, after the amendments passed by the Senate, which introduced preference voting with blocked list leaders and increased the number of signatures required from parties not represented in Parliament in order to stand in elections.
On Wednesday the Chamber had approved the third confidence motion tabled by the government on the first three articles of the law. Thursday saw the final, most delicate, vote. If this last vote had gone against the government, the text would have been rejected, but the cabinet would not formally have been obliged to resign.
The most significant changes are contained in the first two articles, which were approved through a confidence vote. They introduce preference voting alongside blocked list leaders and set out the rules for electing both the Chamber and the Senate under the new system.
The signature threshold for parties without parliamentary representation has also been raised, from 1,500 to 6,000, and the rules on gender representation have been amended.
A third article addresses single-member constituencies in the province of Bolzano, while article 8 introduces one of the most anticipated changes: the right to vote for people living away from their registered place of residence.
The confidence vote is a mechanism that allows governments to fast-track legislation and limit debate and filibustering by the opposition. Under this procedure, MPs vote on the government's text as presented, without the ability to propose amendments.
The government stakes its survival on the outcome, if the Chamber votes it down, the administration automatically falls.
The issue of first-term MPs’ pensions
Faced with the threat of a government crisis, it was widely expected that most MPs would back the reform.
There is one date that Italian political scientists are all trying to pinpoint precisely: the moment when the current legislature reaches 4 years, 6 months and one day of its total five-year term.
On that date, first-term MPs become entitled to a parliamentary pension (around 1,500 euros, payable only from the age of 65).
For the current government, that threshold falls on 14 April 2027, and Italian political history shows that it is very unlikely that an election will be called before then.
There is nonetheless concern that the Constitutional Court could overturn the reform, which would complicate the government's plans and expose the right to fierce criticism during the campaign.
The opposition has identified three potentially unconstitutional elements: the majority bonus in the Senate, the requirement for parties without an established ballot logo to gather 300,000 signatures, and the absence of any requirement that at least 40 percent of lead candidates be women.
According to critics, the law potentially leaves Italy in political deadlock.

1 dead in Poland’s second school knife attack in 2 days, amid ‘copycat’ fears
Two others were injured in the incident at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw, officials say
A 15-year-old former pupil killed one employee and injured two others at a Polish primary school on Thursday wearing a helmet-mounted camera, the second school stabbing in two days, possibly in response to an internet challenge, authorities said.
A 37-year-old woman who worked as a caretaker had died in the latest attack, which took place at around 9am local time in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw, officials said.
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old wounded 10 people including himself at another school in Ostroleka, northeastern Poland, and police detained a 17-year-old in Sierpc in north-central Poland on suspicion of planning an attack.
“We fear a grim copycat phenomenon,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk told an emergency meeting.
“We are facing an extraordinary situation … for the first time, we are dealing with a killer who wore a helmet-mounted camera, intending to film the knife attack.” It was not clear whether the attack was actually filmed.

Turkmenistan celebrated 35 years of independence with a vast parade through Ashgabat, as the country set out its ambitions for the decades ahead.
Turkmenistan has marked 35 years of independence with parades across Ashgabat, joined by international partners including the United Nations.
Permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN General Assembly in 1995, remains the cornerstone of its foreign policy and has shaped its economy, with growth above 6% and public debt below 2%. Gas is the backbone, led by the vast Galkynyş field, while ports, motorways and education are expanding.
Celebrations also honour the ancient Akhal-Teke horse breed, as the country pairs pride in its heritage with ambitions for the next 35 years.

Rally Estonia put on WRC calendar also for next season
FIA and the WRC promoter unveiled the calendar for next season's World Rally Championship on Thursday, with Rally Estonia also included. The event will take place on the roads of southern Estonia from July 22-25.
In August this year, the FIA World Rally Championship's promoter changed hands, with French automotive technology company Cosmobilis and private equity investor Park Square Capital acquiring WRC Promoter GmbH. The new owners aim to make the championship and its individual rounds even more attractive, turning each rally into a major event offering a wide range of entertainment alongside exciting racing.
The championship's new CEO, Eric Boullier, also visited Delfi Rally Estonia this summer and was highly impressed by what he saw. He praised the high standard of organization and the organizers' ambition and ability to combine world-class rallying with a comprehensive sports and entertainment experience.
Following this year's rally, the Rally Estonia team held several further meetings with representatives of the promoter. These discussions resulted in an agreement for Rally Estonia to remain a round of the World Rally Championship in 2027.
"Rally Estonia's continued inclusion in the WRC calendar is a major recognition of everyone who has contributed to the event's success. A big thank you to the Estonian state, local governments, private sector sponsors and the entire organizing team and of course to local residents, rally fans, drivers and teams," rally director Urmo Aava said.
"WRC Delfi Rally Estonia is much more than four days of top-level racing. It is a major international event that boosts Estonia's economy, supports regional development, generates tax revenue for the state and provides memorable experiences for tens of thousands of spectators along the stages and hundreds of millions of viewers across various platforms. The desire of foreign visitors to return to Estonia and recommend us to their friends creates value long after the rally weekend has ended," Minister of Culture Heidy Purga added.
WRC Rally Estonia will be the ninth round of the 2027 FIA World Rally Championship, taking place from July 22–25. The 2027 WRC calendar will feature a total of 15 rounds.
The WRC is set to become even more global in the coming years, with the United States also hosting a championship round in 2027. The series will also enter a new era with the introduction of new Rally1 cars and technical regulations. Several new private teams are expected to join the championship, while Ford recently announced that it would return as a factory team after a decades-long absence. These developments promise to make the championship even more exciting and competitive.
Of the 43,894 unique spectators who attended this year's WRC Delfi Rally Estonia, foreign visitors accounted for 31.9 percent or 14,002 people. According to a study, the event generated an estimated €44.9 million in additional revenue for Estonian businesses, up 36 percent from 2025. Direct tax revenue associated with this turnover was estimated at €8.3 million.

Greece agrees up to $4 billion US arms deal, sources say
ATHENS, Oct 8 - Greece has agreed to spend up to $4 billion upgrading more of its F-16 fighter jets and buying advanced missiles from the US, two senior sources told Reuters on Thursday, a day after a visit by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Greece had already planned to spend about €28 billion by 2036 to buy US made F-35 fighter jets and helicopters, and to build the "Achilles Shield" a multi-layer anti-ballistic and anti-aircraft system with Israeli-made weapons.
"The agreement includes new advanced missiles and bombs for the F-16 Viper the F-35 fighter jets, and the Black Hawk helicopters. Also the upgrade of old F-16 fighter jets to Viper version," a senior defence Ministry official told Reuters.
The official added that most of the procurements have been included in the government's multi year defence plan and will not put additional pressure to the country's financials.
A senior foreign ministry official confirmed the above, adding that the cost will be spread over several years.
Rubio said on Wednesday in Athens that the two NATO allies had agreed on a joint security plan for counterterrorism information sharing between their law enforcement agencies.
Greece agreed to buy 20 Lockheed Martin F-35 fighter jets and 35 Sikorsky UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters in 2024. Is upgrading about 82 F-16s to Viper version and wants to upgrade 37 more Block 50s to Vipers at a cost of about $1 billion.
The move is part of Greece's bid to modernise its armed forces as it emerges from the 2009-18 debt crisis that led to years of austerity.
Greece spends nearly 3.5% of its gross domestic product on defence, a higher proportion than many other NATO countries, due to its long-standing dispute with Turkey. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Senior advisor to Mike Huckabee blocked and altered reports critical of Israel, investigation finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:57:48 UTC
22:57:48 KST

David Milstein, a senior adviser to U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, repeatedly blocked or substantially altered reports critical of Israel in an effort to present Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in a more favorable light to the administration in Washington, a New York Times investigation published Thursday alleges.
For the investigation, Times reporters interviewed 15 current U.S. officials who had worked with Milstein in some capacity, as well as nine former diplomats who helped provide background. The newspaper also obtained or reviewed dozens of documents, cables, memos and other internal communications that it said showed Milstein’s involvement in changing embassy reporting.
Most of those who spoke to the Times said they did so out of concern that Milstein’s actions were undermining standard diplomatic work. Some also expressed concern that, in certain cases, his actions contradicted President Donald Trump’s stated policies.
One example cited in the investigation took place in late March, at the height of the war with Iran, when Israel quietly approved more West Bank settlements at once than ever before. A sharply worded, urgent report on the move never reached the U.S. administration. According to three U.S. officials, Milstein blocked it.
A similar case occurred in April, when senior IDF officials warned that settler violence in the West Bank could ignite a new Palestinian uprising. Embassy personnel tried to relay those warnings to Washington, but Milstein prevented the reports from being sent in their original form, according to three officials.
Instead, Milstein praised Netanyahu’s “new and unprecedented initiatives” to combat violence in the West Bank. The report was titled: “Government Acts Forcefully Against Escalating Violence in the West Bank.”
Another case involved members of Congress who requested information about the deaths of nine Palestinian Americans in the West Bank over the past four years. According to multiple officials, Milstein blocked a detailed report prepared by embassy staff, effectively thwarting lawmakers’ efforts to obtain the information.
The main findings in the blocked report showed that in most cases the investigations had made very little progress, that some files had been closed and that no one had been prosecuted over the deaths, according to those officials. Instead of sending the report, Milstein argued that the embassy should send a letter stating that Israel was handling the investigations properly.
Officials who spoke with the Times said that, shortly after returning to the embassy in Jerusalem at the start of Trump’s second term in the White House, Milstein began insisting on approving outgoing correspondence from the embassy section dealing with Palestinian affairs.
The volume of reporting fell from several reports a week to only a handful a month, because some staff members stopped writing reports out of fear that Milstein would block or rewrite them, those officials said.
According to several officials, Milstein’s interventions went far beyond those of any of his predecessors. They and others said they were speaking out because they feared officials in Washington were receiving a distorted picture of Israeli actions through key diplomatic channels.
Milstein’s efforts, they said, helped shield the Netanyahu government from potentially harsher responses by the Trump administration.
The Times noted that it is unclear to what extent Huckabee was aware of Milstein’s actions. Both Huckabee and Milstein declined the newspaper’s requests for interviews. Huckabee is required to approve most major reports and decisions made by Milstein, but officials said the adviser sometimes acted on his own.
According to those officials, Huckabee at times worked with Milstein to withhold information or present it differently to the administration. In other instances, however, he believed Milstein had gone too far and stopped him.
Milstein’s efforts to influence embassy reporting were first exposed about a year ago by the online magazine of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a Washington think tank that advocates reduced tensions and greater restraint in U.S. military policy.
The Times investigation, however, presented documented evidence and previously unreported cases in which Milstein allegedly sought to tilt information in favor of the Netanyahu government. The documented activity, the report said, continued throughout the past year.
Those who spoke with the Times included career government officials and political appointees, including strong supporters of the U.S.-Israel relationship.
Concern over Milstein’s conduct also spread to senior administration officials in Washington, including in the White House, who expressed frustration to colleagues over some of his actions, according to four people.
It remains unclear whether or how Milstein’s interventions affected White House policy toward Israel. Since Trump declared a year ago that he would not allow Israel to annex the West Bank, he has rarely spoken publicly on the issue.
In response to questions sent to the embassy about Milstein’s actions, Huckabee did not address the specific cases described in the investigation.
“The events in the investigation are so incomplete, in fact, that they are consistent with other ridiculous efforts by the Times. I personally and categorically reject the allegations presented in the investigation,” he said.
The U.S. State Department said: “The entire State Department team remains focused on advancing President Trump’s America First agenda.”
Who is David Milstein?
Milstein is a familiar figure in right-wing circles in the United States and Israel, and has repeatedly arranged meetings between Huckabee and senior Israeli officials. Still, he is not especially well known in either country, and his role as a gatekeeper for information flowing to Washington had received relatively little attention until now.
His stepfather is right-wing radio host Mark Levin, a close ally of Trump. Netanyahu has also appeared on Levin’s program several times in recent years. The connection among the three is well known in Washington and at the embassy, officials in Jerusalem and Washington told the Times.
Milstein identifies as a conservative and longtime Republican. He previously served as an aide to pro-Israel Texas Sen. Ted Cruz from 2013 to 2018, before moving to Israel to study at a Jerusalem yeshiva. In 2020, he took a job as an aide to then-U.S. Ambassador David Friedman.
As an adviser to Huckabee, Milstein is now one of the most senior officials at the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem. According to the Times, he functions as a kind of chief of staff for the ambassador.
Huckabee has authorized him to oversee much of the mission’s portfolio, particularly developments in the West Bank and Gaza. His responsibilities include reviewing and editing information sent to Washington, including the reports he allegedly softened in Israel’s favor.
Officials with professional familiarity with Milstein said he goes to unusual lengths to portray Israel positively. They said he has blocked critical reporting, rewritten reports to convey a different — sometimes opposite — message from the original, and delayed approving drafts until the issue was no longer relevant.
One prominent case cited in the investigation occurred in the summer of 2025, when dozens of Palestinians arrived at a food distribution point in Gaza run by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, or GHF, which was backed by Jerusalem and Washington.
U.S. diplomats drafted a report for the Trump administration warning that the foundation’s distribution process was chaotic and deadly, and cautioning about additional “mass casualty incidents.”
According to officials who saw the original report, Milstein rewrote it to declare the GHF operation a success, while omitting the mass casualties.
The discrepancy did not go unnoticed at the White House, which saw a striking gap between news reports and embassy reporting. As a result, White House and State Department officials sought a clearer picture of events and, on at least two occasions, contacted embassy staff directly to obtain a more reliable account.
Former U.S. diplomats who spoke with the New York Times said distorting information sent to Washington should raise serious concerns.
“The embassy should tell Washington everything — the good, the bad and the ugly,” said Dan Kurtzer, who served as U.S. ambassador to Israel under President George W. Bush.

2026-10-08
16:57:36 EEST
22:57:36 KST

A Russian air strike on two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people and injured 18 on Thursday, 8 October, Ukrainian authorities said. On the same day, a drone attack disrupted operations at Russia's largest Yandex data centre in the Ryazan region.
The attack in Kramatorsk struck a street near a public transport stop at around 10am, setting buses on fire and leaving bodies and debris scattered across the road, according to Ukrainian police and emergency services.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service confirmed 33 deaths and 18 injuries, while Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin later reported that the number of injured had risen to 19. Authorities suspended public transport in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk following the bombing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of deliberately attacking civilians and said doctors were treating victims whose conditions remained critical.
"This strike will not go without our response. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this," Zelenskyy said in a statement on telegram.
Filashkin also accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting buses carrying passengers, saying the attack demonstrated Moscow's disregard for civilian lives.
The bombing struck Kramatorsk, one of the last two major cities in northern Donetsk under Ukrainian control. Together with Sloviansk, the city forms part of Ukraine's defensive positions against Russian forces seeking control of the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in the region.
The attack followed a Russian strike on an apartment building in Pryluky, northern Ukraine, on Wednesday, which killed at least 22 people, including five children.
Separately, Russian drone strikes on Kyiv killed three people and injured 14 on Thursday, according to the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
Ukraine's air force said Russia had launched 142 Shahed-type drones overnight, including 82 jet-powered variants. Ukrainian air defences reported intercepting or suppressing 126 of them.
Meanwhile, a drone attack struck a data centre belonging to Russian technology company Yandex in Sasovo, southeast of Moscow.
According to reports, the attack caused a fire and forced Yandex to suspend operations at the facility.
Yandex confirmed disruptions to its cloud infrastructure and reported power supply problems affecting one of its availability zones.
Open-source intelligence groups Exilenova+ and ASTRA identified the affected facility as Yandex's Sasovo data centre.
The facility houses tens of thousands of servers supporting Yandex's internet services and cloud computing operations.
Yandex initially acknowledged an infrastructure incident without identifying its cause. Russian regional authorities and Ukraine's military had not publicly commented on responsibility for the strike.
The Sasovo facility stands within the industrial complex of machine-tool manufacturer Sasta, which produces equipment used in Russian manufacturing, including the defence, aerospace and energy industries.
Britain placed Sasta under sanctions in 2024 over its involvement in Russia's defence sector. Western restrictions on exports of advanced electronics to Russia would complicate the replacement of equipment damaged in the attack.
Open-source monitoring groups reported disruptions to some Yandex services, although public outage trackers showed no evidence of widespread failures across the company's main consumer platforms.

South Africa pushes for local medicine production
South Africa is stepping up efforts to manufacture medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients locally to reduce reliance on imports and strengthen its ability to secure critical medical supplies during future health emergencies, the government has said.
President Cyril Ramaphosa, accompanied by Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Professor Blade Nzimande and Health Minister Dr Aaron Motsoaledi, toured the FuturePharma facility at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in Pretoria. The facility is expected to strengthen South Africa’s pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities by helping researchers move technologies from laboratories towards large-scale production and commercialisation.
”The facility will also support local API and medicine production, helping to reduce dependence on imports and strengthen security of supply,” the Government Communication and Information System (GCIS) said.
The move towards greater domestic production is aimed at giving South Africa stronger control over the availability of essential medicines while building local pharmaceutical capacity.
According to GCIS, one of the major objectives of the facility is to close the gap between scientific discoveries and medicines or pharmaceutical technologies that can be produced commercially. ”It will provide researchers, innovators and industry partners with access to specialised infrastructure and expertise to advance technologies towards manufacturing, while supporting technology transfer and skills development,” GCIS added.
This means pharmaceutical innovations developed by researchers could receive the technical support and infrastructure required to move beyond experimental laboratory stages and towards manufacturing.
The facility is also expected to form part of South Africa’s preparations for future pandemics and other major public health emergencies. The Covid-19 pandemic highlighted the risks countries face when they are heavily dependent on international supply chains for medicines, vaccines and other critical health products.

Chinese parcel service Speedaf challenges Swiss Post
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:55:20 UTC
22:55:20 KST

Chinese parcel service Speedaf challenges Swiss Post
Chinese online retailers Temu and Shein are creating a flood of parcels into Switzerland. A Chinese logistics firm is looking to capitalise on this phenomenon.
Massive advertising and aggressive low prices: the Chinese online retailers Temu and Shein are already firmly established in Switzerland, and are rapidly taking market share away from local online shops.
Now a Chinese logistics firm is also making inroads into the Swiss market. Speedaf is currently setting up a parcel network here which, according to Swiss federal technology institute ETH expert Stephan Wagner, could quickly reach a significant scale.
More
Chinese retail platform Temu challenges consumers and retailers
This is because the planned sorting capacity of up to 50,000 parcels a day is substantial for a new entrant, says the professor of logistics. At full capacity, this would amount to around 15 million parcels a year.
Speedaf could also put pressure on the dominant logistics providers – Swiss Post and DPD – in terms of pricing. Wagner points out that little can be said about the pricing structures at present. However: “It may well be that parcel delivery becomes cheaper in the medium term.”
Furthermore, there is certainly room for another strong player in the growing parcel market. This is particularly true given the sharp rise in parcel imports from China. “And this is precisely the area Speedaf intends to focus on initially,” said Wagner.
Speedaf is currently building its own Swiss parcel network. Plans include a sorting centre covering around 4,000 square metres, capable of handling up to 50,000 parcels a day, plus regional distribution centres in Zurich, Bern and Lausanne.
Founded in 2019, the logistics company has been operating in Switzerland for a few months.
The company is already active in more than 30 countries and handles parcels from Shein, Temu and Aliexpress, amongst others.
The Chinese parcel giant ZTO Express is one of its founding shareholders.
According to Wagner, Chinese logistics firms are increasingly seeking to organise international transport themselves, right through to the last mile in Europe.
Should Speedaf establish itself firmly in Switzerland via international parcel delivery, the Chinese logistics firm could become a serious competitor for Swiss Post.
More
Swiss lawmakers demand curbs on Chinese online retailers
“If the network is stable and deliveries are reliable, Swiss mail-order companies and smaller firms could also switch to Speedaf,” Wagner said. “That would certainly pose a threat to Swiss Post.”
Switzerland’s small size an advantage
Furthermore, Switzerland’s compact geography is fundamentally an advantage when it comes to building a nationwide network, Wagner added. “With one distribution centre and a few depots, you can cover a lot of ground here quickly. In larger countries such as France, that’s not so easy.”
However, the costs are high. Wagner considers it sensible that Speedaf intends to rely on local delivery partners for the last mile. This enables market entry without first having to build up its own fleet of vehicles and a large number of delivery staff.

A traffic accident can be handled without the police or paperwork — how to use the European Accident Statement in Diia and whether your “driver’s license” will be taken away
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:55:11 EEST
22:55:11 KST

A traffic accident can be handled without the police or paperwork — how to use the European Accident Statement in Diia and whether your “driver’s license” will be taken away
Kyiv • UNN
The European Accident Statement in Diia is available when there are no injured parties and both drivers agree. After it is completed, licenses are not confiscated and no report is drawn up.
From now on, the full process of completing a European Accident Statement can be done directly in the Diia app — without traffic jams or paperwork. This was reported by Oleksii Biloshytskyi, Head of the Patrol Police Department, according to UNN.
According to Biloshytskyi, Diia will automatically fill in the required data from official registers, which will help complete the accident report faster and avoid errors during completion.
When you can complete a European Accident Statement in Diia:
- only two cars are involved in the accident, with no trailers, and both are at the scene of the collision;
- there are no injured or dead persons;
- no property other than the cars has been damaged;
- both participants have valid compulsory third-party motor liability insurance policies;
- the drivers are sober and are not under the influence of medications that may reduce attention or reaction speed;
- the participants have reached an agreement regarding the circumstances of the accident.
Important: if the other driver does not have the Diia app with verified documents, complete a paper European Accident Statement.
If you have not reached an agreement regarding the circumstances of the accident, call the police at 112 or 102.
Will your driver's licence be taken away after completing it?
No. You settle the situation with the insurance company without involving the police, so the driver's licence is not confiscated and no administrative report is drawn up.
How do you complete a European Accident Statement?
Diia → Services → For Drivers → European Accident Statement.
After both drivers sign via Diia.Signature, the data is sent to the Motor (Transport) Insurance Bureau of Ukraine and the insurance companies.

In attacks on Ukraine from the territory of Belarus, Russia likely used Belarusian Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks, as well as a network of repeater stations on Belarusian territory, to help provide stable signals to Russian Shahed-type drones used in mass attacks on Ukraine, two Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14, 2026.
The revelation came two days after Russia sent hundreds of drones, hugging Ukraine's northern border, in a rare a mass attack targeting regions in western Ukraine on Sept. 12.

Poland will change procedures for military aircraft and helicopters that engage objects entering from the direction of Russia, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Sept. 28, 2026.
Under the current peacetime procedure, Polish pilots must fly close enough to visually confirm a target in Polish airspace before firing at it.

Gold coins seized at Estonian-Russian border put up for auction
Nearly €400,000 worth of gold coins found hidden in a truck seat at Estonia's Luhamaa border checkpoint are now up for grabs after authorities put them up for auction.
The Estonian Tax and Customs Board (MTA) is auctioning 157 gold coins, valued at about €390,000, that were seized at the southeastern border crossing last year.

A criminal investigation was opened over an alleged attempted sanctions violation and to determine who owned the coins. After the owner could not be identified, a court ordered the coins forfeited to the state.
The coins are being auctioned in small lots through Osta.ee, a local online auction site similar to eBay. Bidding on the first eight coins runs through October 14.

FDA-approved epilepsy drug may help reverse osteoarthritis damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:52:56 UTC
22:52:56 KST

FDA-approved epilepsy drug may help reverse osteoarthritis damage
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- Yale School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Researchers at Yale have identified a promising new approach to osteoarthritis that could do more than simply ease pain. The epilepsy drug lacosamide appears to block a protein involved in both pain signaling and cartilage destruction, helping damaged joints shift back toward repair in preclinical studies.
- Share:
For millions of people with osteoarthritis, pain and stiffness can make everyday activities increasingly difficult. Common treatments, including over-the-counter medications and steroid injections, may reduce symptoms for a time, but they do not prevent the underlying joint damage from progressing.
New research from Yale suggests a different approach. In a study published in Bioactive Materials, scientists found that the medication lacosamide can serve two purposes in osteoarthritis, reducing joint pain while also reversing cartilage damage. The effects were particularly strong when the drug was delivered directly into the joint using a specialized hydrogel.
Why osteoarthritis damages cartilage
Osteoarthritis is often called a condition caused by wear and tear, but that description leaves out much of the biology involved.
Within a healthy joint, cells known as chondrocytes help maintain cartilage by continuously balancing the creation of new tissue with the removal of old material. Osteoarthritis disrupts that balance. Cartilage begins to break down faster than it can be replaced, eventually allowing bones to rub against one another. As the disease advances, some patients may ultimately require joint reconstruction procedures such as a total knee replacement.
"There is a major unmet need in osteoarthritis," says the study's principal investigator and Charles W. Ohse Professor of Orthopaedics & Rehabilitation, Chuan-Ju Liu, PhD. "We need therapies that don't just mask pain but actually change how the disease progresses."
At present, no medicine approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration can both stop osteoarthritis pain and prevent the structural breakdown of cartilage. The work led by Liu suggests that it may be possible to address both problems with a single therapeutic strategy.
The researchers repurposed an existing medication and paired it with an advanced gel designed to keep the drug inside the joint. The approach could potentially preserve joint tissue while delivering sustained pain relief without relying on addictive opioids.
A protein linked to pain and cartilage loss
The research focuses on Nav1.7, a protein that functions as a sodium channel. These channels act as microscopic gates in cell membranes and play an important role in electrical signaling.
Nav1.7 was long thought to operate primarily in specialized nerve cells that transmit pain signals to the brain. More recent work from Liu and his team, however, revealed that the protein is also highly active in chondrocytes, the cells responsible for maintaining cartilage.
Nav1.7 is relatively quiet in healthy joints. In osteoarthritis, however, its activity increases substantially. The researchers found that this heightened activity can intensify pain signaling while also pushing chondrocytes toward breaking down the cartilage they would normally help preserve.
That makes Nav1.7 an unusual therapeutic target because it appears to influence both the sensation of pain and the physical deterioration of joint tissue.
"When Nav1.7 becomes dysregulated, it contributes to both joint degeneration and pain," Liu says. "Our findings suggest that Nav1.7 is a dual-acting target. By blocking this single protein, we can potentially quiet the pain nerves and tell the cartilage cells to not only stop breaking down but start repairing as well."
Epilepsy drug shows potential for cartilage repair
Instead of creating an entirely new medication, Liu's team tested drugs that already inhibit sodium channels. Among them, lacosamide produced strong biological effects at considerably lower concentrations and offered a better safety profile than older drugs in the same class.
Lacosamide is already used as a treatment for epilepsy, but the researchers found that its effects on cartilage depended heavily on the dose.
More was not necessarily better. At an ideal low concentration, lacosamide encouraged cells to produce proteins involved in building cartilage while also suppressing processes that break tissue down. When the concentration was either too high or too low, those benefits began to fade.
"This tells us the system is finely tuned," Liu notes. "There is an optimal range where the drug helps restore balance without overcorrecting. What stood out was not just its effectiveness, but how little of a dose was needed."
Further investigation revealed that lacosamide also changes the way cells communicate. The drug stimulated the release of two beneficial signaling proteins, HSP70 and midkine.
HSP70 helps cells respond to stress and supports tissue repair, while midkine helps regulate inflammation and protect joint tissue from degeneration. Together, the proteins appear to create conditions that are more favorable for maintaining cartilage.
"These proteins create a supportive environment for cartilage maintenance," Liu explains. "They allow the effects of the drug to extend beyond individual cells and influence the entire tissue."
Smart hydrogel keeps the drug inside the joint
Oral treatment with lacosamide was effective in preclinical testing, but drugs taken by mouth circulate throughout the body, increasing the potential for unwanted effects elsewhere.
The researchers therefore investigated intra-articular injection, which allows the medication to be placed directly inside the affected joint.
There was still a significant problem to overcome. "The knee joint, which is also the most common location for osteoarthritis, naturally acts like a leaky bucket," Liu says. "The body's drainage system can clear out liquids injected into the knee within hours."
To keep the medication in place longer, the team created a specialized hydrogel made from Collagen II. The material responds to temperature. It remains liquid while inside a cool syringe, then becomes a firm, jelly-like material after reaching body temperature.
Once inside the joint, the gel acts as a storage site for lacosamide, keeping the medication concentrated in the affected area while gradually releasing it over several weeks.
"The hydrogel acts as a local reservoir," Liu says. "It holds the drug in place in the location it is needed most and releases it slowly over time. It transforms a daily pill into a long-lasting, local treatment that stays active for a month or longer."
In the same preclinical studies, one injection of the lacosamide-containing gel every four weeks prevented cartilage loss more effectively than taking an oral dose every day.
Existing drug could speed clinical testing
One important advantage of lacosamide is that the medication is already approved for use in people. That could make it possible to move toward clinical studies in osteoarthritis patients more quickly than would be possible with a completely new drug.
Lacosamide has also been tested in humans with certain nerve-related pain conditions caused by Nav1.7 mutations. Those results give the researchers greater confidence that the effects seen in laboratory studies could eventually translate into meaningful pain relief for patients.
The work also reflects a broader direction in medicine that combines drugs with advanced biomaterials to control exactly where and how treatments are delivered. If the approach proves successful in people, it could eventually reduce the number of procedures patients need, limit unwanted side effects, and provide longer-lasting protection against structural joint damage.
"We are not just developing a treatment," Liu concludes. "We are developing a system that allows the medicine to work more effectively where it matters most. Our goal is to move beyond symptom control and towards true disease modification. This effort brings us closer to that reality."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Yale School of Medicine. Original written by John Ready, MS. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chaopeng He, Guiwu Huang, Lida Moradi, Jingwei Bi, Xinyu Yang, Xin Liu, Xudong Cui, Arya Varthi, Daniel H. Wiznia, Stephen G. Waxman, Wenyu Fu, Chuan-Ju Liu. Collagen II hydrogel-mediated sustained delivery of lacosamide attenuates cartilage degeneration and pain in osteoarthritis. Bioactive Materials, 2026; 61: 640 DOI: 10.1016/j.bioactmat.2026.02.045

Canadian Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:51:46 UTC
22:51:46 KST

Canadian Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Swedish Academy praised the 76-year-old poet and essayist’s work for being ‘bold and inventive’.
Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, the award-giving body has announced.
Carson was selected “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy said in a statement on Thursday.
The 76-year-old, whose work is praised for blurring the lines of poetry and fiction, and for giving ancient works new translation, is also a professor of classics.
She has written more than 20 books, some of which have been adapted into plays, and has received numerous literary awards.
“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” the academy said.
“She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work. Her translations from Classical Greek may be regarded as independent works in their own right.”
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy, which awards the prize worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m), said Carson “was very taken by surprise”.
“We didn’t have so much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind.”
Shortly after the announcement, Carson reacted to her win to Icelandic broadcaster RUV. “Crazy. I think they’re all crazy … Well, you know, it’s crazy,” she said.
Carson, who was born in Toronto, also spends time in Iceland, where she also has citizenship.
One of her most notable works includes the Beauty of the Husband, a poignant and moving book-length narrative poem depicting a doomed marriage.
The Trojan Women, published in 2021, is a graphic retelling of Euripides’s ancient story, infused with modern vernacular.
In August 2024, she revealed in the London Review of Books that she was living with Parkinson’s disease.
The Nobel Prize, awarded by the Swedish Academy, is widely considered the most prestigious international award in literature.
Last year’s prize was won by Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai.
Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in literature, science and peace have been awarded since 1901.
Literature was the fourth of this year’s Nobels to be announced this week, following medicine, physics and chemistry. The peace winner will be announced in Oslo on Friday.

A top adviser to the US ambassador to Israel has systematically suppressed, delayed, and rewritten internal diplomatic cables to shield the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from scrutiny by Washington, The New York Times reported Thursday.
David Milstein, an influential gatekeeper at the US Embassy in Jerusalem since April 2025 and principal aide to US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, repeatedly stymied assessments intended for senior policymakers, according to an investigation based on interviews with more than a dozen US officials and reviews of internal State Department records.
In late March, Israel approved record-breaking occupation expansions across the occupied West Bank. Embassy personnel drafted an alert warning that the move risked violating US President Donald Trump's explicit red line against annexation. Milstein quashed the memorandum, framing the land acquisitions as a domestic matter before sending a revised text claiming the move addressed unspecified humanitarian needs of occupiers.
Milstein similarly altered reporting on surging violence in the occupied West Bank. When Israeli military commanders warned that attacks by occupiers could trigger a widespread Palestinian uprising, he blocked the dispatches suggesting that Israel failed to take action. Instead, an embassy cable authored under his name praised Netanyahu's initiatives and claimed authorities were actively combating the unrest.
The aide also suppressed a detailed embassy inquiry into the killings of nine Palestinian Americans by Israeli forces and occupiers, effectively thwarting accountability requests from members of the US Congress. Despite findings showing investigations stalled without criminal charges, the mission forwarded an alternative letter claiming active cooperation with Israeli authorities.
Milstein also edited dispatches regarding aid distribution by the US-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation to describe the operations as successful, removing diplomatic warnings that the process was "chaotic, deadly," and risked "mass casualty events."
Staff members noted that the interventions caused reporting from the embassy's Palestinian affairs section to drop from several weekly cables to a few per month and prompted some officials to bypass official embassy channels to obtain unfiltered ground intelligence.
"The elements of the story The New York Times is trying to assemble are so lacking in fact that it ranks up with other Times farcical endeavors," said Huckabee. The US State Department said its personnel remain focused on advancing the administration's foreign policy priorities.

Syria calls for independent probe into sinking of ship in Black Sea
Oct 8 - Syria called on the International Maritime Organization and Bulgarian authorities on Thursday to conduct an independent investigation into the sinking of a cargo ship in the Black Sea, whose 10 crew members including 9 Syrians were missing.
The investigation should look into why search and rescue operations stopped before the fate of the missing crew was determined, said Mazen Aloush, director for international relations of the Syrian General Authority for Ports and Customs.
Bulgaria said on Wednesday it had halted its search for the crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone about 70 nautical miles (130 km) off its coast. Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov said no trace of the sailors had been found and that the rescue operation would not resume.
The ship, the Alfa Watan, was attacked early on Tuesday in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Aloush said.
It remains unclear who carried out the attack.
Aloush added the authority was closely monitoring the incident and condemned the targeting of a civilian commercial vessel, saying it represented a serious violation of maritime safety and a direct threat to sailors' lives, as well as international trade routes.
He urged authorities to use all available technical means to locate and inspect the wreckage to help establish the cause of the incident, and said the case should not be closed before all available avenues had been exhausted to determine the crew's fate.
He also called on international organisations and maritime bodies to strengthen measures to protect commercial shipping and crews in the Black Sea amid growing risks to maritime transport in the region.
Russia has struck cargo ships in the Black Sea with drones and missiles during its war with Ukraine.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Wednesday that the nature of the cargo and the direction of travel of the ships could point to Russia, but said there was no evidence allowing Sofia to directly attribute responsibility.
Russia's embassy in Sofia said the merchant vessel was not among targets hit by Russian drones. REUTERS

Iran strikes tankers outside Hormuz in signs of expanding campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:49:25 UTC
22:49:25 KST

Two commercial vessels were hit within 24 hours — one off Qatar, the first attack in that area in six months, and one off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman — as IRGC-affiliated outlets suggested Tehran had extended operations beyond the crucial strait.
Iran's armed forces struck two commercial tankers outside the Strait of Hormuz within 24 hours this week, in what appeared to be a deliberate expansion of attacks beyond the strait, as Iranian officials issued a fresh wave of warnings against the United States.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said several projectiles hit the oil and chemical tanker Acers, flagged in Antigua and Barbuda, 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal in Qatar on Wednesday. Casualties were reported.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel and said it was heading toward the Strait of Hormuz.
It was the first attack in that area in more than six months.
In a separate incident on Thursday, Vanguard reported a fire on a tanker some 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, which it identified as likely the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalgout.
The UKMTO had not recorded the incident, and the cause of the fire was not immediately clear. NASA's FIRMS fire-detection system confirmed the blaze, and US military aircraft — including two KC-46 tankers, a KC-135, a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and several helicopters — were over the area at the time.
Iran and media affiliated with the IRGC did not officially claim responsibility for either attack. IRGC-affiliated outlets implicitly suggested that Tehran had "extended the scope of its operations against commercial vessels that violate Iranian laws and regulations in the Strait of Hormuz to waters beyond the strait."
Both incidents fall outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas shipments normally pass. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began in late February, after Iran and the US imposed concurrent naval blockades.
"The distance between you and us is determined by our missiles," Acting Defence Minister Majid Ebn ol-Reza posted on X on Thursday.
"Yesterday the Gulf of Oman, today the Indian Ocean and tomorrow the Bay of Pigs. If you make a mistake, you will see a new set of dividing lines.," ol-Reza added in an apparent reference to a failed, US-backed military landing on the southwestern coast of Cuba from April 1961 aimed at overthrowing the communist government of Fidel Castro.
Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior military adviser to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, had earlier warned that if the US or Israel attacked Iran again, Tehran could extend the war "as far as the Indian Ocean or other places," adding that Iranian forces had prepared contingency plans for worst-case scenarios.
Ebn ol-Reza was appointed acting minister after Aziz Nasirzadeh, Iran's then defence minister, was killed on 28 February — the first day of the war — alongside several other military commanders. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Mehrdad Akhlaqi as a permanent replacement, and parliament is due to hold a confidence vote on 18 October.
Iran's army spokesman said separately that its forces were ready to carry out pre-emptive operations, if necessary, to prevent what he described as "any aggression or attack by the enemy."
At a midterm election campaign rally in Nebraska, US President Donald Trump defended the decision to go to war with Iran. "This is a small price to pay for keeping the world and our country safe. They can destroy a city. Let them destroy it. Let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," he said.
At a separate rally in Texas on Wednesday night, Trump walked back those remarks after criticism. "We protect our own cities. We will not allow such a thing to happen," he said.
US President Donald Trump defended the launch of war against Iran at a midterm election campaign rally in Nebraska, stating that "this is a small price to pay for keeping the world and our country safe."
"They can destroy a city. Let them destroy it. Let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," Trump said.
However, in another speech in Texas on Wednesday night Trump responded to criticism of his controversial remarks two days earlier about a possible Iranian attack on Los Angeles and San Diego.
"We protect our own cities. We will not allow such a thing to happen," he said.

Estonian Spa Association: There may not be enough customers for all new spas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:49:00 UTC
22:49:00 KST

Estonian Spa Association: There may not be enough customers for all new spas
Several new spas are set to enter Estonia's market in the coming years, but Aire Toffer, CEO of the Estonian Spa Association, warns that there may not be enough solvent customers to fill both the new and existing facilities.
Toffer said that the completion of several new spas is planned for the end of next year and the beginning of 2028. In her view, an incorrect impression may have formed about the spa market, as if large amounts of money were circulating there.
"These perceptions have arisen from the fact that during school holidays and on Saturday evenings the prices in spas are very high," she explained. Toffer said these are isolated days when visitors have time to go to the spa, which makes it possible to charge higher prices.
She said that starting spa entrepreneurs may lack an understanding of what the cost side of spas looks like, such as electricity and water consumption. "It's worth looking at companies' financial reports — the accommodation sector is not a very profitable business," Toffer noted.
Still, she is optimistic that every product has a consumer if it is created in the right place and is distinctive and innovative. But at present, according to Toffer, Estonia does not have enough solvent customers to fill all spas.
Gross: if you do it well, there should be enough customers
Next year, a spa hotel will rise by Lake Viljandi, owned by Lääne‑Virumaa entrepreneur Oleg Gross. He said that if you do something, you must do it very well. "And if you do it very well, there should be enough customers," he added.
Gross noted that a spa must offer a premium‑class product. "Besides, life has shown that Estonians have started going to spas more," he said. Gross explained that although foreign tourism has decreased, Estonia's climate encourages Estonians to visit spas more. He stated that a spa hotel is not a profit project but rather an emotion project. "But that it would start running losses — I don't believe that," he said.
According to Gross, there is room on the spa market for one more spa. At the same time, he noted that many developers have built a hotel with a spa only with bank loans and have no other business. "But we have a parent company in food retail," he said.
Gross said that if the spa should run a slight loss in its early years, he does not plan to sell or close it, and the spa will be kept alive by force if necessary. "It will get going in any case, there is no doubt about that," he noted.
According to Toffer, whether every spa will have enough guests does not depend solely on Estonian visitors. "Many other things also play a role here — for example, how accessible Estonia is, whether we have flight connections, what will happen with airBaltic," she explained. Toffer stated that when designing a tourism service, foreign visitors are always considered as well.
Foreign visitors are also needed
"Certainly, we also need to do something at the national level to find visitors from other target markets outside Estonia who would come to Estonia because of the spas," she said. Toffer explained that this requires better marketing messages and promoting Estonia even more as a health‑oriented country.
While it is often visible how various companies close their doors because customers do not have the money to visit them, this is not seen much with spas. "Perhaps spa entrepreneurs have been more patient and have become accustomed to the fact that this is not a very profitable business," Toffer suggested.
She explained that in the current economy most entrepreneurs are trying to make ends meet, and if many more spas are added, it is not excluded that someone may have to close their doors.
"Entrepreneurs have a very high tax burden, and our VAT is unreasonably high compared to neighboring competitor countries," Toffer said. She added that if someone decides to end their activity in the current economic environment, they cannot be blamed for it.

French economists urge $140B deficit reduction, sweeping policy reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:48:42 UTC
22:48:42 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
France’s Council of Economic Analysis urged policymakers to reduce the public deficit by €125 billion ($140 billion) by 2032 and overhaul public policies, Le Monde reported Thursday.
All 23 members of the council, which advises the prime minister, signed its first collective note since 2014, warning that policies pursued over the past three decades had become unsustainable.
The economists identified population aging, deteriorating public finances, weak productivity growth and declining educational performance as major challenges, alongside rising poverty and wealth inequality.
They warned that higher interest rates could trigger an uncontrolled increase in public debt, forcing France to repair its finances urgently on terms it could no longer determine.
The council recommended achieving roughly half the proposed deficit reduction during the first two years to restore market confidence and stabilize debt within five years.
Drawing on previous reports, it outlined 150 possible measures, including freezes on central and local government spending, changes to pension indexation, higher taxes and reductions in business subsidies.
The options include restoring housing or wealth taxes and raising value-added and corporate taxes.
The economists also proposed scaling back research tax credits to limit windfall benefits for large companies.
They argued that the adjustment could not fall mainly on a small section of the population or depend on uncertain future growth.
Alongside fiscal consolidation, the council called for €4 billion in additional annual investment in schools, wider adoption of digital technologies and artificial intelligence, and a “France 2040” innovation program.
It also urged stronger climate adaptation measures and higher taxation of large inheritances to address inequalities linked to inherited wealth.
The appeal comes seven months before France’s 2027 presidential election.
