US retaliates after being labeled disinformation threat in EU – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:48:12 UTC
22:48:12 KST

US retaliates after being labeled disinformation threat in EU – media
Washington has reportedly pressured several governments to withdraw their support for a conference organized by an EU-funded “anti-disinfo” NGO that designated the US a potential source of foreign disinformation.
The event host is EU DisinfoLab, one of Brussels’ info-gatekeepers deployed to scapegoat and smear dissidents opposing the bloc’s political course. The NGO notoriously launched its career by labeling online critics of French President Emmanuel Macron as “Russophiles.”
Organizers of the #Disinfo2026 conference in Vilnius, Lithuania, reportedly classified the US as a “foreign information manipulation and interference” (FIMI) actor, according to two news outlets with insider sources in Brussels. The EU normally uses the term to describe alleged malicious online activities by geopolitical rivals such as Russia and China.
By the time the conference opened, the logos of the EU’s diplomatic service, the European External Action Service (EEAS), and the foreign ministries of Canada and Lithuania had disappeared from all material, leaving only the French Foreign Ministry and the Vilnius city administration.
Rapporteur, formerly known as Euractiv, attributed the changes to a pressure campaign initiated by American writer Michael Shellenberger, who withdrew as a speaker after learning that the US had been designated a FIMI actor.
Politico cited the US State Department and cables instructing American embassies to convey Washington’s objections.
“Labeling the United States a ‘FIMI threat’ – a term normally reserved for describing influence operations of adversaries – undermines shared goals and should alarm those involved,” officials told the outlet.
Experts in (spreading) disinformation
The Russiagate hoax, involving a concerted campaign by former US President Barack Obama and his secretary of state, Hillary Clinton, to falsely claim US President Donald Trump was somehow compromised by links to Russia, helped fuel the emergence of an industry of self-described experts in combating online disinformation and misinformation. Critics have accused such organizations of serving as proxies for government-backed censorship that authorities cannot impose directly.
Belgium-based EU DisinfoLab first attracted widespread attention in 2018, when it alleged Russian efforts to amplify a political scandal involving Macron’s security aide, Alexandre Benalla, who had been filmed assaulting protesters while wearing police equipment.
The NGO’s research identified alleged “Russian bots” and “French Russophile” Twitter accounts supposedly fueling public outrage over the affair. Critics questioned its methodology, prompting the organization to publish detailed information about the accounts it had studied, including those of opposition politicians Jean-Luc Melenchon and Marine Le Pen.
In 2022, the Belgian Data Protection Authority (APD) fined EU DisinfoLab €2,700 ($3,000) and its lead researcher, Nicolas Vanderbiest, €1,200 ($1,300), while formally reprimanding both. The regulator, which investigated the case in cooperation with France’s data protection authority, the CNIL, found that the researchers had unlawfully processed personal data revealing political opinions and exposed users to potential discrimination through political profiling.
The decision prompted French National Rally MEP Virginie Joron to question whether EU DisinfoLab should continue receiving funding from Brussels. Grants allocated by the European Commission to the NGO over the years have added up to at least €1.4 million ($1.6 million), according to financial disclosures.
It’s a small disinfo world
EU DisinfoLab’s leadership reflects the close ties between the Western “counter-disinformation” industry and government-backed infowarfare operations.
Board member Emma Le Mesurier is the widow and former colleague of James Le Mesurier, a former British Army officer who helped establish the White Helmets in Syria. The Western-funded group aided jihadist forces in overthrowing President Bashar Assad.
Fellow board member Andy Pryce is a veteran British diplomat who launched and led the Foreign Office’s program intended to thwart Russian strategic communications. His name also appeared in the “UK Cluster” of the Integrity Initiative, a British-funded media manipulation project exposed by the leak of its internal documents in 2018.
Former board member and researcher Camille Francois worked on an investigation into the 2016 “Russian interference” in the US on behalf of the Senate Intelligence Committee.
Laser-focused away from Western disinformation
The EU DisinfoLab annual conference program includes a yoga session and discussions of “identity-based disinformation” and “Russia’s global information war.” Cases of debunked Western disinformation, plentiful as they are, received little attention.
One example was the alleged Russian attempt to jam the navigation system of a plane carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over Bulgaria last year. The story unravelled when Bulgarian authorities said their monitoring systems had detected no GPS interference, contrary to statements by EU officials.
A similar case last month involved a claim that a Russian drone had nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, which Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store stated during a joint press conference. However, Moldovan authorities later clarified that Zelensky’s flight from Chisinau to Oslo had merely been briefly delayed by a drone alert. The drone in question crashed some 160 km from the airport.

'Leaves in the Wind': a song from a world where only sound remained  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:45:11 UTC
22:45:11 KST

On Monday 12 October, Justinas Stanislovaitis releases a song and music video from his mu‐ sic-theatre performance “Where the Sound Remained” – on what a person is worth once the applause has stopped
Vilnius – On Monday 12 October 2026, the Lithuanian singer-songwriter Justinas Stanislovaitis offi‐ cially releases the song and music video “Leaves in the Wind” (in Lithuanian, “Vėjo Blaškomi”). The song comes from his music-theatre performance “Where the Sound Remained” (“Kur liko garsas”), a post-apocalyptic story about a man who, at the end of the world, must finally face the question he has spent his whole life avoiding.
The performance is set in an imagined apocalyptic landscape. The cities are empty, the power has failed, and people fight to survive – for warmth, for food, for somewhere safe to pass the night. In such a world everything must justify its weight: what to carry, what to leave behind. And yet one musician sets out with the bare essentials – and a guitar.
That small gesture becomes the question at the heart of the piece. What is a song for when the only task left is to stay alive? What remains of a musician with no stage and no audience? “Am I worth any‐ thing if no one is listening? Am I valuable without approval?” The questions echo through an aban‐ doned concert hall where people once rose from their seats to applaud – and where now there are only empty chairs, darkness and the low flicker of a fire.
“Where the Sound Remained” explores the origin, essence and meaning of the human need for recog‐ nition: where the longing to be seen comes from, what recognition truly is, and what it means. Is our worth measured in applause, ratings and the gaze of others – or was it given to us before the first per‐ formance ever began? It is not a question reserved for those on stage. In one form or another, almost everyone asks it today, whatever their work – teacher or doctor, programmer or builder: am I of any value when no one notices what I do?
“Leaves in the Wind” is one of six original songs in the performance, each arriving at the point where words are no longer enough. Its chorus sounds almost like an answer the singer offers himself:
Maybe we’re just leaves in the wind,
Dreaming where the blue skies begin.
Still we rise while we can,
Leaving our light where we land.
The music video opens onto a cinematic world of muted, earthy colours: a journey across open country, fire and wind, and translucent memories drifting through the frame – the things that stay with a per‐ son even when everything around them has fallen apart.
The song is released in both English and Lithuanian. It is also the way into Stanislovaitis’s chamber concert programme “Between Silence and Light”, in which his original songs stand alongside his own interpretations of songs by Leonard Cohen, Sting, Nick Cave and Peter Gabriel. On stage: Justinas Stanislovaitis (voice, acoustic guitar) and Martynas Vaičekauskas (accordion, keys and lumzdelis, the traditional Lithuanian wooden flute). Concerts are planned in Riga, Gdańsk, Toruń and Vilnius – dates and venues are to be announced shortly at justinasstanislovaitis.lt.

Syria Demands Answers Over Sunken Ship off Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:44:57 UTC
22:44:57 KST

Syria has asked Bulgarian authorities and the International Maritime Organization to conduct an independent investigation into the sinking of the ALFA WATAN, according to Syrian General Directorate of Borders and Customs representative Mazen Alloush, while the wreck lies at a depth beyond the current underwater inspection capabilities cited.
Alloush told Agence France-Presse that Damascus wants an investigation to establish what happened to the vessel and determine why the search and rescue operation was stopped.
“The crew consisted of ten sailors, nine Syrians and one Egyptian, whose fate remains unknown,” Alloush said.
Nine Syrian sailors are still missing after the ALFA WATAN sank, Alloush announced, as cited by BTA. The Syrian Seafarers’ Union said contact with the crew had been lost and that no survivors had been found.
Syria has also asked Bulgarian authorities to disclose the reasons for ending the search and rescue operation within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
According to data published by Maritime.bg, the damaged ALFA WATAN lies at an estimated depth of around 2,000 meters. The Bulgarian government has said an underwater examination of the wreck could potentially be carried out with assistance from partners including the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) and NATO, the specialized media outlet reported.
EMSA currently has the capacity to conduct underwater inspections at depths of about 1,500 meters with remotely operated underwater vehicles, an agency source told Maritime.bg.
It remains unclear whether the other vessel involved in the incident, the ABLE, has sunk or is still drifting, Maritime.bg reported. No merchant vessels traveling through the area have reported receiving information about the ship.
Maritime.bg said the multi-purpose frigate Verni is sailing toward the area where the two merchant vessels were struck to survey the site.
The European Commission is providing Bulgaria and Romania with satellite data concerning the attacks in the Black Sea. EMSA has also indicated that it is ready to examine recovered debris free of charge.
The Syrian authorities’ request comes after the search for the crew of the ALFA WATAN was called off.
Syrian citizens have posted photographs and messages on social media mourning relatives they believe died at sea. Among them is Walaa Melhem, who said her brother Tarek was among those lost, while Yasmin Merei shared a photograph of her 26-year-old nephew Raed, who worked as a cook aboard the sunken vessel.
The Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS) has said Bulgaria should pursue joint action with Romania and Turkey over security in the Black Sea.

Latvijas Banka is issuing a symbolic collector coin 'Chestnut'  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:44:44 UTC
22:44:44 KST

On Thursday, 8 October, Latvijas Banka will issue "Chestnut", a silver collector coin with gilded details, symbolically depicting one of the heralds of autumn. The coin gives a new expression to a work by the artist who won Latvijas Banka's open design competition on the theme of nature last year.
Chestnut trees were first introduced to Latvia around the turn of the 17th–18th centuries and were found mainly in the parks of manors. One of the great chestnut trees served as the inspiration for the prose masterpiece Straumēni by Edvarts Virza. Beneath the branches of the chestnut tree, the household and their guests are depicted celebrating or resting after a day's work. In the early 20th century, the renowned Latvian landscape painter Vilhelms Purvītis immortalised a grove of these trees in his painting Blooming Chestnut Trees. A small number of sweet chestnut trees (Castanea sativa) also grow in Latvia, mainly in Kurzeme.
Figurines fashioned from chestnut fruits have become favourite playthings for children, and chestnuts are also believed to have healing properties. Carrying a chestnut in one's pocket is believed to protect against misfortune. For women, good fortune has traditionally been associated with a chestnut in the left pocket; for men, in the right.
The chestnut coin is like a talisman, embodying all the positive qualities of the tree and its fruit. In Latvian, the word for chestnut tree is used in both the masculine (kastanis) and feminine (kastaņa) grammatical gender. This means that the tree, and now the coin, belongs to everyone. Yet the reasons for carrying it in one's pocket remain individual.
The collector coin "Chestnut" was designed by artist Kaspars Līdums, who entered and won the 2025 design competition on the theme of nature with his design proposal.
The collector coin will be available for purchase only on the website e-monetas.lv/en from 12:00 (noon) on 8 October. The price of the coin is EUR 147.00; the purchase limit for one buyer will be 3 coins. The mintage of the coin is 3000. The coin has been struck by UAB Lietuvos monetų kalykla in Lithuania.
CHESTNUT
Face value: 5 euro
Weight: 23.00 g
Shape: irregular; the longest distance between the edges of the coin, measured through its centre – 35.00 mm
Metal: silver of .999 fineness; with gilding
Quality: proof
Maximum mintage: 3000
Struck in 2026 by UAB Lietuvos monetų kalykla (Lithuania)

Obverse
A relief depiction of a chestnut fruit with its spiny husk and a gilded fruit shown from the front. The inscription "5 EURO" is arranged in a semi-circle at the top, while the year "2026" is placed at the bottom.
Reverse
A relief depiction of a cracked chestnut husk with part of the gilded fruit shown from the back. The inscription "LATVIJA" is arranged diagonally at the top.
Edge
Plain, gilded
The horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) was introduced to Latvia around the turn of the 17th–18th centuries, first appearing in the parks of manors. It soon became a favourite tree for lining roads and avenues and for planting beside homes, valued for its rapid growth, shelter from the wind, and magnificent blossoms. Many chestnuts have grown into venerable trees, reaching at least 23 m in height and 3 m in circumference. One such tree stands at Billītes, home of writer Edvarts Virza in Jelgava Municipality. It served as the inspiration for the great chestnut in his prose masterpiece Straumēni. Beneath the branches of the chestnut tree, the household and their guests are depicted celebrating or resting after a day's work. The renowned Latvian landscape painter Vilhelms Purvītis, while living in Tallinn in the early 20th century, immortalised a grove of these trees in his painting Blooming Chestnut Trees. A small number of sweet chestnut trees (Castanea sativa) also grow in Latvia, mainly in Kurzeme.
From its spiny husk emerges a brown, smooth, and round chestnut fruit, cherished in Latvia both as a favourite childhood plaything and a folk remedy. Carrying a chestnut in one's pocket is also believed to protect against misfortune. For women, good fortune has traditionally been associated with a chestnut in the left pocket; for men, in the right. The chestnut coin is like a talisman, embodying all the positive qualities of the tree and its fruit. In Latvian, the word for chestnut tree is used in both the masculine (kastanis) and feminine (kastaņa) grammatical gender. This means that the tree, and now the coin, belongs to everyone. May you always have a chestnut in your pocket!
Activity of Latvijas Banka regarding the issuance of collector coins and 2 euro commemorative coins
Since 1993, Latvijas Banka has issued 98 lats collector coins and 66 euro collector coins. Overall, more than 50 artists from Latvia and 1 artist from Ukraine have participated in designing Latvian coins.
The design of Latvian coins has earned high international recognition. They are regularly honoured with prestigious awards in various competitions. In the 2010 international competition "Coin of the Year", the "Coin of Latvia" received the main prize in the "Coin of the Year" category, while in 2020, the collection coin "Honey Coin" of Latvijas Banka became the "Coin of the Year" – the absolute global winner, as well as took the first prize in the "Most Artistic Coin" category.
The Coin Design Committee of Latvijas Banka, which has been active since 12 November 1993, plays an important role in the coin issuing process. The Committee consists of employees of Latvijas Banka, outstanding experts in Latvian art and culture, as well as artists and scientists.
After the euro changeover, Latvijas Banka has carried on the tradition of issuing collector coin series with motifs characteristic of Latvia and executed in high artistic quality. These coins are legal tender only in the issuing country. They are unlikely to come into general circulation, for, by nature, they are works of art enjoying high demand from the numismatic community and other interested parties.
The face value of collector coins must differ from that of coins in general circulation (it must be, e.g. 5 euro or 10 euro). Their specifications, including colour, diameter, weight, material, etc. have to be cardinally distinctive from those of the coins in general circulation.
For information on the collector coins on sale at e-monetas.lv/en and the Cashier's Office of Latvijas Banka, see https://www.e-monetas.lv/en.
The issuance of 2 euro commemorative coins (2 euro circulation coins of special design) is another area of coin art. Each year, every euro area country is entitled to issue two 2 euro commemorative coins (similar to 1 lats special circulation coins previously issued in Latvia), featuring events of national, European, or global significance. The euro area countries can additionally produce a third 2 euro commemorative coin, provided that it is issued jointly and that it commemorates events of European Union-wide importance.
Commemorative coins bear the same features and the same common or European side as the normal 2 euro circulation coins, while their national sides differ and feature a national commemorating motif.
Euro commemorative coins are legal tender throughout the euro area. This means they can be used – and must be accepted – just like any other euro coin.

Oleksandr Stepura's Skyeton: An Estonian-Based Holding Building Drones for Europe  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:44:34 UTC
22:44:34 KST

The Baltic states have built a reputation as a home for technology companies that think internationally from day one. One of the less familiar examples is Skyeton, a developer of long-endurance unmanned aircraft whose holding company is registered in Tallinn. Founded by Ukrainian engineer Oleksandr Stepura, the company has spent the last few years reorganising itself into a European group, combining engineering roots in Ukraine with corporate and manufacturing presence across the European Union.
Why Estonia
Skyeton's parent company, Skyeton Holding AS, is based in Estonia. For technology founders from the region, Estonia has become a natural choice for a holding structure. The country offers a transparent corporate environment, fully digital administration, e-residency for foreign entrepreneurs and a strong reputation among international investors.
For a company working in aerospace and dual-use technology, that reputation matters. Partners, customers and investors in Europe want to work with companies that operate within EU law and governance standards, and an Estonian holding provides exactly that framework.
A group spread across Europe
The holding is only one part of the picture. In 2024, the company launched aircraft production in eastern Slovakia, near Prešov, bringing manufacturing inside the European Union. The broader group structure also includes entities in other European countries, reflecting a model that is becoming common among technology companies from Ukraine: engineering talent at home, corporate structure in a business-friendly EU jurisdiction, and production close to European customers.
This distributed setup allows Skyeton to work with European suppliers and partners, take part in EU programmes and offer customers the reassurance of buying from a company based in the Union.
The product: endurance as a feature
Skyeton's flagship product is Raybird, a fixed-wing unmanned aircraft designed to stay in the air far longer than typical drones. According to published specifications, it can fly for up to 28 hours, cover up to 2,500 kilometres and operate at altitudes of up to 4,500 metres. The aircraft is launched from a portable catapult and recovered by parachute, so it does not require a runway.
Long endurance changes what a drone can be used for. Instead of short flights that provide snapshots, a single aircraft can maintain continuous observation of a large area for an entire day.
Why it matters for the Baltic region
Several of the use cases for long-endurance drones are especially relevant to the Baltic states. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania share long land borders on the EU's eastern frontier, and monitoring them continuously is a significant operational challenge. Persistent aerial observation can support border services by covering remote sections where ground patrols are limited.
The region also has an extensive coastline along the Baltic Sea. Maritime monitoring, from detecting oil spills to supporting search and rescue, is another area where an aircraft that stays airborne for a full day offers clear advantages over helicopters. Large forested areas add environmental tasks such as early wildfire detection, while monitoring of energy infrastructure, including pipelines, power lines and undersea cable landing points, has become a growing priority across the region.
A regional voice on dual-use technology
Oleksandr Stepura has taken part in regional discussions on the future of technology and security. At the Lublin Triangle Economic Forum, which brings together Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine, he joined a panel on high technology and dual-use goods. The discussion focused on rising demand for unmanned systems, the challenges facing the security sector and the role of EU funding in developing high-tech industry across the participating countries.
The message from that panel resonates in the Baltics: investment in European technology capacity today is closely connected to the region's long-term security and economic resilience.
From engineering startup to European group
Skyeton's development has been studied beyond the industry itself. IMD, the Swiss business school, published a case study on the company, examining how a startup from Eastern Europe reached technical parity with much larger global manufacturers and the strategic choices it faced as it grew, from moving beyond government customers to deciding whether to sell products or services.
Under Oleksandr Stepura's leadership, the company has followed a path that many technology firms in the region are now taking: build deep engineering expertise, then scale through European structures and partnerships. With its holding in Estonia and production in Slovakia, Skyeton is an example of how Ukrainian technology and the wider European ecosystem, including the Baltic states, are becoming increasingly connected.

Russia’s Defense Ministry proposes establishing rapid response units in military police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:44:26 UTC
22:44:26 KST

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. The Russian Defense Ministry has proposed creating rapid response units within the Russian army’s military police - the relevant draft presidential decree drawn up by the ministry is published on the federal portal of draft normative legal acts.
According to the document, it is proposed to add the term "rapid response unit" to the Charter of the Military Police of the Russian Armed Forces. It specifies that such a unit will consist of two or more military police personnel with an assigned vehicle, "designated in accordance with established procedures to perform, when necessary, duties related to the prompt suppression of crimes, administrative offenses, and/or disciplinary infractions, to detain the perpetrators, to repel attacks on military personnel and civilian staff, on Armed Forces facilities guarded by the military police, as well as to carry out other tasks aimed at ensuring law and order, military discipline, and combating crime among military personnel."
The draft decree also introduces the position of the "patrol duty detail." The patrol duty detail’s duties are planned to include ensuring public order and military discipline within the garrison area and its adjacent territory "within sight and earshot, where military personnel on patrol duty perform their assigned duties around the clock or during a specified period of time."

Human rights group documents 453 Israeli incursions, 69 killings in Syria since 2024
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:43:08 UTC
22:43:08 KST

Laith Al-Junaidi and Ikram Kouachi
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The Syrian Network for Human Rights documented at least 453 ground incursions by Israeli forces into Syria and the killing of at least 69 people between Dec. 8, 2024, and Oct. 6, 2026, according to the Syrian Al-Ekhbariya channel on Thursday.
The figures were included in a report by the group examining the practices and violations of Israeli forces on Syrian territory since the fall of the former regime.
The incursions were concentrated in the southern provinces of Quneitra and Daraa, and to a lesser extent in the Damascus countryside, according to the report.
The network recorded at least 162 cases of arbitrary Israeli detentions. Of those detained, 127 were released, while the fate of 35 others is unknown to the network and their families.
It also documented the demolition of at least 15 civilian homes by Israeli forces following the incursion into Hamidiya village in the Quneitra countryside.
The report documented extensive land-leveling operations in the Jabata al-Khashab Nature Reserve in the northern Quneitra countryside on Oct. 17 and 18, 2025.
In late January, the network recorded Israeli troops spraying grazing lands in Quneitra with a substance whose nature it was unable to determine.
It said Israeli forces resumed land-leveling operations Oct. 4 west of Al-Asha village and Al-Rafid town.
Regarding air attacks, the network documented hundreds of Israeli airstrikes on the provinces of Damascus, Damascus countryside, Hama, Latakia, Homs, Tartus, Sweida and Idlib, without providing an exact toll in the published data.
The figures come amid the continued Israeli military presence inside the buffer zone and at sites around it in southern Syria since December 2024.
On Dec. 13 of that year, the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) said Israeli forces had entered the buffer zone and remained at several positions inside, stressing that the movements constituted a “violation of the 1974 disengagement agreement.”
A UN report issued in September 2025 also documented the continued Israeli military presence in the buffer zone and neighboring positions, pointing to Israeli steps to consolidate its presence in the occupied Syrian Golan Heights and territories it entered after December 2024.
The disengagement agreement signed between Syria and Israel in 1974 provides for the establishment of a separation zone monitored by the United Nations, while Damascus continues to demand the withdrawal of Israeli forces and respect for the agreement.

Giorgia Meloni wins vote on controversial ‘bonus seat’ changes to electoral system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:42:50 UTC
22:42:50 KST

A controversial overhaul to electoral law that critics say is aimed at boosting Giorgia Meloni’s chances of clinging on to power in elections next year has been given final approval by the Italian parliament.
Meloni, the Italian prime minister, says the new system, which introduces a fully proportional model, including bonus seats for any coalition that wins the most votes, will bring about greater political stability, while opposition parties argue that it mainly serves the interests of those in power.
The change was passed in a secret ballot in the lower house with 227 MPs voting in favour and 164 against.
There were protests from opposition politicians who held up signs decrying the law as a “scam” and a “con” when the result was announced.
Opposition parties have vowed to challenge the changes in the constitutional court, arguing that the bonus seat element, which would be granted to any coalition that reaches a vote threshold of 42% of the vote, distorts voter representation.
Another contentious requirement of the changes is that parties and alliances would be required lay out their government programme and name their candidate for prime minister well before a general election.
Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy, had made the vote a test for her ruling rightwing coalition, warning MPs from her allies, including Forza Italia and the League, that, if defeated, the government would face a crisis.
While there are tensions within the coalition, which has suffered setbacks in recent months and is under threat from the rise of new far-right rival Roberto Vannacci, leader of Futuro Nazionale, it has put on a show of unity and has stability on its side after becoming Italy’s longest serving government since the second world war in early September. Whereas the broad leftwing alliance, led by the Democratic party, is highly fractious with no clear leader or programme.
Meloni said the victory was a response to those who wanted to see her coalition divided. “Today we respond with action: we are united, cohesive and determined to fulfil the commitments made to citizens,” she wrote on social media.
Elly Schlein, the leader of the Democratic party, said Meloni’s alliance sought to change the electoral system because it feared losing the next general election, which is officially due to be held before October 2027 but could be brought forward to April or May.
According to a recent survey by Ipsos Doxa, the opposition coalition could reach the 42% threshold if it overcame internal divisions and managed to convince two small radical parties to join forces.

Russian oil supplies to India hinder Delhi-Washington trade deal — report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

22:42:34 KST

NEW YORK, October 8. /TASS/. US efforts to persuade India to stop purchasing Russian oil and to secure market access for American agricultural products remain the main obstacle to signing a trade agreement between the two nations, according to a report by BMI, a unit of the Fitch international rating agency.
"We expect India and the US eventually to conclude a narrow interim trade deal, although the remaining differences make a near-term breakthrough unlikely," the agency said.
The conflict in the Middle East and difficulties in transporting oil from Persian Gulf nations have reinforced India's incentive to maintain alternative sources of energy supplies, the agency noted.
Despite a narrowing of differences between India and the US, purchasing oil from Russia and importing US agricultural products remain the most politically and commercially sensitive matters for New Delhi. Russian oil accounted for approximately 50.8% of India's oil imports in July 2026. India might potentially allow limited imports of US agricultural goods, but importing American dairy products and genetically modified crops would entail significantly higher political costs.
India's effective tariff rate on US goods currently stands at 13.6%, well below the approximately 35% rate set in February. This implies that the direct benefits of the agreement could be limited unless a deal with the US secures preferential access for Indian goods to commercially significant sectors of the American market.
"India will resist costly concessions unless the US offers it a clear advantage over competing exporters," BMI said.
Trade negotiations between India and the US have also become more complicated due to Washington's efforts to reduce the bilateral goods trade deficit, which stood at $58.42 billion in 2025. India could narrow this gap by increasing purchases of US aircraft, energy products, technology, and weaponry. However, such purchases would not resolve US concerns regarding access to the Indian market.

EU representative Dorota Dlouhi-Suliga said the European Union would continue supporting Ukraine’s energy system, including by supplying generators to prevent the worst-case scenario.
According to her, the EU has been helping Moldova strengthen its capacity to receive Ukrainian refugees since 2022. Dlouhi-Suliga did not specify whether the EU was preparing a separate support plan for Moldova and other countries that could receive a new wave of refugees this winter.
As reported by Ukrinform, Sandu said Moldova, Ukraine and Romania should strengthen cooperation on airspace protection amid Russian aggression.

Bangladesh signed a 15-year concession agreement Thursday with UAE-based DP World to modernize and operate a major container terminal at the country’s busiest seaport, as police dispersed protesters opposing the deal.
The agreement covers the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) at Chattogram Port, which handles approximately 44% of the port’s container traffic.

New Sofia Metro Station Set to Open in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

22:40:26 KST

New Sofia Metro Station Set to Open in 2027
Sofia Mayor Vasil Terziev said the Pancho Vladigerov metro station is 90% complete and is expected to begin operating in the summer of 2027.
Terziev inspected the construction work alongside the management of Metropolitan EAD and described the station as an important project for expanding Sofia’s metro network. The facility will connect Metro Lines 1 and 2 and provide a link to the metro depot.
Once the station enters service, the interval between trains is expected to fall from seven to four minutes. Preliminary estimates indicate that the change will improve transport access for around 10,000 to 12,000 additional residents in nearby neighborhoods.
Nikolay Naydenov, Executive Director of Metropolitan EAD, said the station is planned as part of a future intermodal transport hub connecting different modes of transportation.
“We will strive to create more connections of this kind, enabling the integration of rail, road, and urban public transport,” Naydenov said.
A bus terminal is also planned for the area. The aim is to facilitate access to Sofia and encourage people to use the metro instead of private vehicles, which Naydenov said would also contribute to lower carbon emissions.
Naydenov said construction of the section beneath Tsaritsa Yoanna Boulevard is expected to start within the next six months. The plans include a connection with the Ring Road that would allow international travelers, including those from Serbia, Greece and North Macedonia, to leave their cars outside the city and continue by metro.
Another long-term project envisages an intermodal hub in Sofia’s Mladost district near Ring Mall. Terziev said the facility is planned to connect two metro lines with a future tram route and the cable car.
Naydenov said the Pancho Vladigerov station will be the terminus of two lines, allowing passengers to transfer directly between them. He rejected concerns that the arrangement would cause substantial delays for passengers traveling from Obelya.
“It takes place right at the metro station itself. There won't be any such delay. The only delay would stem from the timing mismatch between the trains,” Naydenov said.
He added that the station is also being designed to operate as a railway stop so that future expansion of railway transport will not be obstructed.

Türkiye, China strike satellite technology deal for joint space development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:40:16 UTC
22:40:16 KST

Türkiye and China will carry out joint work on space technologies under a joint R&D, product development and commercialisation agreement signed between TURKSAT and China Satcom.
The 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) continues at the Antalya NEST Congress Centre with Anadolu as the Global Communications Partner.
The congress is organised by the International Astronautical Federation (IAF) and hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and SAHA Istanbul under the coordination of the Ministry of Industry and Technology.
Turkish companies are showcasing their products at the congress while also signing agreements with international partners.
According to information obtained by Anadolu, TURKSAT and China-based satellite operator China Satcom have signed a comprehensive protocol aimed at developing new technologies.
The protocol was signed at a ceremony held at the TURKSAT stand by TURKSAT Deputy General Manager for Satellite Services Selman Demirel and China Satcom CEO Ma Haiquan.
The agreement aims to bring together the engineering expertise of the two countries through joint R&D, product development and commercialisation.
Innovative products and solutions to be developed
The partnership between the two institutions, which began last year with capacity sharing, was expanded through decisions reached at World Space Business Week in Paris.
With the cooperation now moving into hardware and software development, the agreement marks a new phase of joint R&D and production in space technologies between Türkiye and China.
Under the agreement, TURKSAT and China Satcom plan to develop UAV communication systems, satellite-based Internet of Things technologies and smart border security technologies.
TURKSAT will also expand its solution portfolio by applying its existing capabilities in developing end-to-end satellite and communications solutions to new technologies and application areas.
The cooperation will cover the full process, from analysing market needs and developing initial prototypes to testing, validation and commercialisation. Turkish and Chinese engineers will work together to develop new products and solutions.
TURKSAT aims to become a leading technology supplier
Smart border security and Internet of Things technologies are among the other key areas covered by the agreement.
The partnership aims to develop specialised devices for areas without terrestrial communications networks.
The agreement also covers the development of hardware that will allow devices used in sectors such as energy, agriculture and logistics to be managed via satellite in remote areas without mobile networks.
Limited terrestrial communications infrastructure in many parts of the world creates gaps in border security and industrial data transmission.
The TURKSAT-China Satcom partnership aims to develop smart satellite monitoring and IoT systems capable of providing real-time data transmission in remote and challenging areas beyond the reach of cellular base stations or fibre networks.
Through these integrated satellite-based hardware and software solutions, TURKSAT aims to become one of the leading technology suppliers in the global ecosystem.
A joint steering committee with equal representation from the two institutions will also be established to oversee R&D and product development activities, with the work to be reviewed every three months.

Bestselling Hungarian newspaper shut down under Orban relaunches online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:39:30 UTC
22:39:30 KST

Bestselling Hungarian newspaper shut down under Orban relaunches online
BUDAPEST, Oct 8 - Nepszabadsag (People's Freedom), a leading left-wing Hungarian newspaper shut down a decade ago in a blow to media diversity under former prime minister Viktor Orban, relaunched on Thursday as an online news site and weekly magazine.
The newspaper - founded during Hungary's abortive popular uprising against Soviet domination in 1956 - was abruptly closed in 2016 by former owner Mediaworks.
Staff said at the time they believed the move was driven by their coverage of Orban, noting that their publication was Hungary's best-selling daily paper. Mediaworks cited financial losses.
Nepszabadsag's new Editor-in-Chief Akos Toth told Reuters independent journalism in Hungary "needs to return to a very classic, news-based journalism, to ask questions again and not state an opinion."
The relaunch of Nepszabadsag is funded by four Hungarian businessmen mainly involved in real estate investments abroad during Orban's tenure, Toth said.
"They are transparent, not hiding behind complicated company structures," Toth said, adding that, with Orban out of power since his April election defeat, the investors saw a business opportunity in reviving the widely recognised brand.
HUNGARY IS A TOUGH MARKET FOR A NEW OUTLET, EXPERT SAYS
Orban's Fidesz, which had a firm grip on Hungary's institutions for 16 years, is now backed by just one-fifth of voters. Hungary's parliament has set a two-term limit for prime ministers, effectively barring Orban from returning to power.
During his years in power, critics said media pluralism eroded as state media came under tighter government control and several private outlets - including Nepszabadsag - were shut down or acquired by pro-government owners.
Critics then accused the government of silencing dissent, but Orban's government denied exerting pressure on the media and said Hungary met European Union standards on media freedom.
The new outlet will employ about 90 staff members, mostly former employees of Nepszabadsag or left-wing daily Nepszava, which ceased its print edition in May.
The investors acquired Nepszava and rights to the Nepszabadsag brand last month, Toth said, committing to finance operations for two years with plans to break even through advertising revenue and subscriptions.
Market challenges persist, however, with Hungary's media heavily affected by distortions from state advertising channelled to political allies under successive Orban administrations.
Agnes Urban of the think tank Mertek Media Monitor said that market-based advertising money has not replaced state advertising, and companies are more interested in advertising near entertainment content than politics and news.
"It is a tough scene for a startup, and Nepszabadsag will be exactly that after a hiatus of 10 years." REUTERS

Justice Minister Akın Gürlek attended the opening of the International Justice Summit, held at Çırağan Palace under the theme “The Future of Justice: A Common Responsibility for Humanity,” and delivered a speech. (AA Photo)
Istanbul on Oct. 8 hosted the International Justice Summit, bringing together justice ministers, members of the judiciary and law professors from various countries, as Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek stressed that international law must be applied equally to all actors.

Gürlek stressed that international law can only truly constitute law when it is applied equally to all actors.
“A rule derives its legal character not from being applied only in certain circumstances or to certain actors, but from preserving its universal character. For this reason, we believe the international community must take action without further delay,” he said.
Gürlek also underlined the importance of “effectively investigating allegations of violations, ensuring that those responsible are held accountable, preserving evidence, safeguarding the rights of victims, and supporting independent and impartial judicial mechanisms.”

Search warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:38:20 UTC
22:38:20 KST

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home after they arrested him.
The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.
On Thursday, Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.
The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.
The warrants were issued by an Old Bailey judge on 18 February and Mountbatten-Windsor was subsequently arrested the following day, on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.
The arrest followed information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.
Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.
Hilliard said the search warrants were quashed but police had made an application, which would be heard next year, to retain the seized property on the basis that it would have been lawful to take it under a different statutory provision. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes that application.
The judge said: “The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful.”
A senior police source said: “It’s not going to bring the investigation to a halt or affect the chances of success.”
They added: “The news media might say the police messed up. But it was the judicial decision [to grant the warrant] that was incorrect.”
TVP have been in discussions with lawyers from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) about the strength of their case and what evidence they would need for a prosecution.
A TVP spokesperson said: “The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation.
“We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.
“We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.”
Hilliard told the court that the grant of a search warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace) 1984 was conditional on the issuing judge being satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the material sought did not include items subject to legal privilege or special procedure material.
Special procedure material includes documents in possession of a person who acquired them in the course of any trade, business, profession or other occupation – for the purpose of any paid or unpaid office – who holds it subject to an express or implied undertaking to hold it in confidence.
The judge said the presence of legally privileged material was expressly envisaged in the application for the search warrants and that material was likely to be in the possession of Mountbatten-Windsor “who had acquired or created it in circumstances which would make it special procedure material”. He concluded that a lawful warrant could only have been issued under section nine of Pace.
Nick Vamos, the former head of special crime at the CPS, said: “Given the technical nature of the errors revealed today, I expect the crown court to rule in due course that the police can keep the material, or at least as much of it as they would have been entitled to seize in the first place, so they may not ultimately pay much of a price beyond today’s red faces.”
Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.
Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

Türkiye warned that the Black Sea must not become new front in Russia-Ukraine war
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:38:08 EEST
22:38:08 KST

Türkiye warned that the Black Sea must not become new front in Russia-Ukraine war
Kyiv • UNN
The Turkish Foreign Minister said that attacks on civilian vessels and risks to shipping and food security were increasing. At the same time, Ankara is preparing the Mecca Pact for ratification.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan warned on Thursday, October 8, that the Russian-Ukrainian war must not turn the Black Sea into a new front, citing the growing number of attacks on civilian vessels and risks to shipping and food security. UNN reports this with reference to Türkiye Today.
Details
"We must never allow the Black Sea to turn into a new front in the conflict," Fidan said at a joint press conference in Ankara with Hungary's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Orbán.
Fidan said that Europe's security cannot be considered separately from Turkey's security, capabilities and potential.
"Before permanent approaches to security policy are adopted, qualified discussions must be held. Otherwise, it may be too late," he said.
He said that the Russian-Ukrainian war remains one of the main threats to regional and global stability, the publication writes.
"Since the beginning of the war, we have worked persistently to prevent it from spreading to the Black Sea," Fidan said, citing Turkey's "meticulous" implementation of the Montreux Convention regarding the regime of the straits and the Black Sea Grain Initiative as examples of this approach.
Fidan said that the war is now spreading to the Black Sea, where attacks on civilian vessels have become more frequent, posing a serious threat to life, property, shipping and environmental security.
"As countries of the region and the international community, we must never allow the Black Sea to turn into a new front in the conflict," Fidan said.
He said that Ankara is conveying its assessments and warnings on this issue to both sides.
"The efforts of the two countries to gain a military advantage over each other have a serious impact on the safety of shipping in the Black Sea," Fidan said.
He added that Turkish-flagged vessels, vessels owned by Turkey and vessels with Turkish crews had also been affected.
"We are doing everything possible to put an end to this situation," he said.
Fidan said that the attacks not only harm personnel and vessels, but also create risks to food security, especially when grain shipments fail to reach international markets.
"We need to prevent this situation," he said.
Mecca Pact
Fidan also said that Turkey had completed preparations to submit the Mecca Defense Agreement for approval by the country's parliament, emphasizing that the pact is defensive in nature.
"The work required to submit the agreement to parliament has been completed," he said.
Fidan said that the agreement provides for mutual defense if one of its signatories is attacked.
"As soon as a country that is a party to the agreement is attacked, you support its defense. This is not an offensive agreement," he said.
He also clarified that the pact does not allow Turkey to deploy troops to another country's territory to carry out an attack.

The number of Americans filing first-time unemployment benefit claims fell by 2,000 to 197,000 last week, below market expectations, the US Labor Department said Thursday.
The figure for the week ending Oct. 3 came in below the market forecast of 200,000. The previous week’s reading was revised up by 2,000 to 199,000.
The four-week moving average, which smooths out weekly fluctuations, declined by 2,500 to 198,000. The previous week’s average was revised up by 500 to 200,500.
Continuing claims, which track people already receiving unemployment benefits, increased by 17,000 to 1.716 million in the week ending Sept. 26.

The four-week moving average for continuing claims fell by 12,250 to 1.711 million.
In September, the US economy added just 29,000 nonfarm jobs, well below forecasts of 90,000, according to an earlier Bureau of Labor Statistics report.
The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.

A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.
The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.
“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.
“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”
Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.
Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.
However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

EU presses Russia for more details on suspected plague case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:36:31 UTC
22:36:31 KST

Pressure mounts on Moscow to explain the suspected plague case in Siberia, which has put health authorities on edge. Brussels is calling on Moscow to come clean with precise details "as soon as possible".
The European Commission has stepped up pressure on Russia to provide full details of a suspected plague case in Siberia, echoing calls for transparency from the United States and the World Health Organisation (WHO).
Moscow has pushed back,insisting there is no risk of an epidemic.
"Let me say, for the third time this week in the press room: Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible," Eva Hrncirova, the Commission's health spokesperson, said on Thursday.
"We don't have enough information to assess the epidemiological situation, to assess the risks for other countries and to take appropriate measures, if necessary."
The comments came a day after the Commission convened the EU's Health Security Committee, bringing together representatives of the 27 member states, along with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the WHO.
The committee coordinates the EU's response to serious cross-border health threats, allowing national authorities to share information, assess risks and discuss possible measures.
However, Wednesday's meeting ended without any specific decisions because of the lack of reliable information from Russia.
The Commission said it was ready to reconvene the committee at short notice if new information emerged or the situation deteriorated.
"We need information from Russia," Hrncirova said. "It's linked to the Russian membership in the WHO Europe: sharing timely, precise, exact information so that the experts can assess the situation because the situation can have cross-border implications."
The EU delegation in Moscow reached out to the WHO's office in Russia to convey its concerns, the spokesperson said, citing the lack of direct diplomatic contact between Brussels and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Basically the whole world is waiting for the information from Russia," she added.
The case revolves around a female lab worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute, in south-eastern Siberia, who died on 2 October in uncertain circumstances.
Her death was initially attributed to a "pneumonia of unknown aetiology", sparking global alarm and intense scrutiny.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, says the lab worker was "vaccinated and had immunity to the dangerous infections she was working with", and that nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no dangerous pathogens.
More than 90% of those who had contact with her have completed medical monitoring after being placed under strict observation, it said.
WHO has requested details to clarify the lab worker's death, the pathogen that triggered the quarantine measures, and a reported second case, which Moscow called "false".
The US has also urged Russia to provide accurate and timely information. President Donald Trump said he had scheduled a call with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to discuss the suspected outbreak.
"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," a US State Department spokesperson said.
Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria responsible for plague infect the lungs. It is the most serious form of the disease and can spread from person to person. Without treatment, its case-fatality ratio ranges from 30% to 100%.

The Afghan Taliban’s Growing Drone War Against Pakistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:35:00 UTC
22:35:00 KST

Pakistan’s air defense system shot down eight drones after they entered the country’s airspace from Afghanistan on September 23. Four drones were shot down near the border at Torkham and four were shot down near Kohat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In response, Pakistan struck 10 locations in Afghanistan that were being used to launch and store drones by the Afghan Taliban.
This growing use of drones has added a dangerous new dimension to an already fragile Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship. On its western border, Pakistan now faces a two-pronged security challenge: first, the direct use of drones by the Afghan Taliban against Pakistani security positions and other targets, and second, the transfer or facilitation of drone technology to affiliated militant groups such as the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), enabling them to conduct attacks against military check posts and other targets inside Pakistan. What was once primarily a tool of surveillance, propaganda, and battlefield observation has evolved into an instrument capable of extending the reach, precision, and lethality of militant violence.
The Afghan Taliban began using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in 2016, initially for propaganda purposes. Over time, however, their use expanded into operational roles, including reconnaissance, surveillance, and the delivery of explosives. Between February 27 to March 15, 2026 the Afghan Taliban claimed responsibility for 15 drone attacks in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and Islamabad.
The Afghan Taliban procures its drones from a mix of sources, including commercially available platforms, systems obtained through regional networks, and locally modified or assembled equipment. This has made drone technology more accessible and harder to control.
The Afghan Taliban’s 313th Battalion, associated with the Haqqani network, is using one-way attack drones, referred to as kamikaze drones. The Afghan Taliban drones are launched from Kandahar, Nangarhar, Paktia, and Paktika, reducing the distance to targets in Quetta, Peshawar, Islamabad, and Waziristan in Pakistan. Recently, the Afghan Taliban have reportedly acquired anti-drone systems and are preparing to deploy them at the 205th Corps in Kandahar and near Spin Boldak to counter Pakistani drones along the border.
The concern becomes more acute when this capability is viewed alongside the TTP and other militant groups operating from Afghanistan into Pakistan. These groups have shown considerable adaptability in adopting new technologies, especially drones. This low-cost technology gives militant groups capabilities once associated primarily with conventional military forces. For Pakistan, the challenge is therefore not simply the presence of drones, but the growing ease with which this technology can be acquired, adapted and deployed by multiple actors across the border.
Pakistan has so far effectively intercepted cross-border drone incursions from Afghanistan. However, it needs to take further concrete steps, as drone use is becoming a persistent feature of the Afghan Taliban’s military strategy against Pakistan.
The most worrying possibility is not necessarily that Afghanistan will develop a large drone fleet. It is the multiplication of small, relatively cheap systems. A conventional military platform represents a significant investment and is therefore used selectively. Small unmanned systems can be acquired in larger numbers and employed repeatedly. They can observe a security position, identify a target, test air defense responses, and also carry an explosive payload. Even when they cause limited physical damage, they can create disruption, fear, and uncertainty. Pakistan therefore needs to treat counter-drone capability as a central component of national security rather than as a specialized military requirement.
There has already been movement toward domestic drone production. Pakistan’s defense industry and armed forces have experience with UAVs for surveillance, reconnaissance, and combat roles. Indigenous production is important because reliance on foreign suppliers can become a vulnerability during a prolonged crisis. A country facing an evolving drone threat needs the ability not only to build systems but also to modify, repair, and upgrade them according to its own requirements.
Pakistan also requires a layered counter-UAV architecture. The first layer should be detection. Conventional radar does not always provide an adequate answer against small, low-flying drones, particularly in cluttered urban or mountainous regions like Pakistan’s western tribal borderlands. Pakistan therefore needs a combination of short-range radar, electro-optical and infrared sensors, radio-frequency detection, and other technologies capable of identifying unusual aerial activity.
The second layer is neutralization. Depending on the threat, this could involve electronic warfare, communications jamming, spoofing, and conventional interceptors. No single technology is likely to be effective against every type of drone. A layered approach is therefore essential for Pakistan to counter the layered threat.
Pakistan should also invest in artificial intelligence and data analysis. A modern counter-drone system should learn from repeated attacks: launch patterns, flight routes, frequencies, operating times, and target selection. The objective should be to move from reacting to drones after detection toward predicting likely attacks before they occur. Therefore, working in this direction should be a priority of Islamabad.
Airports, power stations, military facilities, government buildings, oil installations, and major communication centers all require appropriate protection. Border management must consequently become more technologically sophisticated. Pakistan’s long and difficult western border cannot be secured through conventional fencing and physical posts alone. Sensors, surveillance aircraft, drones, ground-based monitoring systems, and rapid-response units need to operate as one network. Intelligence sharing between civilian and military agencies is equally important.
At the same time, Islamabad must avoid allowing the drone issue to become part of a permanent cycle of escalation with Kabul. Retaliatory action may be presented as necessary when attacks occur, but military responses alone cannot produce a stable border. Each strike carries the possibility of further retaliation, civilian casualties, and a broader deterioration in relations.
The Afghan Taliban therefore needs to come to the negotiating table. Dialogue does not require Pakistan to abandon its security concerns or accept attacks against its territory. On the contrary, negotiations should be used to establish verifiable commitments by the Afghan Taliban: Afghan territory must not be used for attacks against Pakistan; militants should not receive access to military technology in Afghanistan; mechanisms for investigating cross-border incidents should be created; and both sides should maintain direct communication during crises.

Turkey says Russia, Ukraine increasing attacks in Black Sea ahead of winter
ANKARA, Oct 8 - Intensifying attacks by Russia and Ukraine ahead of the winter are further endangering navigational safety in the Black Sea, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, adding that world powers must not allow the region to be turned into a new front in the war.
NATO member Turkey, which has maintained good ties with both Moscow and Kyiv since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has repeatedly called on both sides to halt attacks in the Black Sea that have also struck Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned commercial vessels. Ankara says it is awaiting responses to a proposal it conveyed to Russia and Ukraine aimed at stopping the attacks and ensuring the safe shipment of grain from the region.
Speaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan said the attacks, which he described as a serious threat to the regional security, were getting worse even as Turkey had already proposed solutions.

"As regional countries (and) the international community, we must never allow the Black Sea to be turned into a new front for conflict. However, unfortunately as you can see, as the war expands, it is also showing its effects in the Black Sea," he said.
Turkey and the United Nations helped to mediate the so-called Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2022 to allow for the safe export of Ukrainian grain amid the war, but Russia withdrew from the agreement the following year, complaining that its own food and fertiliser exports faced serious obstacles.
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on ships and infrastructure facilitating Russian oil and grain exports since July, when Russia intensified its missile and drone strikes on the main Ukrainian grain export hubs of Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi.

Estonia's military conscription no-show rate falls to 2%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:34:00 UTC
22:34:00 KST

Estonia's military conscription no-show rate falls to 2%
The number of young adults failing to report for conscript service in the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) has fallen steadily in recent years, reaching 2 percent in 2025.
A total of 63 call-up selectees failed to report for conscription last year, down from 4 percent in 2024 and 6.6 percent in 2023, the Defense Resources Agency (KRA) said.
KRA Conscripts Office director Krista Juhanson told ERR that those who repeatedly skip required medical assessments without good reason can be subject to official orders and an enforcement fine.
She said fines for failing to attend a medical assessment, which are intended to encourage compliance, are currently capped at €640, with the exact amount depending on the circumstances. Next year, however, the cap will double to €1,280.
"It's important to note that paying the fine does not exempt you from having to attend the medical assessment," Juhanson said.
KRA can impose fines repeatedly, but if that proves ineffective, the agency can seek to suspend a selectee's driver's license or fishing, hunting and firearms permits.
So far this year, the KRA has sought the suspension of 57 driver's licenses. Juhanson said that in practice, these extra measures generally work.
"Once call-up selectees grasp that failing to fulfill their obligations can result in additional consequences, they usually come in for the medical assessment," she said, adding that the goal is to encourage compliance, not punitive.
More flexible medicals
The KRA official also attributed the decline in no-shows in part to a more flexible approach, including a digital pre-assessment review of health records and allowing call-up selectees to choose when and where to have their assessment done.
"That means no more having to spend all day waiting your turn outside a doctor's office," Juhanson said.
Being summoned to a medical assessment doesn't automatically result in a conscription order either, she added, as when and where a selectee will be sent for conscript service are decided only after the assessment.

Has Israel shut the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – or downgraded it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:32:32 UTC
22:32:32 KST

Has Israel shut the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – or downgraded it?
British Foreign Secretary Miliband said the consulate building would remain but would called ‘UK Mission, Jerusalem’.
The British government has said it will retain its presence in occupied East Jerusalem after Israel removed the signage of its consulate amid deteriorating diplomatic relations.
The removal of the signage comes as Israel announced that 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, would have to leave the country and return home.
Britain’s Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, said on Thursday that the consulate building would remain but would be downgraded to the “UK Mission, Jerusalem”.
The Israeli government’s decision to close the consulate followed Miliband’s announcement last month that Britain would ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Here’s what we know:
What did Israel say about shutting the consulate?
In a post on X, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar reiterated on Thursday morning that “no action can be taken against Israel without Israel taking appropriate retaliatory measures”.
In retaliation for the sanctions on the occupied West Bank settlements, Saar outlined the four steps that Israel was taking against the UK, including:
- Removal of British representatives from the International Assistance Centre for Gaza
- Ending British activity to train Palestinian Authority forces in the occupied West Bank
- Closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem
- Prevention of entry into Israel of 12 elected officials and other British citizens involved in “anti-Semitic and anti-Israeli activity”
“We did not want to come to this, but the actions of the Labour government led us here,” Saar wrote, adding that the sanctions and the “hostile rhetoric” of ethnic cleansing of Palestinians had forced their hand against the British government.
“The British Consulate in Jerusalem ended its duties today. The Consul General and 20 diplomats are ending their duties and will leave Israel,” he said, adding that while the building is the property of the British government, Israel has allowed them to operate a task force of seven diplomats in the building with a “very limited scope of activity”.
The minister explained that the decision was also based on an understanding reached with the British government last night.
But isn’t the UK saying its mission will still function?
Yes.
In a statement, Miliband said that the British government had been “clear” that it did not accept Israel’s decision to close its consulate, which has been around for nearly 200 years, reiterating its “longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”
“The UK Mission, Jerusalem is independent, operational, and will continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people.
“This will ensure that we maintain our longstanding British presence and the UK’s role in support of a two-state solution.
“Without an understanding, we would not have the necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises. Accordingly, the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security,” he said.
“We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible.”
“The UK stands steadfast by the measures we took on September 8 , in concert with the international community, in support of a two-state solution to deliver peace and security for the people of Israel and Palestine,” Miliband added.
Reports of reciprocal action against the consulate closure, including expelling one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat who had to leave the country, first came from the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials.
On the consulate’s closure, Stephen Doughty, Minister of State in the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, told BBC Radio on Thursday morning that the British government was continuing conversations with Israel about the issue.
“You can see what’s changed in terms of a name, but crucially a presence remains,” he said.
Asked about reports of a British threat to expel Israeli diplomats, the minister did not comment on it, but said they engaged with Israel in a “mature, responsible and practical debate”.
Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Camille Nedelec said the downgrading of the consulate marked “a low point in UK-Israeli relations”.
So is that a downgraded consulate?
Yes.
While a consulate mainly helps citizens, in this case British-Palestinian nationals, a mission usually refers to a diplomatic representative.
However, according to Vincent Fean, former British Consul General in Jerusalem, it did not “matter” what the consulate was now called.
“The Israeli electorate faces elections on October 27 and I think the plan of the British government is to wait and see what comes from those elections and to deal with whatever government the Israeli electorate chooses,” Fean told Al Jazeera.
“I think that the key point is that Ed Miliband acted correctly on September 8, specifically on the issue of E1 – the red line – settlement the Israelis are planning and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich says is designed to bury the two-state solution,” he added. The E1 settlement aims to link Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem, effectively severing the West Bank in two.
The British consulate first opened in 1839 but closed in 1914 at the start of the First World War. It was later re-established as a consulate-general in 1948 after the British Mandate in Palestine ended.
What led to this?
Relations soured following the new Labour government’s decision to impose sanctions on settlers and illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Miliband announced the measures and said last month that imports of all goods produced by illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank would be banned.
In his speech, he said there was “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank – perpetrated by settler terrorists.”
“The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel,” he said.
“We will continue to support important and valued trade with Green Line Israel precisely because we support the two-state solution, including security and prosperity for Israel,” he added.
However, Israel condemned the announcement last month and called it a “series of anti-Israel decisions by the Labour Government”.
Saar said the “accusations made today by the Foreign Secretary of the Labour Government in the British Parliament were outrageous lies,” and set out the four reciprocal actions.
Is the Israeli action legal?
No.
As the British consulate is in a part of Jerusalem that Israel captured in the 1967 war and has occupied ever since, it does not have the legal right to close the mission.
However, due to Israel’s ongoing occupation of the Palestinian territories, it practically decides what can function in East Jerusalem.
