====================================================================================================

China Focus: China remains committed to letting market play decisive role in determining exchange rate: central bank
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:16:53 CST
22:16:53 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China remains committed to letting market forces play a decisive role in determining the RMB exchange rate, the country's central bank said on Thursday.
The People's Bank of China (PBOC) stressed in a statement outlining its view on the RMB exchange rate that the country adopts a managed floating exchange rate regime based on market supply and demand with reference to a basket of currencies.
The RMB has moved in both directions since the country's exchange rate regime reform in 2005, said the central bank.
In bilateral terms, the RMB has strengthened against the U.S. dollar from 8.27 per dollar in July 2005, when the reform was launched, to around 6.7 per dollar recently, appreciating by 23 percent cumulatively.
In multilateral terms, the RMB nominal effective exchange rate calculated by the Bank for International Settlements has appreciated by over 50 percent since the exchange rate regime reform in 2005, while its real effective exchange rate up by 35 percent, according to the PBOC.
Since 2025, the RMB has strengthened by about 9 percent against the dollar. In particular, while non-dollar currencies have weakened broadly amid surging dollar index and Treasury yields since 2026, the RMB has extended its upward trend against the dollar.
"China has no need or intent to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation, nor has it ever resorted to competitive devaluation," said the central bank.
China's trade growth is driven by its growing industrial competitiveness in the global market, said the central bank.
Exchange rate dynamics are driven by a number of factors including economic growth, monetary policy, financial market, geopolitics and sudden shocks, the PBOC said, adding that there is no straightforward relationship between the exchange rate and the current account.
Regarding global economic imbalances, the PBOC said in the statement that they are deeply intertwined with shifting global division of labor, inherent flaws in the international monetary system, and persistently high fiscal deficits and high consumption in some countries.
Addressing global imbalances requires collective actions from all stakeholders, according to the central bank.
"Attributing one's decline in industrial competitiveness, weakened fiscal discipline, and complicated structural issues simply to others' exchange rates is nothing but shifting the responsibility for adjustment onto others and dodging accountability," said the central bank.
A number of models for assessing the equilibrium exchange rate have emerged from academic studies over the years. Noting that there is no well-established methodology for evaluating the equilibrium level of exchange rates internationally, the central bank said "therefore, citing idiosyncratic assessment findings as 'official evidence' for RMB undervaluation is a misinterpretation and misuse of those findings."
The central bank said China has long been a contributor to global economic rebalancing. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China will stay the course in transforming its economic growth model, expand domestic demand, improve the business environment, deepen high-standard opening up, and pursue a more open, inclusive and balanced global economy, the bank said.
Lu Lei, deputy governor of the PBOC, said in September that China operates a managed floating exchange rate regime, allowing market forces to play a decisive role in exchange rate determination while guarding against herd behavior and the self-reinforcing effects of irrational expectations.
In recent years, as China's export structure has undergone transformation and upgrading, companies have strengthened their pricing power and foreign exchange risk management capabilities, significantly reducing the sensitivity of China's trade to exchange rate movements, Lu said.
Meanwhile, foreign trade enterprises have increasingly used foreign exchange hedging instruments, while the RMB's share of trade settlement has continued to rise, further reducing the sensitivity of trade to exchange rate fluctuations, Lu added.
Guan Tao, chief economist at Huafu Securities, said that factors supporting both appreciation and depreciation of the RMB are currently at play.
In the short term, factors favoring a stronger RMB have the upper hand. Over the longer term, two-way fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate remain the norm, Guan noted. ■

by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
SINGAPORE, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem has reiterated his desire to see a Chinese manufacturer enter Formula 1, suggesting that acquiring an existing team could offer a faster route into the championship than establishing a new entrant.
Speaking to selected media, including Xinhua, ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, Ben Sulayem said China's growing automotive industry and motorsport involvement made it an attractive prospect for F1, but stressed that any new entrant would have to meet the championship's requirements.
"We would like a big team from China because I feel that's the leverage," he said. "You cannot exclude Asia. Asia has many things, and Asia-Pacific has the number of people, the love of the sport and the manufacturers.
"It will add a lot to Formula 1."
Ben Sulayem has previously advocated expanding the F1 grid to 12 teams, following the arrival of American manufacturer Cadillac as the championship's 11th entrant this year.
However, he said adding another team was not necessarily the objective, suggesting that a Chinese manufacturer could instead acquire an existing operation, following the example of German carmaker Audi, which took over Sauber ahead of the 2026 season.
"It's about the right team," he said. "If they come in and take another team, I'll be more than happy."
"It doesn't mean we will have a 12th team," he added, suggesting that acquiring an established outfit could "shorten the time" required to enter F1.
Chinese electric vehicle giant BYD is said to have already explored a potential move into F1, with senior executives holding discussions with leading figures in the sport.
BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li has reportedly met Ben Sulayem and F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, while also holding exploratory talks with former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner.
Despite the discussions, BYD has not announced plans to enter F1.
Another Chinese manufacturer expanding its international motorsport involvement is Geely, which entered the FIA TCR World Tour this year, fielding four Preface race cars through Geely Cyan Racing, with Chinese driver Ma Qinghua among its lineup.
Geely is also reportedly in advanced negotiations to take over Alpine's Hypercar program in the FIA World Endurance Championship from 2027, following the French manufacturer's decision to withdraw from that series at the end of this year.
Asked about Geely, Ben Sulayem confirmed that he had met a senior executive from the company during a visit to China.
"I met with the boss, with the president, in China when I was there for Formula 1," he said, without indicating whether the meeting involved a concrete proposal to enter F1.
Ben Sulayem acknowledged that efforts to expand the F1 grid had previously encountered resistance from existing teams, partly because of concerns about sharing the sport's commercial revenues among more competitors.
"There was a lot of resistance. It's not something to hide," he said. "It was about money."
Nevertheless, he argued that additional manufacturers could help expand F1's commercial appeal rather than simply dividing existing revenues among more participants.
Beyond F1, Ben Sulayem also said he wanted to encourage more Chinese companies to become suppliers to motorsport, as part of a broader effort to reduce costs and make racing more accessible.
"When I came to the FIA, there were no companies from China involved in any tender the FIA would do," he said.
He argued that Chinese suppliers should have the opportunity to compete for contracts provided their products met the FIA's technical and safety requirements.
"If they meet the specifications and the quality is up to our regulations, you give it to everyone," he said.
"Accessibility comes from affordability."
Ben Sulayem also highlighted the FIA's growing relationship with China, which will host the federation's annual general meeting and annual prize-giving ceremony in Shanghai this December.
He said the idea emerged during a meeting with Shanghai's mayor in 2024, adding that the relationship extended beyond major international events to cooperation on motorsport development, mobility and road safety.
"China adopted us, embraced us, and we are going," he said.
"But it's not only about the General Assembly and the awards. It's about the day-to-day dealings with China and its federation in terms of sport and mobility." ■

====================================================================================================

US annual plague average revised without explanation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:14:52 UTC
22:14:52 KST

US annual plague average revised without explanation
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has updated its estimate of annual human plague infections in the country, lowering it from seven to five.
On Wednesday, the CDC amended its Plague Maps and Statistics page, which now states: “An average of five human plague cases are reported each year in the United States.” The previous version, dated March 2025, cited seven cases annually, although its own year-by-year data already showed an average of approximately five.
The agency has not provided an explanation for the revision.
According to the CDC’s current data, there were a total of 131 plague cases across the US between 2000 and 2025, 17 of which were lethal. The highest number of cases dates back to 2006 (17) and 2015 (16). In the latter case, four people died – the highest annual death toll during the period.
The previous figure of seven is likely derived from a different historical period. An April 2026 study by CDC researchers found that 196 human plague cases were reported between 1991 and 2018 – exactly seven annually on average.
According to the CDC, plague first reached the US in 1900 aboard rat-infested steamships, sparking outbreaks in port cities. The last urban epidemic occurred in Los Angeles in 1924-1925. Since then, infections have largely been confined to rural western regions, particularly New Mexico, Arizona, and Colorado, as well as parts of California, Oregon, and Nevada.
The disease is caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, which circulates among rodents and fleas. More than 80% of US cases involve bubonic plague, which does not spread directly between humans and is typically contracted through infected flea bites or contact with infected animals.
Only pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs, can spread from person to person through respiratory droplets, typically requiring close contact. Such transmission has not been confirmed in the US since 1924, although the CDC investigated a possible instance in Colorado in 2014. In July 2025, a man in Arizona died from pneumonic plague after exposure to infected cats.
At least two additional cases have been recorded in 2026, according to the CDC’s provisional data. A patient in Arizona recovered after treatment, while a woman in New Mexico died from the disease in June.
Unlike in medieval times, plague can now be cured with widely available antibiotics. However, early diagnosis and treatment are critical, as untreated plague can rapidly become fatal, particularly in its pneumonic form.
The update comes amid a frenzy in Western media over what they described as a suspected case of pneumonic plague in Russia’s Irkutsk Region. Some reports claimed that a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died on October 2 after developing pneumonia of unknown origin.
Russian health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor acknowledged the death but said extensive testing had found no evidence of infection associated with her laboratory work and insisted there was no epidemic risk. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that the overwhelming majority of media reports about the incident were “false information.”
On Tuesday, Rospotrebnadzor also offered the US assistance in combating outbreaks of infectious diseases, citing recent measles cases and other infections.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning’s Regular Press Conference on October 8, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
21:12:49 CST
22:12:49 KST

At the invitation of Premier of the State Council Li Qiang, President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé will pay an official visit to China from October 9 to 16.
French President’s Diplomatic Adviser Emmanuel Bonne will be in China from October 9 to 13. Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs Wang Yi will hold a new round of China-France Strategic Dialogue with him.
Xinhua News Agency: To follow up on President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé’s visit to China, can you share the program of the visit and China’s expectations? How does China view its relations with Togo?
Mao Ning: President of the Council of Ministers Faure is an old friend of China. It will be his seventh official visit to China since he became the president of Togo, and the visit fully reflects the high importance Togo attaches to our relations. During the visit, President Xi Jinping will meet with him, and Premier Li Qiang and Chairman of the NPC Standing Committee Zhao Leji will hold talks and meet with him respectively. President Faure will also visit Shaanxi, Fujian, and Guangdong.
China and Togo are comprehensive strategic partners. Since our diplomatic relations were established 54 years ago, our traditional friendship has been growing stronger with time. We firmly support each other on issues related to core interests and major concerns, with fruitful exchanges and cooperation across the board, setting a stellar example of equal treatment between big and small countries and solidarity and cooperation in the Global South. We believe that this visit will bring China-Togo relations to a new height and contribute to building an all-weather China-Africa community with a shared future for the new era.
NHK: It was reported that in the meeting between the Chinese and U.S. presidents, President Trump asked the Chinese side to engage in dialogue with Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi and lift export controls against Japan. Is this true? Did the two sides talk about Japan in the meeting? If so, what was discussed?
Mao Ning: China has released readouts on the meeting between the Chinese and U.S. presidents, which you may refer to.
CRI: Russian Presidential Aide and Chairman of the Maritime Board Nikolai Patrushev is now in China for his visit. Can you brief us with relevant arrangements of this visit? What is China’s comment on current China-Russia relations?
Mao Ning: China and Russia are comprehensive strategic partners of coordination for the new era. Under the strategic guidance of President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin, recent years have seen deepened political mutual trust, closer strategic coordination and continuously expanding cooperation that is mutually beneficial between China and Russia. The two sides have set a fine example of a new type of international relations and relations between neighboring major countries.
This is the first visit to China that Patrushev has made in the capacity of the Chairman of the Maritime Board of Russia. Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs Wang Yi and other department chiefs will meet with Chairman Patrushev respectively to exchange views on bilateral relations and cooperation on maritime affairs. China is ready to take this visit as an opportunity to work with Russia to deepen strategic communication, promote practical cooperation, and keep injecting new momentum of development into China-Russia relations in the new era.
CCTV: On October 5, the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council adopted in Geneva by consensus a resolution proposed by China, on behalf of 53 countries, titled “Promoting accessibility for the full enjoyment of all human rights by all.” Could you share more details on that?
Mao Ning: Building a barrier-free environment is consistent with the vision of ensuring support for persons with disabilities and the elderly, and provides important safeguards for enabling all groups to participate equally and conveniently in social life and fully enjoy all human rights. Many countries commended China’s efforts to promote the vision of “accessibility for all,” and believes that it serves the real and pressing needs of developing countries to call for more technical assistance to developing countries and greater international cooperation in relevant fields.
In 2024, the Human Rights Council adopted the resolution with the same title proposed by China. This was the first resolution specifically on accessibility. The adoption of this resolution a few days ago is of great significance for international community to promote and protect the human rights of all groups, actively address population ageing, leverage AI and other emerging technologies to facilitate information exchange on accessibility, and strengthen global governance and standard-setting in relevant areas. China will follow the guidance of the four global initiatives proposed by President Xi Jinping, and deepen its cooperation with various parties to earnestly implement the vision of “accessibility for all,” improve global governance on human rights, and promote sound progress of the international human rights cause.
Reuters: Sources have told Reuters that China plans to put forward senior public health official Song Li as candidate for the top position at the World Health Organization. One of the sources said the planned nomination was a sign that China wanted to fill a void where the U.S. has stepped back at the WHO. Can the ministry share if China has indeed such nomination plans? And if so, is the U.S.’s withdrawal from UN agencies, such as WHO, a good opportunity for China to step in?
Mao Ning: As the UN specialized agency for health, the WHO plays a leading and coordinating role in global public health governance. At present, multilateralism is facing severe challenges, and the development of global public health remains a long-term and arduous task. Amid the changing landscape and new circumstances, the Director-General has a crucial role to play in ensuring the WHO’s steady and sustained progress.
China’s decision to nominate Doctor Song Li as candidate for the WHO Director-General reflects China’s aspiration to work with all parties for a global community of health for all, and demonstrates China’s firm support for multilateralism and the WHO. We believe that if Doctor Song Li is elected, it will help the WHO play a more positive role in promoting the health and wellbeing of all humanity.
CGTN: Regarding the French President’s Diplomatic Adviser Emmanuel Bonne’s visit to China, can you provide the program and China’s expectation?
Mao Ning: During the French President’s Diplomatic Adviser Emmanuel Bonne’s visit to China, he and Director Wang Yi will hold a new round of China-France Strategic Dialogue to have strategic communication on deepening China-France cooperation in different areas and in-depth exchange of views on international and regional issues of mutual interest.
Last December, President Emmanuel Macron made his fourth state visit to China, during which the two heads-of-state had long, in-depth talks and reached important common understandings regarding strengthening China-France strategic communication, staying committed to openness and cooperation, jointly upholding multilateralism and so on. Through this dialogue, China expects to strengthen coordination and collaboration with France on bilateral and multilateral issues and promote the steady development of China-France and China-Europe relations.
Global Times: It is reported that on October 1, the Tokyo District Court conducted the first public trial of Kodai Murata, a former officer of Japan’s Self-Defense Forces who illegally entered the Chinese embassy in Japan. Murata confessed to illegally entering the embassy with a knife without reservation but denied the charge of criminal intimidation. What is China’s comment?
Mao Ning: It is shockingly malignant for a sitting Japanese SDF officer to break into the Chinese embassy carrying a knife and threaten Chinese diplomatic personnel with violence. This incident seriously violates the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, gravely threatens the safety and security of Chinese diplomatic personnel and premises, and exposes deep-seated problems in Japan, including the rampant spread of right-wing impact and lack of supervision and discipline in the SDF. Whether Japan can deal with the matter seriously in accordance with the law will test the Japanese government’s ability to fulfill its obligations under the international law and affect Japan’s credibility and reputation in the world. We once again urge Japan to bring the perpetrator to account and prevent similar incidents from happening again.
Bloomberg: There are reports that Germany’s president is going to be visiting China. Could you confirm that and let us know the schedule and the list of Chinese leaders he will meet?
Mao Ning: Regarding your question, I have no information to share at the moment.

Mao Ning: I would refer you to China’s competent authorities for anything specific. China always believes that it serves the shared interests of China and the EU to stay committed to openness and cooperation, and resolve economic and trade disputes through equal-footed dialogue and consultation.
Reuters: Crowdstrike said in a report on Wednesday that an unidentified actor behind alleged cyber attacks on South Korean financial institutions used China-developed AI penetration testing tool, Chinese language prompt, as well as have left material suggesting possible links to China, including references to Guangdong and a Chinese university. Inside Operation Vivaldi — how Ukraine uses drones, robots to liberate territory in Donetsk Oblast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:12:30 UTC
22:12:30 KST

Drones above, robots below — inside Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine’s push to recapture territory in Donetsk Oblast
Tsyhan, a combat wing operator of the Darts crew of the NAFO, the 66th Mechanized Brigade, assembles a Dart in the Lyman sector, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 11, 2026. (Diana Delyurman / The Kyiv Independent)
DONETSK OBLAST — On a screen, live footage from a reconnaissance drone shows two men in Ukrainian pixel camouflage dashing in short bursts through the ruins of apartment buildings. Then they vanish into a basement.
It is late summer, and the 3rd Army Corps and attached units are fully engaged in a counteroffensive in the Lyman sector called Operation Vivaldi. Russian forces are trying to recapture Lyman, a city in Donetsk Oblast that Russian officials have claimed their forces control. Ukrainian infantry on the ground tell a different story.
For weeks, the operation ran under a news blackout until 3rd Army Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi made it public on Sept. 15. By late September, the corps said it had retaken 176 square kilometers using closely coordinated infantry, air defense, electronic warfare, aerial drone units, and unmanned ground vehicles.
A four-person job
Watching the video feed are drone operators from the 66th Mechanized Brigade, subordinate to the 3rd Army Corps. They are waiting for a batch of Darts, fixed-wing strike drones, to join the fight for Lyman.
Their commander, call sign Deputat, is rushing to bring the drones. His car races down a road beneath tunnels of anti-drone netting, pine forests on either side, a landscape typical of northern Donetsk Oblast. Out of the darkness, a roadside coffee stand appears, glowing faintly. The car speeds past, then turns off onto rough ground.
"Turn on the electronic warfare device," Deputat orders a soldier in the car.
After some time, Deputat stops, quickly unloads the cargo, shakes hands with the soldiers, and drives off. The crew carries the drones into the dugout. They moved into this position only recently, after pushing closer to the front line. The gray zone is less than 10 kilometers away.
Four men live, sleep, and work in the cramped shelter. Crews usually rotate every couple of weeks, but heavy Russian shelling near the positions can delay a rotation.
In one corner is a workstation: a desk with several screens, one showing a video call with other units, another a live map of Donetsk Oblast. The areas marked gray or occupied are different from the picture Russian commanders paint. The soldiers listen to the call as they prepare to join a combined strike.
For hours, units attached to the 3rd Army Corps have been striking a Russian artillery position with HIMARS rockets and drones. According to the 3rd Army Corps, such missions play a crucial role in the operation by pushing Russian mortar and artillery crews out of the area and clearing the way for the infantry.
On the call, someone says, "If I were in their shoes, I'd hop on a motorcycle and get the hell out of there." The soldiers in the dugout laugh. The Ukrainians say the Russian crew won't abandon its howitzer because its soldiers are more afraid of their own commanders.
The strike is delayed. As the wait drags on, the young men grow restless and step out into the dugout's corridor to smoke. Kalash, a soldier with light stubble, is the oldest in the crew. The others jokingly call him Mom. As he cooks breakfast on a camping stove, the smell of scrambled eggs and sausage fills the damp air.
Finally, the duty officer on the call says, "Let's start the mission."
"This is the NAFO crew. We want to join the strike on the howitzer," replies a soldier with the call sign Intelihent, who is piloting today. Every member of the crew can do every job: assemble the drone, prepare it for launch, navigate for the pilot, and fly the strike.
Tsyhan, tall and tanned, assembles a Dart. It reminds him of building Lego as a kid, he says. He and Kalash carry the drone out into the field, set it up for launch, and talk over the radio with the men in the dugout.
"Get out of there," comes the voice over the radio.
"Launch," Tsyhan replies.
The drone must fly several dozen kilometers. Intelihent works the controls while Bratok, a dark-haired soldier, helps him navigate. Back in the dugout, all four stare at the screen, fidgeting nervously on the wooden bench.
"NAFO, locking on target," Intelihent says.
The drone strikes. Direct hit. The men cheer and clink cans of energy drink.
On the reconnaissance drone's feed, a stand of trees bursts into flames. Russian soldiers run out of a dugout and try to put out the fire. Then the feed cuts out. Pleased, the men post screenshots to the platoon's group chat. But someone on the call reports that the smoke is clearing and the target has survived. They must strike again.
"Don't worry, we've got plenty of planes," Kalash tells the others.
But the threat of retaliatory strikes looms over the dugout. Drone operators are among Russia's top targets.
"I think it'll be a few days before they come after us," Tsyhan says.
Eventually, several Ukrainian units working together destroy the Russian artillery position. The 3rd Army Corps said coordination between neighboring units played a key role in the operation.
The men finish the breakfast Kalash made. Some stretch out on camping mats on the wooden benches and sleep fully dressed. Another strike request could come at any moment.
Bratok is on duty, keeping an eye on the screens. To pass the time, he flips through live feeds from reconnaissance drones and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). On the screens, the war plays out in real time across the Lyman sector. The video feed from a ground robot catches his eye: a dirt road, and in the corner a tiny call sign that reads Kuzya.
"Kuzya is a legend!" Bratok says.
read also
Robots take over logistics
Elsewhere in the Lyman sector, Kuzya himself is watching the same feed. The young redhead was one of the first UGV operators in the 66th Brigade's tank battalion. He used to be a driver, risking his life to bring food, medicine, and ammunition to the infantry. He still delivers supplies, but at far less risk. His UGVs can carry half a metric ton of cargo and keep going even after hitting a mine.
The battalion began building up its UGV capabilities in early 2026. They learned how to use ground drones from the 3rd Army Corps. Now, the 66th Brigade ranks among the top five units for UGV use, according to the Delta system's June 2026 rating. According to the team, its 20 operators now cover most of the battalion's logistics, running 100 to 150 missions a month and rarely taking a day off.
At first, the battalion's commanders were skeptical of the robots, until a heavily mined road left them unable to resupply a group of Mavic operators. Today, UGVs play an important role in Operation Vivaldi. The 96th Separate Support Battalion’s robots move ahead of the infantry and clear mines. Some are carried behind Russian lines by drones and launch an assault. But less visible work, logistics, matters just as much.
"Soldiers win battles, but logistics wins wars," says Aibolit, a burly man whose long beard gives him a Viking look. At the UGV hub, he decides which cargo goes on which vehicle.
The increased use of UGVs for logistics in the 3rd Army Corps and its attached units means infantry can reach the front line in armored vehicles or on foot, carrying only light backpacks. Reliable logistics also lets support teams deliver small comforts to the front, lifting the morale of infantrymen who may hold the same position for a month.
Orders come in every day. A soldier can order something in the morning and be drinking a soda in the gray zone by midnight. "It's like ordering pizza," Aibolit says.
"Is the sky clear?"
As evening falls, the men prepare two vehicles, open platforms on massive wheels, for a mission. They load packs of bottled water, fuel canisters, a generator, and sealed boxes of food the soldiers ordered. It takes them only minutes.
"Is the sky clear?" Aibolit asks over the radio.
"Negative. Lancet threat," comes the reply.
"We're holding all movement," Aibolit says.
read also
A drone icon flashes on their screens. It seems to be heading straight for the hub. "Maybe it'll come here, maybe somewhere else," one of them says, and shrugs. The soldiers play it down, saying their town is quiet, yet not a day goes by without a Russian strike. To disrupt Ukrainian logistics, Russian forces freely use guided bombs, including against targets with no apparent military value.
Once the threat has passed, the men drive the vehicles out into the yard. A few minutes later, the robots roll off into the darkness.
Kuzya usually takes the vehicles into the gray zone, where the ground is heavily mined. He knows every pothole and bush on the route. His screen is almost entirely black, except for a stretch of cratered road lit by the robot's headlight.
Along the way, he passes wrecked cars marked with a white "Z." Stray dogs run up and bark at the strange visitor. Before long, they get used to it and trot alongside until they lose interest. Kuzya smiles.
Eventually, the robot stops. Soldiers in camouflage appear on the black-and-white screen and quickly unload the cargo. One walks up to the camera and gives Kuzya a thumbs-up before they disappear into the woods.
Kuzya turns the robot around to reload for the next mission. On a narrow dirt road, it meets another robot, and the two little vehicles circle each other as if they were dancing.
That evening, Deputat drives back from another delivery to his soldiers, beneath the netting, stars peeking through the mesh. A burned-out SUV, recently hit by a Russian Lancet, lies by the roadside.
"When you're coming back from the positions and you see the coffee stand, you know you're safe," he says.

Epicentr has launched a Ukrainian fashion section on its epicentrk.ua marketplace, which currently features more than 100 Ukrainian clothing, footwear and accessories brands, the company's press service said.
"The scale and infrastructure of Epicentr give Ukrainian fashion brands access to millions of potential buyers (...) We want to break the stereotype that designer fashion cannot be represented on a large marketplace. We are convinced that Ukrainian brands can enter the mass market while retaining their uniqueness and exclusivity," Epicentr Marketplace CEO Yulia Pinteskul said, according to the press release.
The company said the new area is being developed in partnership with Kapsula, a fashion retailer specializing in cooperation with Ukrainian manufacturers of designer clothing and footwear.
The new marketplace section was launched in September and currently offers about 10,000 product listings, including brands already known to Ukrainian consumers such as Fiore Bianco, Foberini, get dressed, Inro, J.D.Wool, Marie Fresh, MMSW, MY x MY, OUN, Piel Cosmetics, Rosca, The Lace and Fire Rabbit, among others. In addition to clothing, footwear and accessories, the site also offers beauty, perfume and lifestyle products from well-known Ukrainian manufacturers.
The company said the new category is intended to expand the presence of Ukrainian fashion brands in online commerce. Sellers will be able to use Epicentr's infrastructure for order delivery, fitting and returns.
Customers will receive free delivery, while sellers will pay a fixed UAH 35 fee covering logistics costs if an order is refused or a product is returned, including delivery in both directions.
The company plans to expand the category's product range and attract new Ukrainian brands. Planned technological solutions include a virtual fitting room to help customers determine clothing and footwear sizes when placing an order.
According to the company, epicentrk.ua receives about 25 million visits per month on average. Epicentr's logistics infrastructure includes more than 3,000 parcel lockers and 200 order pickup centers across Ukraine.
The Epicentr group is an omnichannel ecosystem comprising the Epicentr and Nova Linia retail chains, the epicentrk.ua online store, the Epicentr-Ahro agricultural holding, Epicenter Ceramic Corporation ceramic tile plants, the Osmoлoda CBM woodworking enterprise and logistics facilities. As of early 2026, the retailer's network comprised 72 shopping centers in Ukraine.
According to the Unified State Register of Legal Entities and Individual Entrepreneurs, the owners of Epicentr K LLC are Oleksandr Hereha (51.3%), Halyna Hereha (47.97%) and Tetiana Surzhyk (0.73%).

13:09:49 UTC
22:09:49 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said the global financial system remains resilient but warned that lower growth, repeated supply shocks and evolving market structures pose new long-term challenges.
The global financial system successfully withstood recent periods of uncertainty without major breakdowns in liquidity or trading conditions, Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said on Thursday at the Istanbul Economic Forum.
The two-day forum was organized by the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye to address global economic policy challenges by gathering central bank governors and high-level policymakers from around the world, including the US and the UK.
Bailey noted that the world economy currently faces major uncertainties stemming from conflicts in the Middle East alongside vulnerabilities in sovereign debt markets and asset valuations.
He warned that the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence financing created new exposures, even though AI also presented potential growth dividends.
The governor emphasized that weaker potential growth and frequent negative supply shocks, such as the Covid pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, disrupted economic supply capacities.
He pointed out that negative supply shocks pushed inflation and output in opposite directions, which created significant difficulties for monetary policy.
Central banks must make forward-looking judgments and update them as evidence changes to prevent temporary shocks from becoming persistent inflation, Bailey added.
He stated that strong banks and solid corporate balance sheets give policymakers the necessary room to respond to crises without triggering financial collapses.
Bailey highlighted that lower growth and repeated supply shocks weakened public finances and increased pressure on governments to provide support.
He observed that global government bond markets changed profoundly as leveraged investors now play a much larger role than traditional long-term investors.
This new market structure increased the capacity to absorb government debt but also brought greater fragility since deleveraging in one market can spread quickly to others, he explained.
Bailey called for policies that pursue sustainable growth and maintain credible monetary and fiscal frameworks.
He stressed that artificial intelligence and robotics can drive scientific discovery and raise prosperity if authorities deploy them safely.
The governor concluded that financial markets must improve their core resilience to absorb future shocks without amplifying them.

European intelligence services weigh possible fallout after German ex-spy chief's arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:09:27 UTC
22:09:27 KST

European intelligence services weigh possible fallout after German ex-spy chief's arrest
BERLIN, Oct 8 - European intelligence services are trying to find out whether secret information was compromised by former German spy chief August Hanning and what risks this raised, intelligence officials said following his arrest this week.
The arrest of Hanning, a former head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence service, on suspicion of espionage and treason has sent shock waves through the security and intelligence sectors. His former chief of staff at the agency was also arrested.
German media have said the case does not appear to involve Russia. But allegations that hundreds of confidential documents were trafficked, and that intelligence may have been passed to foreign officials, have dealt a blow to the BND's international credibility at a time of rising security alarms.
Days earlier, the current head of the BND said Germany faced a real risk of a violent conflict with Russia, accusing Moscow of mounting a "shadow war" of hybrid and drone attacks.
"This is a total disaster," said a German security official, describing the possible implications for the BND's relations with partner services as "very, very serious".
Hanning, who left the BND in 2005, set up a private consultancy business after retiring from public service and faces allegations of agreeing to pay an official identified as Manfred D. to supply him with confidential documents.
Manfred D., who was chief of staff to a succession of BND heads including Hanning and who retired in March 2026, is accused of supplying him with nearly 2,000 documents, at least some of them classified as confidential.
Hanning is suspected of having briefed foreign intelligence officials using information from the documents. It remains unclear what was passed on and who the other parties were.
Azerbaijan has denied reports of contacts between Hanning and Azeri officials. Prosecutors have declined to comment.
RISK ASSESSMENTS
German media said many of the documents concerned were briefing papers prepared for the Chancellor's office or other senior officials, rather than raw intelligence material.
One European intelligence official told Reuters that some European services were now conducting reviews of the risk to material they have shared with Germany in the past.
Another official from an allied service said they were checking on potential damage and expected all other partner agencies to be doing the same.
A third Western official said intelligence from the CIA was included in documents stolen from the BND. The CIA has not commented on the case.
The allegations cover a period when Hanning was no longer working for the government, but an interior ministry spokesperson said officials were investigating "possible breaches of confidentiality regulations" by Hanning during his service.
Following a victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in a state election in eastern Germany last month, German intelligence officials have fretted about the risk of leaks to Moscow by Russia-friendly officials with access to confidential information.
But the Hanning case has caused particular shock because Hanning and Manfred D. came from deep within the security establishment.
It is a sensitive time for the intelligence services as Germany builds up its defence forces to confront the perceived threat from Russia. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government approved plans this year to beef up the intelligence services, set up after World War Two with much more circumscribed powers than many of their partner agencies.
Hanning has not commented on the allegations. Pluteos, a Swiss-based security consultancy where Hanning served as board chairman, and one of his lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The German news magazine Der Spiegel quoted one of his lawyers as saying their client had confidential documents in his possession but denying he had harmed national security by passing on or selling information to any third parties.
"My client is being wrongfully prosecuted," the magazine quoted a statement from the lawyer as saying.
SPOTLIGHT ON EX-OFFICIALS' BUSINESS CAREERS
The case has again put the spotlight on the business careers of former officials, even where there is no suggestion of wrongdoing. Days earlier, former Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder, who has faced criticism over his links to Russian business and President Vladimir Putin, joined the supervisory board of Russian retailer Hyperglobus.
The parliamentary committee that oversees intelligence services said it was "problematic" that former civil servants with in-depth knowledge of security matters or intelligence take up private-sector roles without being vetted.
Konstantin von Notz, a member of the parliamentary supervisory committee, said Hanning's case made clear there were "structural problems" that the government should address.
"Confidence in the integrity of the work carried out by the German intelligence services must not be betrayed, particularly in view of the clear expectations of our partner intelligence services," he said. "That would be disastrous given the current security situation."
Senior intelligence officials in many countries regularly provide security consultancy services after leaving government service, but officials in Germany said the Hanning case suggested stricter controls were necessary.
Andy Grote, interior minister for the state government of Hamburg, said the case raised questions about "what kinds of employment and business activities should actually be permitted for senior members of security agencies during and after their term of service." REUTERS

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the "gang" in Kiev are part of the same corruption schemes, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
She noted that the EU has firmly embarked on a path of confrontation with Russia, which will only worsen its problems.
TASS has compiled the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman's key statements.
Merz and Kiev "gang" tied to corruption schemes
Ukraine is so deeply mired in corruption that there's little Zelensky can now do to conceal the true scale of the problem: "Ukraine is so deeply mired in corruption that the full extent of the problem can no longer be concealed. Zelensky's efforts to control the flow of information have done little to hide it, leaving only one mainstream television broadcaster while blocking other television news sources."
"Merz and this entire gang, of course, are part of all these corruption schemes. And he is coming [to Kiev] in part to discuss how the money will be distributed after being funneled through the Kiev regime."
Merz made German taxpayers cover the cost by promising Zelensky a new military aid package worth about €1 billion during his visit to Kiev: "These political bankrupts in Berlin have made German taxpayers cover the cost. They had just received concrete results of their policies. They realized that their own citizens not only do not support their policies in their own country, but are demonstrating their absolute rejection of them."
"It seems that Merz is once again emptying his own citizens' pockets, almost as if in retaliation. He is doing so despite their clear understanding of how futile Zelensky's efforts are."
The current German authorities need war, and Merz's actions prove it.
Nord Stream investigation
Russia will continue working through international forums to identify and hold accountable those responsible for the Nord Stream explosions: "We will continue our efforts, including through international forums, to identify and hold accountable not only the perpetrators but also the true masterminds behind this unprecedented terrorist attack."
NATO actions
Moscow views the possible deployment of additional NATO forces in the Baltic states as an escalation: "We unequivocally view the potential deployment of additional NATO forces, including US troops, and the creation of corresponding military infrastructure in the Baltic states as an escalation."
Worsening problems for EU
"The more problems the EU faces because of its own mistakes and miscalculations in its hybrid war against Russia, the more incredible and large-scale plans it attributes to Russia. It accuses Russia of having plans that do not, in fact, exist."
The EU has firmly embarked on a path of confrontation with Russia, which will only worsen its problems: "The European Union embarked on a path of confrontation with our country, initially under pressure from the United States and then simply out of inertia. And this path will not allow it to resolve its pressing issues, indeed, it will never allow it to do so."
The EU leadership "deliberately and consciously chooses to ignore this simple truth."
Merz is coming to Kiev "both to improve his ratings and to escape his own citizens," as well as to avoid criticism and public discontent within Germany.
Moscow has no plans for an armed conflict with Western Europe, and Russia is not threatening anyone: "If Germany's top intelligence official is publicly voicing his own fantasies, that means Europe really is in great danger. Let me repeat just in case: Russia is not threatening anyone. The Russian president and foreign minister have repeatedly stated that Moscow has no plans for an armed conflict with Western Europe."
Statements on Italy
Russia does not interfere in elections abroad, unlike Western countries: "There can be no question of Russian interference in electoral processes abroad. This is not our style. Western political elites openly interfere in election campaigns in full view of the world. At times, they even abduct presidents, put direct pressure on political groups in countries they are interested in, and, as I said, consider themselves free to do whatever they want."
Italian authorities' allegations of Russian interference in elections are disrespectful to Italians: "It is simply disrespectful to Italians to make such statements at the level of the foreign minister or any other minister, playing the so-called Russian card."
Middle East

Germany lifts 2026 growth forecast to 1.3% as exports, public spending drive recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:08:57 UTC
22:08:57 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Germany on Thursday raised its 2026 economic growth forecast to 1.3% from 0.5%, as stronger exports and public spending underpin a recovery despite the Middle East conflict and rising energy prices.
Presenting the autumn forecast, Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche also announced projected growth of 1.1% for 2027 and 0.6% for 2028.
The economy expanded strongly in the first half of 2026, driven primarily by exports and public consumption, the ministry said.
Foreign trade is expected to provide the main growth stimulus this year.
Exports received a boost in the second quarter as buyers built inventories of energy-intensive goods produced in Germany amid global shortages.
Fiscal stimulus through special funds and defense spending is also expected to support public investment and government consumption throughout the forecast period.
Private demand, however, is expected to recover more slowly.
Energy-driven price increases are projected to keep household spending subdued initially, despite continued growth in real wages.
Private investment is expected to recover only gradually next year, held back by geopolitical uncertainty, low capacity utilization, higher material and financing costs, and structural challenges.
The ministry said the outlook remains heavily dependent on developments in the Middle East and Ukraine.
A lasting resolution to the conflicts could strengthen the recovery by lowering energy prices, while persistently elevated commodity and energy costs could put further pressure on businesses and households.

Slovakia’s Fico calls nude Trump statue a sign of EU decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:08:45 UTC
22:08:45 KST

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico on Thursday called for the removal of a satirical statue of U.S. President Donald Trump from the European Parliament, describing it as a “sign of the decline of the entire European Union.”
Writing on X, Fico said that while he does not agree with all of Trump’s policies, “insulting our partners on official premises demonstrates a profound failure to understand the times we live in.”
The sculpture, titled The Orange Plague, was unveiled Tuesday by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt in the Parliament building in Strasbourg. The 2.6-meter work depicts a nude, gold-leaf-covered Trump perched on a frail man’s shoulders, holding a golf club and scales of justice. A plaque reads: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden.”
Advertisement
“It is sad that the leadership of the European Parliament, in its blindness, can no longer distinguish between the legitimate right to hold a different opinion and the actions of spiritually bankrupt individuals, adventurers and lunatics,” Fico added, before asking whether the Parliament would tolerate similar depictions of the French president or German chancellor.
The statue was removed on Wednesday, a spokesperson for the European Parliament said after publication. It was part of a two-day exhibition at the initiative of Danish left-wing MEP Per Clausen.
POLITICO was present at the unveiling, where visitors clamored for miniature replicas of the sculpture, which were distributed in several colors. The statue stands in a prominent spot at the entrance to Parliament’s Winston Churchill building, before the corridor linking MEPs’ and Commission officials’ offices with the plenary chamber.
Galschiøt said the work was intended to confront Trump’s policies and start a debate about how the U.S. president was “destroying the world’s only chance to counter the climate catastrophe.”
Clausen defended the installation in a statement. “If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture … then they have no place on the world stage,” he said.
“MEPs have the possibility to hold cultural events/ exhibitions in the European Parliament … These cultural events and exhibitions by Members shall be authorised in advance by the Quaestors who assess the compliance with the rules in place,” the European Parliament press service said in a statement to POLITICO.
Advertisement
“The rules in place outline that cultural events and exhibitions shall under no circumstances be offensive or of an inflammatory nature or contradictory to the values on which the Union is founded or likely to give rise to disturbances in the designated exhibition areas,” the statement says.
Fico has cultivated ties with Trump, meeting him at Mar-a-Lago in January to discuss closer cooperation, including civilian nuclear energy. He has praised the MAGA movement as “a vision that urgently resonates not only in the United States but across the world.”
The sculpture was previously displayed at protests in Copenhagen and the COP30 summit in Brazil. It is due to appear at next month’s COP31 conference in Antalya, Türkiye.
Trump has not commented on the installation.
Gerardo Fortuna contributed to this report. This article was updated.

Report says German ex-spy chief suspected of passing secrets to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:07:57 UTC
22:07:57 KST

Ayhan Simsek
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
German investigators are examining whether former intelligence chief August Hanning shared sensitive information with a man from China's intelligence apparatus, news magazine Spiegel reported on Thursday, citing several sources familiar with the case.
Hanning's lawyer rejected the allegations. "My client is being wrongly pursued," Leon Kruse told Spiegel. He said Hanning had been in possession of confidential documents, but added: "What is incorrect, however, is the allegation that he passed on information contained in them to the detriment of the Federal Republic of Germany — let alone in exchange for payment." Further investigations will show that, Kruse said.
The federal prosecutor's office in Karlsruhe, which is investigating the 80-year-old on suspicion of treason, espionage and other offenses, declined to comment on the alleged China link.
Prosecutors say nearly 2,000 files were handed over
Hanning led Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, from 1998 until 2005. He was arrested on Tuesday together with his former office director, Manfred D.
Investigators say that after Hanning left the agency, D. supplied him for years with confidential documents from the BND. By June 2022, he had delivered "nearly 2,000 documents" to Hanning, the federal prosecutor's office said.
Prosecutors say Hanning used these documents in at least one case while preparing a security report, as part of his private consulting work, for a member of a foreign intelligence service. They also say he was in intensive contact with another foreign intelligence official. Prosecutors have not named any country.
German public broadcasters WDR and NDR reported earlier that the service in contact with Hanning was not Russian.
Alleged links to a retired Chinese general
Spiegel claimed that the suspected foreign contact is Wang Jianzheng, a retired Chinese major general and diplomat with ties to Hanning.
Wang served at China's mission in East Berlin from 1987 to 1990 and later returned to Germany, most recently as military attache until 2013. He is regarded as one of Beijing's leading experts on Germany.
Hanning made several visits to China after his retirement, Spiegel reported. In 2017, he and Wang apparently met at an official reception in the eastern Chinese city of Huaibei. A city record says the talks covered cooperation and economic development, and that the two jointly visited local companies.
The federal prosecutor's office declined to say whether Hanning's connection to Wang is part of the investigation.

U.K. Expands Sanctions to Cover 90% of Russian Oil Output, Shadow Fleet and Finance Networks

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:07:40 UTC
22:07:40 KST

Britain on Thursday announced sanctions targeting 38 Russian energy companies, shadow fleet oil tankers and financial networks that allegedly fuel Russia’s war effort.
“The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences,” the Foreign Office said in a statement.
London added 17 entities and individuals supplying high-priority goods to Russia, including importers of machine tools and electronics key to the country’s ballistic missile and drone capabilities.
One of the sanctioned individuals is Dutch national Alexander Jan Hendrik Tattersall, who is allegedly associated with the sanctioned Turkish trader Redwing Metal.
Britain sanctioned two Russian energy producers, saying the restrictions now cover more than 90% of Russia’s total oil production capacity.
An additional 12 tankers were also sanctioned, expanding the total number of targeted shadow fleet vessels to more than 600.
Targeting Russia’s alternative payment systems and crypto exchanges used to bypass Western sanctions, Britain designated five financial entities, including one registered in Canada and three in Kyrgyzstan.
The financial measures follow the U.S. Treasury’s recent crackdown on Russia’s A7 shadow banking network, which the U.S. claimed to have processed through sub-agents more than $17 billion in global transactions between January 2025 and June 2026.
The Foreign Office claimed two of the newly sanctioned payment platforms directly facilitated transactions for the A7 platform.

Russian truckmaker signs major deal with Mali

Russian truckmaker signs major deal with Mali
Russian truckmaker KAMAZ has signed a contract reportedly worth about $51.5 million to supply vehicles to Mali, as the landlocked West African country seeks to strengthen its transport network and secure essential supplies.
The deal with the Malian Transport and Logistics Company (SMTL-SA) was signed in Bamako on Wednesday at a ceremony attended by Finance Minister Alousseni Sanou and Transport Minister Dembele Madina Sissoko. Malian broadcaster Kati24 put its value at above 30 billion CFA francs.
In a press release on Thursday, KAMAZ said the contract falls under an intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Mali and aims to expand the country’s capacity to transport food and industrial goods. “In addition to the equipment supply, vehicle repair and maintenance workshops will be established in Mali’s capital, and the possibility of assembling trucks in the country is under discussion,” the company stated.
According to the statement, the parties also discussed spare parts, technology transfer, and training Malian technicians in Kazan, the capital of Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan. KAMAZ did not specify vehicle numbers, models or delivery dates.
The deal comes less than two weeks after Mali’s government approved the creation of SMTL-SA on September 25. The public company is intended to improve transport and storage of strategic goods, including fuel and agricultural products, amid supply disruptions and dependence on regional trade corridors.
KAMAZ already has a supply history in Mali, which Russian state-owned industrial conglomerate Rostec listed among the truckmaker’s African markets in 2023.
The company has also supplied vehicles to other African countries, including Senegal, which KAMAZ described as one of its important export markets. It supplied 167 vehicles to the country, mainly KAMAZ-5460 tractor units for transporting containers from the port of Dakar, and trained Senegalese drivers and mechanics in 2021.
The engagement comes despite Washington’s decision to sanction KAMAZ in June 2022 amid the Ukraine conflict, citing its supply of armored vehicles to Russia’s military.
The latest agreement adds to Mali’s growing economic ties with Russia in recent years as part of efforts by the transitional authorities of the Sahel nation to assert control over strategic industries. In June 2025, Mali launched construction of a gold refinery with Russia’s Yadran to boost national revenues through domestic gold processing, with the state holding a 62% stake. The refinery project followed disputes with Western mining companies, including Canada’s Barrick and Australia’s Resolute Mining, over alleged unpaid taxes and the implementation of a new mining code aimed at increasing state revenues and ownership.

Meetings under the roadmap are expected to be held alternately in Paris and Ankara, with the first planned for the final quarter of 2026, subject to agreement between the sides.

Türkiye has completed preparations to submit the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement to parliament for approval, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, emphasising that the pact is designed for mutual defence and does not authorise offensive military operations.

Ankara weighs defensive support for Saudi Arabia

He said Türkiye and Pakistan had discussed what support could be provided to Saudi Arabia against attacks from Yemen’s Houthi group, while stressing that efforts to resolve the Yemen conflict through peace and dialogue would continue.
Current reporting says Ankara is particularly assessing defensive capabilities, including air-defence support
Fidan warns against Black Sea escalation
Turning to the Russia-Ukraine war, Fidan warned that the conflict must not turn the Black Sea into another front.
“We must never allow the Black Sea to turn into a new front of conflict,” he said, describing the war as a major threat to regional and global stability.
Fidan said Türkiye had worked since the start of the conflict to prevent fighting from spilling into the Black Sea, citing its implementation of the Montreux Convention and its role in the Black Sea Grain Initiative.
He said intensified Russian and Ukrainian attacks ahead of winter were increasingly affecting maritime safety, including Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned vessels and ships carrying Turkish personnel.
Fidan also warned that attacks on civilian vessels threatened lives, property, navigation and the environment, while disruptions to grain shipments could worsen food-security pressures, particularly in Africa.
Türkiye pushes for Gaza aid and political settlement

====================================================================================================

Student Protesters in France are Holding Signs Referencing May 1968. Here’s Why It’s Significant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:04:57 UTC
22:04:57 KST

French students took to the streets again Thursday and blockaded some high schools as they demanded action from the government they say is underfunding the country’s education system. Now in its third week, the wave of protests has seen hundreds of thousands march after rows over staffing shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and dilapidated buildings reached a crisis point.
The protest movement went nationwide on Tuesday, after student unions called for a wider support of their mobilization, with parents, teachers, and activists heeding the call. Some protests have turned violent, with attendees lighting fires and hurling projectiles, and police using tear gas and water cannons. Since the protests began, at least 6,547 people have been arrested or stopped by police, said France’s Interior Ministry. Hundreds of students and police officers have been injured. The French Education Ministry told TIME that as of midday Thursday, local time, 157 schools remain closed.
Throughout the protests, students and other attendees have held up various signs calling for change. A common theme has emerged, as many of the homemade banners mention the year 1968—and more specifically, May 1968. That’s in reference to the nationwide protests initiated by a student movement in 1968 that led to millions of workers striking and nearly toppled the government.
During the blockade of the University of Perpignan Via Domitia on Tuesday, a banner raised on the gates contained a warning, which roughly translated to “You’re trying to pull a fast one on us, we'll give you May '68.” Elsewhere, as students gathered in Reforme Square in Marseille, a protester held a sign that read “Generation 67 is doing May 68,” thought to be in reference to the Gen Alpha 6-7 trend. In Paris, someone held a black and white sign of a larger figure with their hand over the mouth of a youngster, emblazoned with the phrase “sois jeune et tais-toi,” which means “be young and shut up.” That same slogan was used during the 1968 protests.
“1968 was a seminal moment in the protest history of France,” says Chris Reynolds, professor of contemporary European history at Nottingham Trent University. “Not only because of the sheer enormity of what happened, but that it started out as a smallish student protest that within a very short space of time mushroomed to become arguably the greatest strike in French history.”
What happened in 1968 is anything but a distant memory, experts tell TIME. Not only do the youth of France draw inspiration from the rallying of a generation, lawmakers are also mindful of how powerful such protests can be.
“Ever since 1968, there has been a fear within the state that it could happen again,” says Reynolds. “This idea that somehow the students could be the starting point of a movement that would then elicit support from other sectors of society, leading to a much greater crisis.”
What happened in May 1968?
Students at the Nanterre campus of the University of Paris held protests across 1967 and 1968 in opposition of rules they viewed to be too restrictive and conservative.
“It was a crisis of education. At that point, universities were expanding very quickly in the 1960s,” says Robert Gildea, a professor of European and French history at the University of Oxford.
“Universities then were also very conservative and hierarchical,” he adds, noting that a lack of communication between the faculty and students led to growing frustrations.
One argument centered on restrictions on dormitory visits that stopped male and female students staying in each other’s rooms.
In May 1968, when the Nanterre campus was shut down in an effort to dampen escalating protests, the movement moved to the Sorbonne campus in Paris’ Latin Quarter. Students barricaded themselves within the university grounds and called for a reform of the university system, while accusing French President Charles de Gaulle of running a "police state.” Clashes ensued between riot police and student protesters, hundreds of which were arrested. A particularly violent clash in the early hours of May 11 garnered nationwide attention.
The protest movement expanded when trade unions came on board and organized a series of strikes across the country, demanding better pay and conditions for workers in factories and other industries. At the height of the protests, around 10 million workers went on strike, bringing France to the brink and raising concerns in government about the impact on the economy.
President De Gaulle dissolved parliament and cited a state of emergency. He called a snap election in June, which his conservative party ultimately won as French voters gravitated toward the promise of restored stability. The protest movement lost momentum and withered, but it left a lasting impact.
Gildea says many students now reference 1968 from a place of pride, while also warning a revolution could happen if the youth bands together.
“1968 was the last huge explosion of students and workers, which nearly brought the state down,” he says. “The French are very proud of their revolutionary tradition and all subsequent revolutions want to reference it as an appeal for legitimacy.”
In the years since 1968, French students have often taken to the streets to air their grievances, with notable demonstrations happening in 2006 and 2018—all of which have drawn comparisons to 1968.
“It remains this recurring reference point in French history, which seems to be passed down from generation to generation, without fail,” Reynolds says.

Iran is reviewing US feedback on Tehran’s proposed seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and expects to respond within the next few days, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Thursday.
“The negotiation process is still ongoing, and messages are being exchanged through mediators,” Araghchi said, according to the official IRNA news agency.
“We presented our proposal, which was called the ‘seven-day plan,’ and we heard the Americans’ views in response,” he added.
“We are currently reviewing them. I believe we will respond within a few days,” he said.
The seven-day initiative centers on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
What is the 7-day plan?
Araghchi said in late September that Iran could reopen the strategic waterway within seven days if Washington accepted the proposal conveyed through Qatari mediation.
Under the plan, the US would be expected to take agreed steps during the first four or five days, allowing normal navigation through the strait to resume on the sixth day and negotiations on a final agreement to begin on the seventh.
Tehran’s demands include an end to hostilities, the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of restrictions on Iranian oil exports and an end to the US naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The proposal was discussed through Qatari mediation during indirect contacts between Iran and the US on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in September.

Tension in Hormuz
Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz restricted while demanding that Washington fulfill commitments under a June memorandum of understanding. Iran says the waterway will not fully reopen until Iran’s conditions are met and US commitments are implemented.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, while the US later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Washington and Tehran later signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

By Kārlis Mārtiņš Gulbis, Investment Analyst, Signet Bank.
In September the war found its second chokepoint, and markets followed. After Hormuz came the Bab el-Mandeb: the Houthis seized the Yemeni port of Mokha and then Perim Island, which sits in the strait itself. At the same time, drones launched from Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to shut its East-West pipeline, the kingdom’s main route around Hormuz. Brent jumped to around USD 110/bbl, its highest since May. Refined products felt the squeeze most as US diesel hit a record USD 6.53/gal on 22 September, and with midterms on 3 November Trump backed a ban on diesel exports, which had reached a record 1.6m bbl/d in August.
As expected, central banks stopped looking through the energy shock, and three of the majors raised rates within eight days. Then came the flash PMI – US business activity grew at its fastest pace since July 2021, and the selloff that followed carried the 30-year Treasury yield above 5.61% on 29 September, a level last seen in 2002.
The S&P 500 slipped 0.5% and the Dow fell 4.3%, ending a five-month winning streak, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.9% as technology was the only S&P 500 sector to finish higher. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq still closed a second straight quarterly gain. Financials, down around 7%, had their worst month since March 2023, while the STOXX 600 lost 2.5%, ending its own five month run. Gold fell about 6.5%, and Brent eased back to around USD 100/bbl at the end of the month
Back in the hiking business
Strong data left the Fed little choice. August payrolls rose 162k, about three times expectations, and CPI held at 3.4% YoY with energy up 16.3%. On 16 September the FOMC voted 12-0 to raise its target range by 25bp to 3.75%-4.00%, its first hike since July 2023, and 16 of 18 officials projected another hike before year end. Trump replied within hours that US rates “should be 1%, or less”.
The ECB had lifted its deposit rate to 2.50% on 10 September, and the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25%, the highest since 1995, on 18 September.
Five percent and counting
In August the pressure on long-dated debt came from supply worries; in September it came from central banks. Almost all of the 49bp rise in the 10-year Treasury yield, to 5.29%, ran through real yields, with the 10-year TIPS yield up about 44bp, its fastest climb in four years. However, this time a central bank blinked: the Bank of England slowed QT, will no longer sell its longest-dated gilts and paused active sales pending a review before April 2027.
France moved from strained to stressed, as the OAT-Bund spread broke 100bp for the first time since the euro area debt crisis and reached 140bp in early October, when the government presented a 2027 budget built on EUR 54b of savings.
A red carpet and a short extension
Xi Jinping’s 23-25 September state visit, his first to Washington since 2015, came with full ceremony but modest results. The trade truce was extended only to 10 January 2027, two months beyond its November expiry. The two sides agreed lower tariffs on USD 30b of non-sensitive goods each way, Chinese purchases of at least 10m tonnes of US coal in both 2027 and 2028 and a new dialogue on advanced AI, but rare earths stayed unresolved after China’s magnet shipments to the US fell 21%.
Pacing the frontier
On 12 September Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI labs to slow frontier development so safety work can keep up, Sam Altman and Elon Musk agreed. Two days later the Philadelphia
Semiconductor Index fell 5.9% and the KOSPI 3.3%. On 25 September OpenAI paused training of its most capable models after an agent slipped past internet restrictions in testing.
Meanwhile, local opposition blocked or delayed 45 US data centers worth USD 68b in Q2. Spending did not slow however as Nvidia rose almost 3% after a record USD 150b buyback increase.
Micron’s fiscal Q4 revenue reached USD 54.2b, nearly five times a year earlier, and it guided USD 61.5b for this quarter
Firmer dollar and tarnished metals
Currencies remain confined to their familiar range, though shifts in market behavior hint at rising volatility. The dollar has edged toward the stronger side of its neutral zone, and although its next move remains unsettled, we still favor buying it on dips. A EUR/USD climb to 1.1600 would signal renewed dollar weakness, while support at 1.1150-1.1200 should ideally hold, allowing a rebound toward 1.1400-1.1500; failing that, a far steeper decline could follow. Precious metals remain unattractive, with gold especially vulnerable to a deeper fall.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan (R) and his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban (AA Photo)

“The necessary work for submitting the agreement to parliament has reached its conclusion... We have almost completed our own work,” Fidan said at a joint news conference with Hungarian counterpart, Anita Orban, in Ankara.
His remarks came days after the three countries held an emergency meeting of the Mecca pact’s strategic political and defense committee in Riyadh on Oct. 5.
Fidan said the meeting was primarily held to discuss attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, as well as steps needed to institutionalize the alliance.

The Mecca pact was signed in August, shortly before the Houthis launched their offensive in Yemen.
Fidan said Türkiye and Pakistan had also discussed how Ankara could contribute to Saudi Arabia’s defense against Houthi attacks. At the same time, he said Türkiye was working to resolve the conflict through diplomacy and dialogue.
“This is not an offensive pact,” Fidan said. “Türkiye will not send troops to another country’s territory to carry out an attack there.”
The three countries’ defense cooperation comes as Saudi Arabia faces an increased security threat from the conflict in neighboring Yemen, where the Houthis control large parts of the country.
Fidan said the alliance’s institutional structure would also be strengthened as part of the ongoing work.
