Dmitri Teperik: Ida-Viru County should be pro-Estonian, European and successful
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:52:00 UTC
21:52:00 KST

Dmitri Teperik: Ida-Viru County should be pro-Estonian, European and successful
Ida-Viru County must be seen not as a region defined by its problems, but as a source of opportunity for Estonia's future, with long-term investment, local involvement and development essential to the country's prosperity and security, Dmitri Teperik writes.
"I'm from Ida-Viru County." I believe the emotional and substantive meaning of this sentence has changed more over the years than any statistical indicator collected about the county. I remember a time when it was met with a sympathetic nod. I also remember a time when it was followed by a cautious pause. At the same time, I sincerely hope that, before long, it will simply spark curiosity or, better yet, genuine enthusiasm.
I have spent most of my professional life working on security and societal resilience in Estonia, Ukraine and elsewhere. The longer I do this work, the clearer one thing becomes: The most important decisions, those with the longest-lasting impact, are not made in the midst of a sudden crisis. They are made years earlier, on ordinary workdays when passionate election promises and dry statistics are of little interest to anyone.
Once multiple crises strike simultaneously and their consequences begin to mount across different sectors, it is, of course, rather late to revisit someone's decisions or failures to act. This has only strengthened my desire to bring my professional experience back to my home county, not as an outside adviser, but by working on the ground alongside those who live in Ida-Viru County every day.
Over the past few years, I have found many dedicated, like-minded people in Ida-Viru County whose eyes still shine with trust, whose hearts are in the right place and who are firmly in tune with Estonia. I believe there are many more of them.
Ida-Viru is a process
We tend to talk about Ida-Viru County as a border region, industrial, Russian-speaking and shrinking. What else? The list could go on indefinitely, with a statistical table or deeply entrenched stereotype to back up every item. But this describes the current situation, not the direction in which the region is heading. And there is a consequence: When our region is consistently described in terms of its shortcomings, it is offered temporary relief measures rather than long-term investment.
The list of shortcomings can be extended endlessly. Perhaps now is the time to recognize the progress that has been made. Anyone who has lived, worked or regularly visited Ida-Viru County over the past two decades can see and knows just how much has changed. They can actually feel it because the transformation is not just about infrastructure, although that has changed, too. The biggest change is in the people.
Ida-Viru County is a region that has undergone restructuring across several industries within a single generation and the effects will continue to be felt. At the same time, studies conducted in the region reveal findings that challenge the widespread myth of local passivity: Helping neighbors and providing informal mutual support are part of everyday life in Ida-Viru County. People help one another without anyone having to organize them.
What is lacking is neither willingness nor compassion, but safe, welcoming meeting places that people feel are their own, along with trusted channels through which that willingness can translate into decisions. This is a very different diagnosis from passivity and therefore calls for a very different remedy.
Rethinking how we perceive Ida-Viru County is the first and least expensive thing we can do. Ida-Viru County offers a diverse range of resources for building the future: people, industry, skills, culture, nature and experience in navigating major upheavals. Few regions in Estonia have more experience of this kind. I believe that, under the right conditions, Ida-Viru County is capable of bringing renewed socioeconomic vitality not only to the region itself but to Estonia as a whole.
The "Ida-Viru Future 2050" program, launched as a civic initiative, has developed a vision for the region's future based on an extensive public engagement process involving public discussions, seminars, study visits, expert consultations and community workshops. The vision is grounded in the principle that sustainable development emerges when local people feel included in decision-making and believe their contributions matter.
The next decade is being decided now
There is a specific reason why the timing of this discussion matters. The national spatial plan "Estonia 2050" identifies the Ida-Viru urban area — Jõhvi, Kohtla-Järve, Narva and Sillamäe, which function together as a single regional center — as one of Estonia's three regional urban centers, alongside Tartu and Pärnu. The same document identifies it as a key area for Estonia's energy and economic transition. This is not a courtesy gesture, but the position of the Estonian state itself, set out in the country's foundational spatial development document through 2050.
Ida-Viru County is part of Estonia's eastern border region, a stretch of territory extending from the Gulf of Finland to Setomaa where the challenges are the same or very similar throughout: declining populations, disappearing services and stalled investment. The state's own analysis has concluded that this is a matter of national security and societal resilience.
This conclusion has practical implications. In regional policy, the usual question is where each euro invested will generate the greatest return. In national security, that question is asked far less often, although it should be. We do not maintain air surveillance and air defense systems because they are economically profitable, but because without them, the country would be blind and vulnerable. A depopulating border region that is losing hope poses the same kind of risk, only one that develops more slowly and is therefore politically easier to put off addressing.
These choices will come together in the national partnership agreement for 2028–2034. What does this mean for Ida-Viru County in practice? A child starting first grade in September 2028 will be in seventh grade by the time the agreement expires. Their entire school experience — the school building, extracurricular activities, swimming pool, bus routes, teachers' salaries and the next generation of teachers, their parent's or parents' jobs and opportunities for retraining or continuing education, the comfort and safety of public spaces and much more — will be shaped by decisions made over the next year and a half. The previous window of this kind opened in 2021. The next will not open until 2035.
Will the region come to the decision-making table with well-founded proposals or will it arrive largely through media coverage, bringing only its problems?
Pro-Estonian, European and successful
If I had to briefly describe what Ida-Viru County should look like in 2050, I would say it must be pro-Estonian, European and successful.
Being pro-Estonian means that the people who live here, regardless of the language they speak at home, feel a sense of ownership of our country rather than seeing themselves as temporary or permanent guests. Loyalty grows from the state's presence and from local people's genuine ability to make democratic decisions about their own lives.
Being European means building a normal European region where human rights are respected, public spaces are well maintained, public transportation works, services are accessible and businesses compete in the European market.
Being successful means that Ida-Viru County is a hub of socioeconomic activity — a place people come to live, study and work, rather than a place they leave. This is the most difficult of the three goals, but also the most measurable.
These three goals cannot be ranked or separated from one another. There is no point in constructing abstractions that have no personal relevance to anyone. I believe Ida-Viru County deserves the opportunity to foster a sense of belonging. Estonian, European, progressive. Three words, one idea.
So far, we have had varying degrees of success in strengthening pro-Estonian sentiment through language policy, education and culture. This work must continue.
The European dimension can be strengthened further and there is a concrete opportunity to do so: Narva's bid for the title of European Capital of Culture could become a shared undertaking for the entire region and the country. Progress is driven by both grassroots initiatives and major projects in business, urban planning and community life. Most importantly, people should experience the satisfaction of achieving success by making their home county a better place.
All of Estonia safer when things are in order in Ida-Viru County
Security is usually discussed in the context of the eastern border and the Russian-speaking population. This is appropriate, but somewhat incomplete. Societal resilience also depends on whether people trust their country enough to cooperate with it during a crisis. That kind of trust cannot be bought overnight. It is built over decades, not only through modern infrastructure or jobs, but through people's actual experience of having their local voices heard.
Every euro invested in developing employment and education, improving the living environment and strengthening communities in Ida-Viru County is also an investment in security, one that delivers returns even if no crisis ever occurs. When things are in order in Ida-Viru County, the whole of Estonia feels more secure. This works both ways and we know it.
The "Ida-Viru Future 2050" vision has now given rise to the Ida-Viru County Renewal Charter, which sets out concrete proposals on investment, housing, skills and services and community development. Each proposal comes with a measurable outcome to be achieved by the end of 2028. The charter, like the author of this opinion piece, is nonpartisan. It neither supports nor criticizes any political party and is addressed to all political forces and officials involved in preparing major development decisions.
No one claims this plan is perfect. But I would argue that a good plan for Ida-Viru County now is better than a perfect plan in the future. Ida-Viru County deserves more so that all of Estonia can enjoy better, safer and more prosperous lives. Ida-Viru County is not merely a recipient of prosperity; it is a co-creator and contributor because Estonia's prosperity grows when we build it together.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Ukraine Codifies 310-km/h Drone Interceptor as Kyiv Expands Its Counter-Drone Arsenal
Unknown

12:49:54 UTC
21:49:54 KST

Ukraine’s Defense Ministry has codified the Blade interceptor drone, developed by Ukrainian defense-tech company Phantom Defense, clearing the system for procurement and delivery to the Defense Forces.
The company said the milestone moves the Blade from development and testing toward potential deployment with Ukraine’s military. However, codification does not indicate that the Defense Forces have already placed an order for a specific number of units or that large-scale deliveries have begun.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Blade is designed to intercept fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles. It has a reported top speed of 310 km/h, an operating range of up to 30 kilometers and can carry a payload of up to 0.5 kilograms.
The interceptor is equipped with vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) capability, allowing it to operate from sites without prepared runways. Optical (daylight) and thermal imaging cameras are intended to enable operations around the clock.
Part of a broader counter-drone system
The Blade is not designed as a standalone system. It forms part of Phantom Defense’s broader counter-UAV architecture, which combines detection systems, electronic warfare (EW), kinetic interceptors and software for situational awareness and battle management.
Under this model, a separate sensor can detect an aerial target and transmit information to the control system. Operators can then use electronic warfare or a kinetic interceptor such as the Blade, depending on the threat.
Leaked Russian Blueprint Counts 1,000 Weapons to Freeze Ukraine
The system includes a ground control station for flight control, telemetry and video transmission. According to the company, the operator uses a portable workstation capable of operating for at least four hours without an external power source.
The company said the Blade will also become available for procurement through the government-backed Brave1 Market.
Ukraine expands domestic drone production
The codification comes as Ukraine rapidly expands the number of domestically developed unmanned systems cleared for military use.
As of July, the Defense Ministry had codified 413 unmanned aerial systems (UAS) since the beginning of 2026, according to the ministry. Almost all were Ukrainian-made.
The ministry said the number of codified UAS was more than 30% higher than during the same period in 2025 and more than 73% higher than in 2024.
The systems include reconnaissance, strike, FPV, bomber and interceptor drones, as well as signal-relay, target and fiber-optic-controlled systems.
Phantom Defense said it employs more than 850 people and operates production across nine facilities. The company claims an aggregate capacity of more than 100 interceptor drones and 200 EW systems per day, although it has not disclosed how much of that capacity is dedicated specifically to the Blade.
That distinction is important as Ukraine develops defenses against Russia’s large-scale use of strike drones. For interceptor systems, the ability to be produced and deployed in significant numbers can be as important as individual performance characteristics such as speed and range.

Turkey’s foreign minister says Ankara weighing Saudi defence support, rules out offensive role

Turkey’s foreign minister says Ankara weighing Saudi defence support, rules out offensive role
ANKARA, Oct 8 - Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants under a joint defence pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations.
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.
On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Speaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan stressed that the pact was defensive rather than offensive, saying military officials were assessing possible contributions, particularly in air defence, electronic warfare and technical support.
"Yemen's legitimate government forces are already continuing the battle on the ground and Saudi Arabia is supporting them," Fidan said.
"But this is a defensive agreement. When a country party to the pact comes under attack, you stand by it in its defence. This is not an offensive agreement. Turkey will not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory," he said.
Fidan said military delegations would determine Saudi Arabia's operational defence needs and what contributions Turkey and Pakistan could make.
On Wednesday, two officials told Reuters that Turkey was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help its fight with Houthi militants.
Turkish officials have said any support provided at this stage would largely be in a bilateral capacity, as Turkey's parliament has not officially ratified the joint defence pact.
Fidan said on Thursday that work was largely completed for the agreement to be submitted for parliament's approval and that they aimed to send it "as soon as possible".
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defence industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh's technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

“They were smiling as they shot at us”: The Insider speaks with Israelis whose lives were turned upside down on October 7, 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:49:21 UTC
21:49:21 KST

On October 7, Israel marked the third anniversary of the Hamas terrorist attack of 2023. The Insider spoke to three people whose lives were changed forever that day: a survivor of the attack from Kibbutz Be’eri, a Hamas hostage who spent two years in captivity, and a soldier who was among the first to enter Gaza as part of an armored brigade.
- 1.Pyotr Stolba, resident of Kibbutz Be’eri: “Cars and houses were burning, the whole street was littered with bodies”
- 2.Former hostage Maksim Kharkin: “They were killing people and smiling”
- 3.Vitaly Cheberdin, Israeli soldier with the 188th Armored Brigade: “The army had never done anything like this in Gaza”
Pyotr Stolba, resident of Kibbutz Be’eri: “Cars and houses were burning, the whole street was littered with bodies”
On October 7, 2023, several thousand Hamas militants broke into Israel from the Gaza Strip. They initially headed for the Be’eri and Nahal Oz kibbutzim along the border with the Strip. For the first seven hours of the attack — before the army arrived — Be’eri was defended by just 26 people. A total of 101 residents, including 10 children aged from several months to 17 years, were killed. Another 32 residents were taken hostage by the terrorists.
Three years after “Black Saturday,” just one burned-out house remains in Kibbutz Be’eri — a reminder of the tragedy. Its roof has collapsed and its walls are riddled with bullet holes. The house stands on an empty lot surrounded by a large metal fence. Just one year ago, there were more destroyed houses here, but they have since been demolished. Local residents are divided over what to do with the last one – preserve it as a memorial to the attack or remove it so that it does not remind their own children of the horror they experienced.
Pyotr Stolba has lived in Be’eri for 34 years. He immigrated to Israel from Moscow in 1996 with his wife and settled in the kibbutz almost immediately:
“There were two families living in this house: the Kipnises and the Alons. The Alon family was later rescued alive by the Israeli army, while the Kipnis couple – husband and wife – were killed by the terrorists inside the house, which they then set on fire.
At 6:30 a.m. on October 7, Qassam rockets began falling here. Of course, we went into the safe room. I was at home with my wife, my older son, my pregnant daughter-in-law, and my 10-month-old grandson.
We were told not to leave the safe rooms because there were terrorists in the kibbutz. We thought there were just a few of them. No one could have imagined that 400 terrorists would enter Be’eri.
They smashed through the glass balcony door. They shot at the glass and it shattered. They opened the door and came inside. The dog met them and started barking, and they immediately shot it.
They tried to break into our safe room, pulling at the door handle. My son and I held the door from inside. They knocked and spoke to us in English: "Come out, we won’t hurt you." But my older son had served in the territories [in the West Bank], in combat units. He said, 'Dad, we don’t talk to Arabs. Stay quiet.'
We stayed there for 19 hours, until the army rescued us.
The electricity went out half an hour after the terrorists stormed into the kibbutz. While our phones still had battery power, everyone was passing along information. The Losev family from Zaporizhzhia lived near that transformer station. They were close friends of ours. Marina was burned alive in the house. She was identified only by her teeth. Igor was found shot dead near the fence.
Marina was burned alive in the house and identified only by her teeth, while Igor was found shot dead near the fence
The terrorists were drinking on my balcony and shooting at the road. They used heavy machine guns to shoot anyone who drove past or tried to escape. They shot at chandeliers and the TV. A tree burning next to the house heated the roof tiles until they glowed and began to fall. My wife said, 'Listen, the house is collapsing!' I said, 'All we can do is pray. There’s nothing else we can do.'
When the army arrived, we went outside – everything around us was burning. Cars and houses were on fire; bodies lay in the street. The dead were everywhere: terrorists, Israelis. Children, women, and men lay on the sidewalks and in the roads.
We were taken from there to a hotel by the Dead Sea. That’s where we learned who had been killed and how. One of my friends said, 'I don’t know where my wife is, where my daughter is.' It turned out they had been killed.
I returned to Be’eri four months after the attack to get the local printing press running again. My wife and I now live in temporary housing and are preparing to move into a new home. A new military base has been built next to us. I think that will give us some protection in case of a sudden attack.
We never doubted that we wanted to return, because this is our home. But some families do not want to come back because of the trauma. Maybe with time it will somehow fade, but it’s impossible to ever completely forget that day."
Former hostage Maksim Kharkin: “They were killing people and smiling”
On October 7, Maksim Kharkin went with friends to the Supernova music festival, which was attacked by Hamas. Maksim was held hostage for two years:
“I had never been to Supernova before. It was a huge, very well-organized event, with all the necessary permits. There was police and internal security. We went there to enjoy ourselves and listen to music.
But at 6:27, a massive rocket attack began. That’s when I realized the war had started. The road was cut off, and the terrorists were already advancing. I ran into a field. At some point, a friend called me: ‘Max, where are you?’ I said I’d managed to get about 100 meters away. He asked, 'Max, come back and help me. I don’t know what to do.'
The shelling could already be heard from all sides. But they weren’t shooting directly at us yet – there had been no direct contact.
I heard my friend’s wife screaming into the phone: 'Max, help me, save me.' So I went back.
We decided to lie down in a ditch. The shelling was coming from all sides – from both sides of the road and from the direction of the party itself. The terrorists were advancing from two sides, calmly spraying everything with gunfire: rat-a-tat-tat-tat.
At some point, they reached us – and that was it. My friend managed to fire a shot. He had his service weapon, and he took one of them down, but he was immediately shot in the back.
They first shot at my head, but the bullet whistled over it. By then, I had basically given up hope.
I saw them killing everyone who was there. They were smiling – killing people and smiling. They let their victims scream out their pain, plead and cry. Then they shot them with a smile.
There was a young guy running around with a camera. I called him the “wedding photographer.” He walked around filming everything, enjoying himself.
You see how many of them there are — thirty here, another hundred there. And they’re in no hurry. Everything is fine, everything is great, it’s a celebration.
They tied my hands, pulled a stocking over my head, and took me to the Gaza Strip with another hostage. Every second could have been my last.
I decided I was already a dead man. They brought me to Gaza with my hands and feet tied and pushed me to the floor. I fell to my knees first, then they shoved me again and I fell face-first onto the floor. When I first fell to my knees, I realized that from that moment on, every second I was alive, every breath I took, was a gift.
“When I first fell to my knees, I realized that from that moment on, every second I was alive, every breath I took, was a gift.”
We were held in ordinary homes in the Gaza Strip. Apart from Hamas fighters, the only people we had contact with were the heads of the households. Their sons, boys around 15 to 17, carried machine guns and could casually transport grenades and ammunition in UNICEF bags.
If one of us did something wrong – for example, if they saw someone talking to another hostage, even whispering or communicating with their fingers – you could get a beating for that.
The house where I was held came under fire, and the upper floor was destroyed. After that, I was moved to an underground tunnel. I spent another year and four months there. Some tunnels are designed for people to live in. They can have tile, floors, and entire rooms — basically apartments. Ours was nothing like that. It was a transport tunnel. There were just concrete beams, about 20 centimeters wide and a little over a meter high. Then came a concrete arch of the same thickness, another beam, and another beam on the floor. That was it. The entire tunnel was built that way.
How did we use the toilet? I dug a hole, and that’s where I went.
At one point, there were six of us. We came down with every illness imaginable, including COVID. We never left the tunnel. Your condition gets to the point where you stand up and immediately start swaying. You can’t walk properly; you’re constantly staggering.
There was no light. The only light was a small LED bulb, if there was one. Sometimes there wasn’t. If they called you from one room to another and you didn’t have a flashlight, it was pitch-black. You couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing.
We were fed infrequently, and it got worse as time went on. Especially during the last five months, we could easily go 27 to 30 hours without eating. Lunch was a tablespoon of some kind of sauce and half a pita. I weighed just 50 kilograms when I came out. When I entered the tunnel, I weighed 90 kilograms.
Hamas guards had a separate room for themselves in the tunnel. There was a core group that stayed there permanently, while others rotated in and out. They had a room like ours, only larger — with a satellite TV, a kitchen and food.
We’d get the shit beaten out of us, then they’d interrogate us, then we’d get the shit beaten out of us again. 'Who are you? Where are you from? What’s your mother’s name? Your father’s? What did you do in the army? Where did you come from? Why did you come here?' We had to make up some kind of half-true story.
Hamas fighters hardly ever spoke to the hostages. From time to time, they would tell us something demoralizing or offer food or other concessions in exchange for converting to Islam. Eventually, I converted to Islam, which let me wheedle a radio out of them — supposedly to listen to prayers recorded on a memory card. They had deliberately broken off the antenna, but the base was still there, along with a manual tuning dial.
I studied a little physics at the Suvorov military school. I understood that as long as electricity was running through the cables in the tunnel, you couldn’t pick up anything. But when the power was off, a cable could work as an antenna. Everyone told me, 'You’re crazy. What waves? What radio? You’re making this up.' We put it under the cable – and suddenly we had a signal!
There was no electricity in the wires from 5:30 p.m. until 9:30 a.m. That was when we listened to all sorts of things – stations from neighboring countries: Egypt, Syria, Lebanon. We quickly picked up the Israeli military station Galei Tsahal. That’s where we got our news and learned what was really happening.
I think I managed to pick up Vesti Moskvy once, or at least hear Russian being spoken. That was hugely important because I hadn’t spoken Russian with anyone for two years.
At the moment we were released, at 7:30 a.m., they lined us up and said that nothing was over yet. If anything went wrong, they would either kill us on the spot or, at best, send us back into the tunnel. From the start, I told myself I wouldn’t believe we were free until the door of the Red Cross armored Land Cruiser closed behind me.
When it did, I exhaled for the first time. But you’re still there, and they’re still all around you."
Vitaly Cheberdin, Israeli soldier with the 188th Armored Brigade: “The army had never done anything like this in Gaza”
In late October 2023, after three weeks of bombardment, the IDF launched a ground operation in the Gaza Strip. The stated goals of the operation were to destroy Hamas’s military and governing capabilities, return the hostages, and prevent further attacks on Israel.
During the operation in Gaza, tens of thousands of people were killed, and around 85% of buildings in the Strip were damaged or destroyed. The figures were cited by Nikolay Mladenov, the UN High Representative for the "Board of Peace," who is respected by both Israelis and Palestinians.
Israeli soldier Vitaly Cheberdin entered Gaza in December 2023 with the 188th Armored Brigade. According to him, the troops had initially been preparing for possible fighting in Lebanon, so the deployment south came as a surprise:
“The army had never done anything like this in Gaza. Before that, they had only entered small areas. It’s densely populated there, which makes fighting, especially with tanks, extremely difficult.
On the first day, we had to advance about 10 kilometers in our tanks and bring in several battalions so the security services could begin operating there. When we entered Gaza, I saw the sky glowing pink from the explosions. Hamas fighters started firing back. Something came flying in our direction.
We just kept moving forward, firing as we went – they shot at us, we shot back. I saw houses, movie theaters, cars, things exploding. It was like something out of a movie.
One of my unit’s main tasks was to search for Hamas weapons depots and tunnels. We mostly went to Hamas fighters’ homes looking for weapons. If we found anything – a weapons cache or other infrastructure – we blew it up on the spot.
There were also addresses where hostages were believed to be held. That was a priority for everyone, but honestly, we didn’t expect to find anyone. Whenever there was a small operation involving hostages, we dropped everything and focused entirely on it.
We didn’t want to kill anyone, but it happened. Once, we started entering a house, reacted to movement, and shot a woman. Everything was filled with smoke; the house was already on fire. There was also a dead girl inside, though it wasn’t clear what had killed her – a tank or infantry fire. Three girls were still alive, around 14 or 15 years old, along with an adult woman and two men. We took them all outside.
We gave the women food right away. The men were initially in their underwear. Obviously, that’s all they could wear when they came out. We then brought them blankets, and after some time handed them all over to the Red Cross. We fed the civilians and shared our food with them.
A man started coming out from somewhere. He was shot in the head. I don’t know by whom. He immediately fell backward, his brains blown out. His family came out behind him; they were spared.
“A man started coming out from somewhere, was shot in the head, and his family came out behind him – they were spared”
Civilians suffered mainly because Hamas put them in harm’s way. Hamas fighters don’t look like they do on TV, either. Most walk around in flip-flops and shorts, carrying a grenade launcher or a Kalashnikov. They often hide among civilians — it's guerrilla warfare.
Once, our unit spent the night in a girls’ school. I went into the teachers’ room and started looking at photographs from school parades – pictures of them supposedly destroying something resembling Israel, trampling on it, pretending to slit its throat. They’re steeped in hatred.
I still have a girl’s album that I took from one of the apartments. She draws beautifully, she has talent, but the pictures — she drew the Islamic Jihad symbol, terrorists, Yasser Arafat.
I’ll never forget this image: you’re standing in a building on high ground, with the whole city spread out below, and it’s burning — burning intensely. And you realize you’re part of all this, that you’re the reason for it.
COVID was going around there for a while. I felt sick, but I got through it relatively easily. My gunner, though, just collapsed. He was in the tank as we were attacking and advancing, lying unconscious in the back with a temperature close to 40°C. He couldn’t take part in anything and just rode along with us. We pressured the officer, and they took him back to Israel that same evening. He ended up in the hospital.
In total, I spent four months in Gaza. The first time, I came out more or less okay. But the second time, I had a completely dead look in my eyes. I didn’t feel like doing anything.
You drive into Israel and there’s so much light. We were like frightened idiots. A friend told me that when he got home, he walked into the room, went up to his mother, and asked, 'Can I turn on the light?'
The first day I got home, I couldn’t sleep because it was so quiet. The birds are singing here, while over there you had mortars pounding."

India’s Modi accused of cutting millions of Muslims from electoral roll
Protests have erupted in India after authorities removed millions of names from the electoral voter roll, requiring them to show documents to prove they have the right to vote.
Over 130 million names have been cut, with opponents saying the move has disproportionately targeted India's 200 million Muslims, who are unlikely to support Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu-nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
People have also reportedly been removed for being "dead", even though they are still alive.
The move followed an order from the Election Commission of India, appointed by Modi, to clean India's voter roll of duplicate, dead, and ineligible voters.
The poll body says the exercise identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent "foreign illegal immigrants" from casting ballots.
Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities.
Millions appealing the decision are still stuck in court, denied their right to vote during the election earlier this year.
Members of Modi's BJP have long claimed that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's electoral rolls.
The Prime Minister and his party have been accused of anti-Muslim rhetoric and policy, particularly around elections, including using dehumanising or stereotyping language about Muslims, calling them "infiltrators" and suggesting they "have more children" in a way that implies a demographic threat to Hindus.
Protests demanding that election commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down have grown since the report, with a demonstration in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday expected to draw large crowds.
Opposition parties also say the commission is striking off legitimate voters to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party.
The Indian Express alleged last month that key decisions linked to the large-scale revision exercise were likely taken without approval from two of the three election commissioners.
The Election Commission of India (ECI), a constitutional body, has rejected the allegations. It says all its decisions were unanimous and legally valid.
The Supreme Court has ordered the government and election body to explain decisions linked to the voter-roll revision.
The court has also examined the legality of the revision exercise.
In May, it allowed the election commission to proceed with the nationwide exercise, while calling for safeguards to protect eligible voters.
Another hearing is due next week.
The protests follow millions of students taking to the streets this summer in the "Cockroach Protests" over exam leaks, the nation's high unemployment rate, and limited opportunities for its youth.

Medium-term borrowing costs for UK government hit 19-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:47:49 UTC
21:47:49 KST

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has urged the chancellor, John Healey, to agree a budget that reassures financial markets after the UK’s medium-term borrowing costs hit a fresh 19-year high.
With investors offloading government bonds previously considered safe havens amid fears of rising inflation, Bailey told all governments caught in the crosshairs of financial speculators that they needed to avoid market turmoil that raises the interest paid on debt.
Recent dramatic moves in government bond markets have been driven by international factors, but will increase the pressure on Healey ahead of his tax and spending announcement on 28 October.
The yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds had risen 0.06 percentage points by lunchtime in London, to 5.515%. That was the highest level since July 2007, when the global financial crisis was starting to unfold.
Yields on 20- and 30-year UK government bonds, which are known as gilts, also rose significantly, to their highest level since as long ago as 1998. Yields go up when bond prices go down.
Yields later dropped back on a day of volatile trading, but analysts said further conflict in the Middle East would push them up again as concerns increased about inflation becoming embedded in many major economies.
Meanwhile, the benchmark oil price rose by more than 5% to $105.3 a barrel amid escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast.
Diesel prices at UK pumps hit £2 a litre last week, leading to concerns among central banks that inflation will surge over the coming months, leading to higher interest rates and burgeoning government debt financing costs.
Speaking at a conference in Istanbul, Bailey said he would not meddle in government policy, but he had one observation for Healey after the recent bond rout dramatically increased UK borrowing costs.
“Whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets,” he said.
Realistic commitments to rein in debt would help curb demands for higher returns from investors who might sell when there were shocks like the outbreak of the Iran war, he said. “In other words, such commitments are needed more than ever when these negative shocks occur.”
Economists believe rising borrowing costs and a weaker growth outlook are likely to have wiped out around half of the £24bn buffer against Labour’s fiscal rules that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, built up at the time of her spring statement in March – perhaps significantly more.
Healey is expected to raise taxes at the budget to partly rebuild that cushion, as well as paying for policy interventions including the six-month VAT cut on electricity bills and a modest energy support package for the poorest households.
Some economists are warning the chancellor not to go too far in rebuilding the Treasury’s headroom, however. Andrew Wishart, of Berenberg Bank, said: “Raising taxes to keep the surplus close to the size it was in the March forecast (ie to ‘maintain the headroom’) would do unnecessary damage to economic incentives.”
He argues that gilt yields are likely to come back down over the next year, with the Bank of England likely to make fewer rate rises than the four that investors currently expect.
The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates at its November meeting to tackle surging inflation, echoing moves already made by the European Central Bank, Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan.
The bond selloff has intensified across big economies in recent days, as oil prices have soared, with no resolution of the Middle East conflict in sight.
Investors appear to be anxious about higher inflation and runaway government spending. France has been hardest hit, as Paris battles to pass a budget, but the selloff has been widespread.
Reuters reported that European Central Bank officials and eurozone finance ministers were preparing on Thursday to make representations to the French government to pass a 2027 budget to calm bond markets.
Investors are worried about the country’s large budget deficit and 2027 presidential election. Its 10-year bond yield has jumped nearly 80 basis points since the start of September and hit its highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%.
An EU official said finance ministers were unlikely to make a public plea, but would call for a budget that brought down annual borrowing.
“That’s kind of a no-brainer. So I would expect this to be the main message,” the official said.
Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), has urged governments to tighten their belts in response to rising bond yields.
“My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said, ahead of next week’s IMF annual meeting in Bangkok.
Higher yields not only push up costs for indebted governments, but have knock-on effects for borrowers across the economy, including homeowners and businesses.
The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has tried to rein in yields on the US’s long-term debt by increasing buybacks of its government bonds, known as treasuries, but the policy appears to have had little impact.
Yields on the 30-year treasuries targeted by Bessent’s policy were about 5.235% when he announced the doubling of buybacks in August, but have since surged above 5.7%.

Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:47:46 UTC
21:47:46 KST

Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- La Trobe University
- Summary:
- New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.
- Share:
Archaeologists from La Trobe University have described 18 newly published hominin fossils from South Africa, including a second skull fragment belonging to Homo erectus. The discovery adds stronger evidence that the species was present in southern Africa 2.0 million years ago, about 200,000 years earlier than traditionally believed.
The fossil collection also includes remains of P. robustus. Those specimens suggest the species was undergoing gradual evolutionary changes as it adapted to shifting environmental and climatic conditions.
Fossils From South Africa's Cradle of Humankind
The fossils come from Drimolen Main Quarry in South Africa's 'Cradle of Humankind,' one of the world's richest sites for remains of ancient human relatives. Although the quarry was discovered in 1992 and excavated through 2019, many of the fossils recovered there had never been formally described and remained largely unknown to science.
Researchers from La Trobe, working with colleagues in South Africa and the United States, have now analyzed and described another 18 fossils from the site. The remains have been assigned to Homo erectus and P. robustus.
In research published in Annals of Human Biology, the team reports the first known adult Homo erectus fossil from Drimolen. The specimen is about 2 million years old, making it roughly 200,000 years older than adult Homo erectus fossils discovered elsewhere, including specimens from Dmanisi in Georgia that date to about 1.8 million years ago.
"Homo erectus is the first species of hominin that researchers broadly agree fits within our own genus Homo and is likely directly ancestral to us. Drimolen preserves evidence for the first appearance of this species 2 million years ago; however, the original fossil, DNH 134, belonged to a child aged between two and four, and there was uncertainty about what the adult version may have looked like," lead researcher Dr. Jesse Martin said.
"This paper publishes a new adult fossil attributed to Homo erectus, DNH 127, providing further confirmation that this species first appeared in southern Africa 2 million years ago."
Two Human Relatives Took Different Evolutionary Paths
The newly described fossils also provide evidence that P. robustus changed over time. Between about 2 million and 1.8 million years ago, the species developed larger teeth and more powerful chewing muscles.
According to Dr. Martin, the contrast with Homo erectus is striking. While Homo erectus was developing a larger brain and smaller molar teeth, possibly as a result of eating more meat, P. robustus retained a brain only slightly larger than that of chimpanzees. At the same time, it evolved enormous molars suited to grinding and crushing tough, hard foods, functioning much like a mortar and pestle.
"These two human species shared the same landscape and are both preserved in Drimolen cave. While we know that Homo erectus and the lineage leading to us was ultimately the successful one, 2 million years ago P. robustus outnumbered Homo erectus at Drimolen by more than 10 to one. During this time period, it was our ancestors that looked like the outside long-odds chance to survive," Dr. Martin said.
Fossils Reveal Evolution in Action
The Drimolen fossils also help researchers compare P. robustus populations separated by about 200,000 years.
"This paper confirms that the P. robustus fossils from the 2-million-year-old Drimolen Cave are slightly but importantly different from the P. Robustus fossils at the 1.8-million-year-old Swartkrans cave.
"During this 200,000-year period, P. robustus teeth became even larger, and so did the muscles associated with chewing. Hominin fossils are so rare that generally the differences between them are huge, and researchers are left to make educated guesses regarding what existed in the missing parts of the fossil record.
"However, the large number of fossils from Drimolen, some of which are published in this paper, allow an unprecedented insight into the micro-evolutionary changes that shaped human ancestors.
Dr. Martin said researchers had already recognized that the Drimolen population of P. robustus was distinctive enough to receive a separate subspecies designation, P. Robustus ukusa. The newly described fossils provide additional support for that formal classification.
The research involved scientists from the Palaeoscience Labs, Department of Archaeology and History, La Trobe University, Palaeo-Research Institute, University of Johannesburg, Evolutionary Studies Institute, University of the Witwatersrand, and Department of Anthropology, Washington University.

Journalists analyse intercepted Russian plan to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:46:00 EEST
21:46:00 KST

Journalists analyse intercepted Russian plan to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure
Journalists from Skhemy, an investigative project by Radio Liberty, have examined a Russian plan to pressure Ukraine, which identifies as priority targets for strikes "nodes" near Ukraine's western border through which electricity is imported, major hydroelectric power plants and even nuclear power plants.
Source: Radio Liberty
Details: The journalists obtained a copy of the Russian plan from sources in Ukrainian forces and studied it in detail.
The plan intercepted by Ukraine concerns Russia's strategy to cut electricity and heat supplies to Ukraine's major cities by up to 90%.
"One of the largest attacks took place on the night of 29-30 September, when hundreds of Russian strike drones and ballistic missiles were launched against the energy infrastructure of the capital and Kyiv Oblast," Radio Liberty recalls.
At least three of the facilities attacked that night – two combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and one thermal power plant in Kyiv Oblast – were identified by Skhemy journalists as being included in the Russian plan.
The plan, apparently prepared by the Russian side and provided by Ukrainian intelligence, was presented to Ukraine's partners in Paris on 17 September by Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal at the energy meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format), Radio Liberty notes.
The copy of the plan contains an analysis of Ukraine's energy capacity and calculations of the number of missiles, drones and bombs Russia would need to cut major cities such as Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa off from electricity, heat and water.
The list of facilities "to be hit" includes nuclear power plants alongside small boiler houses.
However, the plan assesses them solely in terms of Ukrainians' electricity consumption in gigawatts, without any mention of the potential nuclear threat, the analysts note.
The plan identifies four priority targets: power generation and electricity supply, water supply, sewage and heating.
The first priority is to disable "nodes" near the western border through which electricity is imported from Europe.
These include cross-border power lines, high-voltage substations near the border and interconnectors – systems linking the power grids of Ukraine and EU countries, receiving European electricity and transforming it before transmitting it further into the country.
The plan also refers to major hydroelectric power plants, located mainly on the Dnipro and Dniester rivers, and the shutdown of three nuclear power plants – South Ukraine, Rivne and Khmelnytskyi. The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant has been under Russian occupation since March 2022.
The plan lists a total of 60 key targets, including the aforementioned hydroelectric and nuclear power plants and interconnectors, as well as thermal power plants, combined heat and power plants, substations, boiler houses, wastewater treatment facilities, pumping stations and other state and municipal facilities on which electricity, water, sewage and heating depend.
The plan says that such attacks would require basic types of weapons: up to 770 Molniya and Geran UAVs and Dan-T/Banderol drone-launched cruise missiles, as well as 170 FABs (here and throughout the article, a modification of a high-explosive aerial bomb equipped with a universal planning and guidance module) and 75 Kinzhal aeroballistic and Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The plan contains a detailed calculation for each facility, specifying how many weapons and of what type would be needed to disable it, Skhemy reported.
So, two Iskander missiles are envisaged for the destruction of a nuclear power plant (the plan refers to an "outdoor switchyard" – a high-voltage installation located outdoors that receives and transmits electricity). Accordingly, six missiles are required to destroy the equipment at three nuclear power plants.
As for hydroelectric power plants, up to 25 Molniyas, Gerans or Dan-T/Banderols, or three Kinzhal missiles, are allocated for each.
"In other words, for the destruction of 10 major Ukrainian hydroelectric power plants, depending on the distance to the launch site or line of contact, the document calculates a total of up to 30 Molniyas (for facilities located up to 60 km from the line of contact) and around 240 Gerans and Dan-T/Banderols, which can be replaced by Kinzhal ballistic missiles (probably up to 30)," Radio Liberty says.
For combined heat and power plants (five transformers), the calculation is likewise 25 Gerans and so on, or three Kinzhal missiles per facility. The plan also says that each combined heat and power plant could require around 25 FAB-500 bombs and five Iskander-M missiles.
For a substation (three transformers) or an interconnector, the calculation is 15 Molniyas and so on, or three Kinzhal missiles per facility. For housing and utilities infrastructure, it is 25 FABs or five Iskanders per facility, while a boiler house would require 20 Gerans.
Moreover, next to the section on boiler houses, the authors of the plan explicitly note that "due to their proximity to residential areas, the use of other types of weapons could result in civilian casualties".
The Russian plan specifies the types of weapons to be used "depending on the target and distance".
For example, it lists Molniyas and FAB-500s for distances of up to 40-60 km; Geran-4, Dan-T/Banderol and Iskander-M for 60-500 km; and Kinzhal, Kalibr, Oreshnik and Zircon for more than 500 km.
The capital's facilities occupy a special place in the plan, with Kyiv's energy system analysed and presented in detail.
The authors of the plan note that the capital's energy system is fairly extensive but identify five substations in the "Kyiv ring" serving different parts of the city as its "bottleneck", or more precisely, its weak point.
"Overall, according to the document, hitting 12 key substations in the three cities mentioned above should halt up to 90% of electricity supplies. For this, the authors of the document specify 40-50 Molniya drones and 130-140 Geran-4 or Dan-T/Banderol drone-launched missiles," Radio Liberty says.
Experts interviewed by the journalists say the plan is not a final operational plan but rather a set of calculations.
They also say this is not a new tactic, as Russia has systematically attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, turning cold and darkness into a weapon.

UK imposes new sanctions on Russia’s oil, shadow fleet, war supply chains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:45:00 UTC

UK imposes new sanctions on Russia’s oil, shadow fleet, war supply chains
The UK Foreign Office said this in a statement, Ukrinform reports.
The sanctions target 38 legal entities and individuals. In particular, restrictions were imposed on Russian oil companies Zarubezhneft and INK Capital. The UK Foreign Office said Britain had become the first G7 country to impose sanctions on Russia’s four largest oil companies. The latest measures mean that UK sanctions now cover more than 90% of Russia’s oil production capacity.
In addition, 12 more oil tankers were added to the sanctions list, bringing the total number of vessels from Russia’s shadow fleet under UK sanctions to more than 600. According to the Foreign Office, these vessels are used to circumvent sanctions and transport Russian oil, including through deceptive practices and the use of false flags.
The Foreign Office noted that the new sanctions target not only vessels already at sea but also those facilitating the supply chain used to transport Russian oil around the world.
Another 17 legal entities and individuals were sanctioned for supplying Russia with so-called Common High Priority goods. These include machine tools, electronics and materials needed to manufacture ballistic missiles, drones and other military equipment. According to the UK Foreign Office, Russia obtains some of these goods through third countries. The ministry said it was identifying those involved and taking appropriate action against them.
The UK also imposed sanctions on three cryptocurrency exchanges, two payment platforms and a related individual suspected of helping Russia circumvent financial restrictions. According to the Foreign Office, two of these entities processed transactions through the A7 financial network, which is backed by the Kremlin. Last year, it reported processing more than $90 billion in transfers.
“The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences… By sanctioning these companies, we’re not only stemming the flow of Russian oil money, but cutting off the routes used to circumvent our sanctions regime by making it harder for major Russian oil companies to rebadge their oil under the name of an unsanctioned entity,” the UK Foreign Office said.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 1, the United Kingdom announced a new sweeping package of sanctions against Russia aimed at weakening the Kremlin’s war budget, countering propaganda, and holding accountable those involved in the torture of Ukrainian civilians and the deportation of children.

Eight survivors rescued from the rubble as fears of further collapse slow operations in Istanbul’s Maltepe district.
At least two people have been killed after a seven-storey building in Turkiye’s Istanbul partially collapsed, officials said.
Emergency crews were trying to reach at least two people who were believed to be trapped, authorities said on Thursday.
The cause of the collapse was not immediately known, and an investigation was under way.
The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, caved in before dawn in the district of Maltepe, on the Asian side of Istanbul, a city that is bisected by the Bosporus Strait.
Residents from the upper floors were safely evacuated while search teams rescued eight more people from the rubble.
The rescuers recovered two bodies and were trying to reach two people still believed to be inside, according to the Istanbul governor’s office.

He warned that the building was at risk of further collapse, hampering the rescue efforts. Nearby buildings were also evacuated for safety, the governor said.
Istanbul and other parts of Turkiye are undergoing an urban transformation programme that aims to replace old and earthquake-prone buildings with safer housing.

“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
“The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.”
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said it was open to renewing a constructive dialogue despite South Korea’s move.
“Despite Seoul’s decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to resuming constructive dialogue, even if it will take some time,” a foreign ministry spokesman said, adding that Kyiv believes “diplomacy should prevail over emotions”.
South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his United Nations General Assembly address last month.
South Korea accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement relating to the transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.
The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers have expressed their desire to resettle in South Korea because they could face persecution if repatriated to North Korea.
South Korea had said it would accept them because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.
South Korean officials said the nondisclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North.
There have been no comments from North Korea’s state media on the soldiers’ transfer. But the North has previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and its key ally, the United States, and focused on bolstering its nuclear programme since 2019.
South Korea has provided $445m in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100m in aid to Ukraine during a meeting with Zelenskyy.

GELENDZHIK /Krasnodar Region/, October 8. /TASS/. Bio-ecological settlements, due to be developed in a number of Russian territories, may be based on a network of Arctic integrated emergency rescue centers of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations that already cover the Arctic regions, Acting Head of the Research Institute for Advanced Research and Innovative Life Safety Technologies at the Ministry of Emergency Situations' St. Petersburg University Sergey Ivakhnyuk told the 3rd International Bioprom Forum.

"This system may be based on the existing network of Arctic integrated emergency rescue centers, which already covers key logistics routes and most important territories of the Arctic Zone. Bio-settlements will act as a risk management framework."
In order to implement this approach, it is necessary to move forward from separate centers to their distributed network as outposts, he continued.
"This is a modular, autonomous solution that, first of all, ensures the settlement's safety, while it is located in the transport accessibility zone off the central hub, serves as its outpost and an additional base for deploying forces and assets in a remote area," he said.
The ministry's reference point in a bio-settlement will become not just a station on duty, but will act as a training ground in Arctic conditions, thus specialists will be able to train personnel right on the spot. Additionally, such a system offers an option to develop the institute of volunteers, involving local residents, and to carry out scientific research.
The project was supported by Mikhail Kovalchuk, President of the Kurchatov Institute National Research Center, who noted it was quite promising given the Northern Sea Route development. However, he suggested to eye the existing settlements along the Northern Sea Route, many of which are currently abandoned. They could be developed to create outposts, since they still have infrastructures. In his opinion, it would be easier to restore such settlements and create bio-ecological settlements on their basis.

New report says transgender law caused “profound” suffering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:42:38 UTC
21:42:38 KST

New report says transgender law caused “profound” suffering
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The law governing how transgender people could change their legal gender had profound physical, psychological, and social consequences, according to a report by Radboud University released on Thursday.
Researchers conducted 28 in-depth interviews with trans and intersex people, as and studied Health Council and parliamentary papers to reach the conclusions found in the report, titled An Inhuman Law.
The report, commissioned by the education ministry, “examines how the law and its conditions impacted the lives of trans and intersex people, as well as the forms of harm, coercion, and loss of autonomy they experienced”.
From 1985 to 2014, trans people had to meet a series of criteria to change their legal gender. Until 2001, they had to be unmarried, so some were forced to divorce their partners.
They also had to undergo physical adaptation “as far as medically or psychologically justified” and be permanently infertile, which meant having the uterus and ovaries or the testicles removed.
Some 2,000 people are thought to have been affected by it, the Volkskrant reported on Thursday.
“You have to negotiate with society, with doctors, and with God knows who.
And you no longer have time for yourself,” one trans woman who participated in the study said.
Junior education minister Judith Tielen said the report “helps us learn from what happened at the time”.
The bill was controversial when it was proposed in 1982. The CDA felt that without requiring physical changes, it would be too easy to change genders, which would also allow gay couples to marry and for men to avoid conscription. But D66 and PSP (which would eventually become GroenLinks and then Pro) were opposed to any surgical or medical requirements.
In 2021, the government apologised to all transgender people who were forced to accept being sterilised and to undergo body modification and take hormones if they wanted to change their gender on official documents.
The apology followed legal action by the Transgender Collective in 2019, which said that the law conflicted with the European Convention on Human Rights. In 2011, the Dutch law was also the subject of a damning report by Human Rights Watch.

The exhibition—conceived by the Italian Embassy in Zagreb and the Italian Consulate General in Rijeka—celebrates the historical journey of this accessory, which originated in Croatia and later became a global symbol of luxury, elegance, and Italian craftsmanship, of which the Talarico brand stands as a paragon of excellence. From its very beginnings, the company has cultivated a passion for detail and quality, creating a product that today stands as an authentic icon of “Made in Italy.”
The exhibition is part of a wide range of activities promoting Italian design and “Made in Italy” organized by Sistema Italia in Croatia and, thanks to a collaboration with the Split City Museum, will be open to the public in Split through November 8.

Kansas Has Emerged as a Senate Battleground State. Here’s Why It Matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:39:51 UTC
21:39:51 KST

Kansas has emerged as a surprise battleground in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections.
The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years, but Republican Sen. Roger Marshall now faces a close challenge from megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton—with repercussions that will extend beyond Kansas, as Republicans fight to keep their Senate majority this November.
An Emerson College/Nexstar Media survey of 750 likely voters showed that Hamilton had 45% of support next to Marshall’s 43% as of September. In comparison, Marshall won his 2020 general election with 53% of the vote, topping his competitor by 11 points.
Read More: Congress Is Headed for a Massive Turnover
In this race, Marshall has the financial upper hand. His campaign had reserved $2.3 million in advertising as of Oct. 2, compared with $590,000 reserved by Hamilton’s campaign, according to AdImpact figures reported by the Associated Press. Including outside groups, nearly 10 times as much advertising had been reserved to support Marshall as Hamilton.
Marshall also has Kansas’s recent voting history on his side. President Donald Trump carried the state by 16 points in 2024—a sizable Republican advantage.
Trump’s influence in the state may have once helped Marshall, who has in turn been a staunch defender of the President. He backed Trump's disproven claims of election fraud in 2020 and voted to acquit him during his second impeachment trial in February 2021. He has also publicly supported Trump’s sweeping immigration agenda.
Notably, Trump gave Marshall his “Complete and Total Endorsement” in September, lending his support to the incumbent as the race tightened.
But Kansas sentiment toward the President seems to have shifted since 2024, and a connection to the presiding Administration could hurt Marshall more than it helps. Experts say a confluence of dissatisfaction with the economy, escalating gas prices, and migration raids in the state have turned a once-obvious outcome into a deadlocked race. Given those concerns, there is the potential for Hamilton’s “X-factor” to sway Independents. About 29% of registered Kansas voters are unaffiliated, according to the Associated Press.
The Cook Political Report shifted the race from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican” on Sept. 23 and then moved it again, to “Toss Up,” on Oct. 6. Such predictions have not gone unnoticed by the GOP.
This campaign season, the Republicans’ Senate Leadership Fund has reserved $8.2 million for Kansas, according to AdImpact—a figure that would historically be seen in a traditional swing state like North Carolina. It marks a significant investment in a seat once seen as relatively sure—and signals to voters that the GOP is envisioning a tight contest.
Sen. Thom Tillis claimed that it is “almost statistically impossible” for Republicans to keep the House.
“I want my party to be in the best position for elections. And we’re going to take a little bit of a hit this season, and recover from it, I believe,” Tillis said on MS NOW’s The Beat on Monday.
Even Trump has expressed concerns about the midterms, bluntly addressing the potential of a blue wave while speaking at an Oklahoma rally for gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei last week.
“I feel a little foolish, you know. I’m saying, ‘Go out and vote, go out and vote.’ [They’re] gonna win in the last half, but still go out and vote,” he said. “We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states.”
How Trump could affect Marshall’s Senate race
According to Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, the biggest challenge for Marshall’s campaign is the U.S. President.
She tells TIME that Kansas voters are blaming the Trump Administration’s policies for their economic issues—pointing to the war with Iran hiking up fuel prices; tariffs affecting the agriculture, aerospace, and other sectors; and the threat of a trade war with Canada.
“The agricultural industry is suffering right now,” Middlewood says, claiming that this is a significant issue in a state where agriculture is the largest economic driver and contributes $62 billion and close to 150,000 jobs. “At the same time, it is harvest season, and diesel prices have gone up, and so farmers and ranchers are really struggling in the state.”
Beatty also points out how Trump’s plan to lower grocery store beef prices by temporarily lifting or lowering tariffs on foreign beef imports—including Argentinian beef—angered Kansas cattle ranchers.
Separately, the Kansas Livestock Association’s political action committee declined to endorse Marshall this year. The association had backed his 2016 House campaign and his 2020 Senate campaign.
“Several cities were also upset by unannounced ICE raids,” Bob Beatty, chair of the political science department at Washburn University in Kansas, tells TIME. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) swept through major cities including Dodge City, Garden City, and Liberal in September. ICE made 104 arrests in southwestern Kansas, according to the Justice Department. City and state officials—including Marshall—said they were not notified in advance about the raids.
“From the outside it's almost as if Trump is purposely hurting Roger Marshall,” he says.
TIME has reached out to both the Marshall and the Hamilton campaigns for comment.
“Trump is not only nationally not very popular at the moment, but there's been a number of things that he's done that have specifically ticked off Kansans of all stripes—not just Democrats,” says Beatty.
In September’s Emerson survey, Trump’s approval in Kansas stood at 40%, with nearly half of likely voters naming the economy as their top issue. His national approval rating stands at 32%, according to a Reuters/IPSOS poll published Monday.
Why unaffiliated voters matter in Kansas
Kansas is seen as a red state nationally, but Middlewood says that there is a strong “libertarian” sentiment throughout the state, and a large percentage of independent voters that need to be swayed for a candidate of either party to win.
“There are actually more registered unaffiliated independents in the state than there are Democrats, and because of that, those voters really make the difference and decide pretty much every election,” she says.
While national economic policies are potentially harming Marshall’s campaign, Middlewood and Beatty say that Hamilton’s charisma, persona as a pastor, and his middle-of-the-road politics have allowed him to appeal to undecided voters. September’s Emerson poll shows that Hamilton is leading among Independents, at 42% to 27%.
“Democrats have a very good candidate Adam Hamilton came into the race as a masterful speaker and communicator as a pastor,” Beatty says. “He's been a very good fundraiser. So he's raised the money that's needed to get his message out, and he's been actually consciously aware of how Democrats win in Kansas.”
A potential path forward for Democrats
Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly is a Democrat. Beatty says that candidates from her party have had an easier time capturing the gubernatorial vote by appealing to voters as advocates of Kansas—in terms of education, roads, and property tax policies—than as a function of the Democratic Party.
Conversely, he says: “Republicans have traditionally been very good at nationalizing the U.S. Senate races in Kansas—tying the Democratic candidate to the national Democratic Party, usually the most extreme versions of the national party, and they've done it successfully.”
Beatty notes, however, that the race is incredibly close—and he says that it would not be entirely surprising if Hamilton did lose to Marshall, considering the numeric advantage for Republicans.
“This is a state that has not seen a Democrat win since 1932, so we'll believe it when we see it,” he says. “But Hamilton is certainly making a lot of believers out there.”

Airline chiefs say can't fully guard against rogue pilots after flydubai attack
BRUSSELS/LONDON, Oct 8 - Airline executives said safety standards remained high after a flydubai co-pilot attacked the captain with an axe last week in an alleged attempt to crash the plane, but acknowledged it was hard to guard against a rogue pilot.
The comments, among the first by airline chiefs since the attack, highlight the industry's struggle to address safety and security concerns after an incident that caused the jet to plunge 16,000 feet in 30 seconds.
The flydubai co-pilot was eventually overpowered by passengers after the injured captain opened the cockpit door. A passenger helped stabilise the plane before a standby crew member who was on board landed it safely.
"If you have somebody who is a mad person in a cockpit, it's very difficult to legislate for it," Ryanair Group Chief Executive Michael O'Leary told reporters on the sidelines of an Airlines for Europe (A4E) press conference in Brussels.
'NO ABSOLUTE SAFETY'
Reuters reported this week, citing two Israeli officials familiar with the investigation, that the flydubai co-pilot told interrogators in the UAE, where he is in custody, that he had planned the attack before joining the Dubai state-owned airline.
The UAE has not announced any formal charges against the co-pilot and it is not known if he has appointed legal counsel.
Saudi Arabia has opened an air accident investigation into the incident, Reuters reported, while experts assess the implications for aviation safety alongside the separate UAE-led criminal probe, three people close to the matter said.
Lufthansa Chief Executive Carsten Spohr said it was impossible to prevent every incident and that aviation safety standards remain high. He said that the last comparable case involving a pilot occurred more than a decade ago.
A Germanwings Airbus A320 crashed in the French Alps in 2015 after the co-pilot locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately flew the aircraft into a mountainside, killing 150 people.
"We have to face the fact that there is no absolute safety and security in this industry," Spohr told reporters, adding that mental health screening of pilots was already robust. REUTERS
