She reimagined antiquity and changed the modern world: what is known about the 2026 Nobel Prize laureate in Literature
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:38:55 EEST
21:38:55 KST

She reimagined antiquity and changed the modern world: what is known about the 2026 Nobel Prize laureate in Literature
Kyiv • UNN
Canadian writer Anne Carson became the 2026 Nobel Prize laureate in Literature. She was honored for her innovative dialogue with the classical tradition.
On Thursday, October 8, the Swedish Academy announced the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. The award went to 76-year-old Canadian poet, writer, and translator Anne Carson. She is known for works that combine ancient mythology, contemporary culture, and personal experiences. One of her best-known works is the verse novel "Autobiography of Red."
UNN has compiled everything you need to know about this year's Nobel Prize in Literature and the artist who received this prestigious award.
Who was in the running for the Nobel Prize in Literature
Ahead of the announcement of the winner's name, on September 7, the British publication The Guardian published a list of writers whom bookmakers considered the leading contenders for the award.
Among the favorites was 73-year-old Chinese writer Can Xue, whose real name is Deng Xiaohua. Her work is distinguished by its experimental style, surreal plots, and unusual narrative structure. The writer has repeatedly attracted the attention of the international literary community.
Another contender for the highest honor in literature was Japanese writer Haruki Murakami. The author of the novels "Norwegian Wood," "Kafka on the Shore," and "1Q84" has remained one of the best-known candidates in Nobel Prize predictions for many years.
Among the other writers who could have received the prestigious award were Australian author Gerald Murnane, American novelist Thomas Pynchon, Canadian writer Margaret Atwood, and British-American author Salman Rushdie.
What is Canadian writer Anne Carson known for, and why are her books worth reading
As the Swedish Academy noted, Carson received the award for bold and inventive work that, in a playful dialogue with the classical tradition, created new forms for contemporary literature.
Who is Anne Carson
The future writer was born in 1950 in the Canadian city of Toronto. She received an education in classical philology, studied ancient Greek literature, and for many years combined her writing with translation and teaching at universities.
A distinctive feature of her work is the combination of poetry, prose, scholarly research, and ancient mythology. The writer often uses ancient Greek plots to tell stories about contemporary human experiences, including love, loneliness, loss, and the search for one's identity. The study of the origin and meaning of words occupies an important place in her work. Carson has repeatedly emphasized that etymology is the starting point of her creative process.
In addition to writing her own works, Anne also translated ancient Greek authors, including Sappho, Sophocles, and Euripides. Her work in this field stood out because of its distinctive approach and was often perceived by readers and even critics as independent literary works.
Why the writer was awarded the Nobel Prize
One of the main features of Carson's work is her rejection of traditional literary boundaries. In a single work, she may combine poetic lines, historical research, personal memories, and philosophical reflections. This is why the Swedish Academy took note of her ability to create unexpected connections between authors from different eras. For example, Carson compared the ancient Greek poet Simonides with the German-language poet Paul Celan, and the historian Thucydides with the British writer Virginia Woolf. This approach allowed the artist to reinterpret classical texts in a new way and go beyond familiar genres.
Anne Carson's best-known works
One of the writer's most significant works is considered to be "Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse," published in 1998. Carson based the work on the ancient Greek myth of Geryon — a winged red giant killed by Heracles. However, in her interpretation, the mythological monster becomes a sensitive young man who experiences a difficult childhood, falls in love, and tries to understand himself. The story explores unrequited love, traumatic experience, and emotional dependence.
Another well-known work — "The Beauty of the Husband" — was published in 2001. It consists of 29 poetic episodes devoted to a woman's complicated relationship with her unfaithful husband. Each episode contains a reference to the work of the English poet John Keats.
A special place in Carson's work is occupied by the book Nox, dedicated to the memory of her brother Michael, who died in Denmark. This unusual edition takes the form of a box containing pages with photographs, letters, and texts. Through the prism of a personal story, the writer reflects on death, memory, and the impossibility of fully knowing a loved one.
How Carson changed contemporary literature
In the following years, the writer continued to experiment with form. Her work Float consists of 22 separate booklets that readers can open in any order.
The writer and translator also collaborated with artists, choreographers, and theater and opera directors, turning literature into part of broader artistic projects. In the view of the Swedish Academy, it was precisely this freedom in using language, genres, and artistic forms that secured Carson a special place in the international literary community. The Nobel Committee believes that her work demonstrates how ancient narratives can remain relevant across millennia, helping contemporary readers reflect on universal human experiences.
Books by Nobel Prize laureate Anne Carson available for purchase in Ukraine: where to order them and how much they cost
Anne Carson's books can be ordered in Ukraine. Prices for English-language editions start at 823 hryvnias, although most books are delivered from the United Kingdom.
In particular, Anne Carson's books are available from the online bookstore Yakaboo. As of October 8, several of the writer's best-known works are available to order, including poetic novels, collections of poems, and experimental prose.
Autobiography of Red ("Автобіографія червоного") can be purchased for your personal library for 823 hryvnias. Ukrainian readers can also order Glass, Irony and God ("Скло, іронія і Бог") for 1,236 hryvnias.
Another available edition is The Beauty of the Husband ("Краса чоловіка"), which costs 1,318 hryvnias. For 1,400 hryvnias, you can purchase Decreation — an experimental collection combining poetry, essays, dramatic texts, and other literary forms.
At a similar price, If Not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho ("Якщо ні, то зима: фрагменти Сапфо") is also available.
It should be noted that all the books mentioned above were printed in their original language. Ukrainian translations are not yet available to readers in Ukraine. The estimated delivery time for books from the United Kingdom is 15 days. Prices and the availability of individual editions may change.
How the Nobel Prize laureate is selected
The Nobel Prize in Literature is awarded by the Swedish Academy, which consists of 18 members. The process of determining the winner takes several months and involves several stages of selection.
Each year, the Academy receives approximately 300 nominations for candidates. In the spring, the Nobel Committee reviews their literary achievements and draws up a preliminary list of approximately 20–25 writers. The list is subsequently reduced to approximately five candidates. During the summer, Academy members study their works, after which they vote in the autumn. To be awarded the prize, a candidate must receive more than half of the votes.
It should be noted that information about the nominees and the decision-making process remains confidential for 50 years.
What reward does the winner receive
In 2026, the Nobel Foundation increased the prize amount from 11 million to 12 million Swedish kronor, which is approximately 1.2 million dollars. The decision was made to mark the 125th anniversary of the presentation of the first Nobel Prizes. The foundation explained that the increase in the award is intended to preserve its value in the long term.
The ceremony will take place on December 10 in Stockholm. The laureate will receive a medal, a diploma, and a cash prize.
Who previously received the Nobel Prize in Literature
In 2025, the laureate was Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai, known for his novels about the crisis of society, human existence, and the power of art. In 2024, the award went to South Korean writer Han Kang; in 2023, to Norwegian playwright and novelist Jon Fosse; and in 2022, to French writer Annie Ernaux.
Overall, from 1901 to 2025, the Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded 118 times. Its laureates included 122 writers, 18 of whom were women.

Exclusive: G7’s 100-million-barrel pledge tied to unfinished March emergency oil release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:38:00 UTC
21:38:00 KST

The October G7 announcement aims to accelerate and complete the IEA’s March emergency oil-stock release, rather than add a new 100-million-barrel pledge to the original 400 million, according to a document seen by Euronews.
The G7's proposed release of up to 100 million barrels of oil to curb soaring energy prices aims to complete the outstanding portion of the 400-million-barrel emergency release coordinated by the International Energy Agency (IEA) in March, according to an internal document seen by Euronews.
"Of its 400 million barrels, 326 million have been released. Because some members over-delivered, the 100 million barrels in the G7 statement can be covered within the existing action if everyone fulfils their commitments," reads the document.
The IEA members backed accelerating the March releases and completing them “as soon as possible” at an IEA meeting alongside the European Commission on 7 October.
The rush followed an ultimatum from Washington, which pressured Europe to release more of its crude oil and diesel or face an export ban on diesel. Global oil markets remain volatile with ongoing disruption in the Middle East, and Brent crude oil traded at $105 on Thursday.
IEA chief Fatih Birol said that Middle Eastern crude flows are recovering significantly. However, refined-product flows, like diesel or jet fuel, remained severely constrained, with disruptions to Russian refining capacity and China's export ban adding to the squeeze.
At the IEA-EU meeting, all participants backed prioritising diesel stocks given the current tightness in the market, with IEA data showing "a real physical disruption in diesel supply".
Several European governments have already fulfilled their obligations, while others still have national procedures to complete. While the political agreement exists, delivery depends on national decisions over how strategic stocks are counted and released.
Greece, Italy and Portugal have met their pledged commitments. Emergency oil stocks from France, Germany, the Netherlands and Spain are under assessment.
Portugal questioned how effectively the IEA handles the emergency release and said it will only consider new commitments once all members have delivered their existing ones, noting that about 50 million barrels remain pending at EU level, according to the document.
Greece wants to know how much time the March release has bought so far.
Demystifying G7's language
The internal document seen by Euronews clarifies the G7's somewhat ambiguous wording in its latest announcements.
On 2 October, the group said it would fulfil its commitments through a 100 million barrel coordinated release over four months, including a substantial front-loaded diesel release within the first 20 days. It linked the move to the “immediate and full implementation” of the March 2026 commitments.
The Commission referred Euronews' questions about the details of the latest G7 announcement to the IEA. But the IEA didn't reply to Euronews' requests for clarification on volumes and refined products.
In its 7 October statement, the G7 said participants in the IEA-EU meeting "emphasised their commitment to delivering on the March 2026 Collective Action".
The March action was an extraordinary response to the Middle East supply shock, which followed the United States and Israeli military attacks against Iran on 28 February and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
IEA members originally agreed to make 400 million barrels available to the market, with the bulk of the contribution coming as crude oil and European countries supplying a greater share of refined products.
Fresh, new release could come
The IEA said members still hold around 1.1 billion barrels of publicly held emergency stocks, including more than 200 million barrels of diesel.
The Paris-based agency didn't rule out further releases if necessary. For now, it is trying to squeeze the remaining barrels from the mechanism agreed seven months ago.
The IEA said the March releases had already helped plug part of the supply gap, but stressed that diesel markets remain particularly tight, making the October action different in emphasis from March.
The next political test comes on 15 October, when the IEA Governing Board gathers governments to settle the details of the operation, including volumes, timing and the type of refined oil products to be released.

Zelenskyy responds to Rubio: You cannot negotiate with Russia and talk about a diplomatic stalemate at the same time
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's statement that the war cannot be ended diplomatically because the situation has reached a "stalemate", and called on the US to help Ukraine gain air superiority and increase pressure on Russia.
Source: Zelenskyy speaking to journalists in Pryluky, where a Russian missile struck an apartment block on 7 October, killing 22 people, including five children
Quote: "We have heard about many different moments during the war. Many hopeless situations, difficult corners and so on. We – people, leaders, politicians – drive ourselves into a corner… Even on the first day of the war, we were not in a corner. Because one person tried to drive an entire nation into a corner, and the nation rose up and defended its state." [Zelenskyy's references to a "corner" are a wordplay on the Ukrainian translation of Rubio's "stalemate" as "глухий кут" ("dead end"), which contains the word "кут" ("corner") – ed.]
Details: Zelenskyy added that getting out of the corner is not difficult and that this requires increasing economic pressure on Russia, giving Ukraine access to Starlink over Russian territory and not negotiating with Russia on future projects.
"You see, you cannot negotiate economic projects for the future with the Russians on the one hand and, on the other, say that we are at a… diplomatic deadlock. We are not at a diplomatic stalemate. Shut down their entire economy. Shut Russia's mouth. Do not feed them with your sales. Just impose sanctions on their weapons. Open Starlink to us, to Ukraine," the president said.
He recalled that the US had already done this when it attacked Iran, when "Israel had complete control of the skies over Iran".
Quote: "So that means that when you need it, it works like that… Just control the skies to protect yourself. The US has this capability. For them, it costs nothing to help Ukraine. And I said frankly: 'Give it to us, help us protect our skies and dominate the skies. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table. Why? Because he will lose everything. Three, two months – he will lose everything.' And we are waiting for the Chinese to develop this equivalent and hand it over to the Russians. So where is the truth, where is the honesty? What corner? This is called unwillingness."
Background: Rubio earlier said that ending the Russia-Ukraine war through diplomatic negotiations is currently "proving elusive" because the war has reached a "strategic stalemate". He acknowledged that diplomatic efforts are failing because Russia is demanding full control of the Donbas and Ukraine refuses to accept it.

BRUSSELS/LONDON – European airlines could face more than another year of elevated fuel costs and higher fares due to the Iran war, Ryanair Group CEO Michael O’Leary said on Oct 8, in the first warning by an executive that the knock-on effect could spill into 2028.
The Iran war has driven jet fuel prices sharply higher in 2026, squeezing airline margins despite widespread fuel hedging.
Jet fuel is currently about 50 per cent more expensive than it was pre-war, and is likely to remain at those levels for the next 12 to 18 months, O’Leary told reporters at an Airlines for Europe (A4E) press conference.
“We are all facing an enormous cost challenge next year,” he said, though he said he did not expect supplies to run out any time soon.
Analysts have warned that Europe could face a jet fuel supply shortage into the fourth quarter.
“There is no question over availability of jet fuel in Europe this winter, or frankly into next summer,” he added.
Pricier flying
O’Leary said he expects fare increases to continue in the months to come, particularly as many carriers are substantially less hedged on jet fuel costs moving into 2027.
He previously said ticket prices could be up to 20% higher next summer as a result of rising costs.
“The airlines cannot survive unless they pass on these insanely higher fuel costs in the form of higher offers, and the customers will have to pay,” O’Leary told journalists on the sidelines of the press conference, adding later that the situation was already a “full-blown crisis”.

"For our part, we will consistently continue our efforts, including on international platforms, to identify and punish not only those who carried out this unprecedented terrorist attack, but also its true masterminds," the diplomat said.

Only in Germany are law enforcement and judicial authorities continuing to pursue the case, albeit in a highly peculiar manner. According to Zakharova, the Hamburg Higher Regional Court recently refused to allow the Nord Stream operators to participate in the proceedings concerning the pipeline explosions. "Moreover, the court concluded that the damage inflicted on the companies’ interests was not existential, that they could defend their economic interests through civil proceedings, and that they did not require special protection during the criminal hearings scheduled for mid-October," she added.
Zakharova went on to say that a press release issued by the Hamburg court in this connection indicated that the proceedings were limited to determining the degree of culpability of the sole defendant, a certain Sergey K., in complicity in a war crime involving prohibited methods of warfare and an attack on a civilian facility. "Everything else, including a comprehensive examination of the circumstances of the case, falls outside the scope of the hearings," she stated. "It turns out that they are interested only in how this defendant physically committed his crime, while the fact previously established by Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office that he was acting on instructions from Ukrainian government agencies remains outside the purview of the German judiciary."
"We are not surprised by this turn of events. In four years, Germany’s much-vaunted 'impartial' and 'independent' judiciary has shown no interest whatsoever in identifying and bringing to justice the true instigators and masterminds of this terrorist attack. Now the German judicial authorities have also joined efforts to cover up the truth, apparently unwilling to expose the ideological architects of the pipeline explosions, including those based in Ukraine, which the German authorities continue to support with unwavering determination," Zakharova stressed.

Two days earlier, on October 1, a Russian Shahed-type drone struck Kyiv’s Pivdennyi Bridge as a metro train was crossing, according to footage and eyewitness accounts shared online.

Ukraine’s Drones Hunt Down Russian Osa Air Defense System—and Strike It Twice, Video

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Drones Hunt Down Russian Osa Air Defense System—and Strike It Twice, Video
Ukrainian drone operators struck a Russian Osa short-range air defense system twice on the Donbas front, according to footage released by the Signum Battalion of the 59th Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems on October 8.
The video shows Ukrainian drones engaging the Russian surface-to-air missile system during a broader series of strikes against military equipment and logistics.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Signum operators highlighted the irony themselves, playing on the system’s name—Osa means “Wasp.”
“We ‘stung’ the Osa twice,” the battalion said.
The same footage shows Signum operators targeting Russian logistics across the Donbas, including pickup trucks, UAZ vans, cargo trucks, semitrailers, and other vehicles used to move troops, ammunition, and equipment.
The battalion said its crews routinely work against the routes Russian forces depend on to keep frontline units supplied, with the Osa becoming one of the more valuable targets caught during the latest operation.
The 9K33 Osa is a Soviet-designed mobile short-range air defense system developed beginning in 1960 and introduced into service in 1971. At the time, it was notable for combining its target-acquisition radar, tracking radar, and missiles on a single amphibious vehicle, allowing the system to operate without separate radar vehicles.
Built on the six-wheeled BAZ-5937 chassis, the Osa was designed to accompany ground forces and protect them from low-flying aircraft and other aerial threats. Its radar can detect targets at distances of roughly 30 kilometers, while later variants can engage targets at ranges of around 10 kilometers.
The system underwent several upgrades during its service life, including the Osa-AKM introduced in 1980, which brought improved tracking and enclosed missile canisters.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system using FP-2 strike drones, with footage showing the system burning before its ammunition detonated and tore the vehicle apart.

The FSB's sabotage campaign in Europe: Russia's war on Western arms makers – and what it means for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:36:00 EEST
21:36:00 KST

The FSB's sabotage campaign in Europe: Russia's war on Western arms makers – and what it means for Ukraine
A disaster was narrowly averted in Germany in summer 2026. On the night of 4-5 August, unidentified individuals attempted to attack Leipzig airport with three explosive-laden FPV drones. Their target was a Ukrainian Ruslan aircraft operated by Antonov Airlines. The Ruslans are an important link in the military logistics chain, transporting cargo not only for Ukraine but also for NATO countries more broadly.
A source familiar with the incident told Ukrainska Pravda that the Ukrainians had three strokes of luck that night. The explosive on the first drone failed to detonate, the second drone crashed into another aircraft, and the third never made it into the air. Police found it only a few weeks later on the outskirts of the airport. Something had apparently spooked the perpetrator.
According to Politico, investigators soon noticed similarities between the drone's warhead and other improvised explosive devices found in caches set up by Russian agents elsewhere in Europe.
The brazen sabotage attempt in Leipzig marked a new escalation in the hybrid war targeting Europe's military sites and defence industry facilities. OSINT analysts have noted that the attacks are becoming more frequent and increasingly systematic.
The Russians themselves are no longer hiding their hand: the arms factories of Ukraine's partners are in their sights.
"It's a secret. A military secret," Russian leader Vladimir Putin said when asked by reporters whether Russia could attack facilities in the UK defence sector.
Ukrainska Pravda looks at Russia's sabotage campaign across Europe and whether it could put continued support for Ukraine at risk.
Fifty incidents involving hybrid attacks in a month
Russia has repeatedly tried to put a bomb under EU support for Ukraine – both literally and figuratively.
The OSINT tracker Malcontent News has logged 497 acts of hybrid warfare across Europe since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. In 454 cases, its analysts identified direct links to Russian or Belarusian hybrid operations. The attacks have taken many forms: cyber-attacks, vandalism, sabotage, arson and incursions by unknown drones.
OSINT analyst Clément Molin estimates that 50 incidents have been recorded across Europe since the start of September alone, many of them likely linked to Russia's hybrid campaign. At least 10 incidents over the past two months have involved the defence industry or military logistics.
Russian intelligence services are behind the planning and organisation of these operations, but they turn to civilians to carry them out. Members of local criminal gangs serve as the Kremlin's intermediaries, seeking out recruits and paying them in cryptocurrency for each job. Former Wagner Group recruiters have also taken part in the process. Ukrainian migrants recruited by the FSB are also frequently among the perpetrators.
Using local residents gives sabotage operations a convenient cover, making them look like industrial accidents or acts of anti-war, environmental or pro-Palestinian activism. But the same approach can also undermine the operation itself. Untrained recruits are prone to mistakes that trained professionals would know how to avoid.
In Leipzig, it was precisely this kind of mistake that helped avert a tragedy.
Sabotage
Most acts of sabotage across Europe between 2022 and 2025 were not aimed at defence industry facilities. Instead, they appeared designed to threaten or intimidate. In most cases, police and counter-intelligence services managed to thwart the attacks – and, in some instances, even prevent assassination attempts.
For instance, in 2024, Russia planned to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German defence giant Rheinmetall, which supplies weapons to Ukraine. The plot was foiled by the US and German intelligence services.
In 2026, the picture has changed dramatically. Defence industry facilities have been increasingly drawn into the sabotage campaign.
One of the most notable incidents was a fire at the Czech drone and optical systems manufacturer LPP Holding. The blaze damaged production facilities and destroyed stock in the warehouse.
Despite the damage, the company said the planned delivery of 40 attack drones to Ukraine remained on track. Czech police immediately determined that the fire had been deliberate and investigated it as a possible terrorist act.
A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group claimed responsibility, accusing LPP of manufacturing weapons for Israel. The company rejected the claim, saying it has no cooperation with Elbit Systems and does not manufacture equipment for Israel. LPP and Elbit Systems announced a partnership in 2023, but the deal was never realised.
LPP suggested that the pro-Palestinian cover story could have been a Russian covert operation aimed at disrupting the company's cooperation with Ukraine.
Another suspected act of sabotage targeted transformers and power-line pylons supplying KNDS and MBDA, major European defence companies that manufacture missiles and ammunition. The attack left 3,000 homes without electricity, and graffiti reading "Action against war" was found nearby.
And the Russians themselves did not stay silent.
On 15 April, Russia's Ministry of Defence released a list of 21 Ukrainian and European companies producing drones and drone components for Ukraine. It gave the addresses of their manufacturing facilities and named the sites themselves. The accuracy of the list is difficult to verify from open sources. But the message was hard to miss.
"When strikes become a reality depends on what comes next. Sleep well, European partners!" Dmitry Medvedev, former Russian president and current deputy chairman of the Security Council, wrote in a comment on the matter.
Four months after Medvedev's comment, a failed sabotage operation in Leipzig showed that Russia was prepared to take its confrontation with Europe a step further.
Fires and explosions hit ammunition depots belonging to arms maker EMCO in Bulgaria on 10 and 12 August. Three days later, a fire followed by explosions broke out at a KNDS ammunition factory in Italy.
Neither Bulgaria nor Italy has officially blamed Russia for the explosions. The authorities have instead attributed them to production problems and human error. EMCO tells a different story, directly linking the incidents to the company's operations and its owner, Emilian Gebrev.
This is not the first time the Bulgarian company has come under attack from Russia. Ukraine has been receiving ammunition from EMCO since 2014 – the same year the first explosions occurred at its depots. In 2015, Russia's GRU military intelligence service attempted to poison Gebrev himself. Similar arson attacks and explosions struck EMCO warehouses again in 2022 and 2023, and investigators found a Russian connection in each case.
In other cases, the Russians were directly accused of sabotage. On 15 August, unknown individuals set fire to Milrem Robotics in Tallinn, which supplies THeMIS ground robots to Ukraine.
The fire was quickly contained, no one was injured, and production carried on as usual. A month later, the Estonian government said the arson attack was an act of sabotage orchestrated by Russian intelligence.
Another incident took place in Slovakia in late August. Local police foiled an arson attack on a Skyeton production facility in the east of the country, where the Ukrainian company manufactures unmanned systems. Company representatives told Ukrainska Pravda that Russian operatives also regularly attempt to target its facilities in Ukraine.
Similar incidents have been reported in Poland, France and Germany. Fires at production facilities belonging to WB Electronics, Delair, Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing have been linked to Russia's military intelligence.
Explosions of unknown origin have also rocked Serbian defence factories producing weapons that end up in Ukraine.
Not every explosion or fire at a defence facility is necessarily an act of sabotage. Rising orders and the rapid expansion of production inevitably bring about the occasional accident.
For instance, a fire broke out on 17 September at ZVS Holding, an ammunition manufacturer owned by CSG (Czechoslovak Group), in Slovakia. CSG spokesperson Andrej Čirtek told Ukrainska Pravda that the company has no information linking the fire to sabotage.
Čirtek said: "The fire broke out during roof renovation work carried out by an external contractor. Based on the findings available so far, the most likely explanation is that the fire was related to the renovation work. However, the investigation by the relevant authorities is still ongoing, so we do not want to speculate about its final conclusions."
How Europe is responding
By carrying out such operations across Europe, the Kremlin is probing how far it can go. Moscow is gauging European countries' responses to sabotage and testing NATO's resilience, taking care not to cross the threshold that could trigger the Alliance's Article 5.
Beyond the immediate damage, acts of sabotage can help map the infrastructure supporting military logistics and reveal vulnerabilities that could become targets in a future conflict.
This is precisely why the arson attacks on defence factories are only part of the picture. There have also been reports of railway tracks being blown up, drones flying over strategic airfields, communications being jammed and other provocations.
Europe has yet to develop a unified response to these events. In the cases mentioned above in Bulgaria and Italy, the governments have refrained from directly accusing Moscow, apparently out of concern that doing so could further escalate tensions.
Other countries take a more sober view of the threat from the east and are seeking ways to counter Russian sabotage. Germany is perhaps the most active in this effort. Its law enforcement and security services are searching for weapons caches that Russian operatives may have set up in preparation for future attacks.
Germany is also putting together a broad package of measures to counter Russian sabotage and cyber-attacks. Special forces are being deployed in strategically important cities across the country to protect critical infrastructure against drones and deal with explosive devices. Police units will work alongside them. Ukraine has been sharing its experience with Germany in this area.
A source familiar with the situation in Leipzig told Ukrainska Pravda that the German law enforcement agencies handled the attempted attack on Ukrainian aircraft particularly well.
"The first thing the German authorities did after the investigation was not to disclose what they had found, but to explain how they would prevent this from happening again," the source said. "They thoroughly analysed everything that happened on the day of the attack and have since introduced a great many security measures to ensure that such acts of sabotage do not happen again. Yes, they were unable to prevent it, but ultimately, the situation served as a wake-up call for them."
Other European countries are also taking active steps to counter the threat. Romania and Germany, for example, have been detaining civilians suspected of collaborating with Russia. Poland has deployed 10,000 troops to protect critical infrastructure after explosions damaged railway tracks. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have set up joint investigation teams to investigate terrorist attacks and acts of sabotage.
A European intelligence official told AP that European intelligence services are now committing as many resources to countering Russian sabotage as they do to combating terrorism.
Defence companies are also tightening their security measures. Representatives of Milrem Robotics told Ukrainska Pravda that the company is changing its approach to security following the arson attack on its premises.
"Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the security situation in Europe has clearly changed, and defence companies must take this into account," says a Milrem Robotics representative.
Will acts of sabotage affect support for Ukraine?
Another clear aim of Russia's sabotage campaign is to weaken European support for Ukraine and reduce the flow of aid.
So far, Russia has failed to achieve this. Most companies have suffered financial losses, but supplies have continued uninterrupted. Some factories temporarily lost production capacity, only to return to normal levels later. The way these sabotage operations have been carried out also suggests that, for now, intimidation is the main objective rather than disruption.
The choice of targets is also telling: Russia is carrying out these operations in countries that are actively helping Ukraine strengthen its defences. By contrast, in countries that provide little support to Ukraine, such as Hungary, no such incidents have been recorded. Moscow is therefore trying to make ordinary Europeans feel the cost of supporting Ukraine.
As warnings of a potential conflict between the EU and Russia become more frequent, European and US intelligence agencies are increasingly highlighting the expansion of Russia's hybrid war against Europe. European governments, too, are beginning to recognise the scale of the threat.
One of the key messages at the 2026 Munich Security Conference was that European leaders must accept this reality and act on it.

PepsiCo cuts earnings outlook as North American recovery takes longer than expected

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
PepsiCo lowered its full-year earnings forecast Thursday as a slower-than-expected recovery in its North American business weighed on profitability despite stronger international demand.
The US food and beverage company now expects core earnings per share to grow 2.5%-3.5% in 2026, compared with its previous forecast targeting the low end of a 5%-7% range.
It expects annual net revenue growth of about 6%, at the upper end of its previous guidance of 4%-6%.
Third-quarter revenue rose 5.6% from a year earlier to $25.27 billion, exceeding analysts’ expectations. Adjusted earnings of $2.34 per share also topped forecasts.
Net income attributable to PepsiCo increased to $3.05 billion, or $2.23 per share, from $2.6 billion, or $1.90 per share, a year earlier.
Organic revenue, which excludes the effects of acquisitions, divestitures and currency movements, increased 3.1%.
“Our business in North America performed below our expectations and represents a meaningful opportunity for improvement,” Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Ramon Laguarta said in prepared remarks.
North American beverage volumes declined 2%, while food volumes in the region were unchanged.
Chief Financial Officer Steve Schmitt said the turnaround in the company’s domestic operations was progressing more slowly than expected.
International operations remained a stronger contributor, accounting for 41% of revenue so far this year, according to Laguarta.
PepsiCo is focusing on product innovation and marketing to support its recovery, including snacks with simpler ingredients and added protein or fiber, alongside functional hydration products, energy drinks and zero-sugar beverages.
Laguarta said the company plans to reduce redundancies and discretionary spending to help finance investments in innovation and marketing.

Yandex has blurred all four of its Cloud data centers on its mapping service, including a facility in Russia’s Ryazan region that was reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones on October 8.
The locations were identified by Russian outlet Verstka, which reported that the facilities are in Mytishchi, Moscow region; Sasovo, Ryazan region; Kaluga; and Vladimir.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Satellite imagery in Yandex Maps shows the sites blurred, while searches for their addresses do not indicate that Yandex data centers are located there. It remains unclear when the company began concealing the facilities.
Verstka noted that other organizations also appear to operate at the same sites. Yandex provides limited information only about its Kaluga facility, where the service marks a checkpoint, although the displayed location is imprecise.
The concealment drew attention after the Yandex data center in the Ryazan region suspended operations following a drone attack on October 8. A fire broke out at the facility after the strike, according to the report.
Yandex described the attack as an "incident" that affected part of the facility’s infrastructure. The company reported that employees were working to restore the damaged systems.
The disruption highlights the vulnerability of Russia’s civilian digital infrastructure to drone attacks reaching facilities deep inside the country. The Ryazan incident affected one of the four locations that support Yandex Cloud infrastructure, as identified by Verstka.
The Sasovo data center shares its industrial site with the Sasta machine-tool plant, which was hit in the same overnight strike. Sasta manufactures CNC lathes, milling machines, and five-axis machining centers, and is reportedly integrated into supply chains supporting production of the Iskander tactical ballistic missile system.
The company faces sanctions from the US, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Canada, Switzerland, and other countries over its links to Russia's military-industrial sector.
The data center itself has a stated electrical capacity of up to 12 megawatts and is designed to host tens of thousands of servers. Widespread Yandex Cloud disruptions followed the attack, though a direct link to the damage has not been independently confirmed.

The EU extended sanctions against Russia for hybrid attacks for another year
Kyiv • UNN
The Council of the EU extended sanctions against 80 individuals and 20 organizations until October 9, 2027. The restrictions provide for asset freezes and a travel ban.
The Council of the European Union has extended until October 9, 2027, sanctions against individuals and organizations responsible for Russia’s destabilizing actions abroad. This was reported by the press service of the Council of the EU, according to UNN.
Details
Today, the Council decided to extend for one year — until October 9, 2027 — the individual restrictive measures against persons responsible for Russia’s destabilizing actions abroad, in view of Russia’s ongoing and intensified hybrid activities, including foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) against the EU, its Member States and partners
Restrictive measures related to Russia’s destabilizing activities currently apply to 80 individuals and 20 legal entities. Those individuals and organizations included on the list are subject to an asset freeze, while EU citizens and companies are prohibited from providing them with funds, financial assets or economic resources. Individuals are also subject to a ban on entering and transiting through the territory of the EU.

An exhibition in Sofia tells the story of St. Francis of Assisi
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:34:26 CEST
21:34:26 KST

The figure of St. Francis of Assisi and his depiction in art are the focus of an exhibition hosted by the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, marking the 800th anniversary of the saint’s death.
                                    
The exhibition begins with the earliest depictions that emerged after Francis’s death, which occurred in Assisi on October 3, 1226, and traces the interpretations of his figure through the centuries, including those by non-Catholic artists. From Cimabue and Giotto to Giovanni Bellini, Caravaggio, and Pietro da Cortona, all the way to Adolfo Wildt, Mimmo Paladino, and contemporary artistic expressions, the exhibition explores the historical and religious dimensions of the saint through images.
                                    
A section is also dedicated to the graphic arts, comics, and cinema, with references to Roberto Rossellini’s *Francesco, giullare di Dio* (1950), Franco Zeffirelli’s *Brother Sun, Sister Moon* (1972), and Liliana Cavani’s *Francesco* (1989). The initiative is presented by the Italian Embassy and the Italian Cultural Institute in collaboration with the Academy and is part of the program of international events dedicated to St. Francis promoted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation. The exhibition is produced by Cms Cultura of Bologna.  The exhibition is scheduled to run from tomorrow through November 30.

German poll finds most voters reject Merz reform course
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:33:42 UTC
21:33:42 KST

Ayhan Simsek
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Most Germans say Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s reform drive is heading the wrong way, and the conservative leader has fallen to a personal low, a survey published on Thursday found, as the anti-immigrant AfD holds a clear lead in voting intentions.
The poll for public broadcaster ZDF found that 59% of respondents believe the coalition’s planned and partly adopted changes to pensions, health care and long-term care are going in “the wrong direction.” Only 30% said the measures are on the right track. Supporters of Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance were the only party camp with a majority in favor, at 66%.
Most voters were angry about what they saw as an unjust distribution of the costs. Some 80% said the burdens are distributed unfairly, against 12% who called the distribution fair. On the social-insurance changes, 77% said they do not believe the government will make an important contribution to solving the problems.
Chancellor sets a personal low
The poll asked how respondents view each politician, on appeal and record, from +5 (very positive) to −5 (very negative). Chancellor Merz scored −2.0, slightly worse than −1.9 in September, a new personal low and his weakest rating in the series so far.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) stayed narrowly in first place at 1.3, down from 1.4. Manuela Schwesig, the SPD premier of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, scored 1.1. Hendrik Wuest, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia from Merz's conservative CDU, scored 0.8.
Anti-immigrant AfD holds its lead
If a general election were held this week, the poll projects the right-wing AfD at 28%, ahead of Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance at 21%.
The center-left SPD, Merz’s coalition partner, would remain at 13%. Among the opposition parties, the environmentalist Greens would gain 1 point to reach 15%, the socialist Left Party would remain at 12%, and the liberal FDP would receive 3%.
The figures suggest that, if a snap election were held, Merz’s CDU/CSU alliance and the center-left SPD would fall short of a parliamentary majority.
Majority sees AfD as threat
Some 68% of respondents said the AfD is a danger to democracy in Germany. But 29% disagreed. Disagreement was higher in the former eastern states, at 42%, than in the west, at 26%.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency classified the AfD in 2025 as a confirmed right-wing extremist endeavor, citing anti-democratic positions and ties to right-wing extremist groups. The party rejects that finding and is challenging it in court.
Asked about proposals to ban the AfD over its alleged anti-democratic goals, 43% favored outlawing the party and 51% opposed it. Opposition was higher among supporters of Merz's conservative CDU/CSU alliance, at 54%, and among supporters of the liberal FDP, at 55%.
On cooperation, 45% said other parties should refuse in principle to work with the AfD, including 70% of SPD supporters, 76% of Greens supporters and 79% of Left Party supporters. As many as 53% said parties should decide case by case, including 54% of CDU/CSU supporters, and 86% of FDP supporters.

Beyond Deference: India’s Bangladesh Reckoning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:33:00 UTC
21:33:00 KST

On October 6, Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi called on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi. It isn’t unusual for heads of Indian missions assigned to critical or sensitive bilateral stations to provide direct update or receive specific strategic directives during visits or consultations in New Delhi. Modi’s office maintains an active and hands-on approach to foreign policy implementation, making direct communication and briefings with key diplomatic personnel a standard part of administrative routine. However, Trivedi’s case and the circumstances of the meeting are rather unique.
Trivedi was appointed as India’s high commissioner to Bangladesh in April 2026, a rare political appointment to a key neighboring diplomatic mission. A businessman and a politician of the ruling BJP from the eastern state of West Bengal, he has direct access to Modi and does not need to route his meetings through the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). His appointment to Dhaka in April 2026, replacing a career diplomat, came at a time when bilateral relations between India and Bangladesh had hit a rough patch.
Bangladeshi demands for the deportation of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has found refuge in India since August 2024, has been a particular sore point. India has ignored repeated pleas by the new BNP government and its predecessor interim government to extradite Hasina, despite the existence of an extradition treaty between the two countries since 2013. The treaty’s terms (Article 6) allows either country to refuse extradition if the offense is of a political nature.
Three days before his meeting with Modi, Trivedi’s response to a direct question at the Bay of Bengal Conversation (BoBC) 2026 in Dhaka had hit the headlines. The BoBC is an annual international conference with participants from over a hundred countries comprising world leaders, policymakers, diplomats, researchers, academics, experts, and civil society representatives organized by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS). I participated in the conference, held this year on October 3-4, as a panelist and a guest of the CGS.
A participating Bangladeshi student asked the Indian high commissioner: “When will India send back Hasina?” Trivedi appeared to diplomatically avert the direct query and instead passed the buck to the Bangladeshi military, who had sent her to India on a military aircraft before she even resigned from her post. Moreover, Hasina was meant to be transiting via Delhi to a third country, which never actually materialized. This put New Delhi in a quandary.
“At that point in time, she [Hasina] was still the prime minister of Bangladesh. We had hardly any choice on that. It was our duty as a neighbor to accept the reality of life,” Trivedi said. He added that New Delhi cannot set a deadline for her return, as her extradition request is under review as part of the legal process. “Nobody can give you a time frame [over Hasina’s return],” he concluded.
While no press statements were issued, the meeting between Modi and Trivedi may reflect an effort on New Delhi’s part to gauge Dhaka’s mood from its own representative. Dhaka has ignored the MEA’s invitations to new Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to visit Delhi. In fact, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, who attended the same conference, was categorical in saying, in a subsequent media interview on the sidelines of the BoBC, that the “principal challenge” in planning Rahman’s visit to India are the activities of Hasina, who he termed a “terrorist,” and her team, who are there. Trivedi could be suggesting a course correction in New Delhi’s policies toward Dhaka.
Since November 2025, India’s MEA has maintained that the formal request for Hasina’s extradition is being “examined as part of ongoing judicial and internal legal processes.” Yet, these “processes” remain inconclusive even after 11 months. While New Delhi is unwilling to sacrifice its former ally, it hasn’t closed the door to mending ties with its eastern neighbor, given their interdependencies and strategic compulsions.
New Delhi still envisages that a visit by the Bangladeshi prime minister to India could create opportunities for an exchange of views and break fresh ground in normalizing relations, but it has yet to embark upon a path that will create the enabling environment necessary for such movement. To the contrary, India’s actions have not inspired much confidence in Bangladesh.
First, from time to time India has allowed Sheikh Hasina to issue press statements denouncing the BNP government, despite Dhaka’s objections. Second, India continues to forcibly deport “illegal Bangladeshi migrants.” A large part of the process involves physically pushing these people under the cover of darkness into Bangladeshi territory while ignoring Dhaka’s objections to such a practice. Third, while Dhaka’s imports from India have risen, restrictive trade measures implemented by both countries have stifled Bangladeshi exports to India. Fourth, the number of visas issued by India’s missions in Bangladesh, mostly for medical patients to access India’s affordable private healthcare facilities, has fallen sharply. Fifth, even two months after Dhaka informed Delhi of its choice for its next ambassador to India, India hasn’t approved the posting. This can be seen as a pressure tactic at its very best.
The irony is that, to New Delhi’s discomfiture, Dhaka is carving out a new framework to deal with India. India is used to conformity and deference from its small neighbors while conducting its neighborhood policy. While that worked for New Delhi for almost 15 years, as long as Hasina was in power, the Rahman government has emphasized its desire to pursue its India policy based on two principal pillars: strategic autonomy and a principle of equality, as it sees itself as an emerging middle power and a major hub in the Bay of Bengal region.
In his opening address at the BoBC 2026, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman emphasized the importance of dialogue, partnership, and mutual respect in strengthening regional and global cooperation, while highlighting various national priorities for Bangladesh — including the protection of national interests, economic stability, institutional reforms, investment, and social safety nets. This translates to Dhaka revisiting its relations with a number of countries, including China and Pakistan, heightening New Delhi’s concerns of being surrounded by a hostile neighborhood – ironically, the same misguided calculation that led to poor relations with Sri Lanka during the Indira Gandhi period.
This new outlook on the part of Dhaka has led it to voice its preference to possibly join the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, which has caused much consternation in New Delhi’s policy circles. More importantly, this further implies that Bangladesh’s negotiations with India to share the water of rivers such as the Ganga and Teesta will start afresh rather than being rolled over as extensions of the lapsing agreements, which Dhaka now considers “flawed.”
Predicting the direction Bangladesh-India ties will take in the coming months is thus a challenge, but the Trivedi episode offers a useful marker of where things stand now. New Delhi appears caught between its reluctance to part with a longtime ally and its recognition that the costs of inaction are mounting. Dhaka, for its part, has made clear that it will no longer treat India’s comfort as the central principle of its own foreign policy. Unless India moves beyond symbolic gestures and ambiguous legal processes to address the substantive issues on the table, the relationship risks settling into a prolonged standoff rather than the hoped-for course correction hinted at by Trivedi’s remarks.

Taiwan opposition continues push for NT$20,000 cash payments

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT legislative caucus secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said Thursday that the party will continue pushing for NT$20,000 (US$630) cash payments to citizens.
CNA reported that Hsu said the KMT would not withdraw its proposal despite the Cabinet’s plan to distribute NT$10,000 next year. She argued that higher-than-expected tax revenue could cover the payments without additional government borrowing. Citizens should benefit from economic growth, particularly gains from the AI industry, she said.
The Cabinet has allocated NT$235.7 billion for NT$10,000 cash payments in its proposed 2027 central government budget. The finance ministry said the first payments could be made on Jan. 26, ahead of the Lunar New Year, if lawmakers approve the budget by Jan. 5 and the president promulgates it by Jan. 20.
Hsu said the KMT’s proposed NT$20,000 payment this year would be separate from the Cabinet’s planned NT$10,000 payment in 2027. She said the KMT proposal would use excess tax revenue, while the Cabinet plan would be funded through next year’s central government budget.
Citing finance ministry figures, Hsu said tax revenue reached NT$3.07 trillion from January through August, up NT$619.1 billion from the same period last year. She estimated that about NT$470 billion would be needed for the payments if additional tax revenue reaches NT$1 trillion by year-end.
Hsu argued that the additional revenue came from the efforts of businesses and the public and should be returned to citizens. She accused the Cabinet of citing fiscal discipline to reject larger payments while spending heavily on what she called failed energy policies.
Hsu urged the government to manage the additional revenue responsibly and ensure that citizens share in economic growth. She said the KMT would continue pressing for the NT$20,000 payments.

Christa Pike is ‘up and walking’ for first time after failed execution, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:32:46 UTC
21:32:46 KST

Christa Pike is “up and walking” in hospital, her lawyer said, just more than a week after she survived two lethal injections during a botched execution in Tennessee.
The recovery marks a dramatic turnaround after Pike was declared brain dead on Monday, before waking up and beginning to speak on Tuesday. Her ordeal has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty.
Stephen Ferrell, a lawyer on Pike’s legal team, told the BBC that she was able to walk, but remained mentally foggy. “What’s been described to me is that physically there’s quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she’s not able to use them very much,” Ferrell said.
“She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far,” he added.
Pike, 50, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber on 30 September, after receiving two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital.
After the botched execution attempt, one of her lawyers called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered.
Pike’s team is seeking psychological support for her, given that “clearly is necessary now”, Ferrell said. On Wednesday, Pike was described as “angry and confused” after regaining consciousness.
Ferrell said of Pike’s mental state: “I think it’s kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she’s also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she’s going.”
He said it remained to be seen whether Pike makes a full recovery.
“I assume [Pike’s condition] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don’t know that yet.”
On Wednesday Randy Spivey, another attorney for Pike, said she was unable to move her arms and has pneumonia and a blood clot. Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm.
Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year, but they continue elsewhere.
On Wednesday, Texas executed Jamaal Howard by pentobarbital. He was convicted of murder in 2001 for fatally shooting convenience store clerk Vickie Swartout during a robbery. Howard’s lawyers argued the execution should be halted, given the issues the drug had caused with Pike, but a series of courts refused.
Meanwhile Donald Trump this week approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. Hasan is due to be shot to death on 3 December; his execution is set to be the first carried out by the US military since 1961.
Pike’s lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.
There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins – which were problematic, a fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of all these factors.
Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995.
According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her.
Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years.
Pike’s attorneys have argued that her original legal team failed to present evidence about the sexual and physical abuse she suffered during childhood. Lee blocked Pike’s request for clemency. He has since ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”.

Ukraine strikes Yandex data center housing two of the company’s supercomputers
A Ukrainian drone attack started a fire at a Yandex data center in the town of Sasovo, Ryazan region. No one was injured, but the data center has completely halted operations.
Yandex has warned that some of its services may be unavailable, and users are already complaining about outages at Yandex. Problems are also reported to be affecting Yandex’s main service, Yandex Cloud, as well as the Yandex Disk and Yandex Documents services that depend on it. Outages are also hitting the websites of Cian, Russian Railways, and the administrations of several regions.
Shares of Yandex, one of Russia’s leading IT companies, fell more than 3% amid the strike, according to data from the Moscow Exchange.
The strike hit the grounds of the Sasta machine-tool plant. Ryazan region authorities did not name the plant, saying only that the roof of “one of the enterprises” caught fire after the Ukrainian attack.
Sasta manufactures pipe-threading machines, and its products are shipped for export and to machine-building plants across Russia. Sasta also provides a production base for defense enterprises, the independent Telegram channel Astra explains. The plant is on the sanctions lists of several Western countries.
Yandex’s data center has occupied part of Sasta’s former premises since 2014. In September, center employees showed off its equipment and said they work specifically in Sasovo, Ryazan region.
The Sasovo center houses two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, which are used to train neural networks: “Lyapunov” and “Chervonenkis.” Chervonenkis is the company’s most powerful supercomputer, the independent science-focused outlet T-invariant writes. In 2021, it ranked 19th in the world’s Top 500 supercomputer list. It later entered the second hundred of the rankings amid difficulties updating its infrastructure because of sanctions.
Yandex has not yet reported on the condition of the supercomputers after the strike. The third system, “Galushkin,” is located in Vladimir.
It is unclear whether the plant or the data center was the intended target. Ukraine has not officially commented on the strike.
The attack on Yandex’s data center came shortly after Russia began striking similar Ukrainian infrastructure. Since September 23, data centers belonging to at least eight companies have been damaged or destroyed, and Russian forces have attacked some of them more than once. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed the data centers “provide for the processing and transmission of intelligence data in the interests of the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
Many see this as a continuation of Russia’s campaign to pressure Ukraine and its residents and destroy the Ukrainian economy. Russian forces have also struck bridges, gas stations, railroads, shopping centers, and warehouses. In recent weeks, the Russian military has been striking Kyiv almost around the clock.

Fed’s Waller signals further rate hikes as inflation stalls, AI spending drives up costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:31:36 UTC
21:31:36 KST

Emir Yildirim
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
US Federal Reserve (Fed) board member Christopher Waller forecast that the bank may need to impose additional interest rate hikes to return inflation to the 2% target if incoming economic data continue to meet expectations, speaking at the Istanbul Economic Forum on Thursday.
Waller provided a comprehensive assessment of the American economic outlook at the summit held by the Turkish Central Bank, noting that further tightening may be needed to accelerate progress toward price stability.
The two-day forum was organized by the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye to address global economic policy challenges by gathering central bank governors and high-level policymakers from around the world, including the US and the UK.
The Fed decided to hike rates by 2 basis points to 3.75-4% at September’s Federal Open Market Committee meeting after maintaining rates for nine months, following 75 basis points of cumulative rate reductions across the final three meetings of last year to combat labor market softening.
Waller stated that the fight to cool inflation had stalled while employment stabilized in the first half of this year, partly due to energy price spikes amid the Middle East conflict.
Waller had initially supported maintaining rates on the assumption that regional wars would be short-lived, but hopes for a swift resolution have since waned. Analysts say high oil prices could persist through next year due to damaged production infrastructure and low inventories.
Recent acceleration drives up future inflation estimates
He noted that while artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investments surged and drove up the prices of high-tech products, ongoing trade disputes threaten to exert further inflationary pressure through new tariffs.
He mentioned that he backed the September rate hike not only because of August consumer prices but also because of months of evidence showing resilient hiring and stubborn inflation.
He is not overly concerned that tighter conditions will lead to a significant domestic slowdown, as economic activity accelerated in the second half of the year.
Waller was concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation was driving up future inflation estimates among consumers, investors and price-setting businesses.
He noted that interest rate projections among Fed officials show the likely direction of monetary policy, but future rate decisions will hinge on economic data.
“If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal,” he said. “But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time.”
American consumers show resilience
Regarding Treasury bond yields, Waller stated that the rise in borrowing costs stems from strong economic growth, higher productivity forecasts and expectations of further policy tightening.
He warned that the trillions of dollars that artificial intelligence firms could borrow in the coming years to fund their massive investments could boost the US government’s borrowing costs.
Waller noted that American consumers have shown resilience amid banking, geopolitical and pandemic shocks, in response to a question about whether household finances might suffer under high food and energy prices.
As for AI, Waller called it a “revolutionary technology,” expecting its advent to boost productivity in the coming years as it transforms how quickly work is conducted. However, the impact of expected productivity gains has yet to be clearly reflected in overall economic data.
“(AI) is going to have an impact on jobs, but we’ve known that about every technological change that's ever happened — some jobs disappear, new jobs are created,” he said, noting that the elimination of existing jobs is immediately visible while newly created jobs remain difficult to foresee.
He added that he expects AI to cultivate a broad and shared ecosystem of competitive firms rather than collapse into a zero-sum monopoly that could lead to an economic crash.
He mentioned that the expansion of private credit funds and their potential risks to commercial banks fuel financial stability concerns. He added that well-governed private credit funds pose limited systemic liquidity risks because they lock in capital over multiyear periods and are not obligated to meet on-demand redemptions.

Iran has now warned regional countries that any attempt to open new routes for oil exports would be considered hostile, a senior regional official close to Tehran told Reuters.
It was part of a plan agreed by both Iran's political leaders and its Revolutionary Guards, the official added.
'Iran has no intention of allowing control to slip from its hands'
"Iran has absolutely no intention of allowing control of the Strait of Hormuz to slip from its hands, and has plans ready to block routes that some regional countries have for exporting oil," a senior diplomat in the region briefed by Tehran told Reuters separately.
"This could involve missile and drone attacks on ships, or sending boats to scare ships away," the diplomat added. "It plans to continue this policy of fear and threats," he said.
In recent months, Gulf oil producers have rushed shipments of oil through channels that hug the Omani side of the strait before transferring the oil in open waters in the Gulf of Oman with aerial support from the US, sources have told Reuters.
In the latest incident in the past 24 hours, projectiles struck a tanker some 51 nautical miles off the coast of Qatar inside the Gulf, British navy agency UKMTO reported.
Maritime security sources said the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged chemical tanker Acers had been hit by multiple projectiles north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal with minor injuries sustained by its crew.
“The Acers strike raises the prospect of a wider combat area affecting approaches to Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq,” maritime risk intelligence group Pole Star Global’s subsidiary Clearwater Dynamics said in a report on Thursday.
The vessel's operator, listed in shipping databases as Antigua and Barbuda-based Valvoria Shipping, could not be reached for comment.
"The recent spate of Iranian attacks seems to have dampened the appetite of shipowners to sail through the Strait," said Jakob Larsen, chief safety & security officer at shipping association BIMCO.
"The Iranian threat appears to have increased."

Spain snap election puts ties with Israel on the line, Prime Minister Sanchez at risk - interview
