Female genital mutilation (FGM) in Brussels: “a bigger problem than thought”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:20:49 UTC
21:20:49 KST

Almost 9,800 girls and women in the Brussels Region have undergone female genital mutilation (FGM) or are at least at risk. This is unacceptable, says GAMS Belgium, an organisation which is taking to the streets on Saturday to protest against gender-based violence.
Female genital mutilation (FGM) in Brussels: “a bigger problem than thought”
This summer, posts defending female genital mutilation circulated on social media. They are also reaching parents and young people in Brussels. That is why, on Saturday 10 October, on the eve of the International Day of the Girl Child, GAMS and its supporters are gathering outside Central Station to say ‘no’ loud and clear, as they did previously on 22 August in countries including Mali and France.
What proponents pass off as ‘tradition’ has a face. A girl from Anderlecht is travelling to her parents’ family home in the summer. What she doesn’t know is that a family member thinks it is ‘time’. Every year before the summer holidays, GAMS receives enquiries from worried mothers, grandmothers and sisters, as well as teachers and doctors who fear precisely this.
Female genital mutilation (FGM) is any procedure in which the external genitalia of a girl or woman are partially or completely removed or injured without medical justification. It ranges from the removal of the external part of the clitoris to the almost complete closure of the vaginal opening. The consequences last a lifetime: pain, infections, complications during childbirth, sexual difficulties and deep psychological trauma.
The problem is more widespread than many people in Brussels realise. There are more than 23,000 women living in Belgium who have been subjected to FGM, and over 12,000 girls are at risk if no preventive measures are taken. In the Brussels Region, this correponds to nearly 9,800 girls and women who have undergone the mutilation or are at risk. These figures date from late 2020, and every new study to date has shown an increase. The figure is believed to be a significant underestimate of this form of gender-based violence, which occurs in 94 countries worldwide and is the fourth leading cause of death among girls and women in African countries where the practice is carried out.
A trip to country of origin...
The mutilation rarely takes place in Belgium itself. The greatest risk arises when travelling to the country of origin, sometimes with a girl who is left behind there. That is why GAMS launches a prevention campaign every year ahead of the summer period. Last year, the focus was on protective parents, as they are the ones who can put a stop to this intergenerational trauma, even if it sometimes takes all their strength and courage to stand up to social pressure.
Why does it still happen? Not because parents want to harm their daughters. FGM is a social norm. A girl who has undergone FGM is regarded as a full member of the community. Anyone who refuses risks exclusion and a break with the family. No religion prescribes it. At its core, it is about control over women’s bodies and sexuality. FGM is not a cultural practice, but gender-based violence.
Social exclusion and discrimination, a language barrier, uncertain residence status, poverty and dependence on family abroad place girls in an even more vulnerable position. Anyone who thinks this is a problem for ‘others’ would do well to take a look at themselves. FGM is an umbrella term. Broadly speaking, any procedure on the genitals without medical necessity and without free, informed consent is a form of mutilation. This happens in Belgium too, even if we do not call it that: an unnecessary episiotomy during childbirth, a ‘husband stitch’ to narrow the vagina, or operations on babies with variations in sex characteristics (intersex children). In each case, someone else decides what constitutes an acceptable body.
A 'husband stitch' is a non-medical practice whereby an extra stitch is added during perineal repair after childbirth to tighten the vaginal opening for the male partner's sexual pleasure.
Stricter laws? No, that doesn’t seem to be the answer. Since 2001, FGM has been explicitly made a crime in Belgium, even when carried out abroad. What is lacking are the resources to carry out prevention on a structural level. Punishment always comes too late.
A cultural shift is already underway, driven by the communities themselves. The ‘Community Voices’ are initiating dialogue in their own languages and through their own networks. GAMS itself was also founded by the communities themselves, by a number of courageous role models, including Khadidiatou Diallo. GAMS also calls for a cultural shift within a broader social context, to tackle patriarchal gender roles and ensure that women’s bodies are no longer used as pawns in political discourse and public opinion.
"Specifically, we are calling for structural funding for prevention rather than one-off projects; for professionals in schools, the healthcare sector, the Flemish children’s agency Kind en Gezin and its Francophone counterpart ONE and the pupil guidance centres CLB that can recognise the warning signs before the summer holidays; a prevention programme linked to family reunifications and a procedure to bring back girls who are trapped abroad; and men, young people and religious leaders who speak out. A father, grandmother or imam who says ‘not my daughter’ carries more weight than ten leaflets.”
This article originally appeared in Dutch on Brussels media outlet Bruzz .

Gaza has no fully functioning hospital nearly a year into ceasefire, rights group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:20:34 UTC
21:20:34 KST

Gaza still has no hospital operating at full capacity a year after a ceasefire took effect, Physicians for Human Rights-Israel said on Thursday.
The Israeli rights organisation released a report assessing the state of Gaza’s health system nearly a year after the ceasefire began in October 2025.
It said the period has not brought about a genuine recovery of the health system despite a limited increase in the number of hospitals that have partially resumed operations.
“The number of intensive care beds has practically not changed, the shortage of medicines and essential medical supplies has worsened, while thousands of patients remain deprived of life-saving treatments that are unavailable in the Strip,” the organisation said.
“In October 2025, 14 of the 36 hospitals were operating partially. Nearly a year later, the number has risen to 20, but none is still capable of operating fully,” it said.
The report added that Gaza had 103 intensive care beds in October 2025, compared with only 104 in July 2026, noting that kidney dialysis services had failed to recover.
“Dialysis services were available at 17 percent of health facilities in October 2025, falling to 12 percent in July 2026, while MRI services remain unavailable in the enclave,” it said.
The World Health Organization documented at least 143 additional attacks on health care during the first seven months of the ceasefire, it said.
The shortage of medicines and medical supplies also persisted. According to data from Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), 69 percent of medical supplies approved for entry into Gaza between January and May 2026 did not actually enter the enclave, the organisation said.
The report also highlighted the consequences of the closure of crossings and restrictions preventing Palestinians from leaving Gaza for medical treatment, saying “patients are dying while waiting for evacuation.”
“While the need for treatment is increasing, the number of people leaving for medical care is far below pre-war levels,” the report said.
Before October 2023, between 50 and 100 patients left Gaza each day to receive medical treatment, it said.
Between October 10 2025 and mid-September 2026, about 3,423 patients were evacuated abroad, a rate three to six times lower than pre-war levels despite the sharp increase in demand for treatment outside the Strip, according to the report.
According to figures from the WHO’s Health Cluster, Israeli forces killed at least 1,422 Palestinians and injured 5,150 others between the announcement of the ceasefire and the end of September 2026, the non-profit said.
More than half of Gaza dialysis patients die after three years of genocide: health chief
Meanwhile, Gaza’s health chief said that more than half of Gaza’s dialysis patients have died amid Israel’s blockade and the subsequent collapse of the enclave’s health care system during three years of genocide.
Gaza had around 1,400 dialysis patients before the genocide, but that number has now fallen to about 600, Munir al-Bursh, director general of Gaza’s health ministry, told Anadolu, attributing the decline to “deaths caused by the inability to receive regular treatment.”
More than 174,000 wounded people need nearly half a million complex surgeries, but the health care system lacks the resources to carry them out, he said.
Bursh said Israel continues to detain 88 specialist doctors, while its blockade prevents medical supplies from reaching patients in need.
According to Bursh, Gaza’s health services remain in a state of collapse despite the ceasefire.
In September, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented continued shortages of medicines for chronic illnesses, including supplies needed to treat kidney disease.
On treatment outside Gaza, Bursh said more than 20,000 patients and wounded people urgently need to leave the enclave to receive treatment.
He said “arrangements providing for the departure of around 300 patients a day have not been implemented by Israel, with only about 25 patients currently allowed to leave each day.”
UN figures released in April showed that more than 18,500 patients needed medical evacuation, including around 4,000 children.
Bursh called for “urgent international action to pressure Israel to allow medicines and equipment into Gaza, rehabilitate hospitals and allow medical personnel to return, as well as approve the evacuation of wounded people before it is too late.”
Nearly half a million complex surgeries needed
Against this backdrop, Bursh said more than 174,000 people have been wounded since the start of the genocide, with each initially requiring an average of at least three surgeries.
“This means Gaza needs nearly half a million complex surgical procedures,” he said, despite having virtually “no resources to carry them out.”
Bursh warned that Gaza’s health sector is suffering from severe shortages of medicines and medical supplies.
He said “medical stocks have reached dangerously low levels,” with shortages of 52 percent for beds and essential medicines and 56 percent for medical supplies.
“No new medical equipment has been allowed into Gaza since the start of the Israeli offensive,” he said.

NASA is searching for hidden caves to build its first Moon base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:19:20 UTC
21:19:20 KST

NASA is searching for hidden caves to build its first Moon base
- Date:
- October 8, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA is preparing for humanity’s first Moon base with three investigations that will hunt for underground shelters, uncover hidden ice, and track dangerous conditions on the lunar surface. The findings could reveal how astronauts can survive and thrive on the Moon while laying the groundwork for future journeys to Mars.
- Share:
NASA is moving closer to establishing humanity's first Moon base with the selection of three scientific investigations designed to answer some of the biggest questions about living on the lunar surface. The missions will search for underground caves that could shelter astronauts, investigate hidden deposits of lunar ice, and monitor environmental hazards that could threaten future explorers.
The new instruments and technologies were selected through NASA's Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program. They will be delivered to the lunar surface through the agency's CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative as part of its Moon Base Program.
Each investigation will address a different challenge of establishing a lasting human presence on the Moon. Researchers will examine potential natural shelters, identify resources that astronauts could use, and study dangerous conditions that future habitats and equipment will need to withstand. Together, the findings will support NASA's Artemis and Moon Base programs as the agency works toward long-term lunar exploration.
"NASA Science is building the ultimate interplanetary survival guide to ensure that science goes first to the lunar surface to provide our future astronaut crews with the vital information, resources, and safety precautions needed ahead of time to survive the night on the Moon," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "These PRISM selections will directly help NASA minimize risks to our astronauts while maximizing our agency goals as we set up humanity's first lunar outpost in preparation for sending the first astronauts to Mars."
Monitoring Moonquakes and Other Lunar Hazards
The first investigation, Lunar Environment Monitoring Station -- South Pole (LEMS-SP), will establish an autonomous station to track environmental conditions and potential threats over an extended period.
One of its tasks will be detecting micrometeoroids, tiny pieces of space debris that strike the lunar surface. Unlike Earth, the Moon lacks a substantial atmosphere capable of burning up most incoming objects, making these impacts a concern for future equipment and habitats.
The station will also measure the abundance of volatiles, substances that readily turn into gas, within the Moon's extremely thin outer layer of gases. Tracking these materials will help scientists better understand how the lunar environment changes over time.
Another important instrument will be a short-period seismometer, designed to detect vibrations and seismic activity, including moonquakes. These measurements could reveal hazards that NASA must consider when designing structures and installing sensitive equipment on the lunar surface.
By collecting information about impacts, seismic activity, and the surrounding environment, LEMS-SP could help engineers develop safer and more reliable infrastructure for a permanent Moon base.
The investigation will be led by Dr. Mehdi Benna of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County.
Searching for Hidden Caves Beneath the Moon
The second investigation will explore one of the Moon's most intriguing possibilities: enormous underground passages that could serve as natural shelters for astronauts.
Known as Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation (GIMLI), the mission will examine the Marius Hills Pit, an opening in the lunar surface that may connect to an extensive underground lava tube.
Lava tubes form when the outer surface of flowing lava cools and hardens while molten rock continues moving beneath it. Once the lava drains away, it can leave behind hollow tunnels. Scientists believe similar formations may exist beneath parts of the Moon's volcanic terrain.
GIMLI will use geophysical measurements to investigate what lies beneath the pit and determine whether it connects to a larger underground passage. The findings will also provide new insights into the volcanic processes that shaped the lunar landscape.
If large underground spaces are confirmed, they could offer an important advantage for future human exploration.
The lunar surface is exposed to intense temperature changes, harmful ionizing radiation, and frequent impacts from tiny space rocks. Underground lava tubes could provide more stable temperatures and natural shielding from these dangers.
Instead of relying entirely on protective structures built on the surface, future astronauts might be able to use some of the Moon's existing geological formations as shelters.
Confirming the presence and size of these underground spaces could therefore influence where NASA considers placing future habitats and how those habitats are designed.
Dr. Nathaniel Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute will serve as the principal investigator for GIMLI.
Hunting for Hidden Ice and Usable Moon Resources
The third investigation will focus on another resource that could be essential to a lasting human presence on the Moon: water ice.
The Depth Imager with Spectral and Color Optics (DISCO) payload is designed to make the first direct measurements from the lunar surface of ice preserved inside small, exceptionally cold regions known as micro-cold traps.
These areas can remain cold enough for ice to persist because they receive little or no direct sunlight. Identifying where the ice is located, how much exists, and how it is distributed could help scientists understand whether it can become a practical resource for future lunar missions.
Water brought from Earth is expensive to transport into space. Finding accessible ice on the Moon could eventually allow astronauts to obtain water locally and potentially process it into oxygen and hydrogen for other uses.
DISCO will also investigate the physical properties of the lunar surface.
One challenge is understanding what happens when a spacecraft lands. Rocket exhaust can blast dust and loose material away from the ground, potentially affecting nearby equipment and structures.
Researchers will also examine the stability of the terrain to better understand how safely astronauts, robotic vehicles, and other equipment can move across the surface.
Combining these measurements will help NASA develop safer landing and surface operations while advancing technologies that could turn lunar ice into a useful resource for the Moon Base Program.
Dr. Ariel Deutsch of NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley will lead the DISCO investigation.
Building the Foundation for Humanity's First Moon Base
Together, the three investigations will address some of the most important challenges of establishing a sustained human presence beyond Earth.
LEMS-SP will help scientists understand environmental threats, GIMLI will investigate whether underground lava tubes could provide natural protection, and DISCO will examine potential water resources and the behavior of the lunar surface.
The results could influence everything from the placement of future habitats to the design of equipment and the development of systems that allow astronauts to make use of resources already available on the Moon.
"Each new PRISM selection strengthens our ability to deliver ambitious, transformative science to the lunar surface," said Brad Bailey, director of the Exploration Science Strategy Integration Office in NASA's Science Mission Directorate. "These investigations exemplify how Artemis and Moon Base are expanding the frontier of lunar exploration, advancing innovative technologies, deepening our understanding of the Moon's environment, and paving the way for future astronaut missions."
NASA is working to increase the frequency of its lunar missions as it prepares to establish a Moon base. These missions will deliver scientific instruments and new technologies intended to expand American leadership in space science, support a sustained lunar presence, and prepare for more ambitious human exploration.
The agency's CLPS initiative plays a central role in that effort by partnering with American companies to transport scientific, exploration, and technology payloads to the Moon's surface and orbit.
Beyond helping astronauts live and work on the Moon, the knowledge gained from these investigations could prove essential to NASA's longer-term goal of sending humans to Mars.

Who decides what Africa is worth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:19:10 UTC
21:19:10 KST

Can anyone break free from Western bankers? Africa is about to find out
On October 7, the African Union officially launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) in Mauritius, giving the continent its own institution for assessing African sovereigns, companies, and financial institutions. AfCRA is not intended to replace Moody’s, S&P, or Fitch, but to introduce an African source of authority into a system that has long helped determine the price at which African countries can borrow.
On the surface, this is a technical event about ratings and capital markets. But the questions underneath it are political. Who decides whether an African country is a safe place to lend money? Who decides what interest that country should pay? And why should judgements made by institutions far outside the continent carry such enormous weight over the price of African development?
The AU says AfCRA will rate African sovereigns, sub-sovereigns, companies, and institutions. It is designed as a private-sector-driven, self-funded body, with governments barred from owning shares, and is meant to complement rather than simply replace the established global agencies. That may sound modest. In fact, it touches one of the unfinished questions of African independence.
The price of a rating
A sovereign credit rating impacts directly the price of money. A government borrowing to build a railway or refinance debt enters a market in which investors judge the possibility of repayment, and ratings shape that perception. A lower rating can mean a higher yield demanded by investors and can influence the borrowing conditions facing banks and state-owned companies. An apparently technical judgement can therefore become a very material question: How much of the wealth produced by a country must be transferred to creditors simply to obtain capital?
The AU says Africa’s external debt-service payments rose from $61 billion in 2010 to $163 billion in 2024. UNDP research published in 2023 estimated that African countries could save up to $74.5 billion in excess interest and foregone financing if sovereign ratings were based on less subjective assessments. One does not have to accept every estimate, or conclude that every downgrade of an African country is unfair, to recognize the scale of the issue.
African states have real weaknesses: unsustainable debt, commodity dependence, narrow tax bases, incomplete statistics, corruption, and vulnerable currencies. An African agency that concealed these realities would destroy its credibility. But that does not make the existing system neutral. Ratings combine measurable indicators with judgements about institutions, reserves, and policy credibility. UNDP has identified foreign-currency bias and insufficient recognition of informal activity among the structural problems affecting African assessments.
Critics dispute that this amounts to systematic bias. That disagreement is precisely why Africa needs its own analytical capacity. The point is not to guarantee a better grade; it is to stop being the object being graded.
Liberation is also financial
This is where the question of liberation enters. Political sovereignty answers the question: Who governs? Economic sovereignty asks a harder question: Who controls the conditions under which development is possible?
Colonial rule, while occupying territory, organized economies. Railways ran from mines and plantations to ports, commodities moved outward, manufactured goods moved inward, and financial authority remained elsewhere. Independence changed the political map, but much of that economic geography survived. Africa still exports raw materials, imports much of its machinery, and often borrows in currencies it does not control. Rating agencies did not create that structure, but they operate inside an architecture shaped by it.
This is why AfCRA is more important than whether it awards one country BBB instead of BB. It begins to contest who has the authority to interpret African economic reality. The AU says one objective is to strengthen Africa’s voice in global financial governance. Ratings agencies possess credibility that is itself is a form of institutional power.
AfCRA will still operate inside international capital markets. But changing who is authorized to produce credible judgements inside a system can still alter the balance of power within it. Financial independence is built by accumulating alternatives. A continental ratings agency challenges who defines risk. Regional payments systems reduce dependence on external channels. Local-currency finance reduces exposure to currencies controlled elsewhere. Development banks, monetary funds and, eventually, deeper monetary integration push the challenge further.
From Gaddafi to BRICS
Africa has been discussing this architecture for decades. The 1991 Abuja Treaty envisaged deeper economic integration. The 1999 Sirte Declaration, adopted at a summit hosted in Libya and strongly influenced by Muammar Gaddafi’s campaign for a more united Africa, called for accelerating the institutions of the African Economic Community. The AU’s Constitutive Act later provided for an African Central Bank, an African Monetary Fund, and an African Investment Bank.
The AU still describes the intended purpose of the African Central Bank as creating a common monetary policy and eventually a single African currency. This history matters because Gaddafi’s argument about African unity was never only diplomatic. He pushed the question towards the material foundations of sovereignty. Could Africa be genuinely independent if its trade, reserves, borrowing, and development remained structurally dependent on financial institutions and currencies centered elsewhere?
There is a popular claim that Libya was preparing a gold-backed pan-African dinar that would displace the dollar and the CFA franc. That specific claim remains disputed and should not be treated as established fact. What is firmly documented is the wider project: Gaddafi’s pressure for continental union, the Sirte process, and the institutional agenda for an African central bank, monetary fund, and investment bank. The historical question is whether political unity can survive without economic and monetary power.
The same question now appears in another form through BRICS. The bloc has not created a common currency, and predictions of an imminent replacement for the dollar are exaggerated. But it is widening room for maneuver. In 2024, 43.5% of New Development Bank approvals were denominated mainly in Chinese renminbi and South African rand. The 2025 BRICS Rio Declaration also called for further work on cross-border payments and greater interoperability among payment systems.
These are attempts to create optionality, and optionality is where dependence begins to weaken. A country with only one lender accepts the lender’s conditions. A country with several credible sources of finance has bargaining power. The same is true of currencies, payment systems, markets, and rating institutions.
AfCRA belongs in that wider movement. It does not abolish Moody’s, S&P, or Fitch, but it introduces an African source of recognized judgement into a field where Africa has had little institutional power. That can influence how African risk is discussed, what data are considered, and which assumptions are challenged.
What kind of economy are we financing?
Still, cheaper borrowing cannot be the final objective. Africa does not need liberation from expensive debt so that it can accumulate more cheap debt. The deeper question is what borrowed capital produces.
There is a profound difference between borrowing to finance consumption, recurrent deficits, or an extractive enclave that exports most of its value, and borrowing to build power generation, railways, fertilizer plants, machine industries, food-processing capacity, and regional supply chains. The first can reproduce dependency. The second can expand the productive base from which future repayment and development become possible.
That is why financial liberation and productive liberation cannot be separated. And neither can be separated from African unity.
Fifty-five fragmented states, many with small domestic markets and colonial trade patterns, will always negotiate from a weaker position than an integrated continental economy. A mine in one African country should be able to supply a factory in another, financed by African capital, transported on African infrastructure, sold across an African market and paid for through African financial systems. And that is actually the economic content of Pan-Africanism.
National sovereignty has limits when capital, production, trade, and finance operate at continental and global scale. For Africa, sovereignty has to rise to the continental level. The African Continental Free Trade Area enlarges the market; African payment systems can reduce dependence on third currencies; development institutions can mobilize savings towards African priorities. And AfCRA adds another capacity: to interpret and price African economic reality.
When unity becomes power
None of these institutions should be romanticized. AfCRA can fail. If governments pressure it for favorable ratings, it will lose credibility. If it simply reproduces the methodologies of the established agencies with African personnel, its political significance will be limited. And if African ruling classes speak about financial sovereignty while continuing capital flight, raw-material dependency, and unproductive borrowing, the language of liberation becomes another slogan.
Its credibility may even require the agency, at times, to rate an African government more harshly than the established agencies. Independence is not demonstrated by giving Africa better marks. It is demonstrated by producing better analysis.
The launch in Mauritius should therefore be seen for what it is: one institution in a much larger struggle over economic power. African liberation was never completed by lowering colonial flags. It requires control over production, trade, finance, and the circulation of wealth. A fragmented Africa can ask for better treatment. A united Africa can create alternatives.
And that is where financial reform begins to become liberation.

Defense minister: Estonia considering new Datasel settlement proposal
Estonia is considering a new settlement proposal from the Italian-registered ammunition supplier Datasel, Minister of Defense Martin Herem said Thursday.
The Indian businessmen-owned company is in a legal dispute with Estonia over a contract to supply tens of millions of euros' worth of ammunition intended for Ukraine. Herem said he only saw Datasel's latest proposal that morning and thus could not disclose any details.
"I have seen it and we are considering it," Herem said at Thursday's government press conference, noting that Estonia is reviewing the proposal themselves, discussing it with Ukraine and proceeding from there.
"It may ultimately be possible that the Ukrainians will still get the ammunition they need for that amount," he added.
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (ECDI) rejected an earlier settlement proposal from Datasel. In mid-September, the company proposed forming a joint working group with the government, some MPs and the ECDI to resolve the dispute, but the ECDI said the proposal came too late.
The ECDI signed a roughly €70 million ammunition contract with Datasel in 2024, paying about €60 million up front. The ammunition delivered failed to meet requirements, although Datasel has disputed concerns about its quality.
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) launched an investigation into the transactions last month.
The procurement was funded through the European Peace Facility (EPF), not by Estonian taxpayers, with the EU-level funding including proceeds from frozen Russian assets.

France student protests turn violent, over 6,600 arrested as unrest spreads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:18:21 UTC
21:18:21 KST

Rioting linked to student protests in France resumed Thursday afternoon, with Paris police using tear gas to disperse teenagers who overturned trash cans and erected barricades outside Hélène Boucher High School in the northeastern part of the city.
The wave of protests in France, which politicians on the right and center accuse the far left of encouraging for political purposes, shows no signs of subsiding. Over the past 24 hours, the unrest has spread to neighboring Belgium, where similar riots have erupted. In France, protest marches were held Thursday not only in Paris but also in Nantes, Rennes, Bron, Toulon, Marseille and other cities.
Hélène Boucher High School, which has become a major flashpoint for clashes between protesters and police in the French capital, is one of 375 schools, out of approximately 3,700 across France, that were fully or partially closed Thursday because of protest activity. Many of the demonstrators who gathered outside the school wore surgical masks or hooded sweatshirts, apparently to make identification more difficult. At least 12 demonstrations in support of the protest movement were scheduled to take place across the country later Thursday.
The student protests in France began September 17 and gained momentum last week, when students at hundreds of schools, particularly in poorer working-class suburbs such as Saint-Denis outside Paris, began blocking school entrances, occupying roads, setting trash cans on fire and attacking police officers and passersby. The students say they are protesting neglected school infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. The demonstrations erupted as the French government seeks to pass its 2027 budget, which aims to reduce the deficit.
Since the protests began, at least 24 schools have been set on fire or looted, and 85 education workers have been injured. Nearly 800 police officers and 215 teenagers have also been injured in clashes. According to the latest figures from authorities, more than 6,600 people have been arrested across France since the unrest began, most of them teenagers. The Justice Ministry said 1,800 of those arrested would face prosecution, including 1,483 minors. Property damage from the violent protests is estimated at tens of millions of euros.
Opponents of the demonstrations have accused France Unbowed ("La France Insoumise"), the party led by radical left-wing leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a staunchly anti-Israel politician, of inciting violence and fueling the riots. They have also highlighted the involvement of immigrants and their descendants in the street violence.
Palestinian keffiyehs and flags have been visible at many of the demonstrations in recent days, including Thursday morning's protests in Paris. On Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump weighed in on the issue in a social media post, alleging that the demonstrations were not really about conditions in schools but rather reflected uncontrolled immigration and an attempt by Islam to take over France.
According to a poll conducted by Elabe for BFM TV, 72% of French respondents believe the students' demands are legitimate, but 55% believe the protests should end.
Prime minister: 'Political leaders are exploiting anger for elections'
Thursday's demonstrations followed Tuesday's main "day of rage" protests, which drew approximately 266,000 participants according to police and 450,000 according to organizers. Ahead of Thursday's events, a French student union called for blockades of high schools and university campuses, followed by demonstrations outside government buildings across the Paris region and at the capital's Place de la Bastille in the afternoon.
Although the number of schools disrupted has declined over the past two days compared with Tuesday, pressure on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron continues to mount.
The demonstrations against inadequate school funding have attracted troublemakers who are not necessarily interested in the protest movement's goals, alongside labor unions and political organizations. Against this backdrop, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu this week accused Mélenchon's France Unbowed party, which is linked to many of these groups, of attempting to "sow chaos" ahead of the presidential election in April and May. Polls predict that Mélenchon will advance to the decisive runoff, where he is expected to lose to far-right leader Marine Le Pen.
In a televised address to the nation Wednesday, Lecornu acknowledged that students' concerns were genuine and deserved to be heard, promising measures later this month to improve conditions. But he also expressed regret over "the violence, attacks on students and staff, injuries to police officers, schools set on fire or vandalized and thousands of hours of lost instruction, not to mention threats and insults."
He again criticized "political leaders who are exploiting this anger to wage their election battles," in a clear rebuke of the far left and Mélenchon.
Among the demonstrators gathered Thursday outside Hélène Boucher High School in Paris was 18-year-old student Emma Khelil, who came to show support for those manning the makeshift barricades at her former school.
She told The Associated Press that she was concerned about police violence.
"We’re here to defend our rights, not to lose an eye or a hand," Khelil said.
She recalled insulation problems, water leaks and occasional sightings of rats during her time at the school.
"I don’t think the movement is going to lose momentum. As long as things don’t change, we’re going to see the movement grow stronger, and potentially a convergence of struggles, especially with the next presidential election coming up."
Shortly after she spoke, police surrounded a nearby square, the crowd began surging forward and officers fired tear gas toward the demonstrators.
Teenager loses hand, another suffers broken teeth as police warn of escalating violence
France announced Wednesday that it was suspending the use of stun grenades following an incident Tuesday in which a 15-year-old boy lost his hand.
Police said they had been confronted by more than 200 students throwing stones and firing fireworks, and that the teenager picked up a grenade that exploded in his hand. Students, however, claimed he was struck directly after a police officer fired the device toward him.
In another incident last week, a 14-year-old boy named Eden was struck in the face by a tear gas grenade near Paris. According to his lawyer, he lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw. His mother said he is now unable to speak and can drink only through a straw.
The officer involved said in his defense that he had acted in a "split second" to protect a female officer who was exchanging blows with the teenager. He has been suspended pending an investigation.
In recent days, protesters and their supporters have made numerous additional allegations of excessive police force.
In one case, an officer is under investigation for attempted murder after a 17-year-old protester alleged that the officer held his head underwater while trying to arrest him near a river in the northern city of Belfort.
In Tours, in the Loire wine region, a 15-year-old boy suffered partial blindness after allegedly being struck by a police rubber bullet.
Despite the suspension of stun grenades, Lecornu defended the police response against allegations of disproportionate force and denied that security forces had been instructed to confront the young protesters.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told RTL radio that the police oversight agency had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had used excessive force.
The national secretary of the UNSA police union expressed skepticism about the decision to suspend stun grenades, arguing that it was based "on emotion."
"We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, warning that without this crowd-control measure, more confrontations could occur at close range.
"That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he explained.
The national coordinator of the radical left-wing France Unbowed party, known by its French initials LFI, accused the authorities of waiting until "several children had been permanently maimed before Interior Minister Nuñez agreed to stop using grenades against high school students."
Dozens arrested in Belgium as nighttime gatherings banned
Over the past 24 hours, the protests have also spread to Belgium.
In the city of Liège, police used water cannons and tear gas Wednesday to push back several hundred demonstrators. Authorities were forced to send alerts to shopkeepers' mobile phones, urging them to close their businesses because of the rioting.
Nearly 90 people were arrested in the city, and several police officers were injured.
Police reinforcements were dispatched to Liège from Brussels and Antwerp, while Mayor Willy Demeyer issued an order banning public gatherings until midnight Oct. 16, citing what he described as a "real, serious and immediate danger" of renewed clashes and vandalism that authorities expect in the coming days.
Smaller demonstrations took place Wednesday in Mons and Charleroi, while similar protests were held Thursday outside several schools in Brussels and at the University of Liège.
Belgian Foreign Minister Bernard Quintin said radical left-wing activists had infiltrated the student protests in Liège and were causing property damage.
Julien Douet, a member of the Liège Anti-Fascist Front, told local media that Quintin's allegations were "delusional."
In a social media post, Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin declared that "the perpetrators will have to answer for their actions before the courts."
The protests in Belgium, organized through social media chat groups, include demands for more teachers and smaller classes, along with complaints about the country's education reforms. These included an increase in tuition fees for most students in Belgium's French-speaking community, from 835 euros to 1,194 euros ($1,280).
Several Belgian students said they were in contact with their French counterparts.
"We support each other because we're dealing with more or less the same problems," said Alfred, a 19-year-old student.
Amelia Di Salva, a 19-year-old student training to become a teacher, said Belgium's student movement had begun earlier this year and was revived after students saw the demonstrations in France.
"When we saw that nothing was changing without protests, we decided to get started. France definitely influenced us a little."

Estonian team wins grueling week-long adventure racing world championship on Corsica
An Estonian team has won the adventure racing world championship on the Mediterranean island of Corsica, overtaking the world-ranked leaders on the penultimate stage.
This was an improvement on last year's world championships in Canada, where the Estonian team already took silver.
Adventure racing involves a multisport combination of expedition-length navigation, trekking, kayaking and cycling, with teams racing continuously for days.
The foursome of Rain Eensaar, Reeda Tuula-Fjodorov, Tauno Riibak and Timmo Tammemäe, competing as Estonian Ace La Sportiva, finished the 500km course in six days, eight hours and 45 minutes, beating out nearly 100 other teams.
The team passed French squad 400team Altore, leaders of the world rankings, only on the penultimate leg of the race.
The course, which began early Thursday morning, covered more than 500 kilometers with 20,000 meters of elevation gain.
The icing on the cake for Estonian competitors was that another Estonian team, Tactical Foodpack (Lauri Tammemäe, Anita Lehmann, Arvi Anton, Andris Ansabergs), took third place and the bronze medal.
A total of 98 teams took part in the championships in Corsica.

Opposition Leader in Bulgaria Says Ship May Have Carried Troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

21:18:00 KST

Opposition Leader in Bulgaria Says Ship May Have Carried Troops
GERB leader Boyko Borissov, from the opposition, said security service reports at the Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS) indicated that the sunken Black Sea vessel may have been transporting people or troops.
Borissov made the comments during a working meeting with party officials in Petrich, a day after the closed-door CCNS meeting convened by President Iliana Yotova following the sinking of two merchant vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on October 6.
“The intelligence reports state that they were transporting people or troops,” Borissov said.
Borissov was the only participant in Wednesday’s CCNS meeting who did not speak to reporters afterward. He said he had deliberately refrained from commenting because he expected politicians to present selective versions of the discussions for election campaign purposes.
“I told them how Kostadinov would be the first to step out and speak to the media, and then everyone else would recount the specific part that suited their election campaign interests. And that is exactly what happened - with PP, DB, 'Revival,' and the government,” Borissov said.
He called on President Iliana Yotova to declassify the section of the CCNS transcript containing the politicians’ statements, arguing that this would allow the public to compare what was said during the meeting with subsequent public comments.
“And you will see how amusing the comments of those who have already spoken will appear when compared to their behavior inside the room,” Borissov told GERB officials.
Borissov said GERB had supported a Democratic Bulgaria declaration seeking consultations under Article 4 of the NATO treaty following the Black Sea attacks. He said the declaration was also backed by representatives of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS), Democratic Bulgaria (DB) and We Continue the Change (PP), but was not adopted by the council.
“DB submitted a declaration and asked for a vote. I was the first to support it, followed by representatives of DPS, DB and PP. But it was not adopted by the Council,” Borissov said.
He said Revival leader Kostadin Kostadinov had been the only participant to speak openly about his refusal to support a CCNS decision because of the election campaign.
“Only Kostadinov was honest when he said: 'I cannot support any decision by the Consultative Council - firstly, we are in the middle of an election campaign; secondly...' and then he walked out when he saw fit,” Borissov said.
Borissov said President Yotova subsequently proposed removing Article 4 from the declaration because invoking Article 5 would carry the risk of actual war.
“Then Ms. Yotova proposed removing Article 4 from their statement, because it is a very serious article that immediately leads to Article 5. And Article 5 implies actual war. And since drones have been crashing in both Poland and Romania (just like the Ukrainian one that fell on our territory without exploding), we agreed to drop Article 4,” he said.
He said the decision was also supported by Democratic Bulgaria representatives because the security services had not provided the expert assessments needed to establish who was responsible for the attacks.
“The security services say the drones passed by our ship and attacked the others. In other words, the ships were struck quite deliberately; there was nothing accidental about it. Expert analyses need to be conducted; the direction from which the drones came is known. But the services had arrived unprepared,” Borissov said.
Borissov said the services’ reports had not satisfied him and that some information presented at the CCNS was less detailed than reports already available in the media.
He questioned the reported voyage of the second vessel from Egypt to Ukraine, saying the route made little sense for transporting wheat and that its journey had taken 15 days instead of the expected five.
“The services report that the second ship is en route from Egypt to Ukraine - a route where transporting wheat makes no sense. The journey should take five days, yet it has taken fifteen. That ship hasn't been inspected yet - did the crew speak with their families during those fifteen days? What kind of communication took place? The services' reports suggest they might have been transporting people or troops. Whether that’s true or not - that is why everyone agreed to request an underwater drone to go and check it out. But where was that tub for fifteen days? What was it doing?” Borissov said.
He said an underwater drone had been requested to inspect the vessel and establish what had happened.
Borissov also referred to reports of oil transshipments in the Black Sea, saying the issue had not received attention because it did not serve election campaign interests.
“There were accounts of oil transshipments in the Black Sea, yet none of that serves the election campaign, so it goes undiscussed. Meanwhile, a deputy minister stated on bTV that two ships had been hit... It was simply an extremely low level of competence,” the former prime minister said.
Borissov said the logic of the available information pointed toward Russian involvement, but stressed that expert analysis was required before the CCNS could issue a formal position.
“That declaration didn't pass. Afterward, Ms. Yotova and the government began looking for the most timid wording possible. Because, given the current situation, Russia stands to benefit from the sinking of those ships. However, for the Consultative Council on National Security (CCNS) to issue a statement, the results of those expert analyses need to be clear so that we act as a serious body,” Borissov said.
He said he, Ivaylo Mirchev of Democratic Bulgaria, Stanislav Anastasov of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms and Nikolay Denkov of Continue the Change had insisted that Russia be identified as the aggressor in Ukraine.
“Stanislav Anastasov, Ivaylo Mirchev, Nikolai Denkov and I insisted unequivocally that Russia be identified as the aggressor in Ukraine and that this is not a war between equal sides, because one side was attacked. My statement was the strongest,” Borissov said.
He said Yotova had agreed that the phrase “Russia's war in Ukraine” should appear at the beginning of the statement, while Borissov had pushed for stronger wording.
“I firmly insisted that the preamble explicitly state 'Russia's war in Ukraine' and identify Russia as the aggressor. My colleague Denkov agreed, and Stanislav, Mirchev, and I also firmly insisted on this,” Borissov said.
Borissov said the six Black Sea countries had been proposed as a group that should seek a rapid peace to stop the bloodshed and economic losses.
He said he had wanted the public to know that GERB, DPS, PP and DB had insisted on identifying the aggressor, but that subsequent public statements had presented the meeting differently.
“We proposed that the six Black Sea nations seek a swift peace to halt the bloodshed and economic losses. When the vote took place, I said: 'You should state publicly that GERB, DPS, PP, and DB insisted on identifying the aggressor.' Yet, they went out and said the exact opposite. That is why I am insisting that the transcript be declassified,” Borissov said.
He also said that he had attended numerous CCNS meetings during his time as chief secretary and mayor but considered the latest one unusually conciliatory.
“In my roles as Chief Secretary and Mayor, I have been invited to many CCNS meetings over the years, but there has never been one quite so 'peace-loving' as this,” Borissov said.
Borissov described the atmosphere of the meeting as unusually informal.
“It was all jokes and banter,” he said in reference to the meeting with Yotova.
He also said GERB had backed the Democratic Bulgaria call for NATO consultations and that urgent expert examinations should establish the direction from which the attacks came. Borissov said Bulgaria has specialists at the Naval Academy who could assist in determining the circumstances.
“I can guarantee that as long as Balkan Stream is operating, Russian President Vladimir Putin will not strike Bulgaria. That I can guarantee. I hope I am right,” Borissov said.
He also warned about the vulnerability of the Vertical Gas Corridor from Greece through Bulgaria to Ukraine and said the government should focus on protecting the infrastructure.
Borissov additionally called for the VAT on fuel to be cut from 20% to 9%.
GERB leader Boyko Borissov said the security services had reported that the sunken ship could have been carrying people or troops, while criticizing the lack of expert analysis at the CCNS meeting.
Speaking in Petrich, Borissov said the services had told the council that the second ship was traveling from Egypt to Ukraine and that its 15-day journey was inconsistent with the five days he said such a route should take for wheat transport.
“The services report that the second ship is en route from Egypt to Ukraine - a route where transporting wheat makes no sense. The journey should take five days, yet it has taken fifteen,” Borissov said.
He said the vessel had not yet been inspected and that the CCNS had agreed to request an underwater drone.
“The services' reports suggest they might have been transporting people or troops. Whether that’s true or not - that is why everyone agreed to request an underwater drone to go and check it out,” Borissov said.
Borissov argued that political statements after the meeting did not accurately reflect what had happened behind closed doors and urged President Iliana Yotova to release the relevant section of the transcript.
“Politicians' comments bear no relation to what actually transpired inside,” the former prime minister said.
He said GERB had been the first to support a Democratic Bulgaria declaration calling for NATO consultations, followed by representatives of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms, Democratic Bulgaria and We Continue the Change, but the declaration failed to win council approval.
Borissov said Yotova later proposed removing Article 4 from the declaration because of its connection to Article 5 and the possibility of an actual war.
“That is why we agreed, including the DB [Democratic Bulgaria] representatives, to drop Article 4 from the text,” Borissov said.
He said the security services had arrived without the necessary expert assessments, even though the available information suggested the drones had deliberately struck the vessels.
“You are being very timid,” Borissov said he had told the services.

He also said reports of oil transshipments in the Black Sea had received little attention and criticized what he described as the poor quality of the security services’ reports.
Borissov said the council had agreed to await expert assessments before adopting a position and that Yotova had proposed another CCNS meeting once the analyses were complete.
He said Mirchev had also called for state support for companies producing drones in partnership with Ukraine.
Borissov further called for the VAT on fuel to be reduced from 20% to 9%.
He warned that the Vertical Gas Corridor running from Greece through Bulgaria to Ukraine was vulnerable and said the government should pay attention to protecting the infrastructure.

S. Korea warns of AI-aided hacking after bank data breaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:17:00 UTC
21:17:00 KST

South Korea warns of AI hacking after bank data breaches
October 8, 2026
The South Korean government has demanded a comprehensive overhaul of safeguards against hackers after seven of the nation's major financial institutions' cyber defenses were breached last week and the private data of thousands of customers was leaked.
The data breaches go beyond the financial sector, with two of the largest churches in the country and Korea Electric Power Corp. on Wednesday confirming that their online systems had been illegally accessed, although it is not clear whether the same perpetrator was responsible for all the attacks.
On Tuesday, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called for measures to be taken swiftly to halt any further leaks.
"This is a serious situation because this incident is believed to have taken advantage of artificial intelligence, and if AI is used in phishing attacks, it could lead to secondary damage," Yonhap News quoted Han as saying at a Cabinet meeting.
"It is also a serious situation in that similar hacking methods could spread beyond the financial sector to industries, as well as government and public sectors."
Threats to other sectors
Han said government agencies, public institutions, the financial sector and private enterprises all need to "remain vigilant."
Early reports from the US-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike suggest that the attack may have originated in China, although South Korea's Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) said it had identified 28 internet protocol addresses in the United States, Japan, Germany and at least 10 other countries that were involved in the bank breaches.
"South Korea officials are being careful about how they are framing their findings," said Aditya Das, an analyst at cryptocurrency research firm Brave New Coin in Auckland, New Zealand.
In the bank logs, investigators found traces of a tool called ARTEX, an open-source "autonomous penetration-testing" agent built by a Chinese developer, he said.
"It is freely available on the internet and officials have said explicitly that a Chinese-built tool doesn't mean Chinese attackers," Das told DW, adding that the use of multiple IP addresses is likely to be "a ploy by the hackers to hide their tracks."
It appears that the hackers exploited weak authentication protocols in portals used by external loan recruiters, employees' mobile tools and sales-support systems.
Data on thousands of customers lost
According to South Korean media reports, data belonging to as many as 68,000 customers was taken, with Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank among the worst affected. Names, phone numbers, annual income figures, loan limits and their loan products were accessed, along with a small number of national identification numbers.
Das pointed out that if a scammer has a person's name, phone number, income figure and is aware that the individual has recently applied for a loan, a fake "bank security" call can be very convincing to the unwary. Once a victim has transferred funds to an account specified by the scammer, it is very difficult to get it back.
Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul, says the seriousness of the incident goes far beyond the simple exposure of personal information.
"If criminals obtain such information, they may be able to carry out sophisticated financial fraud, identity theft, or highly targeted phishing attacks," she said.
"Another concern is that stolen personal information can be reused or combined with other leaked databases, potentially creating security risks that persist long after the original attack," Lee underlined.
"More broadly, such incidents can undermine public confidence in financial institutions and raise concerns about the security of the financial system as a whole."
While major financial institutions have invested heavily in protecting their core systems, such as internet banking and mobile banking platforms, Lee said they have overlooked other elements of their networks.
"Some auxiliary systems, such as loan agent information portals and internal mobile applications used by employees, appear to have received less security attention," she said, adding that the application of AI by the hackers is another concerning element.
AI makes hacking easier?
"In the past, identifying security vulnerabilities, developing malicious code and conducting attacks against financial institutions required substantial technical expertise and considerable time," Lee pointed out. "Today, generative AI tools can assist with writing computer code, analyzing software vulnerabilities, processing large amounts of information and automating certain stages of cyber operations."
AI is "lowering the technical barriers to cybercrime" and making it accessible to more bad actors. At the same time, the technology is ramping up the speed and scale of attacks to overwhelm cyber defenses.
Given those developments, Lee fears that AI-assisted cyberattacks are only going to become more frequent.
"And the risks will not be limited to financial institutions," she said. "Hospitals, government agencies, energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks and other organizations holding sensitive information may also become increasingly attractive targets."

The ‘Kelvin wave’ hitting California is a potent warning about sea-level rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:16:14 UTC
21:16:14 KST

A slow-moving surge of water called a Kelvin wave is arriving in southern California and looks to be about as large as these waves can get. Though it’s not like the wall of water from a tsunami, the pulse is expected to cause record-breaking sea levels and coastal flooding across the state.
It’s also potentially a preview of what California’s sea levels will look like decades from now because of climate change, says Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources. “What we’ll see at the worst this winter will be something that is closer to the norm later this century in terms of sea level,” he says.
The Kelvin wave, which is currently pushing sea levels about a foot above normal in southern California, originated at the equator as part of the superstrong El Niño happening right now. Normally, trade winds push warm water toward the western tropical Pacific. In El Niño years, these winds weaken or reverse. This bulge rolled slowly east until it hit the northern coast of South America. Blocked by the continents, it spread north and south, becoming what’s called a coastally trapped Kelvin wave. The Coriolis effect caused by the planet’s rotation then pinned the waves against the western coasts of North and South America, preventing the water from sloshing back out to sea.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Kelvin waves are a typical feature of El Niño, says Severine Fournier, an ocean circulation researcher at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California. This year the first such wave originated in January, and several arrived in May and June. And more Kelvin waves are developing and expected to arrive in the next several months. The waves move at about 125 to 155 miles per day, so they take a couple of months to cross the Pacific and about a week to crawl up the California coast.
The one hitting now is about as big as Kelvin waves get, Swain says. “This is an unprecedented El Niño event with extremely strong westerly wind bursts,” he says. The strength of these winds determines how much water sloshes across the ocean. The sea-level rise caused by Kelvin waves typically tops out at about 18 inches, Swain says. California may see sea levels rise by around 14 inches this winter because the size of the bulge attenuates as it reaches the coast like ripples spreading from a rock tossed in a pond, he adds.
That’s not the West Coast’s only problem, though—several factors will exacerbate coastal flooding.
For one, water expands at it warms, and this year’s strong El Niño is expected to bring record-breaking warm water to the California coast. “The temporary ocean level elevation from the combination of these Kelvin waves themselves plus the thermal expansion associated with El Niño could be on the order of two feet or even a little bit higher,” Swain says, “and that’s a very alarming number.”
California also sees seasonal extreme high tides known as “king tides” in November through January that will further push water onshore. And then El Niño also raises the chances of storms in the Pacific, making storm surges more likely this winter. “Particularly in southern or central California, we tend to get stronger waves than usual during El Niño,” says Mark Merrifield, an oceanographer at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego. The result will likely be serious coastal flooding and beach erosion.
All of these effects presage what the state may have to deal with as the planet continues to warm because of continued fossil fuel burning.
Climate change has already driven sea levels up by about eight inches over the past century in San Francisco and La Jolla, Calif., according to a 2022 state-level report. (Local sea rise can differ depending on whether geological forces are also simultaneously pushing up coastlines.) There is uncertainty about future rise, depending on the rate of the planet’s melting of the ice caps, Swain says, but “we expect at least another two feet of sea level rise in California [later this century].” That forecast is similar to the temporary rise that is expected this winter.
“What it really tells us is: if our infrastructure can’t handle this winter,” Swain says, “that means it definitely won’t handle that being the average condition.”

Can Sánchez convince Spanish voters he is their best hope for fairer housing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:16:06 UTC
21:16:06 KST

Even before María del Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday night, a mere fortnight after her eviction from the Madrid flat where she had lived for most of her life, the frail 87-year-old woman had become the enduring face of Spain’s housing crisis.
Her plight – and the wider issue it embodied – had led to street demonstrations, the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.
Abascal’s death now looks set to focus even more attention on housing in the run-up to that election and, in particular, on what her lawyer has called “the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the evident impact and consequences they can have on people’s health”.
With more than 42% of Spaniards identifying access to housing as their main worry and with rents having risen by 80% over the past decade, the most pertinent question may be: why has it taken the eviction of an octogenarian and the accompanying protests to shake Spain’s political class into action? To which the answer could be that, despite years of protests against overtourism and gentrification, the tipping point had not been reached. Now, arguably, it has.
On Thursday, Spain’s state centre for sociological research published polling that showed that 76.3% of those surveyed were in favour of the state intervening in the market “as much as necessary to guarantee everyone’s access to housing”, while 79% believed housing should be prioritised as a constitutional right.
Sánchez’s socialist-led government is keen to persuade voters that it is the only political force that cares about rents and tenants’ rights – hence the emergency measures, which have been redrafted into two new decrees after their defeat in parliament last week. The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases, and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.
“These are measures that, if I may say so, are a matter of simple common sense; a matter of humanity,” the prime minister said on Tuesday. “They unite small property owners and tenants while standing up to vulture funds, precisely because they target only those who view housing merely as a commodity for speculation.”
The measures come almost three years after the prime minister promised to build 184,000 affordable public rental homes. His government has also sought to address soaring housing prices by introducing a law allowing authorities to cap “disproportionate” rent prices in some areas.
Those who had voted down last week’s decrees, Sánchez said, had done so despite studies showing the measures enjoyed “cross-cutting support that transcends ideology”, adding that the public was in favour of regulating “a dysfunctional market”. He is now hoping that at least one of the decrees will be passed by congress’s permanent council, a special body that operates when parliament is not in session. Its approval could go some way to convincing voters that his administration is taking the housing issue seriously.
Others disagree. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, which voted down the measures last week, has said it is a bit late for Sánchez, who has been prime minister since 2018, to suddenly appoint himself Spain’s housing champion.
“Housing has been the big failure of this government but will be the success story of the one that follows it,” he said on Monday. Feijóo, whose party is leading the polls, added: “When a prime minister has been in power for eight years, it’s hard to blame others for what he’s failed to do.” The PP has promised to address the crisis by building 200,000 homes a year, lowering taxes and cutting down on bureaucracy.
However, the PP’s decision to side with the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party to fell the measures has left it looking less than committed to the issue of the day. Sánchez and his allies will be hoping that fact will not be lost on voters as the election campaign kicks off and as trade unions prepare a general strike over housing for 11 November.
Mindful, perhaps, of the distance between his words and his party’s voting history in congress, Feijóo called for people not to manipulate Abascal’s death to suit their own purposes.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he said on Wednesday night. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”
And yet, despite the primacy of housing as an issue, Feijóo opted to start his campaign in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, where at least 141 people died as tens of thousands tried to cross over from neighbouring Morocco at the end of July. The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing, which saw about 80,000 people enter Ceuta, has been criticised at home and abroad. Speaking in the territory on Wednesday, Feijóo promised that its safety would be at the “top of [the] in-tray” if he became prime minister.
Vox, meanwhile, has responded to Absacal’s death by posting footage of a TV interview in which she said she held Sánchez responsible for what had happened to her. The far-right party accused the socialists of using “the suffering of an elderly person to stage a campaign to hide the government’s responsibility in the housing disaster”. It also suggested that Sánchez had visited “ruin and death” on Spain in the form of the floods that killed 230 people in Valencia two years ago, last year’s nationwide power cut, the deadly train crash in southern Spain in January, and recent events in Ceuta.

Drone strikes hit Eritrean vehicles around the northern city of Adigrat overnight, with witnesses reporting destroyed lorries and retreating troops, days after Ethiopia expelled Eritrean diplomats and Eritrea severed ties.
Ethiopian drone strikes have targeted Eritrean forces who had reached a northern Tigrayan city, a conflict monitor and witnesses said on Thursday, amid fears that the renewed fighting in the African country might turn into a wider regional war.
The strikes came as the Tigray People's Liberation Front-led seven-group rebel coalition continued to push against federal forces across northern Ethiopia, with fighting reported in Afar and Amhara regions since the coalition announced its offensive last week.
Eritrean troops crossed the border this week and were positioned around the Ethiopian city of Adigrat in northern Tigray, according to multiple sources.
Conflict monitor ACLED said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in the Adigrat area were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight between Wednesday and Thursday.
"There were many, many drone strikes yesterday. Some Eritrean lorries have been destroyed. They are no longer in the streets," one witness, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told AFP.
Another witness in Adigrat, who also asked for anonymity, said they had heard a "massive explosion during the night".
"I also saw Eritrean military vehicles that had been hit by a drone," they added.
A third witness said Eritrean troops appeared to be retreating north.
Relations between the two neighbouring countries, which fought a border war from 1998 to 2000, have deteriorated again in recent months.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing rebels in its northern Tigray state, and the two countries severed diplomatic ties last week.
The government in Asmara in turn accuses Ethiopia of supporting its own opponents, and of looking for a pretext to invade its territory and seize direct access to the Red Sea.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Meskel said on X that Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Neither Ethiopia nor Eritrea has responded to questions about the fighting.
Alliance turned ugly
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, cutting off the latter from access to the Red Sea.
After years of war and tension, relations improved markedly after Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed rose to power in 2018, an effort he was rewarded for with a Nobel Peace Prize.
Eritrea even fought alongside Ethiopia during the latter's 2020-2022 civil war against the TPLF.
But the relationship deteriorated soon after, with Eritrea voicing anger over the terms of the peace agreement that ended that war and, later on, Ethiopia's claims that it has a right to sea access.
Abiy's rhetoric escalated to claim that allowing Eritrea's independence was a "mistake," as Ethiopia accused Eritrean troops of crimes against civilians during the 2020-2022 Tigray war.
This and other accusations prompted Eritrea to blast Ethiopia for allegedly "floating false flags to justify the war that it has been itching to unleash for two long years".
Sparks flew again in February, when Addis Ababa accused its neighbour of sending troops across the border, an allegation Asmara slammed as "false".
Addis Ababa has further pointed a finger at Eritrea, but also at Sudan and Egypt for allegedly supporting the TPLF-led alliance in the latest escalation of fighting.
Last Thursday, Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara, while Eritrea responded that it would "sever all diplomatic ties".

Italian opposition accuses Meloni of rewriting election rules to stay in power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:15:15 UTC
21:15:15 KST

Italian opposition accuses Meloni of rewriting election rules to stay in power
The political opposition in Italy has accused Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition of attempting to rewrite the election rules in a bid to remain in power, over a controversial reform that would award bonus parliamentary seats to winning alliances in next year’s general election.
The new bill has cleared three confidence votes in the lower house of parliament, with the final secret ballot scheduled for Thursday. It passed on Wednesday by 228 votes to 144, bringing the government closer to securing ultimate approval for the overhaul.
The reform would replace Italy’s current electoral system, which combines directly elected constituency seats with proportional representation, with a fully proportional system that rewards the winning coalition with additional seats if it secures at least 42% of the vote.
Meloni’s ruling coalition has claimed the reform will ensure more stability, although opposition parties have condemned the proposal, accusing the coalition of changing the rules because it fears losing the 2027 election. They have also questioned whether the proposed system of awarding bonus seats is constitutional.
“Fear, lies, contempt, and failure. These are the characteristics of an electoral law passed at the last minute in the final year [of the parliamentary term],” Anna Ascani of the opposition Democratic Party said, according to ANSA.
The reform would replace Italy’s current system, which combines directly elected constituency seats with proportional representation, with a proportional system that rewards the winning coalition if it secures at least 42% of the vote in both chambers.
The winning alliance would receive a bonus of 105 parliamentary seats – 70 in the lower house and 35 in the Senate. If no coalition reaches the threshold, or different alliances win the two chambers, seats would be distributed proportionally without the bonus.
The bill would also require coalitions to name their candidate for prime minister before the election and allow voters to express preferences for up to three candidates on party lists. Critics argue that leading candidates would still be effectively guaranteed a seat.
Meloni has rejected claims that the reform is designed to benefit her coalition, insisting it would ensure political stability regardless of who wins. “I don’t think it’s a law that serves the center-right, but whoever wins the elections will have the numbers to govern,” she said in June.
The overhaul has also raised concerns within Meloni’s own coalition. Some lawmakers fear the new rules could instead benefit a united center-left opposition or smaller rival parties, according to the Financial Times.
The bill has already passed the Senate and faces its final hurdle in the lower house, with Italy’s next general election due in 2027.
