Alessandro Baricco in South Africa: A Journey Through the History of Opera
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:54:28 CEST
20:54:28 KST

Writer Alessandro Baricco’s South African tour concluded last night at the Baxter Theatre in Cape Town; after Johannesburg, he brought his program dedicated to the history of Italian opera to the Western Cape before a packed house. The events were organized by the Italian Cultural Institute in Pretoria with the support of the Italian Embassy in Pretoria and the Italian Consulate in Cape Town.
                                    
One of Italy’s most celebrated contemporary writers, Baricco brought two extraordinary “Opera Lecture Recitals” to South Africa. A profound and passionate connoisseur of music and opera, he presented a selection of famous arias, offering the audience glimpses into music history and anecdotes about storytelling, opera, and composers, before giving the stage to the singers of Opera UCT (University of Cape Town).
                                    
Baricco took the audience on a fascinating journey through an era when opera was, in fact, at the center of culture and social life. Composers were the true stars of the show. Baricco’s format thus made a highly successful debut in South Africa as well.
                                    
Baricco explained to the audience how music was the universal language of the time and how, in the early days, the wealthy would go to the theater partly to find a wife or husband. He then illustrated the difference between opera buffa and opera seria and how, ultimately, almost all operas revolve around a love story that may have a happy ending or end in tragedy. He also emphasized that, although composers were almost exclusively men, the true heroines and the strongest characters in the stories were often women. He even explained how music was capable of conveying emotions that could strike directly “at the heart.”
Baricco recounted with a touch of irony how Rossini was so popular that, after composing three or four operas a year for a time, he was able to retire relatively young to Paris and live off the fortune he had accumulated thanks to his success. The audience responded with great appreciation, alternating between laughter at his jokes and long rounds of applause at the end of the performance.
                                    
The Lecture Recital featured a selection of famous arias from the operatic tradition: “Io ti lascio, perché uniti,” an aria from *Il matrimonio segreto* by Domenico Cimarosa; “Madamina, il catalogo è questo” from Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s *Don Giovanni*, which was particularly appreciated by the audience for the piece’s irony; “Mira, o Norma” from Vincenzo Bellini’s *Norma*; “Una furtiva lagrima” from Gaetano Donizetti’s *L’elisir d’amore*; “Miei rampolli femminini” from Gioachino Rossini’s *La Cenerentola*.
                                    
The evening concluded with what Baricco described as the last great golden age of opera in the early 20th century, represented by “Vissi d’arte,” from Giacomo Puccini’s *Tosca*.
                                    
Joining Baricco on stage were Lisa Engelbrecht on piano, Molly Dzangare (soprano), Rosa Vita van der Dussen (mezzo-soprano), Landula Hambile (baritone), and Vuyani Halam (tenor).

Seasonal flu wave expected to start in mid-December in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:54:04 UTC
20:54:04 KST

Seasonal flu wave expected to start in mid-December in Switzerland
With the arrival of autumn, the season for respiratory infections has begun in Switzerland. While the flu and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are still circulating to a limited extent, cases of Covid-19 are already on the rise in some regions.
However, the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) does not expect a full-blown flu wave until mid-December. The scale of this wave remains difficult to predict, it told Keystone-ATS news agency. It will depend in particular on the population’s immunity, the virus variants in circulation and the weather conditions.
The same applies to Covid-19 and RSV, which can cause serious infections, particularly in young children.
+ Swiss researchers sequence genome of 1918 Spanish flu virus
For the time being, the situation is developing in line with the health authorities’ expectations. According to the Sentinella surveillance system, flu and RSV remain at very low levels, while Covid-19 is gaining ground.
A typical pattern
This trend is by no means unusual. In recent years, Covid has generally peaked in the autumn, ahead of the winter waves of flu and RSV, the FOPH notes.
In recent weeks, around 120 cases of Covid-19 have been reported each week in Switzerland and Liechtenstein, compared with 10 to 20 during most weeks of the summer. However, the circulation of the virus remains lower than during the same period in previous years. During the first week of October 2025, more than 500 cases had been recorded.
Other respiratory viruses, which are responsible in particular for colds, also circulate in autumn. This is the case with rhinoviruses, which are not, however, monitored within the FOPH’s reporting system.
At the same time, some manufacturers of flu vaccines are reporting delivery delays to doctors’ surgeries, hospitals, care homes and pharmacies.
However, this is not a shortage, but merely a delay, emphasises Simon Ming, spokesperson for the FOPH. People at risk, like the rest of the population, still have plenty of time to get vaccinated if they wish.

Over 2,000 Gazans died awaiting medical evacuation amid siege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:54:01 UTC
20:54:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Over 2,000 Gazans have died awaiting medical evacuation amid Israel's continued siege
More than 2,000 Palestinians have died while waiting to be evacuated from Gaza for medical treatment since the closure of the Rafah crossing in May 2024, the territory's health ministry said on Wednesday, as Israel's siege continues to prevent thousands of critically ill patients from accessing treatment abroad.
The ministry said 2,027 patients had died while awaiting evacuation, while approximately 21,000 others urgently require treatment outside the devastated Palestinian territory.
Among those still awaiting evacuation are 5,600 children, 2,800 patients requiring cancer treatment and 194 people whose conditions are considered immediately life-threatening.
Another 2,000 patients are classified as emergency cases, according to the ministry's latest figures.
The numbers reflect the continuing humanitarian consequences of Israel's continuing siege of the territory and the collapse of Gaza's healthcare system, nearly a year after a so-called ceasefire, which was supposed to allow the entry of humanitarian aid, came into effect in October 2025.
The Rafah crossing, Gaza's main gateway to Egypt, was closed in May 2024 following Israel's military offensive in the southern city, severely restricting the movement of patients requiring specialised treatment unavailable inside the territory.
Although limited medical evacuations have taken place through alternative arrangements, the number of Palestinians requiring treatment abroad continues to vastly exceed the capacity of evacuation programmes.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) coordinates medical evacuations alongside Palestinian health authorities and other partners, with patients requiring referrals, security clearances and arrangements with receiving hospitals before they can leave Gaza.
The ministry's latest figures come as a new report by Israeli rights organisation Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) found that Gaza's healthcare system has made only marginal progress towards recovery during the first year of the ceasefire.
According to the report, none of Gaza's hospitals has returned to full operation, while the territory remains without a functioning MRI scanner.
The number of partially operational hospitals has increased from 14 to 20 since October 2025, but intensive care capacity rose by just one bed, from 103 to 104, according to figures covering the period up to July 2026.
The report also found that dialysis services had become less accessible, with the proportion of medical facilities providing them falling from 17 percent to 12 percent.
PHRI cited earlier Gaza Health Ministry figures showing that at least 1,570 patients, including 264 children and 505 cancer patients, died while awaiting evacuation between October 2023 and 2 July 2026.
The newer ministry figure of 2,027 deaths covers the period since the closure of Rafah in May 2024 and should not be added to the earlier total.
Israeli authorities continue to prohibit the transfer of Gaza patients to hospitals in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, despite legal challenges from human rights organisations.
In July, Israel's Supreme Court declined to intervene in the policy at that stage, leaving medical evacuations dependent on arrangements with third countries.
Rights groups say that the restrictions prevent patients from accessing established Palestinian medical facilities capable of providing life-saving treatment.
The ministry said the continued delays were placing thousands more lives at risk, with Gaza's damaged hospitals unable to provide many forms of specialist and emergency care.

Israel's long road to a Gaza without Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:53:47 UTC
20:53:47 KST

Breadcrumb
With or without 7 October: Israel's Gaza endgame was always ethnic cleansing
In April 2023, six months before the 7 October attacks, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a meeting with Yoav Gallant, his then defence minister, and Alon Davidi, the mayor of Sderot - an Israeli city built on top of the historic Palestinian village of Huj.
Gallant and Davidi casually joked about flattening Gaza to rebuild Jewish-only settlements on its ruins. “I would also like to build in Beit Hanoun (in Gaza), but I will settle for Sderot,” said Davidi. Gallant replied, “In order to build in Beit Hanoun, you first need to flatten the area there.”
A month earlier, Israel’s Minister of Settlements Orit Strook said explicitly, “I don't know how many years it will take...returning to Gaza will take a lot of sacrifices. Gaza is part of the land of Israel, and we will return to it one day.”
Strook was reiterating what the deputy head of Israel’s Knesset, Limor Son-Har Melech, said the same day. “Our task now is to return to the settlements in Gush Katif and rebuild them,” he said, in reference to Israeli settlements in Gaza that were evacuated in 2005.
Israel’s finance minister and de facto ruler of the occupied Palestinian territory, Bezalel Smotrich, had also promised on the eve of the Netanyahu government’s formation in December 2022 that Israel would “return” to rebuild Jewish settlements in Gaza.
Three years into Israel's war, these statements now sound like prophetic declarations of intent.
Beit Hanoun was levelled to the ground during the war, just as Gallant said. Earlier this year, Limor Son-Har Melech led a group of settlers deep inside Gaza, planting trees to mark the first step towards rebuilding settlements in the enclave. He bragged: “Gaza will be Jewish, because only in this way will we ensure victory.”
Israel Katz, meanwhile, Israel’s new defence minister, has formally announced intentions to start building settlements in Gaza.
That is why Israel's military rabbi Amichai Friedman described the month of October 2023 as “the happiest month of my life”. He added, “We're finally realising who we are. All of this land is ours. The entire land, including Gaza and Lebanon. Gush Katif is tiny compared to what we will get with God’s help to achieve... We will destroy everyone.”
An ambition decades in the making
Seven months before 7 October, Israel’s former defence minister and right-wing politician Moshe Yaalon sounded the alarm that Israel’s “Jewish supremacist” ministers, whose beliefs, he said, reflected “Mein Kampf in reverse”, wanted to provoke “the final war” of “Gog and Magog.”
Yaalon warned that Smotrich and Ben-Gvir would try to provoke Palestinians, through massacres, for instance, to use any Palestinian retaliation as a pretext for the 'final battle'.
As soon as Itamar Ben-Gvir became Israel’s security minister, he rushed, as Yaalon anticipated, to abuse Palestinian prisoners to ignite that war. Some of his first decisions were to ban pita bread for detainees, reduce their shower time to two minutes per day, overcrowd their cells, and let a Palestinian hunger striker, Khader Adnan, die in solitary confinement.
The cruelty meted out to Palestinian detainees is thought to have served as one of the core justifications, and strategic drivers, for Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar to launch the 7 October attacks on Israel.
But even without Hamas’s attack, the concept of ‘transfer’, or ethnic cleansing, has long been embedded in official Israeli policymaking.
“You shall continue to live like dogs, and whoever wishes may leave… It's possible that in five years, there will be 200,000 fewer people, and that's an enormous thing,” said Israel’s then defence minister Moshe Dayan shortly after the 1967 war.
The “live like dogs or leave” dichotomy was reiterated in 2017 by Smotrich in a manifesto Israeli pundits themselves described as “genocidal.” Smotrich gave Palestinians three options: submit to living as inferior subhumans, leave the land, or resist and get killed.
Israel has used this policy in Gaza since the 1948 Nakba. Even before it captured Gaza officially in 1967, the Israeli government sought to push for mass migration from the enclave through intimidation, bribery, periodic massacres, and destruction of vital infrastructure.
After Gaza fell under Israeli occupation, Israel used more force, coercion, destruction, intimidation, and bribery to empty Gaza.
When Israel imposed a blockade on Gaza in 2006, economic warfare and starvation were systematically imposed, punctuated by periodic “high-tech killing sprees” to inflict the maximum destruction possible in order to make the enclave uninhabitable and force its people out.
Before 7 October, about 10% of Gaza’s population (205,000 people) had already emigrated from the Strip since the blockade started. Half of that significant figure were people who left in the five years that preceded Hamas’s attack.
A senior Israeli official even bragged in 2019 that Tel Aviv was “actively pushing Palestinian emigration from Gaza.” The official said Israel was reaching out to Western and Middle Eastern countries to encourage accepting Gazan migrants and even offered to cover the costs of travel.
Israel’s focus on displacing Gaza’s population stems in part from the fact that the overwhelming majority of the Strip’s population are refugees displaced from villages in what is now Israel, leading it to view the population as a persistent potential source of insurgency.
Israel’s then defence minister Moshe Dayan said in 1956, “Why should we blame [Palestinians in Gaza] for their burning hatred for us? For eight years they have been dwelling in Gaza’s refugee camps, as before their eyes we have transformed the land and the villages in which they and their forefathers had dwelled into our own property.”
7 October gave Israel its opening
The 7 October attacks provided a powerful accelerant for Israel’s longstanding displacement of Palestinians in Gaza.
Almost immediately, Netanyahu called on Gazans to leave, while his government ordered the mass evacuation of northern Gaza. The assault also revived an older Israeli conception of the conflict as an unfinished war of national survival, with Netanyahu later explicitly invoking the 1948 War of Independence, or Nakba.
In the first days of Israel’s response, Tel Aviv, with US help, rushed to pressure neighbouring Arab countries to transfer the entire population of Gaza into the Sinai desert under the pretext of “temporary relocation until Hamas is defeated.”
When those countries refused, Israel pushed most of Gaza’s population towards Rafah at the Egyptian border in the hope of pushing them to cross into Sinai on their own. When that failed, Israel invaded Rafah and devastated the city, only to propose sending Palestinians back towards the area again - this time into a so-called “humanitarian city” that Israel’s own former prime minister Ehud Olmert described as a concentration camp.
Even after Israel signed President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan for a ceasefire - which included Hamas’s disarmament, the withdrawal of Israeli troops, and reconstruction - Israel promptly reneged on its commitments and continued to push for building the Rafah ‘humanitarian city’.
The push to empty, and resettle, Gaza
Since the ceasefire began, Israel’s Defence Minister, Israel Katz, has repeatedly emphasised that Tel Aviv’s long-term goal in Gaza remains its total ethnic cleansing.
“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration… I think there is no other solution for everyone’s good,” he said in September, despite Hamas agreeing to lay down its arms. Katz added that Israel remains “organised and prepared to get [Gazans] out – by sea, by air, by every way possible.”
Israel’s Security Minister Ben-Gvir presented a concrete plan in September for the ethnic cleansing of 1.86 million Palestinians in Gaza over the next 7 years, called “disengagement 710.”
Through this scheme, Israel would expel 250,000 Gazans in the first year, 1.11 million by the third year, and the entire population by 2034. During the genocide, more than 100,000 Palestinians have already left Gaza.
That is why, even in the “new Rafah” camp, Israel made clear it would not allow any permanent construction with concrete, but rather would only give the caged population temporary and portable shipping containers to live in, making clear those camps are a mere transit towards expulsion.
The Israeli defence minister made clear that all Israel now needs to “finish the job” in Gaza is a pretext. “When it becomes clear that Hamas is not fulfilling its commitment. Then we will get a green light to advance militarily, territorially, and in other areas as well,” he said.
The same applies to the West Bank, where Katz revealed on Tuesday that the Israeli army has been instructed to plan for a scenario of war with the Palestinian Authority (PA). Despite the PA being Israel’s peace partner and security subcontractor, Katz made clear that Israel is ready to replicate its ‘Gaza model’ in the West Bank.
Any war on the PA “would be short and forceful and would include the use of ground and air forces and special means, the elimination and expulsion of senior officials, the destruction of weapons, and the large-scale evacuation of residents and destruction of terror infrastructure inside the cities and in all refugee camps,” Katz said, referencing the Gaza and Lebanon “models”.
Katz’s threat to the PA is not limited to an Israeli retaliation against violent Palestinian attacks on settlers or soldiers. A “war scenario” would also be unleashed if Palestinians organise a popular uprising.
“There will not be an Intifada lasting years, as there was in the past, but rather a short and forceful war with a clear decision and a change in the reality,” he emphasised.
A political consensus on Palestinian subjugation
The upcoming Israeli election is one of the most heated and competitive in the country’s history. But the one thing that unites the Israeli ruling coalition with most opposition parties is the subjugation of Palestinians.
In 2024, the Israeli Knesset saw an unprecedented moment of bipartisanship in rejecting Palestinian statehood and self-determination. In February of that year, 99 Israeli members of Knesset from both the opposition and ruling coalition voted in favour of a resolution rejecting international recognition of Palestinian statehood. Only nine members opposed the resolution, all of whom were from Palestinian parties.
In June, another resolution passed with only the same nine members opposing it. This time, the resolution rejected Palestinian statehood in absolute terms, even if such statehood comes through negotiations and diplomacy.
In this election cycle, Israel’s former prime minister and opposition leader Naftali Bennet is campaigning on calling the Trump plan for Gaza “unworkable” and opposing the plan’s promise of returning the Palestinian Authority to the enclave.
Israel’s former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman is similarly campaigning on dismantling the PA and resuming military operations in Gaza. Israel’s former war minister and likely the next prime minister Gadi Eisenkot attacked the roadmap for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons in return for the Israeli military’s withdrawal and called it a “capitulation” to Trump “without achieving the war’s objectives.”
The 7 October attacks did not create this Israeli mainstream consensus. At most, it provided the cover of war to make it more flagrant and explicit.
Israel’s stated long-term goal in Gaza and the West Bank is the natural culmination of a settler-colonial project that was created on the premise of grabbing the “maximum land with a minimal number of Arabs.”
Palestinians have for decades been pushed by Israel into ever-shrinking confines with two options left to them: submission or departure.
The only substantial debate about this endgame in Israel’s election is about the pace and packaging of that expulsion and subjugation.
Muhammad Shehada is a Palestinian writer and analyst from Gaza and the EU Affairs Manager at Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor

INTERVIEW - Gaza sports community seeks to revive games after genocide kills 1,000 athletes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:52:04 UTC
20:52:04 KST

Hosni Nadim and Ikram Kouachi
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
- Amputee athletes need prosthetics, rehabilitation and sports equipment to return to competition, says Mustafa Siam
- Sports seen as a tool to help Gaza’s youth recover psychologically and socially after 3 years of genocide, he says
After three years of war that killed more than 1,000 athletes and destroyed hundreds of sports facilities, Gaza’s sporting community is seeking to bring sports back to life.
Mustafa Siam, secretary-general of the Palestinian Sports Media Federation, told Anadolu that the return of sports to Gaza was not just about resuming competitions but also about helping children and young people recover psychologically and socially after three years of genocide.
“Palestinian sports have suffered extensive destruction since October 2023, and statistics show that more than 265 sports facilities have been completely or partially destroyed,” Siam said.
He said 1,014 Palestinian sports figures were killed during the war, including players, referees, coaches and administrators affiliated with the Palestinian Football Association.
Among the best-known figures were international player Suleiman Obeid, who was killed by Israeli gunfire while trying to get food, and Hani al-Masdar, coach of the Olympic team, who was killed in an Israeli strike.
Trying to bring sports back
After the implementation of a ceasefire agreement in October 2025, the Palestinian Football Association held meetings with clubs in Gaza to develop a plan to restore sports activity, Siam said.
Since then, the association has organized four tournaments for senior and youth players, as well as a beach soccer tournament.
Siam said the tournaments’ primary objective was “to restore hope and revive the spirit” among young people and athletes living in difficult circumstances.
“These young people are living in dilapidated displacement camps, and many of them have lost their families, homes, friends or coaches,” he said.
Siam said the tournaments also carried a message to the world that Palestinian youth “have the right to play football and other sports, just like athletes around the world.”
He said the Palestinian Football Association adopted an initiative in May 2024 to establish the Phoenix Cubs center for displaced children in camps. The center currently operates in Gaza City and the central governorate.
“Sports are important for strengthening the psychological and social well-being of children who have lived through difficult circumstances during the years of war,” he said.
He said football could also help preserve and develop young talent, as sports form part of education and social development.
Supporting amputee athletes
Siam said children and young people who lost limbs during the genocide need greater sporting and rehabilitation support, noting that “the number of amputees in Gaza has increased dramatically compared with the pre-war period.”
Before the war, Gaza had amputee football groups and a team, but the number of amputees has risen significantly, including among athletes, he said.
“These players need care and attention, as well as prosthetic limbs and services that can help them practice sports and football,” Siam said.
“Providing prosthetics, rehabilitation services and sports equipment could help establish a team capable of representing Palestine in international competitions.”
“Every one of these players carries a humanitarian message and a painful story they lived through during the genocide,” he said. “It is important to provide the resources necessary to help them return to sport.”
Calls for international action
Siam criticized “the failure of international sports institutions” to take action against Israel over violations affecting Palestinian athletes and sports facilities.
He said the Palestinian Football Association had requested the suspension of Israel’s membership in international sports federations as early as 2013, but no decision had been reached.
He added that campaigns by fans and coaches in Europe had called for measures against Israel.
“International sports institutions should support Palestinian sports and protect Palestinian athletes’ right to compete and represent their country internationally.”
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, while also destroying about 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.

A 3-year-old girl came to visit her aunt in Pryluky, Ukraine. By morning, a Russian missile had killed her grandmother and uncle

A Russian missile strike on an apartment building in Pryluky, a town in northern Ukraine's Chernihiv Oblast, killed 22 people on 7 October, regional police reported on the morning of 8 October. Five of the dead were children: three one-year-old boys, an eight-year-old boy, and a 13-year-old girl, police said.
Russian strikes on Pryluky, Kremenchuk, Oleksandriia, and Kyiv killed 28 people on 7 October, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said. For the town, it was the second deadly missile strike since May. Behind the toll are families like this one: three generations hit by a single strike.
A family visit that ended under rubble
Three-year-old Zlatoslava is now in the Chernihiv Oblast children's hospital, Pryluky district police chief Vladyslav Stoianov told. Her mother, Kateryna, is hospitalized too. The two had come on the evening of 6 October to visit Kateryna's sister, police officer Yuliia Malysh. The girl's father stayed home in Lynovytsia, a village 15 km away.
Yuliia was wounded and is in hospital, Stoianov said. Her husband, Oleh Malysh, was killed. Until recently, Oleh had fought at the front in the Chernihiv Oblast police rifle battalion. The sisters' mother, Liudmyla, had also come over that evening, and she died too. All the family details come from Stoianov, who was describing a colleague's family.
Footage of an emergency worker carrying a little girl from the ruins reached almost all media, Vyhivskyi wrote in the same post. Suspilne first reported that the filmed rescuer had carried Zlatoslava. It then corrected itself: he had carried a different child, five-year-old Zoriana. Vyhivskyi also gives the girl's age as five, and he named the rescuer as State Emergency Service section commander Pavlo Levchenko. With colleagues, Levchenko freed the girl and her mother after the blast threw them out of the building.

Opposition accuses government of borrowing to fund promises in ERR debate

Opposition accuses government of borrowing to fund promises in ERR debate
Coalition parties say the budget deficit is being reduced, while the opposition argues that the governing parties are borrowing money to deliver on their promises.
Taking part in the studio debate were Erkki Keldo (Reform Party), Lauri Laats (Center Party), Riina Sikkut (Social Democratic Party), Rain Epler (EKRE), Aivar Kokk (Isamaa) and Toomas Uibo (Eesti 200).
Host Andres Kuusk noted that the Reform Party had promised to reduce the budget deficit by 0.5 percentage points annually, but that this target would not be met in the coming years.
Keldo maintained that the party was nevertheless reducing the deficit. He pointed out that the forecast for next year's deficit had fallen from 4.9 percent in the spring to 4.4 percent in the summer, while the state budget submitted by the government projected a deficit of 4 percent.
Keldo said the improvement had been achieved through continued spending cuts, adding that the government had already made approximately €1.5 billion in additional cuts.
Aivar Kokk of Isamaa accused the government of concealing spending in the budget. He criticized the submission of a second supplementary budget to the Riigikogu, saying the government was bringing expenditures forward from next year, including €28 million for Rail Baltica rails without knowing where they would be used.
Kokk also argued that the Reform Party's income tax exemption was being financed through borrowing, with the government taking on debt both this year and next to fulfill the party's election promise.
Center Party member Lauri Laats described the state budget currently being prepared as a disaster and called for a comprehensive overhaul of Estonia's tax system.
He criticized the country's reliance on consumption taxes, which he said accounted for 40 percent of tax revenue. Laats said the Center Party would reduce consumption taxes, particularly VAT on food.
Social Democrat Riina Sikkut said her party would not engage in political blackmail when deciding whether to support the budget.
However, she stressed that certain expenditures, including funding for specialized care services, were not ideological matters. She cited a Supreme Court ruling stating that shortages of funding or available places did not absolve the state of its responsibility to guarantee people's fundamental rights.
Sikkut said the Social Democrats planned to submit amendments aimed at supporting vulnerable groups and hoped to secure backing from both coalition and opposition parties.
"These are measures to support vulnerable groups, things the government has left out but which we believe are absolutely essential to address next year," she said.
Toomas Uibo (Eesti 200) expressed hope that future governments would continue reducing the budget deficit by 0.5 percentage points annually.
He said maintaining that pace would eventually stabilize the national debt and allow it to begin declining, although the process would take time. Uibo acknowledged that even achieving a 0.5 percentage-point reduction had been difficult and that a substantial deficit could not be eliminated in a single year.
Rain Epler (EKRE) argued that Estonia had a spending problem and that there were areas where further cuts could be made.
He accused the Reform Party of driving up government expenditure, pointing out that the state budget had grown by more than 50 percent over the past five years while gross domestic product (GDP) had increased by just 4 percent.
Sikkut also criticized the government's approach to spending cuts, arguing that it had reduced expenditure only on paper by shifting some costs into future years.
She said the government's room for maneuver had been limited by its decision to abandon a planned income tax increase that was originally intended to finance the elimination of the income tax "hump."
Estonia switched from a gradual basic exemption reduction scheme to a flat €700 exemption for everyone recently, costing the state in excess of €500 million annually.
"They made the numbers work on paper," Sikkut said, adding that the government had instead chosen to finance the tax change through borrowing.
Sikkut also accused the government of failing to comply with domestic budget rules, which require an annual improvement of 0.5 percentage points throughout the state budget strategy period.
Keldo, however, maintained that eliminating the income tax "hump" had been the right decision.
The debate also covered Rail Baltica, potential spending cuts and excise tax increases.

Semitic, semantic, whatever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:50:58 UTC
20:50:58 KST

Semitic, semantic, whatever
« previous post |
Last Tuesday's post "Pneumatic, pneumonic, whatever" was based on a New York Post headline announcing that "Trump calls reported pneumatic plague outbreak ‘big problem for Russia’". It was implicit in the discussion that the headline writer was ignorant or careless or both.
But yesterday, Bob Ladd pointed out to me that Science magazine committed a similar error in the references to a paper dated 9/25/2026 (Morvai, Boglárka, Kinga G. Tóth, Marianna Boros, Dorottya S. Rácz, Ivaylo Iotchev, Kitti Szabó, and Attila Andics. "Neural evidence that dogs segment the speech they hear with a humanlike consonant bias." Science (2026).
The paper's second reference was to John McCarthy's 1979 PhD thesis, Formal problems in Semitic phonology and morphology — and "Semitic phonology and morphology" is rendered as "semantic phonology and morphology".
Bob's email:
I was going to add a somewhat off-topic comment to your latest post, but I thought you might be interested in this as a separate LLog item.
There's a recent article in Science about how dogs listening to Saffran-style nonsense syllable sequences can pick out recurrent patterns based on detecting regularities in transition probabilities, and that they show the same bias as human subjects do in favour of detecting CONSONANT regularities rather than VOWEL regularities. (I was led to this article by a news story in New Scientist which which kind of garbled the details of the experimental stimuli, so that I went to the original article to figure out what the researchers had actually done.)
The opening sentence of the Science paper begins "Across many languages, consonants are more useful for word identification than vowels…" and goes on to cite work by the likes of Anne Cutler and Jacques Mehler that explored psycholinguistic aspects of this asymmetry. The Science study aimed to see if dogs exhibit the same bias as humans for attending to consonants in speech segmentation, and it reports that they do. Conceivably this would be worth a LLog post for the interest of all those readers who used to annoy Geoff Pullum.
However, what's relevant for "pneumatic, pneumonic, whatever" is that one of the sources for the statement in the paper's opening sentence about consonants and vowels is a reference to John McCarthy's PhD thesis, which is cited as “Formal problems in semantic phonology and morphology.”
The Science paper and its human background deserve a full post, which I hope that Bob will provide for us.
The conceptual gap between that paper and its coverage in the New Scientist should also be mentioned, perhaps with glance at the rest of the (extensive) coverage in popular media (BioTechniques, Neuroscience News, Discover, WaPo, El Pais, Newser, Science Alert, the Times, Earth.com, the Independent, etc. etc.).
There's also the obvious observation that the neuroscience of talking to dogs is one of the most clickbait-y possible current topics, maybe minus only the neurological verification that cats are more aloof, and that some AI agents are developing neurologically optimized vocalizations to steal the loyalty of our pets.

Al-Aqsa Flood and the beginning of Israel's strategic erosion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:50:35 UTC
20:50:35 KST

Three years after the Al-Aqsa Storm operation, the importance of this operation cannot be summarized only in its military dimensions. October 7, 2023, was a point that changed a set of security, political, and media equations in West Asia. This operation occurred under conditions in which the Palestine issue, after years of the siege of Gaza, the occupation of Palestinian territories, the expansion of settlements, and the intensification of pressure on Palestinians, was moving away from the priorities of regional and international policy. The process of normalization of relations between some Arab countries and the Zionist regime had also strengthened the impression that the Palestine issue could be marginalized without a root solution. Al-Aqsa Storm stopped this process and brought Palestine back to the center of West Asian developments.
The first blow was struck against Israel's security image. For years, Tel Aviv had built an important part of its power on a combination of intelligence superiority, technology, the separation wall, surveillance systems, and military capability, and presented this set as the guarantor of the security of the settlements and residents of the occupied territories. But October 7 showed that even such an extensive network cannot create absolute security. More importantly, Israel's internal reports and investigations subsequently revealed serious weaknesses in the performance of the security and military structure. Therefore, the issue was not just the infiltration of Palestinian forces into areas under Israeli control; rather, it was a blow to public trust in the regime's ability to provide security.
Tel Aviv's response to this failure was a widespread war against Gaza. Israel announced big objectives such as destroying Hamas, returning the captives, and creating a new security reality. But the main problem from the very beginning was the gap between the announced objectives and the possibility of their realization. The widespread and destructive war was able to inflict heavy damage on Gaza, but it did not eliminate the political issue of Palestine. Hamas was not removed from the Palestine equation, and the future of Gaza, the manner of governance, the issue of disarmament of the Resistance groups, and even the shape of Israel's relationship with this region still face serious questions.
This is precisely where the concept of "military victory" separates from "strategic victory." An army may destroy a large part of the opposing side's infrastructure, but if it cannot shape the post-war political conditions in accordance with its objectives, military victory does not necessarily turn into strategic victory. The Gaza experience has highlighted this contradiction precisely. Israel was able to employ an enormous level of its military power, but it still faces an issue that existed before the war as well: how can the Palestine issue be solved merely through military means?
This pattern is also observable on the Lebanon front. Israel dealt heavy blows to Hezbollah, but could not remove this movement from Lebanon's political and security equations. The return of clashes in 2026 also showed that even inflicting considerable damage on a military actor does not necessarily mean the end of the threat or a permanent change in the balance. Regarding Iran as well, direct attacks by Israel and America could not remove Tehran from regional equations. On the contrary, direct confrontation highlighted the importance of Iran's missile capability, strategic depth, and regional capacity more than before in the security calculations of West Asia.
From this perspective, one can speak of a cycle: after October 7, Israel entered war to restore deterrence; the war expanded; but the wider the scope of the conflict became, the more the military, economic, political, and diplomatic costs increased, and on the other hand, the main objectives still faced serious obstacles. In other words, the attempt to compensate for one security failure itself led to a set of new crises.
One of the most important consequences of this process was the return of the Palestine issue to the center of world public opinion. Images and reports related to the situation in Gaza, widespread protests in various countries, and increasing political pressures on Israel caused an issue that, before October 7, had been affected by the normalization process in many regional equations, to once again become one of the main topics of international politics. The move by a number of countries toward recognizing Palestine and the increase in disagreement between Israel and some of its Western allies showed that the diplomatic cost of the war for Tel Aviv is also increasing.
Inside occupied Palestine as well, the effects of this erosion have become apparent. The security failure of October 7 intensified the dispute over responsibility for it and exposed the performance of Benjamin Netanyahu and the ruling political structure to criticism more than before. The issue of captives, the continuation or cessation of the war, the future of Gaza, the economic costs of the conflict, and social and political divisions revealed fissures that had existed before but gained greater depth after the war. In this way, Israel was trying to rebuild its image of power and cohesion while simultaneously facing a crisis of internal trust and increasing political pressures.
Even at the regional level, the image has changed. Before October 7, the process of normalization of Israel's relations with some Arab countries could create the impression that the Palestine issue was no longer the main obstacle to the formation of a new regional order. But the Gaza war, and then the expansion of conflicts to Lebanon, Syria, and other places, made this process more complicated. The Palestine issue once again became one of the important criteria of Arab public opinion for evaluating Israel's policies and increased the political cost of approaching Tel Aviv.
Therefore, three years after Al-Aqsa Storm, perhaps the most important question is not how much damage Israel has inflicted on various battlefields; the more important question is whether it has been able to achieve its political objectives. The answer to this question is negative.
Al-Aqsa Storm was a turning point because it showed that the Palestine issue cannot be solved by setting it aside from regional equations. Israel entered a widespread war to restore deterrence, but this war not only did not eliminate the Palestine issue, but brought it back to the center of the world's attention, increased Israel's political and diplomatic costs, made its internal fissures more apparent, and dragged the scope of the confrontation to multiple fronts.
Three years later, therefore, one can speak of a "cycle of failure"; a cycle in which a security failure was answered with war, the war led to erosion, and the erosion created new crises. Perhaps the most important legacy of October 7 is this: Israel showed that it has the ability to inflict very extensive military blows, but it has not yet been able to establish a link between this military power and a lasting political victory. And as long as this gap exists, the end of every war can be the beginning of the next crisis.

Rubio says US committed to Mediterranean undersea power cable
ATHENS, Oct 8 - The US supports an EU-backed undersea power cable scheme in the eastern Mediterranean and will use diplomacy to try to remove any possible hurdles, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a Greek newspaper.
Greece's power grid operator IPTO is developing the €1.9 billion scheme, which aims to link the European mainland to Cyprus and later Israel, but progress has been slow amid a dispute between Greece and Turkey over the maritime area that will be designated for laying down the cable.
Greece wants to resume seabed surveying to determine the route soon, a move Turkey says would need prior coordination between the two countries as it crosses an area under a 2019 maritime deal with Libya, which Athens has rejected.
Rubio said in the interview with Kathimerini newspaper, published on Thursday, that the US was "very committed" to the project as it promotes energy supply diversification, which he said was necessary due to Russia's war in Ukraine and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
"We understand there are some potential impediments, there are some things standing in the way, and we intend to use our diplomatic efforts to remind all parties how important this is to us and why this matters. And I hope to find resolutions," he said.
French investment group Meridiam signed in August an agreement to become the majority shareholder in the project.
Cyprus is the only EU country that has no link to other members' electricity markets, and the cable aims to improve its energy security. REUTERS

Microsoft said its new laptop containing an Nvidia AI chip will start at $2,599, as the software maker tries to bring more artificial intelligence capabilities to its consumer devices.
The Surface Laptop Ultra is now available on preorder and will begin shipping on Oct. 16, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and devices, said at a company event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The computer has the world's first magnetic USB-C port, similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector, along with two other standard USB-C ports, Microsoft said in a blog post.
While Microsoft Windows is the most popular operating system for PCs, the company isn't among the top six PC vendors in terms of unit shipments, according to an estimate from researcher Gartner. As the AI boom matures and chip technology advances, tech giants including Microsoft, Apple and Google are aiming to allow users to run more AI workloads from their devices rather than relying on the cloud.
Users can install and run a variety of models on the new laptop without having to worry about racking up high monthly bills. Microsoft first talked about the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, but is just now providing specifics.
"Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies, wrote on X after the announcement.
Davuluri also said that Meta will introduce a version of its popular Muse AI agent for Windows, capitalizing on the surging popularity of the personal agent, which has jumped to the top of Apple's App store, surpassing ChatGPT.
Microsoft is still trying to solidify its role as a key player in AI. The company offers its own AI models, but they're less popular than leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic and aren't at the forefront in terms of performance, according to one benchmark. Developers are more likely to have used alternatives, according to a recent survey.
This isn't the first time Microsoft has sought to use the AI boom as a way to boost sales of its devices.
In 2024, the company introduced the Copilot+ PC standard, requiring the inclusion of neural processing units that ensure a minimum level of AI performance, along with compliant Surface computers. But Microsoft has since "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences," a spokesperson said.
The new device sports a 15-inch display and weighs 4.4 pounds. It can contain up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory and supply up to one petaflop of computing power. The Blackwell RTX Spark GPU inside the computer has as much processing power as Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server from 2016, which cost $250 million, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at Wednesday's event.
A presenter showed how apps on the Surface Laptop Ultra can route some AI coding requests run on the computer's local GPU, displaying a green leaf icon, and others to the cloud. Through Windows 11, developers can confine coding agents to Microsoft Execution Containers that will prevent unwanted system access.
Microsoft is updating its Windows 11 device setup experience to help people get started quickly with open-source OpenClaw AI agent software.
Microsoft has been releasing its own computers since 2012, and CEO Satya Nadella indicated on Tuesday that the company's position in the market is evolving.
"I think today is the day we'll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours two years from now, five years from now, 10 years from now," Nadella said at the event. "That classic edge that distributed computing will always remain distributed will be more true."

Russian Drones That Entered Poland Were Carrying Polish SIM Cards, Investigation Finds
Polish investigators found SIM cards belonging to Polish mobile operators inside some of the Russian Gerbera drones that violated Poland’s airspace during a large-scale Russian strike on Ukraine in September 2025, according to RMF24 on October 8.
The finding emerged after Polish prosecutors completed their investigation into the incident, which saw Russian drones penetrate NATO airspace during the night of September 9-10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Prosecutors have not disclosed how the Polish SIM cards ended up inside the Russian UAVs, including whether they were stolen, purchased through intermediaries, or obtained illegally through another method. That part of the investigation remains classified.
The presence of local SIM cards is particularly notable because unmanned systems can use cellular connectivity for communications, telemetry, navigation support, or other data functions, depending on how the aircraft is configured.
Polish prosecutors ultimately closed the investigation after failing to identify a specific individual directly responsible for the airspace violation. Investigators nevertheless concluded that Poland’s armed forces acted in accordance with established procedures during the incident and were legally authorized to destroy hostile drones entering the country’s airspace.
The incursion occurred during one of Russia’s largest aerial attacks against Ukraine at the time. Polish forces detected the first airspace violation at around 11:14 pm on September 9, while the final intrusion was recorded at approximately 6:30 am the following morning.
On September 12, Marcin Przydacz, head of the Polish president’s International Policy Bureau, said information available to the presidential office indicated that 21 drones had crossed the Polish border.
Authorities later found wreckage from intercepted or crashed drones across several parts of the country, including the Lublin, Masovian, and Łódź regions. One falling object damaged a residential building, although no deaths or injuries were reported.
Earlier, reports emerged that the Kremlin had been preparing for cross-border attacks since at least July 2025, when Polish SIM cards were discovered inside Russian drones shot down in Ukraine.

Gabriele Moreno Locatelli Remembered in Sarajevo
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:48:42 CEST
20:48:42 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarah Castellani, commemorated Gabriele Moreno Locatelli on the 33rd anniversary of his death. The Italian priest and pacifist, a volunteer with the association “Blessed Are the Peacemakers,” was killed by a sniper on the Vrbanja Bridge on October 3, 1993. “In a world marked by conflict, his legacy as a pacifist remains particularly significant,” said Castellani, offering her thoughts to his family, friends, and the community of Canzo, Locatelli’s hometown. 
The ambassador emphasized how his legacy continues to inspire those who promote reconciliation and interethnic dialogue in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in support of the country’s stability and prospects for European integration, which Italy supports.
                                    
“Gabriele Moreno’s sacrifice is a further reminder to reject all forms of denialism that offend the victims and poison the future,” she concluded. The ceremony was attended by Deputy Mayor Predrag Puharić, citizens, members of the Italian community, military personnel from the EUFOR mission, and representatives of local civil society. Also present were Italian deputies and senators who had arrived in the country as part of the parliamentary assemblies of the OSCE, the Council of Europe, and NATO to monitor last Sunday’s general election.Among the members of the Italian parliamentary delegation, Eugenio Zoffili paid tribute on behalf of the Lombard community, noting that a monument and a street in Canzo are dedicated to Locatelli. “His sacrifice serves as a reminder for our daily work in the service of parliamentary diplomacy, which acts as a tool for dialogue among peoples,” he said. Locatelli was crossing the bridge along with other volunteers to symbolically call on the warring parties to cease hostilities. At that same spot, in April 1992, Suada Dilberović and Olga Sučić—the war’s first two civilian victims—had been killed during a demonstration against the conflict. Shot by a sniper, Locatelli died in the hospital a few hours later.

A Euronews journalist on the ground in Paris' 5th arrondissement on Thursday morning reported that the streets were already filled with students, some of whom had been dragging bins into the streets and chanting since 6:30 am.
One student outside the prestigious Lycée Henri-IV told Euronews that they had come to stage a blockade "to show our full support for the suburban secondary schools."
"They were the ones who started this movement and were immediately cracked down on by the police," they said.
Another student from a technological school in the 5th arrondissement said: "For six months we’ve had no teacher, there’s no supply teacher, and we’re sitting our baccalauréat in that subject."
"At school, to be honest, our living conditions aren’t great," they continued, adding: "Personally, I don’t think it’s normal to finish at 5.45 pm – or rather, 6 pm."
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu addressed the nation on Wednesday evening in an effort to ease the crisis, promising the government would share a plan to respond to the situation by the end of October and denying that law enforcement officers had been "instructed to confront secondary school pupils."
"Their role is to protect property, but above all people; to ensure that the law is upheld; and to allow access to schools," he said.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray also announced on Thursday that he would present an "emergency plan" to address teacher absences within the "coming hours or days."
Protests have at times descended into violent clashes with riot police, resulting in a number of serious injuries, including one teenager who lost his hand.
Unions, rights groups, and students have accused officers of using disproportionate force, but French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has defended the response to the protests and said that authorities would "continue to do what we are doing: maintaining order and intervening proportionately whenever violence breaks out."
France has nevertheless moved to temporarily suspend the use of stun grenades in policing the demonstrations.
Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty International France, welcomed the decision but said further action was needed.
"Protests should not be battlefields. Stun grenades are designed to shock, disorient, and sow panic, often among dense crowds at demonstrations," she said. "Some can cause permanent hearing loss as well as life-changing mutilations due to the blast and shrapnel."
Thousands of people - the majority minors - have been arrested since the protests began.

Nicolás Maduro’s wife to appear in court to push for release from New York jail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:46:58 UTC
20:46:58 KST

The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday.
The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pretrial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been jailed in New York City since early January.
They were captured by US special forces during a shocking predawn assault on Caracas and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism”-related charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Charging documents at the time alleged that Maduro spearheaded a “corrupt, illegitimate government that, for decades, has leveraged government power to protect and promote illegal activity, including drug trafficking”.
Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them. CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected.
The new charging document described how Maduro and his wife allegedly wielded untold horrors to suppress opposition and maintain their control.
Maduro, Flores and other Venezuelan leaders “presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the just-released charging document said.
Maduro and Flores, the superseding indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”. They allegedly “developed and facilitated the systems which they and their co-conspirators used corruptly to amass immense wealth and power, rewarding allies with ill-gotten funds and terrorizing perceived opponents through persecution and violence”.
Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”.
The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power.
“One particular United States citizen was detained in Venezuela and subjected to, among other things, deprivation of food and water, simulated drowning, repeated beatings, electric shock to his testicles, and forced injections.”
Maduro and Flores also put pressure on Venezuela’s judiciary to make legal decisions that supported their efforts to thwart opposition, charging papers alleged. When one official resisted, Venezuelan intelligence agents arrested and tortured their family members, charging papers stated.
“For example, one family member … was forced to drink latrine water; assaulted with tear gas in Victim-1’s cell; threatened that Victim-1 would be killed at gunpoint; and placed in a cold room known as the ‘Freezer’ in which a bright light was left on at all times of day and night and music was blared on repeat,” the superseding indictment said.
This official “ultimately … relented and blocked the opposition figures from running for political office”.
During another alleged torture incident, authorities allegedly abused the friend of a suspected opponent by “asphyxiating him with a bag, applying electric shocks to his testicles and knees, and kicking and beating him with a blunt object”, court papers said.
One torture victim, who was repeatedly interrogated, endured numerous threats “including that his daughter would be kidnapped and raped if he did not confess and name his supposed confederates”, court papers state. “On one occasion, interrogators produced women’s underwear, claiming it belonged to his daughter.”
Shortly after this indictment surfaced, Flores’s attorneys argued for her release in an already scheduled proceeding, pitching house arrest guarded by 24-hour private security. In doing so, they invoked chronic health issues, including cardiac infirmities.
Hellerstein pushed back on this claim, noting that Flores was refusing to have catheterization while detained in general population.
“I’ve undergone it, so I know what it is,” Hellerstein said, noting that it was generally an outpatient procedure. “There’s no pain. There’s no general anesthesia.”
Flores’s attorney then pointed to her high blood pressure. “It’s controllable by pills,” Hellerstein said.
Her team also said in court that Flores dropped more than 25lbs and lost two teeth since her detention.
“For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse than, and perhaps a little better, than when I first met with her [at] her arraignment,” Hellerstein said. Flores’s lawyer said that during her arraignment she was “still bandaged up” from her rough arrest. 
Flores wore dark jail scrubs during her court appearance. She listened to the proceedings with headphones through a Spanish-language interpreter.
The US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, which is prosecuting this case, opposed Flores’s now-failed bail request. Prosecutors have argued that Flores was a flight risk. Prosecutors also maintained that she had received appropriate medical care.
Donald Trump has defended the controversial raid on Maduro, insisting it was a “surgical law enforcement operation”. At Maduro’s first US court appearance, he said: “I’m a kidnapped president – a prisoner of war!”
After Maduro’s forced ouster, Trump worked swiftly to gain access to Venezuela’s expansive oil reserves. In August, Trump announced a new oil agreement with Venezuela – claiming that the US would have “majority” control over 65bn barrels of proven reserves.
Venezuela boasts approximately 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves – the largest in the world. The White House has tried establishing a consistent flow of Venezuelan crude oil to US refineries while boosting US investment into the country’s flagging petroleum industry.
Trump has faced mounting pressure over skyrocketing gas prices in advance of November’s midterm elections. Greater access to cheaper oil and broadened output could help lower costs.
A Guardian investigation found, however, that Trump’s proclaimed “biggest oil deal in world history” is likely to fail due to legal and logistical problems.

Ukraine and Romania opened a new crossing point over the Tysa River
Kyiv • UNN
The "Bila Tserkva–Sighetu Marmației" crossing point has opened in Zakarpattia for passenger cars—up to 400 vehicles per day. Trucks and buses will be allowed through later.
A new road border crossing point, "Bila Tserkva – Sighetu Marmației," has opened in Zakarpattia at the border with Romania. At the first stage, it will operate for passenger cars and be able to process up to 400 vehicles per day. This was reported by the Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine, UNN writes.
Details
To launch traffic from the Ukrainian side, an access road was built and modular infrastructure for border and customs control was installed. On the Romanian side, a border crossing point and a new bridge over the Tysa River were built, connecting the two countries.
"The opening of the new border crossing point is a tangible result of our systematic work to develop the western border. For Zakarpattia, it is an additional route to Romania, while for the entire transport system, it is another opportunity to redistribute flows and reduce the burden on existing border crossing points. It is especially important that we continue developing border infrastructure even during the war. The next stage is to create a fully fledged border crossing point here for trucks and buses," said Mykola Kalashnyk, Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine.
It is noted that this is only the first stage. Development of the border crossing point will continue. Once full construction is completed, up to 400 trucks and 50 buses per day will be able to undergo processing here.

India to Turkiye, can new proposals to broker Russia-Ukraine truce succeed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:45:17 UTC
20:45:17 KST

India to Turkiye, can new proposals to broker Russia-Ukraine truce succeed?
India, Turkiye, Egypt and the US have put forward proposals for ceasefires in bid to protect global energy and shipping.
Ukraine says it has received proposals from India, Turkiye, Egypt and the United States to broker talks with Russia. The offers come as the two adversaries escalate attacks on each other’s energy and port infrastructure with their war now in its fifth year.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha revealed the four proposals at a briefing in Kyiv on Friday and singled out New Delhi’s. “The most comprehensive is India’s proposal,” he said, adding that India had signalled a willingness to play a role for the first time.
None of the proposals aims to end the war. Each seeks a narrower truce, covering energy facilities, ports or commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Here’s what we know:
What is India proposing?
India has not made its plan public. Quoting unnamed sources, however, Indian media have reported it has three parts. According to the Hindustan Times, it would aim to protect infrastructure, keep grain and energy supplies moving through Black Sea ports, and ensure the safety of commercial shipping.
The first part – mutually halting strikes on energy facilities and ports – matches what Kyiv has been demanding. Sybiha said any deal must be a complete energy truce that covers port infrastructure as well.
The second part builds on the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which Turkiye and the United Nations mediated in 2022 but Russia abandoned in 2023.
The third part, protecting merchant ships and their crews, is particularly important to India because Indian sailors have been killed or harmed on Black Sea routes.
The sources were quoted as saying India’s plan goes further than the other three proposals because it covers infrastructure and shipping together. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that it incorporates elements of the Turkish, Egyptian and US initiatives. The Kyiv Post reported that Sybiha also described the plan as addressing a possible ceasefire along the front lines, although other accounts said he gave no specifics.
The proposal likely took shape during Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar’s first visit to Ukraine last month and in a later meeting with Sybiha at the UN General Assembly in New York, also in September. Jaishankar said New Delhi was “trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue”.
What do we know about the Turkish and Egyptian proposals?
Very little. Neither Ankara nor Cairo has published details. Both reportedly focus on keeping Black Sea grain supplies moving by suspending attacks on commercial shipping. Some reports said the two countries proposed a grain truce jointly while others described two separate plans.
Turkiye has done this before. With the UN, it steered the 2022 grain deal, one of the few narrow truces of the war to hold for any length of time. Ankara and the UN are now organising new Black Sea talks with a round planned for October.
Beyond its Black Sea focus, almost nothing is known about Egypt’s proposal. Its interest, however, is clear: Egypt relies on Ukraine for nearly one-third of its grain supplies.
What is the US pitching?
According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Washington has proposed three steps: a mutual halt to energy strikes, a reopening of the grain corridor and a trilateral meeting with Ukraine and Russia, possibly in Abu Dhabi.
The latest effort began in early September when US President Donald Trump’s envoys visited Kyiv and Moscow and secured an agreement in principle for a trilateral meeting. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on September 5 while Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev visited the US twice in September.
The trilateral meeting has since been pushed back. It had been expected to take place in the United Arab Emirates in early October. Washington now wants it in late October, and people close to the talks blamed the delay on Russia.
Washington has also invited Putin to the Group of 20 summit in Miami, Florida, in December. “We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said. The Kremlin said no decision has been made.
At the same time, the US is applying pressure to try to end the war. Trump recently signed a law giving him sweeping powers to sanction buyers of Russian energy.
He has also called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian diesel facilities amid a diesel prices crisis in the US, where Trump faces tricky midterm elections next month. “Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing,” he said on September 13. “He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.” This drew much criticism that Trump instead should focus his comments on Russia, which began the war with its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
He is reportedly sceptical about his own government’s latest diplomatic initiative. People familiar with his thinking have told US media that he doubted Putin would agree to an energy truce before winter.
How have Russia and Ukraine responded?
Sybiha said Ukraine would agree to a truce but with conditions. It would accept an energy and Black Sea shipping ceasefire, but only as a combined package, he said.
He added that Kyiv is also open to an unconditional ceasefire along the current front lines. Zelenskyy backs the US-proposed meeting but stressed it needs “not only Ukraine but also the Russian side” to support it.
Moscow has been warm in tone but has committed to nothing. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia would welcome India’s peace efforts while Putin said Modi has “very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions”, but he did not elaborate.
In private, Moscow appears to have said no. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that Russia has rejected India’s proposal although this has not been confirmed publicly. Ukraine’s agriculture minister said Russia had rejected every Black Sea ceasefire option the mediators have presented.
Why are Global South countries becoming more involved?
Food supplies, the lives of their citizens and fuel prices are all at stake.
“I think it’s clear to many countries that this war is not a localised war, but it’s a war that has these global consequences,” Fredrik Wesslau, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told Al Jazeera.
Russia and Ukraine account for more than a quarter of global wheat shipments, and their attacks on each other’s ports helped push wheat futures to a three-year high in August.
Sailors from countries with no links to the war are being killed. At least five Indian seafarers have died in strikes on Black Sea shipping in recent months along with seven Azerbaijani crew members since June. On Saturday, a Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged ship in a port in the Odesa region killed a crew member. Ukraine, for its part, has targeted tankers it links to Russia’s shadow fleet since July.
The energy war is also being felt in global markets. Ukraine reported more than 194 drone attacks on Russian refineries this year, hitting all 11 of the largest. Bloomberg News estimated that Russia’s fuel output has fallen by more than 30 percent. With Middle East supply already down as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran, global diesel markets are more exposed to the loss of Russian supplies.
Maximilian Hess, a nonresident senior fellow in the Eurasia Program at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said energy is at least as important as grain in driving the diplomatic efforts. He pointed to a “clear frustration” among many countries over high oil prices, which reflect both the Russia-Ukraine war and the crisis in the Middle East.
“Of course, Ukrainian grain is important for them, but the oil-price factor is important there as well,” he told Al Jazeera. “I think it is those commodity-shock concerns that are pushing them to re-embrace this rhetoric, rather than anything else.”
What are the challenges ahead?
Every previous attempt at diplomacy has failed to end the Russia-Ukraine war. A US-brokered, 30-day energy truce in early 2025 collapsed amid accusations of violations on both sides. At talks in Istanbul in May 2025, Zelenskyy complained that Russia had sent a junior delegation with no authority to sign a ceasefire.
In August 2025, a meeting between Trump and Putin in Alaska yielded no results despite Trump claiming to be close to a deal ahead of it.
Wesslau said Washington’s efforts have faltered partly because Trump – who had boasted he would end the war within 24 hours of taking office in January 2025 – has appeared unwilling to put real pressure on Moscow. “The Russians see this, and they conclude that they can continue this war,” he said.
Deep distrust remains. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, said: “Putin never keeps agreements.”
Moscow’s actions on the ground suggest it is in no hurry, Wesslau said “They’re trying to strangle Ukraine, strangle the economy, and make it unliveable ahead of the winter,” he said. He added that Moscow’s occasionally softer rhetoric was aimed mainly at the Trump administration and “has always proved to be a bluff”.
Russia’s terms are another obstacle. Hess said Moscow’s demands have not softened at any point since it launched the war and at times have grown. Putin has demanded all of Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhia regions, including territory Russian forces have never controlled, as well as a buffer zone in northern Ukraine. Moscow is also seeking sanctions relief and military concessions for any Black Sea deal.
“I don’t think it’s a question of who actually mediates. I think it’s really a question of the calculation in Moscow,” Wesslau said. “Fundamentally, the problem is that Putin doesn’t want a ceasefire or a peace agreement. He wants to continue the war. He believes that he can win.”
Analysts said only greater economic pressure is likely to change that calculation.
Wesslau said if Europe can close down Russia’s shadow fleet of oil tankers, “this would be a massive blow to Russia’s war economy.” Hess said the country best placed to shift things quickly is China, rather than the US, by cutting its purchases of Russian oil. However, he added: “I don’t think Beijing is interested in doing so.”
Hess said that unless there is an outside shock, the war “is much more likely to last another four years than another four months”.
