The Azawad Liberation Front (ALF) announced the forced withdrawal of its forces from the city of Kidal in northern Mali.
The group’s spokesperson, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, announced the withdrawal in an official statement.
The decision was made following massive airstrikes by the ruling military junta and mercenaries from Russia’s Africa Corps, which destroyed most of the civilian infrastructure.
The Tuareg command stated that leaving the settlement was a temporary measure aimed at preserving its personnel and logistics.
The city of Kidal has been a key political and military center of the Tuareg movement since the start of the 2012 rebellion for Azawad’s independence, when rebels first drove the Malian army out of the city.
In 2013, as part of Operation Serval, French troops and a Chadian contingent entered the city, driving out radical groups and handing control to moderate Tuareg forces.
In May 2014, an attempt by the Malian army to storm Kidal ended in defeat, after which the city remained under the full control of the Tuareg alliance for years.
From 2015 to 2022, the status quo in the city remained largely unchanged: the UN’s MINUSMA mission was deployed there, while de facto control was exercised by local Tuareg forces.
In November 2023, Malian government forces, backed by Wagner Group mercenaries, managed to temporarily seize the city after a prolonged offensive.
The rebels later regained control of Kidal, launching active operations against government forces and defeating a Russian convoy near Tinzaouaten, which shifted the balance of forces in the war.
In July, Mali’s junta forces, together with the Africa Corps, regained control of the city of Anefis in the north of the country.
The city is located approximately 100 km from Kidal and holds significant strategic importance for controlling Mali’s northern regions.

New Italy election law puts fragile opposition unity to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:34:41 UTC
20:34:41 KST

New Italy election law puts fragile opposition unity to the test
ROME, Oct 8 - A new electoral law approved by Italy's parliament on Thursday was conceived by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's coalition as a way to cement its grip on power after the next election, opposition politicians say.
Yet analysts say the reform, which rewards broad alliances rather than individual parties, could ultimately benefit Meloni's centre-left foes if they can overcome their internal divisions and rally behind a single leader.
The reform gives a parliamentary majority bonus to the largest alliance if it wins more than 42% of the vote, encouraging rival parties to join forces before an election. Meloni says it is intended to increase the prospect of stable government.
OPPOSITION RIVALS CLASH OVER LEADERSHIP
When Meloni drew up the bill, her own conservative coalition was ahead in the polls, but its advantage has been eroded by the emergence of a new far-right group, National Future, allowing a cluster of centre-left parties to edge ahead.
However, a requirement in the new law for coalitions to nominate their candidate for prime minister before any election has laid bare divisions between Elly Schlein and Giuseppe Conte, the leaders of the two main opposition groups, the Democratic Party (PD) and the 5-Star Movement.
"The leadership belongs to the party that gets one vote more. That's not hegemony, it's democracy," Schlein, 41, told a PD meeting last week, making clear she believes the largest opposition force should lead the alliance.
"If there are those who do not recognise this democratic principle, then we will hold primaries," she added.
Conte is indeed pushing for primaries, arguing that voters, not party rankings, should choose the coalition's candidate for prime minister. But a showdown would expose sharp policy differences within the centre-left bloc and personal rivalries.
"Primaries will probably make life worse for the left, because they are a contest in which one person says, 'I’m better than the other,' and that doesn't make cooperation any easier," said Piero Ignazi, a professor of comparative politics at the University of Bologna.
Schlein struck a defiant note in parliament on Thursday as the reform was approved despite centre-left opposition.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," Schlein said.
SUPPORT FOR UKRAINE DIVIDES THE LEFT
Conte, 62, was prime minister from 2018 to 2021 in back-to-back administrations and has made it clear he wants his old job back. He spent much of the summer courting left-wing voters and challenging PD policy positions -- particularly the group's continued support for helping Ukraine's war effort.
Schlein, who has no national government experience, says the PD's lead over its opposition allies in opinion polls means its views must be given more weight.
Latest polls put the PD on about 20% against 12.5% for 5-Star, making it the second most popular party in Italy after Meloni's Brothers of Italy, which is on around 28%.
Alessandro Di Battista, a former senior 5-Star politician who no longer belongs to the party but retains a following among its supporters, said Schlein would struggle to win over parts of the 5-Star base.
"There is a section of citizens who support the 5-Star Movement who wouldn't vote for Schlein even under torture," he told Canale 9 television on Saturday.
Warning that the increasingly bitter rivalry between Schlein and Conte risked playing into the government's hands, he added: "Meloni is already the favourite ... but if they continue like this they may as well not hold the election."
However, Ignazi predicted that despite 5-Star doubts over her leadership credentials, Schlein would win an eventual primary.
"The Democratic Party has many more supporters, who are much more active than 5-Star, so she is the clear favourite," he said.
LESSONS FROM 2022 DEFEAT
The last national election in 2022 used a hybrid voting system that mixed proportional representation with first-past-the-post constituencies dotted around the country.
The PD and 5-Star did not run together, dividing the opposition vote and handing power to the conservative bloc, an experience former Prime Minister Matteo Renzi says should galvanise rather than discourage the opposition.
Renzi, whose small centrist party hopes to join a future centre-left alliance, urged the opposition to embrace any primary contest as a way to expand the coalition's appeal rather than allow it to shred their sense of unity.
"Let's get moving, organise these blessed primaries and turn them into a celebration of democracy," he said last month. REUTERS

Australia's bushfire crisis linked to colonial land-use change: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:34:17 CST
20:34:17 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Forest expansion and thickening after British colonization created landscapes more prone to burning, amplifying the influence of climate change and propelling Australia's bushfire crisis, new research finds.
Researchers from the University of Melbourne, in collaboration with Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation, reconstructed the past 1,000 years of vegetation, fire and erosion in Croajingolong National Park, one of southeastern Australia's most fire-prone forests, according to a university statement released on Thursday.
Published in Nature, the study found that colonization drove cascading changes, including increased fire temperatures, a fourfold increase in eucalypt cover, the transformation of open woodland into forest and increased soil erosion.
The findings provide scientific evidence for the value of cultural burning and the need to integrate Indigenous knowledge into contemporary fire management, said lead author Michael-Shawn Fletcher, a professor at the university.
Climate records showed similarly dangerous fire-weather seasons had repeatedly occurred before colonization, but cultural burning helped maintain open landscapes and limit catastrophic fires, Fletcher said.
"When colonization ended that care, the forest expanded and thickened across the region, loading the landscape with fuel. It is that transformation that has handed control of fire to climate," he added.
Researchers found that the land-use changes predated human-driven climate change, indicating that the current vulnerability of southeastern Australia's eucalypt forests to wildfire has been strongly influenced by colonial land-use legacies.
Sediment records showed that hot fires were followed by a fourfold surge in eucalypts, thickening the landscape and increasing fuel loads. Infrared analysis of charcoal showed that cooler or low-intensity cultural fires before colonization were replaced by hot wildfires afterward. ■

Hungarian section of Budapest-Belgrade railway passes European safety testing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

20:34:15 KST

BUDAPEST, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Testing of the European Train Control System (ETCS) on the Hungarian section of the Budapest-Belgrade railway has been completed, marking an important step toward launching passenger services, a senior official said Thursday.
The ETCS must function properly before passenger services can launch. Hungarian Minister of Transport and Investment David Vitezy said contractors still need to complete track-adjustment work to ensure that the railway can maintain operating speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour over the long term.
This final procedure corrects ballast settlement following construction and load testing and ensures track geometry meets design specifications before a new railway enters service.
According to the construction schedule, track adjustments on the section between Hungary's Ferencvaros and Kunszentmiklos-Tass stations are expected to be completed by the end of October, paving the way for the launch of domestic passenger services and subsequent operations.
Vitezy said that if domestic passenger services run smoothly during the first few weeks, the next phase is planned for December, when trains would operate at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour and international passenger services between Budapest and Belgrade would begin.
He added that although extensive testing, corrective work and verification have been completed, further work remains.
The Budapest-Belgrade railway, linking the Hungarian and Serbian capitals, is a flagship project under the Belt and Road Initiative jointly developed by China and countries in Central and Eastern Europe. It is also the first project to align Chinese railway technology and equipment with the European Union's railway interoperability standards.
The Hungarian section, spanning about 158.6 kilometers, is an electrified railway designed for both passenger and freight transport, with a maximum design speed of 160 kilometers per hour. Freight services on the section officially began on Feb. 27 this year. ■

All illicit gains and related proceeds will be recovered and turned over to the state treasury, the court said.

In return, he accepted money and property worth 10.72 million yuan, either personally or through a third party, the verdict noted.
From 2023 to 2025, after his retirement, Xu also used the influence derived from his former positions via the acts of other state functionaries to help others in project contracting. In exchange, he accepted another 25.87 million yuan in bribes, the court ruling said.
The court said Xu received a lenient sentence because he truthfully confessed to his crimes and disclosed additional bribery facts previously unknown to investigators, while some of the bribery offenses were attempted rather than completed. He had also pleaded guilty, expressed remorse, and actively returned illicit gains, with almost all illegal proceeds already recovered, the ruling said.
The court stated that these circumstances warranted leniency in sentencing.
The case was heard publicly on July 23. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China's highway new energy vehicle (NEV) charging volume rose sharply during the recent week-long National Day holiday, data from the National Energy Administration showed on Thursday.
From Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, the country's highway NEV charging volume reached 163 million kilowatt-hours, averaging 23.26 million kilowatt-hours daily, up 51.42 percent year on year.
These figures reflect both the rapid growth of China's NEV fleet and the growing number of highway charging facilities.
China is the world's largest NEV market. NEV sales and ownership have climbed steadily, partly supported by trade-in programs and increasingly competitive domestic models.
Official data show that China's NEV ownership has reached 48.97 million, or 13.19 percent of all vehicles, with NEVs accounting for nearly half of new vehicle registrations in the first half of 2026.
China has been accelerating the expansion of charging infrastructure as part of its broader push to promote NEVs and cut carbon emissions.
The total number of charging connectors in China has surpassed 24 million, making it home to the world's largest electric vehicle charging network.
About 89,000 charging facilities have been installed at expressway service areas. From January to August this year, these service areas added around 11,000 high-power charging units, roughly equal to the cumulative total before this year.
The National Day holiday, often called "Golden Week," is one of China's busiest travel periods. A total of 2.14 billion cross-regional passenger trips were made over the seven days this year, averaging more than 300 million a day.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China aims to upgrade and retrofit charging facilities at expressway service areas to build an intercity charging network that effectively meets mid- and long-distance travel needs, while also raising the share of fast-charging facilities.
By 2030, the total number of charging facilities is expected to exceed 40 million units, including approximately 300,000 high-power charging facilities, providing enough charging capacity to support more than 110 million electric vehicles. ■

It found social media is deeply embedded in family life, with parents relying on it daily for information, support and connection, while increasingly recognizing its risks and backing stronger protections for children online, the statement said.
Of the 92 percent of respondents who used social media, 96 percent said they used it daily, with 99 percent accessing it via mobile phones, according to the report, which found 44 percent of parents believed social media had a somewhat or extremely negative impact on their lives, compared with 22 percent who reported a positive impact.
Parents cited concerns about children's vulnerability, brain development, bullying, addiction and online predators when supporting delayed access to social media, it said, adding that nearly half said children should be at least 16 before having an internet-enabled smartphone.
The findings highlight a striking contrast between parents' own social media habits and what they want for their children, said Catherine Archer, a senior lecturer at ECU who conducted the research.
"The same experience that makes social media useful for parents also appears to make them more aware of the risks it can pose to children," Archer said.
However, the study found 67 percent of parents reported posting photos of their children online, despite concerns about children's privacy. ■

Lisa Barber, tech editor of the consumer group Which?, says customers’ search history is useful to hackers, so they can launch convincing ‘spear phishing’ attacks.
It’s deeply concerning to learn that hackers have not only obtained customers’ personal details, like email addresses and phone numbers, in the Asos hack, but also their search history.
While many of us would assume that our search history would be uninteresting to a hacker, it can in fact be incredibly useful for criminals hoping to target you with extremely convincing, personalised phishing attacks. This technique, known as ‘spear phishing’, can be hard to spot, as criminals will tailor the communication specifically to you, often using data gleaned from social media accounts and, unfortunately, data breaches.
Shoppers should be especially wary of unexpected phone calls, texts, messages and emails they receive in the coming weeks and months. Eurozone finance ministers, ECB to urge France to pass budget to calm bond markets
Eurozone finance ministers and the European Central Bank will urge France today to pass its 2027 budget to calm bond markets, as French borrowing costs hover at 25-year highs, senior euro zone officials told Reuters.
France is at the centre of a bond market storm, fuelled by worries over the country’s large budget deficit and looming presidential election next year.

Ex-CIA official pleads guilty to nearly $200 million government fraud scheme

Gizem Nisa Demir
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
A former CIA official pleaded guilty Tuesday to wire fraud in a scheme that used fictitious classified programs to finance purchases of Florida real estate and gold with nearly $200 million in government money, CBS News reported.
David Rush entered the plea in federal court in Virginia and faces a maximum prison sentence of 20 years.
His plea agreement provides for the forfeiture of at least $194 million. Assets listed include four Florida homes, 298 gold bars, 35 luxury watches and two BMWs, according to the report.
Court documents cited by CBS describe how Rush invoked classified government activities to authorize spending, direct contractors and gain control of the assets they acquired.
Prosecutors said the property and gold purchases were parts of a single fraud scheme, despite involving different intermediaries and transactions.
About $145 million was routed through companies to purchase properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida, which Rush intended to sell for profit, according to the filings.
To arrange the gold purchases, he told contractors that a top-secret project required deliveries of valuable commodities to unidentified recipients. A contractor’s $45 million transfer to a holding company in January formed the basis of the wire fraud charge. 
'Master manipulator'
The investigation began with a CIA referral to the FBI, the two agencies previously said.
Prosecutors said Rush could access “highly sensitive and classified government programs,” although the charging document did not identify his employer. An earlier affidavit described him as a former employee at the Senior Executive Service level at a government agency in eastern Virginia.
Rush was arrested in May.
During a search of his home, FBI agents seized gold bars valued at about $40 million, along with luxury watches and $2 million in cash. Prosecutors said roughly $38.6 million was still in a holding company’s account.
A federal judge ordered him to remain in custody in June, citing a severe risk that he would flee.
Justice Department lawyers called him a "master manipulator" at the detention hearing, saying he "cannot be trusted" and was "fully willing and able to skirt the rules."

Why REITs aren't getting killed by rising interest rates this time around
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:28:53 UTC
20:28:53 KST

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.
The stocks of real estate investment trusts, or REITs, have long been considered a low interest rate play. That's because they are high-dividend stocks, and real estate values generally rise when rates fall. But some experts are making the case that real estate fundamentals today are outweighing even rising rates.
Correlations between REIT returns and changes in 10-year Treasury yields have repeatedly shifted over time, according to a new report from Cohen & Steers, which notes that the level or direction of rates alone has not been a reliable predictor of REIT performance.
Higher interest rates definitely hurt the commercial real estate sector from 2022 through 2024, as higher costs for borrowing lowered the value of assets. There was also a lot of new supply in several sectors, which caused rents and cash flow growth to slow down. Higher rates made it difficult for new development, but that is what is helping the sector in the current rising rate environment.
"Certainly 100 basis points in the last year on the 10-year [Treasury] is an impingement to the cost of debt and does also mean every other asset class now has to compete with higher yields," said Seth Laughlin, head of real estate strategy and research at Cohen & Steers.
"So you need to get a better yield from your alternatives, and real estate is definitely in that category. But at the same time, what we've seen is acceleration in earnings up to 9% this year. It'll be something similar next year. Call it 8% earnings growth," he added.
As new supply peaks, cash flow growth is improving and valuations are attractive relative to equities, according to Laughlin.
In fact, REIT to interest rate correlations are now at their lowest level in about four years, according to David Auerbach, chief investment officer, Hoya Capital Real Estate. He notes that fundamentals are much healthier than the headlines suggest, and 58 of 98 REITs providing full-year guidance raised their outlook.
"Excluding Data Centers, REIT development pipelines are roughly 40% below their 2022 peak and 2019 levels; Data Centers remain the exception at seven-times 2019 levels," Auerbach wrote in a report titled "The Rate Shock That Didn't Break REITs."
"Solid fundamentals are increasingly doing the heavy lifting, with healthy property-level cash flows, improving earnings visibility, strong dividend coverage, and better balance sheets helping REITs absorb the rate shock," he added.
REIT returns year-to-date are up over 6% according to the FTSE NAREIT All REIT Index. Specific sectors, however, are seeing outsized returns. Hotel and lodging, data centers and senior housing lead with double-digit returns.
Multifamily apartment REITs are still in negative territory, as the sector continues to work through a period of oversupply and weaker rents. Demand, however, for multifamily will grow along with interest rates, simply because fewer people will be able to afford to buy a home.
Other sectors like industrial, regional malls, and even office are seeing positive returns, despite higher interest rates.
"The truth is, under the hood, the economy is really healthy, and I think about REITs as sort of the landlord to the broader economy," said Laughlin.

Canadian poet Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:28:16 UTC
20:28:16 KST

Anne Carson was among the bookies' favourites to win this year, as her body of work eschews easy categorisation.The Nobel Prize committee singled out her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for 2026, “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
The 76-year-old writer is known for her hybrid style, combining poetry and prose, as well as contemporary stories with ancient myth.
The Academy stated: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work.”
Among Carson’s best-known works are her 1986 debut "Eros the Bittersweet", a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature; her 1998 work, often heralded as her greatest, "Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse", a queer coming-of-age story that reworks a Greek poem about Heracles; "The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos" (2001); and "Norma Jeane Baker of Troy" (2019), which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.
Her most recent work is "Wrong Norma", which was published in 2024.
By winning the Nobel Prize, Carson becomes only the 19th woman to win the Nobel Prize for Literature, with recent winners including Han Kang in 2024, Annie Ernaux in 2022 and Louis Glück in 2020.
As of today, the literature prize has been awarded by the Nobel committee of the Swedish Academy 119 times to a total of 123 winners (four literature prizes have been shared between multiple laureates).
Last year's prize was won by postmodern Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art.” Susan Sontag previously described the author as “the contemporary Hungarian master of apocalypse.”
The literature prize is the fourth to be announced this week, following the 2026 Nobels in medecine, physics and chemistry.
Each prize this year comes with 12 million Swedish kronor (€1.07 million). The winners also receive an 18-carat gold medal and a diploma.
The winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced on Friday and the final prize, the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, is to be announced on Monday.
Nobel Prize award ceremonies are held on 10 December, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death in 1896.

Seoul said Kyiv's public disclosure of the repatriation of two North Korean prisoners endangered their families in North Korea, where relatives of those who fall into enemy hands face punishment. Ukraine has rejected South Korea's accusations.

Seoul's foreign ministry announced it was recalling ambassador Park Ki-chan, citing the unauthorised disclosure of information about the handover.
The ministry said it hoped to resolve outstanding issues through continued consultations and that the South Korean embassy in Kyiv would remain open.

Oil shipments to Russia a further complication

Kyiv's reaction came despite Seoul joining the coalition of countries that imposed enhanced export controls on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
In 2024, South Korea expanded its list of controlled goods to more than 1,400 items and tightened restrictions on so-called Common High Priority Items, components Russia procures through third countries for use in missiles, drones and other weapons.
Seoul has also sanctioned Russian ships, companies and individuals involved in military cooperation with North Korea.
In response to reports, South Korea's foreign ministry said Seoul "supports and is actively participating in global efforts to end the war in Ukraine and restore peace."
It declined to comment on specific shipments or the arrival of sanctioned vessels, saying the country strictly observes its own export-control measures against Russia.

====================================================================================================

Mathematicians invented a knitting stitch that stops mistakes from spreading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:25:51 UTC
20:25:51 KST

Despite its tranquil reputation, knitting is anything but boring. One stitch slip-up can cause a defect that spreads across the entire fabric. But does it have to be that way? In a recent paper in Physical Review X, a team of researchers mathematically investigated knitting to invent a new, more resilient stitch.
Knitting is a special form of fabrication in which the two ends of the yarn remain outside the fabric. In knitting, loops from the middle of an entangled yarn are slipped through one another so the yarn holds its position but isn’t knotted together. The knitting process is portable and easy, but the structure also means a tug on one loose end can quickly unravel the whole project. It’s also vulnerable to other quickly spreading errors.
Daisuke S. Shimamoto, a physicist at Ritsumeikan University in Japan, and his colleagues wrapped a three-dimensional model of a single jersey knit stitch—a simple beginner’s stitch—around a doughnut shape called a torus, which preserves the pattern without including any edges at the top or bottom. It basically converts the knit pattern into one giant knot that can be analyzed with knot theory. The scientists projected multiple knit rows on the torus to reveal how defects from one row of stitches spread until the entire fabric unravels. The process is called defect propagation, and the researchers say it’s one of the defining characteristics of knittable fabrics.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Researchers have mathematically described stitch defects in the past, says applied mathematician Alexander Omelchenko of Constructor University in Germany, but only as static objects. This study shows how defects move dynamically across a textile. “It’s a very original approach,” says Omelchenko, who wasn’t involved in this study but originated the topological analysis method used.
One common type of defect propagation is “laddering,” in which a single missed loop slips down a column of stitches, unraveling the whole column along the way. “If one unit cell is disentangled, the cell just below that cell is disentangled, and it is repeated, and it propagates endlessly,” Shimamoto says.
After his topological analysis of the jersey knit, Shimamoto used moves from basic knot theory to design a knittable stitch in which defect propagation can still happen but not endlessly. This “robust knit” is a complex stitch with sweeping loops that cross over through two stitches rather than one, and it reduces propagated defects row by row until they stop. Defects expand only when there is more than one slipped stitch in a row.
Omelchenko appreciates the study authors’ ability to translate math to real life but notes that fully evaluating the possibilities of new stitches by using torus diagrams would be impractically expensive to compute. Shimamoto hopes his work with the robust knit, as a proof of concept, can one day inspire stronger fabric design for manufacturing.
Besides a fascination with fabric, the two researchers have another thing in common: both consulted their mothers’ knitting advice for their papers, and Shimamoto even gave his mother an author credit as a thank you for teaching him how to knit. According to Omelchenko, “It sometimes was a little bit more useful to talk with her rather than textile researchers.”

Britain will update the design of its banknotes — bumblebees, hedgehogs and other animals will be depicted on the pound notes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:24:42 EEST
20:24:42 KST

Britain will update the design of its banknotes — bumblebees, hedgehogs and other animals will be depicted on the pound notes
Kyiv • UNN
The Bank of England selected four animal species for the new series of banknotes following a vote by nearly 500,000 people. The design will be developed over several years.
The Bank of England has identified four species of animals that will become the central images on a new series of banknotes. They were chosen through a public vote. This is reported on the Bank of England website, writes UNN.
Details
The next series of banknotes will feature a barn owl, a buff-tailed bumblebee, a European hedgehog and an Atlantic puffin. Each animal will become the central design element of one banknote of a different denomination.
The selection was based on a vote in which nearly 500,000 people took part. Residents chose from a list compiled by wildlife experts.
The barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and hedgehog were clear leaders in their respective categories. At the same time, the Atlantic puffin was chosen to add diversity and represent the country's marine wildlife and coastline, although other animals received more votes in the overall ranking.
The Bank notes that the process of designing, testing and printing the banknotes will take several years. Portraits of historical figures first appeared on British money in 1970. The new series will preserve this tradition: the portrait of the reigning monarch will also remain on the banknotes.

European Space Agency astronaut urges young people to ‘not be afraid to try’
Unknown

2026-10-08
11:23:47 UTC
20:23:47 KST

Yigithan Yildiz
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut Marco Alain Sieber said the first step toward achieving one’s goals is to take action without hesitation.
Speaking to Anadolu on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in the southwestern Turkish province of Antalya, Sieber said: “I would tell young people that trying is very important because the only way to become an astronaut is to actually apply. It was the same for me.”
“I had always dreamed of it, but I never thought it would become a reality. When the application period opened, I gave it a try, although I thought I would fail,” Sieber noted.
“I did my best and eventually succeeded. So I think you should do what you love and never miss an opportunity to grow and learn,” he said.
Sieber said he was attending the congress for the first time and was impressed by the scale of the event.
“Thank you very much for hosting this tremendous congress. It’s really great to be here in Antalya,” he added.
Organized by the International Astronautical Federation, IAC 2026 kicked off Monday and will run until Friday.
It is co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and the SAHA Istanbul defense cluster and organized by the Industry and Technology Ministry. Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.
The congress brings together representatives of space agencies, companies, universities and research institutions from around the world.

Two-thirds of young Europeans suffered childhood trauma, with lasting life impact, WHO finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:21:21 UTC
20:21:21 KST

Two-thirds of European children experienced trauma that ‘follows them into the classroom, job market and their relationships’.
More than two-thirds of young people in Europe have experienced childhood adversity ranging from domestic violence to the death of a parent, exposing them to poorer mental health and quality of life years later, according to a new report from the World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe.
More than one in five young adults reported experiencing four or more adverse childhood experiences.
“When a child grows up around violence or a household in crisis, we shouldn't be surprised that it follows them into the classroom, job market and their relationships years later,” said Natasha Azzopardi-Muscat, director of health systems at the WHO/Europe.
She added that the extent of the problem is often overlooked and the consequences expand to several aspects of people's lives.
“This isn't a mental health issue in isolation. It's a social and economic one, and it needs every sector at the table, not just health services,” said Azzopardi-Muscat.
The report surveyed more than 26,000 young adults aged 18 to 30 across Europe between November 2025 and January 2026. It measured exposure to nine forms of adversity, such as physical, emotional or sexual abuse, physical neglect, household substance use, household mental illness, parental separation or death, and witnessing domestic violence during their childhood.
“The findings are remarkably consistent. Adverse childhood experiences are at the root of poorer health, social and economic outcomes among young adults across Europe,” said Mark Bellis, from Liverpool John Moores University and academic lead for the study.
The most common experiences were parental separation or death, witnessing domestic violence or suffering emotional abuse.
Exposure to chronic stress in early childhood, which can be caused by these adverse experiences, disrupts brain development, impairs emotional regulation and alters physiological stress response systems, the report noted.
Young adults reporting four or more adverse experiences suffered significantly higher rates of physical pain or discomfort, difficulties with everyday activities like work or study, impaired mobility and self-care difficulties.
Among those who reported exposure to four or more adverse experiences, 76.3% felt they had needed professional mental health support in the previous year, compared with 36.7% of those who reported none.
However, young people most exposed to harmful experiences were also more likely to report that they had not received the mental health support they felt they needed, the report warned.
Breaking the cycle
Without effective prevention and early intervention, harmful experiences tend to recur across generations, the authors warned.
Adults affected by childhood adversity face higher risks of raising their own children in conditions marked by financial stress, domestic violence, and parental mental ill health.
Despite this stark picture, the report noted that even those exposed to more adverse experiences could still achieve positive outcomes.
The good news, Bellis said, is that adverse childhood experiences can be prevented and their impacts reduced.
“With support from policymakers, investment in safer and more nurturing childhoods will help deliver healthier populations, stronger communities and a more prosperous future for Europe,” he added.

Israel reduces British diplomatic presence in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:21:14 UTC
20:21:14 KST

Barricades block the main road leading to British Consulate after the sign outside the consulate was taken down, in east Jerusalem, Oct. 8, 2026. (AP Photo)
Israel said the British consulate in Jerusalem ended its functions on Oct. 8 but that seven diplomats would be allowed to remain in a limited capacity, with the U.K. saying it would continue to offer “vital services.”
The move comes after Israel ordered the closure of the consulate in September as retaliation after London led Western sanctions over violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the Oct. 8 move to downsize the U.K. presence had followed a dialogue with the British government in order to avoid an escalation of tensions between the two countries.
“As I announced, the British consulate in Jerusalem ended its role today,” Saar said in a statement, adding that 20 diplomats including the consul general were ending their missions and leaving the country.
Saar said the building is the property of the British government and that a “task force of only seven diplomats” would be allowed to operate from the premises, “which ceased to function as a consulate today.”
“Their scope of activity will be very limited,” Saar said.
Britain and Israel have “agreed on the continuation of dialogue between the governments, within which both sides will be able to raise issues important to them”, he said.
The U.K. government pledged to continue delivering “vital services” in Jerusalem, saying the consulate general building would remain open and would “be known as the U.K. Mission, Jerusalem.”
The diplomatic emblem and a plaque that adorned the consulate’s facade were removed on Oct. 8.
It was not immediately clear whether new plaques would be put up.
On Sept. 8, Saar ordered the British consulate to close.
At the time, he said Israel would also expel British representatives at a center monitoring the U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan in Gaza, bar British training for Palestinian Authority forces and ban 12 Britons, mostly members of parliament, from visiting.
The retaliation came after 12 countries including Britain, Canada and France announced they would sanction trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, following a surge in settler attacks against Palestinians in the occupied territory.

UK ramps up sanctions against Russian shadow fleet, crypto industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:21:10 UTC
20:21:10 KST

Editor's note: this article was updated with further details provided in a U.K. government press statement released after this article was first published.
The U.K. published 38 new sanctions listings on Oct. 8, targeting ships helping Russia evade existing sanctions and a range of companies in Moscow's military-industrial complex, energy, and cryptocurrency sectors.
"The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences," reads a U.K. government press release.
Among the businesses in the new sanctions listings are three cryptocurrency exchanges and two payment platforms.
Xeltox Enterprises, one of those listed entities has "been involved in obtaining a benefit from or supporting the government of Russia by carrying on business in a sector of strategic significance (...) the financial services sector," reads the U.K. government's sanctions listing.
Russia has increasingly sought to use cryptocurrency, which is hard to track, to circumvent global sanctions, and the new U.K. sanctions target the "A7" network, which is at the heart of Moscow's attempts to evade financial sanctions.
That has prompted the U.K., the U.S., the EU, and Ukraine to target crypto schemes in recent sanctions packages.
Also featuring on the listings are two further oil companies: Zarubezhneft and INK Capital.
"The U.K. was the first country in the G7 to sanction the top four Russian oil companies," reads the press statement.
The U.K. has also added 12 ships to its list of sanctioned vessels accused of being part of Russia's shadow fleet — dilapidated vessels suspected of helping Moscow evade price caps and bans on its trade in oil and gas.
That takes the number of ships sanctioned by the U.K. to 645 and the total number of Russia sanctions to 3,537.

Tallinn Airport lets driverless shuttles run close to airplanes, opening the way to wider airport automation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:20:24 UTC
20:20:24 KST

Euronews Next exclusive: A driverless shuttle now carries aircraft workers and spare parts at Tallinn Airport, with no safety agents on board.
Autonomous cars and shuttles are no longer rare on city streets, but airports with their extraordinary safety rules are a different matter.
At Tallinn Airport, Estonian company Auve Tech is now running its MiCa shuttles on routes passing close to parked aircraft — for the first time, without a safety operator on board. It is a step the company hopes will make driverless transport pay for itself and perhaps spread to other airports.
The Tallinn shuttles serve Magnetic MRO, an aircraft maintenance firm with hangars on opposite sides of the airfield. They move workers, tools and spare parts between the sites throughout the day.
Getting here took years. Auve Tech began testing their tech at the airport in 2023, and the commercial service started in 2025, first with a required safety operator on board. Taking that person out was the hard part.
"When conducting a drive inside the airport, that's a whole other story. You have so many layers of safety rules that you have to comply with," Deivis Sepp, Fleet Operations Lead at Auve Tech, told Euronews Next. "That's why getting the permit is kind of a miracle."
Sepp said the airport's safety board has been reviewing the shuttles' performance data every week throughout the test period.
"Terabytes and terabytes of data have been gathered," Sepp told Euronews Next. "They are not giving us the permit like, 'Hey, just go ahead and do your thing, do the innovation.' It doesn't work like that."
How MiCa works
MiCa is a small electric shuttle that Auve Tech unveiled in October 2022. It is designed for last-mile transport in pre-mapped areas, and it carries up to eight passengers. MiCa is rated Level 4 for self-driving — meaning it can drive itself without a human at the wheel, but only within defined conditions, such as a mapped route.
To ”see” its surroundings, the shuttle uses ten cameras and seven laser-based sensors, which give it a 360-degree view. It does not roam freely between the planes — it follows a fixed route with rules built in and reacts immediately to any potential obstacle.
"It will see enough ahead to make a decision," Sepp told Euronews Next. "We are at a cross section, looking from one place to another, and if it's safe to move, it will go."
The shuttle also reacts to small hazards. Euronews' reporter had to grab a handrail when the shuttle braked hard midway through the ride, apparently for a bird crossing its route.
“Small birds are flying around here, and it detects everything near it," Sepp told Euronews Next. "So of course safety comes first for us."
Humans are still part of the system, but from a distance. The vehicle makes its own decisions, and a remote operator in a tele-monitoring room watches over it.
"The vehicle decides what to do, whether to do it and when to do it," Sepp told Euronews Next. "But if some glitch happens, it will ask permission from the tele-monitoring operator."
Making the sums add up
For Auve Tech, removing the on-board operator is a crucial economic step. Taavi Rõivas, Chairman of the Supervisory Board and a former Estonian prime minister, said a safety operator on board "doesn't make much sense commercially".
"Regulatory needs are there to still have a human in the loop, but one human can supervise or remotely monitor several vehicles," Rõivas told Euronews Next.
He put the break-even point at around three vehicles per remote operator.
"If you look at three vehicles at the same time, see what they're doing, and if necessary give some minor guidance, then we can match the price of human-driven vehicles," Rõivas told Euronews Next.
"Once we can roll out this service in this way, I believe the scaling of autonomous vehicle transportation will be very, very rapid."
Their main client already sees the benefit in cost and reliability. Risto Mäeots, CEO of Magnetic Group, said his company drives "almost 50,000 kilometres every year" between its hangars. Before the shuttles, they had to only use human drivers, which sometimes brought problems of their own.
"We faced a lot of reliability issues. For example, people can get sick, and there was staff turnover," Mäeots told Euronews Next. "It turned out to be a big challenge."
He described transport as a cost centre for a maintenance business, not a source of revenue. He also said the company, which competes with much larger aviation players, has to be inventive to survive.
"We half-joke that we don't have a right to exist because we are a small company against major aviation players," Mäeots told Euronews Next. "So for us to exist, we have to really think out of the box."
"We thought it was going to be predominantly used by people, but now we see an equally important part is spare parts being delivered between the hangars," Mäeots told Euronews Next. Bulky items still travel by conventional vehicles because of the size limits.
Auve Tech now wants to take the model elsewhere. Rõivas said the immediate target is the large number of last-mile shuttle services running in closed environments, such as corporate campuses, where regulators find it easier to allow vehicles without safety operators.
"Globally there are hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of last-mile shuttle services, only in closed environments," Rõivas told Euronews Next. "We see that we can either match the price or outperform the price of the current service."
Interest is coming from Europe, Japan, Abu Dhabi and the US, he said. Other airports’ representatives are visiting Tallinn "pretty much one airport per week" to see the service working. Some consider carrying VIP passengers or move people between gates in such shuttles.
"We are expecting to have, very soon, announcements that much bigger airports than Tallinn will have a similar service up and running," Rõivas told Euronews Next.
Sepp is confident about the direction. "I believe within the next 10 years, autonomous transportation solutions inside the airport will be a common thing to see," he told Euronews Next.

US-led coalition exit shifts more counter-ISIS burden to Iraq and Syria - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:20:08 UTC
20:20:08 KST

The US-led coalition formally ended its Operation Inherent Resolve mission in Iraq on September 30 as its remaining forces and equipment completed their withdrawal, shifting primary security responsibility to Baghdad and raising new questions about how Iraq and Syria will monitor their long frontier against ISIS.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
US Central Command said the transition was part of a planned move toward a bilateral defense relationship between Washington and Baghdad. Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve remains active, with its headquarters relocated to Jordan, while coalition forces continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria.
For Damascus, the shift follows another major change. US forces completed their departure from the al-Tanf garrison in southeastern Syria in February as part of a broader military repositioning. CENTCOM said at the time that American forces would remain capable of responding to ISIS threats in the region and supporting partner-led operations.
The transition raises a central question along the Syrian-Iraqi frontier: Can forces on both sides maintain effective surveillance and intelligence sharing as the coalition’s military footprint changes?
Istanbul-based Iraqi journalist Ali al-Khazali told The Media Line that the most important change after the coalition mission ended has not been a major increase in troop numbers, but a higher state of readiness and greater responsibility for Iraqi forces.
Before the transition, he said, Iraq had worked to build a multilayered defensive system along the Syrian border involving border guards, the Iraqi army, and the Popular Mobilization Forces, backed by fortifications and aerial and technical surveillance.
“Baghdad tried before the coalition’s departure to make the border less dependent on the foreign military presence and to ensure that Iraqi forces themselves hold the ground and manage the file directly,” al-Khazali said.
Iraqi authorities had already expanded concrete barriers, trenches, barbed wire, thermal cameras, observation towers, and drone surveillance along the frontier.
Stronger fortifications, al-Khazali said, do not mean Baghdad can fully replace everything the coalition provided.
Iraqi forces are now capable of handling much of the operational burden inside the country and conducting operations against ISIS cells, he said, but advanced technical and intelligence capabilities remain a more difficult challenge.
US capabilities difficult to replace in short term by Iraq
According to al-Khazali, the United States provided aerial surveillance, drones, intelligence imagery, and sophisticated systems for tracking targets and rapidly integrating information from multiple sources - capabilities that will be difficult to replace completely in the short term.
“Iraq can compensate for a large part of the coalition’s military role, but it has not yet reached the point where it can fully dispense with US support, particularly in intelligence, surveillance, and long-range reconnaissance,” he said.
On the Syrian side, political analyst Firas al-Allawi described similar concerns about surveillance and intelligence capabilities.
Al-Allawi told The Media Line that there are no clear indications of a broad Syrian military deployment or a major increase in troop numbers along the Iraqi border, although limited redeployments may have taken place recently.
“What is available so far does not indicate the transfer of large numbers of troops or major changes along the Syrian-Iraqi border,” al-Allawi said.
Coordination between Damascus and Baghdad exists, particularly in the exchange of security information, he said, but it has not yet reached the level of an integrated strategic security partnership.
Al-Allawi believes some intelligence cooperation is taking place away from public view, with a significant portion occurring within a broader framework that still involves the United States.
“I believe an important part of the information exchange takes place within a broader intelligence cooperation umbrella in which Washington participates, rather than through deep, direct Syrian-Iraqi cooperation,” he said.
A degree of mistrust and caution remains between Damascus and Baghdad, according to al-Allawi, making it premature to describe their cooperation as a fully developed joint security system.
Al-Khazali offered a similar assessment from the Iraqi side. Direct communication channels, information sharing, and meetings between border officials exist, he said, but publicly available information does not indicate that the two countries operate a permanent joint operations room or fully integrated intelligence center.
“What exists is direct communication channels, information exchange, and coordination in some operations,” he said. “But transforming that cooperation into a permanent joint security system is still a work in progress.”
Iraqi officials have previously said Baghdad coordinates directly with Syrian authorities to prevent ISIS infiltration, combat smuggling, and exchange security information.
ISIS operating through small cells, individual operatives, in shift since 2014
The nature of the threat has also changed considerably since 2014.
ISIS no longer needs to move large columns of fighters across the border or capture cities and crossings to pose a danger. The group can operate through smaller cells, desert routes, logistical and financial networks, and individual operatives capable of exploiting gaps in surveillance without the kind of large-scale military breakdown seen during its territorial expansion.
“The most dangerous gap today is not an open stretch of border or the collapse of fortifications,” al-Khazali said. “The biggest danger is the intelligence gap between the two sides of the border.”
The desert corridor between Iraq’s Anbar province and Syria’s Deir ez-Zor region remains particularly sensitive, he said, because small cells and smuggling networks can exploit vast distances and the difficulty of maintaining continuous surveillance.
Al-Allawi identified a similar weakness on the Syrian side.
Syria’s Badia desert and the broader desert belt extending toward Iraq still suffer from limited aerial surveillance and incomplete intelligence capabilities, he said, while the vast geography makes sustained control difficult.
“The area generally remains fragile from both a security and strategic perspective, and the length of the Syrian-Iraqi border makes it even harder to control,” al-Allawi said.
Increasing troop numbers insufficient to rein in ISIS, analyst says
Although ISIS is far weaker than at the height of its territorial expansion, scattered cells in desert areas could use surveillance gaps to regroup or move personnel, money, and equipment.
For that reason, al-Allawi said increasing troop numbers alone will not be enough. Syria needs more advanced surveillance and reconnaissance technology, aerial support, improved equipment, and personnel with greater training in border security, counter-infiltration, and desert operations.
Al-Allawi said improved border security will also require broader cooperation with Iraq, the United States, the international coalition, and Jordan rather than relying solely on a larger Syrian military deployment.
The ISIS detainee issue further ties Syrian and Iraqi security together.
During a 23-day operation that began January 21, US forces transferred more than 5,700 adult male ISIS detainees from facilities in northeastern Syria into Iraqi custody. CENTCOM said the operation was intended to keep the detainees securely held and reduce the risk of an ISIS resurgence.
The end of the coalition mission in Iraq does not sever Iraq’s security concerns from Syria. Iraq now has responsibility for thousands of ISIS detainees transferred from Syrian facilities, while Damascus must prevent remaining ISIS cells in the Badia from using the frontier for movement and reorganization.
Iraqi and Syrian sources agree on one central point: Securing the frontier depends not only on walls, trenches, troops, and surveillance equipment, but on whether information can cross the border faster than ISIS operatives do.

SDE demand €100 million worth of changes in exchange for supporting the state budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:20:00 UTC
20:20:00 KST

SDE demand €100 million worth of changes in exchange for supporting the state budget
The Social Democrats are prepared to vote in favor of the state budget if the coalition backs their proposed amendments, worth up to €100 million, without negotiations.
The Social Democrats voted in favor of sending the budget to the plenary session of the Riigikogu in the parliament's Finance Committee, although they do not intend to support its final passage in its current form. Ahead of the second reading, they plan to submit a raft of amendments, which they expect to be backed without negotiations.
The Social Democrats' demands total up to €100 million. They include larger increases to the salary funds for teachers, police officers and rescue workers, as well as additional funding for special care services and healthcare.
"About €40 million is currently set to be cut from healthcare. We are not prepared to vote for a budget that reduces access to medical care," Social Democratic Party Chairman Lauri Läänemets said.
"If we look at specialized care services, they will need an additional €30 million next year. There may ultimately be a few more proposals on top of these," Läänemets noted.
According to Läänemets, funding could be found for all their proposals. First, the state should take more serious action to tackle the shadow economy. Second, tax breaks for remote gambling should be reversed. Third, the government's reserves should be reviewed.
Õnne Pillak, chair of the Reform Party's Riigikogu group, said the coalition was prepared to reach an agreement if funding sources could be identified.
"It's no secret that specialized care services are an issue close to all our hearts. The budget actually sets aside €37.5 million to reach these agreements. I think this is work we need to get done. I'm glad that at least the Social Democrats are showing a willingness to contribute ideas and put forward substantive proposals," Pillak said.
The Reform Party has also held talks with other opposition parties and unaffiliated MPs. However, there is a fairly clear understanding in the Riigikogu that the Social Democrats are being considered the most seriously, as another MP could leave Eesti 200 before the final budget vote.
The support of an entire party would give the minority government a bigger buffer than that of a handful of unaffiliated MPs. Unaffiliated Riigikogu member Tõnis Mölder said the Social Democrats know this and have set their price very high.
"It has been clear in this building for a long time that the Social Democrats are very keen to join the coalition," Mölder said. "What the Social Democratic Party also needs to understand is that all parties in the Riigikogu actually support increasing funding for special care services. The issue is rather that this budget must not turn into a preelection spending spree. It has to be responsible."
According to Mölder, unaffiliated MPs will take a closer look at the budget over the coming weeks, but their priorities include relief from high energy prices and scrapping the fuel excise duty. On these issues, the government has recently been sending largely positive signals.

CNN, MS NOW, Politico to ask federal judge for extension to protection from White House ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:19:42 UTC
20:19:42 KST

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico are due in Washington federal court on Thursday to ask a judge to extend their protection against being banned from the White House under US President Donald Trump’s order.
Trump’s revocation of the outlets’ access for publishing what he said was “FAKE NEWS” was the latest escalation of his pressure campaign against media coverage he dislikes. He said he might ban other outlets but was unsure it would hold up in court.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily blocked the ban on September 24, finding it likely violated the outlets’ right to fair treatment under the Constitution's Fifth Amendment. He did not rule on the outlets’ claim that the ban violated their First Amendment free speech rights.
The outlets have asked for an order blocking the ban until a final ruling. They say the revocation of their passes was unlawful retaliation for their coverage and accused the administration of coming up with meritless national security concerns to justify the ban.
Justice Department lawyers say the outlets endangered national security by publishing classified information, citing stories about construction of Trump's White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican midterm convention.
Kelly was skeptical of the government’s arguments at a September 23 hearing. Kelly blocked Trump during his first term from revoking CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s White House pass, saying the decision was neither transparent nor fair.
Trump faces low job approval ratings as midterm elections approach
The legal battle comes just weeks before the November 3 midterm elections in which Trump's fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
Trump's job approval ratings are at the lowest of his political career in opinion polls amid concerns over the Iran war and inflation.

Two of Britain’s new E-7 aircraft airborne
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:18:20 BST
20:18:20 KST

Both of the Royal Air Force’s delivered Boeing E-7 Wedgetail aircraft were flying at the same time on Thursday afternoon, the first occasion on which the two have been airborne together.
WT001 came south from RAF Lossiemouth for the orbit areas in the South West using the callsign Boeing 31, while WT002 was out of MOD Boscombe Down as Boeing 38. Between them they represent two thirds of the entire future British airborne early warning fleet. The second aircraft was still being outfitted by STS Aviation at Birmingham Airport as recently as January, so its appearance out of Boscombe Down marks its arrival in the flight test programme alongside the first aircraft.
The Wedgetail is built on the Boeing 737 Next Generation airframe, the same basic aeroplane as the RAF’s Poseidon maritime patrol fleet, and carries the Northrop Grumman Multi-role Electronically Scanned Array radar in the distinctive dorsal fin above the fuselage.
The array has no moving parts, which is the main departure from the rotating radomes of earlier airborne early warning aircraft, and it allows the operator to concentrate the radar’s attention on a particular sector while continuing to scan elsewhere.

The most recent milestone before this one came on 21 May, when WT001 landed at RAF Lossiemouth for the first time, flown by a mixed Boeing UK and Royal Air Force crew. The station has spent a long time preparing for it.
Group Captain Sarah Brewin, the station commander at Lossiemouth, said at the time: “We have been working hard to get ready to operate these aircraft.”
Stu Voboril, Boeing’s vice president and programme manager for the E-7, said: “We look forward to continuing test and evaluation as the aircraft moves closer to entry into service.”
That test and evaluation phase is split between Boscombe Down and Lossiemouth, which explains Thursday’s pattern of one aircraft working out of each. Boeing UK hands the aircraft over to the Royal Air Force once the phase is complete, at which point 8 Squadron takes them on.

Türkiye completes preparations to submit Mecca defense pact to parliament: Foreign minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:18:14 UTC
20:18:14 KST

Türkiye has completed preparations to submit the Mecca defense agreement to parliament for approval, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Thursday, stressing that the pact is defensive in nature and does not authorize attacks on other countries.
"The necessary work for the agreement to be submitted to parliament has been completed," Fidan said at a joint news conference in Ankara with Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orban.
Fidan said he made a final presentation on the matter to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday and that Türkiye has decided to send the agreement to parliament as soon as possible.
Fidan said the agreement provides for mutual defense if one of its signatories comes under attack.
"Once a country that is a party to the agreement is attacked, you stand by it for its defense. This is not an attack agreement," he said.
He also clarified that the pact does not authorize Türkiye to deploy troops to another country's territory to carry out an attack.
"Türkiye will not send troops to another country's territory to carry out an attack," Fidan said.
Mecca defense agreement
Fidan said Türkiye's participation in the Oct. 5 meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee of the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defense in Riyadh was primarily prompted by attacks targeting Saudi Arabia.
He said the extraordinary meeting also addressed several institutional issues, including the structure of the military headquarters, the status of the secretariat and the appointment of a new secretary.
Although the agreement was signed relatively recently, Fidan said institutionalization and practical steps have advanced rapidly.
“The parties are showing through their determination that they are serious about this and want to see concrete results,” he said.
Fidan said the meeting also discussed possible Turkish contributions to Saudi Arabia's defense against attacks by Yemen's Houthi group.
“Yemen’s legitimate government forces are continuing their current fight. Saudi Arabia supports them. But at the same time, we are doing everything we can to help resolve the issue through peace and dialogue,” the minister added.
Russia-Ukraine war
Turning to the Russia-Ukraine war, Fidan warned against allowing the conflict to expand into the Black Sea.
“We must never allow the Black Sea to turn into a new front of conflict,” he said.
Fidan described the Russia-Ukraine war as one of the main threats to regional and global stability, saying Türkiye had worked since the beginning of the conflict to prevent fighting from spilling into the Black Sea.
“We have worked hard since the beginning of the war to ensure that the conflict does not spill over into the Black Sea. Our meticulous implementation of the Montreux Convention and the Black Sea Grain Initiative were concrete examples of this approach,” he said.
Fidan said both Russia and Ukraine are carrying out intense military operations as they seek to gain an advantage before winter, with the escalation seriously affecting navigational safety in the Black Sea.
“Both sides are currently engaged in an enormous offensive to gain a certain military advantage over each other just before winter. This is seriously affecting navigational safety in the Black Sea,” he said.
“We see that Turkish-flagged, Turkish-owned vessels and ships with Turkish personnel are also being affected,” he said, adding that Türkiye is doing everything it can to bring such incidents to an end.
Fidan also warned that disruptions preventing grain carried by ships from reaching international markets are creating food security problems in many countries, particularly in Africa.
“The increasing attacks against civilian vessels pose a serious threat to the security of life, property, navigation and the environment in our region,” he said.
Gaza, West Bank
Turning to Gaza, Fidan said Türkiye is using diplomatic channels at the bilateral, regional and international levels to help end the ongoing situation and secure lasting peace.
He said necessary steps include delivering the maximum possible amount of humanitarian aid to Gaza, allowing the Palestinian National Committee to enter the enclave and take over its administration, and deploying the International Stabilization Force.
“Israel does not have much interest in implementing the Gaza Peace Plan,” Fidan said, stressing the importance of renewed international pressure to end the situation in the enclave.
Fidan said Türkiye would continue its diplomatic efforts despite the wider conflict in the region.
“We are making every effort on every platform to prevent the ongoing tragedy in Gaza, the acceleration of land seizures that have begun in the West Bank, and the planned insidious operations against Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem,” he said.
He described the situation in Gaza as a problem that is “triggering all the fault lines in the region and globally,” saying Türkiye has a vision for a peace plan that would include Israel, Palestine and regional countries.
“We are discussing this with the parties, but intensive diplomatic efforts are needed, primarily with Israel, for the parties to reach this point,” Fidan said.
“We will continue our determined, constructive and result-oriented efforts,” he added.

Flydubai attack: Israel's Transport Ministry sought crew data only after three years of requests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:17:39 UTC
20:17:39 KST

Despite repeated requests from the Israel Tax Authority over the past three years, the Transport Ministry's security division sought access to information on airline crews only after a closed-door Knesset hearing into the attempted flydubai cockpit attack, ynet has learned.
The request came after a confidential meeting of the Knesset's Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee on Tuesday, which examined the attempt by Omani pilot Hamam al-Hammami to crash a flydubai passenger aircraft. Following the hearing, the Transport Ministry's security division requested immediate access to the National Passenger Assessment Center, seeking information about the nationalities of airline crew members.
The Tax Authority confirmed that it had contacted the ministry several times before the attempted attack, explicitly asking it to fulfill its responsibility to appoint an authorized representative who could retrieve information from the center.
Despite those requests, the ministry had not taken the necessary steps to obtain access during the preceding three years.
After finally authorizing a representative, the Transport Ministry was informed that the system was not technically capable of providing airline crew nationality data 48 hours before departure, as required under the legislation governing the center.
Instead, the information becomes available only close to departure, at a stage when it can no longer be effectively used for security screening.
Transport Ministry officials complained about the limitation. However, according to the Tax Authority, the procedure under which crew information is transmitted shortly before flights had already been established with the knowledge and approval of Transport Ministry representatives.
The Transport Ministry disputed the allegation that its security division had failed to appoint a representative despite repeated requests.
"The security division continues to participate in a series of previously scheduled meetings of the National Passenger Assessment Center's steering committee, in order to help define the system and take part in it once it becomes operational," the ministry said.
"Claims that the security division was asked to send a representative and failed to do so are completely detached from reality, since a representative of the division is a member of the center's steering committee."
The ministry added that, regardless of the dispute over representation, the system remained unable to provide information about airline crews sufficiently far in advance.
"In any event, even at this stage, the system is unable to provide the information about airline crews ahead of time, as noted," the ministry said.
The conflicting accounts highlight a dispute over responsibility for obtaining aviation security information, particularly the distinction between participating in the center's steering committee and appointing an authorized official to retrieve operational data.
The revelations come as Lahav 433, the Israel Police's national crime investigation unit, opened a preliminary inquiry Wednesday into suspicions involving senior Transport Ministry officials responsible for aviation security.
The inquiry concerns allegations that officials responsible for security oversight, particularly the screening of pilots arriving in Israel, also worked for foreign airlines, including flydubai, the airline involved in the attempted attack.
Two senior officials are at the center of the inquiry: Avraham "Avri" Cohen, head of the Transport Ministry's security division, and Dvir Rubinstein, director of the ministry's Aviation Security Operations Center. The examination was launched following information provided to police by officials within the Transport Ministry.
The National Fraud Investigations Unit, which operates under Lahav 433, is handling the inquiry, including suspicions of potential conflicts of interest involving ministry employees and the operations of foreign airlines in Israel.
Meanwhile, the investigation into the actions of Omani pilot al-Hammami remains underway. Saudi Arabia is continuing its investigation into the security incident aboard the flight, while the United Arab Emirates is conducting a separate criminal investigation in which Israel's Shin Bet security agency is participating.
Israel has also offered to participate in any aviation safety investigation led by Saudi authorities, but has not yet received an invitation.
Ofer Vaknin, head of the Transport Ministry's aviation safety investigation authority, told Reuters that Israel was prepared to assist with such an investigation. "We are still waiting for an invitation from Saudi Arabia," he said.
Separate investigations are also underway in Australia and New Zealand concerning periods during which the Omani pilot stayed in those countries.
The growing number of inquiries comes as Israeli authorities face questions not only about the attempted attack itself, but also about the aviation security information available before the incident and whether existing procedures were adequately implemented.

Dragon Capital slashes outlook, sees Ukraine GDP dropping 0.5% in 2026, 1.0% in 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:16:25 EEST
20:16:25 KST

The intensification of Russian attacks since July 2026 has inflicted significant damage on Ukraine's economy, prompting leading Ukrainian investment company Dragon Capital to substantially downgrade its macroeconomic forecast: it now expects real gross domestic product (GDP) to decline by 0.5% this year and by 1.0% next year, whereas before the escalation it had forecast possible growth of 1.5% this year and 0.5% next year.
"These estimates are based on the assumption that Ukrainian air defenses will eventually be able to counter jet-powered drones more effectively, but the shortage of interceptors for ballistic missiles will remain a significant problem," the company said in a press release published Thursday.
Dragon Capital recalled that, taking into account the initial consequences of the escalation, it cut its forecast for real GDP growth in 2026 by 0.5 percentage points (p.p.) in early August, to 1.0%, but the latest developments, in particular the expansion of the range of targets attacked by the enemy, indicate that the negative impact on the economy will be more substantial.
A significant part of Ukraine's territory where major industrial assets, including metallurgical enterprises, are concentrated is within the range of ballistic missiles, it said. Although damaged production assets can likely be repaired, the threat of repeated strikes will prevent steelmakers from resuming full-scale operations.
"We believe that grain exports by sea may resume next year as a result of a diplomatic agreement similar to the 'grain corridor' that operated in 2022-2023. However, reaching an agreement covering a broader range of facilities, including the widely discussed 'energy truce,' appears unlikely," the press release said.
According to Dragon Capital, a blockade of Black Sea ports could reduce real GDP by 2.2%, provided that agricultural exports are partially redirected to alternative routes, particularly to Danube ports. If grain exports by sea are unblocked before the start of the spring sowing campaign, these losses could be reduced by 1.5 p.p., to 0.7%.
However, another 1.5% of GDP will be lost due to the shutdown of steel production and, consequently, a reduction in iron ore mining, since it is impossible to redirect these shipments to export under conditions in which the seaports are blocked, the release said.
As reported, the World Bank recently downgraded its forecast for Ukraine's economic growth in 2027 from 4% to 1.5%, while maintaining its estimate for growth this year at 1.2%.
At the end of September, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) downgraded its forecast for Ukraine's GDP growth in 2026 to 1.5% and in 2027 to 2.5%.
Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said at the end of September that he was allowing for a downward revision of the 2027 GDP growth forecast by 0.3-0.5 p.p. from the already incorporated pessimistic scenario (from 1.3% to 0.8-1%) and for 2026 to 0.5%, compared with the current forecast of 1.6%.
The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) lowered its estimate for real GDP growth this year to 1.1-1.2%, compared with its estimate of 1.8% at the end of July this year.
