Medication helps adults with ADHD weigh the negative consequences of their decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:00:29 UTC
20:00:29 KST

Adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder often struggle with choices that require weighing potential rewards against negative consequences. A new experiment reveals that a common stimulant medication improves these choices specifically by helping individuals pay more attention to the potential costs of their actions. The research was published in Psychological Medicine.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsive behavior. People with this diagnosis frequently experience difficulties with real-life decisions, which can manifest as reckless driving, substance abuse, and risky sexual behavior. Every day, humans navigate choices that require balancing the positive aspects of an action against its negative aspects. Buying a new phone brings the benefit of better technology but carries the cost of having less money for groceries.
Neurobiological theories suggest that the disorder involves atypical functioning of dopamine and norepinephrine, which are chemical messengers in the brain that help regulate attention, reward processing, and cognitive effort. Stimulant medications like methylphenidate, often sold under the brand name Ritalin, increase the availability of these chemicals in the brain. While researchers know that stimulants generally improve decision-making, the exact psychological mechanisms driving this improvement have remained elusive.
Mads Lund Pedersen, a psychologist at the University of Oslo, and a team of colleagues conducted a study to break down the specific components of decision-making. They wanted to know if medication helps people by increasing their sensitivity to rewards, heightening their awareness of costs, or simply altering the amount of time they spend thinking before they act.
To answer these questions, the research team recruited 61 adults diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and 63 healthy control participants. The study utilized a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design. The participants with the diagnosis completed the testing twice, once after taking their standard dose of methylphenidate and once after taking an inactive placebo pill. Neither the participants nor the researchers knew which pill was administered on which day. The healthy control participants also completed the testing twice but did not receive any medication.
During the experiment, participants engaged in a computer-based task designed to test how they integrate costs and benefits. First, they completed a training phase where they learned to associate six different shapes with specific numerical rewards and six different colors with specific numerical costs. After learning these associations, they moved on to the main testing phase.
In the testing phase, the computer presented participants with a colored shape for a few seconds. The participants had to mentally combine the benefit value of the shape and the cost value of the color to determine the net value. If the net value was positive, the correct choice was to accept the offer. If the net value was negative, the correct choice was to reject it.
The researchers analyzed the behavioral data using a mathematical framework called the drift diffusion model. This model separates the fast, split-second process of making a choice into distinct cognitive components. One component is the drift rate, which measures how quickly and efficiently the brain accumulates evidence about the choice. Another component is the decision threshold, which represents the amount of information a person requires before they commit to an action, often referred to as the speed-accuracy tradeoff. A third component is non-decision time, which accounts for the physical time it takes to see the image on the screen and press the button.
The results showed that when participants with the diagnosis were given the placebo, they were less accurate than the healthy control group. The mathematical model revealed that the unmedicated participants had a lower drift rate, meaning they processed information about both the costs and the benefits less efficiently. They also exhibited a narrower decision threshold, meaning they acted on less information and responded prematurely.
The researchers also compared how the different groups weighed the positive and negative information. The healthy control participants naturally allowed the cost of the stimuli to influence their decisions more heavily than the benefits. The unmedicated participants with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder showed the reverse pattern, demonstrating a stronger sensitivity to the benefits than to the costs.
Administration of methylphenidate changed how the participants processed the information. The medication caused an increase in the drift rate, but this improvement was highly selective. The drug improved how efficiently the participants accumulated evidence about the costs, while leaving their sensitivity to the benefits entirely unchanged. By boosting cost sensitivity, the medication shifted the overall balance of their decision-making closer to the pattern seen in the healthy control group.
The medication also produced some unexpected effects. Instead of increasing the decision threshold to make participants wait for more information, the drug narrowed the threshold slightly further. However, the medication also increased the participants’ non-decision time. The researchers suggest that the participants might have spent this extra fraction of a second visually encoding the images, which could have improved the accuracy of their stimulus representations and contributed to the higher drift rate observed under medication.
The researchers analyzed individual differences among the participants who had the diagnosis. They found that individuals who reported more severe symptoms in their daily lives had the lowest sensitivity to costs when they were unmedicated. Among those taking medication, higher prescribed doses of methylphenidate were associated with both a stronger sensitivity to costs and a wider decision threshold.
The study includes several limitations regarding how the medication might be acting on the brain. The drug could be improving basic learning and memory rather than the actual moment of decision-making. Because participants had to memorize the values of the shapes and colors during the training phase, the stimulant might simply help them remember those specific values more reliably during the test.
Alternatively, participants might have used simple mental arithmetic to subtract the cost from the benefit. Stimulant medication could enhance this working memory skill independently of how the brain naturally weighs risks and rewards. The study also excluded individuals with severe comorbid psychiatric conditions, meaning the results might not apply to people who have additional severe mental health disorders. Finally, because the medication can cause noticeable physical sensations, some participants might have guessed when they received the active drug, which can influence behavioral performance through expectations.
Future research could separate these potential mechanisms by providing the values directly on the screen, removing the need for participants to memorize the shapes and colors beforehand.
The study, “Selective enhancement of cost sensitivity by methylphenidate in adult ADHD: a randomized placebo-controlled trial,” was authored by Mads Lund Pedersen, Athanasia M. Mowinckel, Sigurd Ziegler, Mats Fredriksen, Atle Bjørnerud, Tor Endestad, and Guido Biele.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Elections have consequences. So do the Trump administration’s exhaustive efforts to undermine them.
Voters will be confident in their choices, but less certain whose voice will count in the face of myriad intrusions by the executive branch. A coalition of Democratic attorneys general are working to make sure voters across the political spectrum have their say.
Led by the attorneys general of Washington, California, Massachusetts and Nevada, 24 states sued to block President Donald Trump’s US Postal Service plot to interfere with voting by mail. Last month, the supreme court upheld our lower court victories and blocked the administration’s unconstitutional power grab, at least for this election.
The law says states decide who receives a mail ballot. The USPS has never had the final say and, according to the American Postal Workers Union, until this year had never in its 250-year history tried to put such arbitrary restrictions on what mail it will deliver.
The case we brought was an important victory in every state, and particularly Washington, where more than 99% of voters cast their ballot by mail. States such as Colorado, Hawaii and Oregon have similarly high mail voting rates. But mail voting is not confined to blue states; it is widely used in red states as well, particularly those like Nebraska and the Dakotas, with large rural populations. It’s also the president’s preferred way to cast his own ballot.
The case of the postal service is just part of the multi-pronged federal attack states are pushing back against. The administration has abandoned the federal government’s traditional role of supporting election security and defending voting rights, work I participated in first-hand as a US attorney.
Recall, in 2020, Trump’s own administration – and particularly the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency – worked to protect the vote and defend the election. Then, efforts to misuse the Department of Justice were thwarted, and Trump relied on insurrectionists to do his bidding. In return for serving honorably, many public servants were sent packing upon Trump’s return to office, and the convicted insurrectionists were pardoned.
Now we have a US solicitor general who described the postal service’s attempt to deprive the rights of millions of eligible voters as only a “modest” use of federal authority.
The Trump administration is not known for its discretion or consistency. While the administration was in court purportedly concerned about election integrity, the president publicly demanded his supporters “cheat like hell” in midterm voting. I don’t think Republican voters want that any more than Democrats do.
We don’t doubt the administration will continue its lawless blitz against voters. Democratic state attorneys general are prepared, and have undertaken the largest multi-state effort to protect the vote in modern American history.
Recent rulings keep state elections on track and show the law is on our side. If Trump attempts to intimidate or discourage eligible voters, or to obstruct the counting of votes or certification of the election, Democratic state attorneys general will take swift action. States have decades of experience countering these threats when lodged by private actors, and they are just as illegal when attempted by the federal government.
Voters can do their part by exercising the right to elect their representatives. The president’s scheming benefits from public doubt and uncertainty. Democracy depends on the participation of its citizens, and every eligible voter should have the opportunity to render a verdict on their elected representatives.
That verdict is unlikely to favor President Trump, who ran on lowering costs, preserving peace, and economic stability, but instead delivered higher prices, hollowed out critical public services, engaged in unprecedented self-dealing, and began a globally destabilizing war with no end in sight.
Presidents don’t decide elections. State attorneys general and the millions of eligible voters we represent will exercise our constitutional powers to help keep it that way.
- Nick Brown is the attorney general of the state of Washington

The Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said they launched another strike on Riyadh’s main airport, after earlier attacks on Saudi Arabia killed three and injured 36.
The Houthis said they targeted King Khalid International Airport on Thursday, soon after an attack on the airport killed one person and wounded eight. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed Thursday’s attack. Another two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on Abha International Airport, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday. The earlier attacks happened on Tuesday and Wednesday, although the authorities did not specify the date of each. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those strikes.
On Thursday, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree warned airlines “for the last time” not to continue their flights in Saudi airspace, calling it a “theater” for Houthi military operations.
A Saudi-led coalition said late on Wednesday that the attacks “will not go unpunished.” It said it had destroyed 82 Houthi military sites across Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf, and Marib in Yemen.
The rebel group has carried out a series of attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s government forces launched a major offensive aimed at recapturing key territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that had been seized by the Houthis. Yemeni forces, supported by Saudi airstrikes, said they had reached Mokha on Monday and driven the Houthis back from the strait, although the Houthis dispute those claims.
The fighting has revived the yearslong civil war in Yemen that created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since the latest exchange of fire began in June, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming and funding the Houthis, which both Iran and the rebel group deny.
It has also opened up a new front in the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran, which began on Feb. 28 with a wave of U.S.-Israeli strikes. The Houthis reportedly received direction from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to capture Mokha last month to threaten global shipping and energy flows through another shipping route. The battle over Bab el-Mandeb has become more important amid new attacks on vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, as Iran seeks to re-assert its leverage over Hormuz.
Attacks on airports
Attacks on airports are a recurrent tactic by the Houthis.
The attack on the Riyadh airport killed a Sudanese national, and injured five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents, and a Pakistani resident, Saudi authorities said. The attack on Abha airport killed a Moroccan woman and an Algerian woman, and injured Saudi citizens, a Bangladeshi resident, and a Filipino resident.
Earlier on Wednesday, Yemeni authorities said ballistic missile and drone strikes targeted Aden international airport in Yemen. One missile landed near the runway shortly before a flight from Cairo was scheduled to land, Yemen’s Transport Ministry said. The Houthis acknowledged a missile strike nearby but said their target was a military camp.
The Saudi civilian aviation authorities also said two airports in the kingdom’s south were attacked on Monday evening, injuring three people. The airports, King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport, suffered material damage, the authorities announced on Tuesday.
Last month, Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of attempting an attack on Mecca, calling it a “red line.” The Houthis denied the allegations, as did Iran.
War widens
Saudi Arabia has sought help from a number of its allies to fight the Houthis. Turkey has sent defensive and technical support, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing officials. Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in August, and the three parties agreed to implement its collective defence commitments earlier this week.
Syria, another Saudi ally, is also weighing providing military aid, Reuters reported, which could include defensive aid or deploying forces on the ground to support the Yemeni offensive against the Houthis. The Syrian foreign ministry did not confirm any potential plan to Reuters and said, “Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries.”
Saudi Arabia also reportedly requested assistance from the U.S., although President Donald Trump has thus far declined requests for direct U.S. strikes against the Houthis. The U.S. has instead provided the kingdom with intelligence support.
Tanker attacks in Hormuz
Although Middle East oil exports have ticked up in recent weeks, renewed attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz have raised the stakes at Bab El-Mandeb, which became a critical alternative route for Saudi oil exports earlier in the Iran War.
Last week, attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest weekly level since the Iran War began. There were at least 12 attacks on oil, LNG, and LPG tankers near the Strait of Hormuz between Sept. 28 and Oct. 5, Reuters reported, citing data from three maritime security sources.
Attacks have continued this week.
India’s foreign ministry reported on Tuesday that 12 crew members were injured after an unknown projectile struck a Panama-flagged oil tanker sailing through Hormuz off the coast of Oman.
An unidentified tanker was also struck by multiple projectiles off the northern coast of Qatar on Wednesday, marking a rare attack deep inside the Persian Gulf. The attack resulted in an unknown number of casualties, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said. Authorities launched an investigation into the incident. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Iran said on Wednesday that it would close “illegal” routes that have been used to bypass Tehran’s blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, including a southern route close to Oman’s coast.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards’ Commander, told the IRGC-linked Fars news agency.
Naqdi said the “few routes” circumventing Tehran’s blockade were created by blowing up rocky passages in the Strait. He said the routes were used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring it to tankers.”
Despite Naqdi’s claims, Middle Eastern crude exports exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days in September, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, which included shipments via Hormuz, the Red Sea, and other routes. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Iran had “lost complete control of the Strait” as the U.S. Navy continues escorting some vessels through the Strait.
“There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he told reporters while on a visit in Athens.
Nevertheless, analysts previously told TIME that increased attacks in the Strait, coupled with the threat to Bab el-Mandeb, could quickly raise shipping costs and disrupt flows. Brent crude again topped $100 a barrel on Wednesday after retreating from nearly $110 a barrel last month.
The White House has also reportedly asked the Pentagon to develop options for strikes on Iran before November’s midterm elections, although no decision has been made. Trump has sought to ease concerns about the war’s economic toll, claiming Iran is holding out in hopes of hurting Republicans in the midterms and predicting that the war will end soon afterward. Strikes before the vote would end a weekslong lull in U.S. attacks on Iran, and could prompt further retaliation from Iran against energy assets and shipping in the Gulf.

How Massive Is Elon Musk’s Trillion-Dollar Fortune? Spend It Yourself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

On any given day, Elon Musk is worth about a trillion dollars. This does not mean that he has a trillion dollar bills sitting in an old-timey vault in a dusty basement somewhere; his wealth is mostly tied up in shares of SpaceX and Tesla. But if he were to cash those out, sell Neuralink and the Boring Company, and scrounge together some extra change, his checking account would hit 13 digits.
“Trillionaire” is an easy enough word to say. It’s fun, even! Rolls off the tongue. But research has shown that the human brain has a very hard time comprehending the actual size and scope of large numbers. “Trillion” sounds like a short hop from “billion,” after all, even though it is in fact 1,000 times bigger. And even if you are somehow able to wrap your mind around that immense scale, it still feels abstract, no matter how many times you compare it to the area of Central Park or the weight of a fleet of trucks. Maybe a better way to visualize a trillion dollars, then, is through what you can actually buy with it.
WIRED has partnered with Neal Agarwal, the proprietor of the consistently delightful website Neal.fun, to do just that. Spend Elon Musk’s Money is a new visualization that lets you, well, spend Elon Musk’s money, on anything from Big Macs to aircraft carriers to the Las Vegas Sphere. It keeps a tally as you go, so you can actually see how far a trillion dollars gets you these days, and it shows the items you’ve bought in a physical space.
WIRED spoke with Agarwal about this new project, why it feels so relevant now, and the state of building things on the web. You can read that interview below, and waste a few hours on Spend Elon Musk’s money right here.
This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.
WIRED: I’ve known about Neal.fun for a long time, I’m a big fan. But describe it for someone who’s never been there.
Neal Agarwal: I never wanted to constrain the site to one thing, so it ended up being almost like a journal at this point. I’ve been running it since I was 19, and it’s kind of a catalog of everything I’m interested in: visualizations, science, weird game mechanics. For me, it’s mostly an exploration of what you can do with a website.
Why is that important to you, the idea of exploring what a website is and means? If there’s one thing I know about you it’s that you love the web.
Very much so. I grew up on the web; I was 8 years old on forums. I probably spent more time in Club Penguin than any real-world walls. I’m definitely a child of the web, and it’s interesting that I’m around the same age as it. It’s a privilege. Painters are working in a medium that’s a thousand years older, a million years older, so a lot of things have already been found out, been fleshed out. But on the web there’s so much that we haven’t figured out yet. I think there’s still a lot of new stuff to discover, and that’s really interesting to me.
I think every medium has distinct things you can do with it. You can turn a book into a movie but it’s not quite the same. There are some things a book is always going to be better at, and vice versa. I think that’s true of the web too. This visualization we’re working on, you can’t print it in a newspaper.
I suspect people might be familiar with some of your individual projects, if not your site itself. To list some off that are huge in my household: The Password Game, Space Elevator, The Deep Sea, Infinite Craft. When something goes viral, as so many of these have, what’s it like on your end? Is it almost boring now to see things blow up?
I think each project has been very different. The ones that excite me the most now are where a lot of people play it and start doing things with it that I did not expect or intend. Within a few days of Infinite Craft launching, people started crafting Japanese words within the game. And they crafted enough Japanese words that they could play the whole game in Japanese. I’ve never released a game before where they unlocked a language.
I had another one called Internet Road Trip; it’s like a simulated road trip but through Google Street View. A Discord formed around that, and people started backseat driving and arguing over which city to go to next, should they make a pit stop here so they can see this monument. People started birdwatching within that game. All these emergent things started happening, and I think the web is really good at that, too. It’s really good at forming communities out of the silliest things, which I find really exciting.
There’s also this contrast with a more closed-off app environment; you don’t really work in apps as a medium.
When I was a teenager I did make some apps, but I always really disliked that Apple and Google had to approve what I could put in them, and you have to wait a week for approval, and if they don’t like your app you have no recourse. So just the idea of having a homepage where it’s like, this is my homepage. Nobody can tell me what to do with it. I can put whatever I want.
We should talk about this visualization, Spend Elon Musk’s Money. It’s sort of a sequel to Spend Bill Gates’ Money, which was one of your first projects, right?
That actually launched with the website itself. I just wanted to showcase how much $100 billion was, which I guess now seems like a little amount of money compared to the trillion we’re working with.
It’s almost quaint, right? The premise is you’ve got a $100 billion counter and a bunch of things you can buy with prices attached to them: a Big Mac, flip-flops, a lobster dinner, a year of Netflix, all the way up to things like a diamond ring, a Ferrari, a McDonald’s franchise, and then up again to the Mona Lisa. And you just keep trying to add it up. What was the response to that game when it first launched?
It was one of the biggest things I’ve launched, and it was really nice to see that the point got across. People understood that this is a way to visualize wealth that isn’t just graphs and bar charts. The game kept finding a new audience over and over again; it was an idea that kept being interesting to people.
And then we come to 2026, and we have a trillionaire in the world, and it felt like maybe the right time to revisit.
Yeah, I think so. There’s a lot more you can do to visualize that, too. That’s why this one is 3D. I think one thing with Spend Bill Gates’ money is, yeah, you can buy 10,000 cars, but it’s still a number on a screen. With Spend Elon Musk’s Money, I want you to see the cars you’re buying on a screen. The amount of physical stuff you can buy—it is an empire.
One thing that I certainly have a hard time with, and I think most people do, is really wrapping your head around what a trillion is. There’s been research that humans are really bad at processing how big the jumps are even from 1 billion to 2 billion, much less getting up to a trillion. Our brains just break.
I think that’s one thing the web is actually really good at, is that you have infinite space. You can visualize these numbers in ways that you can’t do in the physical world. Even for my project The Deep Sea, it’s a 1:1 of the ocean. If you wanted to print that out on paper, it would be a mile long, but on the web you can just keep scrolling and scrolling. So it’s kind of fun to have this infinite scroll mechanic to visualize these huge numbers.
Some of the items carry over from Spend Bill Gates Money, some are different. How did you think about the best mix of options to give people?
This time I was going for more tangible things, so you can visualize it. It’s honestly hard to think of items; once you get to $100 million, there are only so many things out on the market that you can buy. So we have the Las Vegas Sphere in there, and aircraft carriers.
After a point it’s kind of interesting that you’re like, OK, I could buy 1,000 more tanks, what would that really get me? Part of the fun of this one is just the futility of it. At a certain point, what more could a person need?
For sure. I just bought 1,000 monster trucks, and I still have $999,650,000 left.
There were a few different ideas. One is if you had a trillion dollars and just had a stack of money, and as you spend it you see the trillion dollars go down, but it’s actually pretty hard to render a trillion dollars in bills on the page.
I had thoughts of more abstract things. Once you get to a trillion dollars you’re really buying power, so how many companies you could buy or how much influence you have. But for most people, that’s a harder way to visualize things than, like, oh, that is a million racehorses I just bought.
Did you run into any technical challenges building this?
Initially I wanted everything to be 3D models on the site. But if you try to get your laptop to render a million monster trucks, it’s just going to freeze. So I had to do a lot of trickery to get this 3D effect without actually using 3D models.
It doesn’t just tell us about Elon Musk, it tells us about the things we’re buying. I looked back at the original Spend Bill Gates’ Money, and the Big Mac was $2. It’s $6 now. For anything where there’s a direct parallel, you’ve captured a real price jump.
It’s very inflation-adjusted. Which is crazy, because it’s only been six or seven years. If anyone has any recommendations about other items we should add to this, just let me know.

Key points in Italy's new electoral law

Key points in Italy's new electoral law
ROME, Oct 8 - Italy's lower house of parliament on Thursday gave final approval to new voting rules ahead of a general election due next year, completing a reform championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Meloni, whose government last month became the longest-serving since World War Two, says the new rules are intended to increase the prospect of stable government. The opposition says the goal is to favour her ruling coalition at the election.
Below are the main features of the new system.
PROPORTIONAL SYSTEM
The reform introduces a purely proportional system (PR), replacing the previous hybrid one by which around two thirds of seats were elected by PR and one third in first-past-the-post races.
To boost stability, a working majority will be guaranteed to any coalition that wins more than 42% of the vote. Italy's two main camps are Meloni's conservative alliance and the centre-left bloc, which includes the Democratic Party and the 5-Star Movement.
SEAT BONUS
A coalition surpassing the 42% threshold will receive a "majority bonus" of 70 seats in the 400-member Chamber of Deputies and 35 seats in the 200-member Senate.
However, to avoid excessively large majorities, the bonus is capped to prevent the winner getting more than 220 seats in the Chamber and 113 in the Senate.
If more than one coalition passes the 42% threshold, the one with most votes will get the bonus.
PRIME MINISTER CANDIDATE
Each coalition or party running outside a coalition must indicate their candidate for prime minister. However, under Italy's constitution the president formally chooses the prime minister, meaning the party designation will not be legally binding.
MINIMUM THRESHOLDS AND SIGNATURES
Coalitions must secure at least 10% of the vote to enter parliament, while individual parties, both inside and outside coalitions, must obtain at least 3%.
The reform raises to 6,000 from 1,500 the number of signatures parties currently outside parliament must gather in each constituency to field candidates.
Critics say this makes it harder for small or new parties to compete in the elections. REUTERS

Regions Calling: In Irkutsk, Locals Ask 'What Plague?'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Hello and welcome to Regions Calling, your guide to developments beyond the Russian capital from The Moscow Times.
The death of a lab worker at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk region soared to global headlines after local bloggers circulated unconfirmed reports and the head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia named “plague” as the suspected cause.
We spoke with residents of both regions about how the health scare is affecting their everyday lives. We also asked an independent health policy expert to weigh in on Moscow’s handling of the possible outbreak and what risks it poses to the rest of the world.
But first, a look at the latest news from the regions:
The Headlines
- Authorities in the Krasnodar region closed beaches in the Black Sea resort city of Sochi and surrounding areas on Tuesday after an oil tanker caught fire offshore following a reported drone attack.
Ecologists have already warned that the incident could have potentially catastrophic environmental consequences, including water contamination and the release of large volumes of hazardous substances into the air.
- Meanwhile, Yevgeny Naumov, the mayor of the region’s capital Krasnodar, preemptively resigned on Monday after four years in office plagued by controversy.
In January, Naumov signed off on plans to build an Orthodox Church on the grounds of a riverside park despite protests from residents. Since November 2025, more than 30,000 people have signed a petition demanding his resignation.
- A string of deadly bear attacks on humans has continued across Siberia and the Far East over the past few weeks. In the latest confirmed incident, a 55-year-old man was killed by a bear that entered a trailer parked on the premises of a local company in the eastern part of the Irkutsk region.
At least 20 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia since April. In response, lawmakers are reportedly considering lifting hunting quotas, establishing regional population limits and giving local authorities extra powers to control bear numbers.
Authorities in the Krasnoyarsk region said Monday that they have already culled more than 850 bears “as part of the population control measures.”
Read more about reasons behind the attacks in the previous edition of Regions Calling.
- A military court in the Zabaikalsky region sentenced Indigenous Buryat activist Marina Khankhalaeva to 20 years in prison in absentia on charges of organizing an extremist group and participating in a terrorist organization.
Khankhalaeva called the verdict “high praise” and proof that she and fellow members of pro-independence group Tusgaar Buryad-Mongolia “are doing the right thing” in comments to The Moscow Times.
- The former head of Dagestan Sergei Melikov was appointed as a senator from the western Bryansk region in Russia’s upper-house Federation Council last week.
Melikov, who had headed Dagestan since 2020, resigned from the post in May following public backlash over his handling of deadly floods in the mountainous republic.
The Spotlight
“There are no conversations on the streets, no bustle, no fear, no lines at the pharmacies like there were during Covid,” a woman from Irkutsk, the capital of the Siberian region of the same name, tells The Moscow Times.
“There was panic for maybe the first few hours after the news broke. Then memes began to appear online and everyone calmed down,” she adds. “There are so many things going on at once: the fuel crises, the bear invasion, now the plague. People here treat these things as background noise.”
Irkutsk, a region roughly the size of Turkey with a population of 2.3 million people, made international headlines after a 28-year-old employee of a local plague research institute died at a hospital in the Irkutsk suburb of Shelekhov last week.
The highly urbanized industrial region was until now best known for the UNESCO-enscribed Lake Baikal, the world’s largest freshwater lake by volume — that is, before the latest global plague-induced scare.
But for most locals, who say they found out about the possible plague case from social media, little has changed.
“Life goes on as usual in Irkutsk,” another local told The Moscow Times on Wednesday. “Today I met a doctor on the street and asked them about the outbreak. She said that there was one case, but now everything is calm.”
News that the lab worker, Daria Shipilova, may have died from plague first surfaced in since-deleted posts on local anonymous Telegram channels in the early hours of Oct. 2, local independent news outlet Irkutsk Blog reported.
A handful of news outlets soon picked up the rumor and added more unverified details.
The exiled news outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) cited an anonymous source who said the victim was hospitalized after arriving from Thailand, while local TV channel NTS was the first to speculate that the woman got infected after accidentally breaking a test tube containing live bacteria.
Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev confirmed that the head of state health and safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had arrived in the region because of “a suspected case of a highly dangerous infection.”
“All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, the contacts show no signs of illness and laboratory test results are negative,” Kobzev said on Oct. 2.
Rospotrebnadzor also avoided the word “plague” in its first statement on the matter published Sunday, saying Shipilova died from a “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
The first — and only — Russian official to use the word “plague” was Alexei Tsydenov, the head of the republic of Buryatia, which borders the Irkutsk region to the east and south.
“The woman who died — possibly from the plague — in the Irkutsk region had not traveled to Buryatia. There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in the area bordering Mongolia,” Tsydenov said.
Vadim Palko, a journalist at Irkutsk Blog, said he believes that Tsydenov’s statement was more of a calculated attempt to distance himself from unwelcome news that likely upset the Kremlin than a heartfelt urge to reveal the truth to the public.
“He tried, first of all, to protect himself by signaling that all the problems are coming from Irkutsk,” Palko said, adding that Tsydenov’s reaction was likely prompted by rumors that the lab worker allegedly traveled to a “plague hotspot in Buryatia.”
The atmosphere in Buryatia, meanwhile, has been largely similar to that in Irkutsk.
“I found out about the plague from Instagram, from friends who sent me funny reels about it,” said a resident of Buryatia’s capital Ulan-Ude.
“I haven’t been taking any precautionary measures…But now that you have asked, I am thinking maybe I should have? But, actually, what should be done in case of a plague outbreak?” she told The Moscow Times.
This lack of “effective and trusted communication” with the public could prove Moscow’s biggest misstep in handling the plague scare, said Judyth Twigg, a professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University and an expert on Russia’s health system.
The World Health Organization recorded 3,847 suspected human plague cases and 423 deaths across 10 countries between 2019 and 2025. The majority were recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar, but some were also reported in the rural parts of the western United States.
“Residents [of the Irkutsk region] should have received practical guidance…with regular updates, even when the update is that there are no new cases,” Twigg told The Moscow Times.
“It’s what health authorities elsewhere do with plague cases as a matter of routine course, and none of it would have required Russia to concede anything embarrassing beyond the possibility of a laboratory accident,” she added.
Twigg said the measures Russia has reportedly taken appeared operationally sound, including the rapid identification and observation of contacts, isolation measures, precautions scaled to a dangerous pathogen and on-site oversight by specialists.
Today, plague “is not a plausible mass threat to any society with a functioning public health system,” she said, a take echoed by other health science professionals.
“Even though the plague pathogen Yersinia pestis is dangerous and actually causes a very severe and tricky disease, events of the past are not expected to repeat today,” said science journalist Irina Yakutenko, referencing the 14th-century plague pandemic known as the Black Death.
“Beyond the pathogen itself, certain conditions are needed for it to spread: people, rats and fleas who are all constantly in contact with each other,” added Yakutenko.
Rospotrebnadzor announced Wednesday that it has concluded a series of “preventive and anti-epidemic measures” in the Irkutsk region, which reportedly included medical observations of more than 90% of contacts and 5,000 laboratory tests that failed to reveal any dangerous pathogens.
“There are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region,” the health watchdog said.
Meanwhile, the lack of transparency surrounding the incident has already fueled conspiracies that the Irkutsk plague research lab could be part of a state-sponsored bioweapons program.
“Russia's history…provides plenty of reason to ask hard questions. In this case, though, there’s nothing in the public record supporting the conclusion that this civilian surveillance institute was doing something exotic,” Twigg said.
“Transparency would be Moscow's cheapest and most effective rebuttal, but the system isn’t designed to supply transparency.”
Photo of the Week
Residents of Oshurkovo, a village on the left bank of the Selenga River in the republic of Buryatia, put up scarecrows to protest the planned opening of a controversial apatite ore mining site.
“Even the pumpkin knows that apatites equal the death of Baikal. Do you?” says the banner attached to the scarecrow.
State environmental watchdog Rosprirodnadzor greenlit the Russian Copper Company’s mining project earlier this year despite residents and scientists voicing concerns about the threat it poses to Lake Baikal, which is fed by the Selenga.

- “Russia’s Self-Imposed Isolation Reaches a New Frontier: Medicine” by Tatyana Rybakova
- “As Russia’s Permafrost Thaws, Ancient Pathogens Risk Re-Awakening” by Lana Koralova

COP31 organisers aim to break negotiating deadlock with bold climate blueprint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:58:58 UTC
19:58:58 KST

COP31 organisers aim to break negotiating deadlock with bold climate blueprint
- - COP31 organisers in Turkey and Australia plan a presidency-led decision to break logjams and push for a stronger climate action statement.
- - Pacific leaders used the Fiji and Tuvalu pre-COP31 to demand more climate finance, ocean protection and faster action on fossil fuels, as their region faces rising seas and coral loss.
- - Officials and activists warned that Pacific island nations are highly exposed, with Tuvalu facing possible relocation of its population.
AI generated
NADI, Fiji – Organisers of an upcoming UN climate summit in Turkey said on Oct 8 they would prepare a summary text for countries to adopt, as they lead a push for “ambitious” action on keeping the goal of global temperature rise of 1.5 deg C within reach.
The United Nations-sponsored global climate summit – known as COP31 – will be held in Antalya in November, following a “pre-COP” meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu, which wrapped up on Oct 8.
Co-organisers Australia and Turkey vowed on Oct 8 to get negotiators to vote on a so-called presidency-led decision that they would have prepared beforehand.
That would, in theory at least, set a firm and realistic agenda, cutting the endless hours of gruelling negotiations that often dominate COP meetings before votes are taken on individual technical points.
That decision, they said, would focus on binding agreements like one towards electrification, replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels directly, like diesel cars and gas heating, with electric alternatives.
“We feel that a presidency-led decision gives us the best chance of a strong and ambitious outcome at COP31,” Australia’s Climate Minister Chris Bowen said.
“To send the signal to follow the science to keep 1.5 degrees within reach, against the backdrop of the scientific evidence that we will overshoot it. We’ve got to overshoot it for as little and as short as possible,” he said.
Scientists agree that warming above 1.5 deg C relative to pre-industrial times poses grave risks, and nearly 200 nations committed a decade ago to try and keep global temperature rises to this safer threshold.
But with rising sea levels already lapping the coastlines of Pacific nations and the corals that sustain them dying, more firm action on ending the use of polluting fossil fuels is needed.
“The outcomes of this week’s talks are a drop in the ocean given the scale of need, and urgency of the crisis our communities are facing,” Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific, said.
“It is like taking a glass of water to a burning house if we do not urgently act to address the root cause of the existential threat facing Tuvalu, Fiji and all Pacific countries: fossil fuel expansion,” she said.
Vulnerable
Pacific nations used the pre-COP platform to push for more backing.
The South Pacific is among the regions of the world most vulnerable to global warming, from rising seas jeopardising homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.
In a push to highlight the urgent need for action, leaders this week visited Tuvalu, a remote island nation already laying plans to relocate its population of 10,600 if the island nation is consumed by the ocean.
And the region’s leaders pushed throughout the summit this week for oceans and climate finance to be top of the agenda at COP31, as well as maintaining the 1.5 deg C target.
But regional delegates admitted the process is tiring.
“The way that the COP process works is not great, I’ll be very frank,” Pacific climate envoy Tina Eonemto said.
But she said Pacific nations have put their hopes “front and centre” and welcomed plans for a presidency-led decision at the end of COP31.
At a time of rising military budgets in the face of mounting geopolitical tensions, COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey’s environment minister, urged nations to take the climate crisis as seriously as they did defence.
“Tuvalu is disappearing. What good does it do if we take this decision? What good is defending your borders if there is no livable world left?“ Kurum said.
Sea levels are rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to an August UN report.
Up to 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050, with Pacific island countries experiencing sea level rise at twice the global average, it said.
One Pacific delegate said he hopes that voices from the region will be “treated equally and fairly and with all respect” in Antalya.
“That’s the bottom line,” he said. “We have a right to life, and life is a human right.” AFP

Microsoft is bringing more AI to PCs, challenging Apple
Kyiv • UNN
Microsoft introduced a local AI model and Microsoft Execution Containers for the secure operation of agents on PCs. The Surface Ultra will cost from $2,599.
On October 7, Microsoft unveiled an artificial intelligence–based coding model that can run directly on personal computers, as well as a new security technology that prevents AI agents from accessing data without permission. This challenges Apple’s efforts to bring more artificial intelligence to personal devices. UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The software company also unveiled a powerful Surface laptop called Ultra at an event in San Francisco, powered by Nvidia RTX Spark chips. Microsoft is seeking to turn Windows into a platform for AI agents to perform tasks such as writing computer code or carrying out complex business projects on desktop computers and laptops, the publication writes.
For Microsoft, the move is a bet that some of the work currently performed in expensive Azure cloud-computing data centers can be shifted to powerful Windows machines in companies and homes—a market where the company maintains its position and where its customers pay the hardware bills. This, it said, is a market opportunity that rival Apple is also pursuing with its new Mac computers.
For Nvidia, entering the Windows PC market could help it break into one of the last major markets dominated by Intel and Advanced Micro Devices.
As protection against increasingly autonomous AI agents that pose security risks, Microsoft announced the release of Microsoft Execution Containers—an tool that prevents agents from accessing data and performing unauthorized tasks while operating on a laptop or desktop computer. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nvidia will use these tools, said Pavan Davuluri, executive vice president of Windows and Devices.
"We needed to make the desktop the safest place for agents to operate," said Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.
Davuluri said the new tools would allow IT departments to set rules for agents, while the Windows operating system would ensure those rules were enforced on each employee’s computer.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who joined Nadella onstage, said Microsoft’s new execution-container technology, abbreviated as MXC, "will revolutionize how agents are built and deployed."
"Without it, (agents) are a complete failure," he said.
Nvidia is trying to prevent a repeat of the hacking of the Hugging Face artificial intelligence center, while Apple is seeking to streamline the process of giving artificial intelligence agents full access to a Mac computer’s hard drive.
AI is "moving" to PCs
Microsoft also unveiled artificial intelligence models that previously required access to the cloud but can now run locally on powerful Windows desktops and laptops, including Nvidia’s open-source Nemotron model. Davuluri said that version V4 of the model from Chinese artificial intelligence company DeepSeek can run on machines with at least 60 gigabytes of memory and outperform OpenAI’s GPT-5 in some coding and reasoning tasks.
Microsoft is taking a similar approach with its own artificial intelligence assistant, Copilot, dividing tasks between the cloud and individual laptops. "Copilot will still use the cloud for the most complex tasks, but in cases where cost or privacy matter more, it can delegate them to local models running directly on your computer," said Microsoft’s head of Copilot, Jacob Andreu.
Davuluri also said that Meta’s personal AI assistant, Muse, will appear on Windows devices as a native app, using some of Microsoft’s new security tools, and that OpenClaw, an open-source artificial intelligence agent system, can also work with these security tools.
The price question
One of the key problems facing Microsoft and Nvidia is the high prices of these devices after the memory-chip crisis drove them up.
The new Surface Laptop Ultra will cost from $2,599 and rise to $5,899 for a model with a 20-core processor, 128 gigabytes of memory and one terabyte of storage.
An Apple MacBook Pro with a 40-core graphics chip, 128 GB of memory and 2 TB of storage costs $6,700, although these machines cannot be directly compared. Microsoft's base Ultra costs more than Apple's base MacBook Pro, priced at $1,999, but comes with 24 GB of memory compared with 16 GB in Apple's base model.
When Microsoft first proposed the idea of running AI tasks on PCs two years ago to save costs, laptops mostly cost less than $2,000, but Nvidia has increased the price of an AI desktop computer called the DGX Spark by about 75% since its launch, to $6,950, due to rising memory costs.
Two years ago, "the software wasn't ready, but the hardware was. Now the software is ready, and the hardware is too expensive to run it locally," said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. "So it is becoming a situation where only people who have the budget can afford to run AI locally," he noted.

What did South Korea's Foreign Ministry say about recalling its ambassador?

"The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and wil continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end," it said.
Last week, President Lee Jae Myung called for a "public apology" from Kyiv and said South Korea would take "additional measures" if one was not forthcoming. He said that during the prisoner swap, "the Ukrainian side demanded confidentiality and agreed to it, but unilaterally disclosed it."

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, meanwhile, had spoken of a "diplomatic misunderstanding" that he said "we sincerely hope to resolve."

North Korea, meanwhile, sent troops to help Russia reclaim the border region of Kursk that Ukraine was able to partially occupy, and has since celebrated this deployment at home with much fanfare, while seeking closer ties to Putin's Russia.

Italy's Meloni secures final approval for contested electoral reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:54:45 UTC
19:54:45 KST

Italy's Meloni forces through new electoral law ahead of vote, opposition cries foul
ROME, Oct 8 - Italy's lower house of parliament gave final approval on Thursday to a fiercely contested electoral reform championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni which provides the framework for a national election due next year.
Meloni says the new rules are intended to increase the prospect of stable government. The centre-left opposition says the goal is to boost her chances of retaining power.
In a secret ballot, lawmakers approved by 227 votes to 164 a bill introducing a fully proportional electoral system (PR), with a seat bonus guaranteeing a parliamentary majority to any alliance winning more than 42% of the vote.
Under the previous rules, around two-thirds of lawmakers were elected through PR, with the remainder chosen in first-past-the-post constituencies which analysts said may have favoured the opposition.
'WHOEVER WINS MUST BE ABLE TO GOVERN'
"We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary cohesion of any government," Meloni posted on X after the vote. "Whoever wins must be able to govern."
When the reform was conceived, her rightist bloc led in opinion polls and critics said the changes were intended to hand her a handsome majority after the election.
However, the political landscape has changed since the emergence in February of a new far-right party, National Future, which has eroded support for the ruling parties.
Polls now show the coalition trailing the centre-left and some analysts say the electoral reform may backfire on Meloni, whose government last month celebrated almost four years in power, making it Italy's longest-lasting since World War Two.
In a heated debate, centre-left lawmakers accused the government of flouting democracy by forcing through the new rules ahead of an election, against the will of the opposition.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.
One element in the reform obliges each coalition or party running outside a coalition to name its candidate for prime minister before the election.
This puts the centre-left in a bind because the leaders of its two main parties, the PD and the 5-Star Movement, led by former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte, are at loggerheads over who should become prime minister if the alliance wins.
COALITION TENSIONS
Final approval of the reform required four parliamentary votes and capped months of coalition infighting that cast doubt on Meloni's grip on her alliance ahead of next year's election.
The tensions centred on an element of the reform allowing voters to choose their preferred candidates among party lists, reducing the power of the leaders to control which ones are elected.
A compromise was eventually found by which candidates at the top of the lists are automatically given preference, leaving intact the power of the party chiefs to determine most of the candidates who get into parliament.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided, today we responded with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens," Meloni said. REUTERS

Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:53:48 UTC
19:53:48 KST

Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
India was the world’s second-largest arms importer in 2025, partly aided by a historically large naval buildout, according to a Russian think tank that tracks weapons purchases and military expenditures.
The South Asian nuclear power has been rapidly building up its armed forces following a brief clash with neighbor Pakistan last year, triggered by a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir.
India’s identified military imports were worth $6.97 billion, or 5.83% of the global total, and the country is projected to retain the position through 2029, the Moscow-based Center for Analysis of World Arms Trade (CAWAT) said.
Poland came in first with $11.91 billion, while Australia was narrowly behind India at $6.96 billion.
Among the major Indian deliveries cited by CAWAT was the Russian-built frigate Tamal, which joined the Indian Navy in July 2025. Two more Project 11356 frigates are being built at India’s Goa Shipyard with assistance from Russian state arms exporter Rosoboronexport. 
India also commissioned the Vaghsheer, the sixth and final Kalvari-class submarine built by state-owned Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders under license from France’s Naval Group. The six-submarine program was valued at $3.6 billion, according to CAWAT.
The Indian Navy is undergoing its largest expansion in history, with plans to induct or commission 18 warships this year. 
New Delhi imported $25.44 billion worth of arms in the 2022-2025 period, placing it third behind Saudi Arabia and Qatar in CAWAT’s four-year rankings. Its annual imports rose from $3.87 billion in 2024 to $6.97 billion last year. 
The think tank projects India’s arms imports at $45.65 billion over 2026-2029, keeping the country in the second position. Poland is expected to remain at the top with $55.32 billion worth of imports, followed by Germany at $36.48 billion. The forecast is based on existing contracts, officially announced procurement plans, and expected tenders as of December 2025. 
Poland’s rise has been particularly sharp. Its arms imports climbed from $2.17 billion in 2022 to $11.91 billion in 2025, driven by major purchases including US-made Abrams tanks and South Korean K2 tanks.
CAWAT projects global arms imports at almost $633 billion over the 2026-2029 period, up 52.5% from in the preceding four years. The center expects Europe to take a larger share of global demand during the period.
The ranking covers identified commercial arms deliveries and does not include weapons supplied free of charge, including Western military aid to Ukraine.
CAWAT’s methodology differs from that of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), which measures the volume of major weapons transfers using a trend-indicator value rather than their sale price. SIPRI says its figures should not be directly compared with the financial value of arms transfers.

====================================================================================================

Portuguese hospital lets pets visit owners on wards: a new model?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:53:08 UTC
19:53:08 KST

In northern and central Europe, pets stay outside hospitals. At São João, a flexible model combines benefits and safety; no infections yet. "Fear is overblown," says the doctor behind the project.
Since 9 July, São João, one of Portugal's leading public university hospitals, has been opening its ward doors to visits from pets.
The "Pets and Company" project brings together professionals from the One Health São João (source in Portuguese) programme, as well as from the Infection Prevention and Control and Antimicrobial Resistance Unit and the hospital's Humanisation Service. The initiative is part of a wider strategy designed to break isolation and ease the exhaustion caused by long hospital stays.
The therapeutic potential of animals is far from a recent discovery. Countries such as the United Kingdom and Germany have been using them in psychiatric and physical rehabilitation treatments for humans since the 19th century. The term "pet therapy" (animal-assisted therapy) was introduced into the scientific literature in the 1960s by a US psychologist who stumbled upon the healing benefits of these interventions.
In Portugal, trained and certified dogs providing emotional-support sessions have been working for years in hospitals, including São João, in partnership with handlers from associations.
On 30 May 2023, a 77-year-old patient admitted to Cascais Hospital while recovering from a haemorrhagic stroke received a visit from her own dog, in a reunion that took place in an outdoor area of the health unit.
This unprecedented experience is now being scaled up at São João through a comprehensive protocol drawn up from scratch, which goes a step further and normalises the practice of bringing pets into inpatient areas, recognising them as part of the patient's immediate family and offering those who have been away from home for a long time moments of comfort under safe sanitary conditions.
What does the protocol say?
Visits are requested by the health professional, doctor or nurse, who is following the patient and is responsible for flagging up cases, and they are not available to everyone who is in hospital. A case-by-case assessment of risks and benefits is always carried out.
Once informed, the team in charge of the programme assesses whether there is a clinical need and whether infection-control conditions are met in the area chosen for the visit. Other patients are also asked if they are comfortable with the presence of animals.
Once approval is given, the patient's family must provide a veterinary medical certificate proving that the animal's vaccinations and deworming are up to date and that it has behaviour compatible with the demands associated with remaining in hospital facilities.
"Any member of staff, from security guards to doctors or nurses, who sees that something is not in line with the protocol can stop the visit," Filipa Ceia, spokesperson for the One Health São João Group, tells Euronews.
If the animal is "anxious" because of the "noise on the ward", if it appears "aggressive" or "visibly dirty", the visit is "immediately aborted", the infectious-disease specialist and veterinarian warns.
Dogs, cats and even "more exotic species" are allowed, as long as "all the conditions are met", says Filipa Ceia. While it is on hospital premises, the animal must be accompanied by an adult.
Each patient can enjoy these half-hour encounters once every seven days. The project prioritises those who are terminally ill or undergoing long periods of hospitalisation.
To the team's surprise, it is male patients who have most frequently asked to have their pets with them in hospital, although the small sample size does not allow firm conclusions to be drawn. "The fragility in sick men is probably greater. They realise that there are things that matter a great deal in life and they want to have them nearby during their hospital stay," says Ceia.
Benefits for the patient and the animal
Studies on interventions involving trained animals show clear improvements in patients' clinical condition: blood pressure drops and the production of hormones linked to stress and anxiety is inhibited. When the patient's own pet is involved, there is "an even greater benefit", stresses Filipa Ceia.
Euronews followed the visit by Princesa, who went to São João for the second time in 15 days to see her owner, António, who has been in hospital for three months. The dog was brought to the hospital by the patient's wife, who led her on a lead to the ward.
As soon as the lift doors opened, Princesa could not contain her excitement, and the same happened with António.
"My heart was beating with joy. She is like family. She is a daughter to me," confessed the 65-year-old man, who is in rehabilitation because of problems with balance and walking.
His diagnosis has not yet been confirmed, but doctors suspect he suffers from a rare blood disease. The reunion with the dog, who was given to him five years ago after being rescued from the streets, is a balm for the soul.
"It even makes me want to walk better and everything. This is the joy a person gets," he said. These reunions bring "smiles, cooperation with treatment and an incentive to leave hospital", notes Filipa Ceia, who also identifies benefits for the animal itself and even for health professionals.
"Residual" risk
The initiative was launched at the beginning of July and, so far, there have been no recorded infections.
The team behind the project wants to review the protocol at a later stage to correct any shortcomings. Given the procedures in place, a scenario involving "incidents" is, however, "highly unlikely", underlines Filipa Ceia.
In northern and central Europe, infection-control and public-health regulations are stricter. Priority is given to interventions by assistance dogs, and visits from patients' own animals, when they are authorised, usually for those in palliative care, take place in isolated facilities, such as open courtyards or gardens attached to the main building.
Take the example of Sint-Trudo Hospital in Sint-Truiden, Belgium. In July 2023, this health unit opened an independent pavilion (source in Portuguese), connected to but separate from the main building, so that terminally ill patients or those with long hospital stays could interact with their pets. The access (source in Portuguese) for the animals is from outside, via a courtyard, and they are strictly forbidden, in any circumstances, from passing through the interior of the hospital.
Instead of putting up physical barriers by building secondary structures, São João has drawn up a set of rules that, while maintaining clinical rigour, are built into a flexible protocol shaped by scientific evidence.
"There is an excessive fear of zoonotic transmission that is not borne out by studies," says Filipa Ceia. In fact, the infectious-disease doctor notes, "most diseases are more easily transmitted from human to human than from an animal to a human."
"Since we do everything possible to keep safety intact, and since the patient will live with their animal once they go home, the risk really is residual. We need to understand whether, in trying to mitigate risk, we are not depriving patients of the benefit," she adds.
São João's boldness lies not only in the balance between empathy and sanitary control, but also in its autonomy and capacity to humanise care without waiting for lawmakers, unlike in Italy, for example, where progress has been driven by decrees from regional governments.

Survey: 62% of Ukrainians believe neither side is currently winning war
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:53:00 EEST
19:53:00 KST

Survey: 62% of Ukrainians believe neither side is currently winning war
A majority of Ukrainians (62%) believe that neither Ukraine nor Russia is currently winning the war, while 26% say Ukraine has the upper hand and 6% say Russia does.
Source: the results of a survey conducted by Rating Group on 3-5 October 2026
Quote: "An absolute majority believes that currently neither Ukraine nor Russia is winning the war (62%). A quarter speak of Ukraine's advantage (26%), and 6% of Russia's."
Details: The survey also found that 57% of respondents support a cessation of hostilities and seeking a compromise through negotiations. Meanwhile, 13% favour continuing the fighting until the lines of control as of 23 February 2022 are restored. Another 21% support continuing the fighting until the territories of Donbas and Crimea are liberated.
A total of 57% of respondents see seeking a compromise with the involvement of other countries in the negotiations as a realistic way to end the war, while another 26% favour direct negotiations.
Some 35% of respondents oppose territorial concessions in exchange for long-term peace. Meanwhile, 56% would accept such concessions if they were accompanied by security guarantees from the US and European partners, including funding for Ukrainian forces and weapons. Another 3% would accept concessions without any preconditions, while 6% were undecided.
If territorial concessions become a condition for peace, 68% of respondents believe the final decision should be made by the people in a nationwide referendum. Some 17% believe it should be made by the president, while 9% say the Verkhovna Rada (parliament) should decide.
For reference: The survey was conducted on 3-5 October 2026 using computer-assisted telephone interviews (CATI) among 1,000 Ukrainians aged 18 and over.
Respondents were selected through a random sample of mobile phone numbers in all oblasts except for temporarily occupied territories and areas without Ukrainian mobile coverage at the time of the poll.
The results were weighted using current data from the State Statistics Service. The sample is representative by age, gender and type of settlement. The margin of error does not exceed 3.1 percentage points with a 95% confidence level.
Background: A survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology showed that 62% of Ukrainians, like the majority of Kyiv residents, are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, whereas 23% are ready to continue fighting for only a few months or up to six months.

Ryanair CEO sees no European jet fuel shortages into summer 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:52:58 UTC
19:52:58 KST

Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary expects Europe to have enough jet fuel through next summer, but warns that high prices will persist for another 12 to 18 months.
Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said on Thursday that he did not expect jet fuel shortages in Europe this winter or into summer 2027, even as the Iran war disrupts supply chains.
"There is no question, I think, over availability of jet fuel in Europe this winter, or frankly into next summer either, unless there's some unforeseen event," O’Leary said at a press conference organised by Airlines for Europe (A4E) in Brussels.
His comments offer reassurance on supplies, but airlines and passengers still face persistently high fuel costs.
Euronews Business previously reported that lower seasonal demand from November and increased imports from Asia were expected to keep Europe supplied in the coming months. According to Kpler, nearly 900,000 tonnes of jet fuel from Asia were scheduled to arrive over that period.
Those shipments could help prevent shortages, but are unlikely to bring much relief on prices.
“Jet fuel will likely be subject to higher prices, especially as it is deeply linked to the diesel market, which is becoming even tighter and experiencing record prices recently,” George Shaw, Kpler’s senior insight analyst for distillate markets, told Euronews on 23 September.
The European Commission also said on 8 September that increased EU refinery output and alternative imports were meeting European demand for jet fuel, although further disruption in the Middle East could tighten supplies.
Separately, the G7 agreed last Friday to speed up the release of 100 million barrels from strategic reserves to ease pressure on energy markets. On Wednesday, the International Energy Agency clarified that these barrels were part of the emergency stock release agreed in March.
Its members supported accelerating the remaining releases and prioritising diesel because of tight supplies, although the announcement did not specify a release of jet fuel.
Jet fuel prices double
Jet fuel prices have risen faster than crude prices since the war began, as attacks on refineries have disrupted production and widened the gap between the cost of crude and the price of the finished fuel.
According to the International Air Transport Association’s latest fuel price monitor, Europe and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), which includes several former Soviet republics, had the highest average jet fuel price of any region.
Prices averaged $195.95 a barrel in the week ending 2 October, more than double their level a year earlier. Although they fell 1% that week, the global jet fuel premium over crude remained roughly three times its year-earlier level.
"Historically, jet fuel was about somewhere between 10 per cent and 15 per cent more expensive than Brent crude. It's currently running at about 50 per cent more expensive," O’Leary said.
He expected that premium to persist for another 12 to 18 months, citing attacks on Russian and Middle Eastern refineries, along with constraints on tanker availability and refining capacity.
Ryanair said last month that it would reduce its winter flight schedule to limit its exposure to higher fuel costs, cutting its full-year passenger target to 214 million from 216 million.

Lower House gives final approval to new election law
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:52:44 CEST
19:52:44 KST

The Lower House on Thursday gave
final approval to a bill presented by the parties of Premier
Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition for a new election law, giving
it the green light with 227 votes in favour and 164 against.
                                    
The ruling alliance says the new system will make it more likely
that elections produce a clear winner.
                                    
But opposition politicians held up signs calling it a "scam law"
and a "con", when the result of the vote, a secret ballot, was
announced.
                                    
The opposition say the ruling alliance has changed the system
because it fears losing the general election set to take place
next year and wants to minimize the chances of this happening.
                                    
Under the law the old system, a mix of first-past-the-post and
proportional representation, has been replaced with a
proportional-representation system with bonus seats for the
coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches a
threshold of 42%, to ensure it has a working majority in
parliament.
                                    
If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the
Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely
proportional system is used.
                                    
The opposition have said that, among other things, the system of
bonus seats is unconstitutional and are ready to appeal to the
Constitutional Court.
                                    
Coalitions will have to say who their candidate to be premier is
before the election.
                                    
The opposition said this is the government's way to bring in a
reform that it promised by has not delivered so far, the direct
election of the prime minister, by the back door.
                                    
The bill will also give voters the option to express preferences
for up to three candidates out of six on a party list in which
candidates names must alternate according to gender.
                                    
The opposition says that in reality this gives "fake
preferences" as the head of the ticket would always be
"blocked", arguing this was also be a step back for equality,
as, in theory, it would be possible for all the ticket heads to
be men.
                                    
The current system does not give voters any option to express
preferences about which of the candidates on a party list they
want to represent them.
