Denmark’s cyber hotline will remain open until midnight in the coming days following unauthorized access to 8.8 million records in the national CPR system.
The hotline will operate from 8 a.m. to midnight. It normally closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays, the Agency for Societal Security said.
The hotline advises residents and businesses on digital security, fraud and cyberattacks. It can also help people whose identities have been misused.
Residents with a specific suspicion that their CPR number is being used fraudulently can receive help creating a credit warning.
A credit warning alerts companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving loans or credit, making financial identity theft more difficult.
Authorities detected irregular activity in the CPR system on October 2.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information during September.
The records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority, said automated searches appeared intended to identify valid CPR numbers.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating. Authorities have not identified those responsible.
Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates urged residents to remain vigilant.
Authorities advised people never to provide passwords or other confidential information to unsolicited callers or message senders.
Denmark says it is too early to decide whether breach victims need new CPR numbers
Denmark has not decided whether people affected by unauthorized access to 8.8 million personal records will need new CPR numbers, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said.
Egelund spoke after briefing two Folketing committees about the breach of Denmark’s national personal information register.
“I have requested a security review of the entire CPR system,” Egelund of the Moderates said.
She said the findings would determine what changes were needed to restore trust and security. No deadline has been set for the review.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information.
The affected records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
The CPR register can also contain details about marital status, births, family relationships, citizenship, Church of Denmark membership and guardianship.
Egelund said authorities were focused on preventing the stolen information from being used for identity theft, phishing and other digital fraud.
A website and telephone hotline have been established to advise residents about protecting themselves.
The breach has been reported to Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating.
Authorities have not identified who was responsible. Egelund said investigators had not ruled out any possibilities, including international involvement.
Copenhagen apartment listings exceed 2,000 as housing market begins to slow
More than 2,000 owner-occupied apartments are for sale in Copenhagen for the first time since early 2024, according to housing website Boligsiden.
At the beginning of October, 2,057 apartments were listed in Copenhagen Municipality.
That was more than five percent higher than one month earlier and almost twice the number available one year ago.
The increase gives buyers more choice and could reduce competition for individual apartments, said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Sellers must now compete with more properties for buyers’ attention, she added.
Daetz said the changing balance had also led to larger price reductions on Copenhagen apartments.
Every district recorded an increase in listings over the past year.
Copenhagen S, which includes parts of Amager, had 530 apartments for sale at the beginning of October. That was an increase of more than 150 percent from one year earlier.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, said the figures showed that Copenhagen’s housing market was losing speed.
He pointed to slowing sales activity and smaller monthly price increases.
Across Denmark, the number of apartments for sale increased 6.3 percent over the past year.
However, listings of detached homes and terraced houses moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.9 percent nationwide.
German spy chief warns Russia is waging a ‘shadow war’
The head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has warned that Russia is intensifying what he described as a “shadow war” against the country, saying Germany risks being drawn into a violent conflict.
“No other country poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany,” Martin Jäger said during a public hearing in the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, according to AFP.
The hearing took place before the parliamentary committee responsible for overseeing Germany’s intelligence services.
Jäger pointed to a case in August in which a drone carrying an explosive charge was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig. Agents with Russian connections are suspected of being behind the incident.
Germany has repeatedly accused Russia of conducting hybrid operations involving sabotage, espionage and other attempts to disrupt public order. Moscow has rejected such accusations.
Jäger said Russian intelligence services were acting “highly professionally and ruthlessly.”
“Russia is waging a shadow war against us. This undeclared war does not fit into traditional military and legal categories,” he said, according to German broadcaster Tagesschau.
“We must prepare ourselves for further attempts to intimidate us and more interference,” he added.
Germany is one of Ukraine’s largest supporters in its war against Russia.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv on Sunday alongside senior executives from several German defense companies.
Merz, who last week also warned about continued Russian hybrid warfare, announced an additional 1 billion euros, around 7.5 billion DKK, in military support for Ukraine during the visit.
More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.
The 2026 Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands to represent friendship
This year’s Danish Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands in a design focused on friendship and community.
Christmas Seal Foundation board chair Anne Glad Wagner and artist Martin Jørgensen unveiled the seal Monday at Copenhagen City Hall.
The design is titled “The best gifts cannot be wrapped.”
Jørgensen said the children represent the supportive community that young people experience during stays at Denmark’s Christmas seal homes.
“It is about helping children, and therefore I have made them the main characters,” he said. “The Christmas seal homes help children form bonds and believe in themselves.”
Jørgensen has a background in advertising. The foundation selected him because of a graphic style that combines warmth, humor and small visual surprises.
Christmas seals are special decorative stamps sold before Christmas to raise money for the five Christmas seal homes in Denmark.
The homes support as many as 1,000 children annually who experience problems including bullying, loneliness, low self-esteem and poor well-being.
Seal sales cover about five percent of the homes’ operating expenses. Private individuals, companies and foundations provide almost all other funding.
The Christmas Seal Foundation, a Danish charity that operates the homes, has had Queen Mary as its patron since 2004.
Denmark’s Christmas seals were first issued in 1904. This year’s design is the 123rd edition. Copenhagen postmaster Einar Holbøll originally proposed the idea.
Denmark faces mild start to week before cooler and wetter autumn weather arrives
Denmark will begin the week with mild temperatures before rain, showers and cooler conditions arrive from Wednesday, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, the national weather service.
“We will have a mild start to the week with many clouds and locally a little rain from time to time,” meteorologist Anne Borrits said.
A low-pressure system approaching from the southwest will bring more typical autumn weather during the second half of the week.
Monday will begin with some sunshine in eastern Denmark, while most other areas will remain cloudy.
Light rain is possible in Jutland, and temperatures will reach between 15 and 19 degrees Celsius. The highest temperatures are expected locally on Funen or Zealand.
Winds will be moderate to strong from the southwest. Coastal areas near the Skagerrak could experience gales Monday afternoon.
Skies will clear overnight into Tuesday, bringing dry conditions. Temperatures could fall to eight degrees in some areas, though most places will remain between 12 and 15 degrees.
Tuesday will be dry with periods of sunshine.
A low-pressure system will approach from the North Sea during Tuesday evening and Wednesday, bringing rain and later showers.
Conditions remain uncertain through Friday. Temperatures are expected to fall gradually, reaching between 10 and 15 degrees Thursday and Friday.
Strong winds are also possible along some coastal areas.
Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.
Elk dies after collision with car on motorway north of Copenhagen
An elk died after being struck by a car on the Helsingør Motorway near Nivå on Monday morning, North Zealand Police said.
A 36-year-old woman was driving north in the inside lane when the animal suddenly appeared a few meters ahead of her, according to her statement to police.
The collision occurred at 6:10 a.m. between the Kokkedal and Humlebæk exits.
The woman was apparently uninjured. The car’s windshield and rear window were shattered, while its roof and hood were damaged.
The elk was found dead about 100 meters from the vehicle.
Denmark has no naturally occurring wild elk population. However, Swedish elk were introduced to Lille Vildmose in Himmerland beginning in 2015. That population had grown to about 20 animals by 2020.
Authorities also plan to release elk into Gribskov National Nature Park in North Zealand this year.
Wild elk are occasionally seen elsewhere in Denmark. The animals can swim across the Øresund between Sweden and Zealand.
In mid-September, a farm owner near Hundested reported that a roaming elk had damaged a fence before disappearing toward Ullerup Forest.
Morten Elmeros, a senior adviser at Aarhus University’s Department of Ecoscience, previously said that animal had probably swum from Sweden.
Such crossings occur about once every 10 years, he said.
Electric bicycle injuries reach six-year high as imports approach 100,000 in Denmark
Electric bicycle injuries in Denmark reached their highest level in six years as imports of the vehicles continued to rise.
In 2025, 200 electric bicycle riders were injured in traffic, including 133 who were seriously injured. Eleven riders died, according to Danish Road Directorate figures analyzed by insurance company Alm. Brand.
Electric bicycles can reach higher speeds and usually weigh more than standard bicycles, potentially making injuries more serious, said Mathias Kjær Sigvaldason, Alm. Brand’s accident insurance director.
Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.
Imports of standard bicycles fell from slightly more than 500,000 in 2017 to about 350,000 in 2025. Electric models now represent more than one in four imported bicycles.
The figures cover imports, not consumer sales, for which no combined national data are available.
The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Trump voters are not pumped about voting in the midterms, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:04:56 UTC
19:04:56 KST

Trump voters not pumped about voting in the November midterms, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
- - Reuters/Ipsos found Harris voters are far more eager to vote in November than Trump voters, raising a turnout warning for Republicans.
- - Trump’s approval has fallen to 32%, with losses among men, Hispanics, rural voters and other key groups.
- - Cost of living is the top issue, and many enthusiastic voters are driven by opposition to Trump rather than support for him.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Voters who backed Democratic former vice-president Kamala Harris in 2024 are far more enthusiastic about casting ballots this November than those who supported President Donald Trump, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found, in a potential warning sign for Republicans heading into the midterm elections.
The six-day poll, completed on Oct 5, also found that men were more enthusiastic about voting and more certain to cast ballots than women, and that male voters showed signs of shifting towards Democrats. That could signal erosion in Republican support among a demographic that was a pillar of Trump’s 2024 victory.
Some 48% of 2024 Harris voters said they were “very enthusiastic” about voting in the Nov 3 midterm elections, when control of both chambers of Congress is at stake. By comparison, just 30% of Trump voters said the same in the poll.
The findings add to evidence of an enthusiasm gap favouring Democrats and suggest potential cracks in the coalition that propelled Trump in 2024, when he won the popular vote. That coalition was fuelled by strong support from men and gains among Hispanic voters and other demographic groups that shifted to the right in the 2024 election.
The poll also adds to a string of encouraging signs for Democrats, who are widely favoured to win control of the House of Representatives and remain competitive in the fight for the Senate as Trump’s approval ratings have slipped amid voter concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.
Republican strategist Charlie Gerow said the poll’s findings raise the stakes for his party’s turnout efforts, though he expects the enthusiasm gap to narrow as concerns about what he described as far-left Democrats gaining power motivate Republican voters.
“The enthusiasm has to be ginned up among Republicans because turnout is what’s going to determine the outcome of these midterm elections,” Gerow said.
While Trump voters overwhelmingly plan to vote Republican and Harris voters are similarly inclined to vote Democratic, the president’s 2024 supporters are less decided, with 13% saying they aren’t sure who to vote for in congressional elections, compared to 7% of Harris supporters who say the same.
Broad decline in support
The poll, which was conducted nationwide and surveyed 4,506 adults online, showed that just 32% of Americans approved of Trump’s presidency, holding at a record low first marked in a September Reuters/Ipsos survey. The survey has a 2 percentage point margin of error.
Since taking office in January 2025, support for Trump has fallen across every major demographic group, including double-digit drops among Hispanics, men, rural and suburban voters, people without college degrees and evangelical Christians.
One notable shift has come among men, a group Trump won in all three of his presidential campaigns, including by a 12-point margin in 2024, according to a Pew Research analysis.
When asked how they would vote in a congressional race if the elections were today, men in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll picked Democrats over Republicans, 43% to 39%. The four-point Democratic advantage was the widest of Trump’s second term. Men consistently favoured Republicans in 2025 but since August have mostly favoured Democrats.
The warning signs for Republicans reflect growing voter concerns about the high cost of living amid a surge in gasoline and diesel prices following the war with Iran. Trump launched the Iran attacks in February, despite pledging during his campaign not to start new conflicts and to lower costs for consumers.
Cost of living is the top issue on Americans’ minds as they decide how they will vote in November, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Voters cite democratic values as the second biggest issue, followed by immigration.
Republicans continue to hold an edge among older voters, a crucial bloc in midterm elections, when seniors have historically accounted for an outsized share of the electorate. Voters 50 and older still favour the Republican Party over the Democratic Party by 2 percentage points, 44% to 42%, though that was down from an eight-point Republican advantage in December.
Still, the enthusiasm gap looms large for Republicans.
Among all the voters in the poll who said they were enthusiastic, 62% said they were pumped about expressing opposition to Trump, compared to 36% who said they were eager to support the president.
Linda Rivera, a 46-year-old Trump voter in Pennsylvania, said that while she would probably vote Republican if she casts a ballot, she is frustrated with both parties and feels “neither enthusiastic or unenthusiastic” about voting in November.
Rivera, a respondent in the poll, said concerns about widespread voting fraud - which have been repeatedly fanned by Trump and his Republican allies without evidence - have added to her doubts about whether she will vote.
“I have lost faith in the voting process,” she told Reuters. “I have lost faith in both parties. Not just one.” REUTERS

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,830 Troops, 47 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,830 troops, three tanks, and 47 artillery systems over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 8.
The latest figures bring Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,547,780.

Democrats in tight Midwest US races split on trans rights strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:04:42 UTC
19:04:42 KST

Democrats in tight Midwest US races split on trans rights strategy
Oct 8 - After being caught flat-footed on transgender issues in the last US election, Democrats in tight midterm races are pursuing different strategies, with some adopting more conservative stances and others trying to deflect, according to a Reuters review of campaign messaging and interviews with nine party strategists and insiders.
Ahead of the November 3 election, vulnerable Republican candidates have renewed their attacks over transgender rights, a message that political strategists say helped Donald Trump and his party win unified control of Washington in 2024.
In response, some Democratic candidates have moved closer to Republican positions on transgender participation in women's sports and gender-affirming care for minors. Others are seeking to redirect the conversation back to the flagging economy and Trump’s unpopular war with Iran.
The different strategies can be seen most clearly in Iowa and Ohio, states that Republicans have dominated during the Trump era but which now feature competitive congressional and gubernatorial races.
Whether Democrats in these Midwestern states can convince moderate voters they agree with their views on trans issues, or successfully change the topic, could determine how much support they are able to win back from cultural conservatives — and could foreshadow how the party's presidential hopefuls handle the issue in 2028.
Critics warn that moving towards Republicans on trans issues is unlikely to win Democrats new support, and risks alienating LGBTQ voters and the party’s ascendant progressive wing.
DEMOCRATS MOVE RIGHT
In Iowa, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, Senate candidate Josh Turek and congressional candidates Lindsay James and Sarah Trone Garriott have all distanced themselves from progressive positions on transgender issues.
“I oppose letting men in women's locker rooms and voted to let parents, not politicians, make decisions for their kids,” Trone Garriott said in a recent ad.
LGBTQ advocates have criticized such language, saying misgendering transgender women as men represents a betrayal of the party's LGBTQ supporters at a uniquely vulnerable moment.
Since returning to office, Trump has directed the federal government to recognize only two sexes; sought to bar transgender people from military service; restricted transgender girls' participation in women's sports, and moved to limit federal support for gender-affirming care for minors.
“You don't have to capitulate and use Republican talking points to win elections,” said Aime Wichtendahl, the first transgender person elected to the Iowa General Assembly.
Gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand told Politico last month that "girls' sports are for girls." And his approach may be working, with polls showing him favored to become the first Democrat to win the governor's race since 2006.
At a recent town hall he said “I tend to agree” with Republicans that transgender women and girls should be barred from female sports teams.
“Coward!” a man in the room shouted in protest.
'PARENTS KNOW WHAT'S BEST'
Transgender issues have also featured prominently in Ohio, which Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
Republican Derek Merrin, running to represent the 9th congressional district, released a September 10 ad saying that Democratic incumbent Marcy Kaptur had “voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports.”
Kaptur, who faces an uphill race in her recently redrawn district, countered a week later with an ad saying she had “voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids … and boys should not play in girls’ sports.”
The ad was criticized by local LGBTQ organizations, including the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, who wrote in a letter to Kaptur that she was “engaged in a race to the bottom with Republicans.”
Asked for a response to that letter, Kaptur's campaign did not respond.
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, running against Trump-backed Jon Husted, has tried a different approach. A recent ad from Elon Musk’s PAC accused him of supporting an “extremist” agenda under which children are “abused and exploited” through “sex change surgery.”
Brown, who polls show with a narrow lead over Husted, has opted not to engage, framing the attacks as a distraction from more pressing issues: “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” asks one Ohio voter who was featured in a recent ad from Brown’s campaign.
THE ISSUE THAT BOXED IN HARRIS
Among the most indelible ads from 2024’s presidential contest between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris was one that featured the tagline: “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.”
A Democratic Party election report concluded the ads were “very effective” and boxed in Harris, who had previously supported gender-affirming care for inmates in federal custody.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll in April found that 67% of survey respondents supported banning transgender people from competing in female school sports. But the party splits were severe: Ninety-two percent of Republicans said they supported such bans, compared with just 44% of Democrats.
“We have extensive research that shows voters prefer an argument that broadens the conversation to all of us and doesn't leave anyone behind over a divisive narrative that misgenders people and throws them under the bus," said Tyler Hack, executive director of the Christopher Street Project, a transgender advocacy organization.
With their anti-trans attacks, Republicans are “abandoning pocketbook issues in favor of an anti-freedom agenda that is obsessed with politicians making decisions that should be left to parents and schools,” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson Viet Shelton said in a statement, echoing a framing used by Republicans that emphasizes local government control on transgender policies.
Democratic strategist Eric Stern thinks Republicans got “over-confident” about the effectiveness of their anti-trans strategy in 2024.
“I’m skeptical that if there are some low-propensity voters whose wages are being stretched thin because of Trump’s wars and tariffs that they’re going to care about some cultural issue that doesn't impact their lives,” Stern said.
Veteran Republican strategist Charlie Black said the party is right to build on messaging that connected with voters in 2024, and which “might help” in some places, but agreed that "economic issues are predominant this year.”
Hack of the Christopher Street Project added there's no one-size-fits-all approach to such a polarizing topic.
"We want to make sure that candidates talk about these issues in a way that's inclusive and in a way that makes sense for their individual communities," he said, "and that doesn't always look the exact same." REUTERS

Cilia Flores, wife of Venezuela's Maduro, to press for release from US jail

Venezuela's Maduro, wife Flores charged in US over alleged torture
NEW YORK, Oct 8 - Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores both were hit with an additional US criminal charge on Thursday stemming from accusations they tortured political opponents to retain their grip on power in the South American country.
Maduro and Flores were charged with an additional count of conspiracy to commit torture in addition to the drug trafficking charges they previously faced, according to a superseding indictment filed in Manhattan federal court.
In one instance, prosecutors said Maduro in 2013 ordered the arrest of a Venezuelan military officer he suspected of planning a coup.
Members of Venezuela's military counterintelligence directorate then interrogated the officer while shocking the individual with a live electric wire around 20 times and hung the individual by the hands and feet for several minutes at a time, prosecutors said.
In 2022, an American citizen detained while entering Venezuela was accused of conspiring to assassinate Maduro and was tortured by military counterintelligence officers through beatings and shocks to the person's arms, legs and genitals, according to the indictment.
Lawyers for Maduro and Flores did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Flores, 69, and Maduro, 63, were captured by the US military on January 3 in their Caracas home and brought to New York to face the drug charges.
The surprise raid ended the socialist Maduro's 13 years in power in oil-rich Venezuela, which has since boosted cooperation with the US under the leadership of Maduro's former Vice President Delcy Rodriguez.
Maduro and Flores pleaded not guilty to the drug charges and have been held at Brooklyn's Metropolitan Detention Center since their capture. Their trial is scheduled for June 1, 2027.
FLORES SEEKS RELEASE FROM JAIL
Separately, Flores is expected to appear in a US court on Thursday to urge a federal judge to release her from jail for health reasons while she awaits her drug trafficking trial next year.
At a hearing in Manhattan federal court, Flores' lawyers are expected to ask US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein to grant bail so their client can undergo a cardiac procedure and recover in a more comfortable environment.
The lawyers proposed moving her to a residence in the New York City area with round-the-clock private security, and said she is not a danger to the community. The lawyers also said Venezuela's government, which the US authorized to pay Flores' and Maduro's legal fees, would cover the costs.
Prosecutors in the Manhattan US Attorney's Office oppose Flores' release.
They said Flores has received adequate medical care at the detention center, and if released poses an "extreme" risk of flight and danger to the public, including possible witness intimidation.
Prosecutors also said other judges have found it unfair to let some criminal defendants pay for their own out-of-jail supervision, because defendants of lesser means cannot afford it.
Hellerstein's bail decision will not affect Flores' trial or potential punishment. If convicted, she faces a mandatory minimum 40-year sentence.
Flores was Venezuela's attorney general and led its National Assembly before becoming first lady. US prosecutors say she took hundreds of thousands of dollars in bribes from a large drug trafficker. REUTERS

Ruja Ignatova’s Ex-Husband Faces Trial Over €16 Million OneCoin Funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:03:00 UTC
19:03:00 KST

Ruja Ignatova’s ex-husband, Björn S., is on trial in Germany over alleged money laundering linked to financial flows from the OneCoin scheme, with the case involving payments of about €16 million and assets worth millions, according to German publication Diebewertung.
The proceedings at the Regional Court in Darmstadt have renewed attention on the missing "Cryptoqueen" and her former personal and business circle, as well as on what those around her may have known about the origins of the money.
There has been no reliable trace of Ignatova, a Bulgarian national, for almost nine years. The self-styled "Cryptoqueen" attracted investors with promises that OneCoin would create a new financial world and become a major competitor to Bitcoin.
Instead, OneCoin developed into one of the largest international fraud schemes of recent years. Millions of people invested in the project and billions passed through the system before Ignatova disappeared.
While Ignatova remains at large, people from her former personal and business circles have continued to face legal proceedings in Germany and the United States.
Figures concerning the amount of money associated with OneCoin have varied widely over the years. Some estimates have put the total as high as €15 billion.
However, U.S. Department of Justice data provide another figure for assessing the scale of the scheme. Between the fourth quarter of 2014 and the fourth quarter of 2016 alone, OneCoin collected more than €4 billion, or an equivalent amount in dollars, from investors.
The U.S. Department of Justice estimates that the scheme had at least 3.5 million victims worldwide. Internal OneCoin records from the same period show revenue of about €4.037 billion and estimated profit of roughly €2.735 billion.
Even the figures contained in official records therefore point to a scheme of massive scale.
OneCoin was not a conventional cryptocurrency. Its large-scale promotion began in 2014, combining an alleged cryptocurrency with a multi-level marketing operation.
Participants had to purchase so-called educational or OneCoin packages and could receive rewards for recruiting additional members.
At major events, Ignatova portrayed herself as a glamorous businesswoman and promoted the project as a financial revolution. OneCoin was presented as a system that would overtake Bitcoin.
U.S. courts later reached a very different assessment. OneCoin did not possess the characteristics of a freely tradable cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin, while its purported value was set internally and increased almost continuously.
The U.S. Department of Justice now explicitly describes OneCoin as a fraudulent pyramid scheme.
According to U.S. investigators, Ignatova left Sofia for Athens on October 25, 2017. Her publicly documented trail ended after that, with her U.S. indictment having come just days earlier.
She was placed on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in June 2022, and a reward of up to USD5 million is currently offered for information resulting in her arrest or conviction.
As of 2026, Ignatova remains at large and her location is unknown.
Speculation has persisted over whether she was killed. Other theories claim that she could be living under a new identity with support from wealthy individuals or criminal networks.
None of those theories has been established. The FBI continues to regard Ignatova as a fugitive and is conducting an international search for her.
Claims that she is definitely dead or is definitely hiding in a particular country therefore remain speculative.
While her whereabouts remain unknown, her former husband has been appearing before a court in Darmstadt.
The trial against Björn S. began at the Regional Court in Darmstadt in September 2026. The 50-year-old lawyer is accused of money laundering.
Prosecutors allege that he received money that could have originated from the OneCoin scheme. Reports from the proceedings indicate that the case includes two major payments with a combined value of about €16 million.
The investigation also covers money that allegedly reached Björn S.’s accounts through a company based in Hong Kong.
Björn S. has not been convicted of participating in the OneCoin fraud. He is currently standing trial after prosecutors brought charges against him, and the court must determine whether those allegations can be proven.
The presumption of innocence applies until a final ruling is issued.
The proceedings also involve a villa in Bad Homburg, which media reports say was purchased for more than €7 million.
Investigators are examining whether money originating from the OneCoin system was used to acquire the property. A security mortgage has already been registered against the villa.
That issue remains part of the ongoing proceedings and has not received a final judicial assessment.
A central question in the Darmstadt case is expected to be how much Björn S. knew about the source of the funds.
He was not simply an acquaintance of Ignatova, but her husband. Published information says he attended various events connected to her business circle as well as social gatherings associated with OneCoin.
His presence at such events, however, is not the central legal issue. The court must determine what he knew about the origin of particular funds and whether he was aware that they might have come from criminal activity.
The legal position is different in the case of Karl Sebastian Greenwood, who co-founded OneCoin with Ignatova.
Greenwood was arrested in Thailand in 2018 and later extradited to the United States. He pleaded guilty to fraud and money laundering charges in December 2022.
He received a 20-year prison sentence in September 2023. U.S. investigators believe Greenwood personally obtained substantial amounts of money through the scheme.
U.S. prosecutors said he received more than USD300 million, making him one of the central OneCoin participants to have been convicted.
Several detailed investigations into Ignatova’s inner circle have identified Greenwood as a former partner or lover of hers. The fact that the two ran OneCoin together has added another element to the story.

Ship transit through Strait of Hormuz falls to two-month low — Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:01:34 UTC
19:01:34 KST

LONDON, October 8. /TASS/. Commercial vessel transit through the Strait of Hormuz fell to its lowest level since July 23 early this week amid a new wave of escalating attacks on tankers, Reuters reported, citing data from analytics firm Kpler.
On Tuesday, only seven commercial vessels passed through the strait. Average daily oil transit figures in late September dropped by 27% from the month's peak levels, settling at around 10 million barrels per day. This volume represents approximately 74% of the shipping levels recorded prior to the launch of the US and Israeli military operation against Iran in late February this year.
Kpler analysts noted that some tankers continue to navigate the Strait of Hormuz with their transponders turned off. Furthermore, oil exports from the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman coasts have more than doubled during the conflict, reaching 6.7 million barrels per day, largely making up for the losses from reduced transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
The US and Israel launched military operations against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the US resumed its large-scale strikes on Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreement regarding the Strait of Hormuz.

INTERVIEW - More than half of Gaza dialysis patients die after 3 years of genocide: health chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:01:15 UTC
19:01:15 KST

- Dialysis patients in Gaza fell from about 1,400 to 600 due to deaths linked to lack of regular treatment, he says
- Israel continues to detain 88 specialist doctors, he says
More than half of Gaza’s dialysis patients have died amid Israel’s blockade and the subsequent collapse of the enclave’s health care system during three years of genocide, Gaza’s health chief said.
More than 174,000 wounded people need nearly half a million complex surgeries, but the health care system lacks the resources to carry them out, Munir al-Bursh, director general of Gaza’s Health Ministry, told Anadolu.
He said Israel continues to detain 88 specialist doctors, while its blockade prevents medical supplies from reaching patients in need.
The Health Ministry has repeatedly warned that shortages of medicines, medical supplies and equipment, along with a lack of fuel for hospital generators, threaten to shut down essential services.
Gaza has been without regular electricity since the start of the genocide on Oct. 8, 2023.
Israel has also failed to fulfill obligations under the ceasefire agreement in force since Oct. 10, 2025, including fully opening crossings and allowing agreed quantities of food, humanitarian and medical aid and fuel into the enclave.
Health services remain in collapse
Bursh said Gaza’s health services “remain in collapse” despite the ceasefire.
Gaza had around 1,400 dialysis patients before the genocide, but that number has now fallen to about 600, he said, attributing the decline to “deaths caused by the inability to receive regular treatment.”
Thousands of patients with chronic illnesses, including high blood pressure and diabetes, have also died during the war because of difficulties accessing treatment, medicines and medical care, he added.
In September, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented continued shortages of medicines for chronic illnesses, including supplies needed to treat kidney disease.
The shortages have caused complications in dialysis services, including blood transfusions and the suspension of most catheterization procedures.
Nearly half a million complex surgeries needed
Against this backdrop, Bursh said more than 174,000 people have been wounded since the start of the genocide, with each initially requiring an average of at least three surgeries.
“This means Gaza needs nearly half a million complex surgical procedures,” he said, despite having virtually “no resources to carry them out.”
“Patients with chronic illnesses and those requiring continuous follow-up also face difficulties receiving treatment because of damaged hospitals and shortages of medicines and fuel,” he added.
Meanwhile, Israeli attacks continue to cause casualties.
Since the ceasefire agreement, Israel has killed more than 1,460 Palestinians and wounded more than 5,160 others, he said.
Medical supply shortages
Bursh warned that Gaza’s health sector is suffering from severe shortages of medicines and medical supplies.
He said “medical stocks have reached dangerously low levels,” with shortages of 52% for beds and essential medicines and 56% for medical supplies.
“No new medical equipment has been allowed into Gaza since the start of the Israeli offensive,” he said.
Moreover, Israel’s refusal to allow generator fuel and spare parts into the enclave has also disrupted oxygen plants, electricity generators and ambulances, he added.
Operating-room equipment has also been barred from entering Gaza, making surgery nearly impossible, he said.
Patients in need of medical evacuation
On treatment outside Gaza, Bursh said more than 20,000 patients and wounded people urgently need to leave the enclave to receive treatment.
He said “arrangements providing for the departure of around 300 patients a day have not been implemented by Israel, with only about 25 patients currently allowed to leave each day.”
On Feb. 2, Israel reopened the Rafah crossing, which it has occupied since May 2024, under strict restrictions.
UN figures released in April showed that more than 18,500 patients needed medical evacuation, including around 4,000 children.
88 doctors remain detained
Regarding Israel’s continued control over more than 60% of the Gaza Strip, Bursh said several hospitals are located in areas under Israeli control or facing active hostilities.
He condemned Israel’s continued detention of more than 88 specialist doctors, including senior surgeons and prominent medical professionals in Gaza, among them Mohammad Obeid, Hussam Abu Safiya and Ghassan Abu Zahri.
He also said “the prevention of foreign medical delegations with highly qualified personnel from entering Gaza has compounded the shortage of medical staff.”
Bursh called for “urgent international action to pressure Israel to allow medicines and equipment into Gaza, rehabilitate hospitals and allow medical personnel to return, as well as approve the evacuation of wounded people before it is too late.”
Israel has blockaded Gaza since 2007. Around 2.15 million of the enclave’s roughly 2.4 million Palestinians are now homeless after their homes were destroyed during the war, including more than 800,000 living in tents that are unfit for human habitation.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, while destroying about 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.

Hacker claims simple password allowed access to 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers
An anonymous hacker has claimed responsibility for accessing nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, telling newspaper Politiken that a weak password made the breach possible.
CPR numbers are personal identification numbers used in Denmark’s national Civil Registration System to identify residents and access public services.
The hacker told Politiken that the breach occurred on September 11 through a small Danish company with access to the CPR register.
According to the hacker, a leaked password belonging to a former employee allowed entry into the system. The password was reportedly “123456.”
After gaining access, the hacker said they created two computer programs to retrieve CPR information and store it outside the system.
The person’s identity has not been made public, and their account has not been independently confirmed.
The hacker told Politiken they had no plans to sell or publish the personal identification numbers and were “really shocked” by the security weaknesses they encountered.
To describe the situation, the hacker compared it to someone leaving dangerous material unattended.
“Someone leaves a suitcase with 10 kilos of plutonium unattended at a train station. Then a homeless person steals it,” the hacker said.
“Yes, of course you shouldn’t steal other people’s suitcases. But you also shouldn’t leave nuclear material at a train station.”
The hacker provided Politiken with a file containing the CPR numbers.
The newspaper forwarded the file to Emil Hørning, an IT security expert at Danish cybersecurity company Defend Denmark.
Hørning said the hacker’s account appeared credible and that the described method was plausible.
Politiken conducted its interview with the hacker in English through an encrypted communication service.
Danish government proposes tighter senior pension rules to save 800 million DKK annually
The Danish government wants to change how workers qualify for senior pensions, potentially saving 800 million DKK annually by 2030, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Currently, people whose health limits their ability to work to 15 hours a week or less can receive a senior pension up to six years before reaching the state retirement age.
Their work capacity is assessed against their most recent job. Under the proposal, applicants would instead be assessed against all types of employment.
The Finance Ministry estimates savings of 200 million DKK in 2028, rising to 800 million DKK in 2030.
The proposal has divided political parties and organizations.
Anders Vistisen of DF, Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, said his party would oppose the changes.
“We are not going to cut for the worn-out,” he told Jyllands-Posten, citing Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s promises of more dignified retirement.
Ældre Sagen, Denmark’s senior citizens’ advocacy organization, also criticized the proposal.
Deputy Director Michael Teit Nielsen warned that applicants could face longer assessments to determine whether they could work in another profession.
However, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main employers’ association, welcomed the proposal.
Deputy CEO Søren Kryhlmand said assessing workers against the entire labor market would allow those capable of other jobs to remain employed.
The government also plans to increase the separate Arne early retirement pension by approximately 3,000 DKK monthly. Its current maximum is 15,650 DKK per month.
Changing the senior pension scheme, introduced in 2019, requires agreement among the parties behind it before a general election.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard is scheduled to present the budget proposal today.
University of Copenhagen to merge and reorganize faculties from 2028
The University of Copenhagen is changing how its academic departments are organized, with several faculties set to merge or split over the next three years.
The university announced that its Faculty of Theology and Faculty of Humanities will merge into a single Faculty of Humanities and Theology on January 1, 2028.
The Faculty of Law and Faculty of Social Sciences will also combine into a Faculty of Law and Social Sciences on the same date.
Further changes will follow on January 1, 2029.
The Faculty of Health Sciences will be divided into two faculties: Clinical and Public Health Sciences, and Health Sciences. The new divisions will focus on clinical and preclinical subjects, respectively.
The Faculty of Science will also split into two. One will cover traditional natural sciences, while the other will focus on biological, environmental and geosciences.
Despite the restructuring, the university will retain six faculties.
A faculty is a major academic division responsible for particular subjects and degree programs.
The university said most students would not be affected because the content and structure of their degree programs would remain unchanged.
Rector David Dreyer Lassen said the changes were necessary because the university’s faculties had developed differently in size and complexity over the past 15 years.
“When the differences become very large, it challenges our balance, leadership power, and cohesion,” he said.
The University of Copenhagen was founded in 1479 with four faculties: theology, law, medicine and philosophy.
Its faculty structure has changed several times since then.
Today, theology students can pursue studies leading toward the priesthood, while humanities programs include history, English, education and rhetoric.

Leila Stockmarr of the Red-Green Alliance, a left-wing Danish political party, also questioned why families previously considered financially vulnerable would now lose support.
Frederiksen explained that the food checks were introduced to help households manage higher prices for necessities such as food and gasoline.
Asked whether the student grant reductions would outweigh the earlier payments, Frederiksen rejected the comparison.
“Those are two different issues,” she said.

The government’s planned prison unit at Departure Centre Kærshovedgård may take four to five years to become operational, the Ministry of Justice told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The ministry is also working to establish temporary prison spaces at the centre. These are expected to be ready within a few years.

Danish vaccine company Bavarian Nordic has raised its forecast for revenue in 2026, citing stronger expected sales of travel vaccines.
The company now expects total revenue to reach 6.1 billion kroner this year, compared with its previous forecast of 5.7 billion kroner, Bavarian Nordic said in a company announcement Thursday.
The company attributed the increase to better-than-expected sales in its Travel Health business, particularly demand for rabies vaccines in the United States.

Third forecast increase this year

At the beginning of the year, the company expected total revenue of between 5.0 billion and 5.2 billion kroner in 2026.

The Danish Defence will receive a new command system designed to help military and civilian authorities coordinate their responses to drones.
The Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation has signed an agreement with Danish software company Systematic, the agency said Thursday.
“The construction of Denmark’s drone shield is a step closer to the goal with this agreement with Systematic,” Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said.
The system will use artificial intelligence to analyze large amounts of information and identify patterns, unusual activity and potential threats.
The Danish Defence, police and other authorities will be able to access the same information, giving them a shared operational picture from the first drone sighting until the response is completed.
Systematic’s SitaWare software will be installed at several military locations and connected to existing drone defence systems.

The purchase follows an August agreement with Danish defence company Terma. Terma’s system will collect information from different sensors and provide a combined overview of drone activity.
The two systems are intended to work together as part of Denmark’s response to airborne and hybrid threats. The measures follow incidents involving drones over Denmark in 2025.
Denmark records more than 1.17 million state pensioners
Denmark had a record 1,175,187 state pensioners in August, according to figures from the Jobindsats statistical database reviewed by pension company Velliv.
It was the 13th consecutive month in which the number reached a new high.
The increase reflects longer life expectancy and large generations reaching the state pension age. However, many new pensioners continue working.
In July, 24.6 percent of 67-year-old state pensioners remained in paid employment, compared with 10.6 percent in July 2022.
Velliv consumer economist Thomas Gress said the rise could be connected to rules allowing people to earn income without reductions to their own or their spouse’s state pension.
“For some, retirement life is the freedom to leave work completely behind. Others want to keep their colleagues, some hours on the job, and benefit from the generous deductions and subsidies available for continuing working life once the state pension age has been reached,” Gress said.
The growing pensioner population is also increasing public spending. Statistics Denmark said social benefits cost the state 908 billion DKK last year, five percent more than the previous year.
State pensions were the largest expense in the old-age category, costing 170 billion DKK.
Velliv expects the number of state pensioners to continue rising until 2029, when roughly one in five Danes is projected to receive the benefit.

Nearly one million Danes add credit warnings after breach of 8.8 million CPR records
The number of Danes with a credit warning in the national CPR register has almost quadrupled since authorities disclosed a major data breach.
About 970,000 people had registered a warning by October 7, up from just under 250,000 on October 1, the Digital Affairs Ministry said.
“The Danes have taken the situation seriously, and they have acted on the advice that has come from the government and from the authorities,” Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said.
A credit warning makes it harder for someone to obtain loans or credit in another person’s name. It tells companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving applications.
The Agency for Societal Security has recommended warnings for people who have specific reasons to suspect fraud.
Unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people by misusing a small Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system during 10 days in September.
Authorities discovered the activity after the company received an unusually large bill. Each search of the register carries a fee.
The company has not been identified, and authorities do not know who was responsible.
Egelund said it remained too early to determine whether affected people would need new CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.

Denmark proposes ban on sharing AI-generated deepfakes without consent
People in Denmark could gain stronger protection against realistic AI-generated images, videos and voice recordings under a new bill introduced Thursday.
Culture Minister Zenia Stampe of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party, wants to prevent digital imitations of people’s appearance and voices, known as deepfakes, from being shared without their consent.
“With artificial intelligence, you can create manipulated videos and images with a few clicks and share them on social media. It can lead to misinformation and create doubt about what is real,” Stampe said.
The proposal would cover all citizens, including artists, whose performances and presentations could also be protected against unauthorized digital imitations.
Stampe said she had personally experienced having a photograph from her profile turned into a video that appeared to show her speaking.
She described the experience as intrusive, even when such content is labeled as satire.
The minister also pointed to SF, the Socialist People’s Party, politician Karsten Hønge, whose identity has been used in hundreds of fake social media posts about Greenland.
A central aim of the legislation is to make social media companies and other online platforms remove illegal deepfakes quickly.
Satire would remain legal, although Stampe acknowledged that distinguishing satire from unlawful manipulation could be difficult.
She said courts would have to decide whether particular content qualifies as satire or whether that label is being used to justify illegal material.
“It will certainly be difficult, but on the other hand, I also have respect for the fact that we have a very strong tradition of satire in Denmark,” she said.
Stampe hopes the legislation can take effect around the turn of the year.
Denmark expands exemptions from new nitrogen rules for fruit and vegetable growers
More Danish farmers will receive temporary exemptions from new fertilizer restrictions after concerns that the rules could make growing certain fruits and vegetables more difficult.
The Ministry of Nature and Animal Welfare announced that crops including melons, rhubarb, strawberries, table grapes and pumpkins will be exempt from the new nitrogen regulations throughout 2027.
Woody plants grown in nurseries will also be covered by the exemption.
The changes follow a review of the regulations approved by a majority in Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing, in September.
The rules, which take effect at the beginning of 2027, aim to reduce nitrogen pollution from agriculture by limiting fertilizer use.
Nitrogen runoff from farmland has contributed to the deterioration of Denmark’s marine environment.
However, agricultural experts and vegetable producers have warned that the restrictions could create significant difficulties for domestic food production.
The government initially planned to exempt mainly potato growers during the first year. The exemption has now been extended to additional fruit and vegetable producers.
“I am pleased that we have the opportunity to also exempt some berry and fruit growers who otherwise faced major challenges, so they get one more year to adapt,” Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said.
The exemptions apply only to 2027 and are intended to give affected growers additional time to adjust.
The ministry said the newly exempt crops account for a small share of Denmark’s total agricultural land.
As a result, it expects the changes to have only a very limited effect on the nitrogen reductions the regulations are intended to achieve.
Serum Institute expects high flu levels this winter
Influenza infections are expected to reach a high level in Denmark this winter, according to Statens Serum Institut (SSI).
“We expect a winter where influenza will once again be prominent, while COVID-19 appears to remain at a lower level,” Bolette Søborg, chief physician and head of section at SSI, said in an update published by the institute.
SSI expects both influenza A and B to circulate during the coming season.
“Both the number of influenza cases and influenza-related hospitalizations are assessed to potentially reach a high level,” the institute said.
Influenza A has dominated recent seasons, while influenza B has circulated at relatively low levels. SSI said this may mean that the population has less naturally acquired immunity to influenza B, which could make it account for a larger share of infections this season.
COVID-19-related hospitalizations, meanwhile, are expected to remain at a low to medium level.
People aged 65 and over are being offered free vaccinations against both influenza and COVID-19. SSI said the vaccines are expected to provide good protection against the two respiratory infections.
The institute also expects vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, to reduce serious illness among infants.
Since October last year, the Danish Health Authority has offered RSV vaccination to pregnant women. SSI said hospitalizations among infants fell by about 70% during the latest transmission season compared with previous years.
“We therefore also expect that the vaccination will significantly reduce the burden of disease among the youngest infants this winter,” Søborg said.
RSV is still expected to circulate among older children and adults, although for most people the infection causes symptoms similar to a common cold, including coughing.

Denmark proposes up to four years in prison for mediation councils that seek to prevent prosecution
The Danish government has introduced a bill that would make it a criminal offense to participate in a mediation council with the aim of preventing public prosecution of a crime.
The proposed penalty is a fine or up to four years in prison. The bill targets councils that attempt to settle criminal matters outside the Danish justice system.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a Social Democrat, introduced the proposal on Wednesday, arguing that such councils undermine the rule of law.
“It must come to an end that, for example, imams or prominent criminal families can exploit their position to act as judges of law and order and attempt to override the Danish rule of law,” he said.
The proposal revives a bill from the previous government that was not passed before a general election was called in February.
Police have encountered councils in Aarhus
Wammen said several police districts were aware of mediation councils, although he could not give a figure for how many exist.
In 2024, Jyllands-Posten reported that East Jutland Police had encountered such councils in western Aarhus for several years. The newspaper described them as widespread among groups with other ethnic backgrounds.
One anonymized police interview report described a case from 2020 in which a group of “important men” visited the parents of a man who had reported a violent assault.
The visitors wanted to avoid police involvement and suggested compensation for the assault, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Under current rules, a victim and perpetrator can agree to settle a conflict without police involvement, provided there is no criminal conduct such as coercion or witness intimidation. This has made it difficult for police to act against the councils.
The proposed law would also criminalize participation in a council when the purpose is to evade prosecution.
“What we are doing with this bill is that we are taking targeted action against those who sit at the head of the table,” Wammen said.
He cited wiretapping as a tool police could use to establish whether an illegal council was taking place.
“That is because this is something that takes place behind closed curtains and in environments that do not want to talk to the police. That is why we need better tools to combat it,” he said.
The government still needs a majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, to pass the bill. It is intended to take effect on January 1, 2027.

Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.

“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.

Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.

The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.

Before then, parliament will vote this month on the defense agreement Denmark, Greenland and the USA signed in New York.
The agreement has broad political support and largely continues a 1951 arrangement. It also includes two bases the USA wants to establish in Greenland and gives Greenland a stronger independent position.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen thanked Greenlandic leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen for their cooperation during her opening speech.
After New Year, the government will begin legislation restoring Great Prayer Day as a public holiday from 2030.
The restoration depends on employment increasing enough to offset the additional labor created when the holiday was abolished. Socialist People’s Party leader Pia Olsen Dyhr expects the target to be reached.
The government will also reintroduce a citizenship bill covering 2,055 previously approved applicants and their children.
The original bill expired when an election was called. Applicants must undergo a complete new review.
Opposition parties have criticized the government for proceeding before completing a planned citizenship screening system.
Large search bill alerted Danish authorities to breach of 8.8 million CPR records
An unusually large invoice led Danish authorities to discover that unauthorized people had accessed personal records on 8.8 million people, an official said Tuesday.
A small Danish company had legal access to search the national CPR register. Each search carries a fee, and extensive activity produced a large bill.
“There is a very large amount being invoiced, which makes one aware that there has been a lot of activity,” said Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization.
Unauthorized users abused the company’s access for about 10 days in September.
Authorities have not identified the company.
The accessed information consisted mainly of names and addresses, Leihardt said. The CPR system is Denmark’s national register of personal information.
Authorities do not yet know who was responsible or how the company’s access was compromised.
“It is too early to say at this point who is behind it and what method has been used,” said Henriette Erbs of NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit.
She said cases of this type often involve cross-border crime.
Laila Reenberg, director of Denmark’s Agency for Public Security, said digital fraud was an obvious possible motive.
However, she said authorities did not yet know who collected the data or how they intended to use it.
Danish consumer group files complaint over Red Bull advertising on influencer’s platforms
Forbrugerrådet Tænk has asked Denmark’s Consumer Ombudsman to investigate whether Red Bull’s advertising through influencer Rasmus Søndergaard violates marketing law.
The Danish Consumer Council, an independent consumer organization, filed complaints against Red Bull Denmark, Søndergaard’s company and two marketing agencies.
Søndergaard publishes content on Twitch, YouTube and TikTok.
Danish law prohibits marketing energy drinks to consumers under 18 because the products are considered unsuitable for children and teenagers.
Forbrugerrådet Tænk described the Red Bull campaign on Søndergaard’s platforms as the most serious suspected violation of the Marketing Practices Act it had seen.
The organization said Red Bull products appeared frequently in his videos and argued that many viewers were younger than 18.
Miriam Michaelsen, chair of Denmark’s Media Council for Children and Young People, said Danish minors widely use the platforms carrying Søndergaard’s content.
Søndergaard rejected the complaint.
“I make content for adults, and children should not encounter advertisements that are not for them,” he said. “I completely disagree with the complaint, but we are listening, because we must protect the youngest.”
Søndergaard and Red Bull began a formal partnership in 2023.
The complaints also cover DayZeroAgency, which represents Søndergaard, and Ultra, which manages marketing and events for Red Bull.
MobilePay will change its name to Vipps in Denmark from January 12, 2027, the company behind the payment app announced Tuesday.
Some of the app’s nearly 4.7 million Danish users will begin seeing a redesigned logo during the transition.
The app’s functions will not change. Contacts, payment agreements, transaction history and other features will remain available.
MobilePay’s services in Denmark and Finland merged with Norwegian payment app Vipps in 2022, creating a shared Nordic platform.
Vipps MobilePay described the name change as one of the final steps toward operating under a common Nordic identity.
“We know that the new name will require a bit of getting used to,” said Jeanette Hertzum, the company’s Danish country manager.
The company wants users in Denmark, Greenland, Norway, Sweden and Finland to use the same name and logo.
The longer transition period is intended to give Danish users time to adjust before the new name takes effect.
The app will retain MobilePay’s blue color in Denmark and Finland. The logo will change to include the smiling symbol already used by Vipps in Norway and Sweden.
Hertzum said some users would adapt quickly, while others might need more time. The company said assistance would be available to people who need help with the change.

The Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, opens its new parliamentary year Tuesday with a royal visit and a speech from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.

The day begins with a 10 a.m. service at Christiansborg Palace Church for lawmakers, ministers and invited guests.

Henrik Frandsen of the Moderates has been nominated to replace Venstre’s Søren Gade as speaker.
Deputy speaker positions will go to the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Venstre and Danish People’s Party.
The meeting will end with Denmark’s national anthem, led by the Copenhagen Boys’ Choir, the Royal Cantory.
