Breaking Down the Ominous Ending of Below
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

Warning: This post contains spoilers for the Below finale.
Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett) cuts his engine far from shore. Behind his boat, the High Hopes, trails a slab of iceberg the size of a church, netted like a catch. He looks at it for a while. “Nice and deep, about 2,000 meters to the bottom, and not a soul around to give you and your youngsters any grief,” he tells the creature clinging to the base of the ice, the one he glimpsed in the water the day his father died. “Most of my life, you had me scared half to death. But I dare say we’re more alike than I ever expected.” He moves to cut the line.
His confession is where Netflix’s six-part limited series arrives after five episodes of a different kind of dread. Jesse McKeown’s Below opens on a family towing their house across a Newfoundland bay until something drags it under, and for most of its run it behaves like the creature feature that scene promises. Calvin, a widowed fisherman with three kids, teams up with marine biologist Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) as an unidentified cephalopod tears through his hometown of Snook's Arm and exerts a strange psychoactive pull on his son Wade (Charlie Heaton). 
It draws Wade to Little Pot Rock, the island the Penneys fled 40 years earlier, where the Budgells stayed behind: Walton (Shawn Doyle), who knew Calvin as a boy, his elderly father, and his daughter Maggie (Marthe Bernard), who quickly captivates Wade. The Crockers, a wealthy merchant family, own the local fish plant and much of the town, and for decades, long before anything surfaced in the bay, they've pushed to resettle Snook's Arm, moving its residents elsewhere.
The penultimate episode offers Calvin the truth: a mining permit with the Crocker name on it, cobalt and copper under Snook’s Arm, and a plan to move a town rather than pay it what it’s worth. The same day, Fonda chips into a block of harbor ice in the town hall freezer and finds something alive inside. The creature is a mother, and the iceberg is her nest.
Those two discoveries set the finale in motion. The monster the show spent five episodes running from turns out to be a refugee, and the people it kept calling saviors turn out to be the threat. What’s left is a question of what a man does once he can see that. “The whole story has been a kind of slow awakening for Calvin,” McKeown tells TIME. “That’s what the finale is: eyes wide open. What are you going to do now?”
A fine hand
The episode begins small, on the dory Calvin and Wade used to flee Little Pot Rock, the Budgells’ cabin still burning behind them. Calvin thanks his son for saving his life, then admits he was wrong about him. “You and me had a hard go of it since your brother and your sister left, and your mother before that,” he says. “I should never have kept you off those boats. You’d have made a fine hand. I can see that now.”
Heaton describes Wade at the start of the series as a “lost boy,” a young man with “all this energy” who “doesn’t really have anywhere to put it.” The only Penney child who stayed
behind, he spent most of the season looking like a failure to launch. “To finally be trusted, I think, is a big thing,” Heaton says. For Hartnett, what matters is that Calvin can say it at all. “His fear was holding him back and making Wade the person that Calvin was upset he became,” he says.
Snook’s Arm, meanwhile, is emptying, with the military clearing everyone away from the water and the creature in it. The lieutenant overseeing the evacuation is grateful for the Crocker helicopters; with wildfires burning out west, his men are “spread too thin.” Shaking his hand, Jim Crocker introduces Jan (Natasha Henstridge), as his daughter. The night before, the creature went on a rampage when they tried to force her out of the harbor. “Where is it now?” Jim asks, and the show’s title appears over Calvin and Wade, drifting past the iceberg in their small boat.
The nest in the harbor
Fonda spends part of the morning on an informal memorial. She lays Barry’s blue shirt on the rocks above the water and weighs it down with stones. Her one colleague in Snook’s Arm, Barry caught the infection from the creature earlier in the season and in Episode 4 ran to the pier and dove in. Davis calls him Fonda’s “lifeboat,” and says his death helps awaken a “deep well of rage.”
She needs it. In the command tent, Fonda explains that the creature is a deep-water cephalopod, highly intelligent, unlike anything on the taxonomic record, and female. “Her egg sac is frozen in that iceberg out there,” she says. “These waters are too warm for her. Her eggs won’t survive, and she knows it.” As the soldiers confer, Fonda insists the creature, maybe “the only one of her kind,” deserves “to be studied, not bombed from the sky.” One soldier answers with the toll. “Respectfully, this thing has downed three vessels and killed 19 people so far,” he says. “We have a duty to eliminate the threat.” Jim then offers Fonda exclusive access to the remains once the creature is “dealt with.” “She may be the last of her kind,” he says, turning her own words back on her.
Davis frames Fonda’s eventual refusal less as a moral awakening than as the end of a comfortable denial. “It’s easy to turn a blind eye to it until it’s placed very baldly in front of you,” she says. Fonda had “convinced herself she was doing that before” while remaining “pleasantly ignorant.” The creature has never been prey to her, or a trophy. “She’s moving through this whole experience with curiosity rather than vengeance,” Davis says. That’s what makes Jim’s offer so ugly: it asks her to trade the mystery for its corpse.
There is no curse
At the Penney house, the family is packing and cursing Jan’s name when Calvin shows them the mining permit. His speech is the finale’s turn. “All my life, I thought we was cursed, like there was something in our blood, boiled in our bones,” Calvin says. “Blaming myself for every little thing that went wrong: can’t fish, can’t make a living, can’t keep this family together. Turns out, there is no curse. There’s only the Crockers.” A curse is something a family inherits, but a company is something it can fight.
McKeown reads the adult Calvin as a man who took every loss personally because no one told him the truth. “Calvin has been lied to his whole life about what he saw in the water, what happened to his father, the reasons why this town is no longer a viable place to live,” he says. The word he reaches for is “gaslit.” Hartnett hears relief in the speech, and something underneath it: “a bit of guilt for all of the time that he spent feeling that way, and therefore putting pressure on his family.”
A soldier interrupts with orders to evacuate, now. Calvin climbs into the helicopter with his family, reluctantly, and when Mary (Ruby Stokes) tells him to buckle up, he refuses. “I can’t just roll over,” he says. “I just need to stay and see this thing through.” Wade unbuckles his own seatbelt. “If Dad’s staying, I’m staying too,” he says. When Mary begs Calvin to stop him, he won’t: “Wade’s his own man. He can do what he likes.”
Wade scrambles out after his father, and Heaton laughs at the memory of shooting it. “I crawl over everyone like a child,” he says. He finds Calvin’s line sweet precisely because it doesn’t quite fit. “There is something so childlike about Wade,” Heaton says. “He’s got such great energy and exuberance for life.”
With Calvin and Wade’s minds made up, the others start having second thoughts. Jay (Rohan Campbell) and Ruth (Willow Kean) climb out too, and Mary’s boyfriend, Noah (Kaleb Horn), tells her she belongs here. Hartnett says their choice to stay “means everything” to Calvin. “He can’t believe that now they’re standing by him when the guns are out,” he says. “This is insane. But it’s his lifelong wish to reestablish his family unit.”
A solution inspired by iceberg cowboys
Holed up in the old packing plant with Fonda and Wade, Calvin watches the harbor and hatches a plan that sounds outlandish. If the eggs are in the ice and the mother won’t leave the eggs, then move the ice itself. “That ice weighs over 100,000 tons,” Fonda says. “150,000 probably, but it still floats, though,” Calvin replies.
The idea isn’t as far-fetched as it sounds. McKeown met Newfoundlanders who harvest icebergs for a living, selling the meltwater as luxury water and vodka, and describes them as “just wild, crazy, adventurer kind of guys.” The offshore oil and shipping industries taught him the other half. “You can’t melt them, you can’t destroy them,” McKeown says. “All you can do is sort of manage them, and that often means steering them out of the way or breaking them up into smaller pieces.” It made Calvin, whose livelihood adapted around the ice, the natural man for the job. “It’s one of those simple but genius Newfoundland kind of ideas,” McKeown says.
The family reunites in the plant, Mary and Noah last of all, and Calvin, who spent the morning refusing to leave, now tries to send them away. “Now you want to stay?” he says. To Siouxsie and the Banshees’ “The Passenger,” the Penneys rig an enormous net. Wade heads to the shoreline with a rifle to shoot the berg into smaller, towable pieces, hands Mary the heirloom ring Noah had planned to propose to her with, and watches her shots finally crack the ice.
Elsewhere, Jim Crocker sees the creature as a gift. “That is providence,” he tells Jan. “That is manna from heaven. Thanks to her, we have the cover we need to clear this place without a fight.”
The Crockers never needed the creature to be a monster, only to be useful. McKeown frames Below as a story of three families: the Penneys, the Budgells, and the Crockers, split along an old Newfoundland line between the fisherman class and the merchant class. The latter, he says, “sort of represents capitalism” and will “exploit these resources until they’re all gone,” a dynamic he connects to Newfoundland’s overfishing.
Calvin and Wade get two boats around the last remaining chunk and tow it out of the harbor, whooping across the water. On shore, Jim and Jan corner Fonda and ask her to call him off. When she won’t, Jim reminds her whose endowment pays her salary and warns that all of it goes away “right here and now.” “Good,” Fonda says. “I don’t want anything to do with your money.” When Jim reminds her of all the Crockers have done for the community, she has a sharper answer. “You’re not saving the world,” she says. “You’re stripping it for parts, and patting yourselves on the back.”
When Jan moves for Fonda’s radio, Fonda hits her in the face. Davis shot the punch on the production’s final day, in a take or two she remembers as “just sort of sloppy and messy,” which makes the brief dust-up feel all the more real. What stayed with her more was Newfoundland itself. “Every visual memory I have from making this show is like a Turner painting,” she says. “The most beautiful, sublime, terrifying nature you’ve ever witnessed.”
'More alike than I ever expected'
McKeown says the bond at the center of the finale, between a fisherman and the creature tangled up in the worst day of his life, is what the nest reveal sets up. “It would have been much easier for this to be a creature that just had to be destroyed,” he says. Instead, the finale asks Calvin to recognize himself in her. “They’re just trying to protect their youngsters,” McKeown says. Both have also been forced out of their natural environments by powers beyond their understanding.
Hartnett puts Calvin’s recognition in terms of siege. In his reading, Calvin sees “someone who is besieged by the powers that be,” and the kinship comes from a shared certainty. “They’ll do anything to protect them,” Hartnett says. It also explains why Calvin climbed out of the helicopter. “He can do something that he knows is unimpeachable,” Hartnett says. With the forces against Calvin finally clear, he can put himself in harm’s way for something he believes is right. “What else would you do that for?”
For a moment, the sacrifice looks literal. A military helicopter finds Calvin inside the strike zone, and Jim, listening from the command tent, presses the lieutenant to authorize a strike anyway. The lieutenant refuses. The harbor is clear. The people of Snook’s Arm can go home.
Calvin cuts the last rope. The creature rises and glides alongside the High Hopes, and for a long moment, she and Calvin seem to take each other in. McKeown wanted the stillness to feel bigger than a truce. “You realize you’re connected to something much bigger than yourself,” he says of those rare “cosmic moments.” “I think Calvin is having one of those moments.”
It’s just getting warmer
Fonda’s voice carries the episode from there, over aerial shots of open water. Most cephalopods mate once, she explains. After they spawn, they die. When the eggs are ready, the mother stops hunting and eating, gives everything in her body to her young, and uses the last of her oxygen to push her hatchlings out of the deep. Then her ordeal is over.
At the institute, an assistant asks Fonda whether any of the eggs she froze survived. “No,” Fonda
says. “Water’s too warm.” The assistant says that’s sad. “And it’s just getting warmer,” Fonda tells her. “And who knows what’s next.”
Davis has thought about that line more since she said it, through a hot, dry summer in England, and she hears in it a woman who refuses to soften bad news. “Things are horrible, it’s not getting better. I’m not saying this to scare you. It’s too late,” Davis says of the moment. Then Fonda steps outside into the wind, where, as Davis tells it, she “breathes the air and looks at the waves on the rocks and sees a whale pod cresting.” For Davis, that’s the other half of the scene. “That’s beautiful, though,” she says. “I don’t want to not appreciate the beauty while it lasts.” Holding both at once is what the actor took from playing Fonda. “Things are bad, but also things are beautiful,” she says.
Two lonely animals
Snook’s Arm comes back to life. At the Big Squid Distillery & Brewery, Ruth tells Mary and Noah that the Crockers, their first vote tossed out, are already pushing for another. “At least we now know what everyone’s worth,” Mary says.
McKeown is firm that this is not a happy ending. “For me, it’s just a reprieve,” he says. “The Crockers will be back. The glaciers are still melting.” What Calvin won for the town was information: the next offer will come with more money behind it, but “at least they can make an informed decision.”
Calvin watches from the edge of the crowd. Fonda spots him and laughs. “Congratulations,” she says. He tells her he’s glad she’ll get her cut. “It’s the only thing keeping the lights on right now,” she says. He looks at her a beat longer than he needs to. “Will you be around later? I can give you the guided tour.” “Yeah,” she says, smiling. “Yes, I’ll be here.”
For McKeown, the possibility dawns on the characters and the audience in the same instant. “Calvin and Fonda are two lonely animals,” he says. “They’re both in their own little cages at the beginning, and then they go through this thing together.”
The moment surprised the people who made it, too. “We shot that scene, and it just did feel kind of romantic,” Davis says. Hartnett, also an executive producer, wanted a Calvin who doesn’t complain, modeled on the blue-collar Minnesotans he grew up around. A man who keeps his troubles to himself tends to keep his feelings there, too, and that reticence carries into the invitation. “He doesn’t have any game, and I think that’s really lovely,” Hartnett says. Calvin is “now aware that there could be a different future,” he adds. “Is he imagining it yet? I don’t know.”
When Calvin excuses himself, it’s to meet someone waiting at the harbor: Wade. The Waterboys’ “Fisherman’s Blues” plays as father and son board the High Hopes together, and this time, Wade takes the wheel. Calvin’s hand settles on his shoulder. It was one of the last moments of a five-month shoot whose boat scenes were filmed for real, out on the open water, and Heaton remembers feeling “a lot of pride” as production reached the finish line.
Heaton sees Wade arriving somewhere most children reach eventually, if they’re lucky. “You finally get to that point where you see your parents as just people,” he says. “You can kind of understand their choices.” Wade is proud of his father, too. “You want approval from your father,” Heaton says. “That’s like the biggest honor.” For a few seconds, the finale is exactly the family story it kept promising to be.
Then the music sours. The High Hopes slows and stops, and the camera cuts behind the boat to show what the two men are looking at: ice on the horizon, more of it than they’ve likely ever seen. The last shot rests on Calvin’s face, squinting, before the cut to black.
What’s coming next
The ending traces back to McKeown’s first encounter with a berg, on a drive along the Newfoundland coast, when he rounded a corner to find one filling the sky, then another corner, then a dozen. “It’s so beautiful and it’s so majestic,” he says, recalling the “cosmic feeling” of seeing them. But once his mind “kind of recovered,” another thought intruded: “Where are these coming from? … Isn’t that a little bit scary?”
In the premiere, Calvin greets news of a heavy iceberg season as “music to my ears,” because ice is money. By the finale, that bounty reads as a climate warning. “The fact that Calvin sees all these icebergs coming his way should be good news,” McKeown says. “But after everything that he’s been through, he looks at that now and goes, ‘Oh sh-t, what does this mean for our future?’”
For Heaton, the last shot is where the show sheds its genre. Much of the series deals in science fiction and horror, he says, but the icebergs point somewhere more immediate. “At the end, it’s like there’s a very harsh reality of actually what’s coming.” Calvin could move one iceberg, but he can’t move all of these.
McKeown considers Below complete. The six episodes tell a full story, he says, and leaving Calvin in a “slightly ambiguous and unfinished place” is realism rather than setup. He isn’t ruling out a return, though. “If there’s another story to tell with these characters, great,” he says. “But that’s not my intention."
What he wants viewers to sit with is more existential. “That ending is not a cliffhanger, like, oh my God, what’s going to happen next?” McKeown says. “It’s what’s going to happen to us next.” He means the question to travel well beyond Newfoundland. “Climate change eventually will make refugees of us all,” he says. “It will start with the most vulnerable, these people who live on the brink. But eventually, it will come to us.”
Looking back on making Below, Hartnett returns to Calvin, a character he loved playing because he is “someone who tries that hard and figures out that they’ve been trying in the wrong direction for most of their life.” By the end, Hartnett says, Calvin has learned to “trust the people around him, to recognize that he is not holding this world together on his own.”
Calvin is facing the right direction now. Below ends with him gazing out at the water instead of away from it, his son at the wheel and the rest of his family back on shore. He won everything he stayed for, but none of it stops what’s coming. The boy who once leaned over the side of a boat and glimpsed a shape in the water is a grown man now, squinting at the horizon from the deck of the High Hopes. This time, he knows exactly what he’s looking at.

Cuteness Is Political
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

When you think of a military general, the descriptor “cute” probably doesn’t come to mind.
But cuteness may have helped Prabowo Subianto, a former military leader and defense minister, reshape his image to prevail as a conservative presidential candidate in Indonesia’s 2024 elections. His campaign positioned Subianto as a cuddly grandfather-type figure—complete with AI-generated cartoons—despite his controversial military past.
Our recent research suggests that this electoral result isn’t all that surprising. Specifically, we found clear links among specific types of cuteness, purity, and conservatism, revealing important implications for political persuasion and messaging.
Part of our motivation for studying these relationships was that cuteness is ubiquitous now, with adorable puppies, bears, and babies appearing in messaging for everything from sports to toilet paper to political campaigns. By “cute” we specifically mean the attributes of infants—like big eyes, chubby cheeks, round bodies—that elicit a caregiving response, a definition academics have aligned around over the past century.
Marketers have recognized and capitalized on this reality. Case in point: the prototypically cute Hello Kitty brand has generated tens of billions in lifetime retail sales. Cute collectibles like Squishmallows and Popmart’s Labubu dolls trend heavily on social media and were among the most coveted products of 2025.
But the impacts of cuteness don’t seem uniform across groups and individuals. Cuteness draws some people in more than others. To understand why, we drilled into deeper cognitive associations related to the concept of cuteness. Our study, recently published in the Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, featured nine controlled experiments that supported a key finding: conservatives showed a greater preference than liberals for baby-like cute products, and the link was partly explained by the association between that aesthetic and innocence/purity.
We found, in general, that study participants who valued purity preferred cuter versions of a product (e.g., a mug with giant, imploring eyes) to more standard versions. People differ in how much weight they give purity in moral judgments, and conservatives tend to give it more weight than average. Thus, we predicted that conservatives would appreciate cute products more than liberals would.
We collected observations from 3,648 participants across the U.S., U.K., and India and consistently found that political conservatives, on average, like baby-like cute products—mugs, keychains, water bottles, and others—more than political liberals, as measured by purchase intent and other variables. Similarly, we found that the number of searches for cute products (e.g., dresses, toys, bags) on Google Shopping is higher in red states than blue states in the U.S.
Our work shows that moral value systems permeate everyday consumption decisions, often without explicit awareness, and that designing messaging and packaging to reflect a consumer’s moral value system is one way marketers reel in consumers. While our experiments focused on product attitudes, choices, and purchase intentions rather than receptivity to political messages, candidate trust, or voting behavior, the core finding that moral values drive consumers’ basic aesthetic preferences and choices has meaningful consequences for political messaging. The same tips marketers use to design attractive products can be used to craft relevant political messages.
Overall, our research shows that baby-like cuteness is a more powerful attractant for conservative audiences than liberal ones because it signals innocence and purity. This finding is relevant to political strategists, as we’ve discussed, but also to the consumers on the other side of political messages: remember that a cute messenger or mascot shouldn’t substitute for scrutiny of the message itself, especially when it comes to important decisions at the ballot box or in other contexts.

Press review: EU tightens Russia sanctions while Germany eyes return to Russian energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. The EU is rushing to transform itself into an analogue of NATO ahead of elections in Germany and France, as the bloc gives the go-ahead for yet another sanctions package on Russia. Meanwhile, Germany is seeking to resume energy purchases from Russia. These stories topped Thursday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: EU rushing to transform itself into NATO-like bloc amid alleged Russia threat
The European Commission (EC) is seeking an analogue of the North Atlantic Treaty’s Article 4 before a potential change of power in France and Germany, the European Parliament told Izvestia. In NATO’s documents, this clause provides for urgent consultations between allies in case of threats. Brussels fears that Eurosceptics who oppose the strengthening of the EC's powers will come to power in Paris and Berlin. Until this happens, European bureaucratic hawks are trying to shape the EU's foreign policy on NATO, the Russian Foreign Ministry noted.
On October 6, the EC proposed abolishing the right of veto in the adoption of sanctions and the admission of new EU members. Last month, EC President Ursula von der Leyen proposed an Emergency Security Protocol as a mechanism for consultations in the event of threats. The EC is hurrying to do this ahead of the change of power in France and Germany in 2027, Fernand Kartheiser, a member of the European Parliament from Luxembourg, told Izvestia. "She [von der Leyen] is probably looking to act so swiftly precisely before major government changes take place in Germany and France. <...> Public opinion will hardly embrace such a scenario easily, given the current atmosphere of hysteria in Europe. Such an EU-wide step will be perceived by the general public as dangerous," he said.
Kartheiser’s fellow MEP from Bulgaria, Petar Volgin, expressed a similar opinion as he said "the process of the EU transforming into NATO 2.0 has already begun." At the same time, the mass vote for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) shows that more people are increasingly distancing themselves categorically from the militarist policy course being imposed by Brussels and a number of European governments, the politician noted.
Germany should hold a regular parliamentary election in 2029, but the idea of an early dissolution of the Bundestag is becoming increasingly popular. The opposition AfD party is polling at over 30%, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has a record-low approval rating. There is political ground already for a snap vote, said political analyst Yegor Belyachkov, who specializes in German studies.
The initiatives put forward by the EU will be considered as soon as the EU leaders’ summit in mid-October, Thierry Mariani, a French MEP, told Izvestia. "The European Commission is in a hurry, and I guess I know why. It is aware that Marine Le Pen could win in France. Therefore, it is seeking to settle things now, before the French express their opinion," the politician noted.
According to Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department of European Affairs, "the hawkish wing of the European bureaucracy has long been trying to shape the EU’s insufficiently anti-Russian, as they view it, foreign policy on NATO." "Any incident, be it an unidentified drone or problems with Internet connectivity, is automatically blamed on Russia’s 'hybrid' activities," the diplomat explained. "Clearly, all this hysteria does not at least contribute to ensuring stability and security on our western borders," he argued.
Vedomosti: EU approves 22nd sanctions package on Russia
The European Union has adopted a 22nd package of anti-Russian sanctions as EU ambassadors approved it on Wednesday. The measure will soon have to be approved by the EU Council before it comes into effect. This time around, more than 1,500 legal entities and individuals, mostly with ties to the Russian defense industry and the manufacturing of dual-use items, were sanctioned. The blacklisted individuals will be barred from entering the EU, while all their assets on EU soil will be frozen.
Even as the 22nd package does not include any brand-new trade and economic restrictions, it will be the largest ever in terms of the number of Russian individuals and legal entities blacklisted simultaneously, a source in Brussels told TASS. So far, approximately 3,000 individuals and legal entities have been added to the EU’s sanctions list.
The latest sanctions package does not include any industry-wide restrictions as it introduces personal, albeit broad, sanctions, Artyom Sokolov, a senior research fellow at the MGIMO International Studies Institute, told Vedomosti. Tellingly enough, Brussels no longer weighs any deeper sanctions as their effect, including on the EU itself, will be ineffective. Moreover, the fact that the 22nd package is being imposed proves that the range of restrictions has been exhausted. As regards restrictions against Russian lawmakers, numerous Duma members are under sanctions already, but symbolically, recent statements from the EU’s diplomacy chief Kaja Kallas represent a step toward further escalation, as the most vital institution of Russia’s legislative power may be sanctioned, the expert said. According to him, even as the EU lacks any coherent reasons for doing so, Russia has already grown used to similar measures by Brussels, while the State Duma’s functioning will be unaffected by the new restrictions.
The 22nd package of anti-Russian sanctions marks a shift from sectoral restrictions to targeted measures, Alexander Kamkin, an associate professor at the Financial University under the Russian Government, believes. Furthermore, it shows that the EU has exhausted the potential of economic sanctions as it mostly focuses on restrictions on Russia’s military-industrial sector--a move that European governments use to frighten their electorate with--while the imposition of sanctions against the defense industry effectively acknowledges Russia’s achievements in this sphere, the expert argued. Restrictions against Duma members, including those representing Russia’s new regions, were an expected move, Kamkin said, given the EU’s staunchly negative stance toward all government officials in those regions. However, it would be incorrect to suggest that these sanctions could in any way disrupt the State Duma’s operations, Kamkin concluded.
Izvestia: Germany seeking to resume Russian energy imports
Amid underground storage facilities being depleted and gas prices soaring in Europe, Germany sees a clearer benefit in resuming Russian energy purchases. European sources told Izvestia that Germany is interested in restoring energy supplies from Russia. "It would be much better if we could buy energy from Russia again as we did 10 to 20 years ago," one of the sources argued.
Another source said Germany is ready to import gas via the surviving leg of Nord Stream 2: such a scenario would be possible if the conflict in Ukraine ends, he added. "There are all necessary technical capabilities to restart the pipeline, even as no meaningful negotiations are currently being conducted with the Russian side," he noted.
Unless Germany reopens the surviving leg of Nord Stream 2, it will fail to keep its industries operating as before, Steffen Kotre, a member of the German parliament from AfD, told Izvestia. "Germany will no longer be able to run its industrial base the way it was five or six years ago," the parliamentarian pointed out. "We can already see that happening. Falling gas and electricity consumption is clearly due solely to the shutdown of industrial facilities that have become too expensive. Say, in the field of ammonia fertilizers and, of course, everywhere in the chemical industry. Production is being moved to where it is cheaper. And large enterprises are expanding their sites abroad," he added.
In these circumstances, AfD which is leading nationwide opinion polls is openly calling for the repair of Nord Stream. The issue will be discussed at a potential Russia-US-Germany business forum in 2027 as announced by Kirill Dmitriev, head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund and Special Presidential Envoy for Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries, Kotre said.
A full ban on Russian LNG imports from early January may trigger a price spike, and in winter, gas prices on exchanges could easily rise above $1,000 per 1,000 cubic meters and remain there through the season, Igor Yushkov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government and the National Energy Security Fund, told Izvestia. Only two unlikely scenarios - a warm winter or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and stabilization of exports from Qatar - could prevent prices from rising, he said.
In the longer term, the market balance will be achieved not due to the influx of new gas, but through a further decline in its consumption in Europe, as was already the case in 2021-2023, the expert argued. On the one hand, the wave of deindustrialization suits Brussels, helping it to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. On the other hand, amid economic problems, Eurosceptics and forces demanding the return of energy resources from Russia are gaining political weight. The Czech SPD party, for one, which came to power in 2025, advocates for the resumption of purchases of Russian oil and gas. Slovakia too is actively seeking to maintain energy imports from Russia.
Vedomosti: Rumors behind plague case in Russia’s Siberian region explained
Rospotrebnadzor is completing a range of preventive measures in the Irkutsk Region, Irkutsk and Shelekhov after a female employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died on the night of October 1, Russia’s sanitary watchdog said on October 7. No health implications related to infectious diseases have been found, it added. Earlier, Rospotrebnadzor said she had been diagnosed with pneumonia of undetermined etiology. A broader probe did not reveal any microorganisms associated with her professional activities either. The World Health Organization (WHO) is monitoring the situation, its Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus wrote on X.
Plague, including pneumonic, is much less contagious than COVID-19, Andrey Pozdnyakov, an infectious disease expert at Invitro, explained to Vedomosti. It is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis that does not spread over large distances, he said. Consequently, the contagiousness index for plague is significantly lower than that of coronavirus, influenza, or measles, and airborne transmission requires fairly close contact with an infected person. For example, during a recent outbreak of pneumonic plague in Uganda, only two out of 20 people who had been in contact with patients contracted the disease from two deceased patients, Pozdnyakov recalled.
The experience of COVID-19 is not applicable here, Denis Volkov, a sociologist, agreed: back then, a large-scale epidemic broke out, and general lockdowns and disruptions to the usual way of life aggravated people’s anxiety. And the anxiety triggered by the pandemic almost completely subsided two to three years later, he noted.
Panic against the backdrop of news about the situation in the Irkutsk Region started to set in amid coverage in foreign media outlets, Nikolay Bespalov, director for development at RNC Pharma think tank, said. He described the information in overseas media as far-fetched.
US President Donald Trump, too, commented on the situation as he announced a phone call "very soon" with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin. His offer of assistance was not the only response from Washington as the US Department of State and other federal agencies said they were monitoring the situation. The State Department, for one, advised US citizens in Russia to leave the country immediately on its page on X as it also urged others not to travel there, issuing a Level 4 advisory. The European Union expressed similar concerns, while the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it was in contact with Moscow over the epidemiological situation.
Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the US and Canadian Studies Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, sees a deliberate attempt to smear Russia behind the latest US rhetoric. According to him, Washington has responded to the uproar surrounding the Irkutsk incident amid a lack of information. Statements from the United States have been primarily precautionary, preventive, and formal, he said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Experts weigh in on depletion of oil reserves and crude prices
Seven months into the Middle East crisis, global oil inventories have almost been exhausted, Bloomberg quoted CEO of the world’s largest oil company, Saudi Aramco, Amin Nasser as saying at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. A similar assessment was voiced by the chief executive of the world’s largest oil trader, Vitol Group, Russel Hardy. According to him, Western nations have virtually exhausted their available oil reserves amid geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East. This and a shortage of available tankers may push global prices to $200 per barrel, he argued.
Global oil inventories currently stand at less than 6 billion barrels. However, Nasser noted, only 10% of this amount is actually available, with the remainder serving as the operational minimum required for the infrastructure to function. Commercial stocks include crude held in pipelines, tankers, port tanks, depots, storage facilities, and oil refineries. These volumes are in constant use and must be constantly replenished, but withdrawal rates currently outpace replenishment levels.
Besides, Oleg Zhirnov, investment and capital market partner at Kept, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta, a substantial amount of oil in pipelines or storage facilities is needed for those to operate properly. And it cannot be tapped because a minimum fill level must be maintained, he added.
Approximately 1 billion barrels of oil have been drawn from global stockpiles since the Middle East conflict erupted, according to data from the International Energy Agency (IEA). In August, the average rate of drawdown was 3.1 million bpd, and this pace could rise to 4-5 million bpd in the fall, a trend also fueled by the escalating global diesel crisis. If the drawdown of oil reserves were halted, there would be an immediate supply shortfall for consumers, and prices could inevitably surge, potentially reaching $150 per barrel or even higher, Zhirnov warned.
Vladimir Chernov, an analyst at Freedom Global, agrees that Brent prices could rise to $150 per barrel if supplies from stockpiles stop and the oil deficit of several million barrels per day persists. Further large-scale disruptions could trigger brief spikes to even higher levels, and the risk of prices climbing to $200 cannot be ruled out, though that would already represent a crisis scenario, he concluded.

At the epicenter of AI, San Francisco Bay residents take on the technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

From killer-robot protests to tech talks for seniors, S.F. Bay Area residents wrestle with AI
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
San Francisco Bay Area residents, living in the beating heart of the artificial intelligence boom, are just as conflicted about the technology as the rest of the country.
As OpenAI showed off its latest AI assistants in San Francisco last week, protesters outside — some dressed as killer robots —demanded it keep AI away from the military. Thirteen miles away in Oakland the following day, some senior citizens sat down with a group of students to address AI angst at a grassroots tech event.
Even as the clash between tech titans and anxious activists intensifies, the debate about AI is increasingly permeating community events, with the young and old grappling with the changes AI is bringing to their cities and the world.
Many are confused and want answers.
Tech giants such as Meta and Coinbase continue to lay off employees, citing the way AI is reshaping how people work. Tech workers are navigating a crossroads in their careers and a brutal job market.
Oakland resident Assata Olugbala, 81, asked for help removing Google’s AI bot Gemini from her devices after it started offering help she hadn’t requested.
“I’ve never invited it into my space,” she said. “But it starts talking to me and answering questions.”
While debates about building AI that surpasses human intelligence, flashy new gadgets and AI spending tend to dominate tech events, tech talks at last week’s Oakland Tech Week often had a different vibe.
The citywide annual event aims to bring technology to everyday consumers and constituents, and AI was one of its biggest concerns.
The event, which ended Saturday, featured panels and workshops titled “How to build Socially Responsive AI,” “AI in the workplace,” “Can AI Heal Us?” and “Master the Machine.”
AI killed the radio star: DJ chatbots are already chatting up airwaves, humans are pushing back.
Companies based around the San Francisco Bay Area, including OpenAI and Meta, have promoted AI assistants as friendly, cute helpers for tackling tedious tasks. But tech workers, activists and politicians fear that humans could lose control of the technology they’re advancing.
Anxiety about AI’s potential dangers surged last month after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, posting on social media that AI companies, including OpenAI, are “gambling with our lives.” Executives and AI companies have called for a slowdown in the technology’s development, and policymakers have been scrambling to add more guardrails.
Early last week, President Trump and tech executives from Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia and others signed a voluntary accord to “self-police” AI development.
Artificial intelligence stocks tumbled on Monday after American leaders of the AI revolution called for a coordinated slowdown in building more powerful AI systems.
In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed several bills to make AI safer for children and workers. He also issued an executive order to speed up the development of safeguards, including a “kill switch” in case humans lose control of AI.
“AI should expand opportunity — not come at the expense of workers and families,” Newsom said last month in a statement.
At the OpenAI developers’ conference, held at a former military base in San Francisco, the company’s chief executive, Sam Altman, expressed hope.
“I believe that the future, if we get this right, can be much more like a new renaissance than a new industrial revolution,” he said on stage. “AI should be about giving people more power over their own lives, more tools to create, learn, discover, expand knowledge.”
Outside, dozens of protesters held up signs that read “No Killer Robots for ICE,” “People over AI” and “Where is your moral codex?”
They demanded an end to AI surveillance and lethal autonomous weapons, as well as soaring San Francisco rents.
“Sam Altman, get off it. Put people over profit,” protesters chanted.
Berkeley resident Matt Nichols came to the protest dressed up as a killer robot holding a chainsaw. “AI is being used to move us toward a surveillance state with no accountability,” he said.
Lucas Lu walked by the protest, guiding two black-and-white humanoid robots. His employer rents out the robots for events such as OpenAI’s conference. He led them away from the vocal crowd.
Although some people fear AI because they’re worried it could lead to killer robots like those in “The Terminator,” Lu said AI can be helpful.
“It’s actually good at research,” he said. “But I won’t depend on AI to make any decision for me.”
In Oakland, in one event held at Mills College — part of Northeastern University’s global system — titled “Senior Technology Day: Lifelong Learning and Digital Inclusion,” students and senior citizens learned and taught one another about AI.
Participants of all ages expressed concerns about the technology.
“That’s your decision in regard to whether or not you use it,” said Norman Weekes, the AI literacy educator and entrepreneur who presented the topic to the group. “If you never use AI, that’s great, but you should understand it because ... it’s going to affect people you love, if not yourself.”
Artificial intelligence anxiety reached new highs this week as industry leaders highlighted growing concerns that humans could lose control of the increasingly potent technology.
On one hand, people can use AI to build websites or find activities to do. On the other, law enforcement can also request AI conversations, courts can subpoena AI chat logs and chatbots can provide inaccurate information while also flattering people, he said.
Karin Kelly-Givens, 72, uses an AI bot for health questions such as how to understand her blood-test results. Her friends use Gemini to comparison shop for pricey items such as washing machines. But she also grapples with how to use AI.
“Where’s the borderline?” she asked. “What should you not say? What is OK?”
Hayward resident Jason Hughes, 73, downloaded ChatGPT and Claude for the first time. “I might use them both to compare or get more information,” he said.
Activists, tech workers and more are sounding the alarm about AI’s risks and proposing various solutions to curb technology’s risks that include job displacement.
Fremont High School student May Gutierrez, 17, said that although teachers are concerned about AI being used to plagiarize, they’re also using it themselves. The aspiring designer has safety and environmental concerns about AI, so she’s holding off for now.
“Maybe I’m too much of an optimist, but I hopefully believe that people will see the consequences of AI and not necessarily get rid of it, but work toward making it better,” she said.
AIMS College Prep High School student Heven Adugna, who aspires to become a physician assistant, said she uses AI chatbots for research and to help better understand math concepts. Although people are using AI in healthcare, she thinks technology can’t replace everything.
“I would much rather have a sincere person telling me what’s wrong than a robot, so from that aspect, I don’t think AI can really take over,” she said.
The AI craze has intensified in the ‘gold rush town’ of San Francisco, spreading through work and social life.
Olugbala, the Oakland resident who wanted to get Google Gemini off her phone, said she wants to talk to real people using her voice, not bots.
“I want to have more human contact,” she said. “I want to go back and take every opportunity to sit down and get on the phone and talk.”

WIRED’s Midterms Races to Watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The midterm elections are a month away and the candidate pool has never been more WIRED. Races are being run—and likely decided—on Silicon Valley funding, data center debates, AI regulation, extremism, and more. From the contests that will decide the Senate to less attention-grabbing ones that will decide who controls voting in key swing states in 2028, these are the candidates and races we think are most worth watching closely in the weeks to come, and which we'll be keeping an eye on.
Former America PAC lawyer Chris Gober is running to represent Texas’ newly gerrymandered 10th district. Gober served as counsel for the Texas Republican congressional delegation for the 2025 redistricting effort that saw a new, gerrymandered map created for the 2026 midterms—one that was meant to create five new Republican congressional districts.
In addition to representing Musk’s PAC, Gober’s law firm, Lex Politica, has also represented Elevate New Mexico, a limited liability company that ran an advertising campaign supporting a controversial data center project in the state, as well as the Danube Institute USA, a think tank aligned with Hungary’s former right-wing leader Viktor Orban.
According to reporting from The New York Times, Gober was one of several lawyers who advised on the structure of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in the weeks leading up to President Donald Trump’s inauguration.
The 10th district also includes Grimes County, where SpaceXAI and Tesla have said they plan to open a 100-million-square-foot “terafab” facility to manufacture semiconductors. In addition to his legal work, Gober’s LinkedIn lists him as general counsel for a lobbying group called Maven Advocacy Partners, the client base of which includes several defense tech startups. (Its name appears to be a reference to the Department of War’s Project Maven, which is supported by tech companies like Palantir and Anduril.) Gober also appears to run another company called Maven Defense Solutions. Both the company and the lobbying group share an address with his law firm, Lex Politica, and his campaign office.
Gober’s campaign has received $747,550 from the American Mission PAC, a right-leaning super PAC that has itself received funding from Leading the Future, a PAC focused on promoting AI-friendly candidates and policies. Leading the Future has raised over $140 million from Silicon Valley billionaires like OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale, as well as the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz.
This race will be the first in which someone directly involved with Musk and/or DOGE attempts to enter Congress.
A September poll showed Gober leading Rourk 48-41.
Former Pinal County sheriff Mark Lamb ran on a “God, family, freedom” platform and won the GOP primary in Arizona’s 5th congressional district with Trump’s endorsement. He also has ties to paramilitary groups, anti-immigration organizations, and the far-right constitutional sheriffs movement.
Though he may not self-identify as one, Lamb appeared to, at one time, be a constitutional sheriff who gained national notoriety for his refusal to enforce Covid restrictions. He has worked with the election-denial group True the Vote to get sheriffs to investigate elections and has also boosted the role of private militias. He even authorized the formation of a civilian posse while serving as sheriff of Pinal County, in response to Black Lives Matter protests in 2020. He regularly appears on right-wing podcasts, including those hosted by white nationalists and conspiracy theorists.
While sheriff, he was accused of sexual misconduct and racist remarks, though he has denied the allegations.
Arizona’s 5th District is solidly Republican, meaning Lamb is likely to become the first constitutional sheriff in Congress. Lamb will be the heavy favorite.
No polls available yet.
Before launching her congressional campaign, Democratic nominee Lauren Reinhold was a human resources administrator in the Social Security Administration. Like thousands of federal employees, she left her job in 2025 when DOGE and the Trump administration fired government workers, cut programs, and encouraged employees to resign en masse.
Now, she’s running for Congress in Kansas’ 1st district, which encompasses the mostly rural, western half of the state, against three-term incumbent Tracey Mann. The district has long been a Republican stronghold, and Reinhold faces an uphill battle. Though several former federal workers have attempted to run for office in the wake of DOGE’s mass firings of federal workers, Reinhold is one of few that have made it through the gauntlet of the Democratic primaries.
Her race may showcase whether the destruction that DOGE wrought in the first year of the Trump administration will be a real, long-term political liability for Republicans.
No polls available yet.
Democratic nominee for Wisconsin governor David Crowley will be facing off against Republican nominee and congressman Tom Tiffany, who has spent the past six years trying to undermine the democratic process in the US.
In December 2020, as a member of Congress, Tiffany signed up for a Texas lawsuit seeking to invalidate Joe Biden’s victory in the presidential election. He also voted against certifying the results in Pennsylvania and Arizona after the Capitol riot on January 6 and has suggested he would have overturned Wisconsin’s results. This year, he has warmly welcomed the FBI’s baseless investigation into the state’s elections.
If Tiffany wins, as governor he would have the power to appoint some of the state’s top officials on the Wisconsin Elections Commission, giving him the ability to install election deniers to oversee voting for the 2028 presidential election.
A Marquette Law School poll at the end of September found that Crowley led Tiffany by just 3 percentage points, 49-46.
Former Atlanta mayor and Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms and billionaire health care executive and Republican nominee Rick Jackson face a tight gubernatorial race in a pivotal swing state that has continued to be the focus of Trump’s false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.
Jackson has aligned himself with several of Trump’s agenda items. In ads run by his campaign during the primary, Jackson attacked immigrants, trans people, and DEI initiatives. He also ran ads attacking primary opponent and Georgia secretary of state Brad Raffensperger for refusing to cave to the Trump administration’s pressure to overturn the results of the 2020 election. Jackson has supported Republican efforts to redraw Georgia’s congressional map, which would eliminate majority-Black districts, thus favoring Republicans.
Jackson, who said he is invested in a data center in Texas, has also advocated against a moratorium on data centers, instead saying that local communities should choose for themselves whether to allow them.
Bottoms has said she would consider a moratorium and has made health care and expanding Medicaid central to her campaign.
Georgia will likely continue to be a central focus for the Trump administration, both as a place to relitigate the results of the 2020 election and as a critical swing state in 2028. Whoever wins the governor’s race here could determine the certification of future elections and the level to which the state participates in the administration’s national agenda, both with regards to issues like data centers and the erosion of trust in elections.
A recent Rasmussen Reports poll found that Jackson is leading Bottoms, 48-45 percent.
Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed is running against Republican nominee and former congressman Mike Rogers for Michigan’s crucial Senate seat.
Following a bruising primary, El-Sayed's main controversies have surrounded his criticisms of the war in Gaza and US military aid to Israel. This led to accusations he was too soft on antisemitism and too progressive a candidate for the general election. To secure the fractured Democratic base, El-Sayed has announced he will rally with former president Barack Obama in an effort to court Black voters, according to progressive operatives.
He has also sought to cast Rogers as the face of intrusive government surveillance, WIRED previously reported, at a time when voters have expressed privacy concerns around AI and Flock cameras.
Rogers has denied that characterization and, notably, has backed a one-year moratorium on new data center construction in the state, proactively taking steps to insulate himself from the other major tech issue on the trail.
Rogers, who has gone from refuting Trump’s election conspiracy theories to boosting them, has benefited from Elon Musk–affiliated America PAC funding, which has dumped more than $4 million into this race, mostly in negative ads against El-Sayed.
Michigan is a critical battleground state for both parties this midterm cycle because a path for Democrats to take the Senate majority largely rests on retaining this seat. If Democrats lose Michigan, they would need to flip a total of five Republican seats elsewhere.
A recent report from Hill/Emerson College Polling found that El-Sayed is leading Rogers by a narrow margin, 48-46 percent.
Republican nominee and entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy is running against Democratic nominee and Ohio’s former director of department of health Amy Acton in the state’s gubernatorial election.
So far, Big Tech has been bankrolling Ramaswamy’s campaign, through his super PAC. Elon Musk, Jeff Yass, and Bill Ackman have all donated in the millions. Ramaswamy, who was part of the early vision of Musk’s DOGE, has also been endorsed by Trump.
Besides his Silicon Valley bona fides (Ramaswamy’s view on data centers amount to
give everyone with a data center in their community “free electricity”), Ramaswamy has also espoused many of the Trump administration’s views on elections and other electoral policies. Ramaswamy has suggested that the January 6 attack on the Capitol was an “inside job” and, just this year, called on the Ohio legislature to add a constitutional amendment to the ballot that would enact restrictive voter-suppression measures. The governor of Ohio would be in a position to have more power over elections and could deeply impact the 2028 presidential election.
Polling suggests the race is extremely tight. A September poll from YouGov found that Acton maintains a slight lead over Ramaswamy, 48-45.
A number of secretary of state races across the country could heavily impact what happens for elections in 2028. In most states, the secretary of state is the chief election official; they run and certify elections, from county officials all the way up to the Senate. Now, a number of election deniers across the country are running for their state’s top election job.
In Nevada, Republican nominee Jim Marchant is running against Democratic nominee and current secretary of state Cisco Aguilar. Marchant, a former Nevada state representative, is an avowed election denier who was among the most ardent boosters of election denial in the wake of the 2020 election, going so far as to help arrange a QAnon-associated coalition of candidates for the 2022 midterms.
In 2022, Marchant lost out to Aguilar in the race for the secretary of state, but after winning the GOP primary in June, he’ll once again face Aguilar in November. Critically, Aguilar has stood up to efforts to undermine trust in elections over the course of the past four years, but the winner in November will oversee the 2028 presidential election in Nevada, a swing state that went for Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024.
This race is a battle between one of the biggest boosters of election denial and one of the strongest defenders of election integrity.
No polls available yet.
While data centers have been a topic for voters across several key midterm races, nowhere is the debate more relevant than the Ohio Senate race.
Former senator and Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown is running against Republican nominee and former GOP lieutenant governor Jon Husted in one of the most contested races this election season. Husted, who has previously championed data center investments, has become a target statewide for his views.
Trump, who has endorsed Husted’s campaign, is adamantly pro–data center and went out of his way to express his opinions at a recent joint rally in Vandalia, Ohio. "We want them," Trump said. Husted’s campaign quickly issued a statement clarifying that Husted believed data centers were best left as a “local decision.”
Husted has been boosted by the Musk-affiliated America PAC, which has poured over $5 million into the Ohio Senate race, mainly in negative ads targeted at Brown, WIRED has previously reported. The only race in which Musk has spent more, according to federal campaign filings, has been the Senate race in Texas, a battleground state seen as a litmus test for Republicans this cycle.
Meanwhile, Fairshake, a super PAC funded by the crypto industry, is also planning to spend at least $30 million against Brown. (In 2024, when Brown lost his Senate reelection race, Fairshake spent $40 million against Brown, who then served as chair of the Senate Banking Committee and was a big crypto critic.)
According to a Bowling Green University poll, Brown leads Husted by three points, 48-45.
Texas has become a bellwether state for the midterms this November: If Democratic candidate James Talarico defeats attorney general Ken Paxton, the Democrats have a much better chance of taking the Senate majority.
The state has been ruby-red for decades, and Democrats would not have dreamed of this just months ago. But in a perfect storm, and with an unpopular Republican candidate besieged by scandal, Democrats have the best chance in decades of flipping the seat.
Recent approval polls put Paxton at negative 16, a number worse than every other Republican who is running in a close Senate race. Meanwhile, Talarico has been ahead in every public poll since mid-August.
The problem for Paxton is that he cannot exactly rely on Trump to boost his numbers, since the president is also experiencing negative approval ratings both in Texas and nationally. Paxton has been in lockstep with Trump for years, however. Paxton is an OG election denier, having led a failed multistate effort to overturn the 2020 results.
The silver lining for Paxton has been the colossal outside support that Republicans have marshaled to defend the seat. America PAC's biggest spending has focused on the race, pouring millions into defending the Republican’s seat.
Paxton isn’t universally beloved by Silicon Valley, however: Musk's SpaceX is suing Paxton in his role as state attorney general to stop information about its “terafab” operation being released under public records requests.
Talarico has maintained a narrow but consistent lead in polling; dating back to early June, he’s been ahead in all but two of 24 polls tracked by Silver Bulletin.
Republican nominee Riley Owen is running against Democratic nominee Ben McAdams for Utah’s 1st congressional district. Owen briefly served as a White House policy analyst during the first Trump administration and later worked for a startup using drones for conservation efforts. McAdams served as the representative for the state’s 4th Congressional district between 2019 and 2021 but lost to current representative Burgess Owens.
This little-known race has some fascinating funding implications: McAdams has received $1,128,697.73 in donations from Think Big, a PAC that describes itself as supporting “Democratic candidates dedicated to advancing AI innovation in America.” Think Big, in turn, is financed by Leading the Future.
McAdams also has a small stake in a data center project being built in rural Utah that, when completed, is expected to have a much larger power capacity than a controversial nearby project in Box Elder County.
No polls available yet.

Trump Administration Proposes $70K Fee for International Students to Work in U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a rule that would charge schools $70,000 per international student seeking to work in the U.S. through a program known as Optional Practical Training. It marks the Trump Administration’s latest attempt to curb foreign enrollment.
The proposal, published Thursday in the Federal Register and open for comment until Nov. 9, aims to crack down on OPT—a temporary employment authorization that lets students work in jobs related to their field of study and that DHS has claimed has “ballooned into an uncontrolled guest worker pipeline” and become a “magnet for fraud.”
Under the current system, students pay about $500 to apply and are generally permitted to work in the U.S. for up to a year during or after their study, while those in the science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields may get work period extensions.
Under the proposal, schools would have to pay $70,000 for a student’s initial participation—and another $30,000 for each additional program participation—though DHS said it recognizes schools “may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee” to students or employers. Collected fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury.
A DHS spokesperson said in the announcement of the proposed fee that OPT “was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system,” and that “American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”
International students have been in the crosshairs of the second Trump Administration as part of the President’s wider anti-immigration agenda. The Administration has revoked thousands of student visas and heightened vetting of applicants, including by reviewing their social media activity. It also pressured universities and colleges to agree to a compact that includes capping the number of undergraduate students on foreign visas, and it tried to limit the stays of international students to only four years. The Administration has zeroed in particularly on Chinese students amid national security concerns.
While the Administration champions policies discouraging foreign student enrollment as a means to benefit Americans, experts have said that such policies could hamper U.S. competitiveness in the long run.
Why DHS is cracking down on OPT
Since 1947, federal regulations have allowed foreign students to work in cases where employment for practical training is required or recommended by their schools.
But DHS in May alleged it found more than 10,000 foreign students “who claim to be working for highly suspect employers,” and, upon further OPT-linked investigations across multiple states, said it found “empty buildings and locked doors at addresses where hundreds of foreign students are allegedly employed.” Investigators also alleged fraudulent activities, such as “phantom employees,” and suspicious financial transactions.
In its proposal for the new fee, DHS claimed that the program’s growth in the last few years “has exponentially outpaced the number of companies” which it could review and investigate. It said that 194,554 students were granted employment authorization documents in 2024, compared to 160,627 in 2023. The department reasoned that “without the fees proposed in this rule, it cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud and may shut down the program entirely.”
It also said the fee was “necessary to ensure that schools, students, and employers participate in OPT for its intended purpose instead of a means to circumvent the H-1B visa program,” which refers to the work visa that allows American employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations such as technology, engineering, education, healthcare, and finance. OPT has often served as a bridge for students seeking work under H-1B visas, which the Administration has similarly targeted with higher fees.
DHS said it believes that the proposed fee would put the onus on schools “to exercise greater oversight and selectivity” when recommending students for OPT, and it would thus reduce fraud.
Critics call proposal illegal—and anti-American
The proposal, however, like previous attempts to curb foreign enrollment, is expected to face legal challenges. On Oct. 5, educational organizations took the Administration to court following its efforts to limit a similar program, Curricular Practical Training. A $100,000 H-1B visa fee has also been blocked in courts.
“Don’t Panic: DHS has no authority to slap a $70k fee on international students,” Doug Rand, director of the Talent Mobility Fund, an advocacy group for attracting foreign STEM talent, posted on LinkedIn. “Let’s not overreact—this proposed rule isn’t going to fare well in the courts, just as the $100k H-1B fee and other restrictionist policies have been struck down.”
Todd Schulte, president of the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us, said that if the proposal passes, the U.S. “is intentionally pricing itself out of the global market for top talent, especially in STEM fields.”
Results of a survey by the D.C.-based think tank Institute for Progress released Tuesday found that most international students plan to use OPT, but 80% fewer students said “they would likely try to stay” if the proposed fees were implemented. For STEM students eligible for OPT, the survey found that only 15% would likely try to stay. “DHS assumes that for STEM grads, there will be ZERO change in participation,” the think tank’s director for immigration policy, Jeremy Neufeld, posted on X.
Zuzana C. Wootson, deputy director of federal policy at nonprofit organization Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said in a statement that such exorbitant fees would push prospective students to competitor countries. But she also warned that the consequences “would extend well beyond international students. Declining international enrollment would strain institutional budgets, increase tuition pressure on American students, and diminish the educational experience for everyone.”

At the epicenter of AI, San Francisco Bay residents take on the technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

From killer-robot protests to tech talks for seniors, S.F. Bay Area residents wrestle with AI
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
San Francisco Bay Area residents, living in the beating heart of the artificial intelligence boom, are just as conflicted about the technology as the rest of the country.
As OpenAI showed off its latest AI assistants in San Francisco last week, protesters outside — some dressed as killer robots —demanded it keep AI away from the military. Thirteen miles away in Oakland the following day, some senior citizens sat down with a group of students to address AI angst at a grassroots tech event.
Even as the clash between tech titans and anxious activists intensifies, the debate about AI is increasingly permeating community events, with the young and old grappling with the changes AI is bringing to their cities and the world.
Many are confused and want answers.
Tech giants such as Meta and Coinbase continue to lay off employees, citing the way AI is reshaping how people work. Tech workers are navigating a crossroads in their careers and a brutal job market.
Oakland resident Assata Olugbala, 81, asked for help removing Google’s AI bot Gemini from her devices after it started offering help she hadn’t requested.
“I’ve never invited it into my space,” she said. “But it starts talking to me and answering questions.”
While debates about building AI that surpasses human intelligence, flashy new gadgets and AI spending tend to dominate tech events, tech talks at last week’s Oakland Tech Week often had a different vibe.
The citywide annual event aims to bring technology to everyday consumers and constituents, and AI was one of its biggest concerns.
The event, which ended Saturday, featured panels and workshops titled “How to build Socially Responsive AI,” “AI in the workplace,” “Can AI Heal Us?” and “Master the Machine.”
AI killed the radio star: DJ chatbots are already chatting up airwaves, humans are pushing back.
Companies based around the San Francisco Bay Area, including OpenAI and Meta, have promoted AI assistants as friendly, cute helpers for tackling tedious tasks. But tech workers, activists and politicians fear that humans could lose control of the technology they’re advancing.
Anxiety about AI’s potential dangers surged last month after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, posting on social media that AI companies, including OpenAI, are “gambling with our lives.” Executives and AI companies have called for a slowdown in the technology’s development, and policymakers have been scrambling to add more guardrails.
Early last week, President Trump and tech executives from Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia and others signed a voluntary accord to “self-police” AI development.
Artificial intelligence stocks tumbled on Monday after American leaders of the AI revolution called for a coordinated slowdown in building more powerful AI systems.
In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed several bills to make AI safer for children and workers. He also issued an executive order to speed up the development of safeguards, including a “kill switch” in case humans lose control of AI.
“AI should expand opportunity — not come at the expense of workers and families,” Newsom said last month in a statement.
At the OpenAI developers’ conference, held at a former military base in San Francisco, the company’s chief executive, Sam Altman, expressed hope.
“I believe that the future, if we get this right, can be much more like a new renaissance than a new industrial revolution,” he said on stage. “AI should be about giving people more power over their own lives, more tools to create, learn, discover, expand knowledge.”
Outside, dozens of protesters held up signs that read “No Killer Robots for ICE,” “People over AI” and “Where is your moral codex?”
They demanded an end to AI surveillance and lethal autonomous weapons, as well as soaring San Francisco rents.
“Sam Altman, get off it. Put people over profit,” protesters chanted.
Berkeley resident Matt Nichols came to the protest dressed up as a killer robot holding a chainsaw. “AI is being used to move us toward a surveillance state with no accountability,” he said.
Lucas Lu walked by the protest, guiding two black-and-white humanoid robots. His employer rents out the robots for events such as OpenAI’s conference. He led them away from the vocal crowd.
Although some people fear AI because they’re worried it could lead to killer robots like those in “The Terminator,” Lu said AI can be helpful.
“It’s actually good at research,” he said. “But I won’t depend on AI to make any decision for me.”
In Oakland, in one event held at Mills College — part of Northeastern University’s global system — titled “Senior Technology Day: Lifelong Learning and Digital Inclusion,” students and senior citizens learned and taught one another about AI.
Participants of all ages expressed concerns about the technology.
“That’s your decision in regard to whether or not you use it,” said Norman Weekes, the AI literacy educator and entrepreneur who presented the topic to the group. “If you never use AI, that’s great, but you should understand it because ... it’s going to affect people you love, if not yourself.”
Artificial intelligence anxiety reached new highs this week as industry leaders highlighted growing concerns that humans could lose control of the increasingly potent technology.
On one hand, people can use AI to build websites or find activities to do. On the other, law enforcement can also request AI conversations, courts can subpoena AI chat logs and chatbots can provide inaccurate information while also flattering people, he said.
Karin Kelly-Givens, 72, uses an AI bot for health questions such as how to understand her blood-test results. Her friends use Gemini to comparison shop for pricey items such as washing machines. But she also grapples with how to use AI.
“Where’s the borderline?” she asked. “What should you not say? What is OK?”
Hayward resident Jason Hughes, 73, downloaded ChatGPT and Claude for the first time. “I might use them both to compare or get more information,” he said.
Activists, tech workers and more are sounding the alarm about AI’s risks and proposing various solutions to curb technology’s risks that include job displacement.
Fremont High School student May Gutierrez, 17, said that although teachers are concerned about AI being used to plagiarize, they’re also using it themselves. The aspiring designer has safety and environmental concerns about AI, so she’s holding off for now.
“Maybe I’m too much of an optimist, but I hopefully believe that people will see the consequences of AI and not necessarily get rid of it, but work toward making it better,” she said.
AIMS College Prep High School student Heven Adugna, who aspires to become a physician assistant, said she uses AI chatbots for research and to help better understand math concepts. Although people are using AI in healthcare, she thinks technology can’t replace everything.
“I would much rather have a sincere person telling me what’s wrong than a robot, so from that aspect, I don’t think AI can really take over,” she said.
The AI craze has intensified in the ‘gold rush town’ of San Francisco, spreading through work and social life.
Olugbala, the Oakland resident who wanted to get Google Gemini off her phone, said she wants to talk to real people using her voice, not bots.
“I want to have more human contact,” she said. “I want to go back and take every opportunity to sit down and get on the phone and talk.”
