ICE detainees were sprayed with a cleaner during COVID crisis. Now they have a settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

ICE detainees sprayed with toxic cleaner during COVID crisis to get six-figure payout in settlement
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A proposed settlement given preliminary approval by a judge provides compensation to six former detainees who sued over the COVID crisis-era use of a disinfectant at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center.
- The settlement acknowledges that HDQ Neutral can cause serious health problems including chemical burns and permanent eye damage.
WASHINGTON — Six years after he was released from a California immigrant detention facility, Wilfredo Gonzalez Mena has to sleep with his back propped up by pillows, nearly in a seated position, to avoid gasping for air.
He blames his lasting medical issues on the 10 months he spent in custody until September 2020 at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center, about 60 miles northeast of Los Angeles, during which guards sprayed him and fellow detainees nearly around the clock with a concentrated disinfectant meant to guard against COVID-19.
Now Gonzalez Mena, who is one of six named plaintiffs in a class-action lawsuit filed in 2023 over the use of the cleaning solution, is expected to get a six-figure payout as part of a proposed settlement in the case, which was given preliminary approval on Sept. 25 by a federal judge in Riverside. The settlement applies to around 2,700 people detained at the Adelanto facility between March 11 and Sept. 30, 2020, who were exposed to the disinfectant called HDQ Neutral.
“When you least expected it, you would feel the mist,” Gonzalez Mena said. “They would spray us like we were animals.”
The Adelanto facility is operated by the GEO Group, a Florida-based private prison corporation that has faced criticism for years over conditions at its immigrant detention facilities. The company has also pushed back against California laws seeking to increase oversight of its facilities and inform the public about health and safety shortcomings.
Under the settlement, GEO Group and Spartan Chemical Co. Inc., the company that manufactures HDQ Neutral, acknowledged that HDQ Neutral — which is classified as a pesticide — can cause symptoms including blistering, chemical burns, vomiting, permanent eye damage, and damage to the respiratory tract, throat and stomach.
Those findings can now be used by class members who weren’t named plaintiffs and may pursue their own lawsuits, the settlement says.
Immigrants who were detained at Adelanto in San Bernardino County allege that a disinfectant harmed them — and continues to do so.
Neither GEO Group nor the Department of Homeland Security responded to requests for comment. After the lawsuit was filed, GEO Group denied its allegations and said cleaning products are used safely and securely, in accordance with the manufacturer’s guidelines and sanitation standards, at all detention centers.
At the time, a GEO Group spokesperson called the allegations “part of a radical politically motivated campaign to attack ICE contractors, abolish ICE and end federal immigration detention.”
The company later swapped HDQ Neutral for a different cleaning product.
Lawyers from the Los Angeles-based civil rights nonprofit Trial Impact Project who are representing the former detainees called the settlement a victory.
Executive Director Sara Haji referenced other pending lawsuits addressing allegations such as medical neglect, retaliation and substandard food and water. Each one is a different lens into the same problem, she said.
“When a company like GEO settles instead of defending itself at trial, and when it admits that the pesticide it sprayed everywhere can cause serious health problems, it should cause us all to sit up and pay attention to what detained people have been telling us about the everyday cruelty of immigration detention,” Haji said.
The lawsuit alleged that GEO Group engaged in a “months-long poisoning” of detainees when its employees sprayed HDQ Neutral inside the facility. Before the pandemic, staffers had used it as a cleaning product. But as COVID-19 spread, they began spraying the concentrated solution across wide areas, “directly into the air and on all types of surfaces,” the lawsuit said.
Detained immigrants quickly began experiencing the effects, the lawsuit claimed, including nosebleeds, headaches and dizziness.
Spartan Chemical warns that inappropriate exposure can cause the types of effects detainees experienced. Long-term exposure has been linked to asthma and, in laboratory studies on animals, reproductive issues and birth defects.
The EPA’s investigation found that staff and detainees were instructed to apply HDQ Neutral, a pesticide, inside the facility as often as every 30 minutes, without proper ventilation and at a dilution rate that’s double the concentration allowed for disinfectant use.
In 2021, the Environmental Protection Agency found that GEO Group had violated federal law by misusing HDQ Neutral. The report found that staff and detainees were instructed to apply the pesticide inside the facility as often as every 30 minutes, without proper ventilation and at a dilution rate of 2 ounces per gallon of water, which is double the amount allowed for disinfectant use.
In September 2020, a federal judge ordered GEO Group to discontinue use of HDQ Neutral at the Adelanto facility, writing that it had been used “with a callous disregard for the safety of Adelanto’s detainees.”
Among the more than 100,000 pages of documents released during discovery for the lawsuit was an email from a nurse at the facility to Wendy Baca, who was acting health services administrator at the Adelanto facility for Wellpath, the company providing its medical care at the time.
The nurse wrote that patients were arriving with headaches, rashes and blisters, “we believe, due to the chemicals being used to spray.”
“Some of the officers have also reported ‘feeling burned’ after touching their skin with the same gloves that were used to handle the chemical. Please look into this so we do not endanger everyone we are trying to protect,” the nurse wrote.
Baca appeared dismissive of the nurse’s concern. She forwarded the email to GEO Group’s chief of security, asking him to look into it.
“Please also remind them not to put metal into light sockets, run with scissors, or anything usually avoided with a little common sense,” she wrote.
Mark Anthony Ferretiz, a former GEO Group cook supervisor who worked at the Adelanto facility for 14 years until March 2025, wrote in a declaration that his team was told to spray the red chemical “like Lysol.”
“I could taste the spray in my mouth when I used it, and it felt heavy in my lungs,” he wrote.
At some point, the facility’s safety manager brought men from HD Supply to talk to the staff about HDQ Neutral. After learning how often the chemical was being sprayed, one of the men told Ferretiz that it was “rat poison” and that “you’re going to kill someone like that,” he said.
Years later, former detainees such as Gonzalez Mena say they’re still living with the fallout. The former long-haul truck driver said his health deteriorated so significantly while he was detained that, afterward, he could no longer pass the required physical assessment because of his vision and breathing issues.
To make ends meet, he has turned to online resale.
“My wife says that after I was released, I didn’t go back to being the same person,” he said. “I’ve had depression and I often dream that I am there, in that place, and I want to get out.”

He's Running In a District Trump Won By 21 Points. Democrats See an Opening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The odds are still stacked against Justin Pearson.
When the Democratic state representative announced that he would continue to run for Congress in a gerrymandered district five months ago, it was seen by many in Tennessee and Washington as more symbolic than viable. Pearson had originally planned to run in a majority-Black district in the Memphis area, challenging Rep. Steven Cohen, a ten-term Democratic incumbent. Then in May, the Republican-controlled state legislature redrew Tennessee's congressional map, splitting off parts of Memphis and combining it with 14 rural counties. Pearson is now running to represent a district that Trump carried by more than 21 points in 2024.
“We knew this was going to be a harder race after they rigged the maps,” Pearson says in a phone interview. “ It has not deterred us at all.”
This week, Democrats’ House campaign arm gave Pearson’s bid against Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor a vote of confidence, adding Tennessee’s 9th district to its coveted “Red to Blue” list. Campaigns on the list receive “organizational and funding support,” as well as staff resources, training, and strategic guidance, according to a DCCC press release.
The late support comes against the backdrop of a broad national trend of key races shifting in Democrats’ favor. In late September, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report said House Democrats are on track to pick up five to 15 seats. Though Cook still rates Tennessee’s 9th District as a “Solid Republican” seat, emboldened Democrats see a potential blue wave significantly expanding the races in play.
There has been little publicly available polling on the race. A recent poll sampling 400 voters and commissioned by a Democratically-aligned group found Pearson trailing Taylor by four percentage points.
Pearson sees the addition of his scrappy campaign to the "Red to Blue" program shows the party’s leaders see it as more than just a protest against GOP gerrymandering. He says he’s campaigned in all 15 counties in the new district, holding three to four campaign events daily.
“We've been having listening tours, road-to-victory rallies, meet and greets, fundraisers, and of course we're visiting barber shops and beauty shops and churches here in Memphis and Shelby County too, because we're not going to leave any of this to chance,” Pearson says,
A growing backlash in Tennessee to President Trump and the Iran War is also helping, he says, pointing to rural voters who previously voted for Trump that are now canvassing for him. “There are a lot of people who voted conservatively in the past who are farmers, who are very frustrated by the tariffs and what they [the Trump administration] have done with beef imports,” Pearson says. “There are people who are having to spend $1,000 a day on their machineries, diesel fuel, and they know that's a direct correlation to the Iran War.”
Closing the gap
Pearson made national headlines in 2023 for getting expelled from the Tennessee legislature for leading a gun reform protest from the House floor. His opponent, Taylor, has sought to brand Pearson as a “democratic socialist” who is too liberal for the district.
“He causes chaos everywhere he goes, and that’s why the voters in Tennessee’s District 9 will vote for competence over chaos,” Taylor said in a statement to TIME.
Pearson has argued Taylor can’t be trusted to represent the interests of the district’s voters. He highlighted donations Taylor accepted from Elon Musk’s SpaceX. A subsidiary company, SpaceXAI, is seeking to build a massive data center in the Memphis area despite local residents' concerns over environmental impact.
“My opponent…is about making more money for himself rather than protecting and serving the people in our community and in our state,” Pearson says.
Taylor, a former owner of funeral homes who is mostly self-funding his campaign, told TIME he sold his business four years ago and retired at age 54 before running for state Senate. He also accused Pearson of never having a real job and being “a paid protester.”
Capitalizing on voters’ energy
When the Supreme Court issued a ruling in April that undermined a major provision of the Voting Rights Act, it prompted multiple Republican-controlled states to quickly redraw its congressional lines. Tennessee was the first to act, with the legislature quickly approving a new map erasing Tennessee's only majority-Black district. Efforts by civil rights groups to convince the courts to block the new map have so far failed.
Yet the map switch appears to have jolted many of the state’s Democratic voters during the primaries. The Washington Post reported that a fifth of active registered voters in Shelby County, which includes Memphis, cast a ballot in three Democratic primaries for U.S. House seats, the highest level of voter turnout in a decade.
Pearson says Black voters in Tennessee are showing they refuse to be deterred by Republicans’ efforts to dilute their political power.
“This is just another challenge that we are going to face, and we're going to face it together,” he says. “And we're going to show up more than we have in decades. We're going to participate more than we have in decades because our voting rights are on the ballot.”

“I’m sure senator Collins is going to bring this up, but our records have changed: mine has gotten better, hers has gotten worse,” Jackson said, acknowledging that he was once an abortion opponent before becoming pro-choice.
“I think she’s put 55 anti-abortion judges on to the courts, including Brett Kavanaugh, that she knew that he was anti-abortion and that was what he was going to do,” he continued.
“Then, after she voted to put him on there, and she was the deciding vote, he took away Roe v Wade,” he added.
Collins did later argue that Jackson was previously “an extremist when it comes to abortion,” to which the Democrat, who voted to protect abortion access as a state lawmaker after changing his stance, countered: “Was I voting the wrong way? Yeah, and I’ve said that consistently .., the fact of the matter is: I can admit when I was wrong; senator Collins can’t. She still won’t admit that she was wrong in putting Brett Kavanaugh on”.
Republican Senate candidate repeats Islamophobic attacks against Abdul El-Sayed
Rachel Leingang
Heated barbs closed out the contentious debate between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers in Grand Rapids, Michigan on Thursday night.
Rogers ended on the Islamophobic note he sounded repeatedly throughout the debate, accusing El-Sayed of being “bought off by Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaida”.
“We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said.
El-Sayed ended on affordability, closing with his central campaign theme of “money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All”.
“I told you what this debate was going to be: him pointing at me and saying all kinds of foreign names, or him talking about himself,” El-Sayed said.
“And I told you, I’m interested in you. I understand that gas is too expensive. Groceries are unaffordable. I understand that it’s really hard to see a doctor and I want to solve that. And the reason we haven’t is because we’ve got corporate politicians who are going to do the bidding of people like Donald Trump. The war in Iran, the tariff war, all the money he’s taken from pharma, ask yourself if that’s helped you.”
Hegseth falsely claims Obama called 2009 Fort Hood attack 'workplace violence'
In an interview on Thursday with the rightwing network Real America’s Voice, Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, joined Donald Trump in trying to use the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood in Texas to attack former president Barack Obama.
On Wednesday night, Trump made the wildly false claim that Obama had emails from the attacker describing his plans in advance but chose not to stop him.
Hegseth, a former Fox News host, then falsely claimed that Obama had downplayed the attack.
“It was a radical Islamist terror attack,” Hegseth said. “Remember what Obama called it? ‘Workplace violence,’” the defense secretary said, falsely, as Posobiec nodded vigorously.
“I mean, that’s what we’re up against. That’s the worldview we’re up against, it’s ‘workplace violence,’” the supposedly nonpartisan defense secretary continued, referring, incorrectly, to a controversy over how the US military categorized the deaths of the 12 active-duty soldiers killed by Hasan at the time.
Relatives of those killed in the attack by a Muslim service member who later called it revenge for US military operations against Muslim countries, were enraged that the military refused to classify those killed as victims of combat or terrorism, since they were not deployed to Iraq or Afghanistan at the time.
The families sued in federal court, claiming that “the Army has refused to deem the soldiers killed and wounded in the attack eligible for a Purple Heart decoration, with its attendant recognition and medical and retirement benefits.” The suit, which criticized Obama for failing to call the attack terrorism, was dismissed in 2019.
In 2015, during Obama’s second term in office, the military did award the victims and survivors of the Fort Hood attack with Purple Hearts and other medals after Congress changed the definition of who was eligible for the military award to include victims of an attacker who “was in communication with the foreign terrorist organization before the attack” and “the attack was inspired or motivated by the foreign terrorist organization.” Hasan, the army major, did send messages to Anwar al-Awlaki, a cleric at a mosque in suburban Virginia where Hasan worshiped who went on to become a radical cleric and an al-Qaida propagandist. Awlaki was killed in Yemen in 2011 in a drone strike ordered by Obama.
While some experts, including the political philosopher Michael Walzer, have argued that the definition of terrorism should be reserved for attacks on civilians, and exclude soldiers, Republicans continued to criticize Obama for not describing the attack as an act of terrorism, even though he appeared to do so in a 2013 speech at the National Defense University.
After describing the threat from foreign groups that plot “acts of terror” in that address, Obama said, “we face a real threat from radicalized individuals here in the United States.”
“Deranged or alienated individuals - often US citizens or legal residents - can do enormous damage, particularly when inspired by larger notions of violent jihad,” Obama added. “And that pull towards extremism appears to have led to the shooting at Fort Hood and the bombing of the Boston Marathon.”
Mike Rogers has continually leaned into Islamophobic rhetoric against Abdul El-Sayed, attempting to tie him to Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood. The two are repeatedly sparring, with the moderator struggling to keep them on track.
Rogers claimed El-Sayed has refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year or the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, though El-Sayed noted he has condemned both.
But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.”
He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.”
After a 30-second commercial break, moderator Rick Albin said that in his 30 years of doing debates, he’d never seen the sparring continue during the commercial break, but tonight, it did.
The televised Michigan Senate debate, between Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, and Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate, quickly moved on to the topic of tariffs, particularly those on imports from Canada, which affect Michigan as a US-Canada border state. Rogers this week backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on Canada, saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now.
During the debate, Rogers said he called the commerce secretary this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. He said there are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”.
“I’d like to see it end. I think we need to end it,” Rogers said.
El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he only is reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”.
“He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy. Like, just be serious.”
Dr Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, is now debating his Republican opponent, former congressman Mike Rogers, for the first time.
The debate is being streamed live by the NBC affiliate WOOD TV.
Several recent polls show El-Sayed, a former public health official, leading by a slim margin over Rogers.
The tight race has drawn national attention as Republicans fight to keep control of Congress. Questions have swirled over whether the progressive El-Sayed can prevail in a state that elected Donald Trump in 2024.
If El-Sayed were to win the contest, he would make history as the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. His opponents have targeted El-Sayed’s faith and sharp criticism of the Israeli military campaign in Gaza.
In a thinly veiled attack on his faith, Trump incorrectly referred to the Democrat as “Mohammed El-Sayed” and a “Terrorist Sympathizer,” in a social media tirade on Wednesday.
“He knows my name is Abdul,” El-Sayed replied. “He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office.”

USS Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer addresses suicide attempts in strike group
In a brief news conference on Thursday afternoon, Captain Dan Keeler, the USS Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer, addressed widespread reports of mental health challenges faced by his crew during their long deployment.
“For most of my sailors, that this was their first time away from home, their first deployment, their first experience with combat,” Keeler said. “I understand the anxiety that that might have caused, but I can tell you this: our team of professionals on the ship led every single one of those sailors through that experience, and the great majority responded like sailors always do - with honor, courage, and commitment.”
“They are fantastic, fantastic sailors and marines, and they’re going to be cared for continuously on the next coming few months,” he added. “I deployed with five chaplains and a very well staffed mental health team. We got our sailors any care they needed and got them back in the fight when it was appropriate.”
Near the end of the news conference one reporter asked: “Were there some sailors who did try to commit suicide or jump overboard?”
“The key number that I like to focus on is zero; there were no suicides on board. There were no lost lives on on board,” Keeler replied.
“The suicide attempt number,” he went on. “You know, the secretary of the navy put out a number that encompassed the entirety of the strike group,” Keeler said, referring to a letter to Congress from acting navy secretary Hung Cao last month in which he wrote that there had been a total of eight suicide attempts across all the ships in the strike group led by the Lincoln.
“I think that key point has been lost when he, the secretary of the navy, put out the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group, that encompasses several thousand more sailors than what’s on board behind me,” Keeler added.
“We want the suicide attempt number to be zero. Having done this many, many times with the demographics that I have on board and the, you know, the stressful mission that we conduct, that’s unrealistic,” he continued. “That’s why I go to sea with a very, very well staffed mental health team. And when we had acute mental health cases, they immediately get seen by that mental health team and evaluated.”

Pakistani, Bahrain call for de-escalation in Middle East as top diplomats meet in Islamabad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:58:36 UTC
18:58:36 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Pakistan and Bahrain on Thursday emphasized de-escalation in the Middle East amid the US-Iran war and conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group as Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar hosted his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani, in Islamabad.
Dar said discussions with Al Zayani covered the evolving situation in the Gulf, adding that they "emphasized the importance of restraint, dialogue and de-escalation."
“We discussed the need to ensure safety and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb given their importance for regional and global food and energy security,” said Dar.
He said Pakistan “remains committed to efforts for peace and stability in the region.”
The Middle East has seen an escalation of conflicts since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, triggering retaliation by Tehran, which hit American military bases and assets across Gulf nations, including in Bahrain.
Amid the US-Iran war, conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis intensified in September when the Yemeni group seized strategic positions in the provinces of Al-Hudaydah and Taiz, including the port city of Mokha, before advancing to Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Islamabad has played a mediating role between the US and Iran, securing a ceasefire and then hosting the highest-level talks between the warring parties in April earlier this year, and has called for an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Bahraini Foreign Minister Al Zayani said the meeting in Islamabad comes while “the crisis in our region remains unresolved and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz is under daily threat.”
Bahrain “strongly condemns” Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports, saying that targeting airports and civilian infrastructure “is a criminal act, flagrant violation of international law,” he said.
Saudi Arabia’s security “is an integral part of the security of Bahrain and of the GCC (Gulf Council Cooperation),” the Bahraini foreign minister said.
He said he discussed with Dar the situation around the two straits, "underscoring the importance of freedom and safety of navigation and respect for international law."
Tehran has closed Hormuz since the US and Israel initiated the war while the Pentagon has imposed a military blockade of Iranian ports since April.
“We highly value Pakistan’s constructive role” of hosting Islamabad Talks between the US and Iran and "its continued efforts for dialogue and de-escalation,” said Al Zayani.
"We respect each other... we are consistent in our relationship... we feel safe in this relationship," said Al Zayani about Bahrain's ties with Pakistan, stressing: "we understand the constraints on each other."
Boosting ties
After the two foreign ministers co-chaired the third session of the Pakistan-Bahrain Joint Ministerial Commission, Al Zayani said the ties between the two nations have “gained significant momentum.”
Reaffirming “mutual resolve” to strengthen bilateral cooperation in key areas, the two nations next week will mark 55th years of diplomatic relations and have set target of $1 billion in trade transactions.
Bahrain is home to some 134,000 Pakistani citizens and the joint ministerial commission covered cooperation across more than 15 fields as the two sides stress on enhancing people-to-contacts.

Yle poll: Finns Party overtakes Prime Minister Orpo’s party
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:56:31 EEST
18:56:31 KST

The Finns Party has overtaken Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s National Coalition Party (NCP) in Yle’s latest opinion poll, marking the first time the two governing parties have exchanged positions during the current parliamentary term.
The poll, published on Thursday, 8 October, puts the Finns Party in second place with 16.5 per cent support, ahead of the NCP on 16.3 per cent. The opposition Social Democratic Party (SDP) retains its lead with 22.7 per cent.
The Finns Party, led by Finance Minister Riikka Purra, gained 0.2 percentage points from the previous survey, while support for Orpo’s NCP fell by 0.7 points.
The gap between the governing parties stands at just 0.2 percentage points, well within the survey’s margin of error of 1.8 points.
According to Yle, the NCP has not recorded such a low level of support in its polling series since late 2020. The Finns Party last ranked ahead of the NCP when both parties were in opposition at the beginning of the decade.
Tuomo Turja, research director at polling company Taloustutkimus, attributed the NCP’s decline partly to the government’s spending cuts.
"It was not surprising that support for the biggest governmental party declined. The government's saving measures are now fully showing at this stage of the mandate," Turja told Yle.
He said the NCP was losing former supporters to the Finns Party, while some voters remained undecided.
The survey also found that support for the NCP among women had fallen to 12.1 per cent. The SDP leads among female voters with more than 27 per cent, followed by the Left Alliance with more than 16 per cent.
The Finns Party has recovered nearly six percentage points since its low point in spring 2025, continuing a rise that has lasted more than a year.
Meanwhile, the Left Alliance reached a record 12.4 per cent, gaining 0.7 percentage points and closing the gap with the Centre Party, which fell to 12.6 per cent.
Turja told Yle that the Left Alliance had attracted voters from the SDP and Greens. The party has also distinguished itself by refusing to join a cross-party agreement on a debt brake intended to restrict government borrowing.
The Greens received 8.3 per cent support, followed by the Swedish People's Party on 3.6 per cent, the Christian Democrats on 3.4 per cent and Movement Now on 2.1 per cent.
The Centre Party, which previously held third place in Yle's polling, has seen its support settle at around 13 per cent despite criticism of the government over fuel prices.
Taloustutkimus conducted the survey for Yle between 7 September and 5 October, interviewing 2,807 people. Of those, 2,089 expressed a party preference. The margin of error is 1.8 percentage points in either direction.

South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:56:02 BST
18:56:02 KST

South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement on Thursday that "diplomacy should prevail over emotions".
"Despite Seoul's decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to restoring a constructive dialogue - even if it takes time," he said.
Earlier on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said in a statement it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
- Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
  - Published11 January 2025
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

UK scales back Jerusalem consulate after Israel dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:56:00 UTC
18:56:00 KST

UK scales back Jerusalem consulate after Israel dispute
October 8, 2026
Britain has withdrawn diplomats from its consulate in East Jerusalem after reaching an agreement with Israel over the future of the diplomatic mission.
According to Israel, the consulate had ceased operating in its previous capacity. Britain insisted that the building would remain open under the name UK Mission, Jerusalem.
The move follows a diplomatic dispute over British measures targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
What has happened to the British consulate?
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, were ending their assignments and leaving Israel.
Seven diplomats would be allowed to continue working from the building, although their activities would be "very limited," he said.
The consulate's diplomatic emblem and sign were removed from the building on Thursday.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said London had temporarily withdrawn some staff and their families to ensure their safety.
He insisted the mission would remain independent and operational, continuing to provide "vital services" and work with Palestinians.
Miliband said Britain did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which was established in 1838.
Why did Israel order the consulate to close?
Israel ordered the closure on September 8 in retaliation for British measures against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Britain joined other countries in announcing trade restrictions and sanctions targeting settlements and individuals linked to settler violence against Palestinians.
Israel condemned the measures as a diplomatic attack.
The British consulate has traditionally handled relations with Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, separately from Britain's embassy in Tel Aviv.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in 1967 and subsequently annexed it, a move not recognized by most countries, including Britain.
Miliband said Britain would not take retaliatory diplomatic action while talks with Israel continued.
He reaffirmed London's support for a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Kyiv announced in January 2025 that it had captured two North Korean soldiers during battles in Russia's western Kursk Oblast.
The two were among the many thousands dispatched by North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un in 2024 to bolster Russian forces in the border region, making North Korea the only country to send its serving forces to fight on Moscow’s side to date.

California's Proposition 40: the world's first billionaire tax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:53:33 UTC
18:53:33 KST

Breadcrumb
What is California's Proposition 40, the world's first billionaire tax?
Proposition 40 (or Prop 40), also known as the California billionaire tax or the California wealth tax, is a measure that appears on the upcoming California’s 2026 ballot in the United States.
Its aim is to impose a one-time 5% tax on the state’s 200 to 250 billionaires (by net worth) and use 90% the funds for healthcare and the remainder for other social services.
How did Prop 40 come about?
The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare have led to charge to get the measure on the ballot.
Working class advocates have long been pushing for a tax on billionaires, particularly after the 2025 Big Beautiful Bill that redirected funding for healthcare to immigration enforcement.
California has long had an extreme rate of wealth inequality. This was exacerbated during the pandemic, when some of the state’s top billionaires saw their wealth multiply. The state’s billionaires became $500 billion richer last year. Of the 100 wealthiest people in the world, around 85 reside in California as of September 2026.
Who supports Prop 40?
The measure is supported by former Democratic House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, Representative Ro Khanna of California, whose district has one of the highest concentrations of billionaires, and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont (an Independent who caucuses with the Democrats). Sanders is currently touring the state to advocate for Proposition 40.
“Once California passes Proposition 40, trust me, that will not be the end,” Sanders said at a recent rally in California. “If Ro and I have anything to say about it, and we do, we will enact a national wealth tax."
Other politicians, including Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts are pushing for similar measures. At a recent rally in California, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was asked if he supported the measure, he said he wouldn’t comment on California legislation, but that he would support a similar initiative (if it were proposed) in Michigan.
In addition, six Nobel prize-winning economists support the proposition.
Who opposes Prop 40?
Aside from the billionaires who would be taxed, the main opponents are California Governor Gavin Newsom, the California Police Chiefs Association, and the California Medical Association.
The billionaire opponents are spending over $200 million on TV ads against Proposition 40. Google founder Sergey Brin alone has spent $100 million opposing the measure.
In their ads, they say Proposition 40 has loopholes that would allow for middle-class tax increases. Sanders says that no one with less than a billion dollars would see a tax increase under the measure.

Jonathan the tortoise, the world’s oldest living land animal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:53:20 UTC
18:53:20 KST

Jonathan, a Seychelles giant tortoise, is believed to be around 194 years old, making him the world’s oldest living land animal and oldest tortoise ever recorded.
He is believed to have been brought to the island of St Helena in 1882 and still roams the grounds of the governor’s residence.
His extraordinary lifespan has made him one of the island’s best-known residents. False reports of his death have also circulated online, but Jonathan is still very much alive.

Russian, Ukrainian strikes leave at least 56 dead, over 100 injured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:53:09 UTC
18:53:09 KST

Russian and Ukrainian authorities reported deadly attacks on cities and infrastructure on Thursday as Moscow and Kiev continued to target each other amid escalating hostilities.
In Ukraine, a Russian missile attack on the northern city of Pryluky killed 22 people, including five children, and wounded more than 50, Chernihiv Governor Vyacheslav Chaus said on Thursday.
“Twenty-two people died in Pryluky. Among them were five children. Four died at the impact site, and one child died in the hospital,” Chaus said in a statement on Telegram.
Chaus also said a Russian strike hit the regional capital of Chernihiv on Wednesday, setting fire to a three-storey building. Ukraine’s Air Force said its air defences had shot down 117 of 130 strike drones and at least 44 ballistic and cruise missiles launched by Russia overnight.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian Kh-101 missile had struck a residential building in Pryluky, renewing calls for additional air defence systems and ammunition.
“The threat is there every day, and every day, our air defence batteries need to have missiles ready,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Kiev was counting on prompt deliveries and sufficient production by its partners.
A separate Russian strike on two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk has killed 30 people and wounded 18, local authorities said on Thursday.
The Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office said the death toll from the morning attack had risen to 30. The regional governor’s office confirmed the same toll and said public transport had been suspended.
Ukrainian drone attacks reported in Russia
Meanwhile, Russian authorities said a Ukrainian drone attack on the southern port city of Novorossiysk in the Krasnodar region killed four people, including a child, and wounded 29 others. Three of the injured were in serious condition, regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev said.
Kondratyev accused Ukraine of targeting civilians, saying damage was reported to three private homes, five apartment buildings, a church and a kindergarten.
Drone debris also damaged homes and a kindergarten in the nearby town of Anapa, though no casualties were reported there.
Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed its air defences had shot down 596 Ukrainian drones over 11 regions, as well as over the Black Sea and Ukraine’s Russian-annexed Crimea region.
Ukraine’s General Staff said it had struck the Novorossiysk naval base overnight, causing fires at the base and at an oil terminal in the city’s seaport. It described the base as an important hub for the Russian Black Sea Fleet’s ship basing, maintenance and logistical support. The claim could not be independently verified.
Fire sparked at Yandex data centre
A separate drone strike also sparked a fire at a data centre operated by Russian technology company Yandex in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, Russian state media TASS reported.
Yandex said the attack damaged part of its infrastructure, forcing it to suspend operations at the facility and potentially disrupting some services. The company reported no injuries.
Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov said two drones had been shot down over the region overnight, adding that a fire broke out at a local enterprise and windows were blown out in several private homes.
Moscow and Kiev have increasingly targeted each other’s logistics centres, ports and energy infrastructure in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, saying their attacks are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Lithuania plans 4.8 billion euros for defence in 2027, substantial budget deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:53:00 UTC
18:53:00 KST

Lithuania plans to allocate about 4.8 billion euros to defense next year, or slightly more than 5% of gross domestic product, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Thursday.
The planned allocation would be about 36 million euros higher than this year’s military budget. But because of economic growth, defence spending would account for a smaller share of GDP than this year, when the budget provided for 5.38%.
“The priorities for 2027 are to maintain 5% of gross domestic product for defence. As we mentioned, being in the 5% club remains our goal and will be implemented,” Sinkevičius told reporters.
He said the exact figure was still being discussed by the governing coalition and with Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, who wants defence spending to reach 5.1% of GDP.
“The actual amount, compared with this year’s allocated amount, will still grow, the percentage will decrease, but the actual amount allocated for defence and security will increase,” Sinkevičius said.
He stressed that increasing military spending must be accompanied by efficient and transparent use of the funds.
“Is the budget growth sufficient? You can say that the more, the better probably, but I say we need efficient, transparent, meaningful spending,” he said.
Among the government’s main priorities are air defence, the deployment of a German brigade in Lithuania and development of a national division, Sinkevičius said.
He added that 43.92% of this year's defence appropriations had been spent so far.
Lithuania has sought to maintain defence spending at 5% of GDP as it strengthens its military capabilities in response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and deepens NATO cooperation.
Deficit expected to exceed EU limit
Lithuania’s general government budget deficit is expected to reach about 3.8% of GDP next year, Sinkevičius said.
“It seems that the variation is currently about 3.8%,” he said at a news conference when asked about the projected deficit.
That would put Lithuania above the 3% deficit limit set under the European Union's fiscal rules.
Sinkevičius said the government had already made about 1.5 billion euros in planned spending cuts after negotiations to keep the deficit from rising further.
He has previously said that without allowing a larger deficit, the government would not be able to meet its commitments on military spending and other planned increases in expenditure.
The EU’s Maastricht criteria generally require member states to keep their general government deficit below 3% of GDP.
Criticism from Nemunas Dawn
Remigijus Žemaitaitis, chairman of the opposition Nemunas Dawn party, criticised the decision to maintain defence funding at its current level next year.
According to the lawmaker, defence acquisitions are delayed, scandals arise over the use of funds, and some purchases are made outside public procurement procedures. Žemaitaitis said some funds have already been paid in advance, but the goods will be delivered only in one or two years, so he proposed reducing the budget and completing projects already under way first.
Žemaitaitis said he sees no value in being in the so-called 5-percent club, referring to countries that allocate at least 5 percent of their gross domestic product to defence.
“We can leave that 5 percent club. What is the point of being in that club now if you sit in it and do not use the money? We did not use the money, we paid the advance invoices, and we will get the goods a year or two later. I ask, why throw such money into advances, better invest in education, invest in the economy, actually in raising the gross domestic product, in what boosts the economy and what will allow paying off debts in 2028, 2029,” the lawmaker said.

Iotova–Valchev ticket holds commanding lead in presidential election poll

Thursday, 8 October 2026, 12:00
PHOTO gallupinternational.bg
Font size
As Bulgaria’s presidential election campaign gets under way, a clear frontrunner has emerged, with one main challenger some way behind. This is according to a nationwide survey by Gallup International Balkan, conducted in late September and early October.
Incumbent President Iliana Iotova and her running mate Kiril Valchev lead with 44.9% support, followed by former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev, who served as acting Secretary General of the Interior Ministry in his cabinet, on 24.8%. The Vazrazhdane party’s presidential ticket of Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin is third with 10.9%.
The pollsters caution that the outcome of a possible run-off cannot be predicted simply from first-round voting intentions. Much will depend on how supporters of eliminated candidates vote and how effectively the parties mobilise their core voters.
Turnout in the 25 October election is expected to be lower than in the most recent parliamentary vote. The survey projects that between 2.3 million and 2.4 million people will cast their ballots, representing around 36% of eligible voters.

Ancient volcanoes, dinosaurs and healing mud in Pomorie’s planned geopark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:51:46 UTC
18:51:46 KST

News
Ancient volcanoes, dinosaurs and healing mud in Pomorie’s planned geopark
Thursday 8 October 2026 11:53
Thursday, 8 October 2026, 11:53
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Ancient volcanoes, traces of the age of dinosaurs and healing mud are among the attractions of a planned geopark on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast. The project, which would bring together natural, cultural and historical sites in what could become the country’s first geopark, was presented at the Dechko Stoev City Art Gallery in Pomorie. Developed by the Pomorie Local Action Group, it aims to attract more tourists and create new opportunities for local businesses.
“We have been working on this project for two years and will also apply for inclusion in UNESCO’s Global Geoparks Network,” said Pomorie Mayor Ivan Aleksiev. He hopes the geopark will give visitors more to see and do, while drawing tourists to places beyond the town’s best-known attractions.
The planned geopark will cover the whole of Pomorie municipality, as well as an area near the village of Golitsa in Dolni Chiflik municipality, Varna region. Among the sites it will include are three ancient volcanoes near Dabnik, Kableshkovo and Kamenar, the Pomorie Lagoon, Lake Pomorie, the salt pans and deposits of therapeutic mud.
Also included is an area near the village of Kozichino, where geological traces of events dating back some 66 million years have survived. They tell the story of one of the great turning points in Earth’s history – the mass extinction that brought an end to the age of the non-avian dinosaurs.

Gallup: Yotova-Valchev Lead With 44.9% Ahead of Bulgaria’s Presidential Vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:51:35 UTC
18:51:35 KST

The presidential ticket of Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev leads Bulgaria’s presidential race with 44.9% support, according to a nationally representative survey by Gallup International Balkan conducted between September 26 and October 6, 2026.
Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev rank second with 24.8%, while Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin are third with 10.9%.
The remaining tickets included Ivan Hristanov and Stoyanka Cherkezova with 4.1%, Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov with 2.6%, Nikolay Nenchev and Tsveta Kirilova with 2.1%, Ivaylo Simeonov and Kosyo Stoychev with 1.7%, and Ivelin Mihaylov and Yuliana Mateeva with 1.6%.
Gallup expects turnout to be lower than at the last parliamentary elections, estimating that between 2.3 million and 2.4 million voters, or about 36%, will cast ballots on October 25.
The survey found that 52.8% of those firmly intending to vote had already made their choice before the campaign began, describing their decision as “traditional.”
“This indicates the presence of stable and loyal electoral cores supporting the political forces behind the leading candidates. This type of vote is relatively predictable and less susceptible to short-term campaign events - such as political scandals, damaging revelations, or specific media controversies. Thus, these core bases provide fundamental electoral stability for the candidacies backed by major political formations,” Gallup sociologists said.
The researchers said the race at the beginning of the campaign is characterized by a clear leader and a distinct second-place contender. The substantial gap between the two leading tickets and the rest, combined with the expected low turnout, makes a runoff between them the most likely outcome based on current voter sentiment.
Gallup also cautioned that first-round support cannot by itself determine the result of a second round. The eventual outcome will depend on how supporters of eliminated candidates vote, how strongly party bases whose candidates did not reach the runoff are mobilized, and whether the two finalists can win over undecided and peripheral voters.
One in three voters, or 34.7%, said they would make their final decision during the campaign. The survey found that 12.5% decide only at the end of the campaign, including 9.8% in the final days and 2.7% on election day.
The poll found that a candidate’s personality is the decisive consideration for 38.9% of voters, with professional and public reputation, personal charisma, public conduct and background among the factors shaping that choice.
For 24.4% of respondents, the parties supporting a candidate are the determining factor. Gallup said this influence is strongest among core party voters, for whom the presidential choice largely follows established political preferences.
Candidates’ positions on Bulgaria’s foreign policy and geopolitical orientation are decisive for 15.6% of voters. This is more than the 10.1% who identify the overall election platform as their main reason for supporting a candidate.
The survey found that attitudes toward strategic partnerships, European integration, security and major geopolitical divisions could therefore affect the final result.
More than half of voters supporting GERB and the DPS, which are not fielding their own presidential candidates, do not intend to vote on October 25, according to the survey. Gallup said their possible mobilization in a runoff could influence the balance because of the expected low turnout.
The poll was conducted through standardized face-to-face interviews using tablets among 987 adult Bulgarian citizens. Respondents were selected through quota sampling based on age, gender, education and type of settlement.
Fieldwork was carried out from September 26 to October 6, 2026. The survey is nationally representative of Bulgaria’s adult population, with the sample reflecting the country’s demographic structure by gender, age, education and type of settlement.
The maximum statistical margin of error is ±3.2% at a 95% confidence level for a 50% share within the main sample. The research is part of Gallup International Balkan’s independent research program and was self-funded.

====================================================================================================

US probes EU carbon border tax over potential trade barriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:50:58 UTC
18:50:58 KST

The EU's carbon border tax was designed to prevent companies from shifting production abroad to countries with weaker environmental rules — but the US says it amounts to a discriminatory trade rule.
Washington is investigating whether the European Union's carbon border tax is harming US trade and whether plans to expand it would create unfair barriers for American companies, according to an official document published on Thursday.
The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) took effect in January 2026, covering imports of aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, iron and steel.
It aims to level the playing field between European manufacturers and foreign competitors while preventing carbon-intensive production from shifting to countries with weaker climate rules.
Shortly after its launch, several EU countries sought temporarily exemptions for fertilisers, warning that the tax would push up prices and could undermine food security.
Under CBAM, EU importers must monitor and report emissions generated in producing the goods they bring into the bloc. Washington argues that the system is creating financial liabilities for American companies, raising the prospect of fresh trade tensions with President Donald Trump's administration.
The timing is significant. Brussels is negotiating plans to extend CBAM to more products, including washing machines and car parts, while tightening rules to prevent companies from circumventing the tax.
"The USTR (Office of the United States Representative) is seeking comments on the impact of the CBAM on US trade with the EU, as well as the potential impact of the EU’s proposals to expand CBAM coverage. Such comments will help inform continued USTR and US government engagement with the EU on CBAM," the document says.
Washington will examine the impact on costs, regulatory burdens and access to the EU market for American producers, as well as direct and indirect exports and overall trade with the bloc. US companies have until November 9 to submit their views.
The move comes shortly after the World Trade Organisation (WTO) agreed to establish a panel at Russia's request to examine the legality of CBAM. Moscow argues that the carbon border tax creates "significant trade barriers" for goods entering the EU.
Russia also claims that free carbon allowances granted to some heavy industries under the EU's Emissions Trading System (ETS) amount to an "export subsidy" designed to give European manufacturers a competitive advantage, according to the WTO.
EU splits
Within the EU, governments and the European Parliament remain divided over plans to expand CBAM, particularly over which products should be covered, according to a Council document seen by Euronews.
The European Commission says the expansion is intended to prevent carbon-intensive imports from escaping the bloc's climate rules.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU Council presidency and is brokering negotiations, says both governments and Parliament consider the Commission's proposed expansion too narrow. But they disagree over which additional products to include.
Belgium Green MEP Sarah Matthieu told Euronews that the EU should include critical clean tech goods such as solar panels and heat pumps.
Such a move would protect European manufacturers, but critics argue it would also push up prices for businesses and consumers.
The Irish Presidency, which wants to seal the deal at a key meeting on 20 October, has asked EU capitals to identify which Parliament proposals they could accept and where they would be ready to compromise.
Dispute over carbon calculations
Another sticking point is the Commission's proposal to allow certain goods to be temporarily exempted from CBAM in "serious and unforeseen circumstances".
MEPs oppose the measure, arguing that it could weaken the mechanism and give the Commission excessive powers without sufficient parliamentary scrutiny. Instead, they favour financial support for affected industries through redistribution from EU funds.
MEPs also want a tougher system to automatically apply default carbon values to high-risk goods and origins unless specific exceptions are met.
The Council is more flexible, allowing companies to continue using their actual emissions data if they can provide sufficient evidence.
CBAM's default values are calculated using country-specific, sectoral and energy data to estimate the emissions generated in producing imported goods.
Washington, however, argues that the "EU adds a punitive markup" to these estimates, effectively penalising companies that do not provide their own emissions data.
The Irish Presidency has asked governments whether Parliament's approach could create practical difficulties for importers and national authorities – concerns also raised by Washington.
According to the US document, Washington will assess the Commission's original proposal and the competing positions of the Council and Parliament to determine how each could affect American companies compared with their European rivals.
The Commission did not respond to a Euronews request for comment at the time of publication.

Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:49:50 UTC
18:49:50 KST

Russia is concentrating missiles on a smaller, more specific set of targets, and its jet-powered attack drones are part of the reason, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed. Its combined attack overnight on 7 October killed 22 people in Pryluky, the State Emergency Service (SES) said as of the morning of 8 October. Russian milbloggers noted the shift the same day.
Russia often uses concentrated drone and missile strikes to overwhelm localized Ukrainian air defenses and destroy urban centers, ISW noted. Pryluky, where the strike killed children, was one of the areas a Russian channel says drew a significant share of the Kh-101s that night. With winter close, ISW expects the same pattern against Ukraine's energy grid, with jet drones partly letting Russia keep its missiles for priority targets without firing many more.
Missile waves on a few areas, Russian channels claim
Russia launched 48 Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr cruise missiles overnight on 7 October, Ukraine's Air Force reported. It also fired ballistic missiles, Zircon and Oniks anti-ship missiles, and 130 strike and decoy drones, 46 of them jet-powered Shahed-type models.
Russian milbloggers claimed the same day that Moscow had grouped a large part of its missile salvo into repeated waves on a few areas, while other weapons kept stretching Ukraine's air defenses elsewhere. The pro-war Russian Telegram channel Dva Mayora described the change as a switch from striking with splayed fingers to a series of hits with missile "fists." Defenders must then absorb a sharply rising load around one chosen site as one wave follows another, the channel claimed.
Citing Ukrainian monitoring channels, it claimed that roughly 30 or more Kh-101 cruise missiles flew toward Pryluky, Kremenchuk, Svitlovodsk, and Oleksandriia in Chernihiv, Poltava, and Kirovohrad oblasts. It put the Kremenchuk group at up to 15 missiles, Kh-101s and Kalibrs among them, aimed at the area of Kremenchuk and its hydroelectric plant.
Jet drones take some of the load off Russia's missiles
ISW said the jet-powered versions penetrate Ukrainian air defenses deeper and more reliably than propeller models. In ISW's assessment, that partly lets Russia concentrate cruise and ballistic missiles on priority targets without significantly raising missile use. Russia builds about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones a month, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) told Militarnyi in August.
Ukraine spent three years learning to catch Russian drones—so Russia made them fly faster
ISW expects Russia to apply the pattern in a likely brutal winter campaign against energy infrastructure. Russia likely intends to make city life untenable and force Ukraine to capitulate to its demands, ISW assessed. Such tactics have not worked before and are unlikely to work now, analysts added.
They called cheap countermeasures to jet drones and small cruise missiles vital, alongside Western air defense aid such as US-made Patriots, which can stop ballistic missiles. Ukraine has already paired a Soviet-era Kub launcher with American RIM-7 interceptors to catch jet drones.

Meanwhile, Canadian merchandise exports to France rose 53 percent in the first seven months of 2026 from the same period last year, said Global Affairs Canada, the country's foreign ministry.
The figures reflect a broader shift as Canada's export reliance on traditional markets has narrowed while exports to the rest of the world expanded, as Ottawa sought to diversify its trade partners. ■

RCEP fuels Cambodia's trade surge despite global headwinds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
17:49:18 CST
18:49:18 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's trade with Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) member states rose 21.3 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, driven by tariff preferences and trade facilitation, official data showed on Thursday.
According to a report from the Ministry of Commerce, the Southeast Asian country recorded 35.79 billion U.S. dollars in trade with RCEP countries during the January-September period, up from 29.5 billion dollars during the same period last year.
Exports to RCEP members increased by 8.1 percent to 8.03 billion dollars, while imports climbed 25.7 percent to reach 27.76 billion dollars.
The RCEP free trade pact remains Cambodia's largest market, accounting for 61.2 percent of the country's 58.48-billion-dollar total global trade volume over the nine-month period.
China, Vietnam, Singapore, Japan, and Thailand rank as Cambodia's top five trading partners within the bloc.
Coming into effect in 2022, the RCEP unites 15 Asia-Pacific nations, combining 10 ASEAN member states with China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand.
Penn Sovicheat, a secretary of state and spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce, said that the pact has played a vital role in accelerating trade growth locally, regionally, and globally.
"The RCEP is a driving force for our long-term trade growth and a major catalyst for drawing foreign direct investment to Cambodia," he told Xinhua.
Sovicheat said this mega-trade deal, together with other bilateral free trade agreements, will lift Cambodia out of its least developed country status by 2029.
"It provides the economic foundation needed to achieve our goals of becoming an upper-middle-income nation by 2030 and a high-income country by 2050," he said.
Kin Phea, director general of the International Relations Institute of Cambodia, a think tank under the Royal Academy of Cambodia, said that the pact serves as a stabilizing anchor for regional economic integration.
He noted that the deal helps counter global trade headwinds driven by geopolitical conflict, rising transportation costs, and policy uncertainty, even as surging demand for artificial intelligence hardware and technology provides a powerful economic offset.
"Amid rising protectionism and geopolitical rivalries, RCEP proves the enduring value of cooperation," Phea told Xinhua. "Its inclusive framework offers a vital blueprint for stability against global trade headwinds."
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said that RCEP has proven indispensable for safeguarding Cambodia's trade diversification against global protectionism.
"The substantial growth in Cambodia's trade with RCEP partners proves its real-world value," he told Xinhua. "However, Cambodia should focus on narrowing the import-export gap by boosting domestic production and high-value exports."
Mengdavid added that the mega-pact remains a core economic anchor for the kingdom and the wider world.
"Globally, RCEP has unlocked an immense transformative potential. By gradually eliminating tariffs on over 90 percent of goods, it has catalyzed a more robust, integrated, and cost-effective ecosystem for international trade," he said. "Moving forward, the agreement remains central to anchoring the region's economic stability in an increasingly unpredictable global market." ■

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China on Thursday unveiled a plan to expand and improve medical rehabilitation and nursing care services, with measures to increase service resources, strengthen professional training and promote the use of artificial intelligence (AI).
Under an implementation plan issued by the National Health Commission and the National Development and Reform Commission, cities with large populations, a rapidly aging population and growing demand for rehabilitation and nursing care services are expected to have at least one public rehabilitation hospital and one public nursing care facility by 2030.
The plan also aims to provide about 0.48 rehabilitation and nursing care beds per 1,000 people, as well as 0.7 rehabilitation physicians and 1.6 rehabilitation therapists per 10,000 people, by 2030.

The plan prioritizes support for cities at the prefecture level and above with more than 1 million urban residents in expanding and improving medical rehabilitation and nursing care services.
It urges improvements to rehabilitation and nursing care disciplines and programs at universities and vocational colleges, including appropriately expanding enrollment and better aligning training with employment.
Efforts will also focus on ensuring key departments, including intensive care, orthopedics and neurology, have medical professionals with specialized rehabilitation and nursing care skills.
The plan highlights the use of AI in rehabilitation and nursing care services, encouraging the adoption of rehabilitation robots, smart wearable devices and other technologies to support the monitoring of multiple health indicators and provide intelligent rehabilitation training and health management services.
In July, China's State Council unveiled a national health plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), aiming to raise the country's average life expectancy to 80 years by 2030.
It identifies expanding and improving rehabilitation and nursing care services as an important part of broader efforts to develop a high-quality, efficient and integrated healthcare service system. ■

It is documented, substantiated and anchored in a legal record that the world can no longer ignore."
The event, titled "Standing With Truth," brought together Elkayam-Levy, founder and chair of the Civil Commission investigating Hamas' October 7 crimes against women, children and families, and Professor Carol Gilligan, one of the most influential figures in contemporary feminist scholarship.
Gilligan, whose work has shaped decades of thinking about women's voices, ethics, listening and responsibility, praised the commission's efforts to document sexual violence committed during the October 7 attacks and against hostages held in Gaza.
"Denial was one of the most painful manifestations of the rampant antisemitism we have witnessed in recent years," Gilligan said. "You exposed the truth. You broke the silence surrounding one of the deepest sources of pain for Jewish women around the world."
Gilligan said the commission had accomplished the difficult task of transforming accounts of atrocities into an evidentiary record capable of supporting legal accountability. "We stood behind you, and you succeeded in the hardest task of all: turning testimony that others tried to silence into legal truth and laying an evidentiary foundation that can endure for generations," she said.
The discussion came nearly five months after the commission published Silenced No More: Sexual Terror Unveiled, a report of nearly 300 pages examining sexual and gender-based violence committed during the Hamas-led October 7 attacks and against hostages in captivity.
The report draws on years of documentation, investigation and analysis involving thousands of pieces of evidence and witness accounts. It presents the commission's extensive factual findings and legal analysis of the crimes, intended to support accountability efforts and preserve the historical record.
Elkayam-Levy said the report marked a turning point in an effort that began as an urgent attempt to document atrocities before evidence could be lost or dismissed. "What began as an urgent effort to document atrocities became a struggle for truth itself," she said.
She emphasized that the commission's work was not limited to publishing its findings. Its archive was designed to preserve evidence over the long term, ensuring that survivor testimony and documentation remain accessible to future generations.
"Our responsibility now is to ensure that this truth remains strong decades from now," Elkayam-Levy said. "The archive we established will carry this truth forward for generations. The report and evidence are already being used in legal proceedings and will continue to serve the pursuit of justice."
She added that establishing the facts was only the beginning of a broader process of accountability. "The question is what we do once we know," she said. "How do we translate that knowledge into justice and reparations for survivors and families, and how do we turn remembrance into a responsibility to change reality?"
Rabbi Yehuda Sarna, NYU's university chaplain and former chief rabbi of the Jewish community in the United Arab Emirates, also addressed the gathering, emphasizing the responsibility of academic institutions to engage seriously with difficult testimony.
"Universities are places where young people learn not only what to think, but how to hold difficult truths with seriousness, humility and care," Sarna said.
He described the commission's work as an essential resource for students and the wider university community, praising its careful and humane documentation of the October 7 atrocities. "At NYU, where people from many different backgrounds come together, this conversation challenges us to ask: How do we listen when testimony is painful? How do we resist denial? And how do we allow truth to shape our responsibilities?" he said.
The event was attended by NYU faculty members and students, as well as researchers, public figures and other guests.
Three years after the massacre, the Civil Commission continues its efforts to preserve testimony, safeguard evidence and support legal accountability for the crimes committed on October 7 and during captivity.
For Elkayam-Levy, the challenge now is to ensure that the documentation becomes more than a record of the past, serving instead as a foundation for justice, prevention and remembrance. "The archive we established will carry this truth forward for generations," she said.

Animal shelter in Odesa Oblast comes under Russian attack: fire extinguished
An animal shelter in Odesa Oblast has come under Russian attack for the second time in two weeks – this time, the Liubov i Laska (Love and Tenderness) shelter was targeted. A fire broke out on the premises but has since been extinguished.
Source: Oleh Kiper, Head of Odesa Oblast Military Administration; State Emergency Service in Odesa Oblast on Facebook
Details: One dog was killed in the fire and several others were injured.
The fire initially broke out in a car park, where 14 cars caught fire. Another 13 vehicles were damaged by the fire.
The fire later spread to the animal shelter, damaging enclosures and a fence, but firefighters prevented the building from being destroyed.
Despite the firefighters' efforts, one dog was killed and four others were injured. The fire has now been extinguished, and efforts to deal with its aftermath are ongoing.
Shelter head Liubov Kudriavtseva reported that six enclosures had burned down and windows in outbuildings were shattered by the blast wave. Animal welfare organisation UAnimals said that the shelter is caring for 153 dogs, eight of them puppies.
"Shelter head Liubov Kudriavtseva says that the dogs have experienced severe stress and are now frightened [...] We are currently delivering 400 kg of food to the shelter, but it is critically important to rebuild the enclosures so that the animals have somewhere to spend the winter," the organisation added.
The shelter is calling on people to help with the rebuilding effort. It needs materials, skilled workers, animal food and financial assistance.
Kudriavtseva said: "Please help Liubov i Laska withstand this and recover. If you can help physically, please contact us. If you can help financially, we will be immensely grateful for every hryvnia [...]
Do not let our furry friends be left without a safe home. We need you very much!"
Background:
- On 29 September, the Liubliatchi Sertsia (Loving Hearts) animal shelter was hit by a Russian attack. Russian forces struck one of the shelter's buildings, causing a large-scale fire covering more than 400 sq m. The fire also reached the premises where the shelter's head, Olha Shymilina, lived. Three dogs and 10 cats were killed in the fire. The shelter also lost all its food supplies.
- On 7 October, the Sadyba Niushanik bird sanctuary in Kyiv Oblast came under attack. A total of 190 birds were killed and all the equipment was destroyed. The sanctuary also lost medical supplies and bird rehabilitation equipment, while almost one tonne of food for the birds was destroyed.
