Turkish government domestic borrowing securities (DİBS) delivered the highest monthly real return in September, according to data released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) on Oct. 8.
TÜİK said DİBS generated a monthly real return of 1.4 percent when adjusted for the consumer price index (CPI), making it the best-performing investment instrument in September.
Gross deposit interest rates provided a real return of 1.19 percent on a CPI-adjusted basis, while the U.S. dollar, euro, gold bullion and the BIST 100 index posted real losses of 0.22 percent, 0.89 percent, 2.02 percent and 5.79 percent, respectively.
In the three months to September, gross deposit interest rates recorded the highest real return among investment instruments at 4.11 percent when adjusted for CPI. Over the same period, the BIST 100 index was the worst-performing asset, posting a real loss of 9.29 percent.
Over a six-month horizon, gross deposit interest rates again delivered the strongest CPI-adjusted real return at 3.15 percent, while gold bullion generated the largest loss at 15.73 percent.
On an annual basis, gold bullion provided the highest real return, rising 5.3 percent when adjusted for CPI.
During the same period, DİBS returned 3.93 percent in real terms, while gross deposit interest rates yielded a 0.32 percent real gain. The BIST 100 index, the U.S. dollar and the euro posted losses of 4.56 percent, 9.26 percent and 10.97 percent, respectively.

Yemen’s Houthi rebels claimed Thursday that they had hit Saudi Arabia’s main international airport in Riyadh with a missile, while Saudi authorities said three people were killed and 36 wounded in attacks on two international airports.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on X that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile and disrupted airport operations.
“Our armed forces successfully targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile, which accurately struck its target and disrupted airport operations,” Saree said.
The Houthis said the Riyadh airport strike killed three people and injured several others, and claimed it was the third time this week they had targeted the airport.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said attacks on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport took place on Tuesday and Wednesday, targeting facilities at both airports.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, while a Sudanese national died at the Riyadh airport, the authority said. A total of 36 people were wounded.
The Saudi-led military coalition supporting pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it had destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform used in the attack on Riyadh.
The coalition later directly blamed Houthi forces and said it would retaliate.
“The brutal attacks by the Terrorist Houthi Militia on civilian and civilian objects in the Kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished,” the coalition said on X.
The coalition said it had subsequently destroyed 82 “legitimate military targets,” including mountain-based Houthi ballistic missile facilities, command-and-control centers, communication systems and gathering sites.
The conflict in Yemen has increasingly spread beyond the country’s borders since fighting resumed in July.
Saudi Arabia has backed Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which announced a major counteroffensive against the Houthis a day earlier as it seeks to retake additional territory.
The Houthis, who control most of northwestern Yemen, are fighting Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July, when the group captured large areas of the coastline.
The United Nations said Wednesday that more than 200,000 people have been displaced within Yemen.
This week, the Yemeni government said its forces had driven Houthi fighters from strategic positions along the Red Sea coast and around the port city of Mocha. The Iran-backed Houthis, however, said they were holding their territory, while military sources from both sides contacted by AFP reported no major changes on the ground.
The warring parties’ claims could not be independently verified because the situation is changing rapidly and journalists face difficult access.
The Saudi-led coalition said the missile fired at Riyadh had been intercepted, while the Houthis also claimed to have targeted a military supply convoy near Aden, the interim capital of Yemen’s government.
The government’s Saba news agency reported that missiles and drones had targeted the airport in Aden. Citing transport authorities, it said one missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to arrive, forcing the aircraft to divert to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia.
Saree also said Houthi drones and missiles had targeted Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, claiming they had “hit their targets accurately”.
The Houthis also warned passenger airlines against using Saudi airspace.
“We reiterate our call and warning, for the last time, to all international airlines against continuing to operate flights through Saudi airspace,” Saree said.
The Houthis had claimed a second attack on Riyadh’s main airport earlier in the week.
Saudi Arabia has led an international coalition against the Houthis since 2015 and is now supporting the Yemeni government’s effort to reverse the group’s latest advance.
The coalition said Monday that it was providing air support for the government’s counteroffensive.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen’s civil war resumed in July. The Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea last month in the deadliest fighting the country had seen in years.
New fighting in western Yemen on Wednesday killed at least 62 combatants, including 37 Houthis, according to military sources from both sides who spoke to AFP.
Saba also reported that the Houthis fired a missile at Taiz, a city controlled by government forces, injuring five civilians.
“We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit. The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians,” resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
Yemen’s government has said it aims to retake all territory held by the Houthis, much of which has been under the group’s control for more than a decade and is home to most of the country’s population.
The war has created a humanitarian crisis that has left most of Yemen’s population dependent on aid.
Mohammed, a 33-year-old charity worker who fled Mocha for Aden, told AFP Tuesday that “people there are terrified” of the Houthis.

‘Putting biodiversity in our hands’: Four animals selected to feature on UK banknotes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:10:37 UTC
18:10:37 KST

Four animals have been selected to feature on new UK banknotes following a public vote with almost half a million participants.
Historical figures like Winston Churchill will soon be replaced by native wildlife on UK banknotes.
In a public consultation run by the Bank of England, the theme of nature came out on top. A panel of experts then selected a shortlist of plants and animals to be put to the vote.
Half a million people had their say, and the results are now in: the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will represent UK wildlife and feature as the central images on the country's next series of banknotes.
“Nature is more than just scenery, it is the living thread that binds our landscapes, our history, and our future together,” says Scottish wildlife filmmaker Gordon Buchanan, who was part of the expert panel that compiled the shortlist. “To protect nature is to protect the quiet, resilient heartbeat of the land itself.”
Not only could the new notes inspire wildlife conservation, they’re also well positioned to protect the economy.
“The key driver for introducing a new banknote series is always to increase counterfeit resilience,” says Victoria Cleland, chief cashier at the Bank of England.
“Nature is a great choice from a banknote authentication perspective,” she adds, because it lends itself to developing security features that are easy for the public to recognise and distinguish.
Symbolic recognition of UK wildlife ‘overdue and significant’
Nature was the most popular theme among 44,000 respondents in the initial July 2025 consultation, capturing 60 per cent of the vote.
It will replace the current historical figures featured on the reverse side of banknotes, which include writer Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and scientist Alan Turing, as well as the WWII Prime Minister.
“This is a powerful reminder of how deeply people feel connected to and value British wildlife,” says Ali Fisher, founder and director of sustainability consultancy Plans with Purpose. “It’s a beautiful opportunity to put biodiversity literally in all our hands.”
Architecture and Landmarks was the second most popular at 56 per cent, followed by Notable Historical Figures (38 per cent), Arts, Culture and Sport (30 per cent), Innovation (23 per cent) and Noteworthy Milestones (19 per cent).
“The wildlife of the UK is not separate from our culture. It sits in our football crests, our folklore, our coastlines and our childhoods,” says wildlife presenter and activist Nadeem Perera, another panel member. “Giving it space on something as symbolic as our currency feels both overdue and significant.”
How were animals selected for the new banknotes?
A panel of UK wildlife experts compiled a shortlist of 18 options across three categories: mammals; birds; and amphibians, insects and fish.
In the birds category, voters could choose between the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, common kingfisher, Eurasian curlew, great spotted woodpecker and white-tailed eagle. While the amphibians, insects and fish line up included the Atlantic salmon, basking shark, buff-tailed bumblebee, common frog, emperor dragonfly and marsh fritillary butterfly.
Nearly 500,000 members of the public voted, and the Bank of England used the feedback from the consultation to decide on the four animals, one for each denomination of banknote.
The barn owl (Tyto alba), buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) and European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) were the most popular animals in their respective categories.
As the most popular marine animal, the Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica) was included to add variety, making the denominations easier to distinguish, and as an opportunity to "celebrate the British coastline".
Additional imagery on the banknote designs could include other shortlisted animals. They will also continue to include a portrait of the monarch.
'Underdog' animals excluded from banknote shortlist
The RSPA called for Britain's "least-loved" wildlife – such as pigeons, gulls and foxes – to feature on the new banknotes. The charity said this could help change perceptions of "misunderstood" animals and encourage people to see the value of all wildlife.
“What about the pigeons who have been our friends for thousands of years, or rats, with their amazing memories, or even gulls, with their amazing levels of intelligence?," said Geoff Edmond, wildlife expert at the RSPCA. "They are all fascinating wild animals in their own right – and deserve recognition too.”
While pigeons and rats didn't make the final cut, the red fox was an option alongside the pine marten, grey seal, European hedgehog, brown hare and bottlenose dolphin.
"It's great that the Bank of England has pulled together a diverse shortlist... although we would love to see more animal underdogs make the cut," said Dr Ros Clubb, Head of Wild Animals at the RSPCA, following the announcement of the final shortlist.
When will the new UK banknotes enter circulation?
It could be a while before the new nature-based banknotes reach British wallets. The Bank of England explains that they take a number of years to design, test and print, to ensure they are high-quality, resilient and accessible.
The decision on which animal will feature on which denomination is also yet to be made.
It is expected that the first denomination from the next series will be launched over the next few years.
From Norway to Switzerland: Which other European countries champion nature on their notes?
The Bank of England won’t be the first in Europe to give nature a place on its banknotes. Scottish notes already include animals such as mackerel, otters and red squirrels.
Norway’s latest krone series celebrates its long coastline by featuring wave motifs and Atlantic cod and herring.
Switzerland began shifting away from featuring famous personalities on its banknotes in 2016, with wind, water and light among the stars of its ‘many facets of Switzerland’ series. Butterflies, the Alps and dandelion seeds now grace its currency, with a new series set to double-down on native plants and Alpine landscapes in the 2030s.
Nature could also replace architecture on future euro banknotes, with the European Central Bank considering designs featuring birds and rivers across Europe.
Following a contest for EU designers to submit proposals in 2025, the shortlisted themes are ‘Rivers and birds: resilience in diversity’ and ‘European culture: shared cultural spaces’. A final decision is expected to be made in 2026.
“In a cost‑of‑living, climate and nature crisis, small cultural shifts like this matter,” says Fisher. “They help normalise the idea that our natural world is worth celebrating, protecting and investing in.”

Dutch firm uses AI to help drone systems 'talk' on Ukraine's battlefield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:10:02 UTC
18:10:02 KST

Dutch firm uses AI to help drone systems 'talk' on Ukraine's battlefield
KATWIJK AAN ZEE, Netherlands, Oct 8 - A high-velocity drone launched at a disused Dutch airbase by the North Sea roars through the clouds and intercepts a mock enemy target detected by radar and verified using artificial intelligence.
The test by software company Intelic, which has a €30-million ($33.5-million) contract with the Dutch Defence Ministry to upgrade its air defences, is an example of how technology is being developed and provided to Ukraine by European companies to help it defend itself against Russian attacks.
Amsterdam-based Intelic, one of scores of firms operating out of converted hangars at the airbase, now has an office in Kyiv and is helping Ukrainian forces as they face intensified Russian drone and missile barrages in a war in which drones have transformed the battlefield and driven rapid innovation.
In the test in late September, Intelic's AI-powered software, Nexus, used multiple radars, sensors and cameras provided by other companies to identify the projectile as an enemy attack. A reconnaissance drone then verified it was an enemy drone with image recognition.
Although a human made the final decision to launch the AI-guided interceptor drone, the process could be fully autonomous, said Intelic CEO and founder Maurits Korthals Altes.
"Most of these systems use AI at the edge, so in the drone itself, to be able to hit a target, a flying drone for instance, and then actually get intercepted at high speeds," he said.
"But you can also have AI for decision support," for example by assisting a commander in the field, when there is sometimes a window of only a few seconds to decide whether or not to fire on an incoming jet-propelled drone.
The integration between the different systems enables a commander to make such decisions quickly. At high speeds, Korthals Altes said, "you're not so likely to hit it manually, and you need a more autonomous system."
The Dutch government's investment is part of a spending push by the NATO country, which has allocated about €1.4 billion since 2022 to Ukraine's drone programme, making it one of Europe's leading contributors along with Germany and Britain, figures from the Kiel Institute in Germany show.
'CONNECTING TISSUE'
Since 2022, the Netherlands has provided military aid to Ukraine worth more than €12.5 billion, including nearly 1 million drones, the Defence Ministry said.
The Kiel Institute, which tracks military spending in Ukraine, said European aid for drones had jumped from €400 million in 2022, the year of Russia's full-scale invasion, to €1.2 billion in 2025. The figure rose to €1.6 billion in the first four months of 2026 alone, it said.
Kyiv has increasingly sought support from allies to boost its air defences, but European companies provide many different types of drones, which do not always "talk" to each other.
"Right now in Europe, there are over 700 drone manufacturers, and if we want to stay sovereign within Europe, we need to be able to have a system that is the connecting tissue between those different systems," said Anika Kempter, a senior software engineer at Intelic.
She said Ukrainian brigades "might have different drones of different types from different vendors with different screens. Nexus solves this problem. So they can connect all of their drones in one system."
DRONE TECHNOLOGY RACE
During the airbase test, engineers hovered over screens in a mobile command post using an interface that for the first time brings together radar target detection, AI verification and interceptor drones. Each component could be individually selected and operated from the single control panel.
Intelic's command-and-control system is being rolled out on Ukraine's battlefield, where operational decisions are sometimes still communicated via chat apps or phone calls. It supplements Delta, Ukraine's own advanced battlefield management system.
Replacing human communication with autonomous systems shaves minutes off the time between when a drone is detected and forces try to shoot it down, potentially meaning the difference between life and death, Kempter said.
Russia now uses jet-propelled attack drones that fly at high altitude. In the first three weeks of September, Russia launched 2,100 such drones and 136 missiles at Ukraine, killing 288 people, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said.
Drone technology develops so quickly that air-defence hardware can rapidly become obsolete and need upgrading, but Intelic's software can bridge the gap by adding new weapon systems to the platform, said Korthals Altes.
"That's very important in an environment that's unpredictable," he said. "Because nobody really knows how a war or threat would look ... in two years. We have an idea, but we don't know for sure. So that adaptability is key." REUTERS

India on Thursday denied Elon Musk's claim that “certain oligarchs” were blocking Starlink's satellite communication services in the country to maintain their monopoly, terming it baseless.
Without directly naming Musk, India’s Communications Ministry said in a statement that the government has put in “place a fair and non-discriminatory authorisation framework for all telecommunication services, including satellite communication services.”

Two Indian telecom companies, Bharti Airtel and Reliance Jio, signed pacts with SpaceX last year to bring Starlink internet services to the country.
Musk wrote on his platform X that “unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people.”
“You can guess who they are … This is a crime against the people of India!,” he said, responding to a post related to Starlink operations in the world's most populous nation.
India has 958 million internet users, with over 70% internet penetration rate.
Last year, Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Musk in Washington, DC to discuss space, mobility, technology and governance.

Students have blocked entrances to hundreds of high schools across the country since late September, and protests have on occasion been attacked by riot police.
Student union leaders urged fresh mobilisation across France Thursday, with a rally planned in the capital Paris and national education unions calling a general strike in support.
While many rallies have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police—with unions, rights groups and the children saying the police is using disproportionate force.
In a televised address Wednesday evening, the prime minister Sebastien Lecornu attempted to calm tensions, promising a plan to respond to the crisis by the end of October.
Although Lecornu denied that security forces have "orders to confront" minors, many students were unconvinced.
Outside one high school in Rennes, around 60 students had already gathered early Thursday.
Hanaa, an 18-year-old student, told AFP she was "disappointed and unconvinced" by Lecornu's remarks.
"We expected more from him," agreed fellow student Salyna, 17, who said they were also disappointed the government response would not be announced until the end of the month. "This is an urgent situation".
Student 'dialogue'
Suzanne Nijdam, president of university student association FAGE, said they did not have "even the crumbs of an agreement" after a meeting with the higher education minister Philippe Baptiste.
She called for protests to continue outside high schools and government administrative offices Thursday, with "larger-scale demonstrations next week".
As the government tried to adopt a conciliatory tone, education minister Edouard Geffray was to visit a high school in Reims and take part in a "dialogue" with students.
And a fresh meeting between the three main student associations with Geffray and Baptiste was planned for Thursday afternoon.
The students have asked for a direct meeting with Lecornu to present what they say are costed proposals to address their demands.
Student demonstrators—many attending high schools called lycees for children aged between 15 and 18 years old—have complained of missing teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
Classes were partially or completely suspended in 375 schools across the country on Thursday morning, according to the education ministry.
At a high school in Paris, AFP saw adult protesters forming a human chain with their arms between police and protesting teenagers, who huddled together carrying backpacks and placards.
Access to the school had been blockaded with bins and railings, and AFP saw some scuffles between riot police and protesters.
In the southern city of Toulouse, high school protesters waved the French flag and placards, while graffiti on a school wall read: "The police are cracking down on France's children".
Hundreds of students, police and teaching staff have been injured since the protests began, and more than 6,500 people—mostly children—have been arrested.
A 15-year-old lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade, and Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told radio broadcaster RTL early Wednesday that he had suspended the police use of stun grenades in response.
Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct.
The unrest has erupted with just months to go before the 2027 election to choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with far-right veteran candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction.

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the Black Sea overnight, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
A drone attack caused a fire at a data center operated by Russia’s tech giant Yandex in the town of Sasovo in the country’s central Ryazan Region, damaging part of the facility’s infrastructure.
Drone debris fell on the territory of an enterprise in Russia’s southern city of Krasnodar, causing a fire.
A fire also broke out in the industrial zone in the city of Salavat in Russia’s central Bashkortostan Region as a result of falling drone debris after an attack was repelled.

Attack scale
- On-duty air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on October 7 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on October 8, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, drones were downed over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Voronezh, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Orenburg, Penza, Rostov, Ryazan, Samara, Saratov, Smolensk, Tambov, Tula, Ulyanovsk, Moscow, Bashkortostan and Tatarstan Regions, the Republic of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
- More than 30 UAVs were destroyed overnight over the town of Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, the Kamensky, Millerovsky, Neklinovsky, Chertkovsky and Sholokhovsky Districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said on his Max channel.
- Air defense systems shot down 26 Ukrainian drones over the Voronezh Region overnight, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote in a post on his Max channel.
- Air defense forces intercepted two drones over the Ryazan Region overnight, Governor Pavel Malkov said on his Max channel.
Aftermath in Ryazan Region
- A drone attack caused a fire at a data center operated by Russia’s tech giant Yandex in the town of Sasovo in the Ryazan Region, damaging part of the facility’s infrastructure, the company’s press service told TASS.
- There were no casualties, with special services carrying out cleanup operations on site.

- Creating new resources in the cloud infrastructure may currently be limited, with specialists still working to address the consequences of the incident.
- All services in other zones are running normally.

- Windows were also shattered in several private houses.
- There have been no casualties reported so far.
- Emergency services are operating on site.
Other regions

PHOTO YouTube / De La Bona Official
Font size
At the end of a busy summer, Plamen Bonev (De La Bona) presents his new original song “Az sam chovek” (I Am Human). Although the track is only coming out now, the rock singer has been working on the idea behind both the lyrics and music for quite some time. Only recently, however, did the time come for a completely new arrangement, created by Angel Dyulgerov. In “I Am Human”, De La Bona brings together the two sides of his musical style — the more ballad-driven side and a harder-edged sound:
“The melody itself is still ballad-like, and the vocal lines have that ballad feel. As I’ve said before, trends change - musical tastes are constantly evolving. Beats change, sounds change, all kinds of plugins... But the one thing that remains constant is the melody. That doesn’t change: either it touches your soul, or it doesn’t.”
PHOTO Facebook /Plamen Bonev
The video for “I Am Human” was created using artificial intelligence - something that, on the one hand, contrasts with the song’s title, but on the other, reinforces its central message: “I can’t be Superman — I’m just a human being.”
“The human factor cannot be replaced”, Plamen Bonev adds. “I listen to a lot of music, and you can always tell when something has been made by artificial intelligence. Music is an art form; it has to be lived and experienced, and we must not lose the human factor in creating it.”

This winter, Ukraine will be fighting for more than light and heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:03:17 UTC
18:03:17 KST

"Our task, therefore, is not simply to survive another winter. It is to keep Ukraine's frontline cities alive," writes Ihor Terekhov, Mayor of Kharkiv in an opinion piece for Euronews.
Ukraine is preparing for a fifth difficult winter under hostile fire. But for the cities and communities closest to the front, the greatest danger is not simply losing electricity or heat. It is the continued loss of people, businesses and economic life — the foundations without which there can be no meaningful recovery.
As chair of Ukraine’s Association of Frontline Cities and Communities of Ukraine, representing more than 300 communities in the direct midst of the conflict, I see three interconnected challenges that will determine not only how we get through this winter, but what kind of country emerges from this war: energy security, economic resilience and poverty.
The first challenge is infrastructure security
In Kharkiv, we know what it means to lose power and heat after a Russian attack. For some, it can mean the difference between life and death so an effective response by local authorities is critical.
That is why we are no longer simply repairing what has been damaged. We are changing the architecture of our energy system, decentralising generation and building reserve capacity so that one strike cannot leave a large part of the city without essential services.
We have had to rethink education in the same way. When an ordinary school can become a target, safe learning has to move underground. Kharkiv began with classrooms in metro stations and then built underground schools.
These are solutions born of necessity. Over the past four years, Ukrainian cities have accumulated practical experience in protecting critical infrastructure, decentralising essential systems and maintaining public services under sustained attack.
I hope no other European city will ever have to acquire such experience in the way we have. But this knowledge now exists, and Ukraine is ready to share it.
The second challenge is economic resilience
A city cannot survive on repaired buildings and infrastructure alone. It needs businesses, jobs and people who see a reason to stay.
For frontline communities, this is becoming an existential issue. An entrepreneur in Kharkiv or another city under regular attack operates with risks that businesses elsewhere in Europe do not face. Investors see the war risk. Banks see it. Insurers see it.
The result is a paradox: the places that need private capital most are precisely those where capital is hardest to attract.
We need to change that — not by creating economies permanently dependent on aid, but by creating conditions in which businesses can operate and invest despite the risk. Guarantees, war-risk insurance, affordable finance and support for small and medium-sized enterprises should be part of Europe's approach to Ukraine's recovery.
The third challenge is poverty
War does not only destroy buildings. It gradually exhausts families. According to the World Bank's latest estimate, 41.6% of Ukraine's population lived below the national poverty line in 2025.
Behind that number are very painful, personal decisions: whether to buy medicine or pay the rent; whether to remain in your hometown; whether to look for work elsewhere in Ukraine or leave the country altogether.
For frontline regions, prolonged economic hardship therefore carries another danger: depopulation.
A building can be rebuilt. A substation can be replaced. A road can be repaired. It is much harder to restore life to a city once its people have left, businesses have closed and young people no longer see their future there.
This is why I do not believe Ukraine's recovery begins when the war ends. In frontline communities, it has already begun.
If we want people to return tomorrow, schools, hospitals and businesses must function today. If we want investment after the war, we need to preserve our workforce, our businesses and our human capital now.
Europe's support is indispensable to this effort
The European Union has already done an extraordinary amount for Ukraine. For a mayor, that support is not measured only in figures on a spreadsheet. A generator means a hospital can keep working. A transformer means homes have electricity again. Decentralised heating means an entire neighbourhood does not go cold after the next strike.
We are grateful to the European Union for the €920 million package under its 2026–2027 Winter Energy Plan to help stabilise Ukraine's energy system and strengthen its resilience.
But we must look beyond this winter
Not every part of Ukraine faces the same conditions. Proximity to the front affects whether families stay, whether companies continue operating and whether banks, insurers and investors are prepared to take risks.
Future European support for Ukraine should recognise that frontline territories face a distinct combination of security, demographic and investment pressures — and design recovery instruments accordingly.
Supporting these territories is not simply about rebuilding what Russia has destroyed. It is about ensuring that viable communities, functioning economies and people with a future are still there when the war ends.
This matters even more because Ukraine is moving towards membership of the European Union.
European integration is often discussed in the language of negotiating clusters, legislation and the acquis. For most Ukrainians, however, Europe will ultimately be experienced locally — in the quality of public services, transport and energy infrastructure, and in how public money is managed.
That is why transparency, accountability and zero tolerance for corruption must be built into recovery from the start. Not simply because Brussels expects it, but because the trust of our citizens, partners and investors is one of the most valuable resources Ukraine has.
Our cities should not be passive recipients of European assistance. They should be active participants in European integration — and accept the responsibility that comes with it.
Another difficult winter lies ahead. Russia will again try to damage our energy system, weaken our economy and make life in Ukrainian cities increasingly difficult. Indeed their aim is to make it unbearable. For frontline communities, these are not separate problems.
Without energy, businesses stop. Without jobs, poverty grows. Without prospects, people leave.
And once a city loses its people, rebuilding its vital community becomes far harder than rebuilding any structure.
Our task, therefore, is not simply to survive another winter. It is to keep Ukraine's frontline cities alive — with people who stay, businesses that work, institutions they can trust, and a future inside Europe.

Meteors to light up the skies this October: How to watch the Draconid and Orionid showers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:01:36 UTC
18:01:36 KST

From Halloween fireballs to the Hunter’s Moon, here's what to look out for in October’s night skies.
Stargazers will be out in force this month as three meteor showers light up the skies – the first of which is set to peak on Friday.
The Draconid meteor shower is best seen in the evening after dusk, unlike most other meteor showers which are most visible in the early hours, making it more accessible for casual watchers.
This is because the shower’s radiant point in the Draco (dragon) constellation is highest in the sky at nightfall, Royal Museums Greenwich (RMG) explains, and the thin waning crescent moon will only rise just before dawn.
Later in the month, the Southern Taurid and Orionid meteor showers will offer further viewing opportunities, followed by the pre-Halloween Hunter’s Moon on 26 October.
How to see the Draconid meteor shower
Active between 6-10 October 2026, the Draconids are expected to peak on 8 and 9 October when the skies are dark. You are most likely to see them if it’s a clear night.
Choose a viewing spot with an unobstructed horizon and minimal light pollution for the best view. They can be seen with the naked eye, meaning there’s no need to use a telescope or binoculars.
The display is the result of Earth travelling through a cloud of debris from the comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner. The streaks can be caused by particles as small as a grain of sand, according to RMG.
The relatively slow pace of the Draconid meteors mean they are less visible than faster displays, with around 10 expected to be visible per hour under ideal conditions.
What else to look out for in the night sky this October
If you miss out on the Draconids, October offers more opportunities to catch a night sky display. Active between 20 September and 20 November, the Southern Taurid meteor shower will reach its first peak around 14 October. Best viewed between midnight and 3 am, its second peak on 4-5 November is known for producing slow, bright meteors known as ‘Halloween fireballs’.
The Orionid meteor shower is active from 2 October to 7 November and will peak on the night of 21 October. Between three and six meteors per hour could be visible in suburban areas, according to NASA, and few more in darker areas. Named after its radiant, near the constellation Orion, the shower comes from debris shed long ago by Halley’s Comet.
It will be most visible in the early hours of the morning on 22 October, after the waxing gibbous moon sets.
A few nights later, on 26 October, cast your eyes up to the October full moon, traditionally known as the Hunter’s Moon – a name associated with the bright moonlight once used by hunters to track game as the autumn fields grew bare and daylight faded.

African Union launches rival to Western credit rating giants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

18:01:16 KST

African Union launches rival to Western credit rating giants
The African Union (AU) has launched its first credit rating agency in a move it says will advance economic sovereignty, amid longstanding accusations of bias against the continent by Western rating agencies.
The Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), unveiled on Wednesday in Port Louis, the capital of Mauritius, where it will be headquartered, will assess governments, financial institutions, and businesses. The AU says it will operate independently, with governments barred from owning shares.
The initiative follows years of complaints against Moody’s, S&P Global, and Fitch, the dominant Western rating agencies, over their treatment of African borrowers, particularly downgrades during crises. Credit ratings influence borrowing costs and investors’ willingness to lend.
AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf described AfCRA as an “important pillar” in Africa’s efforts to build a stronger and more resilient financial architecture.
“The agency will provide African and international investors, as well as economic partners, with reliable, independent and technically rigorous analysis of African economies and credit risk,” he said, according to an AU statement.
During the launch ceremony, Afreximbank Executive Vice President Denys Denya argued that Western assessments drive up Africa’s borrowing costs by failing to adequately reflect its economic realities. “When lenders don’t see clearly, they charge for the fog,” he said.
A 2023 UN Development Program study estimated that less subjective ratings could save African countries up to $74.5 billion. The AU says the continent’s external debt service rose from $61 billion in 2010 to $163 billion in 2024.
Ghana’s Finance Ministry accused Moody’s of “institutionalized bias against African economies” after a February 2022 downgrade. It said the agency, which cited Ghana’s mounting liquidity and debt challenges, omitted critical information and relied on an analyst who had not visited the country. Last year, Kenyan President William Ruto said global agencies had “deliberately failed Africa,” blaming flawed models and outdated assumptions for inflated borrowing costs.
Earlier this year, Afreximbank terminated its relationship with Fitch, saying the agency’s “credit rating exercise no longer reflects a good understanding” of the bank’s founding agreement, mission, and mandate. The firms have rejected the allegations of unfair treatment, saying they apply the same methodologies worldwide.
Several countries outside Africa have also questioned the fairness of global credit ratings or called for alternatives. In 2023, Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a Eurasian rating agency to provide “absolutely objective” assessments. India’s Finance Ministry alleged systemic bias in sovereign ratings in 2021, while China’s Finance Ministry called a Fitch downgrade “biased” in April 2025.

Car parts giant lends engineers to German missile maker
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:29 BST
18:00:29 KST

ZF, one of the world’s largest automotive suppliers, is providing engineering services to Diehl Defence on selected development projects, and is seconding its own specialists to work alongside Diehl staff, according to the company.
The work spans the development process from concept studies through to testing and validation, taking in design, system development, layout and construction. ZF says the aim is to shorten development cycles, bring expertise in industrial scaling in at an early stage and develop solutions for future defence applications, and it contributes established development processes, scalable organisational structures and long experience in producing quality-critical systems. Diehl Defence keeps responsibility for system requirements and for defence-specific system integration.
Testing and validation make up the other half of the arrangement. ZF supplies test benches, simulation environments and test methods to examine components under realistic conditions, with structured validation intended to establish quality, safety and reliability early rather than late, and the company notes that the physical closeness of the two firms’ sites shortens response times.
Alongside conventional engineering services, the two companies are using temporary employment arrangements that put ZF specialists directly into Diehl projects on site, which the firm says allows short coordination channels and close integration of the teams.
ZF employs around 153,000 people across 162 production sites in 29 countries and reported sales of €38.8 billion in 2025, built on gearboxes, chassis and driveline components for carmakers, a market that has been contracting painfully as European vehicle production falls and the move to electric drive removes the need for much of what it has historically sold.
Defence is where the growth is, and German spending commitments since 2022 have created demand that the established defence manufacturers cannot meet from their own engineering capacity. Diehl Defence, best known for the IRIS-T family of air defence missiles, has been among the busiest firms in Europe as orders for ground-based air defence have multiplied, and finding enough engineers has become as much of a constraint as finding enough factory space.
Rheinmetall has gone furthest in making the same move in the opposite direction, converting automotive plants to defence production, and the pattern of engineering capacity moving from cars to weapons is now visible across German industry.

Covid, Brexit and Liz Truss mini-budget led to lasting decline in mental health, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:00:16 UTC
18:00:16 KST

Brexit, Liz Truss’s mini-budget and other “shocks” over the last 10 years have led to a serious and lasting deterioration in the UK population’s mental health, research has found.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the first and second Covid lockdowns also triggered big rises in psychological distress, as measured by the number of people with depression and anxiety.
The findings come as Prof Peter Fonagy prepares to publish the report of his long-waited government-commissioned inquiry into the dramatic increases in recent years in diagnoses of mental illness, ADHD and autism. It will be published on Friday amid concern that those conditions help explain why a record 2.8 million Britons are too sick to work and almost 1 million young people aged 16 to 24 have become “Neets” – not in education, employment or training.
Researchers led by Dr Annie Jeffery of University College London used data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study of 87,857 people aged 16 and older, which was collected every year between 2009 and 2024, to estimate the mental health impact of those five “systemic shocks”.
“The past decade or so has been tumultuous, shaped by multiple overlapping shocks and ongoing uncertainty and instability that have impacted mental health in Britain,” said Jeffery.
“We have shown that major government decisions and current global events can have substantial impacts on people’s mental health.”
All five events caused immediate and serious damage to overall mental wellbeing across the UK. But the Brexit referendum in June 2016 and first pandemic lockdown in March 2020 caused the most damage, the research team found.
Their analysis of the general health questionnaire’s GHQ-12 screening tool, which measures mental health, found that the UK’s vote to leave the European Union led to an increase in overall mental ill-health equivalent to about 120,000 more people overall seeking a GP’s help for depression.
However, the first Covid lockdown, when the then prime minister, Boris Johnson, told people to “stay at home”, had a much larger impact, as measured by a much bigger rise in the UK’s GHQ-12 score. That jump equated to about 900,000 more people in total visiting a family doctor because they had developed symptoms of depression, Jeffery said.
Russia’s offensive against Ukraine in February 2022 led to about 15,000 more Britons a month seeking a GP’s help for depression. After Liz Truss’s mini-budget in September 2022, which proved disastrous for the UK economy, about 23,000 more people a month visited their family doctor’s surgery because they were depressed.
“We observed increased psychological distress immediately after the Brexit referendum and the first Covid-19 lockdown, with more insidious monthly increases in psychological distress after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the 2022 mini-budget,” said Jeffrey.
Andy Bell, the chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health thinktank, said: “There is clear evidence that Covid had a big impact on mental health. And it makes sense that the other ‘shocks’ listed here would do so, either directly, by making people feel less secure and less connected, or as after-effects, for example the cost of living crisis.
“It’s also clear that rising distress in the population is not due to a single cause but the effect of all these things added together, made worse by years of austerity giving fewer buffers against ‘shocks’ like this.”
Mental ill-health costs the UK £300bn a year, according to research by the thinktank.
The UCL-led team’s findings have been published in the journal BMJ Mental Health. They found that psychological distress had been increasing in the UK from 2009 to a degree that was clinically significant but accelerated from 2015 onwards. Even though the most recent of the five events occurred in 2022, the heightened distress in the population that followed them has persisted and not gone back to the much lower levels seen before 2016, they found.
The total number of people in England in contact with NHS mental health services almost doubled from 2.64 million in 2016-17 to 4.13 million in 2024-25. The number of new referrals the NHS receives every month for mental ill-health has jumped from 360,000 in April 2022 to 530,000 in July 2026 – a jump of 47%.
The huge rise in demand for care – driven by “shocks” causing anxiety, stress and worry – has left NHS services struggling “as more people than ever are reaching out for support”, said Tom Pollard, the mental health charity Mind’s director of policy, campaigns and public affairs.

Co-op Legal Services using AI to rate workers’ phone calls to customers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:00:16 UTC
18:00:16 KST

The Co-op has become the latest employer to place workers under AI surveillance with an automated listening technology that rates every phone call some of them make to customers.
In a system described as “oppressive and dystopian” by a whistleblower, Co-op Legal Services is using AI models to record, analyse and award a percentage score for interactions between agents and customers seeking advice about probate, wills and estates.
A model from OpenAI has been trained to assess more than 50 discrete aspects of each phone call and provide pass and fail scores to managers who use the data to analyse employee performance. One worker said the system can mean their work is monitored by AI for several hours a day as they handle inquiries often from recently bereaved customers.
It comes after the Guardian last week revealed Euan Blair’s AI training company, Multiverse, has started using an AI for blanket monitoring of online classroom sessions, which teachers called “remorseless” and “unnerving”, while Multiverse said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”. Experts have voiced fears that increasing AI monitoring of workers risks increasing stress.
“You are being watched,” said a Co-op worker who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity and said the AI created a sense of distrust. “It’s different from occasionally being listened to for compliance purposes. [You are] being monitored absolutely every word that you say and every time that you utter something … It just feels really dystopian. It’s the thin end of the wedge.”
The Co-op, which operates supermarkets, undertakers, insurance and legal services companies, said it did not recognise the criticism and said its probate advisers were highly engaged. It said it supported colleagues with AI, which is a “key aspect of our quality assurance processes” and helps ensure “our clients consistently receive empathetic expert guidance”.
The AI monitoring is understood to have been introduced in the last couple of months into the work of dozens of legal services staff. It is used in part to identify ways they can boost their sales performance.
The Co-op said the AI is used solely as a support tool, is not a decision-maker, and helps leaders “support colleagues and continuously improve the experience we provide to clients”.
Trade unions have begun pushing back against the spread of AI monitoring. In February Burger King in the US announced it would be using the technology to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions, and this summer, Meta paused tracking of employees’ computer keystrokes amid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash.
“AI is sold as the solution to every problem, but examples like this make it clear that it can diminish sensible workplace practices and intensify working lives for no reason,” said John Chadfield, the national officer of the Communication Workers Union. “Unaccountable computer systems should not be people’s managers, and these hard-working employees demand far more respect.”
“The office is becoming more like a factory now our performance feedback can be given in a more structured way,” said Hayfa Mohdzaini, a senior policy and practice adviser at the Chartered Institute of Professional Development. “Clearly some people have a problem with it. It will be interesting to see how it develops and how much managers need to adjust their approach.”
This year, the International Labour Organization warned about the “psychosocial” risks of AI monitoring, including increasing work-related stress.
“AI systems are being deployed in workplaces in the absence of a comprehensive regulatory framework,” it said. “Preventing the risk of harm by AI use and operation in this context may not be straightforward.”
Caoilionn Hurley, the managing director of Co-op Life Services, which includes legal services, said: “The efficiency of AI over traditional methods allows us to review all customer conversations to ensure we consistently deliver high standards of service, while enabling more informed support, coaching and development for colleagues … Put simply, our goal is to provide expert support combined with empathy and understanding for every client at what can be a difficult time. AI helps us deliver that more consistently, while human judgment, accountability, care and kindness remain at the heart of every client relationship.”

‘Someone else will do it for less’: Refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:00:15 UTC
18:00:15 KST

In a portable building in Kakuma, a refugee camp near Kenya’s northern border with South Sudan, Grace used ChatGPT to research translations of Christian hymns in languages she doesn’t speak. She didn’t know the client, the purpose of her work or whether she would be paid, but as a refugee unable to legally work in Kenya, she needed any opportunity she could get.
Grace, who requested anonymity due to a nondisclosure agreement, prompted ChatGPT to translate the hymn’s English text into the assigned east Asian language. She then used the translation to search for existing versions and find information about its translator, author and Christian denomination. She fed those details to AOP Connect, a crowdsourced research platform owned by British AI enterprise software company RWS.
If RWS deems her work high quality based on six listed criteria, it could award her up to $500 as a “discretionary reward”, according to RWS researcher documents and manuals reviewed by the Guardian. But refugees aren’t guaranteed wages, and most earn significantly less than the maximum without being told why, said Asha Luka Abdallah, a mentor at the Solidarity Initiative for Refugees (SIR), an organization that trains refugees to work in the tech outsourcing industry.
Remote jobs such as content moderation and data annotation have been promoted as a win-win by United Nations agencies as well as global tech companies: refugees get income opportunities, AI and social media companies get a source of cheap labor.
But interviews with more than two dozen refugees in Kakuma show that only one side has clearly benefited. Tech companies have built some of their most powerful tools on datasets handled by precarious workers, including refugees, in low-income countries. But their pay, which was never high, appears to be vanishing as entry-level tech work disappears. The shrinking number of opportunities is driving some to accept gigs for potential “rewards” rather than guaranteed wages, many said.
“It’s one of the things that keeps me awake at night,” Bahana Hydrogene, a Congolese refugee who set up the SIR’s digital skills programs in 2016, said of the increasingly opaque arrangements for refugees. “They can’t get transparent answers from these companies.”
A spokesperson for AOP Connect said the company offers researchers, regardless of location or background, the opportunity to participate in a wide range of projects. The reward structure is communicated “transparently upfront”, as is the nature of the copyright research work, but confidentiality is critical to AOP’s clients, the spokesperson said.
Pay is based on the quality, relevance and timeliness of research submitted, and the AOP Connect platform is “not AI-enabled or used for AI-model training work”, the spokesperson added.
The ‘invisible architects’
Before Grace could become a qualified researcher, she filled out a questionnaire, agreeing to keep her work confidential and complete tasks by herself. Then she was able to potentially earn money through so-called “microwork”, digital tasks broken off of large confidential projects and distributed to remote workers via online platforms.
She logged into AOP Connect to see a list of opportunities and found the hymns research project advertised at $9,000 in rewards available. That figure, however, would be divided among an unknown number of contributors as discretionary “rewards” rather than guaranteed wages, according to a notice displayed on the listing. RWS said higher-quality work leads to higher pay, but there is little transparency about how assessments are made, according to program participants and payment notices reviewed by the Guardian.
Chatbot-assisted research on behalf of mysterious clients offering the chance to win rewards was not what Hydrogene had in mind for when he set up the SIR’s digital skills programs in 2016. He hoped the booming global outsourcing industry would help refugees earn a guaranteed income.
Some highly skilled refugees in Kakuma have found remote work through outsourcing and freelancer platforms to be a gamechanger. Those who did say they worked as web developers and software engineers interacting directly with clients. But most refugees found themselves limited to performing low-paid microwork such as data annotation for anonymous clients abroad, mediated through platforms like Remotasks, the Scale AI subsidiary that left Kenya in 2024.
Life online in Kakuma
Kakuma was originally established as a temporary home for people forced to flee the second Sudanese civil war, later expanding to accommodate people fleeing Somalia, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. More than 30 years later, it is one of the world’s largest refugee camps, with sprawling networks of tin-roofed buildings that make it look more like a permanent town.
On a Thursday afternoon in June, temperatures topped 95F at the SIR’s compound, about 20 minutes away from Kakuma’s main entrance. The arid landscape and severe water shortages around the camp make farming unfeasible, so the more than 300,000 residents are almost entirely dependent on humanitarian aid.
Inside an air-conditioned shipping container computer lab, five students practiced everything from basic digital literacy to full-stack programming. Nearby, three SIR graduates built websites and apps for clients outside the camp in a co-working space where they can access Starlink internet service and reliable electricity.
One South Sudanese software engineer said that, while he has managed to get well-paid work through the SIR and Konexio, a French organization that sources remote opportunities for refugees, he worries about future workers. Entry-level work is disappearing due to AI, he said.
“Senior engineers … are not hiring interns or junior roles,” he added.
The SIR has trained more than 2,000 refugees, connecting more than half with remote tech work ranging from long-term employment to short-term gig work. A few years ago, SIR staff said they could easily find data annotation, transcription and translation work for their students on platforms like Remotasks. Hydrogene said workers regularly took home 500 to 1,000 Kenyan shillings, or $3 to $6, a day before Remotasks shuttered in 2024. While pay was low, it was valued in a place where less than half of households have income, and those that do earn less than $50 a month.
But the microwork economy is often exploitative, said Joan Kinyua, founding president of the Data Labelers Association. The Nairobi-based organization advocates for the rights of what it calls the tech sector’s “invisible architects”, workers foundational to the industry but hidden by opaque supply chains.
Kinyua, who worked many of these jobs, said she noticed wages and conditions for entry-level data annotation eroding as early as 2018. On some platforms, she noticed that even making a small mistake, like outlining an object imperfectly, could cost her pay. Further reductions in pay and opportunities for data labeling in 2020 meant that Kinyua had to work faster for less, and had to be available anytime gigs appeared on outsourcing platforms. Eventually, she was sleeping only a few hours a night.
“You can’t afford to stay away from your computer,” she said.
In Kakuma, refugee data annotators said that at times they were tasked with labeling images and videos of weapons, gruesome bodily wounds and pornography on various outsourcing platforms. As a result, some workers, especially those fleeing wars, experienced post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms after annotating violent material, Hydrogene said. And the opacity of some arrangements meant workers often unknowingly contributed to products they were opposed to. The Bureau of Investigative Journalism found that Somali speakers in Kakuma had done transcription work probably used by the US military, which refugees told the bureau they didn’t consent to.
A spokesperson for RWS said that AOP Connect doesn’t offer data annotation work. Scale AI did not respond to the broader findings on the industry as a whole, saying it was not in a position to comment on the practices of other companies.
Dwindling opportunities
Work became more scarce between 2022 and 2024 as Remotasks closed and automated tools such as ChatGPT took off. Na’amal, a non-profit that links refugees with global employers, noticed clients requesting skilled specialists rather than workers with basic digital literacy.
“As AI became mainstream, some jobs started to dry up,” said Lorraine Charles, Na’amal’s founder.
The International Trade Centre (ITC), a joint World Trade Organization and United Nations agency that has trained digital workers in Kakuma, estimates jobs such as transcription, data entry, translation and web research have declined by about 50% since 2022, said an ITC spokesperson, Susanna Pak. Oxford Internet Institute research similarly shows that growth of popular AI tools coincided with a measurable drop in many of the tech jobs promoted as paths to refugee self-sufficiency.
Merci Biamungu, a refugee trained in 3D modeling, said he regularly received opportunities with guaranteed pay throughout 2023 and 2024.
However, in one of his final projects, he and 20 other workers competed in teams of five to design a 3D model of a potato. The best-performing group received a reward of 15,000 Kenyan shillings, or about $116, split among the five. Now, the AI tools that Biamungu believes he helped train can build 3D images faster, eliminating the need for workers like him, he said.
It’s now been two years since Biamungu has found remote work in tech.
“We used to get three to five jobs per month,” he said. “Now you cannot get one.”
Hubert Sanga, a Congolese refugee who established Generation Aid, another social enterprise that trains and helps refugees find work in tech, said he was seeing entry-level work for refugees collapse as AI expands.
“One hundred per cent of the jobs we are doing right now are really at risk,” Sanga said.
Rewards, not wages
For many, the alternative to these precarious, lower-paid remote gigs is no income at a time when many families in Kakuma face starvation – partly the result of Donald Trump and Elon Musk’s dismantling of USAID last year.
“The language of ‘rewards’ instead of wages shifts risk entirely on to workers, who invest their time and expertise without any guarantee of fair compensation,” said Mark Graham, professor of internet geography at the Oxford Internet Institute.
Hydrogene, of the SIR, said clients within the microwork economy routinely threaten to take jobs to the Philippines or India if he tries to negotiate higher pay.
“AI is taking some of these jobs … and you have more talent available than there are jobs,” he said. “They say, ‘Someone else will do it for less.’”
Na’amal’s Charles has also noticed declines in wages, and as a result is shifting the organization away from microwork entirely. Graphic design, web design and search engine optimization trainings are also being phased out in favor of software engineering, digital marketing and e-commerce, and other jobs believed to be less vulnerable to automation.
But most refugees will struggle to become competitive candidates for such highly skilled jobs, said Konexio’s director, Fabien de Castilla, due to disruptions to their schooling and work experience. If annotation jobs are becoming obsolete, Castilla still believes that other entry-level jobs, such as data cleaning and reviewing AI outputs, might provide opportunities for refugees in the future.
Building better protections
As AI speeds up the refugees’ work, it’s also diminishing their pay. Jobs that used to take days now take hours, reducing billable time, Sanga said.
“If I’m going to take three days to do a job, [the client] says, ‘I’m going to find someone who can do it in two hours,’” he said. “It’s killing us” on pricing, he added.
Diminishing pay has prompted the SIR, Generation Aid and Action for Refugee Life, another organization that trains refugees and sources tech jobs, to push companies to offer higher wages and better conditions. But tech workers told the Guardian they feared pushing for more over concerns they’d be replaced by AI or another worker desperate for a job.
Multilateral organizations like the ITC are trying to understand how digital workers can be better protected. Pamela Coke-Hamilton, the ITC’s executive director, told the Guardian that the loss of the digital economy’s lower- and middle-level workers demands new ways of thinking about collective bargaining.
“We are at a tipping point,” she said. “AI has taken people by surprise with its speed and impact, and we need to ask what labor organizing looks like now. We need guardrails to prevent mass exploitation.”
Though workers and advocates are trying to build those guardrails, they said power ultimately rests with global tech companies, which benefit from an oversupply of cheap labor. But a “race to the bottom” is not inevitable, Graham argues. He’s pointed to the textile industry as a precedent for how pressure can change industry conditions. There, “sweatshop” scandals prompted many companies at the top of the supply chain to commit to responsible business practices at every level.
Sanga believes one practical fix is simple transparency: workers need to know who they are working for so they can understand the value of their labor. When Generation Aid sources work directly from companies, it puts workers in direct contact with the client – a sharp contrast to anonymous platform work.
Milagros Miceli, principal investigator at Data Workers’ Inquiry and research lead at the Distributed AI Research Institute, argues that the supposed choice between no job and a poorly paid one is false.
“Without data workers, tech companies do not have a product,” she said. “So there should be space for bargaining power.”

====================================================================================================

‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:00:15 UTC
18:00:15 KST

When Dr Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu last saw Gloria in Abuja, the young breast cancer patient was so ill that she was in hospital. The cancer had spread to her bones and lungs, and she was struggling with complications from the disease.
Then, at a global conference on cancer thousands of miles away in Hong Kong last month, Bagudu saw her again. Gloria was walking with a stick because of the cancer in her hips, but she was attending sessions, speaking about her experience and advocating for other patients.
“I saw her hopping on the corridor here. I was shocked,” Bagudu recalled.
Bagudu was recounting this story on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress in Hong Kong, attended by more than 2,000 people from 124 countries.
A Nigerian paediatrician and advocate for cancer patients, Bagudu is president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) – the first African to lead the organisation. She takes up the role as cancer cases and deaths are projected to rise sharply, with the greatest increases expected in poorer countries.
“The fact that it [the election of a black person] took so long is a reflection of the inadequacy of cancer care along the entire spectrum in Africa and other low- and middle-income countries,” Bagudu says.
Her election comes as countries across the global south face a growing cancer burden while also struggling with shortages of diagnostic equipment, medicines, radiotherapy services, trained specialists and financing.
According to the most recent figures from the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 20.6 million people were diagnosed with cancer and 9.8 million died from the disease in 2024.
The IARC forecasts an annual rise in cases of 67% to more than 34m by 2050, while deaths could reach 17.5 million, an increase of 79%. Most of the additional deaths are expected to occur in low-income countries.
According to Bagudu, the forecasts reinforce the need to reorientate global cancer policy towards countries where health systems are already under pressure.
“Cancer is tripling and is going to keep on increasing, and the people affected by it most are those from the global south,” she says.
Her ambition is to use the UICC, which represents more than 1,100 member organisations across more than 170 countries, as a bridge between countries with limited cancer services and the research, technology and treatments being developed elsewhere.
“I have this opportunity to be able to bring forth a lot of the problems that the low- and middle-income countries are facing to the global north,” she says.
But Bagudu says access to cancer care cannot be solved simply by building more specialist hospitals. “We keep building cancer centres and we keep seeing that it’s not enough,” she says.
Cancer centres need to be supported by screening, early diagnosis, radiotherapy, medicines, trained health workers and systems that prevent families from being pushed into financial hardship by treatment, she says.
“I’m trying to reduce financial toxicity for the woman in the village,” she says.
That gap is already visible in basic cancer services. UICC chief executive Cary Adams told delegates that less than half of the world’s population has access to diagnostic services, while many patients in low- and middle-income countries pay for care out of pocket.
Only 14% of the estimated 73 million people who need palliative care each year have access to it, according to figures presented at the congress.
Bagudu’s own work in Nigeria has focused on some of these gaps. A paediatrician and founder of the Medicaid Cancer Foundation, she helped establish Kebbi state’s first cancer-control plan and registry during her time as first lady of the Nigerian state from 2015 to 2023.
Her foundation has also worked on cancer awareness and access to treatment for vulnerable patients. She has campaigned for cervical cancer prevention, including the introduction of the single-dose HPV vaccine into Nigeria’s routine immunisation programme in 2023.
In 2024, she became senior adviser to Nigeria’s coordinating minister of health and social welfare with a brief that included women’s health and cancer advocacy. Bagudu now wants to take some of those lessons to the international level, including pushing for new approaches to cancer financing.
She says cancer has never received the kind of global treatment financing mechanism that HIV, tuberculosis and malaria have benefited from. “Cancer has never directly been a beneficiary of global funding for treatment,” she says.
She will support efforts to develop a global cancer financing platform modelled partly on the Global Fund to Fight Aids, Tuberculosis and Malaria, to mobilise resources from governments, donors and other sources to strengthen cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment.
The proposal comes as African governments face competing demands on health budgets, and international development financing is under pressure with significant cuts to foreign aid.
Bagudu also wants greater attention paid to cancers that can be prevented or reduced through interventions already available. She plans to focus particularly on childhood cancers and liver cancer linked to hepatitis.
That prevention must go alongside investment in diagnosis and treatment, particularly as cancer risk is shaped by factors including tobacco use, infections, alcohol, diet and obesity, she adds.
She wants Africa to have a greater role in cancer research, rather than remaining primarily a recipient of discoveries and training from richer countries.
“Research is a little bit more difficult because you have to have the human capacity, you have to have the interest and then you have to have the right environment,” she says.
She points to emerging research centres in Nigeria, Rwanda and Kenya, as well as training programmes that bring African health workers to countries including China to develop skills in radiation therapy, cancer technology and other specialist areas.
The UICC has set targets including reducing cancer mortality by 25% by 2035, reducing exposure to major cancer risk factors by 30% and ensuring that 60% of cancers are diagnosed at an early stage.
Bagudu says the ultimate test of her presidency will be whether the global commitments made in conference rooms reach people far beyond them.

Guidance: Allied Joint Doctrine for the Planning of Operations (AJP-5)
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:03 BST
18:00:03 KST

Allied Joint Doctrine for the Planning of Operations (AJP-5)
Allied Joint Publication-5 is the keystone NATO doctrine for the planning of Allied joint operations.
Documents
Details
Allied Joint Publication (AJP)-5, Allied Joint Doctrine for the Planning of Operations (Edition B Version 1) presents an overarching framework of the key planning principles, considerations and processes that are followed when planning operations.
It describes how planning activities and processes are integrated and coordinated to support decision-making and the production of plans, orders and directives.
This edition is published with UK national elements.
Who should read this publication
AJP-5 is intended primarily as guidance for North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) commanders and their staff. However, the doctrine is instructive to the planning of operations by a coalition of NATO Allies and/or North Atlantic Council (NAC) approved Nations, NATO Partners, partner nations and non-NATO actors and for national planning within the framework of collective deterrence and defence.
It also provides a reference for NATO civilian and non-NATO civilian actors. AJP-5 focuses on the operational level, although it also has utility at the strategic and tactical levels.
