The Man Behind a West Bank Telegram Channel Trying to Keep Palestinian Drivers Safe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The first time we were supposed to meet Anas Hattab, he canceled at the last minute: There was no way to make it from his hometown in Tulkarm, in the northern West Bank, south to Ramallah, where we were meeting, and back before it got dark. That trip, which used to take him an hour, now often takes two to three hours—and some days far longer—because of Israeli military checkpoints on the way. This was one of those days.
At 30, Hattab’s life now revolves around these checkpoints—perhaps more than any other Palestinian in the occupied West Bank. But he has also transformed his community’s approach to them: Nearly 350,000 people follow his traffic Telegram group, which has closed a gap left open by major navigation apps that fail Palestinian users. Local radio stations build their hourly road segments off his dispatches. A routing system used by West Bank companies and a new local app pull his data into their own.
It began in 2019. Hattab was working during the day as a digital designer at a newspaper in Ramallah. When one shift ended, he started another, this time as the paper’s delivery driver. That meant that most nights, Hattab had to drive all around the West Bank. After loading the fresh editions into his car, he would drive north, looping through the cities of Nablus and Jenin, eventually reaching his home in Tulkarm by dawn. He found himself dodging Israeli military raids, settlements he had to route around and, most of all, unpredictable checkpoints, which could cause hours-long delays and where armed Israeli soldiers could search him or his car.
For decades, Israel has restricted or barred Palestinian vehicles from many of the main arteries through the West Bank, while Israeli vehicles pass freely. Popular navigation apps like Google Maps don't account for any of it. They do not mark the 942 checkpoints, gates, and other barriers that now fragment the territory, and they default to what their algorithms deem the fastest routes, many of which run through settlements and areas under Israeli control. A Palestinian driver who follows their directions risks being arrested, fined, or shot.
Navigating these uncertain roads, night after night, wore on Hattab. He knew he wasn't the only one. “People were scared to leave their governorates,” he says. At the core of that fear was an information void. So he began devising a way to fill it, for himself and every other Palestinian in the West Bank.
Seven years ago, Hattab launched a Telegram group called “Road Conditions.” The idea was that people would share information with each other about movements at checkpoints—warn each other about delays or closures, about settler or military presence and violence. Hattab posted the link in local news groups, and waited. They came in a trickle, at first, and then, as checkpoints began to multiply in 2022 and delays got worse, they came in a flood.
As more people joined Road Conditions, the pressure on Hattab mounted. When checkpoints locked down major cities, the number of users could spike, sometimes by thousands at a time. Dozens of commuters would ask about the same checkpoint, and answers would pour in at once. “Clear,” “open,” “closed.” All three could be true within the same hour. "Ten minutes is a long time," Hattab says. "Things change instantly." The questions landed on him, thousands of messages a day. “In the beginning,” he says, “I barely slept.”
When Hattab started Road Conditions, his odometer read 70,000 kilometers. Within four years it read 274,000, inside a territory barely 130 kilometers from tip to tip. It is the equivalent of driving around the Earth more than five times, without ever leaving the West Bank.
What began as a crowdsourced tool for people to help each other navigate the occupied West Bank was becoming an essential utility. To keep Road Conditions reliable, soon after launching the group in 2019, Hattab closed the public chat and asked the most active contributors to become moderators. More than a dozen volunteers now run the feed. Drivers from every corner of the West Bank send them reports, usually with a photo or video. Moderators check these updates by asking others on the ground, cross-checking other local pages, or driving the roads themselves.
As Road Conditions grew, users asked about roads in cities Hattab had never been to. Nothing goes out until he or the moderators have checked it. Before posting a checkpoint is closed, they need to know where it is, whom to ask to verify the update, and what route a driver can take instead. So for six months, Hattab spent his days off driving with no destination. "I'd get in the car, get lost, wherever I ended up, I ended up," he says. He stopped to ask locals for the name of every checkpoint and bypass road until he held the whole map of alternative routes in his head.
After October 7, 2023, a situation that was already dangerous became a crisis. An investigation we published in September, in partnership with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism, and Lighthouse Reports, found that checkpoint delays have increased by more than 50 percent since then. Our analysis found that the average commuter in the West Bank now loses about 77 hours every year taking roundabout routes to avoid checkpoints. Towns that were once quick, 10-minute drives apart have been severed by gates and other obstacles that turn those trips into hour-long voyages. To arrive at our analysis, we went searching for data about checkpoint delays, about when they are open and closed. No official data exists. So our reporting team looked to the Telegram group that Hattab built, scraping the updates that originated from Road Conditions to produce a comprehensive database of the way checkpoints work.
Not long after October 2023, Hattab was driving home at 2 in the morning when a soldier at a checkpoint near the city of Qalqilya stopped him and took his phone. The soldier scrolled through some 20,000 photos Hattab had received on the group of traffic around checkpoints. “You photographed a military site!” the soldier said, then stepped aside to speak with an officer on his radio. The soldier came back and ordered Hattab to delete everything. “I started deleting, in all naivety,” Hattab says. He had erased thousands of photos before the soldier walked back over and told him to go.
“I make sure not to show the military jeeps, not to show one soldier,” Hattab says.
Hattab quit the newspaper and took a job as a sales representative for a construction equipment company because it would put him on a different road every day. “My point is not sales,” he said. “It's Road Conditions.”
Israeli settlers, living in the nearly 150 official settlements and an additional 185 new “outposts” established in the West Bank since 2023—all of which are illegal under international law—have in recent years become a daily threat. In March 2025, at the Yitzhar junction on Route 60, near Nablus, Hattab watched a settler cut off a coffee bean delivery truck directly ahead of him, get out, and beat the driver in the middle of the road. “He was screaming and cursing, armed, beating the driver, grabbing him, punching him, grabbing him again,” he says. Hattab posted the update to the group. That year, the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission documented nearly 5,443 settler attacks. In the first eight months of 2026, it recorded about 4,766.
At 4 o’clock one January morning in 2025, news was circulating about Israeli troops on the road out of the city of Tulkarm. By 7, no one knew if they were still there, and no one wanted to be the one to find out.
Hattab was heading from his home in Tulkarm to Ramallah that morning. He started the car. He turned onto the road that people had been asking about and drove slowly, watching the road ahead.
The path was clear. He posted it to the group. “By the grace of God, it was easy this time,” he says.
Hattab knows the roads better, he would wager, than almost anyone now. When a major junction closes, he can predict the closures that follow across a whole corridor, “like dominoes,” he says. “Think of ants. You set their path with a toothpick on the ground.”
With no institutional support and two young children, Hattab sometimes doubts if he can keep going: “You’re supposed to give your family the best life, not give up stable income for a Telegram group.” To him, it's already more than that.
Other innovators have stepped into the fray, launching new apps and groups to help drivers manage traffic. In 2025, for instance, computer engineers Musab Nuirat and Ahmed Gharib launched A Ween Rayeh (Where Are You Heading?). It’s a Palestinian application that aggregates data to produce a real-time heat map of traffic. It was, by Nuirat’s count, the seventh local attempt to build a functional navigation system in the West Bank. And like nearly all the other efforts, A Ween Rayeh relied on Hattab’s data to update its map.
Hattab knows how important what he’s built has become. So he continues. Hattab knows the operation should be 10 times the size. And he knows he should be able to compensate the moderators. But as a volunteer himself, he has no way to pay them. “I can't give them more than a thank you,” he says.
Hattab considers it his duty. “You know how a taxi driver has souls with him in the car, and he has to drive carefully? Same principle.” Mistakes happen, no one can verify every update in real time. “In the end,” he says, “aren't we living in this country at our own risk?”

NASA Apollo program pioneer Margaret Hamilton dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Margaret Hamilton, scientist on NASA's Apollo program, dies
October 8, 2026
Software engineer Margaret Hamilton, who led the team that programmed the first computers used by NASA's Apollo mission to land humans on the moon, has died at the age of 90.
Her death on September 30 was announced Wednesday by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where she worked from 1959 to the mid-70s.
The university described her as profoundly influential in the field of software development, saying she had "forged new paths in computer science and engineering."
NASA chief Jared Isaacmen paid tribute on X, calling Hamilton "a pioneer whose work helped make Apollo and humanity's first journeys to the moon possible."
How did Hamilton come to work on the lunar program?
Hamilton studied mathematics before moving to Boston, Massachusetts, in 1959.
She began working at MIT soon afterwards, and in 1965 applied to join a lab at the university that was seeking people to develop software to "send a man to the moon."
The lab had won a contract from NASA to build the onboard flight software for the Apollo program.
Hamilton was hired as the first programmer for the project, MIT said, adding that she was also the project's first female programmer.
She initially worked on the first software for the uncrewed Apollo missions, before being promoted to lead the team developing on-board flight software for the crewed missions.
"By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of (Apollo's) Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo's software," MIT said.
"To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement," said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics.
"She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved," de Weck added.
'There was no second chance'
Speaking of her time working on the Apollo program, Hamilton told MIT News in 2009: "There was no second chance. We knew that. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s."
"Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure. Dedication and commitment were a given," she added. "Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust."
"Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers."
Hamilton published more than 130 papers and went on to start her own software companies Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies.
In 2016, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by former US President Barack Obama, whose citation said: "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history. Her software architecture led to giant leaps for humankind, writing the code that helped America set foot on the moon.”

Erik Gamzejev: When businesses shut down, small towns also fade away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Erik Gamzejev: When businesses shut down, small towns also fade away
If local entrepreneurship disappears, then sooner or later even a small town with the most magnificent square will decline, notes Erik Gamzejev.
The centers of Estonia's counties have become ever more beautiful over the years, but alongside improving their appearance, their future is largely determined by how strong and viable local entrepreneurship is.
Valga, Võru, Jõhvi and the capitals of several other counties have gotten themselves cool squares. Dozens of kilometers of bicycle paths have been built around them. New school buildings and recreational areas have been established.
For example, the county center of Ida‑Viru, Jõhvi, is an excellent place to live. Within at most a ten‑minute walking distance from each other there are a kindergarten, a high school, a basic school, a coding school, a stadium, a sports hall, a concert hall, a new music square and promenade, a cinema, a large shopping center and a park with a health trail — all built in this century.
Still this year, construction of a new library‑community house should begin. A large part of people live in the immediate vicinity of all this. Local life should also gain spice and open new opportunities from the Jõhvi film campus with its magnificent studios, which will open next week. It is worth acknowledging Jõhvi's local authorities, who have fought in recent decades for strengthening the county center.
Yet the visibly improved living environment has not been able to prevent the constant decrease in the number of inhabitants. One important reason looks back from the regional wage data page of Statistics Estonia. In the second quarter of this year, the median wage in Jõhvi municipality was €1448. Income tax is still deducted from that. In Estonia on average, the median wage was €1840.
Jõhvi's figure would be considerably worse if it did not have a large share of relatively well‑paid public sector wage earners. In Jõhvi, major employers are Viru Prison, the Defense Forces, and also the Ida‑Viru Central Hospital located nearby in Ahtme, where many Jõhvi residents are working. Also schools, where the average gross salary of teachers reaches close to €3000 thanks to the Ida‑Viru coefficient.
Among Jõhvi residents there are also workers of the oil shale industry. As a result of climate policy, which has messed up Estonia's energy system and destroyed thousands of well‑paid jobs in Ida‑Viru County, their share has significantly decreased, but miners and oil producers who have remained in work still receive higher pay than the Estonian average.
If public sector and oil shale industry people are left aside, then the wage level of the remaining entrepreneurship would be considerably lower than the median wage of 1448 euros in Jõhvi municipality. Jõhvi does not differ significantly from most other regions of Estonia. All counties except Harju County and Tartu County fall noticeably — by several hundred euros — below the Estonian median wage of €1840.
Many local entrepreneurs are in a vicious circle from which it is difficult to find a way out. Because inhabitants — that is, consumers of services — are constantly decreasing, companies cannot grow nor pay employees good wages. Because it is difficult to find a well‑paid job in one's home area, people move away for work, which in turn reduces the turnover of local service providers and creates difficulties in finding employees. Taxes and all other costs are of course just as large for a local entrepreneur as in the capital, where the market and turnovers are considerably larger.
If some nationwide monopoly‑scented large company develops a desire for fatter profit, then it imposes a fixed fee on consumers. And, oh wonder, it gets a green light for this from the Competition Authority.
Local small entrepreneurs have no such possibility, although by the same logic, a similar readiness‑to‑provide‑service fee would have reason to be asked also by a local small shop or hairdresser. Or, thinking over the top, why could these large firms not themselves pay consumers a fixed premium, for example for the readiness to purchase electricity, gas or banking services. If there were no consumers, there would be no business.
In a difficult situation, some local small entrepreneurs try to hide revenues to stay alive, in order to pay fewer taxes. For example, in some service company the payment terminal keeps breaking…
The Tax and Customs Board recently announced that according to their analysis, nine percent of Ida‑Viru workers receive under‑the‑table pay. If we leave aside public sector wage earners — assuming that unreported wages are probably not paid there — then in entrepreneurship this share is still enormously large.
Some entrepreneurs who do not want to go down the path of fraud fight for survival as long as they can, but in the end still shut down their businesses. Suppliers raise prices. Employees want more pay. The tax authority demands its due; for it, the regional‑policy importance of a local entrepreneur has no significance. As a result, the choice of services for small‑town residents becomes smaller.
Local enterprising people, who have often provided work not only for themselves but also for others, turn out to be superfluous. Tired from struggling, they move elsewhere or let themselves be carried in the future on the back of the state's social system. If earlier they brought tax revenue to the state treasury and their municipality, now they become a new expense line.
Most parties talk every four years, when votes are needed from people living outside Harju County to get seats in the Riigikogu, about how important supporting the development of local entrepreneurship is. What this essentially means remains vague.
It is precisely strong entrepreneurship, which creates jobs and brings tax revenue, that is the most important player in advancing local life. Everything else may be and is beneficial. But if there is no entrepreneurship, then sooner or later even a small town with the most magnificent square will fade away.
Therefore, when you see candidates for the Riigikogu in party tents in the coming months, go up to them and ask what they plan to do so that entrepreneurship becomes stronger in Jõhvi, Põlva, Valga, Paide, Kuressaare and elsewhere. Do not settle for general slogan‑like and round answers.
Do not let the conversation be dragged to what their political competitors have previously done wrong. Ask until you get substantive answers about what they themselves will do. If they do not want to end up in an embarrassing situation, then they must be prepared for this exam.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Evelin Kasenõmm: Asia puts drones to work – Estonia should follow suit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:58:13 UTC
17:58:13 KST

By Evelin Kasenõmm, Datel’s head of development.
While Europe leads in regulatory frameworks, Asian countries—particularly China—are rapidly implementing the “low-altitude economy” by integrating millions of drones into everyday logistics, public services, and infrastructure, according to an opinion piece published by Estonian public broadcaster ERR.
Experts note that China’s registered drone fleet grew by 51 percent by late 2025, alongside tighter regulatory and identification controls introduced in 2026.
Rather than competing with Asia on manufacturing scale, Estonia’s best opportunity lies in developing digital services, spatial data solutions, and 3D city models for automated flight management.
To take full advantage of this technology, expert Evelin Kasenõmm suggests that Estonia’s initial strategic move should be establishing two or three permanent drone corridors.
This approach would allow the Baltic nation to leverage its existing digital infrastructure to become a regional leader in safe, automated low-altitude operations.

US, Russia discuss possibility of selling gas to Europe via Nord Stream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:58:06 UTC
17:58:06 KST

Senior Russian and American officials discussed bringing in an American investor for the Nord Stream pipeline projects, sources told Reuters.
Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian president’s special representative for investment and economic cooperation and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, and Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, took part in the talks. Both are also involved in talks aimed at ending the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Dmitriev and Kushner have met in Moscow and New York in recent weeks. It’s unclear how extensively they discussed Nord Stream at those meetings. The topic remains on the agenda, according to sources. Another source told Reuters that the two sides are unlikely to reach a deal in the medium term.
The White House, for its part, said U.S. authorities would need to approve any such deal and that no discussions about Nord Stream had taken place recently.
Kushner views business cooperation as a key factor in reaching a peace agreement, according to Reuters. A deal allowing American participation in the Nord Stream pipelines would let the U.S. profit from energy supplies to Europe after the war ends.
Dmitriev favors resuming sales of Russian gas to Germany. In September, he met with representatives of the U.S. Department of Energy and the Treasury Department and discussed potential U.S.-Russian energy initiatives.
Germany is Europe’s largest energy consumer. It is unclear how interested Washington is in reviving the flow of Russian gas to the country.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, most of Germany’s gas came from Russia via the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipelines. After the war began, the flows stopped and the pipelines came under EU and U.S. sanctions.
Germany and other European countries, which are preparing to defend against Russian hybrid attacks and a possible invasion, are expected to oppose any resumption of Nord Stream’s operations.

South Korea recalls ambassador from Ukraine

Unknown Publisher

South Korea recalls ambassador from Ukraine
South Korea has announced that it is recalling its ambassador from Ukraine amid an escalating diplomatic row between the two countries.
The move comes after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky publicly announced Kiev’s transfer of two North Korean prisoners to Seoul during his address to the UN General Assembly in September. South Korea has insisted that the arrangement was supposed to remain secret, but the Ukrainian authorities have denied that such a precondition existed.
The servicemen in question were reportedly captured in January 2025 in Russia’s Kursk Region, where North Korean troops helped Russian forces repel a Ukrainian incursion.
The South Korean Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Thursday that the country’s envoy, Park Ki-chang, will be leaving Kiev and returning home.
The government in Seoul “hopes that various issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with Ukraine to achieve this,” the statement read.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga previously tried to downplay the spat with Seoul, calling it a “diplomatic misunderstanding” and said he was working to resolve it.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung warned last week that “if the Ukrainian government continues to refuse acknowledging the facts and issuing a public apology, we will take additional measures.”
Kiev’s violation of the non-disclosure agreement is “a matter concerning the dignity of the South Korean people and nation, which cannot be overlooked,” he said in a post on X.
Lee also accused Zelensky’s government of attempting to “bring war to the Korean Peninsula” through its actions.
The transfer of North Korean nationals to South Korea could escalate tensions between the two countries, which technically continued to be at war since the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty. Pyongyang hasn’t yet issued any official comments on the matter.
South Korea has provided Ukraine with humanitarian and financial assistance since 2022, pledging another $100 million in July, but has stopped short of supplying weapons.

Detention
- The Federal Security Service in the Trans-Baikal Region thwarted the illegal activities of two Russian citizens who, acting on instructions from Ukrainian intelligence agencies, were involved in preparing a series of provocations aimed at destabilizing the social and political situation in the region during the State Duma elections.
- FSB officers detained the suspects on the eve of the Single Voting Day during operational and investigative measures.
On suspects
- One of the suspects is a woman who was a member of a precinct election commission.
- It has been established that a member of the Freedom of Russia Legion terrorist organization, controlled by the Ukrainian Security Service and outlawed in Russia, instructed a local woman to join one of the region’s precinct election commissions, the FSB said.

- The second detainee is a resident of the city of Krasnokamensk.
- According to the FSB, he was recruited by the Ukrainian Security Service to gather information on the election campaign and photograph regional government buildings and the recruitment office.
- In addition, he was ordered to set fire to the city office of one of the political parties ahead of the active phase of the vote, using an improvised incendiary device, the FSB added.
Confessions
- The woman confessed to cooperating with the Ukrainian intelligence service, as seen in a video released by the FSB.
- According to her, while browsing various websites in search of an opportunity to earn some money, she was contacted by a man who suggested that she assist him.
- The woman said that he first asked what festive events were taking place in the city and whether locals were gathering and sending humanitarian aid to the special military operation zone.
- The suspect said she had provided him with the requested information.
- According to her, the man also asked her to join a local election commission, which she did.
- The suspect added that her handler had asked her to send photos of a polling station and ballots and to monitor the voting process and possible attempts to rig the election.
- She never received any money from him.
- The second suspect has also confessed.
- He said he had been looking for a job when a person asked him to take photos of recruitment offices and administration buildings.

Investigation
- Investigative and operational activities are underway to establish all circumstances of the illegal activities of the perpetrators, as well as their possible contacts.

Israel says British consulate in Jerusalem ends its operations, few diplomats can remain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:55:05 CST
17:55:05 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 8, 2026 shows an exterior view of the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced on Thursday that the British consulate in East Jerusalem had ended its operations on Israel's orders and that the consul general and 19 diplomats would leave the country, citing "countermeasures" following British measures against Israel. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband disputed Israel's legal authority to close the consulate, saying East Jerusalem was occupied territory. (Photo by Jamal Awad/Xinhua)
JERUSALEM, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced on Thursday that the British consulate in East Jerusalem had ended its operations on Israel's orders and that the consul general and 19 diplomats would leave the country, citing "countermeasures" following British measures against Israel.
The consulate is located in East Jerusalem and is Britain's main diplomatic mission to the Palestinians.
In a statement, Sa'ar said the closure, which was first announced in September, took effect on Thursday.
The building, which remains British government property, will no longer function as a consulate, and the remaining diplomats will operate under a restricted mandate, he said.
Sa'ar said it followed a series of British measures against Israel, including sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and restrictions on defense exports.
Following talks between the two governments, Israel agreed to allow seven British diplomats to continue operating from the building, which will no longer function as a consulate, he said.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband disputed Israel's legal authority to close the consulate, saying East Jerusalem was occupied territory. Israel effectively annexed East Jerusalem shortly after capturing it in the 1967 Middle East war and considers the entire city its "indivisible capital," a claim not recognized by most of the international community.
"We have been clear that we do not accept that the Government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years," Miliband said in a statement.
He said the Consulate General building would remain open as UK Mission, Jerusalem, and continue its work with Palestinians.
Britain said it had temporarily withdrawn some staff and their families for security reasons and intended to rebuild its diplomatic presence in the coming months.
Both sides said they had agreed to continue talks, with Britain pledging not to take reciprocal measures while discussions remained credible. ■

China sees 15.46 mln cross-border trips during National Day holiday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:54:44 CST
17:54:44 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China saw a daily average of 2.21 million inbound and outbound trips during this year's week-long National Day holiday, which ended on Wednesday, up 6.7 percent year on year.
Border inspection authorities nationwide recorded a total of 15.46 million inbound and outbound trips over the holiday week, the National Immigration Administration said in a statement on Thursday.
Mainland residents made more than 4.44 million outbound trips during the period, up 9.3 percent year on year, according to the administration.
Data from major Chinese online travel platforms Mafengwo and Ctrip show that long-haul destinations such as New Zealand and Iceland gained popularity among tourists during the holiday.
Foreign nationals made 682,000 inbound trips over the holiday week, up 5.4 percent from last year, of which 505,000 entries were under visa-free policies, up 9.2 percent.
From January to August this year, China recorded 61.29 million inbound and outbound trips by foreign nationals, up 19.5 percent year on year, including 23.72 million visa-free entries, a 26.8 percent increase year on year.
Since December 2023, when China launched a trial policy granting unilateral visa exemptions to visitors from six countries, it has expanded unilateral visa-free entry to travelers from 50 countries as of September. The policy allows eligible visitors to stay for up to 30 days.
It also extended the visa-free transit period for certain countries from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours in December 2024. There are 57 eligible countries so far. ■

Sea drone vs. air drone: Ukraine’s Sargan-3000 turns anti-aircraft gunner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:54:04 UTC
17:54:04 KST

A Ukrainian Sargan-3000 sea drone shot down a Russian Shahed flying on a mesh radio network, Ukraine's Navy reported on 7 October. Ukrainian sea drones have downed Russian aircraft before, but with missiles. This one used a machine gun.
Russia has been hitting Odesa with air attacks that come in waves with short gaps between them. Guarding the sky over water is harder than over land. Since fall 2025, Russia has also used mesh radio networks to reroute Shaheds mid-flight and dodge Ukrainian air defenses. That leaves Ukraine needing more ways to meet these drones out at sea, before they reach its ports and coast.
A Shahed steered by radio
A mesh-network drone passes its control signals along a chain of radio relays, drone to drone and on to ground antennas. That lets a Russian operator steer it in flight.
In May, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, then a Defense Ministry adviser, said only about 5% of Shaheds had got through in a recent Russian strike, and predicted that Russia would answer with jet-powered versions and strikes near the border. By July, Ukraine was testing jamming against mesh-controlled jet Shaheds, he said.
The Sargan-3000 fired its Protector remote weapon station, Militarnyi reported. The station is a remotely operated 12.7-mm (50-caliber) machine gun with electro-optical sights. The outlet added that the Sargan-3000 is designed for combat missions far from Ukraine's coast.
Built for the open sea
Ukraine's Navy took the Sargan-3000 into service in April 2026, according to Militarnyi. The drone boat has a combat radius of up to 1,600 km. It moves at 40–55 knots and carries up to 450 kg of payload.
In September, a Sargan-3000 sank a Russian uncrewed boat with machine-gun fire. Militarnyi called it the first battle between uncrewed sea platforms in history. Analyst H.I. Sutton wrote that the boat carried a Protector made by Norway's Kongsberg. That is the same weapon station named in the October shootdown. Sutton added that Russian attack sea drones work closely with Shaheds, which can relay the boats' mesh radio signals.

US deportations to Africa 'instrumentalise human suffering' to deter migration, HRW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:52:53 UTC
17:52:53 KST

The US policy of deporting migrants to third-party African countries is against international law and exploits suffering to deter immigration, Human Rights Watch said in a report on Thursday.
After President Donald Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, his administration signed accords with countries in Latin America, Africa and the Pacific to accept foreigners who could not legally be expelled to their own countries.
Since then, the United States has deported more than 500 people to African countries that were not their own, according to data from the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) cited by HRW.
An investigation published in September by the Forbidden Stories consortium estimates that 25,000 people have been expelled worldwide under the programme.
The policy "violates international human rights law and is designed to instrumentalise human suffering as a deterrent to migration", HRW said.
The rights group cited an unnamed US official as having told a Senate hearing that "with countries like Palau or Eswatini, the point is that the Administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere. The point is to scare people."
HRW said it interviewed 24 third-country nationals transferred from the United States to six countries in Africa: Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan.
They described being chained during flights that could last up to 18 hours, without knowing their destination.
Many of the "opaque" deals remain secret, HRW said.
An AFP investigation in early 2026 highlighted pressure exerted by Washington on African countries, such as threats of tariffs, the suspension of visa issuance or aid cuts, to compel them to accept deportees.
Burundi, one of the world's poorest countries, announced early this month that it had agreed to accept US deportees, becoming the 15th African nation to conclude such a deal.

South Korea Recalls Ambassador From Ukraine Amid Diplomatic Rift Over North Korean POWs

17:49:52 KST

South Korea will recall its ambassador to Ukraine amid a diplomatic dispute over Kyiv’s disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul, South Korean news agency Yonhap reported on Thursday, Oct. 8.
The recall comes after weeks of escalating tensions between the two countries, with Seoul accusing Kyiv of violating a confidentiality agreement and saying Ukraine’s subsequent apology did not go far enough.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The dispute began on Sept. 23, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced during his address to the UN General Assembly that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.
The two soldiers were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025 while fighting alongside Russian troops. One was carrying Russian military identification documents, while the other had no identification.
Zelensky said the soldiers had not been easy to capture alive, adding that one had attempted suicide to avoid being taken prisoner. Reports later indicated that the two initially rejected an offer to move to South Korea but changed their minds later in 2025.
Seoul Accuses Kyiv of Breaking Confidentiality Agreement
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung criticized Zelensky after the announcement, saying the public disclosure could create unspecified problems.
Seoul said the two governments had agreed to keep the transfer confidential because of security concerns surrounding the soldiers and their relatives in North Korea.
New Russian Drone Wave Targets Kyiv and Western Ukraine After Deadly Strikes on Putin’s Birthday
Ukraine disputed Seoul’s characterization of the agreement.
Zelensky’s office said South Korea had been informed in advance that the Ukrainian president intended to mention the transfer in his UN speech. Kyiv also argued that Zelensky had not disclosed identifying information about the soldiers or sensitive operational details.
South Korea nevertheless demanded an official explanation and apology, accusing Kyiv of violating the confidentiality arrangement.
The issue became increasingly contentious after Kyiv initially rejected Seoul’s characterization of the agreement.
On Oct. 2, Lee warned that South Korea would take “further measures” if Ukraine continued to refuse to acknowledge the agreement and publicly apologize. Seoul had already summoned Ukraine’s ambassador over the dispute.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the dispute as a “diplomatic misunderstanding” and said Kyiv wanted to resolve it quickly, stressing that South Korea remained an important partner.
Seoul rejected Ukraine’s apology
By Oct. 6, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Sybiha had apologized in messages exchanged between the two sides.
But Cho said the apology fell short of Seoul’s expectations.
South Korea was then considering several possible responses, including recalling its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Hee-chang.
Cho said confidentiality had been agreed upon from the outset and was intended to protect the soldiers and their relatives, who remain in North Korea.
He also offered his personal interpretation that Zelensky may have wanted to demonstrate at the UN that Ukraine had acted appropriately as a liberal democracy.
Fuel shipments add to tensions
The diplomatic dispute comes as Seoul faces separate questions over South Korean fuel shipments to Russia.
A Guardian investigation found that more than 176,000 metric tons of fuel, mostly diesel, were loaded at South Korean ports in July and August and transported to Russia’s Far East.
Seven tankers made 14 voyages, with three of the vessels reportedly under UK or EU sanctions. One sanctioned tanker received fuel through a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters, potentially making the origin of the cargo harder to trace.
The shipments came as Russia faced growing fuel shortages following Ukrainian strikes on its oil-refining infrastructure.
According to the International Energy Agency, Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than two decades, while diesel production was nearly 30% below the level recorded a year earlier.
Data analyzed by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air showed Russia’s seaborne imports of oil products surged in August.
The reported increase in shipments from South Korea began in July, around the same time Lee pledged $100 million for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a NATO summit in Turkey.
Seoul says fuel shipments were not banned
South Korea has rejected suggestions that the reported shipments violated its export controls.
The South Korean Foreign Ministry said on Oct. 8 that refined petroleum products, including commercial diesel and aviation fuel cited in The Guardian report, were not subject to South Korea’s export controls on Russia.
It also said it had not established whether the fuel was actually of South Korean origin and was conducting further checks into the vessels’ routes.
The ministry said South Korea’s overall exports to Russia had fallen by more than half since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
An adviser to Zelensky criticized the reported shipments as being in “sharp contrast” with Seoul’s sanctions policy. South Korea called those remarks “factually incorrect” and “inappropriate.”
North Korea’s role
The two disputes come against the backdrop of deepening military cooperation between Russia and North Korea.
Pyongyang has deployed troops to support Russia’s war against Ukraine and has supplied Moscow with ammunition and other military assistance in exchange for economic and military benefits.
The two North Korean soldiers captured in Kursk were among the first known North Korean troops taken alive by Ukrainian forces.
South Korea, meanwhile, has provided Ukraine with financial and humanitarian assistance but has maintained a policy against directly supplying lethal weapons to countries involved in active conflicts.
Seoul has also emerged as a major global arms exporter, including through multibillion-dollar weapons deals with European countries since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

US-Israeli national charged with wire fraud after using cybersecurity company to pay off hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:49:06 UTC
17:49:06 KST

An Israeli-US dual national and alleged cybersecurity expert was charged with wire fraud in a New York court on Wednesday for paying off cybercriminals while falsely claiming that his company, MonsterCloud, could decrypt ransomware.
According to the US Justice Department, Florida-based 50-year-old Zohar Pinhasi, also known as “Zack Silver” or “Zach Green,” targeted business owners victimized by hackers and ransomware attackers.
He claimed to offer a service that decrypted data as an alternative to paying the hackers off, charging clients large fees while purportedly using “proprietary tools” and “advanced decryption techniques” to recover the victims' data.
To present the company’s services as legitimate, MonsterCloud’s website included “testimonials,” some of which came from paid spokespersons.
Pinhasi allegedly had no special technology and instead contacted the cybercriminals who targeted the clients, paying them for the decryption keys needed to remediate the cyberattacks.
According to the DOJ, in 2019, a paid spokesperson contacted Pinhasi to ask whether MonsterCloud truly used proprietary software to decrypt data. Pinhasi allegedly responded that “MonsterCloud doesn’t hold any Proprietary technology [to] decrypt the ransomware data.”
Pinhasi collected total of $19 million from clients, paid $8 million to hackers
Pinhasi was accused of charging clients significantly more than it cost to pay the cyberattackers’ ransom and keeping the rest of the fee for himself.
In one 2023 incident cited by the DOJ, Pinhasi charged a client approximately $150,000 for MonsterCloud’s services and used only $8,200 of that to pay off the cybercriminal that targeted the client.
Since starting the fraud scheme in 2023, Pinhasi is alleged to have collected over $19 million in fees from clients and paid more than $8 million to cybercriminals.
If convicted of the two counts of wire fraud and one count of wire fraud conspiracy he was charged with, Pinhasi faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison for each count.
Pinhasi pleaded not guilty to the charges and was released on $2 million bail.
Pinhasi previously advised against paying cyberattackers
According to a biography about Pinhasi, he was born and raised in Israel and served in the IDF in the field of security intelligence. After being discharged, he started a business aimed at combating telecommunications fraud.
He moved to Miami and founded an IT company before eventually launching MonsterCloud. Pinhasi eventually came to be known as an expert on ransomware attacks.
According to the 2017 biography, at one point in time MonsterCloud had 70 employees and 7,000 clients worldwide.
Pinhasi previously warned victims of cyberattacks against paying hackers, including in a 2021 interview with The Jerusalem Post regarding a spate of cyberattacks carried out by the Black Shadow hacker group.

‘Demand is growing faster than capacity’: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:46:53 UTC
17:46:53 KST

By 11am on a recent Thursday, Dr Slobodan Mirosavljev had already seen two critically wounded patients at Juba military hospital. The day was barely halfway through, but the surgeon couldn’t say how long he would be at the facility.
A patient shot in the abdomen, head or chest could arrive without warning. A helicopter could bring several critically wounded people from another part of South Sudan. A mass casualty incident could fill the wards within hours.
For Mirosavljev and his colleagues, uncertainty has become part of the job at the hospital, where the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) supports surgeries for weapon-wounded victims of renewed fighting between the military, known as the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF), and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-In Opposition (SPLM-IO), which is loyal to former vice-president Riek Machar, and allied groups.
The conflict has increased the demand for surgical care, overwhelming an already fragile and under-resourced health system in the world’s youngest country. The fighting has intensified in the past year, particularly in Jonglei state, an opposition stronghold, amid a political crisis fuelled by the president, Salva Kiir, sidelining Machar.
Machar and Kiir were members of the Sudan People’s Liberation Army, a guerrilla movement that fought for independence from Sudan, which it gained in 2011, with Kiir becoming president and Machar the first vice-president. South Sudan descended into a bloody civil war in 2013 after Kiir fired Machar and later accused him of planning a coup.
Machar founded SPLM-IO, whose fight against the army in the ensuing civil war killed more than 400,000 people and displaced nearly half the country’s population. The fighting took place largely along ethnic lines, between Kiir’s majority Dinka community and Machar’s Nuer, the second largest ethnic group in the country.
In 2018, Kiir and Machar signed a peace deal – ending the civil war, creating a unity government of the two parties and returning Machar to the vice-presidency. But implementation of the agreement has barely got off the ground, as the two parties are constantly at odds over power sharing.
The renewed conflict was triggered by a deadly attack by the White Army, a rebel group that was allied to Machar during the civil war, on a government garrison in Nasir county in Upper Nile state in March 2025.
It resulted in Machar being charged with murder, treason, crimes against humanity and other serious crimes in connection with the attack, and Kiir suspending him from his post.
The actions have inflamed tensions in the country, with Machar’s supporters saying the charges against him are politically motivated and observers saying they risk jeopardising the peace agreement and plunging the country, where elections are due in December, into full-scale civil war.
The events have also coincided with increased fighting between militias and government forces in parts of the country that has killed hundreds and displaced more than 200,000 people.
Last month, the UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan expressed concern that the renewed violence and political tensions continued to place civilians at risk.
“Visit after visit, we continue to hear from people who bear the consequences of violence, displacement, insecurity and the failures of those with political and security responsibilities to prevent and address those harms,” said the commission’s chairperson, Yasmin Sooka.
At Juba military hospital, patients, medical workers and visitors moved between wards as the rainy season settled over the country. The sounds of footsteps, hospital trolleys and hurried conversations mixed with the steady hum of ceiling fans and the smell of disinfectant.
Some patients recovering from gunshot wounds sat along covered walkways. Others waited on crutches, while patients further along in their recovery carried out morning rehabilitation exercises.
As the fighting intensifies, the facility must be prepared to receive weapon-wounded victims at any time. For the surgical teams, that means there is no such thing as a predictable workday. Mirosavljev said that before midday they had had their morning meeting, received reports from the night shift team, seen critical patients in the high dependency unit, and started operating.
The Serbian surgeon has been working at the hospital since August 2025. He operates on some of the most seriously wounded patients and supervises surgical teams.
His day usually starts before 8am with a briefing, followed by ward rounds, consultations, emergency admissions and operations. Surgeries end in the early evening on typical days, but can go late into the night when critically wounded patients arrive.
Besides victims of political violence, the patients arriving at the hospital include those wounded in communal fighting and cattle-related conflict.
In the first six months of this year, the ICRC evacuated 266 injured people from conflict areas and brought them to the facility. Most cases at the hospital are gunshot wounds, and others include stab wounds, broken bones and explosive injuries. Mirosavljev estimated that one in 10 involve serious head injuries, including bullets entering the skull.
For surgeons, the numbers translate into a daily struggle against blood loss, infection and damage to vital organs.
Some patients require several operations. Every week, the medics receive at least two or three “very difficult” injuries from bullet or blast injuries to the chest and abdomen that need multiple surgeries, Mirosavljev said. For such patients, surgery is only the beginning. “They need a lot of blood; they need a lot of support,” he said.
Blood is among the most critical resources in the trauma unit. The hospital may have about 15 units available, with capacity sometimes reaching 20. A single severely wounded patient can require half of that supply.
Medical teams and hospital management work to find donors, sometimes relying on patients’ relatives and the national blood bank in Juba. But maintaining a reliable supply remains difficult.
The consequences can be serious when several casualties arrive at once. Rose Ochieng, the ICRC’s health coordinator in South Sudan, said the surgical department at Giada military hospital was operating at more than 160% of its bed capacity at the most recent peak this year.
She said: “We are doing what we can to keep pace: adding overflow beds and recruiting more physiotherapy staff. But demand is growing faster than the capacity of trauma services. And it is civilians caught up in the fighting who are paying the price.”
For emergency room nurse Mubarak Jamal, uncertainty begins every morning. Jamal is from Central Equatoria state and has been working at the hospital since 2024. At the outpatient department, there are a limited number of beds. On a normal day, he said, the department sees about 30 patients. Between seven and 10 may be people suffering weapon-related injuries.
Normal days, however, can disappear quickly, Jamal said, recalling that they received more than 93 patients in one day in the last mass casualty situation.
His responsibility is to ensure the emergency department is prepared for whatever arrives overnight – restocking supplies, knowing who is working during the night, and how they will coordinate with the colleagues from the operating theatre and other departments.
And survival is not the end of treatment.
For physiotherapist Lotto Charles, the real measure of recovery is whether a patient can eventually return home and live independently.
Charles, from Eastern Equatoria state, has worked at the hospital since 2016. His job includes rehabilitating the injured. Many of his patients are recovering from gunshot wounds. He lists others: “There are multiple fracture patients, patients with nerve injury, patients with lung collapse, and bedridden patients with extensive soft-tissue injuries who are not able to move.”
His work can include casting broken limbs, managing patients on traction, and helping them regain muscle strength and movement. One day last month, he treated five patients. One needed to have a cast removed, modified and reapplied. Another required exercises to restore knee movement. A bedridden patient was assisted out of bed for the first time.
For Charles, the reward comes when a patient who arrived on a stretcher walks out of the hospital. “That really motivates me a lot – that at least I’m doing something to help the community,” he said.
For Mirosavljev, that makes the difficult days worthwhile. “It’s a good feeling when you do the job, and people survive … and they walk out,” he said.

Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 5% to $105.3 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets.
In the UK, the yield – or interest rate – on the 10-year government bond hit its highest level since July 2007, rising by six basis points to 5.515%. Investors appear concerned that rising oil prices could stoke higher inflation.
The yield on the 30-year bond – the UK’s benchmark cost for its long-term borrowing – rose by three basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998.
The climbing cost of government borrowing places further pressure on John Healey, as he prepares to deliver his first budget, on 28 October.
The market swings came after the Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes against Iran before the US midterm elections. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they would go ahead, were still being debated.
The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up with more substantial action after the midterms, it states.
Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz have reached their highest levels of the war, cutting traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply.
The latest attack came on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit by projectiles off the north coast of Qatar, causing casualties, according to United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.
Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, after Tropical Storm Isaias strengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.
Shell and Chevron said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday.
The Danish shipping group Maersk added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. The rise in energy prices has fed fears about inflation, reinforcing expectations that central banks will have to raise their interest rates in order to control rising prices.
A sell-off in global bond markets continued on Thursday. In France, which has been hit particularly hard over worries about its rising debt and growing spending, the 10-year yield rose by six basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall.
The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by two basis points to 3.504%.
The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by five basis points to 5.331%.
Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%.
In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%. The UK’s FTSE 100 slipped by 0.4% in early trading on Thursday.

HUNDREDS OF ARRESTS

'Too many lies': Netanyahu's ex-military secretary challenges prime minister's October 7 account
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:41:34 UTC
17:41:34 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's 55-page account of the failures that led to the October 7 attacks "does not reflect what really happened," his former military secretary said in an interview partially published Thursday, warning that official transcripts may have been altered.
"It's part of the truth, but not all of it," Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil – who was serving as Netanyahu's military secretary on October 7, 2023 – said in an interview with Israel Hayom. An excerpt of the interview was published on Thursday, with the full interview set to be released on Friday.
"What the public is being told isn't what really happened," Gil charged.
Gil referred to a document that was submitted by Netanyahu to the State Comptroller's Office on February 5. In a press release then, Netanyahu said the document "includes transcripts of security meetings and other documents covering a period of 12 years, starting with Operation Protective Edge [the 2014 Gaza War] and up to the morning of October 7."
However, at the time, Haaretz reported that minutes and summaries of many of the discussions referred to in the document point to a manipulation of the facts, half-truths and omissions.
"There are too many lies in the air," Gil told Israel Hayom. "I had hoped that a state commission of inquiry would be established and would investigate everything, but unfortunately that hasn't happened, and I'm doubtful it will," he added, explaining why he had chosen to speak out now.
The former military secretary is also expected to speak with Channel 12 News on Thursday evening.
In the excerpt published on Thursday, Gil revealed new details about the alleged altering of the record of conversations between Netanyahu and top officials. According to Gil, two weeks into the war, he began noticing that people in Netanyahu's inner circle were "disproportionately" collecting material.
"I decided to reach out to the attorney general," Gil recalled. "I told her that we're at war, and that I'm not looking to blame anybody and I don't want this to be personal. I asked her to clarify the guidelines about what's allowed and what's forbidden regarding stenograms, and that's what happened," he said.
After Gil reached out to the attorney general, Israel Police began investigating whether senior officials in the Prime Minister's Office attempted to change the protocols of cabinet meetings held during the war, as well as transcripts of phone calls made by decision-makers – including Netanyahu – during the first days of the war. One of the suspects investigated by police was Netanyahu's chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman.
"This involves a pattern of criminal behavior by people who believe they can do whatever they please, and the chief of staff acted like someone who felt he could do anything he wanted," Gil said.
"It could be that even back then they were working on the narrative that we see today, that the prime minister was the only one who functioned when [the October 7 attacks] started," Gil said. "This is a grave scenario, but it's plausible. There's another very grave scenario," he added.
"Every commission of inquiry that's established should insist on receiving the full tapes and not the transcripts, because I don't know what's been altered," Gil said, reiterating his concern that the transcripts do not accurately reflect reality. "I would expect the comptroller to do the same, and not rely on partial stenograms provided by the prime minister."
Gil also spoke about the warnings that Netanyahu received before Hamas' deadly attack. While he did not confirm that Egypt warned the prime minister, as has been previously reported, he said the intelligence official's visit to Israel had a reason.
"An Egyptian intelligence plane landed in Israel and was here for just over 60 minutes. That's a fact. A plane like that doesn't come here without any reason," he told Israel Hayom. "Either somebody came to Israel on it to meet Netanyahu, or somebody came to deliver something, a message or an envelope," he added.
"Somebody met somebody or received something, and didn't report it," Gil charged. "And if that happened, and it appears that it did, that has to be reported. And whoever met somebody or received something is still hiding it today."
Netanyahu's Likud party responded to the outlet's interview in a statement saying the report is "fabricated political propaganda against Prime Minister Netanyahu and Likud, aimed at bringing down the right-wing rule and to lead to a left-wing government that will establish a Palestinian state."
Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a member of Likud, accused "all the former generals and IDF chiefs of staff" of plotting to oust Netanyahu. Speaking with Kan public radio, he said they are trying to "throw dust in the public's eye and mislead it."
Gadi Eisenkot, who polls indicate is the leading contender to replace Netanyahu in Israel's upcoming election on October 27, responded to Gil's interview on social media. "Netanyahu misled, deceived and betrayed the trust of an entire nation, while endangering the security of its citizens," he wrote.

Raiffeisen bank raises growth forecast for Swiss economy
Unknown

Raiffeisen bank raises growth forecast for Swiss economy
Raiffeisen’s economists have significantly revised their forecasts for the Swiss economy upwards and expect the Swiss National Bank (SNB) to bring its zero-interest-rate policy to an end in the near future.
In an analysis published on Thursday, the Swiss bank now forecasts growth in gross domestic product (GDP) – excluding the effects of major sporting events – of 1.7% for 2026. The previous estimate stood at +0.8%. For 2027, however, Raiffeisen confirms its forecast of 1.3% growth.
According to the bank, the Swiss economy remains on a path to recovery and has so far been little affected by the consequences of the war in the Middle East. Business confidence has held up even in the face of the renewed escalation of the conflict in September, while second-quarter growth figures came in stronger than expected, buoyed by the dynamism of the pharmaceutical sector.
The bank’s experts have also revised their inflation estimates upwards: in 2026, prices will rise by 0.7%, compared with the previously forecast +0.5%, while for 2027, a rise of +1.1% is expected, up from the previous forecast of +0.8%. The impact of high energy prices is likely to last longer than hoped, while underlying inflation will tend to rise due to the weaker Swiss franc and increased pressure from abroad.
Consequently, Raiffeisen expects the SNB to raise interest rates soon. The Swiss economy is now operating close to its potential, while inflation remains comfortably within the bank’s target range of 0–2%: the zero-interest-rate policy, which has so far supported the economy, therefore appears increasingly inappropriate.
According to Raiffeisen’s analysts, President of the SNB Martin Schlegel could therefore adjust interest rates as early as its next assessment of the economic and monetary situation, scheduled for December 10.

Middle Corridor: Can Bulgaria be a safe gateway for Asian imports to the EU?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:38:00 UTC
17:38:00 KST

Can Bulgaria be a safe gateway for Asian imports to the EU?
October 8, 2026
On the morning of October 6, drones hit two commercial ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, sinking one of the ships and causing alarm and outrage in both Bulgaria and the European Union.
The drone attacks come at a time when the EU is pushing for Bulgaria to become a key entry point for goods imported from Asia to the bloc via the trade route known as the Middle Corridor.
The Middle Corridor, which the EU also refers to as the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, connects Europe and Asia. It begins in China and runs through Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey before reaching the EU.
Although it is mostly made up of railways and roads, short sections of the corridor cross the Black and Caspian Seas.
Bulgaria and the Middle Corridor
The EU has this year declared its intention to bet big on this trade route, a move that could affect Bulgaria's railways, roads and ports.
Bulgaria's land border crossing with Turkey, Kapitan Andreevo, is already one of Europe's busiest, trucks frequently lining up at the checkpoint.
The country also has two strategic ports on the Black Sea — Varna and Burgas — and a new section of a railway line between Istanbul and the Bulgarian border is set to open this fall.
In September, EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos called Bulgaria "Europe's Connectivity Gateway" due to its strategic location on this route.
Wars have disrupted global trade routes
A few months earlier, Kos said the Middle Corridor could considerably cut transport times from Asia to Europe from 45 days to just 15 days and is safer than the two traditional routes for goods being transported to Europe from Asia.
One of these was an overland route via the Northern Corridor through Russia. Trade along this route dropped sharply after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The other route, sometimes referred to as the Ocean Route, sees goods traveling by ship through the Red Seaand the Suez Canal. But fears of disruption caused by wars and instability in the Middle East mean that many goods are now being shipped all the way around Africa — a journey that takes around 45 days. That results in delays and costs for businesses and consumers alike.
All of this explains why the Middle Corridor suddenly seems so attractive — a fact confirmed by Vessela Tcherneva, deputy director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, who is based in Sofia, Bulgaria.
"The Middle Corridor is a project that basically avoids both war theaters that we have near Europe," Tcherneva told DW. "It avoids the route through Russia, and also it avoids the route through the Middle East."
Is the Middle Corridor a realistic alternative?
As promising as it sounds, a lot needs to change before the Middle Corridor can really compete with the Ocean Route.
"You have, first and foremost, security limitations," said Tcherneva. "The security situation in Central Asia needs to really have improved enough so that one can make long-term plans for constructing big projects."
Tcherneva also stressed that weak institutions and bureaucracies in countries along the Middle Corridor are an issue. Russian involvement cannot be ruled out.
"We have seen infrastructure projects in the past not happen because they were not perceived as being in Russia's interest, and the Russians seem to have quite a bit of leverage in the countries along the route," she said, adding that "the outcome of Russia's war in Ukraine is going to have an impact on the success or failure of the Middle Corridor."
Tuesday's drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea are a stark reminder that security on the route could well remain a problem.
In addition, the water level in the Caspian Sea, which is situated on the Middle Corridor, is falling, with climate change as a key driver. This means there is no guarantee that ships will be able to cross it in the future.
Then there is the problem of infrastructure: Ports and railways along the route lack capacity for big increases in trade volumes.
How Bulgaria could benefit
Despite these risks and limitations, the EU clearly wants to see more trade coming through the Middle Corridor, even if it cannot replace existing routes.
In her recent State of the Union speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that the EU wants to improve what it calls "connectivity." It wants to diversify trade routes, increase trade flows and reduce freight transit times.
To do so, it aims to raise €12 billion ($13.5 billion) in public and private investment.
Bulgaria could benefit from this in a number of ways.
"The Bulgarian railways have been underinvested in for many, many years now — for decades. Bulgarian ports would also benefit greatly from investment," Tcherneva told DW. "Developing better road connections from the Mediterranean up, but also east-west, would help, especially the north of the country, which is currently not very well connected. So, there are clear benefits."

Only a third of EU counter-drone programmes will deliver by 2030, leaked report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:37:32 UTC
17:37:32 KST

EU counter-drone investment grew sixfold in 2025, but only a third of programmes will deliver by 2030, a confidential EU report seen by Euronews says, citing fragmented procurement and industry struggling to keep pace with fast-moving drone technology.
Investment in counter-drone technology across the EU surged sixfold between 2024 and 2025, but only a third of the programmes are expected to deliver by 2030, according to a confidential EU report obtained by Euronews.
The 2026 annual defence readiness report, a European Defence Agency (EDA) assessment of national military capabilities, exposes persistent gaps in Europe's defences against drones and urges member states to step up investment in drone and counter-drone technology.
"Investment in counter-drone and very short-range air defence capabilities grew sixfold between 2024 and 2025 in response to the growing threat posed by unmanned systems, although only around one third of programmes are expected to deliver by 2030," reads the report, which was shared with European governments last week.
The EU's eastern flank, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, faces a growing threat from drones, some of which have strayed from the battlefield in Ukraine. On Tuesday, drones struck two commercial vessels in Bulgaria's territorial waters, sinking one.
The EDA found that most member states are investing in drones for surveillance, reconnaissance and target acquisition, while other types of unmanned aircraft continue to attract limited funding despite their growing importance on the battlefield.
EU countries are investing €18.9 billion in drone technologies over 2024-2029, the report says.
"Despite the high level of attention paid to the acquisition of drone and counter-drone capabilities, significant capability gaps and external dependencies continue to affect overall European readiness," the document continues.
Spain, Denmark, Croatia, Latvia and the Netherlands are leading a joint EU project to buy drones and anti-drone systems together and to set up a technology hub to centralise innovation and testing.
However, the EDA points to significant shortcomings: procurement fragmented at national level, limited interoperability, a lack of experimentation capacity and insufficient industrial surge capacity, notably for weaponised drones.
Closing these gaps would cost comparatively little next to other defence capabilities, the report notes, but would demand sustained funding and an agile, integrated approach.
"Industrial capacity has yet to reach the scale and responsiveness required for protracted high-intensity operations, as the pace of technological innovation is outstripping traditional acquisition cycles, creating a persistent risk that capabilities become obsolete before they can be fielded," the report adds.
In short, it says drone technology is evolving so quickly that equipment risks becoming obsolete before it even reaches the battlefield.
The report says current plans and programmes address these challenges but must be paired with adequate doctrine and training.
The EDA also found more than 200 companies producing drone and counter-drone technologies in the EU, a dynamic but fragmented ecosystem that could expand by up to 140% by next year with the right investment framework.
"Industrial readiness in this sector requires agile production ecosystems maintained at the cutting edge of technologies and organised for rapid and massive scaling rather than building up large stockpiles," the report reads.
