Yemen's Houthis claim ballistic missile attack on Riyadh airport
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:58:51 CST
16:58:51 KST

SANAA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Thursday it launched a fresh ballistic missile attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital of Riyadh and carried out missile strikes against government forces near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said in a statement posted on social media platform X that a ballistic missile "accurately hit its target" at King Khalid International Airport, disrupting air traffic. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities of the latest attack claim.
Sarea also issued what he called a "final warning" to international airlines against continuing to operate flights through Saudi airspace, claiming that it had become an area of Houthi military operations. He said the warning did not apply to airspace over the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The latest Houthi claim followed attacks on two Saudi airports on Tuesday and Wednesday that left three people dead and 36 others injured, according to the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on both airports. Sarea said Wednesday that several drones targeted King Khalid International Airport, while ballistic missiles and drones hit Abha International Airport and King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait in the southwestern Asir region.
Later Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said that it had launched a comprehensive operation, destroying 82 Houthi military targets across several provinces, in response to attacks on civilians and civilian sites in the kingdom.
The recent clashes marked the sharpest escalation since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities in the war-torn country.
Yemen's conflict began in late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government, now based in Aden. ■

Schools closed in Malaysia's Johor due to bad air quality
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:58:45 CST
16:58:45 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- All schools in the Malaysian state of Johor are closed on Thursday and Friday due to the worsening haze and deteriorating air quality.
The decision was made as a precautionary measure to safeguard the health and safety of students, Johor Education and Information Committee chairman Muhammad Naqib Md Ghazali said in a statement late on Wednesday.
The school closures affect all 1,198 schools and 617,258 students across Johor.
Johor state has seen some of the worst Air Pollutant Index (API) readings in recent days, with the Segamat area recording an API of 187 as of 10 a.m. on Thursday.
Unhealthy API levels were also recorded in 38 areas nationwide, including the capital, Kuala Lumpur. ■

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Pakistani security forces have killed nine terrorists, including four key commanders, in an intelligence-based operation in the country's northwest Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Thursday, security sources said.

Cambodia's foreign trade up 22 pct in first 9 months of 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:58:36 CST
16:58:36 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's foreign trade volume reached 58.48 billion U.S. dollars in the first nine months of 2026, up 22 percent year-on-year, according to the Ministry of Commerce on Thursday.
Official data showed that the kingdom's total exports rose 18 percent to 27.47 billion dollars from January to September. Meanwhile, imports surged 26 percent to reach 31.01 billion dollars.
China, the United States, Vietnam, Singapore, and Japan were the top five trading partners.
Cambodia's primary exports included manufactured goods such as garments, footwear, travel goods, and bicycles, alongside agricultural products such as milled rice, bananas, cashew nuts, mangoes, longans, and durians.
Its top imports consisted of manufacturing raw materials, petroleum, construction inputs, vehicles, electronics, consumer goods, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetics.
Penn Sovicheat, a secretary of state and spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce, attributed the robust growth to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and bilateral free trade agreements (FTAs) with China, South Korea, and the United Arab Emirates.
"This significant expansion shows that Cambodia is successfully maintaining its key international markets, elevating its position in the global supply chain, and continuing to earn the trust of international buyers," he told Xinhua. ■

Britain says consulate in Jerusalem to remain open as a mission
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
15:58:35 CST
16:58:35 KST

LONDON, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Thursday that the Consulate General in East Jerusalem will remain open, after his Israeli counterpart said the mission is ending its operations.
"We have been clear that we do not accept that the Government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem," Miliband said in a statement on social media platform X, noting that "East Jerusalem is occupied territory."
The consulate, located in occupied East Jerusalem, handles Britain's relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem, as well as in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.
"Following discussions with the Government of Israel, our Consulate General building will not be closing," Miliband said, adding that it would continue to provide services and be known as the "UK Mission."
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said Thursday that the British consulate is ending its operations that day.
Relations between Britain and Israel have deteriorated as Israel has stepped up its military campaign against the Gaza Strip, which has left more than 74,200 people killed over the past three years according to Gaza-based health authorities, while settlement expansion has continued in the occupied West Bank.
Britain announced in September an import ban and additional sanctions targeting settlement expansion, citing "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" by "settler terrorists" in parts of the West Bank.
In response, Israel announced a series of countermeasures against Britain, including that it would close the British Consulate General in East Jerusalem and remove British personnel from a U.S.-led Gaza coordination center.
"We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence, and we will not take reciprocal action," Miliband said Thursday. ■

Programmer who ensured the landing of the &quot;Apollo 11&quot; mission on the Moon has died
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:51:03 EEST
16:51:03 KST

Programmer who ensured the landing of the "Apollo 11" mission on the Moon has died
Kyiv • UNN
Margaret Hamilton died at the age of 90. Her software detected a malfunction and restored the system's operation before the lunar landing.
American programmer Margaret Hamilton, who led the development of the software for the "Apollo 11" mission (Apollo 11), has died at the age of 90. The Guardian reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the engineer's death was announced on Wednesday by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
"At a time when positions such as software engineer and computer scientist had not yet become common, Hamilton, who died on September 30, learned to program under the guidance of a renowned Massachusetts Institute of Technology meteorologist. She continued improving the equipment at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology laboratory, developing software that could detect enemy aircraft," the publication writes.
So, when NASA contracted the institute to create onboard software for the Apollo mission, Hamilton took advantage of the opportunity and joined the work.
"I was attracted both by the idea itself and by the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join, and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
According to the publication, in 1969, several minutes before the "Apollo 11" landing on the Moon, the onboard computer issued an emergency signal. The team then faced the question of whether the mission should be aborted. Ultimately, the spacecraft continued its flight, and the software worked exactly as Hamilton and her team had intended.
"It quickly became clear that the software not only informed everyone that there was a problem related to the equipment, but also compensated for it—it restarted and recovered the highest-priority task. Error-detection and recovery mechanisms came to the rescue," Hamilton said.
In 2016, U.S. President Barack Obama presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom and recalled this incident. "Our astronauts did not have much time, but fortunately, they had Margaret Hamilton," he said.
According to available information, Hamilton is survived by a daughter, a son-in-law, two grandchildren, and four great-grandchildren.
Recall
A piece of the "Apollo 11" spacecraft, which traveled to the Moon with the first astronauts—a strip of golden thermopolyimide tape—is now the central detail of the wedding ring of John Messick, a planning manager at aerospace company Lockheed Martin.

State Veterans Support Service to be established in Ukraine – Veterans Affairs Ministry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:51:00 EEST
16:51:00 KST

The State Veterans Support Service is to be established in Ukraine on the basis of the State Veteran Space digital platform, the Ministry of Veterans Affairs reports.
"A State Veterans Support Service will be created in Ukraine. Its goal is to change the approach to supporting veterans: instead of independently searching for necessary services and institutions, a person will have an assigned specialist who will coordinate their entire route and monitor the outcome," the ministry's statement reads.
It is noted that the Service will operate at both central and regional levels, incorporating a nationwide network of specialists dedicated to supporting war veterans and demobilized individuals.
"Upon receiving information about demobilization or a military medical commission conclusion, a person's data will automatically flow into the 'Oskar' CRM system. Following this, the veteran will be assigned a support specialist, who must contact the individual within 24–48 hours," the department explained.
Specifically, during the initial contact, the specialist will assess the primary needs of the veteran: health status, prosthetics requirements, psychological condition, housing issues, and opportunities for economic self-realization.
Subsequently, an individual action plan will be formulated based on this assessment, which the veteran will be able to approve via the Diia application.
The support pathway will comprise five core stages: preparation for discharge from military service; transition to civilian life; health recovery and psychological support; economic independence and professional self-realization; and socialization and community participation.
Moving forward, the specialist will coordinate navigation through the entire pathway and ensure that essential services are not only assigned but actually delivered.
"The criterion for performance and support must not be the number of consultations or issued referrals, but the actual outcome for the veteran and their family," the Ministry of Veterans Affairs emphasized.
Among other measures, plans include reforming the workload assessment model for support specialists. Instead of the current model, where a single specialist may handle up to 100 cases, a point-based system will be introduced to account for the complexity of each individual case.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:49:14 UTC
16:49:14 KST

Ukraine plans 135 basic mobile shelters for civilians at 28 of its border crossings, the State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development said on 7 October.
Since the start of September, Russian drones have repeatedly struck crossings on Ukraine's borders with Moldova and Romania. Since mid-September, strikes have also reached the Polish border near the Yahodyn crossing in Volyn Oblast. On 13 September, a Russian drone strike set a gas station near the crossing on fire. On 28 September, the blast wave from another strike damaged the checkpoint building. On 25 September, First Deputy Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport Serhii Derkach said Ukraine is exploring with its neighbors whether some checkpoints could move onto their territory. No agreement has been reported. On 2 October, Moldovan Interior Minister Daniella Misail-Nichitin said Moldova had set up shelters next to its crossings with Ukraine and started relocating staff from joint checkpoints.
135 shelters for travelers and border staff
The shelters will stand at the crossings and on the roads leading to them. Regional recovery services in Vinnytsia, Odesa, Chernivtsi, Zakarpattia, and Volyn oblasts are running the purchases. The agency said the shelters will make the border safer for people crossing it and for checkpoint staff.
In Chernivtsi Oblast, one of the 10 tenders the agency lists on Prozorro, Ukraine's public procurement system, covers eight shelters for 50 people each and three for 20 each, Ukrinform reported. They will stand on the approach road to the Porubne–Siret international crossing on the Romanian border. The work is expected to cost UAH 38.5 million (about $855,000), excluding VAT.
Russian strikes on crossings
On 5 October, at about 09:38, a projectile fell near the Palanca–Maiaky–Udobne crossing on the Moldovan border. It ricocheted off the ground into a shuttle bus parked by the barrier and also damaged a control booth. One Moldovan border officer suffered light injuries, and the crossing was suspended, Moldova's Border Police said, linking the incident to Russia's attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Moldovan authorities did not specify the projectile's type or origin.
Overnight on 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing with Moldova, killing two people and injuring three. On 1 September, Russian Shahed drones hit the Orlivka ferry crossing on the Danube, opposite Romania's Isaccea, and temporarily shut it down. Another Russian strike on 6 September halted the crossing again.

Inside Kazakhstan’s historic rock-hewn mosques now recognised by UNESCO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:45:48 UTC
16:45:48 KST

Five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites dating from the 12th to the 18th centuries make up Kazakhstan’s newest UNESCO World Heritage property. The complexes preserve centuries of Sufi tradition alongside much older beliefs.
The World Heritage Committee adopted the decision at its 48th session on 25 July in Busan, South Korea. This follows President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s 2024 instructions to pursue the inscription of these rock-hewn mosques on the World Heritage List.
Set amid the otherworldly landscapes of Mangystau, the newly recognised mosques and their associated sites are named after revered Sufi masters: Beket-Ata, Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe.
In Central Asian Sufism, ‘Ata’, meaning ‘father’ or ‘ancestor’, is used as an honorific for a revered spiritual figure.
Their spiritual lineage traces back to the 12th-century Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. His teachings helped spread Islam among the Turkic-speaking peoples of Central Asia, connecting Islamic practices with older Tengri beliefs and local shamanistic traditions.
The mosques welcome both pilgrims and visitors seeking to explore Kazakhstan’s spiritual, cultural and architectural heritage.
Mangystau – the cradle of nomadic spirituality
According to the UNESCO World Heritage Centre, the complexes reflect the evolution of a distinctive spiritual culture.
They represent “sacred practices in which Islamic Sufi spirituality organically continued and transformed more ancient practices related to ancestor worship, the sacredness of the landscape and the role of spiritual leaders”.
Developed over many centuries, the monuments show how spiritual traditions and practices were adapted to the region’s distinctive natural environment and geological features through local architecture.
Speaking at the 48th session in July, Erlan Karin, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s National Commission to UNESCO and ICESCO, highlighted the significance of the inscription for the country.
“The inscription of the sacred monuments of Mangystau on the World Heritage List was not only a recognition of their significance for humanity as a whole, but also a tribute to the rich history, spiritual heritage and cultural identity of the Kazakh people.”
For local resident Almagul Zhaiman, the sacred sites embody a faith passed down through generations.
“These sacred sites have been preserved because of the faith passed down through generations, the knowledge of that heritage, preserving it and passing it on to our future generations. I believe that is what makes all these mosques so meaningful to us,” she said.
The Sufi masters of the mosques
Karaman-Ata was a Sufi missionary who came to spread Islam in the region. His mosque is believed to date back to the 12th or 13th century, while its associated necropolis is one of the largest and oldest in Mangystau.
For the Kazakhs and Turkmens who lived on the Mangyshlak Peninsula, the necropolis was considered a sacred place. According to local tradition, it was also a site for resolving disputes and negotiating peace. Those who made vows there were expected to honour them, as breaking a vow was believed to bring death and the end of one's lineage.
Karaman-Ata is believed to have been the grandson of Shopan-Ata, a 12th-century mystic revered as the spiritual protector of shepherds and their livestock.
According to tradition, Shopan-Ata was a disciple of the renowned Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. Once part of an ancient caravan route to Khorezm, Shopan-Ata’s site remains an important destination for Sufi pilgrims.
Beket-Ata is said to have regarded Shopan-Ata, who lived centuries earlier, as a spiritual mentor.
Local traditions attribute extraordinary abilities to the 18th-century scholar, healer and architect, including teleportation and levitation.
“He was also regarded as the last and highest-ranking spiritual master among other holy men, which is why he became known as Pir Beket,” said Bakhtiyar Esimbetov, caretaker of Beket-Ata’s mosque.
In Sufi tradition, the Persian word ‘Pir’ refers to a spiritual guide or master, often one who has attained a high level of spiritual wisdom.
The Shakpak-Ata complex served as one of the region’s principal Sufi centres for centuries. Shakpak-Ata is believed to have lived sometime between the 9th and 14th centuries.
Carved into a chalk and limestone cliff, the sanctuary is arranged around a central domed hall with a cross-shaped layout.
Local traditions say the scholar taught astrology and astronomy, as well as ideas linked to the cosmos.
Inside the mosques’ architectural layout
According to local belief, divine signs guided the Sufi masters to the places where they built their mosques.
The sanctuaries are scattered across Mangystau, in western Kazakhstan, a region shaped by its nomadic heritage and geological history. Much of the area was once covered by the ancient Tethys Ocean.
Locally known as “underground mosques”, the complexes were built in natural caves, carved into steep rock faces or dug into the ground, providing shelter in the semi-desert landscape.
Their architectural layouts vary. They include prayer halls, mihrabs, rooms for contemplation and self-reflection, multifunctional spaces and tombs of the Sufi masters, sometimes alongside those of their immediate families.
Some underground cells were carved out for silent meditation and ascetic isolation.
“These underground mosques were places of retreat from society, where people could withdraw from everyday life and devote themselves fully to spiritual purification,” said Yersultan Islam, a local sacred sites guide.
The complexes also feature courtyards, water sources, sacred trees, pathways and cemeteries, some of which date from the 10th to the 20th centuries.
Pilgrims
For centuries, Mangystau’s sacred mosques have been important destinations for pilgrims.
Visitors are expected to dress modestly, while women are required to cover their heads before entering the underground mosques as a sign of respect for the sacred sites.
The sanctuaries attract not only local worshippers but also pilgrims from abroad.
Among them is Dinara Farvazova, whose family travels from Bashkortostan, Russia, to visit Mangystau’s sacred sites year after year.
“We read the Quran here, pray and make wishes. People come here seeking healing, and many see their dreams come true. They then tell their relatives and friends about the place, who come here too.”
Some visitors come in search of a deeper understanding of Islam.
Kaahn Ozturk, a traveller from Turkey, stopped at Karaman-Ata’s mosque during a long-distance motorcycle journey across the country.
“I have lots of questions in my mind, and I just want to find answers. That’s why I’m trying to discover every mosque, every place, every idea about Islam, to understand it better.”
Rinat Aubekerov and his wife, ethnic Kazakhs from Russia, made a pilgrimage to Shopan-Ata, hoping their prayers to have children would be answered.
For Davide Passanante, a visitor from Italy, the appeal was different.
After experiencing the crowds of summer tourism at home, he found a sense of calm in the remote sanctuaries. Travelling with a group of friends across Mangystau’s Martian-like landscapes, he was struck by the region’s spiritual atmosphere.
“I'm very impressed because the religion here is very important. I see how people pray and how they feel, how they think of God every time.”
Easing travel for visitors to sacred sites
The remote sanctuaries are attracting growing numbers of pilgrims from around the world. Kazakhstan is now planning to improve access to the newly listed sites while preserving them for future generations.
A five-year comprehensive development plan, due to begin in 2027, is expected to support tourism at the sites, including restoration work and the development of new visitor infrastructure.
Each sanctuary already has basic facilities where visitors can sleep and eat free of charge, although donations are welcome to help cover maintenance costs.
Plans include building visitor centres at Shopan-Ata, Beket-Ata and Karaman-Ata, complementing the existing centre serving Sultan-Epe and Shakpak-Ata.
“An asphalt road will be built to the site as part of the development plan. We also hope that internet connectivity issues will be resolved,” said Baltabai Balapan, director of the Mangystau State Historical and Cultural Reserve.
The five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites of Mangystau, now collectively inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, are bringing the region’s spiritual heritage to a global audience, inviting visitors to discover its sacred landscapes.

plywood horse doubles turn monument into public playground in seattle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:45:28 UTC
16:45:28 KST

plywood horse doubles turn monument into public playground in seattle
what happens when the horse statue steps off its pedestal? at seattle design festival, studio deng’s flatland horse takes shape as a gateway and a slide, pairing plywood silhouettes with shaggy chenille.
Eight horse doubles bring monumental forms into everyday use
The Flatland Horse by Studio Deng reinterprets the equestrian monument as a set of eight functional horse ‘doubles’ that visitors can climb, touch, sit on, and pass through. The project disassembles the equestrian statue into eight parts. The monumental horse itself is shaped through countless design revisions, with individual body parts selected and assembled into the final official figure. Studio Deng separates these elements into individual plywood silhouettes, each retaining one body part in soft volume while taking on a public function such as a bench, seat, table, gate, slide, mirror, pavilion, or toy.
Birch plywood and chenille give horses a soft, modular form
For the 2026 Seattle Design Festival, themed IN[FLUX], Studio Deng was selected to build and exhibit two of the doubles at Lake Union Park. Gate Horse forms an archway from separated plywood profiles, framing a passage and views of the Seattle skyline through the horse’s negative space. Slide Horse uses the structural logic of a bridge, with a plywood deck spanning four leg frames between a staircase and slide. Its lowered head forms the slide, while the mane becomes a side barrier.
Both installations translate the equine body into flat plywood planes that become more abstract at close range. A selected body part is given volume with brown chenille stretched over a waffle-like framework of half-inch foam core panels attached to the plywood. The textured textile suggests the form of a mane or muscle while adding a softer surface to the structures.
The horses were built from ¾-inch, 13-ply birch plywood, cut and sanded by the design team. Slide Horse was assembled in three units using nails, bolts, and L-brackets for quick installation. After the festival, both structures were unbolted, flat-packed, and reassembled in a courtyard in Issaquah, east of Seattle, allowing the temporary installations to continue in a new setting.
project info:
name: The Flatland Horse
designer: Studio Deng | @studio_deng_
design team: Meichen Wang, Yijia Xu, Qicheng Wu, Chen Yang, Fan Wu, Yangyi Li, Hanlin Cai
fabrication support: Brad McGuirt & North Ballard Chop Shop
organizer: Seattle Design Festival | @seadesignfest
location: Lake Union Park, Seattle, Washington, US

The Indian billionaire investing in Trump's refinery project is also buying more Venezuelan crude
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:41:51 UTC
16:41:51 KST

Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries, which is investing in a historic U.S. oil refinery project proposed by President Donald Trump, has now emerged as the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude outside the U.S.
Trump has been pushing India to buy more Venezuelan oil, but while state-owned oil companies are making opportunistic purchases, Reliance has been the primary buyer, according to Kpler data shared with CNBC. It shows that outside the U.S., India is the biggest destination for these supplies, with Reliance purchasing the bulk of that crude.
"Reliance's Jamnagar complex has been the main destination for Venezuelan crude in India, and we expect it to remain the primary buyer," Sumit Ritolia, lead research analyst at Kpler, told CNBC.
In September, India imported 257,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan crude, of which 76% went to Reliance Industries, data showed. The Jamnagar refinery is the world's "largest and most complex single-site refinery" with crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day, according to Reliance.
Venezuelan heavy and extra-heavy grades of crude are relatively difficult barrels to process and are not universally suitable across India's refining system, Ritola said, adding that the Jamnagar complex is particularly well configured for these barrels.
In March, Trump had announced that the U.S. will build its first refinery in 50 years with investment from India's Reliance Industries. The president had thanked Reliance for this "tremendous investment."
While Reliance has not confirmed the size of investment, Trump in a Truth Social post had said that "THIS IS A HISTORIC $300 BILLION DOLLAR DEAL — THE BIGGEST IN U.S. HISTORY."
Reliance is the most valued company in India, with a market capitalization of more than $169 billion.
Reliance's Venezuelan purchases come at a time when India's procurement of Russian oil has drawn the ire of the U.S., where lawmakers have given Trump the power to impose up to 100% tariffs on countries buying energy from Moscow.
Despite mounting pressure to buy more energy from the U.S. and cut its dependence on Russian oil, the Indian government has insisted that its decisions are driven by the need to ensure energy security for its people.
While oil supplies in September from Russia to India have "moderated" from exceptionally high levels in June and July, that is largely driven by the stronger competition between Beijing and New Delhi and not the threat of tariffs, Ritolia said.
India is the largest destination for Russian crude, securing a supply of 1.82 million barrels per day in September versus China's 1.49 mbd, according to Kpler data, much more than Venezuelan purchases.
For October, 350,000 barrels per day of crude supplies from Venezuela are bound for India, though some of these could land in November because of the long voyage time, Ritolia said.

EU state tightens rules for military-age Ukrainian men

EU state tightens rules for military-age Ukrainian men
Lithuania has tightened temporary protection rules for Ukrainian men subject to military service, becoming the latest EU member state to impose new conditions as Kiev struggles to replenish its depleted armed forces.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly urged European governments to facilitate the return of military-age men to help sustain the country’s war effort. Kiev barred most military-age men from leaving Ukraine after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022 and later lowered the minimum mobilization age from 27 to 25.
On Wednesday, the Lithuanian government approved rules requiring Ukrainians liable for military service to prove they have fulfilled their obligations to qualify for temporary protection. Existing beneficiaries who have continuously retained their status are exempt. Around 52,000 Ukrainians currently hold temporary residence permits in the Baltic country.
Germany has also seen calls for tougher restrictions on Ukrainians. Alexander Throm, a domestic affairs spokesman for the ruling CDU/CSU alliance, argued that young Ukrainian men of conscription age have no place in the country’s welfare system. According to Germany’s Federal Office for Migration and Refugees, the number of Ukrainian men aged 18 to 63 living in the country rose by around 52,000 in the year to March 2026.
Other European countries have already tightened their policies. Poland has scaled back certain welfare benefits, healthcare, and accommodation for Ukrainians, while Norway and Switzerland have limited protection for applicants from Ukrainian regions they consider relatively safe.
The Czech Republic deported 157 Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, nearly five times the number recorded during all of last year, according to Interior Ministry figures cited by RIA Novosti.
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that European leaders face growing public fatigue over the conflict and increasing opposition to continued aid to Kiev.
Despite tightening restrictions on Ukrainians living in the bloc, EU governments continue to channel billions to Kiev. The European Commission announced another €2.9 billion ($3.25 billion) disbursement last week, while €60 billion of its planned €90 billion loan package for 2026-2027 is earmarked for military spending.
Kiev is continuing its controversial mobilization campaign, including the practice dubbed ‘busification’, in which recruitment officers forcibly take men from the streets to enlistment centers, often sparking clashes and protests.
Moscow has accused Kiev of fighting “to the last Ukrainian,” arguing that Western governments are prolonging the conflict by continuing to supply weapons and financial assistance.

In its own statement, Google said it had "fallen short of our own high standards in this instance", adding it intends to fully comply with the LVV order.

Türkiye prioritizes macro-financial stability amid global headwinds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:41:00 UTC
16:41:00 KST

Turkish Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek (AA Photo)
Türkiye prioritizes macro-financial stability and a tight fiscal policy to cushion the impact of shocks while addressing global structural headwinds, Turkish Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said.
Şimşek said on Oct. 8 during the Istanbul Economic Forum's opening ceremony that the government maintained a tight fiscal policy to cushion the impact of shocks and prioritize macro-financial stability.
The two-day forum was organized by the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye to address global economic policy challenges by gathering central bank governors and high-level policymakers from around the world, including the US and the UK.
Şimşek noted that global structural headwinds included conflicts, trade protectionism, high indebtedness, unfavorable demographics, impending climate disasters and artificial intelligence (AI).
The country plans to increase defense spending by 229% in the 2027 budget against the Central Bank's 21% inflation target for next year to build deterrence.
Şimşek added that the value of research and development in defense projects exceeded $100 billion, with around 1,400 defense products and projects, moving the country toward becoming a top 10 exporter.
He said Türkiye ranked among the top three globally for official development assistance and diplomatic footprint.
Turkish Airlines flew to the most destinations compared with other carriers, he recalled.
He also said the government invested in an $8 billion railway project crossing the Bosphorus in Istanbul to connect Beijing to London.
The country also encouraged its neighbors to invest in additional corridors, such as the new development road, to improve connectivity and resilience.
Şimşek pointed out that the nation invested in natural gas and oil pipelines to ensure the availability of energy supplies.
The nation boosted the share of renewables in electricity generation to almost 60% and set an ambitious 35% electrification target, up from 23%, as the COP31 host.
The government responded to global trade protectionism by expanding free trade agreements, holding 54 pacts, with three pending and ongoing negotiations with Japan, Indonesia, the Gulf Cooperation Council and Canada.
He pointed out that tourism revenue jumped ninefold over the past quarter-century, placing Türkiye among the top five global tourist destinations.
Şimşek mentioned that the country had over 50 internationally accredited healthcare facilities and attracted medical tourists for cosmetic treatments.
He said the nation became the world's third-largest exporter of soap operas and ranked second to London in the gaming ecosystem for startups and unicorns.
The country ranked second to China in the global league of contractors and hoped to aid in regional reconstruction, which required at least $1 trillion over the next decade.
Şimşek noted that the nation hosted the sixth-largest number of international students at its universities.
He underscored that total indebtedness remained at 91%, compared with a 230% average for emerging market peers, while public debt to GDP stood at 22%.
The government targeted a 3.1% deficit this year, keeping it well below the 5.8% average for global emerging markets, and reduced current expenditures from 4.6% of the budget to 2.9%.
The administration sought to strengthen its fiscal position by investing in public procurement, state-owned enterprise governance and tax reforms.
Şimşek said the working-age population would continue to grow over the next decade and the administration planned reforms to boost women's low labor force participation rate.
He said the country invested in 5G+ technology, expanded fiber capacity and planned nuclear power plants, including small modular reactors (SMRs), to power AI.
The government also helped small and medium-sized enterprises boost productivity to capitalize on the positive potential of AI.
The administration invested in irrigation and climate-resilient agriculture to combat global warming.
Şimşek remarked that the country frequently tested its ability to recover quickly from difficulties and adapted its policies despite challenges in a tough neighborhood.
He underscored that delivering price stability remained the primary goal of the medium-term economic program while maintaining fiscal discipline.
The minister added that external imbalances remained manageable even though they deteriorated this year because of the war.
He highlighted that real convergence continued as the economy grew slightly more than 3%, outpacing the 1.5% growth of trading partners, while historical growth over the last 25 years stood closer to 5.5%.
Şimşek noted that the Central Bank governor utilized quantitative and selective credit-tightening tools while the government was adjusting its fiscal policy to make support more selective and targeted.
He concluded that recent stress in the asset management sector remained contained and the country maintained plenty of policy space to respond in a shock-prone world.
Touching on the country's disinflation process, the minister said the process had largely stalled this year because of the war, "but we're not giving up."
"This year deficit would have been actually closer to two and a half percent, had we not deployed fiscal space to cushion or to, to slow the pass through from crudes to final products," he added.

Harri Tiido: On Russia's influence activity and even more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:41:00 UTC
16:41:00 KST

Harri Tiido: On Russia's influence activity and even more
In Harri Tiido's commentary series, the focus this time is on Finland and Russia's influence activity. As a broader example, Finland shows how Russia's provocations in foreign countries may begin to undermine the embedded influence, at least it is worth hoping so.
The Finnish Institute of International Affairs (FIIA) published an analysis of Russia's embedded influence in Finland, authored by Sinikukka Saari. I borrow some ideas from there and expand the topic a bit.
The concept of "embedded influence" needs a short explanation. Namely, Russia has for years shaped the strategic environment by embedding its manipulative influence also into seemingly lawful forms of cooperation. This definition of embedded influence activity is also closer to Russia's understanding of subversion.
Talk of Russian hybrid influence is mainly characteristic of the West. What the West calls hybrid activity is rather what Russia calls active measures, that is, subversion abroad. These measures have been known already since Soviet times, when they referred to political influence methods, including spreading disinformation, organizing demonstrations by front organizations, and even murders.
Russia also used embedded influence in Finland, because until the year 2022 Finland's foreign policy sought to maintain pragmatic, cooperation‑oriented and economically beneficial relations first with the Soviet state and then with Russia.
Moscow sought to achieve longer‑term goals by influencing Finland's political decision‑making. Mainly the idea was emphasized that Finland and Russia have unique, mutually beneficial relations based on trust and good‑neighborly cooperation. In addition, a skeptical attitude toward European Union and NATO countries was encouraged, especially toward the Baltic states, who were portrayed as irrationally Russia‑hostile, highlighting against their background Finland's pragmatic and responsible behavior as a neighboring state.
From time to time, attempts were made to carry out carefully calibrated operations so that Finns would not retreat from their previous policy. For example, airspace violations or directing migrants to the Finnish border. It cannot be claimed that these aspirations had no success. In Finland there were decision‑makers who feared that ignoring Russia's investment opportunities for security considerations would give competitors elsewhere in Europe a chance to profit themselves.
I add that certainly there were in Finland — and possibly still are — so‑called dormant influence agents who step forward at the necessary moment. In this context it would be interesting to know how many of them there might be in Estonia. As time passes they age, and in fact it would probably be high time for Moscow to "wake them up," so to speak.
In Finland's case, things were set straight by the start of Russia's full‑scale aggression in Ukraine in 2022; cooperation broke off sharply and Russia was left without its main levers for influencing Finland. Therefore Russia had to move on to ordinary measures — cyberattacks, GPS signal jamming, organizing migration waves, disinformation campaigns and such.
Finland's great advantage is a strong crisis‑preparedness culture and a comprehensive security approach, that is, the readiness of society as a whole to withstand threats. Although despite this, according to the analysis, authorities were slow to understand the risks that accompanied Russia's strategic investments or the acquisition of real estate with Russian money near critical infrastructure and military bases. We know about this thanks to journalism, academic researchers and civic activists. I admit that when writing background stories (link in Estonian) about Russian real estate located in Finland, I used very thorough overviews published in the Finnish media.
The cohesion of society and the broad consensus of political forces in foreign and security policy is a phenomenon worthy of attention. One can only wish that Estonian political forces would also publicly remain in consensus on these issues.
In Finland's case, the example given in the analysis is also interesting: Russian hybrid measures and political pressure often produced the opposite of the desired result. As a broader example, Finland shows how Russia's provocations in foreign countries may begin to undermine the embedded influence. At least it is worth hoping so.
I add some thoughts. First of all, I agree with those who say it is long time to stop talk of Russian hybrid measures or hybrid war. In foreign‑language media, reference has repeatedly been made to the interview of Estonia's foreign intelligence chief Kaupo Rosin (link in Estonian) in the British newspaper The Telegraph, in which he called Russia's actions in Western countries state‑supported terrorism.
A word has its power, and changing terminology would cast new light on this whole set of diversions and sabotage acts. Or then use the definition "warfare with disguised methods." Otherwise there is such whining about the grey zone and hybrid and who knows what. The time should be suitable for this, because several countries have already specifically pointed to Russia as the force behind what has happened on their territory.
From this would follow another possible step that could also be applied here. Namely, charges should be brought against perpetrators of such activities not for hooliganism or vandalism, but specifically for terrorism; surely lawyers will find a proper justification for this.
Because prevention is important and Russia widely uses one‑time actors, including often young people, the change in the basis for such charges should also be widely communicated. In journalism it should be announced that from now on such acts fall under the terrorism paragraph together with correspondingly harsher punishments. It should also be talked about in schools, at meetings with young people, on social media and so on. That is, make those who might feel tempted aware that even a small thing can end very badly.
Decisiveness is also needed in dealing with Russia's shadow fleet, around which there has already long been much pontificating. In a recent publication of the European Union Institute for Security Studies (EUISS), for example, the establishment of special zones at sea is recommended, referring to environmental restrictions, through which only ships with limited emission levels could pass. Old tankers presumably do not belong among them. In addition, the detention of captains and suspicious crew members, to make the profession risky for them. Or also the confiscation of ships or their cargo.
I would add another possibility: to stop shadow‑fleet vessels headed to Russian ports before the Danish Straits, for example due to environmental hazards, insufficient documentation or sanctions. Whether as a NATO operation or as one by a coalition of the willing. And so on…
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Organized group smuggled over 4.7 tonnes of Ukrainian amber abroad disguised as Lithuanian – Prosecutor General's Office
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:40:25 EEST
16:40:25 KST

Under the procedural guidance of prosecutors from the Specialized Environmental Prosecutor's Office of the Office of the Prosecutor General of Ukraine, a notice of suspicion has been served to the organizer and three members of an organized group who allegedly set up the illegal export of Ukrainian amber disguised as stone of Lithuanian origin.
"To legalize the origin of the amber, they used companies in Ukraine and Lithuania. In April 2026, 5.9 tonnes of predominantly small amber, dust, and sand were imported from Lithuania to Ukraine, although the documents indicated significantly larger fractions," the Office of the Prosecutor General reported on its Telegram channel on Thursday.
The investigation established signs of fictitiousness in this import. "In particular, the drivers and the director of the Lithuanian company, who according to the documents were supposed to be involved in the transportation, were not actually in Lithuania, and the Ukrainian company did not make payments under the contract," the prosecutor's office clarified.
According to the agency, the illegally mined amber was subsequently sorted, weighed, and packaged for export at warehouses in several Ukrainian regions. "In the export documents, it was designated as goods of Lithuanian origin," the statement notes.
The prosecutor's office emphasizes that between April and June 2026, more than 4.7 tonnes of amber with an estimated value of UAH 10.7 million were moved abroad under this scheme.
More than 20 searches were conducted while documenting the group's activities.
Four individuals have been served notices of suspicion of smuggling goods committed using official position by an organized group (Part 3 of Article 201-3 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

Rotterdam harbour looks to rabbits to help with expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:39:42 UTC
16:39:42 KST

Rotterdam harbour looks to rabbits to help with expansion
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet is set to announce a €50 million investment in the Port of Rotterdam for nature conservation measures, including releasing rabbits into the dunes, which would allow for harbour growth.
Permits for new businesses and expansion of existing enterprises have been at a virtual standstill for years over concerns about nitrogen pollution in protected areas surrounding the port.
Industry at the port has been shrinking in recent years, hamstrung by a lack of expansion and renovation options as a result of the nitrogen rules as well as pressure on the national electrical grid.
The plans, put together by the government, the city of Rotterdam, and the Port Authority, would involve exotic plants and insects as well as releasing native rabbits into the wild.
According to the project plan, titled “Roadmap to the granting of nature permits in the Port of Rotterdam,” rabbits create a “robust dune ecosystem that is resistant to nitrogen deposition.” The native rabbit population has seen a steep decline due to infectious disease.
The approach could ease some of the gridlock that has followed a Council of State ruling in 2019 on emission limits.
In May 2019, the Council of State ruled the government’s strategy for reducing excess nitrogen was in breach of EU directives on protecting vulnerable habitats and that the way the release of nitrogen was being calculated when assessing construction project licences was questionable.
Since then, efforts to cut pollution so far have largely failed and successive governments have been struggling to find a way to do so.
In June, the Dutch cabinet finalised an agreement on a new package of measures to reduce nitrogen-based pollution in the Netherlands with a budget of €20 billion to implement them.

87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, known as "Maricarmen," has died in Spain. Her eviction from her home in Madrid sparked mass protests over the country’s housing crisis. This was reported by AR, according to UNN.
Details

Romania Orders 12 H225M Caracal Helicopters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:36:33 UTC
16:36:33 KST

Romania has signed a contract to purchase 12 Airbus H225M Caracal multi-purpose helicopters.
The agreement was signed with the French Directorate General of Armaments (DGA) under the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program, the company said.
In the Romanian Air Force, the new H225Ms will replace the aging fleet of IAR-330 Puma helicopters, which were manufactured under French license.
Romania had previously ordered two H215M helicopters in a carrier-based variant, as well as seven H160s and five H145s for civilian and government services.
More than 350 H225 and H225M family helicopters are currently in service worldwide, having been procured by 12 countries, including France, Hungary, the Netherlands, Brazil, and Indonesia.
The Airbus H225M Caracal is a military transport and multi-role helicopter designed for troop transport, medical evacuation, search-and-rescue missions, and special operations support.
The helicopter is equipped with two Safran Makila 2A1 turboshaft engines, each producing more than 2,100 hp, and a five-blade main rotor.
The helicopter has a maximum takeoff weight of 11,000 kg, while its cabin can accommodate up to 28 fully equipped paratroopers or carry up to 4,750 kg of payload on an external sling.
The H225M can reach a cruising speed of up to 260 km/h, has a range of more than 850 km, and can be equipped with onboard weapons, including machine guns, unguided rockets, and self-protection systems.
To engage ground and aerial targets, the helicopter can be equipped with the HForce weapon system, which includes pods with 20 mm NC621 automatic cannons, 12.7 mm FN M3P machine gun pods, as well as launchers for 70 mm unguided or laser-guided rockets.
For fire support and self-defense, 7.62 mm MAG58 machine guns or 13.2 mm machine guns mounted on turrets can be installed in the cabin’s side doors.
In specialized variants, the helicopter can carry Exocet anti-ship missiles for engaging surface targets or anti-tank guided missiles.

Aviation industry representatives are preparing a draft tax consultation on aircraft leasing for the Ministry of Finance — UATA
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:36:11 EEST
16:36:11 KST

Aviation industry representatives are preparing a draft tax consultation on aircraft leasing for the Ministry of Finance — UATA
Kyiv • UNN
UATA has established a working group in response to the Economic Security Bureau’s cases against at least five airlines. Proposals on the taxation of leasing will be submitted to the Ministry of Finance by October 14.
The Ukrainian Air Transport Association (UATA) has established a working group to prepare a package of documents on the taxation of leasing payments made by Ukrainian airlines to non-residents for consideration by the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine. This became necessary because the Bureau of Economic Security attempted to classify aircraft leasing as royalties, affecting at least five carriers. Mykola Shcherbyna, Executive Director of the Public Union "Ukrainian Air Transport Association," told UNN in an exclusive comment.
Why airlines insist on a unified approach to aircraft leasing
As UNN previously reported, since 2024 the Bureau of Economic Security has begun treating transactions involving the leasing of air transport from non-residents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigators’ version, Ukrainian air carriers were required to pay royalties for the rental of aircraft and helicopters. Based on this approach, the BES opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including UIA, "Constanta Airlines," "Windrose," N3Operations, and "Skyline Express." According to UNN, another airline — "Urga" — may also be involved in a similar case.
The criminal cases were opened despite the fact that the airlines regularly undergo tax audits; as of today, only one company has faced objections concerning leasing.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of legislative provisions and that it requires the establishment of a unified state approach.
Earlier, in response to an inquiry from UNN , the Ministry of Finance reported that the taxation of aircraft leasing transactions is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and international treaties of Ukraine. At the same time, the Tax Code of Ukraine does not provide for the possibility of taxing aircraft leasing as royalties.
Therefore, representatives of the aviation industry describe the Bureau’s approach to interpreting aircraft leasing, without changes to tax legislation, as pressure that could destroy the entire passenger and freight transportation sector. According to data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of the aircraft fleet of Ukrainian companies is leased.
To resolve the situation, the issue of aircraft leasing was submitted for consideration by the Committee on Tax Policy, Accounting and Auditing of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the creation of a working group under the Ministry of Finance that would develop a draft general tax consultation on the taxation of leasing payments made to non-residents.
The Ministry of Finance is awaiting documents from the aviation industry
The creation of the working group continued the dialogue between the aviation business and the Ministry of Finance on resolving the issue of taxation of aircraft leasing.
"The Ministry of Finance is working on an issue concerning not the regulation of the leasing market in general, but the application of the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international treaties of Ukraine on the avoidance of double taxation to income received by non-residents in the form of leasing or rental payments for the provision of aircraft for use," the Ministry of Finance reported in response to an inquiry from UNN.
The ministry added that it is awaiting specific examples of leasing transactions being interpreted as royalties, as well as proposals from the aviation industry on how to resolve this issue. After receiving them, the Ministry of Finance plans to develop a general tax consultation that will serve as a mechanism for establishing a unified approach to applying the relevant provisions.
UATA is preparing a draft general tax consultation on aircraft leasing
According to Mykola Shcherbyna, representatives of the aviation industry decided to establish a working group under the Ukrainian Air Transport Association to quickly develop proposals for the Ministry of Finance.
The Ukrainian Association of Aviation and Aerospace (UATA) decided to establish a working group comprising representatives of the aviation industry. It will be headed by Ruslan Melnychenko, chairman of the Legal Committee of the Aerospace Association of Ukraine, an attorney and business protection expert, and chairman of the Legal Committee of the Aerospace Association of Ukraine. Our task is to prepare specific examples for the Ministry of Finance of the incorrect interpretation of leasing transactions as royalties and to develop a draft general tax consultation
He added that Ukrainian airlines had encountered the problem of the Bureau of Economic Security incorrectly interpreting leasing transactions as royalties, and that it was important for this issue to be resolved as soon as possible so that carriers could continue operating under clear rules.
"Leasing aircraft and helicopters is a global practice. Neither Ukrainian legislation nor international law provides for the payment of royalties on the leasing of aircraft. The unilateral change by government agencies in the interpretation, without amendments to legislation, and the criminal prosecution of airlines constitute pressure on responsible businesses that are forced to survive under conditions of closed airspace and pay taxes in Ukraine. This approach poses a threat to the entire civil aviation industry, and this problem must be resolved," Mykola Shcherbyna emphasized.
According to him, the UATA working group plans to collect specific examples of attempts to tax the rental of air transport from nonresidents as royalties, as well as prepare proposals for a unified approach to their taxation. The cases, along with the draft general tax consultation, are planned to be submitted to the Ministry of Finance for consideration by October 14.
A unified position of government agencies on the taxation of aircraft leasing is necessary, one that complies with the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international conventions on the avoidance of double taxation
He is convinced that this format will enable industry representatives, together with the Ministry of Finance, to develop a specific solution to the problem within a short period. If adopted, the general tax consultation should establish the Ministry of Finance's official position on the application of tax rules to leasing payments for the use of aircraft and reduce the scope for government agencies to interpret identical transactions differently.

Slovakia sends military attaché back to Russia for first time in 4 years
Slovakia and Russia are resuming the exchange of military attachés for the first time since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine – a decision that has drawn criticism from the Slovak opposition.
Source: European Pravda with reference to Slovak news outlet Aktuality
Details: During his visit to Moscow in May, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico promised Russian leader Vladimir Putin during their talks that military and diplomatic relations between the two countries would be restored. As part of these arrangements, the countries are resuming the exchange of military attachés after a four-year hiatus.
Fico's government has sent two military officers to Moscow and Bratislava is awaiting the arrival of a Russian attaché.
The last Russian military attaché to serve in Slovakia left the country four years ago. Sergei Solomasov, who held the post, was expelled by the government of Eduard Heger along with other Russian diplomats after Russia invaded Ukraine. Solomasov was also implicated in an espionage case: he bribed Bohuš Garbár, a contributor to the Hlavné správy website, to disseminate disinformation on his instructions.
According to the latest information, Russia's new military attaché in Bratislava could be 46-year-old Maksim Verezhan. The naval officer previously served at the Russian embassy in Rome and has spent the past few years in Moscow.
Slovakia has appointed its military representatives in Moscow. Brigadier General Slavomír Staviarsky will serve as military attaché and Colonel Ivo Gahír will be his deputy.
Tomáš Valášek, an MP from the Progressive Slovakia party, criticised the government's decision to resume military and diplomatic engagement with Russia. He argued that exchanging military attachés would primarily benefit Russia, as the Slovak representative is unlikely to gain access to important information in Moscow.
Valášek also said the Russian military attaché could have an opportunity to take part in disinformation and influence operations in Slovakia, fuel social tensions and sway public opinion towards Russia.
The opposition politician also suggested that the move to restore military relations may have come from Moscow, with the Slovak government simply accepting the proposal.
Background:
- Slovakia's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, justified the return of military attachés by saying that the government is seeking to establish pragmatic relations with Russia.
- Slovak Defence Minister Robert Kaliňák recently said that Bratislava does not regard Russia as a threat.
- Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he does not want Slovakia to become involved in a military conflict "because of some Article 5".
- It was also reported that Slovakia's opposition is demanding explanations from the government and Fico over reports in the German media linking an attempted attack on a Ukrainian drone manufacturer in Prešov to Russian military intelligence.

On Monday strike action is being held across the public sector. Expect disruption: Brussels local transport company MIVB, Flemish local transport company De Lijn and Brussels Airport will be hit on Friday and schools and rail services will be affected on Monday.
National Day of Action and public sector strike to cause disruption on Friday 9 October and Monday 12 October
For the various trade unions, this is at least the 10th major protest against the federal government’s policies. The government’s drafting of the budget is the trigger for the protest this time. The unions fear that ordinary people will once again bear the brunt of the cuts.
ABVV is organising a national demonstration through the streets of Brussels. It will set off from Central Station and head towards Brussels-South Station (Zuid/Midi). “Hands off our pockets” is the slogan calling for the demonstration. “We want to draw a clear line in the sand and warn the government to keep its hands off purchasing power, the cost-of-living index and sales tax VAT,” explains spokesperson Daan Nelen.
ACV has opted for a protest outside the party headquarters of government parties, the Flemish nationalist N-VA, Christian democrat CD&V and socialist Vooruit as well as the Francophone liberals of MR and centrists of Les Engagés. Several hundred activists will take part at each location. The trade union is requesting a meeting with the leaders of each party. At 8.30 am, the procession will halt outside N-VA HQ and the MR, followed by the CD&V, Vooruit and Les Engagés.
The Christian trade union says it wants to convey workers’ concerns to government ministers. The ACV also fears that the government will once again pass the bill on to ordinary people. “Whilst workers have already contributed more than enough. And on top of that, they are paying the price for the rising cost of living, higher energy bills and increasing workloads,” says the trade union.
Both unions also wish again to draw attention to their alternative budget plan: measures that could raise up to 21 billion euros without resorting to harsh austerity measures.
Synova, the independent, formerly liberal, trade union, shares the concerns of the other unions but will not be taking to the streets on Friday. The union intends to roll out its own action plan and engage in dialogue with workers.
The unions day of action will result in disruption
Transit company MIVB in Brussels
Brussels local transport company MIVB expects “significant disruption” to public transport in the conurbation. It does not plan to provide a minimum service.
It will only be able to forecast the exact scope of the expected disruption on Thursday evening. It will provide updates via its social media channels but warns that it will not know the full extent of the impact of the day of action until Friday morning.
De Lijn hit in Flanders
Four in ten buses and trams operated by Flemish local transport company De Lijn will not be running on Friday 9 October due to the national day of industrial action organised by the Christian and socialist trade unions.
The Flemish public transport company announced the expected impact of the action yesterday. De Lijn will operate an alternative service schedule with staff who have indicated they will come to work. 60 per cent of De Lijn’s buses and trams will still be running. Across the provinces, the following percentages of vehicles will be operating:
Antwerp: 58 per cent (Antwerp city: 46 per cent)
Limburg: 61 per cent
East Flanders: 71 per cent
Flemish Brabant: 54 per cent
West Flanders: 65 per cent (Coastal tram: 62 per cent)
NMBS rail services affected on Monday
Anyone wishing to travel by train on Friday will not experience any disruption.
Staff at Belgium's state-owned rail operator NMBS are only taking part in the public sector strike on Monday. It is still unclear what impact this will have on services.
Flights cancelled at Brussels Airport
At Brussels Airport, around 140 flights are expected to be cancelled because ground handling operator Alyzia is affected by the strike. The operator will be operating with a reduced workforce.
According to Brussels Airport, the airlines affected are adjusting their flight schedules and passengers will be provided with information about the status of their flight and any alternatives.
No impact is currently expected on flights handled by a second operator, Aviapartner. This applies to flights operated by Ryanair and TUI fly among others.
Passengers can check which ground handling operator is handling their flight on the Brussels Airport website.
Charleroi Brussels South Airport escapes
All flights at Charleroi Airport are running as normal. However, passengers are urged to leave for the airport in good time. Passengers are advised to check the status of their flight via the airport’s own website or through their airline.
Education also hit
On Friday and also on Monday, there may be disruption in some schools following a strike notice issued by ACOD Onderwijs, the socialist education union.
ACOD Onderwijs will be taking part in the National Day of Action on Friday, as well as in the strike in the public services organised by the socialist trade union on Monday 12 October.
As a result, disruption may be experienced in some schools on both days. Traditionally, ACOD has a stronger presence in the GO! education sector, the official state network.

Russia has shown a drone interceptor built on the Alazan, a civilian anti-hail rocket, Militarnyi reported. The sample went on display at a weapons exhibition that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin toured at the Chebarkul training range in the Urals on 2 October.
Ukraine now sends drones at Russia by the hundreds, by Moscow's own count. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted nearly 900 overnight into 6 October. Russia's missile-based air defense was built to repel aircraft raids and a few cruise missiles, not swarms of low-flying drones.
In May, Ukrainian intelligence said Russia was adding four regiments, 24 battalions, and 162 batteries to counter Ukrainian strike drones. The converted Alazan, which Militarnyi calls an anti-drone system, is one more piece of that search. Meanwhile, the commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brovdi, said his forces struck 300 Russian air-defense assets between January and 19 September.
From hail reagent to shrapnel
Based on the size of the sample on display, the interceptor builds on the Alazan-2M or Alazan-6 series, Militarnyi assessed. The outlet put the stated cost at up to $12,000 per unit but did not say who named the figure. In civilian service, the rocket flies about 10 km, climbs up to 8 km, and carries about 0.5 kg of reagent. For air defense, the developers plan to replace that reagent with a fragmentation warhead.
Militarnyi's analysis of the published photos describes the front end as a steering assembly: four cruciform deflector fins, probably paired with a seeker or a fuze. At the rear sit folding stabilizers and the open nozzle of a solid-fuel motor, held in a metal cradle.
One sample among 300 exhibits
The Kremlin's account of the visit lists more than 300 weapons on display, including interceptor drones, but does not mention the rocket. Propaganda channel Russia 1 aired the interceptor in its report from the visit, and the Kremlin pool of state news agency RIA posted photos.

France's Le Pen opposes Ukraine EU membership over farming fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:31:00 UTC

French far-right politician Marine Le Pen spoke against EU membership for Ukraine on Oct. 7 by whipping up fears that Kyiv's agricultural sector would destroy France's.
Le Pen is leading the polls for France's April 2027 presidential election, and her stance on Ukraine and Russia has already become a key campaign issue for her and her competitors.
"If Ukraine were to enter the European Union, we would be the first to suffer," Le Pen claimed in a video posted to social media.
"We would be the losers, not only in terms of competition with a large agricultural country like Ukraine, but also in the sharing out of Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) (subsidies), because the CAP is a shrinking cake," Le Pen said.
The CAP is an EU program established in 1962 that subsidizes the EU's farming sector, allowing small and uncompetitive farms to continue to exist.
It is also at risk of being reduced already, as Brussels haggles over the bloc's 2028-2034 budget. The fear is that adding a large agricultural country such as Ukraine would exacerbate that situation further.
Le Pen's comments came one day after the European Commission published a communication on the future of enlargement, which noted that the bloc needs to seriously address how to integrate Ukraine's farming sector into the EU smoothly.
Ukraine "will and can become a member of the CAP. Under which conditions, this will be discussed," said the EU's Enlargement Commissioner, Marta Kos, at a press conference on Oct. 6.
"We also have to protect the farmers in the EU, and we are already discussing this subject with Ukraine," Kos added.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said, "We understand the sensitivity of certain segments for European farmers," in written comments shared with the Kyiv Independent.
However, he thinks there are also many opportunities for the EU that come with bringing in Ukraine's farming sector, even for European farmers.
"We do not share the approach under which Ukraine's integration is viewed exclusively as a threat to European farmers," Vysotskyi said.
And Kyiv's lobby for agriculture in Brussels, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB), said that while it understands the concerns of European farmers, it is "increasingly concerned by an excessively protectionist approach towards the integration of Ukrainian agriculture," in an Oct. 7 press statement.
For UCAB, part of the answer lies in communication.
"UCAB has consistently advocated an open and structured dialogue with European farmers, EU institutions, and member states to jointly develop a model for the future enlarged European agricultural market."

From Relic to Infrastructure: Can India's Historic Water Systems Work Again?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

India's stepwells are usually encountered after their useful lives have ended. They are photographed, restored and interpreted as evidence of a water culture that once existed. Beneath the carved stone and descending stairs is a practical question: what happens when a structure built to manage water is put back to work? As Indian cities face water stress, seasonal rainfall and pressure on municipal systems, researchers and restoration efforts are examining whether traditional water structures can function again.
Traditional water architecture was rarely an isolated object. In Ahmedabad, water management was embedded in the organization of the city. Within the historic pols, wells, courtyards and underground Tankas formed part of a distributed system of domestic and communal water storage. A 2026 study in Built Heritage estimates that nearly 10,000 Tankas may still exist across Ahmedabad, many located beneath domestic courtyards.
The Tanka was simple in construction, but its operation depended on several parts of the house working together. Rainwater was collected from roofs and courtyards, directed underground and stored within lime-lined chambers. The structures were typically constructed several meters below ground, using stone, brick and lime mortar, while sloping bases allowed sediment to be removed during cleaning. Water storage was part of the house itself. The building became part of the catchment and storage system.
Related Article
India's Forgotten Stepwells
More than 200 community wells were constructed within Ahmedabad's Pols by the late nineteenth century, while only 14 of the 94 documented stepwells in greater Ahmedabad lie within the historic Walled City. The monumental stepwell is the most recognizable image of India's water heritage. In dense urban neighbourhoods, however, smaller wells and Tankas could be more practical.
In Ahmedabad, the expansion of piped municipal infrastructure and stormwater drainage gradually made household rainwater systems less necessary. The establishment of the Dudheshwar Water Works in 1892 marked part of this wider shift towards centralised supply. Over time, the Tanka remained physically present while its original role disappeared. A Tanka could remain beneath a house for generations, even as the water entering the building arrived through a municipal pipe rather than a monsoon roof.
Ahmedabad's geology offers one explanation for the emergence of the Tanka. The historic Walled City sits over dense clay strata, with groundwater often deeper than 40 meters. In such conditions, digging and maintaining wells could be difficult. Collecting rainwater close to where it fell provided another option, particularly within a dense urban fabric where larger water structures were difficult to accommodate. The courtyard became a catchment. The floor became a threshold to an underground reservoir. The house became part of a water system.
The 2026 Built Heritage study's survey found that 90 percent of the residents questioned expressed willingness to reintegrate Tanka water into the urban system, although the study also identifies significant barriers around governance, ownership, incentives and water quality.
Bansilalpet Stepwell in Hyderabad provides a different case. For decades, the seventeenth-century stepwell had effectively disappeared beneath a dump. Its restoration involved removing approximately 2,000 tonnes of debris, after which a freshwater source was identified around seven meters below ground. The restored well was reported to have a water-carrying capacity of approximately 2.2 million litres.
The restoration also addressed the surrounding precinct, including rainwater-harvesting measures and changes to surrounding infrastructure. Reports on the restoration record the well's association with the water supply of Gandhi Hospital. Bansilalpet does not yet show that restored stepwells can supply cities at scale. The available evidence demonstrates water recovery, storage capacity and a deliberate attempt to reconnect the site with water management. It has not yet established its long-term contribution to Hyderabad's overall water balance.
The harder problem begins once the water starts flowing. A Tanka depended on more than its masonry chamber. Its operation depended on seasonal cleaning, preparation of roofs and pipes, decisions about when to begin collecting rainwater and knowledge of how the system should be maintained. The 2026 research found that some surviving Tankas remain in use, while others have deteriorated or been repurposed. Water quality also varies, with some existing systems requiring treatment before water can safely be consumed.
Who maintains a privately owned Tanka if it contributes to a neighbourhood water system? Who tests the water? Who pays for repairs? How does a municipal authority regulate infrastructure located beneath private homes?
The researchers argue that the existing governance framework lacks mechanisms to incentivise citizen participation and heritage-based water reuse. They propose a model combining municipal capacity with community involvement. The system depends on routines of cleaning, testing, maintenance and shared responsibility. Without those routines and responsibilities, restoring the masonry does not restore the water system.
Amritvarshini Vav in Ahmedabad is another distinct case. Built around 1723 within the Walled City, the stepwell has an unusual L-shaped plan and extends more than 15 metres below ground. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation records that the structure was recharged in 2004. Recharging the well brings one of its original functions back into use.
Reusing a historic water structure also introduces change. Contemporary safety requirements, water-quality standards, public access and urban infrastructure rarely correspond exactly to historic conditions. A restored water structure may therefore need to accommodate systems that did not exist when it was built. Continued use can also be part of its survival. New interventions can change how a historic water structure is experienced. A stepwell restored for public use may become a civic space, a heritage attraction, or both, depending on how the surrounding program is designed.
The restoration extended beyond the well itself into the surrounding public realm, introducing new infrastructure and uses around the historic structure. The restored site now functions both as a water structure and as a civic and heritage destination. At the scale of the house, the Tanka transformed a roof and courtyard into a water catchment. At the scale of the Pol, wells became shared resources within a dense neighbourhood. At the scale of the city, stepwells connected water and public life. Their effectiveness depended on how they worked with surrounding buildings, people and environmental conditions.
Today, these systems could supplement existing municipal infrastructure. Heritage buildings could contribute to rainwater management. Courtyards could become storage systems. Existing structures could be adapted for continued use. Such a shift would also require coordination between architecture, water policy, municipal authorities and the communities that maintain these systems. The Tanka worked because the roof, courtyard, reservoir and routines of maintenance formed one system. Bringing it back into use therefore depends on whether the buildings, institutions and communities around it can support that system again.
